The game gets a bit repetitive after 600 hours so the best way to enjoy it is to play overhaul mods which let me to have over 1400 hours. This game is a masterpiece and I will always be coming back to play this game at least once every year. My wish was for elden ring be the first live service game from fromsoft, adding new DLC which contains new relics, more weapons and new bosses yearly with cost of $40 to $50, Regardless of that I am looking for future projects from fromsoftware and hopefully one day they will release a sequel to elden ring.

Как бы я не бомбил на элден из-за сложности и пустого открытого мира, но с*ка, какая же эта афигенная игра. Раньше считал ее вовсе шлаком, и во время прохождения тоже, но после второго босса (годрик) я понял, что эта игра - шедевр. Игра по большей части отличается от своих предвестников (трилогия дс) из-за опен ворлда, и что ты можешь на время скипнуть босса и в любой момент с ним сразиться. Многие считают это минусом, некоторые вовсе считают это казуальным, но по мне это не так. Начну наверно с плюсов игры. В этой игре прекрасно абсолютно все; сюжет, который вполне себе интересный, в целом весь лор который прописан до мелочей, лвл дизайн локаций, сайд квесты нпс (мой самый любимый с миллисентой, данг итером и с ренной), система прокачки, разнообразия пушек, талисманов и прочей фигни, кастомизация перса, боссы (не учитывается те которые в дандже) и всякая всячина. атмосфера у этой игры присутствует, веет неким вайбом берсерка (хотя в целом, элден буквально экранизация берсерка). я так давно не получал таких эмцоий как от элден ринг, и я даже не жалею что потратил 2к на стим версию, потому что в игре буквально дофига контента которые в общей сложности займет 100+ часов. Сам я наиграл 120+ часов (70 на пиратке, 50 на лицухе) и то не до конца облутал весь мир. Из минусов я могу перечислить только пустой опен ворлд и однотипные крипы, на этом все. Повторюсь, настоятельно рекомендую к покупке. Эта игра однозначно заслужила игру года, т.к буквально лучший соулслайк эвер, в котором прекрасно абсолютно все. Моя оценка 10/10. Шедевр от Миядзаки.

This game is a masterpiece and, imo, the best souls game. They converted it into open world in such a beautiful fashion you forget this is their first time at it. One thing I love about this game particularly is the philosophy of if you can see it you can go to it. For example seeing the Forge of the Giants from Limgrave or Miquella's Haligtree from Mountaintop of the Giants. There's just such a great sense of wonder and discovery to this game that I think makes it stand out so much. What I'd give to be able to play this game for the first time again. The bosses here are super good too. Yes, there are some stinkers like Godskin Duo and they tend to overuse some bosses (I'm looking at you Ulcerated Tree Spirit), but across the board they are really strong. I think of Dark Souls and the only bossfight I thought was good was Ornstein & Smough. Here, there's Mohg, Morgott, Placidusax, Radagon, Elden Beast (yes I love this fight), Malenia (I learned to love this fight), and more. The ost for this game is equally strong. If you like souls games, this is a must buy. If you like open world games and a challenge, this is a must buy. Honestly, if you like gaming in general and are up for a challenge, this is a must buy. I would only hesitate to recommend this if you don't like the slow-paced combat of these games or just aren't generally fond of the game challenging you.

I played until completion to leave this review, finishing through spite rather than enjoyment. My playthrough was late and apart from knowing about Ranni and Rykard through memes, I went in completely blind as a big Dark Souls 1 and 2 fan. The game wasn't what I expected and for the first few days of playing, I went where I thought I was supposed to go and just hit wall after wall after wall. Whether through the luck of it being open world, but I roamed around until going north and just felt powerless against everything. I'd tough it out against what I thought were boss looking enemies in the overworld only for them to not drop anything after trying to kill them for an hour. Or randomly get ambushed by a pack of something, which I learned is the games favourite thing to do. It took a long time to realize enemies were meant to be avoided unless progression was blocked. My intent to not look anything up and play a dex build was tossed when I genuinely felt like stopping, because I was endlessly frustrated at nothing being consistent and the general gameplay. Enemy poise and my ability to parry was completely up in the air, I'd break poise against soldiers in armour but an emaciated ghoul with a knife could have super armour in or outside attack animations. Enemies I thought I could parry, were unparriable so I'd end up dying trying to get a pattern down and thinking I was failing. Even when successful, it was just too risky for the fact that from start to finish the game is a one-two hit kill fest if you're not specifically built for each threat, which I wasn't. This is made even worse from the fact that so many enemies in the game have multiple moves with 3-8 hit strings, whether a knight or some sort of boss. It felt so oppressively designed, not in a fun to overcome but sheer irritation to perfect dodging one attack only to be hit by a follow up attack designed to hit if you did. Then if you do manage to avoid getting hit, the enemy immediate acts again with no delay, no breathing room whatsoever. Shield the attacks instead, you get staggered and killed first combo. This is why despite really liking all the different weapon arts and weapons themselves, there was little point. Mobs tended to die easily to anything yet anything a stage higher only let you hit once between combos or leaping away to do a ranged attack or summoning 8 of its mates to swarm you to death. Unless you use a Greatsword, then a few more enemies than normal can be staggered easily. I assume that's why I saw to many shadows use them and why enemies with them were so strong. I grew to hate the open world and the endless one note ambushes and beginners traps that were no different to each other just so frequent you got numb to it. Spirit Ashes being a requirement annoyed me at the start because I wanted to have that 1 on 1 challenge. Then they annoyed me even more when it regularly became a 2v2 race to try and kill one enemy before the spirit was killed. I can't honestly tell you a boss I liked fighting, for the first half of the game as a dual thrust wielding/twinblade dex build, to the Dark Moon Greatsword INT build I switched to at the end because I couldn't deal damage anymore. I didn't feel like I overcame a challenge, only kept trying till I got a pattern each time that let me succeed. I only stuck it through to the end because I paid for this and wanted to see Ranni's ending for myself. I assumed this game would be like Dark Souls, slow, consistent and methodical. Complete unfairness would be kept minimal and bosses were fair but challenging once you understood. Exploration would be rewarded, not met with 1000 ambushes to a crafting item. No, it's an action game with an open world and no leniency. I felt like I was in Devil May Cry but I wasn't Dante, I was the random mob he styled on. If you like that sort of thing, good for you. This isn't the souls gameplay I was looking for.

This review is more about a very positive impression than a game description. Not necessarily meaningful if you don't know Dark Souls games. I love the Dark Souls games but I always got stuck at some point with about 3 possible enemies that I couldn't defeat even with reading tips. These games are hard and I guess I'm not good at this. However, when I saw Elden Ring at a sale I was on the fence but boredom won and I didn't regret it at all. I find it so much better with the much more open world approach. If I get stuck somewhere I go back to easier places. There are so many secrets and hidden things that it's impossible to find all of them at the first or even second go through. Or I sneak around in much harder areas hoping to find better equipment without fighting (and dying). Another aspect I really like are that you can summon ghosts that fight for you. Even if you are not good at fighting with hectic key presses, studying enemy moves and creating an effective build (all of that applies to me), over time you can upgrade your ghosts and at some point they can defeat bosses for you. You might wonder why I like playing this if I'm so bad at this. It's the ambience, visuals and strange beings you meet. There is a really beautiful and strange world to explore. I absolutely don't mind revisiting areas in this game if I'm (or my ghost) to weak to continue. I just enjoying playing it.

I replayed this game yet another time to finally get through the DLC, starting completely fresh, a choice I'm very satisfied with. This remains a mastodontic masterpiece, though not a flawless one. There's a fair amount of bloat and balance issues that unfortunately carry over into the expansion as well. The DLC itself is stunning in visuals, artistic design and scope, but occasionally feels a bit sparse. None of that changes the bottom line: this is an absolute must-play. Some would argue it's From's magnum opus: a decade of design experience distilled into a massive, cohesive artwork. Personally, I prefer their smaller, more focused titles like Sekiro and Bloodborne, but I still deeply adore the world of the Lands Between. I can only recommend everyone experience it at least once.

Elden Ring as a game has many baffling design decisions, many of which somehow work. Typical of Souls games, the story is not straightforward and instead told primarily through the environment, flavour text in items and the enemy designs. In terms of visuals and storytelling, the game rewards exploration, attention to detail and perseverance (be prepared to do many awfully designed quests for your lore!) The quest design is some of the worst we've seen in any Souls game. Anyone who thinks the quests are well designed in Elden Ring I am convinced they have not tried to do a quest without a wiki. Several NPCs will hint to where they will be next, but the location is so generic and nonspecific you could actively search for them and miss them because, SURPRISE they were tucked away in this little corner behind this rock you forgot to look behind. If the hardest part of your quests are figuring out where to find the next parts to continue it, your quests are badly designed. It's strong points in gameplay are the high levels of build customisation, including large varieties of weapons, skills, talismans and armour. Unfortunately, there are many points where it feels like player choice was not prioritised to the detriment of the game. Several weapons are seemingly stuck with skills that aren't even unique to them. Many skills are badly designed, clearly meant more for show than actual practical use, and if they were made better they would make for interesting additions to builds. Although I really like skills and spells in Elden Ring, they cause a majority of the balance problems, despite how fun they are. Many skills/spells can easily be slotted into any build for immediate power due to low stat requirements. Any build is just a few steps away from broken territory, even the simplest, most basic ones. If you're just using a big bonk stick, you'll quickly realise that jump attacks are insanely overpowered in PvE, easily staggering large enemies and bosses. There are a handful of "no-brainer" talismans that are so strong you might as well always have them equipped unless you really need to squeeze in something for your build. This ultimately leads to my point that Elden Ring is a very unbalanced game with many overcentralising mechanics. It's no wonder the community is so uptight about how you play this game. Ultimately, I think balance of single player games still matters. I would prefer more balanced options that are competitive with each other, and also less "no-brainer" choices that are just the obvious picks. In the end, Elden Ring is a Souls game, and in Souls games knowledge is power. Practically every Souls game has mechanics where if you know how to use them you can utterly break the game, but Elden Ring is so full of them it's very easy to just accidentally happen upon them.

Elden Ring completely pulled me in from the moment I first stepped into Limgrave. Seeing that massive world open up for the first time was honestly overwhelming in the best possible way. I remember just standing there, trying to decide where to go first, immediately making the questionable decision to wander off and explore [spoiler] before arriving at the first church [/spoiler]. That feeling of freedom is what makes this game so special. Every road, ruin, cave, or suspicious corner felt worth checking out because the game constantly rewarded curiosity. Even after hundreds of hours, I still kept finding hidden items, new paths, or entire areas I somehow missed before. The bosses and world design were easily my favorite parts. Getting destroyed by the Tree Sentinel early on was humiliating but hilarious, and it perfectly taught me what kind of game I was facing. Finally defeating Malenia after all the frustration, scarlet rot, and repeated failures felt incredibly satisfying. The game feels difficult, but fair, and every victory actually feels earned. I also loved diving into the lore, (even if most of it came from outside sources rather than the game directly - which is a personal choice in the end) Compared to Dark Souls III, this game takes everything I loved and pushes it much further. The open world, the freedom to explore, and even small quality-of-life improvements like traveling freely between Sites of Grace made the experience feel bigger and smoother without losing the soul of a FromSoftware game. Elden Ring may not be the hardest or fastest Soulslike ever, but it absolutely feels like one of the most memorable. It is one of those rare games where getting lost is not frustrating because it is the entire point. 10/10, currently replaying it too.

The level design is masterful, each region has its own identity and mood, and legacy dungeons like Stormveil and Leyndell are some of the most carefully crafted spaces I've ever explored in a game. The cutscenes are genuinely stunning, the art, the lighting, the scale and the Soundtracks ofc. If you want to start a FromSoftware game, Elden Ring is your go-to, It's far more beginner friendly than people make it out to be, yes there are hard parts, but the summon system is there for a reason, struggling with a boss? Call for help, It genuinely makes the experience more accessible without taking anything away from it. And the DLC, At 40€ Shadow of the Erdtree is a steal, the amount of content, new areas, new weapons, and bosses it brings feels closer to a full sequel than an expansion, If you loved the base game, this is non-negotiable.

In my humblest of opinions, Elden Ring is kinda... My favorite is dark souls II so make whatever assumptions you'd like, but after I first beat the game I was left feeling really meh. I couldn't bring myself to replay it the same way I want to replay DS2 or Sekiro, but I have regardless to make new characters or play with friends, just never beaten it again. Fromsoft really pushed themselves with this game, and it shows. They struggled with enemy variety in that I want to say 40% of enemies are reskinned version of other enemies, and infamously, each miniboss appears five or so times at least across the entire game. Exploration doesn't really reward the player with much, with most rewards being basic loot you can find on enemies or flowers or berry bushes and stuff. The world, however, feels a little empty. Even though dying worlds are their formula, it's really out of place here in my opinion. The game's lore revolves around the fact that the lands between are a lived in world full of colorful diverse characters, and yet I found most NPCs woefully out of place. The capitol was a huge let down for me, for example, and the roundtable hold is plain strange in my opinion, with merchants who you'll want to move between (one selling smithing stones and the other providing upgrades) being on polar opposite sides of the hub... Oh my lord and the dungeons - the dungeons as a whole are a perfect example for how tired I think the devs were while working on this game because the dungeons are the lamest and least inspired parts of this game. They are essentially the same structure with the same enemies for the most part, with ♥♥♥♥ loot at the end oh my lord. Each of them follows the same formula as well, really sad in my opinion. Fromsoft tried to accomplish A LOT of things with this title and I think they landed securely in an in-between place where there are great and egregious things at once, but mostly, the game is good. I want to throw some serious shade at Shadow of the Erdtree DLC. What the hell man. It was just a slog, the areas were uninteresting, others felt uninspired and kind of pointless. The boss movesets seemed AI generated if I'm being honest, felt so unpredictable. Maybe I just wasn't good enough but holy hell the amount of shockwaves and double hit attacks (where you dodge the first part but get hit by the second while you're coming out of a roll) were commonplace. The hippo boss was insane, and I mean that in a good and bad way. It's because of all these facets I never actually reached Mesmer, just got so bogged down by those aforementioned aspects compounding onto me throughout my playtime. I've beaten Nioh 1 and 2 and those have some INSANE and irritating bosses but Shadow of the Erdtree gave me little to feel excited about in terms of pushing through. Oh my lord and the DAMAGE they deal is bonkers. Unironically, my favorite boss in all of Elden Ring was Godrick the Grafted - so much personality, BEST soundtrack in the game IMO, cool concept and phases, but whose moveset and behavior didn't feel chaotic, or plain silly like some of the bosses felt. Call me a normie, but that's my hill I guess. Anyways after all that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, it's still a fantastic game, just a flawed one, as they all are. I hope that Fromsoft either improves on their tried and true formula with ideas to keep it fresh (meaning dead worlds etc) or either tries really hard to remedy what made Elden Ring suffer in my eyes - feeling empty and feeling un-lived in. I also hope they take a look back at their masterpieces like Sekiro to reach a better synthesis of their different combat systems. Elden Ring at times could've really benefitted from being more like Sekiro, but instead just felt like DS3, even with guard counters.

I feel like it's such an important thing to discuss what makes these games feel "intimidating" at first. After my 2nd playthrough, I gotta say, this is one of THE best games I have ever played. And I am bummed at myself for holding off on playing for so long because how the community and others have made the game sound like it's impossible and too tough to understand. What I've been encouraging my friends with is to just give this game at least 6 hours of chance, let yourself understand the basics of leveling up attributes and learn what "builds" are and weapon scaling. Everything beyond that is yours to explore in the way you want to. There's little homework to be done and more freedom. The combat isn't too difficult if you let yourself explore the world everything it's got to offer so that you can upgrade your character and builds. The game and it's world design does a really good job at putting you in the exact locations where you need to be, and there is always a choice of coming back stronger to certain areas if it wasn't. There's a fun challenge in all of the bosses, none of them are "impossible" to beat, you just have to be smart going in what's needed for the fight. Let yourself try hours at a single boss. I can't really say much else other than there are enough ways to make the game easy for yourself. And I encourage new players (like me) to give these games a try.

Elden Ring isn’t just a game — it’s a cathedral of chaos, wonder, and triumph carved into the soul of modern gaming. From the first step into Limgrave to the final clash beneath shattered gold, every moment feels like walking through a living myth painted by gods and madmen. The world is breathtakingly vast, dripping with mystery, beauty, and terror around every corner. Every castle, every crypt, every forgotten battlefield tells a story without begging for attention — it simply exists, daring you to uncover its secrets. FromSoftware didn’t create a map; they forged an odyssey. The combat is razor-sharp, brutal, and endlessly rewarding, demanding mastery while making every victory feel earned in blood and fire. Boss fights are spectacles of pure legend — monstrous, majestic, and unforgettable. Few games capture the feeling of true adventure, but Elden Ring resurrects it with overwhelming grandeur. This is not merely open-world design; this is art, ambition, and excellence fused together in one merciless masterpiece. It respects your intelligence, tests your patience, and rewards your courage like no other. Elden Ring stands as a towering monument to what gaming can achieve when creativity is unchained. A once-in-a-generation masterpiece. Beautiful. Savage. Eternal. 10/10 — a crown jewel forged in the flames of greatness.

I wish I could forget everything and play this game again with fresh eyes. In 25 years of gaming, I have encountered nothing like it. The game gripped me the moment I stepped into the world - a landscape that is grand, mysterious, and entirely free to explore. It refuses to hold your hand. I vividly remember my first major boss battle in Stormveil Keep with Margit taking over 30 attempts (later I learned this was entirely optional but recommended). There were many a rage-quit night before the eventual victory...and when he finally fell, the adrenaline and dopamine hit was unlike anything else. I was immediately hooked into the cycle. 60+ hours later, the scale of the world and the technical achievement remain staggering. From the highest peaks to the expansive underworld, the world is packed with puzzles, hidden treasures and unmarked quests. Nothing feels repetitive; no two encounters play out the same way. While I’ve stayed strictly in single-player and avoided the save-file corruption issues or invasion fiascos reported by others, my experience has been seamless. However, be aware that these are ongoing issues which I'm not sure are being resolved. In brief, Elden Ring is a masterpiece of world-building. Developers are already taking notes on how to craft an adventure this immersive, and they should - this game sets a gold standard.

This was my first ever FromSoftware game, and it was a great introduction to the souls games. Saying that this game is a 10/10 is an understatement. The open world is truly magical, straight out of a fantasy book (thanks George R. R. Martin). I can't go 10 steps on Torrent without finding a dungeon, beating the boss, and get either a mushroom, or a god-slaying weapon as a reward. The combat is stellar, and I could tell that the variety of builds is huge with the range of armaments, arts of war, talismans, and spells. Since this was my first souls game, the bosses were an extremely difficult, and the moment I tried to recuperate during combat, the bosses did not hold back to attack. Every boss and enemy spiked my focus, learning and avoiding their moves/abilities. All these factors would be for naught without the incredible music. Some of my favorite music comes from bosses such as Mohg or Godfrey, and the ambient music from Leyndell was not only soothing, but told a story of a great city in ruins after a war. There were many times of frustration, but the game improved my perseverance and patience. Before fighting Malenia, I thought I would beat her within 10 tries. 10 tries turned to 20 tries, and 20 tries turned to 2 weeks. Even after many defeats, I stilled fought, and through patience I eventually gained Malenia's Great Rune. To sum it up, it's a pretty fun game. 10/10

From the very first moment I launched this game, I knew I was about to experience something special. It’s honestly one of the rare games that completely pulls you into its world and makes you forget about time. Every small detail feels carefully designed with passion, from the atmosphere and soundtrack to the gameplay mechanics and progression system. The developers clearly understood what players actually want: a game that is fun, rewarding, immersive, and endlessly enjoyable. The gameplay itself is incredibly satisfying. Whether you’re exploring, fighting, grinding, building, or simply discovering new mechanics, the game constantly gives you a reason to keep playing. There’s always something exciting waiting around the corner. The pacing is perfect because it never feels too slow or overwhelming. Instead, it keeps you engaged for hours without becoming repetitive. Even after spending a huge amount of time playing, the experience still feels fresh and enjoyable. One of the strongest parts of this game is the atmosphere. The world feels alive in a way that many modern games fail to achieve. Every location has its own identity and charm, and the visuals create such an immersive environment that you genuinely feel connected to the game world. Combined with the soundtrack, which fits every moment perfectly, the experience becomes unforgettable. There were many moments where I simply stopped playing for a second just to appreciate how beautiful and well-crafted everything looked. The progression system is another reason why this game stands out so much. Every achievement feels rewarding, every upgrade feels meaningful, and every hour invested feels worth it. The game respects the player’s time while still providing enough depth to stay engaging long-term. It manages to balance challenge and enjoyment perfectly, which is something many games struggle to do nowadays. What impressed me the most is how much passion and care was clearly put into this project. You can tell the developers genuinely cared about creating a memorable experience instead of just making another generic game. The amount of polish, creativity, and attention to detail is honestly incredible. Bugs are minimal, performance is smooth, and the overall quality feels extremely high. Another thing I absolutely love is how replayable the game is. Even after finishing major content, I still find myself wanting to come back again and again. Whether it’s trying different strategies, exploring hidden content, improving skills, or simply enjoying the atmosphere, the game never loses its charm. Very few games manage to create this kind of long-term attachment. The community surrounding the game also deserves praise. It’s always enjoyable discussing strategies, sharing experiences, and seeing how passionate other players are. A strong community usually says a lot about a game’s quality, and this one definitely has one of the most dedicated player bases I’ve seen. Overall, this game exceeded every expectation I had and easily became one of my favorite gaming experiences in a very long time. It delivers amazing gameplay, fantastic design, immersive world-building, rewarding progression, and endless entertainment. If someone is looking for a game that truly feels worth their time and money, this is absolutely one I would recommend without hesitation. It’s the kind of game that reminds you why gaming is such an amazing hobby in the first place. A masterpiece in every sense of the word.

[u]An absolute must‑play within the FromSoftware lineage.[/u] Elden Ring takes the studio’s signature challenge‑driven design and expands it into a sweeping open world that feels endlessly explorable. While it departs from the tightly structured progression of Dark Souls 1–3 (a format I personally prefer) the shift still brings a unique strength. The Lands Between evoke the same sense of boundless possibility that made Skyrim so iconic, rewarding curiosity with challenging encounters, layered storytelling, and a level of discovery rarely matched in modern RPGs. However, this sense of discovery didn't come without drawbacks. The sheer freedom of pathing makes FromSoftware’s already cryptic questlines even harder to track, often to the point of feeling overwhelming. NPC arcs can become fragmented or unintentionally skipped, and the open structure occasionally disrupts the narrative flow, creating moments where major story beats feel out of order or disconnected from the intended progression. Regarding the graphics, it’s impossible not to highlight the sheer beauty of the world FromSoftware has crafted. Every vista, dungeon, and battlefield feels meticulously composed, often looking more like art then the video games of past. Whether standing still to admire the horizon or caught in the chaos of combat, nearly every moment feels screenshot-worthy. It’s a visually astonishing experience that elevates the sense of wonder throughout the journey.

Elden Ring is basically a beautiful open-world fantasy designed to repeatedly humble you until you somehow become the very demon that once bullied you. You start out as a weak little homeless corpse with a stick getting folded by random soldiers, horses, dogs, gravity, and anything larger than a squirrel, while the game casually tells you to "go explore" like the entire map isn't trying to personally assassinate you. The bosses are incredible, mostly because they kill you so many times you develop a toxic relationship with them, but eventually the suffering pays off and suddenly a dual-wielding nightmare deleting enemies in three hits while dramatically walking through explosions. The world is gorgeous, the lore makes zero sense unless you watch a 6-hour video essay, and the online messages from other players range from helpful to clinically insane. We hated every second of getting destroyed...and immediately came back for more. 10/10 emotional damage simulator 😅

Would prefer if I could give this a "meh", but there are so many frustrations honestly so far. I'll possibly update once finishing, but wanted to produce some thoughts on the game at this point in my playthrough. I'm going to start with just some things about Elden Ring, and then some issues with FromSoftware in general. I'd not played a mage/sorcerer in any previous Souls games, so wanted to try it here, and basically the literal level 1 spell you start with is just better than basically 99% of anything you'll encounter in the game. Who tf designed that? It's ludicrously bad. You'd think "oh cool, I just spent 5-10k on this new spell, surely it must be better than the literal starter spell!" Yeah, unfortunately you'd be wrong about that. This game feels very empty a lot of the time. Most of the game is just running around through fields, trying to guess at where the game wants you to go. Finding the areas suitable for your level is also pretty bad, as you can literally walk for 10 seconds out of somewhere massively underlevel for you, straight into massively overlevelled enemies. Most FromSoftware games do this, which again feels pretty stupid. I like that you *can* get to higher level areas in these games, but it shouldn't be just a case of "oh I turned right instead of left and now I have to grind away 10 minutes to try to get my souls back without getting 1 shot lol". Most actual buildings that you'll find (like the whole, massive sunken town area in the West side of the map) are inaccessible. What's the point in making a massive area with all these buildings etc., and just... None of them serve literally any purpose whatsoever. I also feel like this specifically does not work very well when they just try to rehash the same FromSoftware formula over and over, because whereas in previous Souls games, you will naturally encounter an NPC that is crucial to the story or to being able to buy certain items for certain builds, this game does the same thing except over SO much empty space. For example, they put the primary mage trader in a random hole in a random ruin in the middle of nowhere behind a miniboss. How does that make any sense gameplay-wise? You're not going to naturally encounter them like you would in other Souls games so putting random NPCs in random places makes way less sense than in any previous games. If you don't literally look that up to start with (i.e. remove your own immersion), you're likely to not encounter them for ages if you don't happen to go in that direction early on. I'm 15 hours in so far, and have found 0 pairs of gloves, and no real usable armour or shields lol. I imagine if you want to actually get some, it's again going to be a case of "yes, we designed this so you have to look up a guide!" Very engaging, immersive and fun. They literally self sabotage the atmosphere in their own game by doing stuff like this. I love the Souls themes for the most part, but it's impossible you immerse yourself when your only option in these games is you HAVE to look up a guide in order to have any sort of gameplay enjoyment (more on that later). The whole collecting/crafting stuff in this game feels very un-thought through, very much like it was shoehorned in without much direction at all. You just end up picking up stuff most of the game that you never use, never need to use and that has almost no value. It doesn't feel like a main feature for you to utilise, it doesn't feel rewarding, and it pretty much exclusively used for stuff like making arrows. The controls feel worse in some cases and a step backwards (again). No idea why, but FromSoftware simply is incapable of making good decisions with controls, or from ever actually just building on their previous game(s). This game for example, unlike in several of their previous games, they have decided to remove being able to move the camera slightly when locked onto an enemy. Why? You want to look around slightly whilst fighting an enemy you're locked onto? Not possible. Changing targets when locked on also doesn't work half the time, and even actually just locking on can often be a struggle. They add a horse, so you're often moving faster whilst fighting in bigger, more open areas, and yet you have no way to quickly look around you a little bit whilst travelling? Just no thought behind it honestly, the number of times I'm stuck locked onto an enemy and because you're covering more area, you just run into more enemies that you can't easily just look around at. I've also had so many times when I've been running away whilst my camera is facing an enemy, pressing to lock my camera, and it just spins my camera to face the front instead of locking onto the enemy that is in the open, central in my camera to begin with. This then causes your movement to completely change, and feels awful. Getting stuck on a candelabra in a dungeon because you tried to lock onto an enemy and the camera spun round instead of locking, or running off of a bridge you're traversing because you tried to actually play the game and fight an enemy, very fun... The game looks very good, but there are many, many reused assets & enemies which kind of detracts a bit from how good the game looks. Make a few really great looking buildings/areas/enemies and then just reuse the living ♥♥♥♥ out of them. ### Moving onto FromSoftware in general: My biggest issue with the Souls games is the developers just never really seem to know why they're doing things, or they never really have the motivation of making something actually fun to play, more just to make it difficult/frustrating to deal with just for the sake of it. Take weapon damage for example: for those who are unaware, there are so many hidden elements that determine how much damage you do. It seems like a completely arbitrary system that punishes being intelligent or creative and having ideas, and kind of lazy to be honest; basically, adding hidden crutches that prevent you from actually being able to utilise things like your stats in any real sensical way, and saving them having to actually try to balance things properly because the hidden crutches just add hidden limits to everything you want to do. You'd think "hey, I want to play as a mage, I'm going to focus mainly Int at the start". Wrong, you just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ your experience. "I want to put some points in dexterity to-" WRONG, start again. It's really does reduce the fun when the game actively punishes you for not going and trawling through 100 guides and documents (not provided by FromSoftware, of course) to find exactly the right stuff to do. Why do players need to go and look through a spreadsheet and plugin 10 different numbers in order to actually know whether a weapon is better to use? And even then, there are then a dozen more elements like swing speed, animations etc. that can still mean a weapon is better/worse, that there is literally no information for within the game. It honestly makes these games so unimmersive and takes away a lot of the joy of playing them, because you literally have to go and *research* every single thing to know whether it's actually not just going to be miserable to use. They can never just decide on a reasonable list of useful stats to include in the games, they seem to change it EVERY single different Souls game, and most of them are literally just useless and a waste of precious levels, and this game is absolutely no different.

Took me 4 attempts of coming back to this game but I finally got it and finished it, I initially went a health build with mace and shield but swapped to mage then to a strength build. I understand why Elden Ring was GOTY. Elden Ring has a good mix of biomes with their own themes. There are a lot of eye candy pieces that I loved. effects are just as pretty, very edgy animations/designs, very visually pleasing. This game like the other souls games ran very well on my system. Gameplay you know what to expect from a souls game, off the bat the world is huge and sprawling. The additional mechanics such as your mount to travel about adds an element to the combat and platforming. The magics system is probably at it's best in this game. Every build is satisfying but you will find the classic i-frame rolling at the centre of combat. There's mechants and a central hub you unlock as you play which you will goto often to help you along the way and unlock new armour, abilities and spells. Plot is on par with what to expect, less is more and world storytelling is at the forefront. Saying that you will find NPCs that will guide you and aim you alongside the map. A note which I don't think every gets pointed out is the voice actors are all great in these games. As I don't want to drag this on as this game has been out for years now, please find some quick pros and cons. Pros: Fluid, fast, fun, rewarding combat that is small part frustration and large part satisfying. World is vast, beautiful go in any direction and you'll find something new and some areas truly are epic. Game breadcrumbs you nicely and I believe the pacing is fair. Cons: It is a me thing and take with a pinch of salt, but I can dislike the travelling and exploring in the said vast open world, the mount you get is fast and agile, but I really just prefer a more dense, concentrated world/game area. Games with empty lands whilst give you scale of the world can be quite boring, Elden Ring is quite generous with it's enemy placement/things to do so you aren't always travelling feeling burnt out. Takes a few hours of baby steps before you start ramping up in power, whilst you can go anywhere some areas are incredibly unforgiving at the start. Runes/Souls or whatever you want to call the experience currency can feel arbitary in how it rewards you. Some enemies that might be brutal or health sponges may award nothing and some that are easily dispatched can give you loads, I don't know how it works but some enemies aren't even worth it, so you might just sprint past. TLDR: Can see why this was GOTY, took a few times to get it but it's really fantastic, I can't wait to come back to this in a few years and enjoy it all over again. I'd play as raw as you can and look at a guide when really stuck. Sometimes it's easier to try a different area if a place is really difficult and enjoy exploring as the game is full of new things always.

25 hours on PC, 500 hours on console… and Elden Ring still finds new ways to humble me. You’d think after 500 hours I’d be some kind of god. Nah. I load in feeling like the main character and 10 minutes later I’m getting folded by a random enemy hiding in a bush like it’s their full-time job. This game is just Dark Souls but open world and somehow *more disrespectful*. You’re riding around thinking you’re free, then boom—dragon, tree sentinel, or some absolutely unhinged boss appears out of nowhere to remind you you’re not built like that. Boss fights? Either you first try them and feel like a legend, or you get stuck in a loop of: “ok this time I’ve learned the pattern” *dies instantly* But that’s the thing—when it clicks, it REALLY clicks. Clean dodges, perfect timing, clutch heals… you start moving like you actually know what you’re doing (for about 5 minutes). The map is huge, the music is great, and there’s always something new to find—usually something that ruins your day in a creative way. Would I recommend it? Yes. Will you suffer a little? Definitely. Will you stop playing? Not likely.

Elden Ring is simultaneously From Software's best and worst game. It is worth every penny spent and if you are looking for an answer to the question if you should buy it or not, look no further : Go and play the game ! Maybe even consider using the Seamless Coop Mod to enjoy your time together with friends ! After all, this is From Software and the game won GOTY 2022 not without a good reason. This being said, here is the critique i have to offer considering the highly debated topic of ranking the Souls born Games: The Peaks are incredible, and the lows are mostly just minor annoyances, but it keeps an odd place in the Soulsborn lineup by being the only open world title so far. It is also the best or worst start you can have to the genre depending on what you enjoy in these games. The major issues consist of the multiple reuse of the same bosses over and over again to a point where you are asking yourself if they even had enough time to finish the game or if they just filled holes before release. Sometimes the reuse is explained and makes sense story-wise. Other times it is just as random as encountering a lion inside the supermarket next door. The same goes for some dungeons. Controversially, the game gives the player the option to use spirit ashes as a way to make fights easier and more manageable, which also results in some fights feeling unbalanced if you don't rely on these mechanics to assist you (This argument only applies if you want the same journey as in the Dark Souls Series where u don't get Spirit Ashes to Assist you). On the flip side of the coin, Elden Ring just delivers when it comes to visual designs as well as the boss design generally. The consistent and smooth combat allows the game to make enemies faster than previous titles and results in fights being exciting, punishing and ultimately more rewarding. It also shines when considering re-playability, since the game gets considerably more fun when you know which path to follow and which annoyances to avoid. This is paired with a huge number of weapons, spells and equipment which are balanced to make every build and play style viable. One can thus also heavily influence the difficulty of the game by changing the order in which to tackle the main tasks and spending an unlimited time leveling up in between bosses. Therefore, i conclude the game to be a well-known friend of Schrödinger: The best and the worst Soulsborn game you might play, and you only know what it is once you look inside the Box.

My journey into Elden Ring began with confidence. I stepped into this majestic, mysterious world… and immediately locked eyes with a gigantic knight on a horse. “Ah,” I thought. “You are mine.” Reader, I was not his. I charged in at level 1 like a hero in a prophecy. The prophecy was written by a liar. I died. Then I died again. And again. After ten attempts, I began to suspect that perhaps the game and I had… different expectations. But here’s the trick: the world doesn’t shove you down a hallway. It whispers. Golden lights guide you forward, fires let you rest, and somewhere out there is your destiny… probably holding a weapon the size of a small building. And scattered across this hauntingly beautiful world are messages from other players. Helpful guidance, you think. “Treasure ahead.” You follow it. It’s a bloodstained cliff. Another message: “Try finger, but hole.” No further explanation. Just vibes. The gameplay loop is simple: Fight. Roll. Die. Fight better. Roll faster. Die with slightly more dignity. Then suddenly… you don’t die. You win. And when you level up enough, you return to that smug, oversized boss that bullied you earlier… and absolutely erase it from existence. Sweet, vengeful poetry. Or, if you’re feeling less heroic, you summon help. And that help is almost always a nearly naked warrior with a pot on their head and two swords, who arrives like a feral tornado and deletes the boss while you’re still figuring out which button is “heal.” Visually? Stunning. Every landscape looks like it was painted by a melancholic god. Mechanically? Brutal. Your keyboard and mouse will develop trust issues. Emotionally? YOU DIED. After roughly 10,000 deaths, 4 playthroughs, multiple dragon-related incidents, and being humbled by creatures that might actually be gods… I highly recommend it.

This is one of those games that stays with you long after you finish it. I completed Elden Ring on May 4, 2026, and honestly, the only word that fits is: peak. I’ll be direct—I was wrong about this game at first. I went in expecting to dislike it, even hating on it early on. But somewhere between the struggle of the early hours and the intensity of the mid-to-late game, something changed. It didn’t just get better—it pulled me in completely. Looking back, I regret ever doubting it. As my first Souls-like experience, this set a very high standard. I’d rate it an 8.5/10. Open-world games usually aren’t my preference, but that’s a personal bias—not a flaw of the game. In fact, the world design here proves why this genre works so well when done right. What truly makes this game unforgettable is the feeling it gives you. The bosses are unique, challenging, and demanding. Every victory feels earned. When you finally overcome a difficult fight, it’s not just progress—it feels like a genuine achievement. Few games capture that sense of accomplishment this well. Visually, the game is also stunning. If you can run it at max settings, the environments are nothing short of breathtaking, adding even more weight to every moment of exploration and combat. I just finished it, and already I miss it. That says everything. This isn’t just a game you play—it’s one you experience and remember. And yes, beating Malenia? That’s a flex I’ll carry proudly. If you’re reading this and wondering whether you should buy it: do it. Even if it looks difficult, even if you get stuck—it’s always possible to push through. And when you do, it’s worth it. 100% recommended.

Elden Ring is widely considered one of the greatest video games of its generation, not because it is flawless, but because it successfully combines ambitious design, deep gameplay systems, and a uniquely rewarding sense of discovery into a single, cohesive experience. Developed by FromSoftware, the game builds upon the “Soulsborne” formula while expanding it into a massive open world, creating something that feels both familiar and groundbreaking at the same time. One of the most important reasons Elden Ring is so good is its open-world design. Unlike many modern open-world games that rely heavily on markers and checklists, Elden Ring trusts the player to explore naturally. The world, known as the Lands Between, is vast and filled with hidden dungeons, bosses, and secrets. This creates a sense of genuine discovery—players are not just completing objectives, they are uncovering mysteries. Critics often describe the world as “rich” and “imaginative,” with an enormous scale that encourages curiosity and experimentation . Another major strength is the gameplay itself, especially the combat system. Combat in Elden Ring is deliberate and challenging, requiring timing, patience, and skill. Every enemy encounter has weight, and every victory feels earned. The difficulty can be intimidating, but it is also what makes the experience so satisfying. As one review notes, mastering the combat provides a “profoundly satisfying” feeling that keeps players engaged despite repeated failures . This balance between difficulty and reward is a defining feature of the game. Character customization and build variety also contribute to the game’s quality. Players can choose from a wide range of weapons, magic types, and playstyles, allowing for a highly personalized experience. Whether someone prefers melee combat, ranged attacks, or spellcasting, the game supports multiple approaches. This flexibility encourages replayability and experimentation, making each playthrough feel unique. The artistic design and atmosphere are equally important. While Elden Ring may not be the most technically advanced game graphically, its art direction is widely praised. The environments—from haunting castles to golden fields—are visually striking and memorable. The game’s lore, partially written by George R. R. Martin, adds depth to the world, creating a sense of history and mystery that players piece together through exploration and subtle storytelling . However, it is also important to acknowledge that Elden Ring is not perfect. Its difficulty can be a barrier for some players, and certain aspects of the open world can feel unclear or even frustrating. Some critics point out issues like uneven pacing, occasional technical problems, and moments where exploration feels aimless . These flaws prevent it from being universally accessible, but they also contribute to its identity as a challenging and uncompromising game. In conclusion, Elden Ring is an exceptional game because it successfully blends exploration, challenge, and creativity into a single experience. It rewards curiosity, skill, and persistence in a way few games do. While it may not appeal to everyone, its ambition and execution have earned it a place among the best games ever made

Where do I begin? By the time I was done with it, the game left me completely disappointed. Most of the negative reviews have captured all the significant problems with this game so I'll keep it (relatively) short. My favorite games in the Fromsoft catalogue are Dark Souls and Sekiro (also among my favorite games of all time). These games feel deliberately designed; Dark Souls made you feel like exploring a dangerous land, and Sekiro's combat system is truly one of a kind. But Elden Ring? It's a video game ass video game. Everything in this game exists for the player's benefit. Side dungeons almost always end in boss fights with a treasure chest to reward the player. Stakes of Marika make it convenient to fight bosses. Sites of Grace abound so that you never feel the tension of exploration (also free fast travel). Every single death in this game will only be due to bosses, or sometimes gravity. Don't wanna fight overworld enemies? Get on Torrent and ride away. The open world is simply a collection of all the dungeons they made spread horizontally. Is the open world truly open then? Nope, there's a strictly linear progression with some side stuff along the way, with arbitrary progression gates like Morgott's Seal and Great rune requirements. Balance is literally non-existent. Is the combat good then? It's basically Dark Souls combat again. There's a gazillion weapons, but they all mostly play the same, you know how it is. Boss fights are now true shonen anime style affairs, wait for your turn and dodge while the boss does his wombo combo and then poke. Repeat all over again for a 100 bosses, and the nail in the coffin is that a significant portion of them are repeats. Not even remembrance bosses are spared. Don't even get me started on the DLC. I was genuinely excited to play this game, and sadly, this made me question the future of Soulslikes from Fromsoft. I guess we'll have to wait and see.

ELDEN RING features one of the best open worlds I've experienced in a game, with different dungeons, areas and secrets to be found in every corner. You might find your build defining weapon, talisman, or spell in this cave, maybe after defeating a certain boss, or doing a certain questline - which is what adds the incredible depth people have praised ELDEN RING so heavily for. Now, ELDEN RING is probably the best game ever made, (still not my favourite lol) along with it's absolutely stellar DLC but it does have one major pitfall for me - since it's open world, replays do have this checklist feel to it - since you already kinda know where everything is and what path you need to take to get to a boss to progress further in the game, or whatever talisman you need etc. it results in a fresh playthrough being a horse riding simulator for an hour. This is only a problem if you plan to replay, but it doesn't totally ruin the experience. (including Xbox playtime, I have around 400ish hours on this game and have probably beaten it 10 times over and I've 100%'d it on PC) I would also like to say they really mastered every type of combat in this game, mage builds are actually really viable in a souls game for once, so there's so many different playstyles meaning on a replay you could also try something new and enjoy it a tonne but eventually you will end up covering all the stuff you want to do (or maybe not everyone is different with souls games and the like this is just my opinion) ELDEN RING is great buy it or eat my shoes

Definitely my favorite game of all time. First I'm going to talk a little about the lore because it's probably my favorite part of the game. The lore is extremely deep and well-hidden, but not so well-hidden that it's almost impossible to make reasonable guesses on past events (looking at you, Dark Souls II). The lore community is still very active and come up with new hypothesis all the time. The combat is very good, and spells can often mesh well with your regular weapons. The main bosses are all really great, and PvP is fun (especially at lower levels). There are lots of unique consumable & throwable weapons and buffs, lots and lots of decently unique spells (although there is one particular group of spells that are just slight variations of the same thing). There are a huge number of weapons, and special "ashes of war" you can attach to them which give an extra special attack on top of their existing moveset (even bows and magic staves can have them). The exploration is also pretty good. The game does tell you where to go to an extent, but there are no minimaps, or giant markers on your screen, or even on-screen instructions, only what NPCs tell you in the game, so you get to make all of the decisions on where to go instead of the game directing you around. Exploration is driven by "I wonder what that thing over there is". It is a large game, but the game does a decent job at hiding exactly how big it is on your first playthrough, so it shouldn't feel too terribly daunting at first. There are also lots of little minor locations, caves, and dungeons for you to do. They can be a repetitive, but they contain lots of useful loot, and the puzzles tend to get harder & dungeons get longer as you get further into the game. The game is also absolutely beautiful; everything looks like a painting. In my opinion, even better than Dark Souls III environments, which are also incredibly beautiful. The DLC is very very excellent, even better than the base-game in my opinion. It feels completely packed compared to the base game, and the bosses are generally very good, challenging, and rewarding. The dungeons are much more unique, even with unique bosses you can't fight anywhere else, unlike the base game dungeons. Also the weapons and spells are all really cool and fascinating, and every single location is just so beautiful and unique. It's crazy!!! At full price, this game is worth it.

I purchased Elden Ring and got around to playing it recently, only to find the game freezing for 2 to 3 seconds every few minutes, making it completely unplayable. This is a well-documented issue with countless forum threads and YouTube videos confirming it. My machine had no trouble running Spider-Man 2, Black Myth: Wukong, or Lies of P. The problem is clearly with the game itself. What makes this especially frustrating is that this is not a new or obscure bug. Players have been reporting this freezing issue for a long time, and FromSoftware has done little to nothing to address it. When a problem is this widespread and this well known, leaving it unresolved is not an oversight, it is a choice. Selling a product you know is broken for a significant portion of your playerbase and doing nothing about it is simply not acceptable. At some point, the developer and the platform that profits from selling it share responsibility for that. Of my 2 hours and 57 minutes of playtime, the vast majority was spent attempting to debug the freezing issue, not actually playing the game. I requested a refund, not because I didn't want to play it, but because I couldn't. Steam denied it, citing their 2-hour/14-day policy without any acknowledgment of the circumstances. The support experience was worse than the technical issue. Three different agents gave me copy-paste responses. One assured me refunds are considered "case by case" but offered zero explanation of what factors were actually weighed. When I asked them to consider that I only launched the game for the first time days ago, or that nearly 3 hours on a 100+ hour game hardly constitutes taking advantage of their policy, I got silence. Then they closed the ticket. As a software engineer, I'd never tell my customers to debug my product on their own time. Steam apparently has no such qualms. The platform I trusted to protect my purchases hid behind a rigid policy to retain a modest amount of money from a customer with a completely legitimate complaint about a broken product. If you're thinking about buying a game and playing it at your own pace, the way gaming used to work, think twice. Steam's refund policy doesn't protect that. Buy it, launch it immediately, and decide within 2 hours or you're on your own.

My first souls-like as it isn't exactly my type of routines, and thus is this review's perspective: - It's beautiful. It's a relaxing exploration of a dying world with spam-able mobs. - It's annoying. It gets cheeky with mobs that don't play the same rules as others or yours. - It's repetitive. 50 easier mobs only require the same moves repeatedly (usually stun-locked and can't survive a full combo). Cheekier mobs can only be fought with the same exploitive moves 50 times. They respawn. - The mob diversity and how that tells the story is quite amazing. - The combat control is not very responsive and balance is not intuitive. It's a long list. - Fighting dragons aren't the problem. They're more like learning music. The real challenges are fighting your own character's animation sets (about 3 out of 5 animations are self-destructive), animation queues and delays that triggers after your current (very slow) one, and the camera looking too far up or too far down, blinding you. I lost that fight often. - I've rage-quit only twice. Once was the first 1.5 hours when a horny guy at a large castle ♥♥♥♥-blocking me, who eventually taught me to explore elsewhere rather than follow "directions" (basically, "Don't trust the game"), which I ended up enjoying quite a bit. Then another an hour ago when I got too bored with the routines and started rushing bosses and seeing if I can use any other moves beyond 2 for 10 minutes each, which was a stern "no, don't trust the game". Considering the reputation of souls-like, I thought that wasn't so bad. Though, I was hoping that'd be due to some difficulty barrier, not how counter-intuitive it felt, especially after so many of these games the company has been making and how well received they have been. Souls-like is still not my type of game. But I know many people enjoy these type of routines, and I do enjoy watching them playing or analyzing. Definitely nurture this shiny tree, I'd say.

A Late but Honest Review of Elden Ring This is a very late review, so you'll easily find better and more detailed ones out there. Still, here are my thoughts after finishing the base game and working through the DLC.Elden Ring was my first proper FromSoftware game, though I had already played several souls-likes (Hollow Knight, Blasphemous, and others). The Good: The base game is excellent. There's a huge amount to do, the world looks stunning, and the bosses are the highlight — they're epic, memorable, and the main reason to keep playing. The world design is outstanding. It's beautifully interconnected, and if you can see a location in the distance, you can usually find a way to get there. It gives a real sense of freedom and exploration, similar to Breath of the Wild. Combat is intense and punishing, which is both its greatest strength and biggest point of frustration. Enemies are aggressive, and groups can quickly overwhelm you if you're not careful. There are also quite a few "cheap" enemy placements, traps, and surprise attacks that feel unfair at times. That said, playing completely blind, I found it to be a hard but mostly fair challenge overall.One standout feature is the enemy variety: almost every regular enemy has around 15 different attack animations, and bosses often have double that. It makes fights feel dynamic and replayable. The Not-So-Good: The story is my biggest complaint. It's extremely vague and unclear for the first 40+ hours. Even after that, huge parts remain unexplained, forcing you to watch video essays or read wikis to understand what's actually going on. Many systems, item descriptions, and lore details are so obscure that it's often hard to know what you're supposed to do or why something matters. If I could change one thing about the game, it would be making the story and key information clearer. Crafting exists but can largely be ignored if you don't enjoy it. However, I strongly recommend paying attention to weapon upgrades using smithing stones. I neglected them for too long and definitely suffered for it. Music and sound design are solid and atmospheric, but not particularly memorable or thematic. Performance is decent (see pc specs) but not perfect. Frame rate dips into the low 40s (and sometimes lower) can happen, especially during intense boss fights or in the DLC areas. It’s noticeable and occasionally frustrating. DLC: The Shadow of the Erdtree DLC is very much worth the price. It's nearly as large as the base game and feels like a full expansion. I’d recommend saving it until you’ve nearly finished (or fully completed) the main game. Very similar in quality to the Witcher's blood and wine expansion. Final Thoughts: Is Elden Ring the greatest game of all time? Not for me. Would I tell anyone to avoid it? Absolutely not. It has an incredible amount of quality and allure. The exploration, bosses, and sense of discovery are top-tier.That said, story and clear motivation are what keep me most engaged in games, and in that regard, The Witcher 3 is still my gold standard. Elden Ring doesn’t come close there.If I had to give it a score, I’d say a strong 9/10. Pro tip: Install a simple boss tracker app on your phone (the game doesn’t track progress for you), and don’t be afraid to look up guides when you get stuck. It’ll save you a lot of frustration without spoiling the magic.

The best RPG and Action game I have ever played so far. At the time I am writing this, I have finished two playthroughs and I am getting ready for a third. This is also the first Souls-like I have finished (excluding Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice) Starting off with a few cons: * The combat system is not beginner friendly, but given you have the time and patience, it is definitely worth the time learning it. * There are also some bosses with annoying gimmicks such as [spoiler]the Godskin Duo and sometimes the Elden Beast[/spoiler], but the game provides you with tools to help you in areas that you struggle. * The mechanics are not perfect by any means. Some bosses take up a majority of your screen or lack a good enemy lock-on feature, leaving you with little visibility. * There are some armor sets and weapons that you may have to grind unreasonable amounts of time for, as those have very low drop rates. Fortunately, you are not forced to grind for specific items to make progress, but it is frustrating spending a lot of time doing repetitive grinding for an item you want. Now, for the pros of this game: * Very fun progression. It is really fun to see the story progress, as well as seeing what other areas and equipment you can find as you progress. * Great character aesthetics. The character creator is incredibly fun to mess with and you can make some really nice or even funny looking characters. There are also dozens of armor sets and equipment that you can mix and match to express yourself fully. * Very fun build system. There are thousands of possibilities for different builds you can make and styles you can use. The game provides you with weapons that you can change the affinity of as well as abilities (some special weapons are not customizable, though). You may also use different types of spells (offensive and defensive) along those weapons. * Very fun combat system. Not only do you have access to different equipment and stats, but you can also fight enemies in ways that you find most fun. Bosses are really engaging and challenging, but still allow for players to express themselves with different builds. * Beautiful visuals. The art direction for the world, enemies, and player equipment are amazing. The graphics fidelity is great as well even at lower settings. Overall, this is my number 1 favorite game so far (tied with Terraria for very similar reasons), and I am looking forward to trying out other FromSoft titles.

There is a specific kind of magic in Elden Ring that most modern games are too afraid to touch: the magic of the unknown. From the moment you step out into the windswept fields of Limgrave and see the Erdtree looming like a golden titan over the horizon, the game makes you a promise: if you can see it, you can go there, and if you go there, you will find something that was worth the trip. Unlike the "theme park" style of most open worlds where you are led by the hand from one icon to the next, Elden Ring treats you like an adult. It trusts your curiosity. You might follow a trail of glowing statues to a hidden catacomb, or chase a invisible beetle across a beach only to find a weapon that changes your entire playstyle. It creates a sense of "organic wonder"—that feeling of stumbling upon a massive underground city like Siofra River by accident and realizing the world is three times larger than you ever imagined. The combat is a brutal, beautiful dance of trial and error. It’s not just about "git gud" anymore; it’s about "git creative." If a boss is smashing you into the dirt, you don't have to beat your head against a wall. You can leave. You can go find a better spell, summon a pack of spectral wolves, or level up your sword. It gives the player agency over their own difficulty level without ever needing an "Easy Mode" button. Every victory feels earned, and every defeat feels like a lesson. But perhaps the most hauntingly beautiful part is the world itself. Built on a foundation laid by George R.R. Martin and brought to life by Hidetaka Miyazaki, the lore is a tragic tapestry of fallen gods and broken dreams. You aren't just playing a game; you’re an archaeologist picking through the ruins of a civilization that was once magnificent but is now rotting from the inside out. The bosses aren't just monsters; they are tragic figures—the General Radahn holding back the stars themselves, or the Lunar Princess Ranni seeking a path through the dark. Ultimately, Elden Ring is a masterpiece because it restores a sense of mystery to gaming. It reminds us that games don't have to be predictable or safe. They can be vast, terrifying, beautiful, and deeply rewarding all at once. It’s a game that respects your intelligence and rewards your bravery, and that is why it will be talked about for decades to come.

Elden Ring / S.O.T.E – FromSoftware’s False Messiah 166 hours played – completed main game and DLC - Elden Lord ending Rating: 6/10 Elden Ring presents itself as a once-in-a-generation masterpiece. At first, it really feels like that’s true. The world is huge, the atmosphere is incredible, and moments like seeing the Scadutree for the first time genuinely feel unforgettable. But the longer you play, the more that image breaks down. What is sold as a perfect masterpiece slowly reveals itself as a messy, inconsistent experience built on frustration and unclear design. What starts as awe quickly turns into frustration. Exploration often feels unclear or pointless, progression can feel like aimless wandering, and the game frequently fails to guide the player in any meaningful way. Instead of leading you through its world, it often leaves you lost in it. Pros Elden Ring does have strong build variety. There are many weapons, spells, and playstyles, letting you customize your character in different ways. The world and art design are also impressive, especially in the DLC. Areas like the Gravesite Plain and Cerulean Coast look beautiful and atmospheric, even if they sometimes feel like the only consistently strong part of the experience. Boss designs also look great visually. Rennala, Radahn, Maliketh, and Malenia all stand out in appearance, even when their gameplay design is heavily flawed. Cons This is where the illusion completely falls apart. Boss fights are often overly aggressive, filled with heavily delayed attacks that deal inconsistent but extreme damage. Instead of learning through fair repetition, many fights feel like trial-and-error until you survive a messy attempt. Even with high HP, you often feel like you never have enough; Artificial difficulty makes boss fights feel poorly balanced rather than challenging. Malenia is the clearest example—visually incredible, but completely undermined by mechanics like her two Scarlet Aeonia attacks(one-shots), Waterfowl Dance, grab, and healing on hit and block, which can erase progress instantly and make fights feel unfair rather than rewarding. Consort Radahn continues this problem with overwhelming pressure, visual clutter, and attacks that feel difficult to read rather than difficult to master. Messmer stands out only because he is one of the few bosses that actually feels fair, readable, and well-paced in comparison. Most other bosses devolve into waiting simulator gameplay—dodging long, repetitive combos just to get a single hit in. Strength builds feel unnecessarily punished, while faster builds like bleed or magic often outperform them significantly. Wins don’t feel earned—they feel like relief that the fight is finally over. Reused Content A large portion of the game also suffers from heavy reuse of bosses, enemies, and dungeon layouts. Many encounters feel copied and pasted with minor variations, which makes exploration feel repetitive rather than fresh over time. Open World & Direction The open world suffers from a serious lack of direction. Exploration is often not rewarding, but confusing and time-wasting. You can easily spend hours in areas that do not clearly contribute to progression, with very little guidance on where you should go or why. Compared to structured open-world games like Breath of the Wild, Elden Ring feels less like a guided experience and more like a massive pile of content with no clear structure holding it together. Even Melina, who is supposed to guide the player, feels poorly implemented. She disappears for long stretches, returns inconsistently, and ultimately her death happens so randomly, making her character fail to provide meaningful direction or emotional weight. Her role feels underdeveloped and almost irrelevant to the actual experience. Story & Endgame The story is extremely unclear unless you look outside the game. Most of it is hidden behind item descriptions or external lore explanations instead of being properly told in-game. By the end—especially in the DLC—you’re left with major moments like Consort Radahn and Miquella cutscenes that look important but feel confusing and underdeveloped in context. The base game ending also suffers. Radagon is a solid fight, but the Elden Beast immediately after feels like a drawn-out, frustrating fight filled with delayed attacks, constant running, no room to get damage in, and magic attacks that feel unfair, making the entire fight a huge disappointment rather than a meaningful conclusion. Overall, the Elden Lord ending feels more tedious and boring than satisfying, making it feel more like “oh, that’s it, I guess I beat the game” rather than an impactful, worthwhile journey. Conclusion Elden Ring (including SOTE) is not a well-made game and is heavily overrated for what it actually delivers for its price tag. It presents itself as a flawless masterpiece, but that image does not hold up under real time spent playing the game and calling out poorly made game design. The more you engage with it, the more its flaws become obvious—unclear direction, inconsistent boss design, and storytelling that feels too vague to be satisfying. While it does have strong moments in world design, atmosphere, and build variety, these highs are constantly undermined by frustrating gameplay systems and poor pacing decisions. In reality, Elden Ring is a 6/10 experience rather than a 10/10 experience—a game with massive ambition and beautiful presentation that is consistently dragged down by flawed execution. A false messiah: impressive on the surface, but deeply inconsistent underneath. Truly A Waste Of Time And Money.

get gud? But no, kind of really. This game taught me the difference between challenging, but fair, and challenging, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Early on, I thought I was dying to some nonsense, but I eventually learned a couple of things that helped me. Boss encounters are not flailing skirmishes to button-mash your way through. There's input buffering; the game stores how many times you press attack. You have to be methodical in your attacks, and you have to respond to the boss's moveset. You're dancing here, you're not brawling. You realize that, and you realize that you're learning to dance with the boss and find the windows to punish, the game opens up in miraculous and interesting ways. Now you can just max vigor and strength, slap wild-strikes on the rusted anchor, and go to town. That's valid, it's also kind of ridiculously fun. Stacking poise and simply wild-strikes'ing a dual-sword wielding boss in the DLC was hysterical. But there's so much nuance to appreciate in this game. So much music, so much design. If a boss slaps you around, there's a better'n fair chance there's either a mechanic you haven't learned, or a tool that'd make the fight easier (sentry's torch for black knife assassins, as an example.) now in fairness. Much of this knowledge, the game doesn't give you. It comes from wikis and guides on youtube. Which sucks to a degree; I feel like a game should come with all the tools you need to overcome the challenges there-in. ultimately though, I do recommend this game. There's always mods if you want to change the flavor of your base experience. So if you're going to get this game, i'd recommend three things. 1: don't worry about runes. You can always farm more runes. Focus more on learning to move AROUND the boss, not just panic roll. I've lost millions, i'll make millions more. It don't matter. 2: Give yourself patience to learn. Everything in this game wants to slap you around. Learn from it. Appreciate the lessons you're being taught. the guides are your friends. you don't have to min-max your builds, but there's lots of good information out there to help you learn and grow.
