Planning on coming back and updating this review at some point because I know its a bit unfair of me to rate it negatively after having only scratching the surface of the game (from what I've heard/seen) and only having played it for 4 hours BUT: within those 4 hours I barely got to play the actual game. I don't have much experience with souls-likes but I have played my fair share of RPGs. In fact, one of the things I hate the most about most modern RPGs is the amount of hints and 'recommended paths' they do. I don't need a hint to pop up when I can't solve a puzzle within the first 30 seconds of encountering it and I don't need NPCs to use no-so-subtle dialogue to tell me which path may be harder or which path will have more dire consequences. At this point if you're a fan of souls-like games you might be thinking "Oh Elden ring would be perfect for you! There's no hand holding at all." Except no hand holding doesn't have to mean no tutorial/unrepeatable tutorials and bad interface design, but it does in this game. I don't know if that's because this game may not have been originally intended for PC and therefore may have been poorly adapted for mouse and keyboard players but in my experience so far, it's really sucked. Boxes that should be clickable aren't, you can't use the escape key to exit out of some menus, you can't pause the game even though its just you playing, among other pains. Now I know some players bask in the brutality of it but the reality is that its a primarily single player game, meaning if players deviate from the intended way to play, who cares? They're enjoying the game the way they want to. I personally have never 'pause-buffered' or used menu shortcuts to give me an advantage against difficult enemies in any game, nor do I intend to, but not being able to pause a single player game when some sort of IRL circumstance calls is quite frustrating. Additionally, the tutorial sucks and returning to the game is incredibly difficult. I have tried returning to this game twice now since I first played it, each time giving it roughly an hour to an hour and a half. Both times I have spent nearly 30 minutes trying to understand the combat mechanics and the equipment menu. It's not that either is incredibly difficult to use, it's that they are poorly explained and difficult to learn. I've played several other games that have the formula of 'dodge roll' 'heavy attack' 'light attack' 'block/parry' but in all of them all I have to do to learn what buttons do what is hit the pause menu and look at controls. In Elden Ring, even when I do that it simply lists 'dodge roll' 'strafe' 'backstep' as one button. And on top of that that same button is used to turn light attacks into heavy attacks. Sure I can adapt, figure out what conditions need to be met for my character to perform a 'strafe' instead of a 'dodge roll' or a 'backstep', but I don't want to relearn every single time I return. And if you're thinking "Huh, what kinda guy only plays a game for an hour or two then doesn't come back to it for a month??" I'd agree with you because normally I do enjoy a game for a full playthrough, however many hours that may take, but with Elden ring, every time I've given it a try, I've experienced more frustration than I have had fun. So when I come back to my computer for the next session a day later, I decide not to play it. And games are meant to be fun. So maybe your personal takeaway can be that you need to give it more time to transition from frustration to fun than I did.

This game holds a very special place in my heart as the first FromSoftware game that I played, especially since I first played it after searching for the next game to play like BOTW and TOTK. I've bought the game twice now (first on console where I have hundreds of hours) and now on Steam, and I've fallen back in love with it after having taken a break for a little while, and I have to say, there really is nothing quite like it. It is the only 10/10 game I have ever played in my opinion, and that 10/10 score is well deserved, the game does everything perfectly, between the amazing open world that has been masterfully crafted, and the infinite replayability with its innumerable builds and styles of play. On top of that, the story of this game runs extremely deep, and is incredibly interesting (I highly recommend checking out some Youtube videos on the topic). But what I think Elden Ring does the best is the design of the world itself, and the life that is scattered throughout it. It does what BOTW and TOTK couldn't quite accomplish, in that it spreads enemies and NPCs out enough so that they aren't crowding each other, while leaving nowhere so devoid of life that it is boring for the player, and makes sure that there is always something for the player to do that isn't tedious or just straight up annoying. I truly cannot recommend it enough, 10/10 and my favorite game of all time.

What a great game that I wish I had picked up sooner! What kept me away from FromSoft game's was the complete hard-stop I experienced back with DS1 (PTDE) at Blight Town. Manditory difficult jump(s), poison, with high fall probability in a scaffolding-type ladder/maze area... died so many times until I simply got frustrated and uninstalled the game... although I had thoroughly enjoyed it up to that point. Things I love about this game: 1) large beautiful open world just begging to be explored... having trouble with a boss? go explore, level up, and come back later 2) exploration is often well rewarded 3) tonnes of sorceries, incantations, armor, weapons, Ashes of War, and summons to mix'n' match for a variety of play-styles and builds 4) crafting can turn pickups into useful items... like bombs, cures, xp boost, item find boost, etc. 5) map marker system super helpful 6) There are "natural" spots in the game near site's of grace that make "time efficient" XP farming "easy" when you were either (a) looking to reach item stat requirements, (b) wanted to force a level up to spend all your runes before attempting a difficult fight, or (c) needed more runes to purchase items. The first spot I used was inside a castle just outside the final boss room... there was a giant there just down the steps that I could kill easily, rest, and repeat whenever I wanted/needed more runes. What i wish the game had: 1) a side quest tracker / journal - the site's of grace point you along the main story path, but you have to manually make note of "side quest details" you find via conversations with NPC's... if they mention a place/person make sure you come back to talk to them later after you've visited who/where they the mentioned to move the side quest along. Sometimes it's hard to know if the conversation was just delivering background/lore or giving you a side quest. Things I'm not a fan of: 1) side quests can auto-advance / skip milestones if you pushed ahead too far either via exploration or progressing the main quest. very easy to do if you didn't realize you had a side quest with the absence of a quest tracker / journal 2) I generally don't do well with "jumping puzzles" and die... so more a me issue than the game. There are a number of spots/areas where parkour (and selective falling) is important... especially if you want to explore/traverse all areas... so far I've managed to accomplish most without too many deaths. Things I hate about the game: 1) Nothing comes to mind. At the time of writing this review I have yet to complete the game. I'm nearing 130 hours on my second character... I abondoned the first character (80-90 hrs) after figuring out they had "botched side quests". I've yet to decide if I'm going to try the "backup/restore my save file" method for reaching all the endings or if I'll just replay the game 3 times... I have a feeling I'd replay this game anyway, but getting the achievements out of the way in this playthourgh (via save backup/restore) could take the pressure off and/or eliminate the possibility of not unlocking or choosing the desired next ending achievement by mistake.

Writing reviews about games this big and this popular always feels weird, because it's not possible to say something that haven't been said already. Obviously the game is amazing so instead of praising it I'm just gonna list my minor annoyances. - Horse Combat - It's just bad, you can't roll, weapons' movesets are non existent. Luckily horse combat is optional. It is recommended for dragon fights as it trivialises them, but you are never required to engage with this mechanic. - Crafting - It's completely pointless. Instead of collecting/buying useful items, now you have to go through one more hoop to get said items. I've went through the entire game crafing maybe 3 different items. It doesn't hinder the experience, but the game just didn't need this system. - Open World - I just don't like open worlds. The "level" design gets worse, because now there are huge empty spaces which you have to run through. Imagine how much better the game would have been if ER wasn't open world. Imagine getting a DS1, but with 5x the number of maps. It would have been glorious. I'm glad that legacy dungeons and castles are still a thing and I have enjoyed them very much, but I'm just annoyed they were separated by some peak Ubisoft-like gameplay - "mindlessly going from marker to marker". Another fallout of the open world design is that balance gets thrown out of the window. By the time I reached the final boss I was level 165 with no farming. At such an absurdly high level I was able to face tank Radabeast while mashing LT like a monkey. I enjoy clearing all the content there is and sadly open world games are not balanced around clearing all the content. As much as I like complaining, that's it. The game is otherwise stellar and if we exclude my personal dislike for open worlds the only real issues with the game are crafting and horse combat which are fully optional.

One Ring made by the evil lord Sauron Hidetaka Miyazaki, One Ring to rule them all, One Ring to find them, One Ring to bring them all and in the darkness bind them, In the Land of Japanese software development warehouse building where Shadows lie. Elden Ring is not worth your time due to the profound curse placed upon the game's core design by the evil man who made it. The game aims at being infinitely replayable, but each of its assets is designed in a narrow fashion - so much so that the world does not feel as open as it is rather episodic. Each and every instance in the game is instrumented to be seen and encountered in a specific way which makes the experience of world exploration predictable and less exciting after playing for the first time. The dificulty ranges of the various explorable regions of the game world are awfully imballanced, so much so that it's less enjoyable to avoid choosing a linear path through the game on later playthroughs. The game world's incredibly size makes this issue even more frustrating - in order to experience something new on a subsequent playthrough, the player has to cross massive distances which are increasingly less and less aproachable the further he is from the starting point, ultimately discouraging exploration and narrowing the game experience to a single, most optimalized path of progression. There are only so many ways to reexperience the game's world without being severely discouraged and punished. And so ultimately, the game world's size and the quantity of its assets is severely nullified as the various paths to approach them are tragically so very limited. The game's world becomes eventually too predictable and the premise of experiencing the game in a fresh way nonexistent, which is not fun. Let it be pronounced and heard, Elden Ring could be legendary, but it is not, and won't be, unless FromSoftware developpers cease to practice the habit of forgetting a game once it's been created, despite the quantity of bothersome features still present and still widely acknowledged. One may recall the pathos of never properly finishing Lost Izalith in their previous game Dark Souls, an area of the game so very unique and all the more so disappointing for being critically underdevelopped. I feel very simillar about Elden Ring. As a former world of warcraft player, I see fit to pronounce a variety of ideas which could severely improve the experience of Elden Ring if they were ever developped, as they are present in that particular game, and although a very different game at that, still possesing a massive world and the spirit of an rpg game. Those ideas would be: There should be a variety of start points in Elden Ring, or at the very least, it should be possible to cross into other regions of the game from Limgrave without being stupefied and severely punished as much as is the case now. There should be more low level regions surrounding Limgrave so as to increase replayability and the possibilities of exploration on future playthroughs. And yes, despite the existence of various teleportation chests in Limgrave, the fact that the places you are sent to are completely above Limgrave's difficulty makes them less relevant as a travel feature. There is not enough enemy variety at each of the game's various places - an occasional "rare enemy spawn" or the promise of a "rare item drop" would be a solution to this issue. And lastly, there should be more paths connecting the various regions and places of the Elden Ring world and more accessible ways to connect the game's many features. In conclusion, Elden Ring nowhere near as fun as enjoyable after the first couple of playthroughs, it becomes stale and predictable rather too fast, and that is a completely nonsensical feature for a game of such high ambition and such quantity of the game's features.

Before anything, GET A CONTROLLER. I thought that Mouse and Keyboard will always be the way to go and that controller is for lazy people, GET THE CONTROLLER. Now on to the actual review. This game is unlike anything I have ever played before. It literally just launches you into the most hostile, uninviting, and dangerous setting and that's it. All you have is the "Armor" you are wearing and the will to become the Elden Lord. This game will NOT hold your hand, and it might seem weird and awkward at first but it is the best thing they could have done. The exploring alone is unparalleled, the map is deceptively ENORMOUS, and trust me, if its your first run, you will not BELIEVE the magnitude of this game. The boss fights. Cinematic. Are the fights hard? ABSOLUTELY! Are they incredibly frustrating? YOU BET! Does being stun locked and hit by 6 hits in a row when you accidentally ran out of stamina and held your shield and get killed when the boss was literally one shot and now you need to get a new controller cuz yours somehow ended up smashed to pieces on the floor make you want to rip out your hair? this might be one of the worst games i've ever played; i genuinely don't see where the glaze comes from. i always try to look for positives in a game first, but it's hard to find ANYTHING to like about elden ring. no, i did not finish the game, but with a game like elden ring you don't need to finish it to gauge its quality. after all the game is extremely repetitive and lackluster (an excuse of an open world game), which is one of my main gripes. i don't inherently have an issue with parries in combat systems, but the way that elden ring does it is not satisfying at all and feels extremely forced and, not only skill-less, but also soulless. sure, you can dodge attacks, or make a really cool build, but in the end the gameplay always bogs down to, "parry, swing, swing, parry, swing, occasional unparriable attack, swing, swing, big stun damage choreographed attack..." repeat until you either die or win. there isn't really much merit in making varied builds if it doesn't change the gameplay at all. that's like, if when equipping a sword as demoman in tf2, instead of swinging the sword, you throw it in an arc and get headshots for more damage. that's effectively what elden ring is with its build "variety". or, of course, you could just make a super OP build... but then where's the gameplay? what SKILL are you guys seeing in this? learning enemy patterns doesn't count, because you'll be doing that in ANY game. ergo, there is nothing that makes elden ring's combat unique save for its own poor game design. the world is pretty good looking, but it felt extremely empty and unrewarding to explore. you could either find some niche enemy to fight, or a guy that sells you incrementally better weapons, or both, or neither. maybe it gets better as you explore the map. but the open world shouldn't force me to progress its story for it to... open the world (side note, i don't mean the game can't gradually open up its world or be something similar to BOTW, but one, i was already WAY past the tutorial, and two, it isn't acceptable when there isn't anything to explore in the first place.) i can't speak on story much, but from what i have seen, it feels extremely misguided, fragmented and meandering. what is the message of elden ring's story? i get that not every story needs to have some super impactful message, but, if elden ring isn't one of those games, what is there to merit about its story? the fact it has cool character designs? you can go to some random place and find a tiny piece of lore? this isn't ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ undertale, it doesn't work. seriously i do not recommend this game to anyone who has any self respect and actually wants the games they play to be of quality and substance. this might work as parryslop for the majority, but it really isn't all that.

♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. This game has changed my life. I am not joking. Many people talk about how the Soul's games challenge them in real life just as much as in game, but it actually cured my mental health. Not as escapism, but as a solution to my problem's with addiction and rage. Elden Ring challenges you; in your patience and resilience, as well as the gaming industry; with masterclass in game design. Elden Ring is the greatest game ever made. Period. Almost everyone here in the reviews are saying the same thing, it's basically fact. It's tied with Portal for being my favorite. It is FromSoft's magnum opus. I struggled to get into this game for over three years. I originally got the game near launch, and it was my introduction to the Soulsbourne series. I knew they were hard games, but I didn't expect it to be so hard to GET into. The performance wasn't great on my old system which also hindered my progression. I put it down. I started playing other games that didn't challenge me. They were easy in comparison, easy to play, easy to enjoy, just...easy. I felt a little empty, defeated, and I felt bored. I bought Sekiro knowing it's different to the other games in the series thinking maybe this one's for me. It turned out to be the most difficult of the bunch and I didn't get too far lol. But a few months ago I re-downloaded Elden Ring (I had 3 hours on record), and gave it another shot. I had a beefier PC and I just felt the FOMO, because I knew it got amazing reviews. I stepped into the Lands Between and I was hooked. I failed for hours, I shut down the voice in my head saying "told you so", I shut down the rage, and I took a deep breath and went again and again. I beat the first boss and I felt an adrenaline run, this high that felt more powerful, more invigorating than my addiction. I beat the next boss, and the next and the next. I was hooked. I hooked on the process of beating them. I got to the end of the game in tears not only for the masterpiece this game is in story, gameplay, world building etc. but also my progression as a human being. I'd grown so much. I was in therapy for my health during this whole time and in every session I was relating my health to Elden Ring. I was obsessed, obsessed with the real life results. I felt purpose in areas I lacked purpose before. I tackled my issues like I tackled bosses. I learnt their weaknesses from failing again and again, I learnt openings, I learnt control, and patience. I wanted to beat this game (addiction) so hard I could beat anything else thrown my way. I've been clean for six months now and I am so filled with joy and hope. I know I spoke about mainly me in this review, but we already know about how amazing this game is, and I think it is important to share our experiences with it. I can definitively say this game is art, for the reasons listed above. This game is perfect and I will forever cherish my time with it, wishing only to experience it all again for the first time. Good luck, have fun. Don't you dare go hollow. julesy.

I tried to play this game 4 times on and off for about 3 years and finally, it clicked. Once I stopped being scared of losing runes and levelled up my Vigor and weapon early on, the game was a blast. PROS: The game rewards you for 1. Exploring, with a great number of useful items hidden in optional dungeons. 2. Attention to detail, such as reading the weapon and item descriptions, These often reveal useful hints and lore information. 3. Not button-mashing, with boss battles often requiring rhythmic timing and patience. Every button press has consequence as you really cannot panic roll or heal whenever you want. It is very fulfilling when you go up against a boss multiple times, learn all their combos, what not to do and finally beat them. Elden Ring: A Breathtaking Baptism of Fire A Masterpiece Reviewed from the Perspective of a Soulsborne Virgin For years, I avoided the "Souls" genre. The infamous reputation of punishing difficulty, unforgiving mechanics, and the dreaded "YOU DIED" screen kept me safely in my comfort zone. But the sheer gravitational pull of Elden Ring was impossible to ignore. I finally took the plunge, fully prepared for misery. What I found instead was one of the greatest, most awe-inspiring gaming experiences of my entire life. 🌍 The Lands Between: An Unrivaled Sense of Discovery From the very first moment you push open the heavy doors, step out into Limgrave, and witness the glowing, colossal Erdtree dominating the horizon, you realize this is no ordinary open world. Zero Hand-Holding: There are no cluttered minimaps, no endless checklists, and no GPS markers telling you where to go. You are guided purely by your own curiosity. Organic Exploration: See a bizarre, ruined castle on a distant cliff? You can go there. Stumble upon a hidden elevator in the woods? It might take you to an entirely breathtaking underground universe. The sense of genuine discovery is unmatched in modern gaming. ⚔️ The Crucible of Combat: Brutal, Fair, and Addictive Let’s address the elephant in the room: Yes, Elden Ring is incredibly hard. The enemies hit like freight trains, and the bosses will relentlessly test your reflexes and your sanity. But here is the secret that veteran Souls players know, and the profound lesson this game taught me: Death in Elden Ring is not a punishment; it is an education. Every time you die, you learn a new attack pattern. You learn when to dodge, when to block, and when to strike. The combat is weighty, deliberate, and requires your full attention. When you finally land that killing blow on a boss that has wiped the floor with you twenty times, the adrenaline rush and the sense of sheer, hard-earned triumph are absolute perfection. 🛡️ Why It’s the Perfect First "Souls" Game Previous games in this genre often trapped you in a narrow corridor with an impossible boss, forcing you to "git gud" or quit. Elden Ring fundamentally changes the formula by giving you the ultimate weapon: Freedom. The "Walk Away" Strategy: If a boss is destroying you, you don't have to smash your head against a brick wall. Simply summon your spectral steed, Torrent, ride off in the opposite direction, explore some dungeons, level up your stats, find a better sword, and come back as a demigod to exact your revenge. Spirit Ashes: The game introduces summonable spirit companions. Having a pack of spectral wolves or a legendary knight fight by your side is a massive help for beginners, taking the heat off you so you can heal or attack. Limitless Potential: Whether you want to be a massive armored tank swinging a sword the size of a car, or a squishy wizard blasting enemies with cosmic lasers from across the room, the game accommodates every single playstyle. 🏆 The Final Verdict Elden Ring didn't just teach me how to play a Soulsborne game; it completely rewired how I experience video games. It doesn't treat you like a child. It demands your respect, tests your perseverance, and rewards your bravery in ways no other game does. It is a dark, beautiful, and unforgettable masterpiece. Final Score: 10/10 – A generational leap in gaming. If you, like me, have been terrified to try a Souls game, let this be your sign. Step out of your comfort zone. Arise, Tarnished. The Lands Between are waiting for you.

Elden Ring (Elden Ring) is one of the most ambitious open-world action RPGs ever made. It takes the core “Souls” formula—methodical combat, challenging boss fights, and cryptic storytelling—and expands it into a vast open world that genuinely rewards curiosity. Exploration is the game’s biggest strength: stumbling onto hidden dungeons, optional bosses, or entirely new regions often feels organic rather than scripted, and the sense of discovery is consistently strong. Combat is deep, flexible, and highly customizable. Whether you prefer heavy melee builds, magic-focused playstyles, or hybrid setups, the game gives you meaningful tools to approach encounters in different ways. Boss fights are a major highlight, often visually spectacular and mechanically demanding in a way that feels rewarding once you learn them. The world design also supports experimentation, letting players tackle challenges in multiple orders rather than forcing a strict path. That said, Elden Ring isn’t without flaws. The difficulty can be uneven, with some bosses feeling dramatically harder or more polished than others. The open world, while impressive, can occasionally feel repetitive in its side content (similar dungeon layouts, reused bosses, etc.). And the game’s storytelling remains intentionally vague, which some players find immersive, but others find too opaque or emotionally distant. Overall, Elden Ring is a landmark game that successfully translates the Souls formula into a massive open world without losing its identity. It’s not perfect, but its sense of scale, freedom, and challenge makes it one of the most memorable RPGs in years.

# 🎮 Why *Elden Ring* is worth your time Imagine stepping into a massive, haunting fantasy world where **every hill hides a secret, every ruin tells a story, and every enemy could destroy you**—unless you outsmart it. That’s *Elden Ring*. Developed by FromSoftware and shaped with worldbuilding by George R. R. Martin, this game takes the brutal combat of *Dark Souls* and drops it into a **fully open world called the Lands Between**, where you can go almost anywhere from the start. ([Wikipedia][1]) It’s not just a game—it’s a **challenge, an exploration sandbox, and a mystery you slowly unravel**. --- # 🌍 The Core Experience (What You Actually Do) * Explore a **huge open world** on foot or horseback (your mount “Torrent”) * Fight enemies and bosses using **precise, skill-based combat** * Build your character however you want (magic, swords, stealth, hybrid, etc.) * Discover hidden dungeons, secrets, and lore without hand-holding * Optionally play **co-op or PvP** with other players ([Wikipedia][1]) There are no quest markers telling you what to do next—**you figure it out**. --- # 🔥 The Pros (Why people love it) ### 1. A truly massive, rewarding open world This isn’t filler content. Exploration constantly pays off with weapons, bosses, and secrets. ([GameScribe Daily][2]) You’re encouraged to wander—and you’re almost always rewarded. ### 2. Deep, satisfying combat Combat is **deliberate and skill-based**—timing, stamina, and positioning matter. ([TechRadar][3]) Every victory feels earned, not handed to you. ### 3. Huge build variety You can play however you want: * Heavy knight with a giant sword * Spell-casting mage * Agile rogue * Weird hybrid builds The flexibility is massive and replayable. ([Play Versus Games][4]) ### 4. Rich lore and atmosphere The story isn’t spoon-fed. Instead, you piece it together through: * Item descriptions * NPC dialogue * Environmental storytelling It creates a **mysterious, immersive vibe** unlike most games. ([GameScribe Daily][2]) ### 5. Tons of content There’s easily **100+ hours of gameplay**, with more than most players will ever fully complete. ([Trusted Reviews][5]) ### 6. Genuine sense of accomplishment Beating a boss in *Elden Ring* feels like: > “I earned this.” That emotional payoff is one of the game’s biggest selling points. --- # ⚠️ The Cons (What might turn you off) ### 1. It is HARD—very hard There’s no easy mode. You will die. A lot. That’s intentional design. ([Trusted Reviews][5]) ### 2. Minimal guidance The game barely explains: * Where to go * How quests work * What stats do New players can feel lost or overwhelmed. ([My Blog][6]) ### 3. Story is vague If you want a clear, cinematic narrative—you won’t get it. You have to **interpret and piece things together yourself**. ### 4. Some repetition in side content Not every dungeon or boss is unique—some reuse ideas or layouts. ([TechRadar][3]) ### 5. Occasional technical issues Minor performance hiccups or pop-in can happen, depending on platform. ([My Blog][6]) ### 6. Not very accessible * No difficulty settings * Limited accessibility features This can exclude more casual or time-limited players. ([My Blog][6]) --- # 🧠 Real Player Perspective (from the community) From Reddit, one player summed it up bluntly: > “The feeling of wonder and triumph… is like nothing else” ([Reddit][7]) But others note: * It can feel confusing or frustrating * Some bosses or systems feel unfair or unclear ([Reddit][8]) So yeah—it’s not universally loved. --- # 🏆 Final Pitch If you want a game that: * Respects your intelligence * Doesn’t hold your hand * Rewards persistence and curiosity * Gives you unforgettable “I DID IT” moments 👉 *Elden Ring* is one of the best modern RPGs ever made. But if you want: * Relaxed gameplay * Clear direction * Easy progression 👉 This might frustrate you more than entertain you. --- # 🎯 Bottom line **Buy it if:** You like challenge, exploration, and deep gameplay systems **Skip it if:** You hate dying, getting lost, or figuring things out yourself --- If you want, tell me what kind of games you usually like, and I’ll tell you straight up whether *Elden Ring* will click with you or not. If you’ve ever thought, “I’d love a game that humbles me, confuses me, and still makes me say ‘one more try’ at 2am,” then Elden Ring is basically your soulmate. This game drops you into a massive, mysterious world with almost zero hand-holding. There’s no “go here next!” flashing sign. Just vibes, danger, and the distant glow of a giant golden tree judging your life choices. You’ll wander, you’ll get lost, and you’ll absolutely walk into places you have no business being. And that’s kind of the magic. Combat feels incredible until it doesn’t, which usually means you just got flattened by a boss the size of a small building. Every defeat somehow feels like a lesson, even if that lesson is “maybe don’t roll off a cliff next time.” When you finally win, it’s not just satisfying. It’s victorious in a way most games can’t touch. The world design is honestly unreal. One minute you’re exploring peaceful fields, the next you’re in a nightmare dungeon wondering who approved this emotionally. And the bosses? Equal parts terrifying and cool, like you’re fighting living legends with anger issues. The only “downside” is that the game expects patience. If you want something easy and straightforward, this might test your sanity. But if you’re up for a challenge and love the feeling of slowly mastering something tough, it’s incredibly rewarding. Final verdict: Beautiful, brutal, confusing, and completely addictive. You will suffer. You will improve. You will keep playing anyway. ⭐ 10/10. Would get destroyed again.

The exploration is incredibly tedious thanks to how broad and depth-less the open world in. Content is highly repetitive and you really have to search every nook and cranny to find items that are potentially extremely useful. In prior Souls games there were a limited number of paths, but you could always expect a path to lead to something interesting, useful, challenging, or any combination of those. In this game the open world is just there to waste your time as you mindlessly slog through your 4th crypt that both looks, feels, and plays exactly like the last three in the hopes that this one drops something you might need Far too difficult compared to prior Souls games, and not in a way that I find engaging. Rather than demanding that you face challenges head on, the game throws absurd enemies in your way, then strongly encourages you to go around exploring the map until you can take down your opponent through mostly brute force. I got all the way to the sword-dog boss, couldn't beat him, then summoned and felt like I had cheated myself out of the legitimate souls experience and haven't been able to get back into it since. Sword-dog just had far too many attacks, extremely long sequences with small windows of opportunity for punishment or recovery, but summoning made it completely trivial because all the aggro got soaked up by my spare. Why do I have to pick between ferociously difficult or mind-numbing? The entire series was known for a hard, but fair philosophy that rewarded patience, and here we are with this stinker of a title I went back and played through the bulk of Dark Souls 3 with the impression that I had just grown tired of the series, but my enjoyment for it hasn't faded at all

What a weird game - exceptionally high highs, really low lows. If this is your first FromSoft game (as I imagine it was for a majority of its players), this game will be an undisputed masterpiece. For Soulsborne veterans, not so much. The game is still great, but its "merely" great. If you've played your fair share of FromSoft games, you will inevitably feel how derivative Elden Ring can feel. "What's this spell? Oh its literally Lightning Spear. Hey look, its the Claymore! Same moveset and everything. And this item? Ah its Red Tearstone ring with a different name". Elden Ring is essentially Dark Souls 3 with some of Dark Souls 2's design ideology, wearing a Breath of the Wild costume. The open world is a fun addition, but I personally don't think it adds anything exceptionally meaningful to the formula. Having to scrounge around for resources to craft a basic fire pot is not mechanically interesting enough to warrant the extra time wasted doing so when in previous games you can just buy them off a merchant. Then there's the balance. Of course brainless mongoloids will mindlessly yap about gitting gut (which is sometimes completely valid), but this ignores the problem the game has. Some builds will tremendously struggle and some will breeze through due to the design ideology of the enemies and bosses. Enemies are fast, often use ambushes, and have combos that can almost 100% to 0% you. This goes X2 for bosses. Late game bosses are caricatures of themselves - they have a stupid amount of HP, they are insanely fast, they jump around the map while you impotently try to catch up, they are almost always huge so that locking on while they do their anime dashes makes it hard to keep track, and they can easily combo you from full to dead unless you have 50+ Vigor. UGS enjoyers will struggle immensely, UGS + no summons is basically unviable. The game very much seems to have been designed with summons/co-op in mind, which can be either good or bad depending on your preference. The game at least looks phenomenal - not graphically, textures/effects/lightning basically haven't improved since DS3. The game looks incredible aesthetically. The Liurnia landscape is a painting (literally), and Nokron is one of the most breathtakingly beautiful spaces I have ever seen in a video game. The endings are underwhelming, but of course they are - that's GRRM's signature move. TL;DR - a masterpiece of normies, a pretty good if flawed entry for seasoned FromSoft players

Elden Ring is different from previous Souls games, but it as amazing - the developers achieved expanding the Souls gameplay fomula without destroying the core. If I had to describe the game in simple terms, I would say it is a bit like Dark Souls + Far Cry. There is a ton of exploration that gets rewarded, lots of POIs and map objectives and it all sits on top of the core Souls combat system. The game looks AMAZING, it is stylish and still keeps a dark and brooding atmosphere. The game is HUGE compared to other Souls games, there are so many placed to explore, they all look great and different and there is always something to find there - NPCs, bosses, loot, ... The first playthrough (whole map explored, most of the loot, almost all achivements) took my about 100hrs + ~30hrs for a NG+ playthrough to unlock all missing endings and do all NPC quest lines. The game brings a lot of QoL improvements compared to older Souls games, the gameplay overall is very smooth. Stakes of Marika alone save so much time and frustration. And there are some new features like Ashes of War, Spirit Summons and crafting. The music is good, but I would rank it below all 4 Soulsborne games, not by a lot, but still. A lot of the soundtracks are "generic epic music", but it has two or three special tracks. Bosses overall are more difficult compared to previous titles - the bosses are more aggressive and active and a lot of them have mutliple phases. The boss design in this game sometimes is quite lazy though and can be very frustrating: - Input reading - Unnaturally delayed attacks - Very, very long attack combos that leave very little time to attack yourself - Attack combos that look the same but add extra moves when it is convenient - Animation & stagger cancelling !!! The game was entirely completable with a purist solo melee-only build, but quite frustrating at several points. There is only one boss I didnt manage to beat on my first playthrough without using a Spirit Ash, but finally managed it on NG+ with the purist build after a dozen tries. And its not that the boss is just difficult, it is simply unfair (read issues above, especially the stagger cancelling is unheard of - the boss staggers, but cancels the stagger animation to instead hit you before you can finish your own attack trying to take advantage of the stagger - wtf). At the same time, the game is also completable for casuals and players new to the series - there are dozens of buffs that can be applied before and during a fight, there is a ton of strong ranged options and players can summon Spirit Ashes and other players for help. And this gets me to the few negative aspects (on top of some lazy boss design). While I applaud the effort to make the game more accessible to new players, I think the difference between using and not using the tools the game provides you with, is too big - there is just too much "possible" help in the game and it really trivializes most bosses - many bosses can be soloed by your summons. When I summoned a Spirit Ash for the aforementioned boss fight, I suddenly managed it first try, without changing anything else. The game feels less tight and a bit less well designed compares to other Souls games - towards the end the game started to drag a bit and a lot of map design decisions feel a bit random and less deliberate. But thats to be expected when the size of the game increased so much. And as always, there are some issues with input lag/ignoring, but combat overall feels very fluid and smooth. I cant really complain much, the game is amazing, almost perfect, Game of the Year 2022 was well deserved.

Elden Ring is one of those games that doesn’t try to impress you — it just throws you in and lets you figure things out on your own. There’s no proper direction, no step-by-step guide, and no one telling you what to do next. At the start, it feels confusing and a bit unfair, but slowly you begin to understand how everything works… and that’s when it clicks. You die a lot, you get stuck, and you question your build, but every time you come back a little better. And when you finally beat something that once felt impossible, it actually feels earned. The freedom is what makes it special. You can play however you want, build your character however you like, and explore at your own pace without being forced into a single path. The world is quiet, sometimes beautiful, sometimes unsettling, but always interesting — every area feels unique, and there’s always something hidden waiting to be discovered. It’s not an easy game, and definitely not for everyone, but if you stick with it, it becomes something unforgettable. After finishing everything, I can confidently say it’s one of the best games I’ve ever played.

Elden Ring is a good game. Extremely overrated and overhyped but still a good game. The game is praised for its open world but the world has nothing to offer besides Legacy Dungeons and pretty views. The rewards you often get for exploring is combat. You can't even use so many spells and weapons because your build doesn't allow for it. The starting open area is the best one but every thing that comes after is a dip in quality. The starting Legacy Dungeon is also the best and densest. FromSoftware's fixation on making everything vague just for the sake of it harms the game rather than making it more immersive, fun and enjoyable. Most of the time you are running across an open area hoping to find something good but again, all you are rewarded with is the beautiful art of this game and not something that immerses you in the world. Going from level-based game design to a fully fledged open world also requires you to add some interesting content in the open world. Hiding a large area that you accidentally found whilst exploring is fun until you realise that area had basically nothing and you just rode across your horse for a boss fight. There are so many areas with books scattered around so why can't I read them? Why do I always have to read item descriptions to understand what's going on? Those items often provide only a line or two worth of lore. This stupid game design needs to change if they are making an open world game. The smaller dungeons follow a very basic formula. You go in, explore until you find a lever, that lever unlocks the boss room, kill the boss. That boss you fight is either the easiest part of the dungeon or the most stupid enemy-type that ever graced your screen. Often times you can just trade blows with the boss but sometimes they put a boss which is too big for that arena, has no stagger or duo bosses which are not designed to be a duo. There really are no good small dungeon bosses in this game. The first Legacy Dungeon, Stormveil Castle, is the best one. The second one, Raya Lucaria, is also good but not as good as the first one. The third one, Volcano Manor, had a lot of potential but it's quite short. The fourth one, Leyndell, is huge but again, not a lot to do there except kill enemies or find something that doesn't go well with your build. The last one, Elphael, is also good but it's not close to Stormveil. There are no Legacy Dungeons (or at least they are not good enough to be called that) in two main areas. I am not too happy with the bosses in this game. Many ♥♥♥♥ bosses have been copy and pasted in different areas. You fight the same ♥♥♥♥ boss multiple times. I have no idea how they thought that THIS boss is good enough that players won't mind fighting them for the 5th time. Most of the main bosses are good and it's fun to learn their moveset but some bosses have complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ attacks and hitboxes. The first main boss you fight is infamous for his delayed attacks and relentless combos. I think DS3 found a really good balance between the player speed and the boss' speed but Elden Ring is more in favor of the bosses rather than the player. I don't enjoy dodging a 5-10 move combo for 5-10 seconds just to land one attack. There are not many dodge and attack windows in this game (unlike DS1 and DS3). You dodge, dodge, dodge, dodge, attack, dodge, dodge, attack. Not fun. All of this criticism doesn't mean the game isn't good or fun. I had a blast on both of my playthroughs but Elden Ring, in many ways, is a step back for FromSoftware and it not as great as everyone makes it out to be. One thing Elden Ring excels at is build variety. You have so many options to go for and change your playstyle. There are so many different types of weapons like swords, greatswords, colossal swords, daggers, katanas, whips, axes, greataxes, freaking perfume bottles, wands and even shields to play from. Not to mention all the cool armor sets you can mess around with to create a pretty unique looking character. Despite all the negativity in this review, I will still give Elden Ring a 8.5/10. It's a good game but not the pinnacle of open world games. Not even close to that.

This was my first Souls game ever, it had its ups and downs, cause this type of game is bound to tilt you sometimes, wether a hard boss or mechanics that you struggle with in particular, sometimes traps where a mob will push you off a cliff, etc. BUT, all in all, this was an amazing experience. The journey is awesome, i'm not a fan of the little mobs around to confront or elites, i much prefer the boss encounters but it's still fine and Elden Ring just allows you to mostly avoid all that, you can just skim pass riding Torrent or running sometimes. In my first playthrough I killed almost all bosses of the base game + dlc (in total i'm pretty sure i'm missing less than 10 bosses), ofc in a way this meant some bosses i found later, i was a bit overleveled making it a bit too easy but ye, I just wanted to "catch them all". It's a game you should really blindly explore and enjoy and don't stop just cause you get stuck at some boss, it can be frustrating, just go do something else, explore a different zone, take a break, because after killing it, the more you struggled the more you enjoy the fact you passed that obstacle. This was pure yap, just play the game, it's a 10/10, not the hardest souls game according to the genre veterans but if you're new to that type of games, this is one of the best experiences for a new souls gamer. Some other details: - Lore: It's okay, it's not bad but a bit confusing sometimes and A LOT of it, has tidbits in quests, bosses, scrolls, making it a bit complex, it's nothing crazy but I still think it's a pretty nice supporting plot for the game and with enough important secrets for the lovers of lore diving, there's a lot of good youtube videos that expose you to the deeper lore of the game and they're a nice watch - Graphics: the view is amazing, you feel how giant the world is, insane sized areas with massive structures, one of them pretty early in the game, it's very good for players who love "old fantasy aesthetics", everything is really beautiful, bosses designs also, the weapons, "arenas", legit everything - Audio: Just like the massive feel of the world, the soundtrack also gives that idea, with a very "epic" feel to it, one of the best games in this regard also, it's pure joy - Performance: Super fine for when I started playing it (was a decent time after release I guess, like 2y after?) and my PC is already super old CPU wise (Intel 6700) with a good GPU (AMD 7800 XT), there were maybe 1 or 2 zones and bosses where the visual effects would tank my FPS a bit but since that was pretty rare, it was wtv, plus again, my fault having such an old CPU. - Bad stuff i can remember: Questing in this game is definitely a bit of a challenge sometimes, for the main importanty storyline I think it's fine, but for side quests it's hard to know what to do sometimes or how can affect rewards or outcomes, sometimes I just used google, didn't really ruin my experience but something to keep in mind Think that's about it, just play the game, it's awesome and gives you a good amount of hours, especially if you buy during sales. The game is not terrible but it is just not good enough. I 100% all Dark Souls/Sekiro games and as a successor to this franchise it is exhausting, boring, it feels off. What is dislike: - The main selling point - the open world - is actually its biggest flaw. Everything i remember in a positive way are the legacy dungeons like Stormveil Castle which is a closed off area that has nothing to do with the open world. It was fun exploring, but riding through generic forests or small castles or mini dungeon etc. is so boring, you just run past everything. Stop with the open worlds, you have nothing to tell, nothing to fill it with, it is not "a revolution in gaming", stop it. - 90% of the items you find are useless, it feels underwhelming to explore anything after 20 hours ingame - Too many recycled bosses (that giant space mantis whatever at the end of that one cave had me laughing, absolutely terrible decision to reuse that boss) - The camera is a disaster again. It is the - I dont know - maybe 7th iteration of this kind of game and camera still sucks like in the first Dark Souls. Make walls transparent when you are forced into a corner and move the camera back, make the camera zoom out when fighting giant bosses, I want to see more than a foot of the enemy, I must know what he is about to do. I know what my character does, I do not have to see him up close. - Generally too many giant bosses, too many dragons, towards the end of the game they put 2 dragons in an area and to top it off, another optional boss battle - a dragon - yay! Sorry but fighting a dragon in an action game has always been terrible. It is no fun, it is meant to be fought with heavy machinery or something, not in a sword fight. Stop making 1 on 1 dragon vs human fights every 2 hours. It is exhausting. Put one dragon fight in there and make it special, not generic. - A lot of the bosses have too long combos and they also change up the attack patterns so I cannot really learn the boss because the openings are sometimes there, sometimes not, so I always have to assume there is no opening to get a hit or two in. It felt more of a gamble most of the time, or trading blows - The balance is off. I wanted to solo the game and I did until the late game super bosses, there I was stuck and after a few attempts I tried summoning spirits for the first time. It was ridiculous, it made the game so easy that I beat almost every boss from that point forth first or second try. Having a companion is too overpowered but solo it felt impossible (e.g.: one boss turns the arena in a constant bleed build up, solo I felt there was no way as a melee class to do this fight. Maybe with more practice it is possible but I felt too tired to try it more often solo) - There are so many checkpoints in the world so they had to turn up the damage of common enemies. Some generic dog in the late game area hits you? Say goodbye to half of your health bar. Just run past everything until you find the next checkpoint - Too many convoluted questlines intertwined with eachother. Do not talk to this guy if you have not spoken with this guy somewhere in the south and before killing that boss! Annoying, exhausting. Dark souls had this too but it felt more possible because the characters appeared at locations you definetely come across and in order. Yeah open world ruins this too. - Crafting is such a weird mechanic in the game. It is nice to have but you do not need it at all but because of crafting there are thousands of worthless items to collect in the world. Mushrooms, berries, twigs... sorry but just a waste of time again. Why should I create a firebomb if I can just run up to the enemy and punch him in the face? - I used an Xbox 360 controller and the input delay was bad. The game had a real problem with accepting new inputs from me in fast fights. Lets say I used a heavy attack with a long attack animation and then pressed the button for heal during the attack animation but then realize "oh no, I cant heal i need to roll" so I keep spamming roll the game still thinks I want to heal although there were at least 3 new "roll" inputs after the heal input. - I do not want to spoil but the final boss is the perfect metaphor for this game: boring and generic - even the name. What I liked: + The first 20 hours of the game felt great, gearing up, exploring two legacy dungeons. After that it went downhill fast. + Music is alright I guess + Many builds, weapons, spells and armors available + Some decent and memorable boss battles (but not too many) + The hitboxes are actually not that bad, I remember them being quite bad in the Dark Souls series but they have improved, not a lot of instances when I thought that an attack should have hit or not have hit me + The scenery and cutscenes can be nice to look at I still have to play the DLC but I cannot bring myself to play it, I am burnt out, bored.

Anywhere you go, there is something to find, a vista to enjoy, and a story to piece together, if you care to. One of the things I enjoy about Fromsoft games when I first played DS2 was finding hidden routes, new areas, and quests that I never even thought to look for or was oblivious to the whole time. That has never been more true than in this game. You can think you know this game inside and out, and then you'll be like me and stumble across an entire area that you never even knew was there. I also at times found myself thinking "man, as gorgeous as this game is, some of these areas only have a few bodies and a mushroom or two..." and then if you care to look closer you'll find a story in the arrangement of the bodies, the other items around, and also begin to enjoy the open areas that are serene in their existence, as horrifying as some are. Because while you are fit to become the Elden Lord, the universe does not care about you, and this land has existed for millennia longer than you, but may not last much longer after. You are at the tail end of the world-shaping history of this land, and while the pretty settings and grandeur are staggering... This world is old. It has been built upon centuries beyond centuries of kingdoms and nature and gods and goddesses and fighting and celestial conflict. You are but a speck in the glory of Grace and its many enemies. I like making a battlemage, using a shield and sword and yet also wielding some of the most powerful spells known to Tarnished. I love this game and look forward to trying out many others of the hundreds of possibilities for a build in my future hours. For all the praises I will lavish upon this game, the horse mechanics are just almost not perfect. They work amazingly most of the time, until you're in a fight and suddenly Torrent just *poofs* out from under you, landing you on your back and getting you killed. If you somehow survive, you can call him again... and he's obviously not dead. You don't even have to use a flask 9 times out of 10 to summon him after he disappears. And this poofing he does makes the whole Rowa fruit mechanic to feed fruit to Torrent actually pointless and proving that for everything they nailed, some things were just not executed well, and it's sad they made it through to the final product. Of course Torrent deserves all the berries, but the mechanic itself was described as decidedly combat-focused and not immersion. By the Guidance of Grace, I found the will to fight. May you also take up the call to become the Ruler of All that is Golden, the Elden Lord.

This game is honestly one of the most immersive open-world games I’ve ever played. The exploration feels very natural and not forced at all, because the game doesn’t constantly guide you. Instead, you’re encouraged to discover things on your own, and that makes every finding feel more meaningful—whether it’s a hidden dungeon, a strong enemy, or just a really beautiful environment. What stands out the most for me is the boss fights. They are challenging and sometimes frustrating, but that’s exactly what makes them memorable. The music during these fights plays a huge role—it builds tension and often gives goosebumps, making the whole experience feel more intense and cinematic. The combat system also requires patience and adaptation. At first it can feel difficult, but over time you start to understand the mechanics and improve your skills. This creates a strong sense of achievement whenever you overcome a tough challenge. Overall, Elden Ring delivers a complete experience: - engaging gameplay - a vast and detailed world, - and an unforgettable atmosphere. It’s the kind of game that not only entertains but also leaves a lasting impression. 100000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000000/10

It’s a work of art – one that is bold, brilliantly executed, and deeply rewarding at every turn. Calling it a game would be like calling the Sistine Chapel a building. The first time you walk into the Lands Between, the world FromSoftware has built takes your breath away. Gold fields, volcanoes, crystal caves, swamps, a coliseum in the sky – all set in this magical land. Every biome is a painter’s dream. Every inch of this massive world is filled with secrets, secrets hidden behind every cliff, every crumbling ruin, every hidden underground passage. The story of the Lands Between is the story of the archaeologist. The tale is told in pieces and shards. It is a puzzle for players to assemble, and an epic and heartbreaking myth as compelling as any you’d find in Greek literature. We’ve known what open-world games were. Maps full of icons, waypoints and linear objectives leading to the next big moment. Elden Ring isn’t that game. There are no quest markers, no arrows on the minimap. It’s your journey. Two people could play 100 hours in the Lands Between and have completely different stories. I love that. The best part is it scales problems to curiosity. It trusts the player completely. I can't think of a game that does that these days. It is a game where every battle is a conversation. A timing, a positioning, a patience. Bosses are not just hurdles to jump over. They are dances to learn. The Margit that kills you 20 times becomes your dance partner and you learn the rhythm of the dance on the 21st time. Few media give you that sense of achievement when you finally get a challenge. You’ll have more arrows in your quiver, Ashes of War, sorceries and incantations, but Elden Ring is arguably the most expressive and accessible FromSoftware game to date, while still retaining that difficulty. "Boss Design as High Art" “Radahn, the Starscourge,” a knight so powerful that he holds the stars in place with gravity sorcery, rides across a beach as a symphony of guitars and violins fills the heavens. “Malenia, Blade of Miquella,” might be the most technically demanding and artistically beautiful boss ever dreamed up. Maliketh, Morgott, and Rennala aren’t just enemies; they are stories, tragedies, and secrets. The encounters aren’t just hard, but they’re also heart-wrenching. The game is a hit, but it’s also created a culture. The asynchronous multiplayer aspects of messages inscribed on the dungeon floors and the ghostly presence of other players means that your lonely adventure isn’t a lonely adventure. And the DLC expansions like Shadow of the Erdtree show it’s not a ceiling, but a foundation. For many, it’s the best DLC in gaming. Elden Ring is bold, beautiful, hard and deeply moving. It doesn’t coddle the player. Instead, it delivers one of the most immersive and emotionally satisfying experiences interactive art has ever delivered. It’s not just the best game of its generation. It sets a standard for all future games that will be judged by it for years to come. 10. Absolutely perfect. And then some.

Definitely the greatest game I’ve ever played. I’ve put more hours into it than any other game I own, and it almost always has something new to show me. Just the other day despite being on NG+13 I discovered that you can use a telescope in Limgrave and several other zones to get a bird’s‑eye view of the area. I have no idea how I overlooked that for so long, but I did. I even found a super weak Deathrite Bird or whatever it’s called in Liurnia that I somehow missed twelve times in a row. I’m only mentioning this so that anyone who hasn’t played yet understands just how much game there is to play. There’s a bit of a learning curve for newcomers, but the game does a great job teaching you the basics in the first zone. It shows you the core controls, subtly guides you with eye‑catching landmarks and architecture, teaches you how to find map fragments without treating you like an idiot, introduces NPCs without forcing unskippable dialogue, and gives you the freedom to go wherever you want without punishing you for doing side content instead of the main story. It’s also one of the few games I’ve played that genuinely rewards curiosity and punishes it just as often. One chest might give you a useful item, while another might teleport you to a cave across the map. Sometimes that glowing blue item at the end of a corridor really is that easy to grab, and other times the floor collapses right before you reach it. There are plenty of surprises and unexpected events, and there’s a ton of fun gameplay for just about any preferred playstyle. There’s lots of room for experimentation and an abundance of items, armor, and weapons to discover. I could go on for hours about the creatures, environments, spells, incantations, the subtle lore hidden in item descriptions, and the overall worldbuilding. If anything I’ve mentioned sounds appealing, then I think you should give it a try.

Main run was a bloodhound fang dex build which I tried my best to clear every corner of the map, I'm pretty sure I cleared every cave, dungeon, side boss, etc. I used the elden ring wiki and the story map progressions online to help make sure I wasn't missing anything. Is it a perfect game? No. Is it peak Souls experience (apart from extra value added by other Souls games because of personal nostalgia)? Yes. Death is common and yet Death is not punishing. The game provides maximum freedom for players to explore and also control their builds and destiny. The game's movement mechanics are probably the weakest element but the combat is refined and rewarding. The community will note that this game has some very specific "smart boss" mechanics that are very challenging and you will need to learn how to cope with them. It is, however, 100% possible to learn to cope with them with a little time and patience (which, after all, is what these games are all about). And let's not forget the best part: This is a stunningly beautiful game! Even at 300+ hours of playtime I'm still in awe over how beautiful the game is. If you like Souls games, then you should play this one. If you don't like Souls games but you want to play it anyway then do it. If you are unsure, then do it.

I really want to like Elden Ring as I loved the Souls series and I have tried many times to like it but it has so many issues that I personally have with it that make it not click with me like Demon's Souls or Dark Souls did. I think my biggest problems are that the open world while it seems cool just doesnt work with Elden Ring so well, if you explore it with no direction, you can end up in areas that feel just straight up unfair and it can be really frustrating to find where you are supposed to go at whatever level you may be at and sometimes you just have to wonder if its a skill issue or if you are genuinely in the wrong place. Ontop of this, if you are a completionist like I am with souls games then it can be really hard to find bosses or areas that you may have missed without needing to pull up a guide every 5 minutes which just feels annoying and tedious for no reason. Another big problem I have with the game is that the boss designs are just horrid. It feels like they upped the speed of the bosses since Dark Souls 3 to match how quick they were in Sekiro, but the problem with that is that in Sekiro, players were given a parry to avoid damage and tools to exploit any bosses weaknesses, in Elden Ring, you are given nothing to help and while majority of the bosses arent too bad with how spammy they are, they have other issues. Some are way too overused, some are just straight up stupid gimmick fights and some are just straight up boring. Its hard to find bosses in Elden Ring where I sat there and thought to myself "okay this was actually good" Another issue I have with Elden Ring is the fact that base game co-op is straight up just unplayable and takes away many features without using the seamless co-op mod, they disable your horse in base game and block off a lot of areas so that open world that was a big selling point of the game is just completely gone if you are like me and are someone who loves exploring open world games with others. Its not all bad though, Elden Ring has some very gorgeous places and backdrops and I genuinely think that the amount of content you get is wholeheartedly worth the full price of the game even if you just played it once. Some of the characters have some very interesting storylines and the replayability is really high with how many weapons, builds and ending you can get. And thats not even counting the DLC. All and all, I think that Elden Ring is a DECENT game, but I will NEVER understand how people glaze it and say its the best game of all time or anything like that, and if I could I would leave a maybe review but I cant and I personally dont like the game and don't think it lives up to the scores it has or the hype around it.

My review of Elden Ring After 100 hours!!! And after completing the game 100% I can say it’s not just a game — it’s a legendary masterpiece! At the very least, it’s a complete game. A world with this level of beauty, scale, depth, and visual variety — from lush, green natural lands to desert regions and volcanic areas, from snowy realms and dragon-infested worlds to even an underground world. From the moment you enter the game, you realize you’re standing before the greatest game of the century — perhaps even the greatest thing ever created in gaming. The world design is carefully crafted and precise, but nothing surpasses the mastery and precision of the boss fights. Literally, Souls games are the only ones that have perfected boss combat — where you must memorize the boss’s moves, learn their fighting style, and master dodging with the correct timing. And since we mentioned timing, how can we not bring up parrying with shields — a unique and excellent feature in Souls / Souls-like games. The story has a depth that pulls you into deep thought, and the soundtracks transport you to another world, making the experience even more incredible. The variety of weapons — from magic, swords, bows, and spears — along with the diversity of skills (Ashes of War), adds even more richness. By the way, the game isn’t primarily based on magic, yet it contains hundreds of spells — meaning it even surpasses games that are built around magic, like Hogwarts Legacy. I don’t even know how to describe the greatness of the bosses to you. You’ll face some of the greatest bosses in Souls games — I’m talking about General Radahn, the Starscourge, descendant of war, the Red Lion, breaker of kings, shedder of blood. And I’m talking about Malenia, Lady of the Sword, the undefeated Blade of Miquella, the lone flower of the Elden. And not to mention Godfrey, the first Elden Lord, warrior of kings, breaker of thrones, the White Lion, the embodiment of raw power. The game is difficult and gives you nothing easily, but it rewards every effort you put in and every skill you learn. Every step is calculated, every decision carries weight, every moment is full of excitement, and every minute you spend in the game is a unique experience. Elden Ring is the crown of gaming. It doesn’t just deserve Game of the Year — it deserves Game of the Century. They made this masterpiece in just 5 years, which is honestly insane. Even the biggest studios couldn’t pull off something like this in that time. And yeah, I don’t regret spending a single penny on this game. Thanks, FromSoftware.

[h1] Elden Ring is a masterpiece, and even thought it is not perfect, deserves your time. [/h1] The experience of going through this magical land where every landmark is an actual place you can visit, explore, and earn amazing rewards from, it has no rival, and I loved every second of it. It is a difficult game, and the balance is somewhat inconsistent. There are noticeable discrepancies between items, enemies, bosses, and weapons. The game has an insane difficulty spike toward the end (the Mountaintops of the Giants had me wondering if I had some kind of debuff), and the fact that the final stretch includes repeated bosses or multiple bosses at once takes away from what should have been a truly amazing ending to such a rich story. And with all of that in mind... I still cannot recommend this game enough. Please give it a try; the exploration, the bosses, the lore, the environment, and the world where everything takes place all deserve your time. Thank you, FromSoftware, for such an incredible experience.

It’s hard to overstate just how completely Elden Ring redefined what a modern open-world game can feel like, because it doesn’t just hand you a map full of checklist objectives—it trusts you to get lost, to struggle, and to discover things on your own terms, which makes every victory feel genuinely earned rather than scripted. The world itself feels ancient and indifferent, filled with haunting landscapes, cryptic lore, and enemies that don’t scale to your comfort level, so when you finally overcome a brutal boss or piece together a fragment of the story, it sticks with you in a way most games can’t replicate. What really elevates it is the balance between freedom and challenge: you can wander off in any direction, build your character however you want, experiment with weapons, magic, or sheer stubborn persistence, and the game never punishes creativity—it rewards it. At the same time, it maintains that signature tension where even a small mistake can cost you everything, which keeps you fully engaged instead of coasting. There’s also something special about the quiet moments, like riding through a golden field at sunset or stumbling into a hidden underground city you never knew existed, that give the experience a sense of awe and mystery that few games achieve. It respects your intelligence, your patience, and your curiosity all at once, and that combination—freedom, difficulty, atmosphere, and player-driven storytelling—is what makes it feel less like just a game and more like a personal journey, which is why I consider it the best of all time.

[h1]For My First FromSoftware Title, quite the journey. 9/10[/h1] The FromSoftware games were always something I had always wanted to play, but never really got the chance to. They are games that I have always watched people play, whose lore I have occasionally watched, but whose Soulslikes such as Code Vein, Blasphemous, and Hollow Knight/Silksong were what I generally played. I am overall fairly familiar with the many... [i]quirks[/i] these games provide, and it was only because this game was a gift that I was able to play this game. This makes it my first ever FromSoftware title. At the time of writing, I do not own the DLC for this game. I mainly played Offline, and only really turned on Online Mode to see funny messages and to complete a couple of side quests. So where does that leave me? At the time of writing I have just beaten the final boss of the game and achieved the [spoiler]The Age of Stars[/spoiler] ending. The Stat Spread at the end of my playthrough are as follows (these are with certain kinds of gear you will find throughout your playthrough): [list] [*]Level 136 [*]Vigor 55 [*]Mind 13 [*]Endurance 41 [*]Strength 65 [*]Dexterity 20 [*]Intelligence 10 [*]Faith 21 [*]Arcane 10 [/list] So Elden Ring could be summarized as Dark Souls, but Open-World. The Lands Between had some extremely beautiful locations, challenging bosses, and [i]so[/i] many secrets to find that I wasn't able to find them all in my first playthrough. I also generally played on High Settings, and only experienced stuttering in the late game areas and 2 bosses. Only had 1 game crash, 60hrs in. I went with primarily a Strength, Dex, build in the early game; but late game I basically messed around with Strength, Dex, and Faith. I do like using summons, and did so for pretty much every important boss fight in the game, yet I did not equip a single spell or incantation. I didn't use an Ash of War until the 70hr mark (around level 80 for me) and the flask that gives buffs until basically 90hrs in (level 130). By base game standards and talking with peers, I was pretty overleveled for dealing with the final boss; ending at level 136. My starting class was the Wretched Class, so I started at level 1 and all of my stats were 10. No armor, and only a club. I figured this would give me an unbiased look at the game instead of gearing me to a specific playstyle as I had no idea how or when I could respec my stats. I can say with confidence that I have a massive skill issue when it comes to recognizing enemy attack patterns, dodge rolling, and parrying. I basically fell for every single feint the bosses did and several of them took at least 10 attempts to complete. Yet through the power of perseverance, summons, and being over-leveled it is certainly possible to complete the base game. This is most certainly a game that is not for everyone, but I think one's ability to stick with it would provide an incredible experience. I only really have 2 major issues with this game: [list] [*]Not being able to fast travel out of Catacomb/Cave system sucks. Generally, I had found myself dying in these, but I always had to walk out of them. Sometimes these underground areas are the closest Fast Travel Point to where I want to go; but this usually means that I had to wait for an elevator to come down, then ride it all the way back up only to then fast travel. [*]The overworld map needed to have more layers to it. Several Fast Travel Points are technically underground or indoors despite being on the overworld map, and I had frequently gotten mixed up with which points I wanted to go. In general, I do wish the maps also showcased interiors; but I am sure that is just a me thing. [/list] If I had to give some tips for newcomers, it would be the following: [list] [*]Don't be afraid to run away from a fight [*]Not every boss is required to beat the game [*]Explore to your heart's content [*]Don't be afraid to look up some things like item locations or dungeon navigations. [*]Summons are cool to use and don't be discouraged by other people you call you bad for using them. This is a mainly single player experience, and you get to decide how to play it. [/list]

Elden Ring is not just a game—it is a landmark achievement in modern game design, a culmination of decades of refinement in action RPG mechanics blended with an unparalleled sense of discovery. From the very first moment you step into the Lands Between, the game establishes a tone of mystery, scale, and quiet grandeur that few titles in gaming history have ever matched. It doesn’t hold your hand, it doesn’t bombard you with instructions, and it certainly doesn’t rush you. Instead, it trusts you—and that trust is what makes the experience so powerful. At its core, Elden Ring succeeds because of its open-world design. Unlike many open-world games that feel bloated with repetitive tasks and markers, Elden Ring’s world is dense with meaning. Every ruin on the horizon, every strange structure tucked into a cliffside, every glowing item in the distance feels intentional. Exploration is not a checklist—it’s a genuine adventure. You are not guided by quest logs or GPS markers, but by curiosity. That sense of organic exploration brings back a feeling that many players haven’t experienced since childhood: the thrill of not knowing what lies ahead. The combat system is another pillar of its greatness. It builds on the precise, punishing mechanics that FromSoftware has perfected over the years, but expands them with greater flexibility and creativity. Whether you prefer heavy melee weapons, agile dexterity builds, powerful sorceries, or hybrid playstyles, Elden Ring allows you to shape your character in meaningful ways. Every enemy encounter feels deliberate, and every victory feels earned. The difficulty is often discussed, but what truly defines it is fairness—when you fail, you understand why, and when you succeed, it’s because you adapted and improved. Then there are the bosses—arguably some of the most memorable encounters in gaming. Each one feels like a test, not just of skill, but of patience and observation. They are visually stunning, mechanically diverse, and emotionally impactful. Some feel tragic, others terrifying, and a few even awe-inspiring. The game doesn’t just throw obstacles at you; it presents challenges that feel like legends within the world itself. The atmosphere and world-building elevate Elden Ring even further. The Lands Between feel ancient, broken, and layered with history. There is a sense that everything you see has a story behind it, even if it’s not immediately explained. The game’s storytelling is subtle and environmental, encouraging players to piece together the lore through item descriptions, dialogue, and observation. This approach respects the player’s intelligence and rewards those who choose to dive deeper. Visually, the game is breathtaking—not necessarily because of cutting-edge graphics, but because of its art direction. From golden fields bathed in sunlight to haunting underground cities lit by ghostly stars, every area feels distinct and memorable. The soundtrack complements this perfectly, shifting from quiet, ambient tones during exploration to intense, dramatic compositions during boss fights. What truly sets Elden Ring apart, however, is how all of these elements come together into a cohesive experience. It is not just a collection of great systems—it is a world that feels alive, mysterious, and worth investing in. It respects the player’s time, intelligence, and curiosity in a way that few modern games do. In an industry often driven by trends and formulas, Elden Ring stands as a bold reminder of what games can be when developers prioritize vision and craftsmanship. It doesn’t try to appeal to everyone in a conventional way; instead, it commits fully to its identity—and in doing so, it becomes something extraordinary. Elden Ring is not just one of the best games of its generation—it is a defining moment in gaming history. A rare masterpiece that will be remembered, studied, and celebrated for years to come.
