Sat down and realized I somehow haven't wrote a review about how good this game is. Probably because it seemed like such a tall order to talk about everything that makes this game good, so instead, I'll try to just hit the major beats. Elden Ring is Miyazaki/Fromsoft's Mangum Opus. Everything they learned from making the Soulsbourne series perfected and planted into a MASSIVE open-world. The first playthrough alone could take a Souls veteran 100+ hours to complete if you want to explore all the areas and side quests. I myself have only done about 4 playthroughs plus the DLC experience and I still find myself coming back to play bits and pieces here and there but I find replaying through the entire game something that I'm not usually willing to put time into. If you've never played a Fromsoft/Souls-like game you might not want to start with this one. The mechanics and quests are intricate and run DEEP you'll find yourself looking at a guide or the wiki for every single thing. I personally hope that the next installment is a smaller more linear experience similar to Dark Souls but set in the same universe, though I would not complain about another open world again. Regardless, if you have the time to commit to learning this game or are already a souls-like player then I think there is insane value here. Just about every aspect of this game is phenomenal. Music, graphics, sound design, gameplay, lore, depth, variety, environment, co-op. The only aspect of this game that I see complaints about is the level of difficulty, especially in the DLC and especially if you're on NG+ like I was. To wrap it up, Elden Ring is in my opinion one of the best fantasy/RPG games ever made and there's maybe even a case for it being one of the best games of all time.

This game is the absolute manifestation of perfection in gaming. As a fairly new player to the souls-like genre, I was worried initially. Not that I wouldn't like the game, I was rather worried about mechanical confusion. I was worried about the fact that I couldn't understand the game. This primarily stems from the fact that the lack of guidance can be problematic. That doesn't mean I want the game to literally take me by my hand and lead me to the ending, but complete lack of guidance makes the game less enjoyable for me. Elden Ring balances this perfectly. Yes, there were some things that required research, mainly new mechanics, but the guidance is firm and telling enough to give me breathing space. The game clearly tells you "go in that direction, and you will progress in some way", and then hints at what is optional. Its not written anywhere clearly, like in a quest log, but there are subtle and simple ways of guiding you that do not spoil you the game. Something that should also be noted is the method of storytelling. I had to learn this externally, but the game does not "tell a story" through collectibles, which is boring. The game tells a story by the environment. Almost everything in this game has a reason for its location, appearance, and behavior. Bosses tend resemble their personalities in the way they move, attack, speak, everything. The environment is shaped in such ways to tell a story. An NPC being concealed doesn't have to be just a visual decision, it can resemble something deeper and important. Not a lot of games take it to such a depth and often things looks the way "just because they were designed that way". A knight can have a very consistent pattern of attacking that does not change, because it literally "keeps calm". A teacher can test you, be consistent, and incredibly calm, but then once you fight his "real self", he throws away the composure, and becomes much more violent and desperate. The game does not have a perfectly linear gameplay, but it does not fail at "telling where is the main progress" either. if a fight feels too hard, you should come back later once you are stronger. Or you can switch up your strategy and lure the enemy somewhere. Weapons are not perfectly universal, and tend to have specific uses for specific situations. So holding onto one single weapon is not very ideal here, because experimenting is rewarded. A common complaint I see is the difficulty of this game. And I agree this game is difficult, but there is also a clear distinction between "difficult, because RNG", and "difficult, because of complex mechanics". there are games that are difficult only because of RNG, meaning you barely control the outcomes, the random elements do instead. These games tend to be much more frustrating, because you can learn only a very limited range of things, because there is so much outside of your control. But here? The game is not difficult, because of a ton of elements that you basically cannot control. The game is difficult, because of mechanical complexity. Bossfights, for example, are difficult, because you need to learn patterns. Learn patterns, recovery windows, read the enemy movement, tune your equipment,... Each death that happens has a clear reason. If you happen to die, you always know why and what killed you. The visual clarity is strong enough that you notice it and physically see it. This is the type of difficulty that is much less random and actually is fair. A boss can be extreme hard, but still can be extremely fun, even if you repeatedly die over and over. You never have to deal with the boss being extremely random and unpredictable. This is the closes to a skill-based game you can ever get. Yes, there are downsides. Especially in the engine. The game is obviously meant to be played with a controller, and on a console. That does not mean its unplayable on a keyboard, I would say the experience is pretty okay, but some keybinds can feel weird, and you may need to change them. The game is also permanently locked at 60fps, so your 1000hz monitor is useless here. And while unlocking it is possible, it can have some unpredictable outcomes, like some animations breaking, or acting weirdly. Not to mention that the engine is not really suited to hyper-optimize games. Foliage can be an issue, mainly around forests and trees. It can lower your fps on high settings, despite having capable hardware. I would also enjoy a bit better explanations of some systems. Not to necessarily add new explanations to gameplay mechanics, but to rather make the existing ones more clear and understandable. In the end I would say that the game is absolutely amazing. Its not often that I get so excited from games, and this one really made me enjoy gaming the same way when I was a young kid completely new to gaming. The price is a little high with small sales, but I would say its definitely worth it!

Do not expect this to be "open-world Dark Souls". It has excellent soulslike levels, with a vast emptiness between - the rest is between Skyrim and Shadow of the Colossus. Combat speed sometimes goes overboard, and some monsters are beyond grotesque (giant ants. Whose idea was it to make them this realistic?? And don't get me started on Colossal Fingercreeper). But guard counter is as satisfying 80 hours in as it was the first time. Overall, the combat lacks polish - enemies hit you through walls and pillars, there are no plunge attacks. It works well when it does, but enemy design quite often draws it back. On the bright side, there's a hand cannon. And crossbows are finally functional. Open-world nature of this game clashes violently with its DS1-style quest structure - so if you meet a character you think has a quest, read online where to meet them next. There is exactly one quest in the game where rewards tell you where next. Quite a few things feel videogamey - every Ruin has exactly one(1) treasure chest. But then there's lore, and aesthetic, and all the actually good areas (though those start rather late).

No hyperbole this is best game ever made, certainly my favorite game of all time. You get a quite possibly one of the biggest worlds to explore with TONS of interesting things to do and see, hundreds of weapons and builds to experiment with, amazing bosses that feel just right in terms of difficulty, and just an incredible, almost magical sense of atmosphere and scope on top of a great story with memorable characters, twists and turns, and hype moments. All of that, and the DLC manages to push the game even further, from one of the greatest games already to one of the best pieces of media of all time. It combines everything great from every other Fromsoftware game into one creating an almost best of their previous endeavors. (The stealth from Sekiro, expanded version of the world exploration of Dark Souls 2, atmosphere and fast paced combat of Bloodborne and Dark Souls 3, and the quieter more subdued feeling of Dark Souls 1 and Demon Souls) If my hours in it weren't enough to tell you, I love this game, and if you're just getting into Souls games, Elden Ring and it's DLC make for a great starting point. I also think this is one of the easier Soulsborne games too. There's multiple ways to break the game an hour in, some builds are totally busted and make the game a cake walk (Iron Ball *cough cough*) and the checkpoints before some bosses are way more forgiving than they were in the other Ssoulsborne games too. Highly HIGHLY recommended, 10/10, a real work of art in every sense of the word.

An Absolute Beast: Fun! Die! Fun! Die! Elden Ring is an absolute beast of a game. Fun! Die! Fun! Die! That's the cycle, and I wouldn't have it any other way. There are literally 100 different ways to play this game. Whether you want to be a tanky strength bonk lord, a flashy mage raining death from afar, a dex bleed ninja, or some unhinged faith/incantation build — the game supports it all. The build variety and freedom keep it fresh even after dozens of hours.I killed way too many rats hunting for Rune Arcs (seriously, those little bastards became my personal nemesis), but other than that... no real grind. No tedious farming sessions that suck the soul out of you. You can just explore, fight, and level up naturally as you go. Some of the "easiest" moments were actually the hardest. And don't even get me started on gravity — that invisible boss has killed me more times than any actual enemy in the Souls series. Falling off cliffs, ledges, or just misjudging a jump in the middle of nowhere... classic. The world is massive and packed with secrets. Every new area feels like a discovery, and the boss fights range from "holy crap this is beautiful" to "I want to throw my controller." The open-world freedom means you can completely avoid (or come back way overleveled for) the things that frustrate you. If you're into challenging action RPGs with insane replayability, breathtaking exploration, and that sweet "I finally beat it" dopamine hit after dying 10 times, this is peak gaming. Just be ready to laugh at your own deaths — especially the ones caused by the environment. Highly Recommended. 10/10 Best game I've ever played. Not even close. Miyazaki built something that doesn't feel like a game sometimes. The world is connected in a way that makes you feel like you're discovering something real. You walk into a new area and the atmosphere alone tells you what happened there before you read a single item description. The lore is scattered everywhere and when you finally piece it together it hits harder than any story that was just handed to you. You start in Limgrave thinking this is the whole game. Then you beat Godrick and step into Liurnia and just stop. The scale hits you instantly. Then Raya Lucaria appears and somehow blends Harry Potter and Halloween and Bloodborne into one place and it works perfectly. Then you clear it and walk into Altus Plateau and a royal orchestra starts playing and you see the capital in the distance with the Erdtree towering over everything and you realize you haven't even scratched the surface. And I didn't even mention Nokron, Eternal City, Nokstella, Eternal City, Siofra River, Ainsel River, Lake of Rot, Deeproot Depths,Mohgwyn Palace... The exploration never stops doing that to you. Every time I wanted to quit I told myself just one more area just check that one spot and suddenly hours were gone. The dungeons the caves the open world are all designed in a way that makes discovery feel addictive. I spent 200+ hours on a single playthrough without NG+ leaving no corner unexplored no item behind. Not 100% completion. I did Something harder than that. From the crumbling towers of Farum Azula to the rot-soaked beauty of Elphael every area has its own identity. You don't just travel through these places you feel them. And through all of it you're just a Tarnished with nothing slowly becoming something the entire world thought was impossible. Then Messmer opened his mouth. "Those stripped of the grace of gold shall all meet death in the embrace of Messmer's flame." I sat there for a second just processing that. The OST doesn't play fair. You reach Radagon the final boss of the base game and the music starts. Then it hits you. That theme is a reimagined version of the main menu track. FromSoftware told you how this story ends before you even started playing and you never noticed. There's no word for that feeling. Promised Consort Radahn's theme in the DLC does the same thing differently. It hits like a war anthem and never lets go. Combat is punishing but never cheap. You die because you made a mistake and deep down you know it. That's what separates it from everything else. Every open world game feels hollow after this. Every RPG feels like it's missing something. Miyazaki figured out something that nobody else has and probably never will. Nothing else comes close.

If Miyazaki speaks, I listen. If Miyazaki gives his opinion, I agree. If Miyazaki appreciates something, I appreciate it. If Miyazaki has 100 fans, I am one of them. If Miyazaki has one fan, I am that one. If Miyazaki has no fans, I do not exist. For the lost, he is their beacon. For the hungry, their feast. For the blind, their light. For the crippled, their support. For the warrior without purpose, his path. If Miyazaki creates a world, I lose myself in it. If Miyazaki forges a challenge, I face it. If Miyazaki punishes me, I learn. If Miyazaki makes me suffer, I thank him. If Miyazaki hides a secret, I will uncover it. If Miyazaki writes a story, I will decipher it. When everything seems calm, I hear the rumble of a hidden boss. When I think I've won, a second phase begins. When I fall a thousand times, I rise a thousand and one. When despair consumes me, I find another wanderer’s message: Don’t give up, because pain is fleeting, but glory is eternal. Because in every defeat, there is a lesson, and in every victory, a sacrifice. Because in his world, we are not mere players. We are souls in search of meaning.

9.5/10 TL;DR: A beautifully crafted open world with exceptional combat variety and style along with environments that are bound to leave you startstruck. However, obscure NPC questlines and lack of in-game tracking can make for a frustrating time without external tools if you are looking to explore all. Detailed Review: Pros: - Boss fights feel like an intricate dance, with clear punish windows while still subverting expectations on subsequent attempts with their delayed or unpredictable attacks. - Excellent build diversity, especially hybrid/quality builds like Faith-Arcane or Strength-Intelligence. - Stunning, vast landscapes that encourage exploration due to the mystique they carry. - Dungeons are generally well-designed, with occasional unique gimmicks that break monotony and keep it fresh. Cons: - NPC questlines are rather obscure and difficult to follow organically. - No in-game checklist or tracking for collected items, making completionist runs unnecessarily reliant on external tools like MapGenie (Scadutree Fragments I'm looking at you). - Just like any other FromSoftware game, ELDEN RING also doesn't explain much about its mechanics making it difficult to recommend to a lot of casual players. Shadow of the Erdtree DLC: A very vertical and puzzle like map layout makes it very interesting but also frustrating to navigate the Land of Shadows. The performance is overall worse compared to the base game and a lot of bosses like to do attacks which are too long (almost like cutscenes). Despite all of that, the beautiful landscapes, more weapon variety and a good story made it quite engaging for me.

This is an excellent game for players of a particular sort: A. You like a game with a rich open world feel. The landscape is sumptuously rendered and can be interesting to explore. B. You do not want what fans call "hand holding" your way through the adventure. There is little intuitive about what the player is to do next other than a general cardinal direction. ("Hand holding" also applies to understanding the interface of the game which is not especially intuitive unless you have played other Dark Souls games.) C. You like pointlessly hacking and slashing your way through enemies for the only reward to level up" so you can defeat more challenging enemies until there are no more enemies to defeat. As for A, Elden Ring is in the class with the very best games of the sort, Skyrim, BG3, Dragon Age, etc. Regarding B, there can be much appeal to this philosophy. However, unless one has countless hours to devote to exploration and experimentation, the feature can be frustrating. This is especially true regarding the interface and menu systems if one is new to the Dark Souls way of doing things. For example, multiple icons appear on the screen announcing some aspect of the gameplay, but with zero tutorials, there is no way of knowing what these mean or how to take advantage of them. HP, Mana, Stamina, are pretty commonly understood for anyone who has ever played a video game. Of the dozen or so other indicators, there is little intuitive about how to interpret them. In addition, Menu items and inventory control is vast. That could be a good thing. Knowing how to manipulate and change items in your inventory, it will take you awhile. Of course, the player always has the option to consult the various player guides and walkthroughs for help, but: 1. That defeats the purpose of no "hand holding: in the first place. 2. The interfaces are so complicated the guides are sometimes hard to follow even still. As for C, my personal taste is that progress in the game only by killing virtually everything that moves is an unimaginative approach to game design. It lacks subtlety that better games employ to create an intriguing storyline. There is never any banter that gives the fights scenes emotional value - leveling up is pretty much the one and only point. There is never any negotiating with an adversary to obtain your reward without a fight. 95% of the living characters are out to kill you on sight. The other 5% only provide you information or an item of need, but rarely with any condition or side quest. There is virtually no subtlety here. The closest to subtlety is that when you are underpowered, you can sometimes sneak past the bad guy to obtain the reward. For my preference, the Cardinal Sin of Elden Ring is it takes itself so seriously. There is a dearth of whimsy or humor. Out of thousands of NPCs with which I have interacted, only one made me laugh. 15 seconds out of 58 hours provides a really grim world and experience. When it first came out, Skyrim was much like this. However, fans developed mods to add some entertaining NPCs and side-quests. Over the the years, Skyrim became a much better game. but Elden Ring makes modding cumbersome, as opposed to BG3 which incorporates modding into the interface, and Skyrim which incorporated fan mods into the later editions. One final aspect of the game bears noting. Leveling up requires the player to collect "souls," hence all the killing. However, if you die in a battle, you lose the soul point you have collected. On the plus side, this requires to player to plan strategically, especially since you cannot save before entering a fight as with so many other games. It creates a unique challenge to gameplay. However, the downside is it promotes a "use it or lose it" approach to resource management and an excess of passivity and reluctance to experiment in gameplay. This appeal to some because it gives each battle higher stakes, but is also frustrating when player has worked an hour to build up enough resources to level up and then loses it all. Add to this, that the game is glitchy. I have had it freeze up in the middle of a battle in which I was doing well to find on rebooting, I had "lost" the battle and my resource along with it. BOTTOM LINE. Very pretty game. The kinds of frustration it creates will appeal to some, but turn off others. It lacks any motivation that appeals to human emotion other than self aggrandizement of killing others to get to the top. It engages no human emotion other than simplistic greed. Ironically for a game dependent on the collection of souls for advancement, the game itself lacks soul in its design. I will continue to play it for a time if for no other reason than to get my money's worth out of it, but I cannot recommend it to anyone who seeks joy in their role play gaming. I will add, I thoroughly object to this game being listed as an "RPG." There is NO role to play other than Executioner. It should be listed as a first person shooter. I have made this mistake with Steam before and will not do so again.

This game and its dlc has given me a solid 125 hours of solid content I love the lore and exploring this world so much. Played with a variety of builds and most work well. I really struggled with any kind of glass cannon build. My biggest complaint is that it feels like you need 50 to 60 vigor and 30 to 40 endurance to play as a scrub like myself. Feels like any less in theses stats and you'll get two to three shot killed or run out of stamina blocking one attack/dodge rolling a 12 plus swing combo by a boss. Without a shield, hell, most boss attacks nearly kill you while blocking with just a sword. Wish there was a perfect block mechanic for two handed swords so there was a little more depth than just dodge rolling every attack. Kind of like how you can parry some boss attacks. In Elden Ring you'll have to trial and error what you can parry/block/roll/or jump over the game will not tell you. Which is fine, but most late game bosses have almost endless poise and stamina so they never really stop flailing. Hell, almost most endgame area basic enemies have infinite stamina it feels. The absolute death nail for this game being so frustrating is frame trap attacks. Now I think the most egregious frame traps have been fixed that are unfair by the devs standards. IE consort Radahn stuff, but most bosses just get so many damn free hits on you. They'll hit you somehow on the initial downswing of a sword or slam attack even though the attack is no where near you. Any weapons based enemy or boss has parry and dodge timings are all over the map. Sometime its the start of the swing or it could be the very end of it. You just don't know and there are so many areas and enemies that as a normal person you never get good naturally at this combat system. Bosses move so damn much in this game it makes The Dancer from DS3 look like its in slow mo. I think I spent more time getting rolled around and chasing the boss in this game than I did fighting and enjoying the dodging and learning attacks. Because even if you know the bosses attacks the game just hates you and no matter how perfectly you play you'll get hit and staggered and then hit 3 more times because apparently every boss should get 4 free hits off of one attack. Also I think every major boss has a grab attack now. So much of this game is artificial difficulty. I absolutely love this game and the world, but the combat is stuck in ds2 era when it could've been amazing or expanded on from Sekiro. Not being just Sekiro combat pasted over but idk?? perfect blocks/parry/ and step dodges could've been fun to master. I know there's a million weapons so how do you make a combat system and animations for all that? idk but i'm sure the millions souls games have made could fund it. It'll never get added, but for future games, please either move the camera out based on how big the boss is or let us adjust how far the camera sits in a fight. SO many bosses take up the entire screen and I no see good so I get bonked to death by angry dude. I cant overstate how much I love and am frustrated by this game. So much good held back by a very clunky and outdated combat loop where you never feel like a master. also CURSE YOU BAAAAAAYYYYYLLLLLEEEEEEE!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

Highly recommended. I paid $65NZD for this game which kept me entertained for 59 hrs. Fantastic value for money for a single player campaign with optional co-op fortification. This game is just flat out fun, it takes you on a journey. You start out weak with weak weapons, even lesser foes are a challenge - and taking on a group of such foes is unwise. But you level up, you get stronger - the challenge is still there. The environment adds challenge, a tough enemy can be despatched quickly if you can hit them off a ledge, or get them up against a wall and go Mike Tyson on 'em. The animations are superb, the swordsmanship in this game is downright beautiful. There's a constant feeling of 'I wonder what's over here' or wanting to test things out. Honestly, this game is just monstrous, I definitely see myself playing through it again. And experiencing all new 'wow' moments when I do.

This game WILL NOT STOP FREEZING. Every couple of minutes it will completely stop rendering anything. The game itself will hold, but then speed up a second to "catch up" to where it thinks the player should be. If you're mid-jump, you end up falling. If you're in a fight, you drop your guard. I have a great computer it is not a question of processing or graphics power - the developers just did a poor job of porting the game to PC.

Game is awesome, everybody knows that. However my negative review is due to poor PC game optimization. With my specs I can play all modern games in 4k, however I have to play this one in 1440p. I spent about 6-7 hours trying to fix the issues. None of the solutions over internet worked for me, eventually thanks to some data analysis, chatGPT and I guess luck, tweaking some BIOS settings on my cpu cores I was able to have the game working smoothly (at 1440p). However I still see some drops of FPS here and there, but luckily nothing game breaking at this point. Still, the game offers a massive amount of content and replayability. Whether you're a Souls veteran or new to the genre, Elden Ring delivers something special. 10/10

However, there are so many lows to average aspects (repeated bosses and dungeons, some bosses you fight them later as lesser enemies, performance till today isn’t optimized even with strong PC, meaningless open world design that simply doesn’t work with souls-like formula, boring combat and weapons, artificial difficulty, and it feels like riding a horse simulator. I really think if this game was developed by Ubisoft or Bethesda, we would have seen completely different reaction. In short, this is 7/10 game due to the high highs of it, but considering all the flaws and the unjustified long length, I don’t recommend it. It is a great piece of art but not fun game.

Every boss fight goes like this: Enter arena with confidence Immediately get humbled Whisper “okay THIS is the run” Die in 12 seconds Repeat for 2 hours Win by pure luck and emotional damage The Samurai experience is basically: You feel like a god against regular enemies You feel like a wet noodle against anything with a name Also, who designed these enemies?? Why does every boss have: 17-phase combos Delayed attacks specifically timed to ruin my dodge Personal hatred toward me At this point, my character is max level but I, the player, have learned nothing except fear. I remember hearing about Elden Ring for the first time in 2022. A lot of my friends hyped the game up as one of the greatest of all time. and ranted and raved about how innovative it was. I had never played a "souls-like" game in my life and thus wasn't very interested. Fast forward to ~2024, I started to dip my toes in the genre. My first was a game called Mortal Shell. I liked it. Then I played through Sekiro (also from fromsoft) in 2025 but got hard-stuck on the final boss. In 2026, I decided to try Elden Ring for the first time. I bought it on sale for I think around 30 dollars. From the first couple hours, I was totally entranced by this game. My friends were not kidding - this game is legitimately a modern masterpiece. The Pros: The map is absolutely shockingly massive. The overworld map alone feels much larger than any other game I have ever played. And then you find out about the wells, and realize "♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, It gets even bigger." Most games that have large maps have long stretches of barren, lifeless areas that artificially increase the size. Not Elden Ring. Not at all. EVERY area of the game is not only breath-takingly beautiful, but also filled to the brim with unique structures that even transform and change as you reach milestones in the game's story. There are hundreds of unique enemies, mini-bosses, and bosses to fill in the aforementioned map. Exciting, challenging encounters lay waiting around every corner to be discovered by the player. You'll be walking through a dungeon, and all of a sudden - "WHOA WHAT THE F**K IS THAT THING" - you'll be attacked by an abomination. Skeletons. Lizards. Dragons, Worm people. Dogs. Crazy villagers. etc. Each enemy and boss has their own unique attacks and animations and it absolutely never gets old. It is a very refreshing change from most modern video games, that largely reuse the same "pool" of attacks and animations without really caring about the gameplay becoming boring. What's the point of enemies without weapons, right? Good news - Elden Ring has hundreds of unique ones to choose from, most of which can be further modified with "ashes of war" found throughout the game. You want to wield a battle-axe that makes people bleed? Done. What about a sword that freezes enemies? Done. What about a giant hammer that poisons? Done. The customization is borderline limitless. And the armor in this game is largely the same way. There are tons of different sets to choose from or mix and match, that raise certain attributes to fit your particular playstyle. No matter how you want to play, this game has options for YOU which is awesome and shows they really deeply thought about the combat from an early stage of development. The voice acting in this game is another thing I'd like to highlight. It is absolutely perfect. Every enemy. Every boss. Every NPC. There were many times during this game that the voice acting gave me chills - which is very rare for me and especially in video games- such as mohg's "NIHIL! NIHIL! NIHIL!" or Godrick's "Forefathers one and all, bear witness!" This game FEELS like you as the player are actually living in this huge fantasy landscape. It's amazing. The cons: It pains me to really say anything negative about this game because I, like many others, consider it a legitimate modern masterpiece to gaming. However, with that being said, there are a few things I must critique. The storyline, while there, certainly feels a little bit lacking to me. The developers absolutely give you bits and pieces of a story throughout the game but it is largely through experiencing the world and going to different areas. It feels a little bit disjointed and confusing at times. Some particular bosses in this game have legitimate "Guaranteed hit" moves. It's a souls-like game, so of course there's going to be stuff like that and what I'm about to say isn't a "major" critique but remains true to me. I feel like a lot of bosses (particularly late game bosses) should be a little more choreographed than what they are. Some bosses are programmed to essentially do "random mix ups" meaning they can chain an attack with another attack or this other attack or this other attack. They essentially randomly pick from a set of moves. In theory this is cool, until you encounter a boss like Mohg, lord of blood or Malenia and then you want to smash your controller into bits and pieces. You are going to be hit by a lot of attacks that will have you going "wait a second, that wasn't even close to me wtf" and you aren't tripping. Some attacks really, literally, can look or feel as though they are clearly dodged and just.... aren't. On the flip-side, some attacks are virtually guaranteed regardless of how you want to dodge/roll. Malenia's "waterfowl dance" is a perfect example of this. Although *technically* dodge-able, if you are close to her when she does it? Son... It's over. There are memes online that say the best thing you can do when she does waterfowl close range is to just exit and try the run again until you get a tamer mix-up and lowkey?....... they're accurate LMFAO. I just really wish that wasn't the case. Your success, particularly in late-game bosses, often feels like you're just waiting for a fight where they don't do X attack or don't have such punishing mix-ups. The fight that I finally killed Malenia she only did waterfowl once in phase 2. There were other fights where she'd do it 4-5 times and again, if you get a fight like that (which mind you is rng) it is ACTUALLY just over unless you're a perfect god with thousands of hours on these types of games. Again, not a major critique because it's a souls-like game - just a personal preference. I like bosses that have more choreographed attacks. If this part is putting you off from trying this game - Don't worry! This game has lots of fights that are fairly choreographed and very fun!! There are only really 3-5 bosses in the whole game that I would consider just outright unfair in the sense that your success is literally just waiting for good rng. And believe me, when you run into them in your journey... you'll know. (lol) My only other gripe with this game is how it does quests. I considered tying this part in with the storyline critique but my issue is with characters that aren't necessarily "needed" for the story and thus I feel it deserves it's own section. A lot of the quests in this game are - and I am not exaggerating in the slightest - Find X character here at random location on the map. Then talk to them and find them here in totally different area opposite side of the map. Then talk to them and find them here in this totally unrelated area of the map opposite to that. If you want to do a particular ending or just help particular npcs - you will 100% without a doubt need to search up how to do some things. I personally wanted to save Melina from her death and so I did Hyetta's questline. It was horrifically painful to experience before I succumbed to using google for help. Her questline in particular is absolute, total dogs*it so much so that it's actually unbelievable. Her questline involves an invisible door that you open with a pressure plate some place in a random dungeon on the map. For real. I am not exaggerating.(LMFAO) Remember how I said that you will need google for certain parts? I really mean that. I don't think it is actually possible as a solo player to find certain things without it. And I got to say - that right there is my biggest critique about this game. Even if the developers included vague dialogue like "I'm going to the mountains of ____" or something just to give the player a general idea of where to look for them to advance their quest would be all they would need to do to fix this. All in all, Elden Ring is an absolutely INCREDIBLE game. Despite having a few cons, I believe the pros vastly outweigh them. It is one of the best games of all time, and I would have paid double full price if I had known.

From did impossible! First time in my life I was bored to death while playing a From game. Why? Because there is nothing in this game. Nothing new, I was going here and there pointing at things with thoughts: "this boss is from Bloodborne", "this room is from Dark Souls" etc. Its ok at some degree, but here it was too much. Basically creative bankruptcy. Nothing to remember. Yes, it's beautiful, but it makes the situation even worse: the world is so gorgeous and yet its too big and too bland. Everything takes so much time: battles, traveling, exploring, examining lore. Why? Why game exists after horribly empty Leyndell? Why it takes 100h to beat? What's the point? The point is lost in this vast sea of content. Nothing to love. From the fist King's Field From games were complete, whole: with philosophy, questions, logic. This game has only content, no author's questions, it's just a product, it's not art. This game has no soul. Because of that there is no reason to explore it. There is nobody to talk to (I mean author's voice, author is mute!), no statement, no argument, no mystery. Nothing. Just endless Santa Barbara. Who are all these characters? Who cares? From was making adult non-indy games until now. They were like the only one who were doing that. And now, it's gone. Because of that there is no reason to play this game, there is no connection between you and author. You should play because it's cool and it's difficult, and it's hype. So that after beating it you can say that you did beat Elden Ring. The problem is, in DS for example, there were even better reason: after beating it I understand what this whole thing is about, I see the world, I understand it's philosophy, it's now part of my life experience. The only experience in Elden Ring is understanding your physical abilities and patience. It's boring, I have no reason to prove myself or somebody anything. I guess classic From is over, now they are making CoD in fantasy-action games. Good luck, thank you for King's Field, Demon's Souls, Dark Souls and Bloodborne. Also I'm changing my review of Sekiro to positive, because at least Sekiro was honest and not pure content. It had soul, it had story, it had (not gigantic like in DS) heart. I was naive by criticizing it for it's problems in 2019. Elden Ring is much worse. I cannot even compare.

My journey with soulslikes started right here with Elden Ring. The world is masterfully crafted brutal, harsh, mysterious, and filled with stunning locations. Unlike many other titles, this game doesnt treat the player like an idiot. The obscure side quests add a lot of flavor, theres zero chance you wont miss something during your first playthrough. The combat system is excellent, with beautiful animations and spectacular effects for spells and incantations. While the difficulty especially the overused delayed attacks can be off putting at first, the game becomes even more enjoyable once you master the mechanics. As an RPG fan, the open world really spoke to me, though I understand its not for everyone. Personally I think it gives the game much higher replayability than the linear Dark Souls titles, as every new run can feel completely different. Now, what you really need to look out for is the lack of a save anywhere feature... just kidding! Honestly, one of the main issues is those previously mentioned delayed attacks practically every single enemy has them! Another downside is the heavy boss recycling. I would also point out that the rewards for clearing catacombs are often unsatisfying, usually just being spirit summons. And finally, optimization issues? Im not sure what to call it exactly, but there are micro stutters that can ruin a fight. I dont think its a hardware issue, even after upgrading from an RTX 2060 to a 5060 Ti 16GB and from an i5-10400F to an i7-11700K, absolutely nothing changed in that regard. Interestingly, these stutters dont occur at all on a handheld like the Lenovo Legion Go. Overall, I highly recommend it, a game easily worth hundreds of hours. Definitely in my top 10.

When I first played Elden Ring, I thought it was great, but not necessarily one of my favorite games. A big part of that is that I have a ton of respect for the world design of the original Dark Souls, and I feel like Elden Ring's Open World can lose a lot of the marvelously layered world design that makes Dark Souls legendarily fun to explore. The fact of the matter is that this is partially the case, but it is part of what makes Elden Ring legendary. Elden Ring is one of the greatest Dungeon Crawlers of all time. Most people do not think of it as one, but it is. Sure, the open world is gorgeous and well-designed, but I actually find its endless vaults and tombs to be marvelously compelling. The better designed "Legacy Dungeons" are obviously great, but this game is a fantastically fun one to play through when you delve below the earth to see what's hidden in the old and forgotten places. I imagine that it's only better with some sort of randomizer and I cannot wait for the days when I've forgotten enough about Elden Ring to by surprised by it once again.

From the creators of Bloodyborne and Dark Souls, you essentially get a glorified dating sim that is confusedly also an open world RPG. The areas are vast and beautiful yet the main attractions remain the women in this game. You have Ranni the Witch. I don't need to tell you how popular she is. Let's just say 4373 is a large number for people dedicating "art posts" to her. Then you have Melina, your first maiden. That childhood friend/neighbor girl character who has been helping you along the way throughout out your quests and just waiting for you to notice her. Soft spoken yet meaningful in her words and easy on the eyes. Just don't show her the three fingers, she's not into that...Then you have Fia. The deathbed companion. The character you go to after dying to the boss over and over again. Why? Because if you can't feel the warmth of a woman's body in real life, might as well pretend to feel it in a triple AAA game from Miyazaki. And to maintain realism, whenever you hug her you get debuffed, just like how it feels to hug women in real life; it doesn't last long, its lackluster, and you keep coming back for more while losing your grip on reality. Then you have Hyetta. She's the gal with an appetite. Feed her some grapes and she'll be over the moon. Feed her enough, and she will show you her three fingers (pun intended). You also have the amazon goddess of snoo snoo herself, Nepheli...the one with daddy issues. I know Gideon said he "adopted her" but...cmon. The guy who is all knowing wouldn't know how to court a barbarian women? Really?. That aside, the cutest one...the tsundere that sets your heart on fire...Dung Eater-chan. I swear...his eyes are as brown as the left over basketball sized chocolate mud babies I leave in my toilet after a hearty Taco Bell breakfast. A character of rigour and personality. The characters are as diverse as the regions you play in. The weapons are unique and all usable up to end game. The only regret I have with this game is not being able to continually fight bosses like you could in Sekiro for example. That was a huge missed opportunity. TLDR: You either get frame Moghed or you mew hard enough to be Elden Lord. In essence, a game I will never put down and the true successor to Dark Souls.

this is my first and last souls game, and i won't replay it once i finish it. The game is hard but you already know that, the thing is it's mostly hard because the controls are janky, the camera and targeting are bad af and you can't break animations. I'm not good yet and it took 40h for me to start getting it, but even now i feel half my deaths are unfair af. Idk why people like that so much but it's too frustrating and the ratio dopamine/frustration isn't worth it.

I don't understand why people say souls games aren't hard. They are definitely hard when you are underprepared, which happens alot if you haven't played these games before. But they can extremely easy if you are overprepared without limiting yourself (farming, memorization, etc). Honestly, play how you want to play, don't dwell too much on the challenge from these types games because it differs from player to player (personally i hate the enemies that don't stop attacking). Don't compare difficulties of other games to this. Nor is this game too hard because its bearable. In the end, its an adapt to game or suffer. That being said, this is far from my ideal type of game due to lack of creativity for the player near the end of the game when they max out their stats. The atmosphere really good but I started to get tired of fighting similar bosses. Using the Serpent Spear on Rykard was so amazing (maybe I like whacking large bosses) but not having any of that feeling at the end of the game felt underwhelming (chasing the final boss feels annoying than hard)? At some point I started to spam either Carian slicer or Zamor Ice Storm and its hard to change the build because the other spells are kinda butt tbh (and changing builds requires an investment which is kinda weird to me). And no, Horseback battles with Torrent is cool only for a few fights. Lastly, how do people play this game blind sometimes? there is so many missable items, quests, events, etc (YES THAT INCLUDES THE STORY ITSELF), and be able to lock yourself out of. It might be little obvious sometimes but finding that one random npc to start the quest or learning that event that locks you out of ending isn't fun (atleast to me). Some say that gameplay should come first before the story but I find it best when they come hand to hand. They just feed you bosses but its up to the player to come across and piece together the story, but I struggle to fill in the cracks for the story sometimes. So don't think I could talk about the story itself. Its a 8/10, had a pretty fun time, reading player messages, watching cutscenes, exploring the world (the best part of the game), listening to the godlike ost, etc. Idk if this is a hot take but I wish the game was shorter (more areas for using Torrent and less areas with elevators or ladders).

Elden Ring is a disappointing experience. I recently completed both Dark Souls 1 and 3 (I'm not an expert by any means) and went on excitedly to play Elden Ring but it ended up being a huge mistake. This game is pretty and the story is at least interesting and I understand why the masses would like this game but having played it myself I think it's not a bad game per say but it is not a good Souls game. The open world structure actually feels detrimental to the game and sometimes the exploration can be very confusing (especially the Rauh Ruins in the dlc that are easily the worst offender in that regard). The enemies drop very little runes which ended up being a problem as it meant this game was the first Souls where I ended up having to farm levels to progress. The difficulty feels very artificial as well, from the midgame onward the enemies feel very spongy, have a ton of poise and deal a huge amount of damage, so much so that it's common to get two shotted in the end game. As for the bosses, they usually have a very cheap attack pattern where they attack a lot very fast and deal a truckload of damage, so it's not really a matter of skill issue and more a matter of luck in the latter bosses. There's also a lot of things that feel re-used and areas that feel samey wich is a shame because Dark Souls 1 for instance had some pretty nice diversity in areas in my opinion (granted not all of them). In the end, in my opinion, I feel like you should pass up on this game. It is simply not a good Souls game and the difficulty is way too high for very little reward; in the end, the only real regret I have is that I played too much of this game and I can't get a refund anymore.

8 hours in. I have died more times than I can count. I have thrown my mouse across the desk. I have questioned every life decision that led me to this moment. This game will humble you. That first boss? He doesn't care about your feelings. That second boss? Still doesn't care. The WORLD doesn't care. You are nothing here — just a little guy in a big, brutal, breathtakingly beautiful world that wants you dead. But here's the thing — every death teaches you something. Every "YOU DIED" screen is just the game whispering "try again, but smarter." And when you finally land that killing blow after your 47th attempt? Pure. Unfiltered. Euphoria. The world design is jaw-dropping. Every corner hides something — a secret path, a terrifying enemy, a reward that makes the suffering worth it. I've only scratched the surface in 8 hours and I already know this is one of the greatest games ever made. Do I recommend it? Absolutely. Is it hard? Disgustingly so. Will it break you? Yes. Will you love every second of it? Without a doubt. Would suggest

Elden ring, at its core is a massive open world game, with deep buildcrafting, and hidden storytelling. the amount of times i would be on my way somewhere, and would get distracted by something new, (A new boss/ dungeon) was way more than i can count The world: Most open world games are filled with empty space, with no rewards. this game has something for you to loot and discover around every corner. The dungeons: the dungeons are FILLED with secrets. Fake walls, invisible floors, hidden mini bosses, hidden GIANT bosses hidden weapons and gear. there is so much to find in them, between parkour, and simple searches and the "how can i get there?" The Bosses: this is what makes the game so intense and addicting. The way it challenges you, and the amount of times you have to fail in order to learn, and then win. you will lose to a lot of the bosses, but when you win... you will FEEL that win. The gear: the way Souls games chooses to make you build has always been amazing. every combo can be good with the right set up, the longer you play... the stronger and more skilled you will get with that gear. The DLC: the DLC was much harder than the base game, but it was also very fun. Conclusion: My first and only 10/10 game i will play this game again, and then likely again. it is THAT good if you're unsure if you should buy it, understand these games aren't for everyone, this game WILL challenge you! but if you try, you can beat it!

Ashen one… no, Tarnished. 97 hours have passed since I first set foot upon the Lands Between—and still, the call of grace burns bright. I came as one untested. A stranger to the works of FromSoftware. A fool, perhaps… unready for the weight of such a journey. Yet the world did not bend to me. It broke me. Again and again. And still… I rose. What is Elden Ring, if not a cruel teacher? Its lessons are carved not in words, but in defeat. Each fallen boss, each lost rune, each ambush in shadow—these are its scripture. And through suffering, I learned. The Lands Between are vast beyond reason. Golden fields that whisper false peace… rot-choked swamps that cling to your very soul… castles that loom like forgotten gods. Every path beckons. Every corner hides wonder—or death. I have cursed this game. I have walked away from it. And yet… I always returned. For in its harshness, there is beauty. In its silence, meaning. In its struggle… triumph. To those who have yet to begin: know this. You will fail. You will be lost. You will despair. But if you endure… You may yet become Elden Lord. *Verdict: Praise the message.*

Elden Ring is a massive achievement, but the difficulty sometimes feels like its coming from the wrong place. After putting in over 100 hours, I have a few thoughts. The Good: World & Play The level design is genuinely amazing. The way the world is built is top-tier; these levels are expansive, twisting, and turning into each other in ways that are actually hard to wrap your head around. It’s beautiful to look at, and the enemy variety is awesome. The 'come up' of getting stronger is where it really shines. The Bad: Controls & "Artificial" Difficulty I found the controls to be ridiculous, I don't think making a game harder with cumbersome controls is good design. The queue up system for inputs acts so strange that I found myself still making mistakes even after 100+ hours. The amount of times I have accidently dismounted from my horse its unbelievable, call me bad, but this is my experience. Bad physics isn't a puzzle, it's just frustrating. Same goes for some of the site of grace layouts; tedious for no real gain. The Ugly: Narrative & Inventory The story makes very little sense. Call me a smooth brain, but FromSoft just doesn't tell a good story I almost never knew what I was actually doing.. The lack of explanation carries over to items, I have a million things in my inventory, most of which where useless, or that I had no idea how to use. Managing it all was a chore; when the expansion started I had to look up what the first item did. Why? Multiplayer: PVP & Coop The PVP was mostly try hards wasting my time, the native coop is quite clucky and I highly recommend Seamless Co-op mod, it made the experience a lot better for me. It removes a ton of the friction from cooperative play. Performance: My PC is a literal god computer, and I’m still seeing 40 FPS at times. Lul. Final Take: Its a gorgeous, expansive world with fun boss fights, and great multiplayer held back by clunky UI and controls. I still recommend it, its a fun game, but its probably going to piss you off at times.

I will add this preface to my review, now that I have played for sixty hours: Everything I wrote below is still true, but the game is absolutely beautyful, and riding around in the world is fantastic. I will also say that I now believe that some of the problems I mentioned below stem from weird hitboxes, especially on the player character. I loved Dark Souls 1, and think Dark Souls 2 is a fine but flawed game. Elden Ring is beautiful, but it sucks! Mechanical Death contraptions clip so badly, that you can't solve the puzzle without dying first. Quite a few attacks bypass your shield, without animating the shield actually being pushed aside, and your stamina isn't touched, your hp is just suddenly drained even though your shield should have protected you. I can't believe From Software released such an unfinished game, and three years later they haven't fixed anything! Within two hours of playing the game, I lost all desire to ever play a From Software title ever again, and I was really exited to finally try this game. I have now played three additional hours, and I can say that dodging slow moving ranged attacks apparantly doesn't work for a certain miniboss near the beginning of the game. Did From Software forget to implement quality assurance because they got high? Many hours later, this game is so full of Bed of Chaos moments, that I'm not sure I will actually want to finish the game. Also it is absolutely insane that the game is so easy to play as a sorcerer. My two main beginning chararacters are a faith based melee fighter, and a ranged int based magic-user. I think one of my main complaints with this game, is the lack of visual feedback. In Dark Souls 1 I could visually see why something failed and why my character got hit, that is not the case in this game. Addendum after having played a lot more. I'm really not sure wether I actually enjoy the game or if I'm continuing because of some weird stubborness. The clipping in this game is really inexcusable, there are such glaring faults, like when giant creatures clip through entire buildings in the combat arena. How From Software actually justified to themselves shipping such a buggy product I don't know. They certainly can't have any pride in their craft.

Elden Ring is a masterpiece and easily earns a solid 10/10. It takes everything great about FromSoftware’s previous games and expands it into a massive, open-world experience. The world design is one of its biggest strengths. The Lands Between are vast, mysterious, and full of secrets. Exploration feels rewarding, with hidden areas, bosses, and items around every corner. The sense of discovery is unmatched. Combat is excellent, offering a wide variety of weapons, builds, and playstyles. Whether you prefer magic, melee, or a mix of both, the game gives you the freedom to play how you want. Boss fights are challenging and memorable, pushing players to improve and adapt. The atmosphere, music, and art direction are all top-tier, creating a dark and immersive world. The lore is deep and intriguing, even if it’s not always directly explained. While the game can be difficult and occasionally frustrating, that challenge is part of what makes it so rewarding. Overall, Elden Ring is an outstanding game with incredible world-building, gameplay, and depth. It stands as one of the best RPGs in recent years.

You're better off playing on consoles. Edit: Ok, I finally managed to fix the stuttering issue. Turning off variable refresh rate in windows graphics settings, and hardware accelerated GPU scheduling for good measure did it for me. So here is my final review. I enjoyed Elden Ring much more this time around than during my first playthrough. I went in with a few specific protocols because Elden Ring is a game that breaks if you do not cooperate with it. If you are a thorough explorer, it is easy to trivialize the challenge by over-leveling. To counter this, I spent my accumulated runes on purchasing in-game items instead of levels, by the midpoint of the game, I stopped leveling altogether. Furthermore, your horse, exacerbates an age-old problem in these games by making it easier than ever to run past enemies. To stay engaged, I made a point of fighting any enemies that aggroed toward me. Because the combat can feel like a stagnant, simplistic system that turns monotonous after a few hours, I constantly respec'd my character to try different builds. Incorporating various Ashes of War and elemental damage types brought much-needed variety to the gameplay. Finally, I found that the 2D map is far too detailed, it spoils the sense of discovery and can turn the game into a Ubisoft-style checklist affair. I ignored the map throughout the entire playthrough, relying on it only for fast travel when resting at a Site of Grace. With these self-imposed rules in place, Elden Ring is a much more enjoyable experience, making it easier to appreciate the impressive work that went into the open-world design. The world is highly vertical, with constant elevation changes that make the act of navigation inherently interesting. You will rarely traverse a flat, empty expanse for long, instead, there are cliffsides, ravines, and hills everywhere that force decisions and encourage attentiveness. A seemingly flat horizon might suddenly give way to a cliff, and if you are mindlessly galloping on your horse, you will fall to your death. This same feeling of handcraftedness extends to the visual design. In my Bloodborne review, I commended Fromsoft for creating these cinematic framings while the player maintains total control, whereas other developers resort to wrestling control away from the player and restricting their abilities to achieve a similar end. Fromsoft managed to one-up themselves by replicating this accomplishment in an open-world format. It is incredible how the game can look like a painting from every angle while control of the camera remains entirely in the player's hands. On top of that, the density of content in the open world is unprecedented, there is simply something to do in every square inch of the map. In the first region alone, you can spend upwards of 30 hours exploring every nook and cranny. If you get tired of the monotony of running around in the open world, there are a number of caves and catacombs you can find through natural discovery. These give you a short burst of that classic, structured Dark Souls experience, complete with traps and ambushes in tight spaces and a boss at the end. This turned out to be an addictive loop to cycle between. One thing you wouldn't expect to survive the transition to an open world is the impressive enemy variety the Souls series is known for. Elden Ring surprises by filling virtually every sub-region with unique enemy types. Although understandable compromises have been made, even the repeated enemies tend to have unique movesets to make them feel distinct. While all of that is happening in the open fields, Elden Ring also features these imposing structures that you can view from a distance, which then seamlessly transition into expansive multi-layered dungeons when you get up close. These areas are fully explorable and packed with shortcuts, interesting enemy encounters, secrets to find, and bosses with high-level presentation. Although there are a bit too many sites of grace in these areas for my liking. Fromsoft wasn't content with this, however, so they hid entire underground regions below this vast surface that already possesses a daunting size. These underground areas themselves contain even more secrets worth dozens of hours of content. This is an insane escalation of what I praised Dark Souls 1 for. There is so much more to be said about this gargantuan game, which took me a little more than 200 hours to finish. If nothing else, Elden Ring is a monumental achievement due to its sheer scale and its ambition to make the experience feel as curated as a linear game, in spite of its size. For the most part, they accomplished that, but it requires that you negotiate with the game. Still unforgivable that the game doesn't work perfectly straight out of the box though so be mindful of the technical issues.

What can i say about Elden Ring that hasn't already been said? It's a game that will be talked about as one of those games that define the generation it released in, Much like it's spiritual predecessors Dark Souls, Bloodborne, and Sekiro. Elden ring embraces the best elements of gaming. It bombards you with vistas that beg to be explored. The combat is the best, most diverse, and quite honestly the easiest its ever been due to the seer amount of weapons, tools, and consumables that combine so beautifully, that you can literally buff the humble hand held fire torch to kill literal gods. The Story telling is the most overt its ever been, i'm not going to spoil anything, but it lays out why you are doing what you are doing whilst telling you all of the key characters in the intro cutscene. From Software combined that classical story telling with its own unique deep interactive lore that needs effort to find and decipher. The game is so content rich that if you just follow the critical path you will have a 40 to 60 hour game, i lick, sniff, and explore every crevice of a game when i play them and my first playthough took me well over 200 hours. It's not a game without flaws though, some of the side, and mini dungeons can feel very similar even if they mostly have their own twists, puzzles, and enemies. Speaking of enemies there is a few bosses that are used several times and a certain one in particular because infuriating as it has a bit of a wonky hitbox. Overall its a 10/10 game,, and if not one of the best games of all time, its certainly one of the best games of its generation.

[h1] The TL;DR [/h1] Elden Ring is what happens when you take the tight, punishing combat of Dark Souls and set it loose in a world that actually rewards your curiosity. It is massive, beautiful, and occasionally makes you want to throw your controller into the sun—and yet, you’ll keep coming back for more. [hr][/hr] [h1]The Breakdown[/h1] [b] 1. Exploration (10/10)[/b] Unlike most modern open-world games, there are no "towers" to climb to reveal map icons. You see a weird building on the horizon? You can go there. You see a massive well in the middle of a forest? It probably leads to a literal underground galaxy. The sense of discovery is the best in the industry. [b] 2. Gameplay & Combat (9/10)[/b] Variety: Whether you want to be a colossal-sword-swinging tank, a sneaky assassin, or a wizard nuking bosses from afar, the build variety is staggering. Difficulty: It is hard. Really hard. However, it’s the most "accessible" Souls game. If a boss is beating you senseless, you can just leave, level up elsewhere, and come back later. Spirit Summons: A new mechanic that lets you summon AI ghosts to help in fights. It’s a literal godsend for solo players. [b] 3. Visuals & Atmosphere (10/10)[/b] The art direction is carrying the heavy lifting here. Every "Legacy Dungeon" (like Stormveil Castle or Raya Lucaria) feels like a masterpiece of gothic architecture. The scale of the world is genuinely intimidating. [b] 4. Performance & Technical (7/10)[/b] This is the only real "tarnish" on the experience. PC Port: Still capped at 60 FPS. Stuttering: Even on high-end rigs, you might see occasional frame drops in specific areas. Ultrawide: No native support without mods (which disables online play). [hr][/hr] [h1]Pros & Cons[/h1] ✅ [b] Pros:[/b] Absolute freedom to go anywhere. The "Horse" (Torrent) feels great to control. Incredible boss designs (mostly). Hundreds of hours of content for a single purchase. ❌ [b] Cons:[/b] The UI is still a bit clunky (standard for FromSoftware). Some late-game bosses feel slightly "unfair" with infinite stamina. The story is told through item descriptions—don't expect a cinematic movie plot. [hr][/hr] [h1]Final Verdict[/h1] If you have any interest in RPGs, you owe it to yourself to play this. It doesn't hold your hand, but that’s exactly why winning feels so good. [h3]Final Score: 10/10 (Masterpiece)[/h3]

Refunded. Despite being released in 2022, this game has no support for common-place monitor aspect ratios, only working with 16:9, meaning that unless you're still using a techno-peasant-grade monitor, you're going to end up with black bars on the sides. For a game where one of the primary selling points is its graphics, this is an absolutely unbelievable level of developmental laziness and incompetence. The days of calling monitors "wide" or "ultra-wide" is long gone. There are no wide monitors. There are no ultra-wide monitors. There are simply monitors, and they come in all different sizes and ratios. That is why it is so hard to find a game published within the last 15 years that doesn't support multiple monitor aspect ratios. It's hard to find even an indie developer these days who doesn't accept this as undeniable fact. But somehow a major developer like FromSoftware never got the memo. So here's a negative review for wasting my time.

I want to preface this review by saying that I have not played Dark Souls or any similar boss-focused fight games, and I am guessing this genre is just not for me, which may color my strong dislike of this game. I played for 45 minutes before requesting a refund (which I have never done before on a game). Positives: This game is very beautiful in its environmental production with some stellar fight mechanics. I can also see how people would get an adrenaline-boost when faced with battling the monster bosses as well as the intellectual challenge of finding ways to overcome their overwhelming power over you. Negatives: The story is basically Lord of the Rings (which I love) but void of any heart or soul or character ambitions. The playable character lacks motivation and I do not know what I am trying to accomplish by seeking the Elden Ring. The game is also extremely difficult, which is fine except that it forces the player to grind hours trying to beat a boss who I don't even understand why I should be trying to defeat. I could see a scenario where I dedicated hundreds of hours into this game only to achieve nothing, which is why I decided not to waste my time with it. It is basically fan-fiction for Lord of the Rings where you play as a nameless Easterling (evil man) fighting in Sauron's army and have to defeat all the big-bads of the franchise without even knowing who they are besides their names or what the One Ring does or why you are trying to wield power over it in the first place. The gameplay is also very repetitive: basically you go and attack something, try to kill it, and then go onto something else to kill, then heal, then often re-kill all of these monsters again and again and again. And your reward for these battles? Some random loot that is so difficult to understand it is like getting paid for farm work with NFTs. If you like hack and slash games without story or purpose, this may be a great time suck for you. Otherwise, it is truly a waste of your life.

[h1] Elden Ring is one of those games of games. [/h1] [h2] Intro [/h2] Took 150 Hours for me to 100% (and do the DLC). It's about 4 playtrough. I love this game and it is truly one of the games you have to play if you are into souls-like. The first playthrough is a bit rough. It takes a while and you die... a lot. Slowly you understand how the game works and how much exploration there is to do and you begin to lose yourself in the world. I'm 100% sure that i missed a bunch of things in the main game and DLC. [h2] The Good ! [/h2] [h3] The Exploration and environment [/h3] The exploration in this game is truly incredible. HIDDEN STUFF EVERYWHERE. Invisible walls, hidden platforms, Invisible floors, deadly traps, enemy ambush, dragon ambush, ball ambush (yes ball ambush, don't ask). There is so much to see and to do that it might be overwhelming. The game never take you by the hands and pushes you to take your time and to explore every nook and cranny of this Grand world. yes i used Grand with a big G because everything looks massive. The environment, from afar (we'll speak about that further down) is magnificent and beautifully handcrafted. The environment also contribute a lot to the storytelling of the game. [h3] Storytelling and Design [/h3] The storytelling and design of the game are a bit weird, but not in a bad way. If you are familiar with Darksouls you already know that but the story is told via item description and enemy design. If you want to read then oh boi, you are going to have fun with the descriptions. Every item has his own description which ground it in the lore. It's even better for the items which comes from bosses. Every enemy also contributes to the storytelling just via their designs. Some are really disgusting though so don't stare too heavily :) [h2] The Bad ! [/h2] There is not much bad to say but there is still some problems that me or others i know encounters. So.. what is it?? So, still in 2026, the game is locked in 60 fps. It also doesn't support widescreen. There is still some hiccup with the perfomances too. Other than that, no guidance from the start may be detrimental to your experience because you may miss actual features and plots. You see for yourself if you see it as a negative or a positive. Most People won't interact with the story of the game other than via the cinematics because the game doesn't show you that the items can be interacted with in another way than equipping it. [h2] Tips ! [/h2] If you have a hard time against a boss, go explore, get new gear, level up. Your best friend is reading and talking to npcs. Quests are not written in a journal so you may want to take note of what npcs tells you. [h2] The End! [/h2] [h2] Thanks for reading! [/h2]

I really appreciate the beauty of the landscapes in this game. The environments are carefully designed, with impressive details that create a strong sense of immersion. Whether it’s vast open fields, mysterious ruins, or darker and more hostile areas, each location feels unique and contributes to the overall atmosphere. Exploring these places is not only visually rewarding but also adds to the feeling of adventure. Beyond its aesthetics, the game is highly enjoyable because of its combat system. Fighting enemies and especially powerful bosses provides a real sense of challenge and accomplishment. Each encounter requires attention, strategy, and patience, which makes every victory feel earned. The difficulty is part of what makes the experience engaging, as it constantly pushes the player to improve. However, it’s true that the game can feel frustrating for beginners. The mechanics are not always easy to master at first, and the difficulty can seem overwhelming. Early defeats are common, and progress may feel slow. But once you spend some time learning the gameplay, understanding enemy patterns, and improving your character, the experience becomes much more enjoyable. What initially seemed difficult starts to feel rewarding, and the game gradually becomes easier to appreciate and have fun with.

Review & Genre Analysis: Elden Ring Elden Ring is an action RPG created by FromSoftwareAG, and falls under the categorie called “Soulslike”. Essentially, it means it’s a difficult game where the player can choose a lot by themself and don’t realy get a direction set. But it’s also what makes it so interesting. In Elden Ring, you get to explore a huge open world called the Lands Between. The catch tho is that, it does’ t tell you what to do. Essentially, you are left to explore and fight enemies on your own. At first, it can get quite confusing, but it is also quite nice to be free to choose your own path. The combat is possibly the most important part of Elden Ring. You cann’t just press buttons and expect to win. You have to get to know your enemies and be quite patient. On top, you will lose many times, but it’s part of the experience. Each time you lose, you will also learn something new, making it quite satisfying when you finally beat an enemy. A big difference between Elden Ring and older games like Dark Souls (1-3) is, that it is an open world designed game. This means that if you are unable to beat a boss, you can leave and come back later when you are stronger. This is possibly why it is a bit easier to play. Compared to the other “soulslike”-games it’s completely up to you where to go and who to fight in which order. The graphics are also a prompt where elden ring got a lot of compliments from players as well as form judges. The game has a lot of variety in the world, such as castles, forests, dark caves, and it all looks detailed and realistic. The enemies are also creative and, in some cases, a bit creepy. The music is good, but it’s not too distracting. Sometimes it can get a bit overwhelming tho because when there are bosfights or special enemies the muisc get catchy and pushy. However, the game is not perfect. There is no real quest log, and it’s not clear what you're supposed to do at some points, which can get a bit frustrating. It’s also worth mentioning that, if you have not played a Soulslike game before, this might not be the best game to start with. There are often too many questions for the player if you aren’t used to soulslike games. Therefore it might be better to start with a game which has more guidelines and quests to follow along. Considering the game genre, it’s clear that Elden Ring is a good game in the Soulslike genre because it improves the genre and shows the direction in which it can be taken. It does this by including the original elements of the Soulslike genre, such as difficulty and abstract storytelling, but it also includes an open-world element, which makes the game more accessible and makes it one of the best in recent years. In conlcuision it can be siad that, Elden Ring is a great game for a certain type of player but may not be the game for everyone. It’ s for people who enjoy a challenge and like to explore on their own. People who enjoy a clear direction and a relaxed experience might not get satisfyed here.

There’s a point where praise starts to sound exaggerated, but Elden Ring somehow pushes past that and still earns it. This isn’t just another great RPG. This is FromSoftware’s opus magnum. The kind of game that makes you wonder how anything is supposed to top it. In an era where nearly every developer is chasing the open-world formula (especially after The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild) Elden Ring doesn’t just follow the trend, It perfects it. The world isn’t just big for the sake of being big, it’s ALIVE. Every direction you move in, there’s something waiting; whether it’s a hidden dungeon, a terrifying boss, a new weapon, or some quiet detail that pulls you deeper into the world. Every bridge, every ruin, every mountain, every empty-looking field somehow has purpose. Exploration doesn’t feel like a checklist, it feels like curiosity that is constantly being rewarded. And at its core, this is what makes Elden Ring such a perfect RPG. You don’t need to have played any previous FromSoftware titles. You don’t even need to fully understand the story. You could skip every line of dialogue and still walk away with an unforgettable experience. But if you do choose to engage with it? That’s when the game opens up even more. The lore, the characters, the side quests, they’re all layered in a way that rewards attention without demanding it. You’ll find yourself actually caring about what happens next, listening more closely, exploring more thoroughly, and getting invested in a world that never forces you to care, but makes you want to. Combat is where the game truly tests you. Bosses are brutal, sometimes frustrating to the point of disbelief and broken controllers/keyboards, but beating them? That feeling never gets old. Every victory feels earned. Every new encounter makes you wonder not just how you’ll win, but what kind of fight it’s going to be. And the tools you’re given to face those challenges are just as impressive. Weapons, armor, spells, abilities, EVERYTHING feels handcrafted and meaningful. Whether you’re running a raw strength build, a dexterity bleed setup, or diving into magic, faith, or even dragon-based abilities, the variety is insane. Every build feels viable, and more importantly, fun. Visually, the game is just as powerful. The landscapes are massive and hauntingly beautiful. The lighting, the textures, the atmosphere, it all works together to create moments where you genuinely have to stop and just take it in. Everyone’s first screenshot is the Erd Tree after the elevator for a reason. The music elevates everything even further, turning already intense encounters into something unforgettable. This is the kind of game that doesn’t just pull you in, it CONSUMES your time without you realizing it. You’ll want to explore everything. Collect everything. Understand everything. And somehow, even after hundreds of hours, it still doesn’t feel like enough. With over 400 hours put into the game, most of that in pure, unmodded gameplay, it never once felt boring. And if you decide to go beyond that into the modding scene, you’re looking at hundreds of additional hours of fresh experiences layered on top of an already massive game. At full price, Elden Ring is more than worth it. The amount of content, the level of detail, and the sheer quality of the experience make it one of the best value games out there. So honestly? Stop reading the endless reviews. Stop scrolling through the million opinions. And just go play Elden Ring. Because this isn’t just one of the best games ever made. It might be the one everything else gets compared to from now on. Praise the Sun \o/ and go become an Elden Lord
