Maybe this is where I officially become the old guy yelling at games. Because somewhere along the way, “bigger” replaced “better,” and nobody seems to question it anymore. Elden Ring is what happens when you take every questionable idea during development and decide not only to keep it but double down on it. The real difficulty is genuinely in your effort to remember that you’re playing something critically acclaimed, because so much of the experience feels confused, stretched thin, or undercooked. I forced over 40 hours into this. Having played every mainline Souls game, I had to see it through. I wanted to know what the “final form” of this formula looked like. Now I know. The disappointment is as vast as the empty landscape, and the confusion is immeasurable. This isn’t a case of “you need a break from the game.” This is a case of needing a break because of the game because of its design, its systems, its world, and the constant feeling of randomness pretending to be depth. It’s not challenging in a meaningful way, it’s not rewarding in a satisfying way it just slowly drains you. Not from difficulty, but from repetition, confusion, and the sense that everything is just slightly off. You’re not playing a game anymore, you’re enduring one. And my patience ran out around the 40-hour mark. To put it front and center: The big selling point here is the open world. And like most open worlds, it proves a simple rule: scale does not equal quality. What you get isn’t a carefully crafted experience, but something closer to an “MMO from 2008 but with better lighting.” Vast, empty landscapes filled with enemies awkwardly standing around like they’re waiting for their shift to start. Half of them look like they spawned in five seconds ago, the other half like they forgot to despawn. Instead of the tight, interconnected level design that made earlier Souls games work, you now roam what feels like the Scottish highlands populated by idle mobs, copy-pasted assets, and the occasional enemy placed on a hill or in a ditch for dramatic effect. Not because it makes sense, just because. I can sense the confusion in the mobs themselves. Hollow soldiers guarding a broken cart. Patrols defending a handful of rocks in the middle of nowhere. Entire camps built around absolutely nothing of value. It feels less like worldbuilding and more like someone forgot to remove placeholder assets. Whatever themes were intended are completely lost, overwritten by sheer randomness. At times it feels less like exploring a world and more like wandering through a very expensive early-onset dementia simulator. To make this scale even remotely playable, the game introduces a mount. And this is where the domino effect really kicks in. The world is too big → you get a mount → encounters lose structure → enemies become filler → combat turns into drive-by hits or stamina management on horseback. What used to be deliberate level design is now replaced with wide open killing fields and loosely scattered content. Combat has also gone in a direction I personally can’t stand. After Dark Souls II, things have been getting faster and more “spectacle-driven,” but here it hits rock bottom. What used to be methodical combat is now closer to button mashing with extra steps. Most fights boil down to abusing dodge invincibility frames and hammering heavy attacks until something breaks (guard or poise). Repeat from start to finish. If that’s “skill,” then sure. To me, it feels more like exploiting a system than mastering one. Then there’s crafting, which might be the most pointless system in the game. Enemies rarely drop anything meaningful, materials are scattered everywhere with little thought for what, where, or why, and the whole system feels like it exists just to justify itself. You end up running around committing wildlife genocide deers, turtles, birds, rabbits just to craft items that could have easily been sold by a vendor. It adds nothing but menu clutter and busywork. And even when the game does give you loot, it quietly undercuts it somewhere else. Rune (souls) gain from regular enemies is so low that it might as well not exist. Your actual income comes almost entirely from bosses. Everything else either gives too little or takes too long to be worth the effort. So the usual gameplay loop “farm a bit, get stronger, try again” barely functions. There’s no real incentive to clear areas, no satisfying buildup of progress. If you’re underleveled, you’re not grinding your way up you’re waiting for the next boss payout. At times it feels like you’re more likely to grow bored than actually progress through effort. The core issue with the game: it constantly adds systems without improving the experience. More space, more mechanics, more items but less purpose. There are moments where you can see what the game could have been. But its dead and buried under repetition, filler, and design decisions that work against each other. Honestly, it’s almost worth playing just to witness how all these pieces somehow fit together into something so mediocre, so confused, so boring.

There are great games. There are masterpieces. And then there’s Elden Ring - a game that feels like a once-in-a-generation moment. And apparently not even Miyazaki's true ideal of a game. We do not deserve what this man and FromSoftware have for us. [h1] TL;DR [/h1] [h3]Pros:[/h3] -Massive open world: Seamless exploration with secrets everywhere -Freedom: Build, playstyle, and path choices are very flexible -Combat depth: Challenging, skill-based, and satisfying -Lore & atmosphere: Rich, mysterious world co-created by George R.R. Martin -Replayability: Multiple endings, bosses, and builds -Fantastic mods [h3]Cons:[/h3] -Difficulty spikes: Can be punishing for newcomers -Opaque mechanics: Some systems (stats, crafting, progression) aren’t well explained -Navigation: Open world can feel confusing without guidance -Sparse story clarity: Narrative is subtle; some may find it hard to follow -Extremely sparse sidequest story: Extremely difficult to follow side quests as a new player - narrative is extremely subtle, and NPCs randomly cark it if you don't meet their needs... -Terrible online/co-op play (the typical FromSoftware co-op experience) From the first step into the Lands Between, you realize something is different. There’s no rush, no pressure like the other installments from FromSoftware - just a vast, mysterious world stretching endlessly in every direction, quietly daring you to explore it with music in-hand blessing your ears. And when you do? It rewards you in ways few games ever have. Every hill hides a secret. Every ruin tells a story. Every unexpected encounter - whether it’s a wandering boss, a hidden dungeon, or a breathtaking new region - feels like it was placed there just for you to discover. This is freedom done right. Combat is the culmination of everything FromSoftware has learned over the years. It’s tight, punishing, and deeply satisfying. Whether you’re a spellcaster raining destruction from afar, a heavily armored juggernaut trading blows, or a nimble rogue dancing around enemies - every playstyle feels powerful when mastered. And yes - it’s difficult. It will knock you down without hesitation. But unlike anything before it, it also gives you the tools to rise again. You can go somewhere different. Farm runes and level yourself to become unstoppable. Or you can do it the old fashion way - spawn, die, spawn, die, spawn, die... Explore somewhere else. Get stronger. Come back wiser. Victory is never handed to you, but it’s always within reach. The boss has to defeat you forever, but you only have to defeat it once. The world design is nothing short of breathtaking. Not just in scale, but in intention. The Lands Between feel alive, ancient, and deeply interconnected in ways that constantly surprise you. And the moments… the bosses… the music… Standing before something that seems impossible, failing, learning, adapting - and then finally overcoming it. That feeling? Elden Ring perfects it. Flaws? Minor ones exist - but they fade into irrelevance compared to what this game achieves as a whole. And just when you thought Elden Ring had already said everything it needed to say… the DLC arrives and somehow raises the bar again. Shadow of the Erdtree isn’t just an expansion - it’s a statement. It’s almost absurd to say this, but the DLC alone sparked “Game of the Year” conversations… again. Not for a new title. Not for a sequel. For an expansion. That’s the level we’re dealing with here. It feels less like extra content and more like a second masterpiece layered on top of the first. And then there’s the difficulty. This is where it hits. If the base game gave players more freedom and flexibility to overcome challenges, the DLC reminds you - very quickly - where this series comes from. The enemies are relentless. The bosses? Absolutely ferocious. Every fight feels like it demands your full attention, your best build, and your willingness to adapt or be crushed. Let's not give people flashbacks of pre-nerf Consort Radahn. That old feeling is back. That “I don’t know if I can do this” moment. Followed by the attempt. The failure. The adjustment. And eventually… the triumph. The world itself is darker, denser, and even more haunting. There’s a weight to everything here. A sense that you’re stepping into something forgotten and dangerous. Exploration feels tense again. Every corner could be your next mistake… or your next breakthrough. And somehow, even after hundreds of hours in the base game, it makes you feel small all over again. That’s not easy to do. Most DLCs add content. This one redefines the experience. It reminds you why you fell in love with Elden Ring in the first place, then pushes you further than you expected to go. 10/10 – A landmark achievement. Play it. Experience it. Remember it.

I was disappointed with the character creation because the visuals look dated, and ugly. I spent an hour trying to get a likeable face, but that hour was not an enjoyable one because it felt like a battle to see meaningful changes. After starting the actual game, the cutscenes were stills not even animated stills or in-game video. A minor gripe, but it undeniably conveys the feel of an indie production, not a AAA title—which is not OK if the goal is to achieve AAA standards. The interface looks and feels like it was made circa 1998, you know, that era where developers hadn't really had time or experience to figure out what works well for an interface system. The tutorial was frustrating because explanation text boxes kept popping up, not centered properly with quickly written text, child-like, noob indie feel. Incomprehensible clickable "messages" scattered about the environment, and some kind of ridiculous voting system for those messages popping up in this horrible interface, was torture. The combat system while probably not terrible, does not have a fluid feel such as can be experienced in games like Oblivion, Skyrim, Ghost of Tsushima, or Guild Wars 2 among others. It felt very slow, clunky and out of sync. Enemy combat behavior was too simple, the animations merely rudimentary, and their death sequences uninteresting. I didn't get past two hours, but, after checking with Gemini AI, apparently there are no populated towns or "complex" NPCs--the likes of which can be found in the aforementioned games. From the outset, with a story that felt dull and barely existent along with an indie-feel to most other elements: interface, visuals and combat, I could not find a reason to continue, and so I requested—and received—a refund. Thank you.

TL DR: Play ds3 or something For a game that has received such high praise I did not expect to become so dissapointed. The game is praised for breaking the curse of bloated open world games, yet falls into the same pitfalls. Every hour feels more boring than the last. Open world and progression The first hours of this game feels fresh and exciting. There is lots to explore and the scenery is stunning, yet this feels like the most the game has to offer. Past a certain point the world loses its appeal, due to the insane amount of repeat bosses, dungeons and ruins. This is a shame, because there is a good amount of unique and fun bosses and dungeons, but the amount of trash I have to wade through the get there is painful. This is made worse by the fact that bosses who feel unique and powerful are casually thrown back into the game when the devs feel the need to fill their massive open world. Not only does the game bore me with repeat dungeons, but they actively ♥♥♥♥ on any good experience I just had. The progression system in this game seems to actively contradict what it means to be an "open world". In Dark Souls 3 the progression was pretty straight forward. You complete an area, you get stronger, you get to the next area and the enemies have also gotten stronger. It is a linear game, so thats what you would expect. Yet elden ring copies this formula with little concern for how this would affect the open world experience. Early on it is established that the player has to explore the world. Both the Iron Sentinel and Margitt teaches this to the player as if you go fight them as early as possible you'll be massively underleveled. This does not reward exploration, this punishes the player for not doing so. Whatever I'll level up. I explore some stuff, get stronger, complete stormveil castle. After this the game takes a weird turn for me. I go to Liurna of the lakes, but by doing so Caelid becomes massively underleved. Atleast games like the witcher 3 tell the player what the recomended level is when such an artifical barrier is set up. There is fun to be had in the world, yet that is only when the game feels like dark souls 3. The so called legacy dungeons are fun, precisely because they took what fromsoftware had mastered from previous releases. It is almost like this is because the game becomes more linear, the enemies are more tighly packed, healing becomes restricted creating tension and consequences, and because the map becomes both interesting to traverse and look at. Oh wait, that is what every other fromsoft game is known for. Combat This franchise has become synonymous with difficulty. It is dissapointing to see fromsoftware forget why that difficulty was interesting in games like ds3. The whole reason is that the difficulty felt fair and that the player could overcome it by reasonable means. Fundamentally this game still feels like ds3. The same core mechanics are still here yet the bosses have become more agile, more dyanmic, they have more delayed attacks, more aoe attacks and overall more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The whole point of the game is that I can take all that to the face and learn something, yet on every new run the boss decides that it can chain another combo in a series of absolute tomfoolery, where if I even dare try to get a light attack in, I get a stick shoved straight up my ass. The fact that the AI can chain up attacks like this promotes a passive style of play, where I am left up eating scraps when the boss eats a 9 course dinner. Then there are attacks that are just completely ridicuouls. Rykard's earthquake, Malenia's waterfowl and tons of other aoes or grab attacks. Their timings range from delayed, arbitrary or non existant. This game is incredibly insistent upon difficulty for difficulty's sake. The game has tons of gimmicky ways to offset difficulty, but I find them to be just that, a gimmick. Summons are at the core of this, yet the game fails to convince me that it was balanced around them. Bosses becomme laughably easy when using them, since they can usually only target one at a time. Gimmicks only push the problem back. Why are they needed? Are fights too hard or just not rewarding enough when using the core mechanics? Story and narrative Despite the harsh words above, this has to be weakest part of the game. There are some fun moments to be had exploring and there are fun bosses to be fought, however the answer as to why the player is doing this seems non existant. This game borrows the same principles from soft have worked with. That is to tell a vague story with item descriptions. In elden ring it works less than ever. In dark souls 3 the vague story could be tied to the very themes themselves. The world felt hollow, because it literally was. Humanity was fading away and that was the motivation for the whole journey. Elden Ring shares this same broken world premise, yet struggles to captivate me. Why does the player blindly follow the path to become elden lord when no one else does? Even when this game wants to pretend that it is a good rpg, every quest follows the same trends: blindly gain persons trust, go fetch item, npc dies or you kill them. This is made worse by the fact that I need a wiki glued to my ass to find the npcs in this vast world. Every quest feels impersonal, becuase they are. Joining volcano manor and killing other tarnished holds no weight. Killing demigod after demigod changes nothing, nothing happens to the world and no one acknowledges my effort. There is no change troughout the plot, the story is still the same. Kill boss, collect the rune. If I had not played the first half and was put into the game, there wouldn't be much I missed in terms of the main story. People often state that this game isn't trying to tell a regular story. It wants to be vague and doesn't want to "handhold" you throughout. This feels strange when in the first 10 minutes I meet 4-5 npcs, who i will continue to see throughout their sidequests. The game wants to tell a obscure story, yet still wants to use npcs and dialogue in a traditional sense. This ends up being boring, because of the aforementioned tropes. The ingenuity of fromsoft storytelling, seems to lie in the item descriptions. They tell the lore of various parts of the world, but I couldn't bother. 1 Why should I care when the lore so often depicts random "fun facts"; Why should I care about the backstory of some random enemies when the narrative is still the same? Kill, loot and move on. 2 The act of stopping to read is a lazy way to utilize the video game medium. If read dead 2 and the like get critique for being too much like a movie, then elden ring wants to be too much like a book. I feel like just observing the community is a great affirmation of item descriptions being bad: Why do people watch lore videos, when you can play the game? A game that supposedly fixed open world gaming still commits the same mistakes. A game that wanted a rawer experience with less map markers outsourced the problem to the wikis. A game that was supposed to be the newest iteration of souls combat feels derivative and cheap. In the end this game struggles from wanting to cater to as many as possible: Being open world to challenge the AAA market and being more difficult to cater to the loudest fromsoft fans, but to make the game feel fair it is offset with gimmick summons. I would not recommend this game simply because there are better fromsoft games.

If I could give this game a "mixed" I absolutely would. This game is utterly fantastic. It has incredible environments and exploration, so good that that aspect alone carried me through 3 playthroughs. The boss fights, when done well, are extremely rewarding and feel like a hard yet fair challenge. It's everything else that drags it down for me. The terrible boss fights are *really* terrible. So much so that they drag down the experience for a while. Also, the quest design in this game is bafflingly bad. They tried to keep the vague, cryptic quests of the original Souls games and put them in an open world format where 90% of players will likely never return to the specific area the NPC decided to move to. Of course there are hints to where they've gone, but unless you've got a notebook keeping track of it there's no way to follow all 10-20 questlines organically. That said I don't think the quests even add much to the game and you can beat the game without progressing any of them. There's a lot to love about this game, and even more to learn to love. Yet the downsides can't be ignored. This game is a trailblazer yet suffers from some obvious flaws that just kinda carried over from past games. I guess whether or not you should buy this game is how much you're able to tolerate and if the highs of this game resonate with you, which it definitely did for me.

Elden Ring isn’t just a game—it’s an unforgettable experience that completely redefines what open-world action RPGs can be. From the moment you step into its vast, hauntingly beautiful world, you’re met with a sense of wonder and discovery that very few games have ever achieved. Every landscape feels meticulously crafted, from golden fields stretching into the horizon to eerie, shadow-drenched ruins that whisper stories of a forgotten age. The level of freedom is astonishing. You’re not just following a path—you’re forging your own legend. Whether you choose to charge headfirst into danger or carefully explore every hidden corner, the game rewards curiosity in ways that constantly surprise and delight. There’s always something new to uncover: a hidden dungeon, a breathtaking vista, or a powerful piece of gear that completely changes your playstyle. Combat is nothing short of phenomenal. It strikes a perfect balance between challenge and satisfaction, demanding skill, patience, and strategy. Every victory feels earned, and every defeat pushes you to improve. The sheer variety of weapons, abilities, and builds allows for endless experimentation, making each player’s journey uniquely their own. What truly elevates Elden Ring, though, is its atmosphere. The world feels alive with mystery and history, even in its quietest moments. The subtle storytelling, combined with a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack, creates an emotional depth that stays with you long after you put the controller down. In every sense, Elden Ring is a masterpiece. It’s bold, ambitious, and executed with incredible precision. Whether you’re a longtime fan of challenging RPGs or completely new to the genre, this is a game that demands to be experienced. It doesn’t just meet expectations—it exceeds them in ways that feel almost magical.

A Love Letter to the Lands Between If you are a fan of SoulsBorne games and you’re wondering if this is worth it—stop wondering. Get this game. It is an absolutely beautiful, massive masterpiece. To me, it feels like the ultimate "Greatest Hits" collection of FromSoftware; a perfect blend of the Dark Souls trilogy’s depth, the haunting atmosphere of Bloodborne, and the sharp DNA of Sekiro. What makes it special: True Freedom: The game gives you a little nudge at the start, but then the leash is off. You are free to roam a breathtaking open world filled with more items, gear, spells, and secrets than you’ll know what to do with. The Challenge: The bosses and enemies are legendary. Every corner of the map offers a new challenge that feels rewarding to overcome. A Quick Note for the Co-Op Travelers: If you want to experience this journey with friends without the constant threat of invasions, do yourself a favor: search for the "Seamless Co-op" mod and play your way: It deactivates the standard Easy Anti-Cheat (which, let’s be honest, you don't really want on your system anyway) and puts you on a private "server." You can set a password for your group and toggle invasions on (1) or off (0) as you see fit. Ignore the Gatekeepers: You aren't harming the official servers or bothering anyone else’s experience. If anyone tries to tell you off for choosing not to be invaded, let them cry. Those aren't "real" Souls players. Real players want you to enjoy the game. Bottom line: This is an incredible journey. Play it how you want, enjoy the world, and be happy. See you in the Lands Between!

Elden Ring was my first FromSoft game. I play very few 3rd-person action games, and very few open-world RPGs, so I was way out of my element. However, by the end of my 225-hour playthrough, I loved it! Elden Ring was an epic adventure unlike any other I have played. I played without using the wiki or any external guide other than seeking occasional hints from a trusted friend. My favorite aspect of Elden Ring was the world and level design. The towering verticality, the epic scale of it, the huge vistas. I loved how the world was designed to showcase views of faraway castles and mountaintops, enticing me to discover and explore them. I loved the way the dungeons and sub-areas twist and wind on themselves, making clever use of vertical space. Exploration is one of my favorite activities in video games, and Elden Ring was a dark wonderland of discovery. There were constant surprises waiting in every tunnel, behind every castle wall, atop every rugged peak. The 3rd-person melee combat was very unfamiliar to me. It was brutally difficult initially, but I used loading screens tips to gradually learn some mechanics. I lacked the dexterity and experience to properly time melee attacks, dodge-rolls, and blocks, so I brute-forced my way through much of the game by attacking with ranged spells and running away. Even if I never got very good at the combat, I was glad that levelling up my character had a meaningful impact on my success. Whenever I was not able to progress in a certain area because the enemies were too hard, I could always go somewhere else to make progress, then come back later with better stats and gear. This was a huge upside to the open-world design. Ultimately, the game felt tough but (mostly) fair. It did provide many conveniences to the player -- for example, never losing my loot, and using the same currency for levelling up as for purchasing at merchants. The generous abundance of instant-travel points and the tireless double-jumping super-horse made map traversal easy. My least favorite aspect of Elden Ring was the unwieldy feeling of having to manage character animations constantly. Getting smacked by an enemy while my character slowly did his "stand up" animation. Some animations queued; some didn't. Some animations could be cancelled, some couldn’t. Not being able to block because I'm still doing a spell cast animation. Going off a cliff because my horse had to do its "turning around" animation. And most fatal of all, the unstoppable "I'm out of mana potions" animation. Elden Ring features a quest system which is very obscured to the player (i.e. no quest log, no quest markers) but is also very conditional (i.e. there are unseen conditions determining whether a quest can even be started, progressed, or completed). Unfortunately, this is a very player-unfriendly combination. I appreciate games which don't hold the player's hand, and as such I kept a very large and thorough document about leads and mysteries I wanted to pursue. However, I found instances where a quest character did not appear where they were supposed to, because I hadn't reached some other unrelated checkpoint yet. Or reaching some unrelated checkpoint caused the quest character to not appear, despite the insistence to the contrary of some clue or dialogue I had found. There were also instances where reaching a destination was not tied to any intuitive geographical progression or clues, but by finding a teleport from one arbitrary location to another. Anyway, those gripes aside, Elden Ring was an incredible journey, full of struggles and triumphs. Exploring and discovering this dark and mysterious world was fully absorbing, and I felt incredibly accomplished when I finally reached the end.

Elden Ring is arguably the most accessible From Software title, mixing the polish of Dark Souls 3 with a true open world as seen in other popular AAA studio RPGs, rather than the 3D Metroidvania worlds seen in Dark Souls 1-3, Sekiro, and Bloodborne. This gives the player an even higher degree of freedom to explore the world. If something is too tough, Elden Ring expects the player to just go do something else and come back later. The boss design is among the best in FromSoft's entire catalogue, up there with Sekiro and Dark Souls 3, and exceeding both at times. Overall, Elden Ring is a masterpiece and anyone who is even a little curious about it should give it a try.

After a thorough 230 hour playthrough, I find it dishonest not to give this game the tagline it deserves. MASTERPIECE. Objectively and subjectively. Don't let the soulslike snobs discourage you. This game is HARD, no question about it. But for that same reason is so rewarding. No run is the same, not even close. The world is massive and dense. There is so much to explore and to do. The gameplay is smooth and addictive in the best way possible. So many build possibilities, so many cool weapons. There are only two things that keep it in third place for me. One is the fixed frame rate. 60 is enough on paper, but only if it's guaranteed. And in my experience it wasn't. I know they do it for stability reasons, but uncapped frame rate in 2026 seems like a no brainer to me. The second reason is the story. I'm a kind of guy that appreciates a non-linear story that doesn't necessarily spoon-feed you the details. But I barely cared about the story here unfortunately. I just wanted to play the game, which is of course a good thing because it's a GAME at the end of the day. However, that's why Cyberpunk 2077 takes second place for me, because it's equally fantastic on the gameplay front, but the story is way more human and relatable. The first place is held by Sekiro, which aside from the perfect gameplay, in my opinion has the best balance between mystical and human elements. Nonetheless, Elden Ring deserves its 2022 GOTY title and much more, because it has achieved something incredible. As a 25 year old man, I rarely find a game that I cannot put down. I'm happy to say that this is one of those cases. I totally recommend it for every video game enthusiast, even the more casual ones. I say give it a shot.

1000+ Hours and Still Going Strong (Overwhelmingly Recommend!) I originally planned to write this review after my first playthrough, which took me about 100 hours. I took my time exploring every corner of the Lands Between, doing side quests, hunting for items, and soaking in the world. But the game hooked me so hard that I kept coming back for more runs, waited for the Shadow of the Erdtree DLC, crushed its bosses, grabbed every achievement, and now I’m sitting at over 1000 hours. This is easily one of the best games ever made—perfect for both newcomers dipping their toes into FromSoftware titles and veteran Souls players looking for something fresh. What stands out most is the incredible freedom and flexibility. The open world lets you go almost anywhere from the start, tackle challenges in whatever order you want, and experiment with literally hundreds of build possibilities. Weapons, spells, ashes of war, talismans—everything combines in ways that keep the game feeling new even after hundreds of hours. After hitting around 700 hours on vanilla runs, I dove into mods. Adding new weapons, quality-of-life tweaks, and especially the Seamless Co-op mod completely transformed the experience. It makes co-op smooth and unrestricted—no more summoning limits or session drops. I got my friend back into the game, and now we’re running modded playthroughs together, exploring, fighting bosses, and having a blast. The modding scene is super accessible, and co-op has never been easier or more fun. Whether you’re playing solo, grinding for that perfect build, or teaming up with friends, Elden Ring delivers an unmatched sense of discovery, challenge, and beauty. The world is breathtaking, the combat is deep and rewarding, and the sense of accomplishment when you finally take down a tough boss is unbeatable. If you’re on the fence, just buy it. 1000+ hours later, I’m still finding new things to love. Masterpiece. 10/10, would get invaded by again. This version keeps your authentic voice and story but makes it more readable, punchy, and appealing to other Steam users. It highlights the strengths (freedom, replayability, mods/co-op) while sounding genuine from someone with massive playtime. Feel free to tweak any details!

The peak of the Soulsborne series, a game that takes everything From Software has done to the next level and delivers a rich and deeply satisfying experience. The gameplay is very similar to Dark Souls, but much more expansive, with a wide variety of unique builds that guarantee a completely different playstyle depending on your weaponry. On top of that, there’s the open world, which is Elden Ring’s biggest standout feature compared to other From Software games, and it’s sensational. The game makes you want to explore every corner of the map and rewards you generously for finding secrets and dungeons, offering excellent game design in both open areas and castles, dungeons, and cities. Another major highlight in Elden Ring is the boss fights; even though many are repetitive, the ones that matter to the game are simply the epitome of what can be called epic—Malenia, Radahn, Dragonlord Placidusax, and many others that simply leave you speechless with the intensity of the battle. Even though I got beaten up a lot, I couldn’t get angry or sad about the defeat, since they were so cool that I always had fun trying again. The game’s art is vibrant; you can really see the effort the art directors put into creating such a masterpiece. The colors are bold and perfectly capture the setting, and the structures and designs are pure art—a real feast for the eyes. And along with great visuals, we have an incredible soundtrack that, even though I don’t consider it quite as memorable as those in the other games, is still very good and immerses you in the game’s medieval atmosphere. Elden Ring is almost a perfect game—the pinnacle of what years of game development and refining ideas could achieve—and a game that leaves a mark on your life. It’s only not better than Bloodborne because I’m stubborn and I really love it.

Can't believe I'm saying this...but it's finally over. It's taken me well over a year, well over 100 hours, multiple lengthy hiatuses, and lots of outside help to finish my first playthrough, but I finally did it. And it was worth it. The high you get from beating really difficult boss after several or even dozens of attempts simply cannot be easily replicated. First off, I had never and still have never played any traditional "Dark Souls" games as of this writing, so your mileage may vary if you're already familiar with that game series and genre. Imagine, if you will, an impossibly large open world that's bigger than Breath of the Wild, with way more darkness and depression than Twilight Princess and Majora's Mask combined. Unlike most RPG's you may have played, there's no journal, no quest log, nor dialog history. So that makes keeping track of quests and storylines difficult if not impossible unless you have an eidetic memory or use pen and paper to keep your own notes, or like me just used the Elden Ring wiki when all else fails. And compared to how vast this game is, there's comparatively few NPC's to interact with, and very few "quests" in the traditional sense. You may not even notice you're in the middle of a quest. To add to the difficulty, there's no save scumming or reloading here; you're stuck with every choice you make, no matter how mundane or incidental. There's also arguably no pausing in this game either, certainly not when you're in combat, so plan accordingly. And the game explains very little to you, including some mechanics that people only figured out much later after the fact through data mining. I was advised to look up a character build that I wanted to target in advance, otherwise this game could have been too difficult if not impossible to complete. While doing so takes some of the mystery out of the game when it comes to truly customizing your own character, I learned upfront that some stats are completely wasted depending on the weapon and playstyle you want to use. In my case, "strength", despite what the name suggests, was not needed as much as stats like dexterity for increasing damage with the weapons I wanted to use. Thankfully, there's a mechanic later on to re-spec your character so you can theoretically re-spec into a completely new character build mid-playthrough if you want to change things up. I took advantage of this late game once I unlocked some particular weapons. Admittedly, the "blink and you miss it" part of this game gets really obtuse sometimes. One quest I was doing requires you to pay attention to options available at a very specific grace (basically a save point), and another quest I was only able to continue after paying attention to a very casual reference in an NPC's dialogue. So don't be ashamed to look up where NPC's can be found during their questline, as this world is so vast it is quite probable that you completely miss them otherwise, unless for some crazy reason you desire to do playthrough after playthrough in this game all on your own. At least the New Game+ is an option once you finish your first playthrough and I believe ever subsequent playthrough afterwards. Make sure you have some sort of ergonomic way of playing this game, otherwise you'll wreck your finger joints. I used a HORI PS4 first person shooter controller. There's enough replay value to this game to warrant more playthroughs...one day. Maybe I'll even get the DLC for this game as well. But after experiencing what this game had to offer, I just need a really long nap.

The game is both amazing and miserable in equal measure. If you like immersive dark fantasy open worlds with strong environmental story telling, there's a lot to love. As a role playing sandbox, the exploration is unmatched. The downside is, the moment to moment gameplay can be straight up hostile. Encounters feel deliberately mean spirited with enemy swarms, traps and intentionally frustrating set ups around environmental hazards just to ruin your day. Even if you're having a great time with it, the game feels like it wants you to be having a bad one which can be exhausting over long stretches. That being said, the artistry is incredible and the experience can be just as fun as it is miserable. It's up to you whether that trade-off works. If you're looking for a solid RPG and don't mind being personally victimized along the way, it's worth a try.

I played Demon’s Souls years ago and came to Elden Ring after finishing Tainted Grail. I was expecting a challenging 3rd person Action-RPG but spent my first 20+ hours feeling like I just wasn’t connecting with it before I realized that in spite of its massive open world, skill leveling, and item looting, it’s really more comparable to a NES game than something like Skyrim. Sure, it gets compared to Zelda but it’s more like Zelda II than the newer releases. However, I’ve come to think of it more like Super Mario Bros. (meets Ninja Gaiden). You’re going to die. A lot. While there’s an overarching story, it’s secondary to the gameplay and there’s not one way to play, so whether you want to try and collect every “coin”, find all the secrets, or just race to the end - it’s your game to play however you’d like. Also, don’t overthink the characters and creatures you encounter. Some are there to advance the story but everything else is an extension of the game’s mechanics and exist to be a challenge and/or exploited (rune farming is basically bouncing on the last turtle in 3-1 to get all the lives). I’m now 60’ish hours in and although it wasn’t what I thought I was getting into, I’m glad that I stuck with it. While they’re both dark fantasy games set in a broken world, it’s basically the inverse of Tainted Grail which was a very immersive story driven experience with decent gameplay. Elden Ring is a gameplay driven experience with a decent story. It may look like a modern game but it has the heart of a retro experience. Or at least that’s my 40 years of gaming impression.

Elden Ring is one of the most beautiful and difficult open-world games I have played. It's one of those games that you will never regret buying. Elden Ring offers an extremely detailed and atmospheric open world, filled with hundreds of hours of gameplay. Anything from random enemy encounters to way too overpowered boss encounters that will make you sit on the edge of your seat. As with other games from FromSoftware, the difficulty can be challenging, but it gives you a large selection of tools to help you along, like the option to summon NPCs, creatures, and even other players. And the option to venture out into the Lands Between, into dungeons and places not even close to your level, makes it a place for a curious mind. Elden Ring's boss fights are probably what makes it one of the best RPGs in my opinion. Everything from the cutscenes, avatars, and voice acting during the boss fights makes it a memorable and truly epic experience. The different types of design and mechanics from boss to boss are what keep the combat exciting throughout the journey. And with a deep and incredibly fascinating lore, if you take the time to understand it, and several different endings, it really is a game of the decade. Few games manage to create such a vast world while still keeping exploration meaningful and rewarding. In short terms, "Elden Ring is a masterpiece." Final verdict: 10/10, five stars, and so on.

I thought I would only play Elden Ring for a little while, like other games, but it turned into one of those games where you look up and it's 3 a.m. and you're still fighting the same boss over and over. I was really bad at first. I didn't know what I was doing, so I just walked around Limgrave and got killed by everything, even the tree sentinel. The game, in a strange way, teaches you to be patient. Every death teaches us something, even if it seems unfair at the time. Malenia was my first real wall. I fought her with two random people in co-op, and for some reason, we killed her. I went back later and did it again, mostly by myself with mimic tear, but the mimic died after about 30 seconds, so the fight turned into a long 13-minute duel. I used comet azur sometimes, but I kept missing it, so most of the fight was just me trying to stay alive and slowly wear her down. After that, I tried out a lot of different builds. In the end, I had a dual katana bleed setup with rivers of blood and uchigatana with seppuku. That build is crazy once it gets going. When the bleed procs, bosses just melt. Before that, I spent a lot of time farming runes at Mohgwyn Palace, where I killed Albinaurics with the sacred relic sword Golden Wave. At some point, I realized that I had basically become an albinauric killer. I also aimed for 100% achievements on Steam, which required me to find all of the bosses and legendary weapons and spells. I nearly started a new run because the bolt of gransax is missable, but fortunately I was able to grab it. It took about 100 hours and a lot of trial and error to complete that final accomplishment, so it felt strangely emotional. This is the most rewarding game I've ever played, but it can also be cruel, confusing, and unfair at times. If you persevere long enough, you gradually transition from feeling completely destroyed by everything to feeling like a true boss.

Writing a review for such a generational game is really hard, especially because I don't share the common sentiment that Elden Ring is one of the best games of all time. The gameplay is fine, it manages to be as polished as Bloodborne's or Sekiro's while keeping (and surpassing by far) the build and weapon variety of the Dark Souls trilogy. However, I quickly grew tired of the countless ganks, infinite combos, delayed attacks and insane tracking that the game likes to throw at you at every corner. Another thing I'm not a huge fan of is the open world. While it's far from a generic empty AAA slop open world, it still introduces a lot of "padding" to the experience. Most of the items you find on the ground are just boring crafting materials, most of the dungeons have the same generic copypasted bosses, etc. The open world also makes following NPC quests basically impossible without looking up their locations (because they often move to places you have already explored before starting their quest and have no reason to come back to). In general ER feels like a less tight and cohesive experience compared to DS or Bloodborne and has much more unnecessary bloat. The graphics and art direction department is probably the only one I can't complain about, most areas in the game are genuinely stunning and the colorful, saturated world of Elden Ring felt like a breath of fresh air after the desolate greyness of DS3. The music is not as good as previous FromSoftware titles imo, but that's a really high standard. Overall, Elden Ring was a mostly enjoyable experience with some highs and lows, and while it didn't resonate with me as much as the other FromSoft titles I've played, it was still definitely a net positive.

This is one of those games that will never make you regret buying it. Elden Ring offers incredible replayability, countless build possibilities, a massive open world, and hundreds of bosses and enemies to encounter. The diversity in this game completely blew my mind. There is an unbelievable amount of content packed into it, and every playthrough can feel different depending on how you approach the game. The boss fights are one of the strongest aspects of the game. The cutscenes, atmosphere, and voice acting during boss encounters make them feel truly epic and memorable. Every major boss feels unique, both in design and mechanics, which keeps the combat exciting throughout the journey. The difficulty scaling is also handled very well. Like other games developed by FromSoftware, the game can be challenging, but it gives you many tools to make things easier if you want. Using spirit summons such as Mimic Tear or Tiche can make difficult bosses much more manageable. The co-op system is also fantastic—many players in the community are very supportive and are willing to help others defeat bosses if they are struggling. One of the best parts of the game is exploration. The world of The Lands Between constantly rewards curiosity. When I first started playing, I thought only Limgrave, Weeping Peninsula, and Stormveil Castle were the main areas of the game. But after defeating Godrick and stepping into Liurnia, and later reaching Altus Plateau, I was shocked. I realized I hadn’t even explored 10% of the entire map. Besides the massive overworld, there is also a huge underground world with hidden places and mysterious locations. Exploring these areas feels magical and often leads to powerful items, secret bosses, and beautiful environments. Every cave, ruin, and catacomb usually contains something valuable that you can only discover by exploring. Another thing that makes the game special is the freedom it gives to the player. You can approach fights in many different ways—melee builds, magic builds, hybrid builds, or even your own creative builds like becoming an assassin or samurai. This flexibility is one of the main reasons the game has such strong replay value. If you ask me about the cons of the game, honestly there are almost none. Some players might say the story is not presented directly, but that is very subjective. The lore is actually incredibly deep and fascinating if you take time to understand it. In fact, the story and world-building feel so rich that they could easily inspire a movie or series. The only minor issue I faced was fall damage, which can sometimes be frustrating, but it’s manageable once you learn the map better. In my opinion, this game has top-notch graphics, music, characters, and gameplay. The soundtrack during boss fights is phenomenal and adds a lot to the tension and excitement. The game is also fairly well optimized, although it is locked at 60 FPS. Overall, Elden Ring feels like a once-in-a-generation gaming experience. Few games manage to create such a vast world while still keeping exploration meaningful and rewarding. It constantly surprises you with new locations, enemies, and secrets even after dozens of hours of gameplay. Final Verdict: 11/10 – A masterpiece of a game. Already my game of the decade. I will definitely buy the DLC in the future. This game is absolutely worth every penny.

Back in 2011 my friend got me to play Dark Souls. I loathed it. I had no comprehension of the game's stats, general level layout, or mechanics. I let myself be lead around by the nose and more or less gifted an electric zweihänder that I could barely lift to carry me along. Fast forward to 2022, this new Elden Ring game is being lauded as the greatest thing since sliced bread. And I was skeptical. It wasn't until a coworker, a silly man in his late 50s proudly declared that he was 'the Elden Lord', if he could beat it so could I. So I bought the game. I decided I wanted a faith/strength build as I quite adore the paladin archetype. So I picked that class- But I could not understand in the slightest what I was doing. I ran along and somehow ended up in Liurnia before I'd even seen a boss. One lobster chase later I was ready to put the game down and get back my money. Then my friend stepped in. He gave me simple instructions; "Pick wretch so that you are introduced to the game's mechanics slowly over time. Then, pick any direction and follow it in a straight line and see where your adventure takes you- It is after all an open world game." So I made a wretch, with literally nothing to lose but my precious loincloth and stick. I settled on my first objective, *find pants*. And so I left in a straight line heading east by north-east. I entered Caelid. Right at the gates I was greeted by the invader, Anastasia. I understood her move-set instantly, she was Maneater Mildred all-over. She killed me, several times. But in the end I got her- And I felt accomplished. I traveled further into Caelid and eventually came upon a merchant who sold me pants. There after I entered a divine tower and ran into a black flame cultist who flattened me. A bit flummoxed I returned to my friend. "You're certainly in the wrong area, return to the tutorial area and head due south.", he said. There I met Gronk the Magic Potato Dog- but I digress. I kept to this pattern, pick a direction and see what I find. Found my favorite weapon in the game, the iron cleaver, and thereafter I came to enjoy my goofy clueless romps across the Lands Between. I got into a pattern of never keeping runes on me- they would go to waste as I wasn't any good. And I kept at this, and eventually I beat the game. Then I beat it again, and again. Until I'd had all the achievements. I learned mechanics, that if you encounter an obstacle it can be overcome with just a bit of wit and preparation. And throughout I was joyful for Anastasia numerous returns. Though.... As someone who went through Mohg's fight twice without either macguffin I can say clearly, ♥♥♥♥ Mohg.

A game that expertly combines gameplay, narrative, visuals, and world building, making for an unforgettable experience overall. Whether you want to unravel the mysteries of a brutal fantasy world, have your skills tested in challenging yet fair combat, or escape to a place like no other, this game has you covered. Personally speaking, the main highlight of this game for me is its narrative and world building combined. You have your basic plots and characters, which are compelling and enjoyable in their own respects, but I love how a majority of this game’s stories are told through character dialogue, environmental storytelling, and item descriptions. Like one giant puzzle that can be completed and interpreted in a number of ways, with there being no “right” option to most in-game quandaries. Allowing for the game to have increased longevity, since the appeal of debating this games lore is likely to be the main appeal to this game. Decades down the line, at least. Along with making the world as a whole more interesting, as everyone who explores it gets to enjoy and see it in their own unique way. The only problem I have with this game is its multiplayer. It works great when you want to play with strangers and don't have to worry about the progress of others, but it can be a slog when trying to do a whole playthrough with friends and/or family. The way the in-game cooperative play currently works has tow major flaws, in my opinion. Firstly, the player who is summoned doesn't get any of the benefits and rewards (besides Runes, maybe, the duo main in-game currency and levelling up resource) when completing the host players boss or dungeon. Making it so that if both players want to progress at the same pace, they will effectively have to do each segment of the game twice or thrice, depending on how many people are playing together. Which, can make each part of the game played together feel more tedious and annoying for all players involved. Secondly, since you can only summon players for the specific parts of the game mentioned above, it effectively makes it impossible to play any open world parts of the game together. Though, given the loopholes some players have found, it would be more accurate to say unnecessarily convoluted. And, given how one of the main appeals to this game to most players, including myself, is its open world nature, you are heavily incentivized to not partake in a good percentage of this games content. At least, if you wish to play the whole game with your friends/family, that is. Which, be it intentional or not, is a pretty strange and poor decision in my opinion. The popular Seamless Co-Op mod does fix both of these issues, so I would highly recommend installing and using that if you wish to play this game with others. Besides the multiplayer, this game is a masterpiece, and is easily in my top three favourite games of all time currently. Thus, I would highly recommend all of those interested in buying and playing it to do so. It is well worth the price in my opinion.

[h1]Elden Ring is not hard. It is annoying.[/h1] There is a difference. A hard game tests timing, judgment, adaptation, and consistency. Elden Ring often tests patience instead. Too many fights are built around bosses flying to the other end of the arena, chaining disengages, or forcing long chases that add nothing except downtime. That is not difficulty. That is irritation. Even Miyazaki has described Elden Ring as being designed to reduce hard progress walls by letting players leave bosses for later and by making it easier to get help in multiplayer, and he has also said FromSoftware “expect” players to use outside help like guides and community knowledge. In other words, even the design philosophy seems to assume players will route around build problems instead of solving them strictly within their own build. That becomes a problem when the game counter-picks you. Want to play a Holy paladin? Fine, until the late game starts stacking major holy resistance on the exact bosses that matter most. Community strategy references for Radagon and Elden Beast routinely note heavy holy resistance, broad status immunity, and a practical push toward physical damage over many themed setups. And that gets to one of Elden Ring’s biggest issues: build fantasy is not evenly respected. Bleed and frost are allowed to feel explosive and rewarding, while poison often feels undertuned by comparison unless you build around very specific synergies. By the end, a lot of players are not expressing a build so much as learning which builds the game still permits. That imbalance is one reason so many discussions keep converging on bleed and frost as the stronger status options. The boss design has similar problems. People love to brag about the boss count, but the raw number is inflated by repetition. A huge number of “bosses” are reused, remixed, doubled up, renamed, downgraded into normal enemies, or upgraded from normal enemies into bosses. So yes, Elden Ring has a lot of bosses on paper, but in terms of truly memorable, one-off headliners, the number feels dramatically smaller. There is a reason one recurring criticism of the game is that the open world is stuffed with repeated encounters rather than consistently new ones. That repetition undercuts the game’s sense of wonder. When a “boss” is just something I already killed three times in a mine, a catacomb, and then later saw wandering around as a regular enemy, it stops feeling like a boss and starts feeling like recycled content with a health bar. The camera does not help. Large or hyper-mobile bosses have been a complaint since launch, and Elden Ring still has encounters where the camera is a bigger enemy than the moveset. Fire Giant, Elden Beast, and Maliketh are the obvious examples. If the boss is too large to read cleanly up close, or too erratic to track cleanly at medium range, then target lock becomes part of the problem instead of part of the solution. That is not a satisfying skill check. Then there is the final stretch. Radagon and Elden Beast do not feel like a final exam for the game’s build variety. They feel like a rejection of it. Radagon shrugs off or resists a wide range of things, and Elden Beast is notorious for broad status immunity and strong elemental resistance, especially to holy. The result is that many builds arrive at the finish line only to discover they are effectively nerfed for reasons that have less to do with player execution than with the damage types the game decided to invalidate. So what happens? A lot of players converge on the same practical answer: simplify the damage profile, lean physical, survive the chase, and work around the arena-wide movement. That is not build expression. That is funneling. Elden Ring is still a very good game. The world is striking, the art direction is exceptional, and when the combat clicks, it really clicks. But I am tired of people describing every frustration in this game as proof of brilliance. A boss sprinting away for the fifth time is not genius. A giant enemy breaking the camera is not genius. Copy-pasting bosses into caves and later turning them into normal mobs is not genius. Making entire archetypes feel invalid in the late game is not genius. That is not “hard.” That is annoying.

Quite good overall, though being open world both adds and detracts from it in huge ways. You get a huge world and beautiful sights and many environments, but very poor interconnectivity and all the usual open world problems. Even though it's Fromsoft and they're usually quite independent in how they design stuff, there are numerous things in ER which feel like they're only there because every other open world game does it. The pointless crafting, easy fast travel from anywhere, copy and paste caves/catcombs, fast movement on a mount, etc. Doesn't feel tightly designed at all. Thankfully they did avoid losing all identity and the map isn't littered with question marks. The world feels huge. But after a while it starts to compress because you wind up teleporting everywhere and never actually travel to places anymore. It's a conceptually flat, there is little of the intricate interconnectivity which Fromsoft is known for. Because of this there's little reason to revisit places. You don't need to and you don't really have time. I feel like the world should've been more creatively shaped at a fundamental level, like maybe some crazy spiral around the Erdtree. Being able to teleport anywhere when not in combat, being able to escape instantly with the horse, and the very high frequency of the teleport spots really takes away a lot of the danger from the game's open world. With little friction in moving from place to place, there is no real planning/survival aspect like Dark Souls has. Engaging with it is a bit dull aside from the pure exploration and beauty of it. It's shallow, like most open worlds. "Why is it always mushroom...?" And speaking of the horse... Torrent has no personality at all because it has no interactivity or world presence. You just teleport onto it instantly and then it disappears when you get off. A far cry from something like Shadow of the Colossus and Agro. Torrent isn't a companion but a movement mode. This looser integration of gameplay/world/narrative is pretty noticable compared with DS. ER feels more generic, with nothing like Humanity or hollowing or whatnot. The game is at its strongest when you're in an actual level. A castle, a city, a swamp, etc. Classic Souls stuff. The bosses are also great fun and a huge spectacle, though the difficulty can be a bit extreme at times because they do crazy high damage. There's plenty of praises to sing but I'm not going to bother lol Random thoughts: - Having to use an item to see player summon signs is silly. - Calling the different grades of smithing materials [1] [2] [3] [4] is pure dullardry. Just reduce the number of them and stick with shard/chunk/slab. Making it so fine grained is pointless and annoying. - My god I cannot keep these character names straight, I never stopped confusing them the whole 80 hours. They're just too similar and come up too infrequently. Melina, Malena, Maquela, Marika... Godfrey, Godwyn, which one was which again??? The story is spread out over such an expanse of gameplay time that I constantly forgot. - Despite being a new world, ER looks and feels very much like DS3. There are so many things that are obviously reused from DS3, from animations and attacks to environmental props and story themes, that at times it feels a bit ridiculous to call it a new world with a new name. But in other ways it does have its own identity so it's not too bad, just an odd feeling. - Left stick deadzone is absolutely terrible, just like Dark Souls 2. Fortunately I was able to fix this by adjusting the response curve in Steam Input. - Caelid looks like a No Man's Sky level (don't @ me)

Elden Ring stands as a seminal achievement in interactive myth-making. One thing this game does is encourage an approach to character progression. Whether you prefer the visceral, heavy-hitting cadence of a colossal sword or the distance of glintstone sorceries, the mechanical framework is amazing. The game really shines when you start experimenting with making hybrid builds, like mixing stats like Strength and Faith or Dexterity and Arcane to create a build that feels entirely personal. The lore is this game is really mind-blowing as it doesn't just hand you a plot, it sort of force you to piece together a tragic mystery of a broken world. As a "tarnished" which is sent into the world long after signifcant events occur, witnessing the aftermath of a war that fractured reality itself and creating a narrative depth it make the game feel both haunting and monumental. A game that truly earns its title of GOTY and will undoubtedly remain a cherished masterpiece for many.

The character designs and enviornments are beautiful, unique and interesting. The voice acting is just... incredible. [h2] The bad: [/h2] This section will be longer than the one above, that doesn't mean that Elden Ring is a bad game though. I just want to talk about this a bit more in-depth, at least as much as I'm able to. It's late. Spirit summons are this games ''''easy mode'''', and I think they're not very well thought through. Some spirit ashes are extremely overpowered and carry bad players through the game. Even some of the less OP ashes can carry you a little too much. YOU'RE here to fight the boss, not other people. I wish the system was reworked a bit to make it a bit more interactive, alongside some nerfs ofc. Same thing goes for general summons. Player summons are a different topic. The biggest issue with this game imo is that it focuses a bit too much on ''quantity > quality''. There's lots of weapons but many are outclassed, bad or just poorly balanced. There's many different dungeons to explore, but most of them look and feel the same. There's a whole lot of bosses to fight, but many are repeated encounters. Too much filler overall and it really brings this game down for me sometimes, coming from someone who explored the vast majority of this games available content. I think the tutorial should be improved to be less wordy. I'd like to have it be longer though and maybe have it teach the player some mechanics better. Not too much hand holding though, one of the good things about ER is that it (usually) doesn't hold your hand. Some other QoL changes would be nice, like having a pause screen, no input delay on rolls (would require some less restrictive input binding) and a couple of other things. I think some boss encounters weren't that fun / had more potential, but most I enjoyed. I wish some weapons had cooler AoW / some type of AoW interaction [spoiler] (Dragon Greatclaw having Endure as it's only AoW is criminal) [/spoiler]. Torrent feels underbaked and is a more boring way of fighting some bosses. Having to click on a menu to revive Torrent is also a... weird choice. Quest design is needlessly confusing and the game not showing you numbers for talismans is weird - aka the game needs a wiki and that's lame! [h2] Conclusion: [/h2] Elden Ring is a great game, but that doesn't hinder it's weaknesses from bleeding through... even bleeding a little much sometimes. I enjoyed it so much despite those weaknesses, it was absolutely worth playing.

A mighty open world beast of a game. That having been said, it plays less like Dark Souls 3 and more like a single player MMO RPG in which you explore big spaces, collect stuff, and then summon your phantom buddies for a raid boss. Trying to play it solo is doable, and fine if you like that, but much of Elden Ring's nuances as a combat loop are how mounted gameplay and summonable parties transform combat. If you forgo those, it plays like a less well paced version of Dark Souls 3. If you include them, it becomes a more unique and memorable experience. Also, this game is big. No, bigger than big. Bigger than bigger. It is simply biggest. As a result, having too much pride to use all your tools (magic, summons, Torrent,) in gameplay can very easily kill the pacing by having you get stuck on a boss. This game is too big for mindless completionism or stubberness if you are not actively enjoying those things throughout the playthrough. It's a game, play it how ever feels right in the moment and you will come to understand why it is a classic. If you try to treat it like Dark Souls 4, it will likely just feel like slower paced DS3. Big thumbs up overall.

Spectacle and buzzwords over substance. The open world is empty and repetitive, mostly just a time waster in between the real highlights of the game that they refer to as "legacy dungeons". Many parts of the world do look very good, but I would much prefer double the legacy dungeons which are generally well designed and engaging. The best this game ever felt for me was when I had a complete character in NG+2 and could just run past all the tedious open world stuff and not bother with any of the copy-paste dungeons or remote crevices where one useful item might be hidden. The game design is completely obvious, I feel no immersion because nearly every enemy and especially the bosses have been programmed based on the way players will react to them. Enemies hold their attacks for long periods of time or perform stilted combos designed to roll-catch and punish reactive or panicking players. Then there are large spectacle pseudo cutscene moves that are cool the first couple times and then just become boring and ruin the pace of the fight. None of them feel like an organic enemy in the world, just bare game design tuned to force rote memorization of their movesets or spectacle for the sake of it. I can appreciate the difficulty of it, but it ruins any kind of immersion or world-building for me. The story seems a level more depraved than any of the previous games, but you don't really have to pay attention to it. Overall a bad direction for the series and a major disappointment for me as a long time fan. I still like it better mechanically than Dark Souls 3 but find it to have less replayability because of Elden Ring's large scale making new character builds an incredible chore. The series has been on a downward slide since Bloodborne and this game is my exit point, I have neither purchased the DLC nor do I plan to in the future. There is plenty more that could be said, but its probably not worth it at this point. Some bonus gripes: Body Type 1 and 2 instead of male and female, expected from a game that is chiefly concerned with marketability, (buzzwords, flashy clips, difficulty memes) but still disappointing. Also as of March 2026, the game will not launch. It has an error after Easy Anticheat fails to initialize. I'm sure there is probably some sort of fix or workaround for this, but I now consider it a blessing that I was stopped from playing it again. I did a fresh install after not playing for year hoping to just mess around for a few hours and then it wouldn't launch making me realize immediately that I never want to play it again, and finally convincing me to put at least some of my thoughts on the game into a review.

Tl;dr Elden Ring is the best Souls game so far, it is very replayable thanks to its Ash Of War based gameplay. Elden Ring, which has an eye-catching art style, has greatly increased replayability by making it feel different every time it is played, thanks to the many Ash of War content it contains. Since the main motivation of Souls games is that they make you feel like you are improving even more as you play with a different build every time you play and fight bosses, I can say that Elden Ring is the one that does it best. There are two elements that can undermine replayability, one of them is farming items and the other is long runs. These two can undermine the feeling of replaying a bit, especially farming items, because if you research well enough in long runs, you will see that there is always a shortcut to your destination, but farming items is always torture no matter what you do. Open world design decision is so good for souls games. You're already ready for search new things and open world game design let you do what are you want. Overall Elden Ring is the best souls game you can play and replay. Good bosses, good music and awesome art style, what more could you want in a game?

Elden ring is a game that you cannot pause, even in offline mode. Every other aspect of the game is permeated with this same sort of smug, sickeningly arrogant design philosophy. It's a game that totally realizes its vision, but this vision is so far beyond awful it is genuine difficult to describe how bad it is. It's central thesis is that what is obscure, cumbersome, or difficult is good. And that's it, there are no other design considerations. The game is terrible at explaining itself. Towards the end of it there is an area with invisible enemies. You can't see them without an item that is found very, very far from this area. No one so much as hints to the player where the item is, or even that it exists. If you do stumble on it, the default stats display for the item tells you nothing about it being special. Buried in a different menu page that normally just contains item related lore is a brief message telling you the item lets you see invisible enemies. Just awful design. Staggering and being staggered by enemies is a *huge* part of the game. A weapon's stagger stat is probably more important than its ability to deal direct damage. Luckily, the equip menu displays this stat where it is easily viewable. Just kidding, there is no where in the game you can see this stat at all, for any piece of equipment, ever. At least you can see a stagger bar that shows you how close enemies are to having their stance broken. Just kidding, there's nothing like that anywhere in the game. But at least you can see a stagger bar for the player character. Just kidding...Well, you get it by now. Elden ring just feels so, so sickeningly bad to play. Player movement is ponderously slow, and there is a noticeable delay before the player executes any attacks. I just can't overemphasize enough how *unmotivated* the player character behaves as they lethargically, limply swing their weapon. And that's not even taking into account the restrictive stamina system. But, if you spend enough time leveling up endurance, you can eventually circumvent this problem. Just kidding, welcome to "soft caps". Far before you can increase your stamina to the point the game doesn't feel like a slog, you start getting massively reduced returns. Like, you can still put more points into endurance, but it only increases stamina by one measly point per level. In fact, Elden Ring mostly robs the player of feeling stronger as they level up. You can definitely find a lot of weapons, and those weapons can definitely be upgraded, but I've never seen a better example of illusory progression than the effect player attribures have in this game. Even endgame weapons that scale "well" with dexterity give something like a 0.33 percent increase in damage for every level of dexterity. There is also not even a remote semblance of different character attributes being balanced, the best build, for every type of character, is always one that emphasizes vigor to gain HP. Focusing on any other attribute instead is playing a challenge game. The worst thing about the game is how it generates difficulty. Remember how I told you that the player lacks any sort of agility? Well, the developers decided that meshed well with a lot of platforming and (usually lethal) fall damage. Enemies also have every movement related advantage that the player doesn't. In addition to turning invisible, they can charge, sprint, dodge quickly and energetically, teleport, and don't seem to care about stamina or MP. Another thing enemies do so often it I consider it to be the game's trademark, is attack the player from across the level with devastating ranged abilities. I'm talking about what basically amounts to artillery, and does tons of damage and knock the player down. And when I say "across the level" I don't just mean they aren't super nearby, I mean it is often genuinely difficult to figure out where these attacks are coming from because they originate so far away. My favorite terrible thing the game does is this: player attacks terminate when weapon swing arcs hit an obstacle. The game *meticulously* checks for these collisions when the player attacks. And so, when I ended up in combat with an enemy on the other side of a wall, I thought "ah, I'm safe, the game is super careful to check if obstacles block swings." And then the enemy attack totally ignored the wall and hit me anyway. Generating difficulty in games is both very easy and very hard. It's easy to put obstacles in front of the player, but hard to do it in a way that feels fair. Elden Ring feels like a game where the developers didn't come remotely close to understanding this, and instead generated challenge in the most lazy and uncreative way possible. It feels like the work of a self-absorbed amateur. There are so, so many more terrible things I could say about this game, but unfortunately I only have limited space.

Three times, I've tried to like this game. The internet makes such a big deal of it. Every time, I fail. The mechanics feel like they push back. And in some games, that works for it, forces you to wonder, to jiggle the handles, to test and begin picking a mystery apart. Here, it feels less like a mystery, and more like they're manufacturing confusion. Some of the arbitrary rules don't seem like they're grounded in the world, but in game balance, and there doesn't feel like there's more depth to some of them than that. The character gets clear signals that the player can't interpret without a lot of experimenting, and we don't know what that signal is. NPCs that should PROBABLY warn you that you'll die if you mishandle the stuff they give you, don't. And why? Because mystery, I guess. Corrupting the narrative to make it more mysterious, like a sitcom where the main character turns stupid when the plot needs him to misunderstand. I know it's probably a good game for the right kind of player. It's too popular not to have captured its own niche with skill. But I can't recommend.

Elden Ring is a perfect example of how an action RPG should be made. After several playthroughs, I can confidently say that it is one of the greatest games ever created. The amount of content in this game is astonishing. Visually, the game is beautiful, with pleasant graphics and incredible art direction. At times the game looks absolutely breathtaking. I still remember the first time I entered Liurnia of the Lakes after defeating Godrick. I spent minutes just standing there and taking dozens of screenshots. The same happened when I first visited Nokron, the Eternal City. The views were unforgettable. I also remember the first time I entered Caelid. The atmosphere there is completely different. The region immediately creates a powerful sense of danger and hostility, especially when you encounter the very unfriendly wildlife that inhabits that land. Every location feels magical and carefully designed. Wherever you go, you will always find something interesting. Hidden caves, ruins, unique landmarks, secret paths, and valuable loot are everywhere. The world constantly rewards curiosity and exploration. The number of points of interest across the map is enormous, and exploring never feels pointless. The music and ambience add even more immersion. The soundtrack perfectly supports the atmosphere of the world and its mysterious tone. Gameplay is outstanding. The player has access to a huge variety of weapons, spells, armor sets, and abilities, allowing you to create a build exactly the way you want. You can play as a heavily armored warrior who withstands powerful blows from bosses, strike quickly with a magic katana while dodging every attack, or become a powerful mage capable of destroying enemies with devastating spells. The number of possible playstyles encourages multiple playthroughs, and eventually you will want to try them all. The story is also very interesting. Learning about the world, its history, and its characters feels rewarding. Every NPC you meet leaves some kind of impression, and many of them are memorable in their own way. The game does have a few minor issues. Player versus player combat can sometimes be frustrating. If you play in co-op, you may be invaded by other players who are extremely experienced and focused entirely on defeating you. These encounters can interrupt your progress toward a boss and force you to spend resources dealing with invaders who constantly harass you during your run. Despite a few minor imperfections, Elden Ring remains an extraordinary experience. Its vast world, incredible art direction, deep gameplay systems, and constant sense of discovery make it a truly remarkable game. It is a title that sets a very high standard for the entire action RPG genre and will be remembered as one of the greatest games ever created.
