Imma split my feelings about Elden Ring into two paragraphs. This is just my opinion, I recommend This game but can also understand why people don't enjoy all aspects. [h1] MAIN GAME: 6/10 [/h1] If you like high fantasy games you will probably enjoy Elden Ring. I personally had a hard time getting into it, I beat it, but damn did it feel slow at times. I think this was the easiest souls game so far, which isn't super bad, probably good for people getting into this kinda game, but it made some aspects of the story feel unsatisfying. PROS: - Awesome world building cut scenes - Cool lore is scattered around forcing you to look for explanations to why things are happening (which i like exploring so that was cool) - The open world is fun to explore and has a lot of areas to see with pretty views - Most fluid combat system compared to older games - You meet game changing NPCs early on - Graphics were amazing CONS; - NPC questlines feel unimportant and unless you really wanna hear them out, or follow them, the game doesn't do a good job of making you care about them compared to other games. - the first half of the game lacks direction - The game is objectively easy. The hardest boss is optional which makes the main story feel weak. The hardest main boss is the first one you fight, after that they were super easy and didn't match the lore attached to them. - The repeating nonmain bosses was annoying, i think i fought the ulcerated tree mini boss guy like 15 times in one play through. All in different areas, to the point where id finish a dungeon and be like hell yeah boss time and then just be disappointed that its another ♥♥♥♥ ass different colored ulcerated tree. - The NPC quests are so hard to track without looking it up. I think that is why its hard to care about them. You see them in the [spoiler] roundtable [/spoiler] and then they are just gone somewhere on the large ass map, and if you end up missing them because its a large ass map, then their quest line fails. i enjoyed it by the end, but i think it was the DLC that pulled me in. With out the DLC i was uninterested in the story. I can see why people enjoy it, but the main game alone to me was weak compared to other titles. [h2] The DLC 9/10 [/h2] The DLC for Elden Ring was fire. I really enjoyed exploring the new areas, learning about the NPCs views, and connecting the dots between the main games story and the DLC. The DLC Reminded me of how it felt to play DS3, so if you liked playing that you would enjoy the DLC PROS: - boss fights had impact, they were hard, it felt satisfying to slay them and their fights made sense with story cues. - the world was large but not large enough to lose story impact - Graphics and cutscenes were amazing - The story was easy to follow, i didn't ever forget what my objective was and puzzles were solvable without googling the quest i was working on. - The DLC made the NPCs quests feel important, you see the NPCs in the DLC more then you see the main story NPCs in the main game and you can talk to them enough to have an opinion on their views by the end - The big bad at the end is constantly hinted at everywhere, and makes you question if your doing the right thing constantly which made the DLCs story feel impactful CONS; - The ending man, All that lead up and no cutscene at the end. You learn so much about the final boss leading up to it and there is no closure. Its such a hard fight too (which i liked btw), but no real closure or cutscene. i loved the reveal of the final boss just left wishing there was more after. Over all Elden Ring was a good game, Id recommend it, it just was a little disappointing at times, and felt unsatisfying throughout parts of the story.

I've played about 2700 hours on the PS4 version as well. This game is art that I still lack the language to describe properly. Almost everything about the experience is deliberate. The depth of this game cannot be overstated because I'm not sure it has been fully experienced, by anyone. The amount and level of human skill, talent, effort, and love embodied here is a continually-unfolding treasure. After all this time, I still make new discoveries. Of course, it's imperfect. In some ways it leans into this, which is itself beautiful. But this is sometimes done to a level that overshadows the experience. Around mid-game the bigger problems start to pile up: - Atrocious targeting - Eaten or poorly-queued inputs (particularly jumps, jump attacks, flask uses, crouches, and steed whistle uses) - Hitboxes that are too large on enemy attacks and too small on yours - Basic enemies that read your animations in three frames and too often interrupt your actions at the last possible moment - Basically scripted deaths, as the developers have explained, to give you stories to tell your friends - Ranged attacks that are designed to fail under far too many common circumstances - Boss fights that are unrewarding, monotonous, and performatively frustrating As you move into later portions of the game these problems go from noticeable to oppressive. The shadows lift once you learn to deal with these things semi-reliably, but it does take time.

This is a good game. Yes a good game not an excellent one. It certainly doesn't live up to its hype and one of its biggest flaw, actually being its open world. But first lets get to the good parts of the game: - combat: still works great, with a lot of different enemies and movesets to keep you busy experementing. - legacy dungeons: these are smaller areas that kinda work as the level-like areas in former Dark Souls entries and they are most of the time very good, like you are used to, with shortcuts great enemy placement etc. Some of them are very short, but most of them are really great and are parts where Elden Ring shines and shows that FromSoft is still capable of pulling that sort of quality out. - enemy design: again one thine I really enjoy much also in former entries and here in Elden Ring the enemy designs show a great variety and range from standard soldiers to intersting fantasy species to creepy horror apperances. A little caveat come already here, when enemy types pop up at areas where they seemingly dont belong - Mechanics: Overall I admire how much depths of mechanics is put into the game. You have upgrading, can change affinity of weapons, can calll Spirits to help, which you can also upgrade, you can mix your own potion, use great runes, make your own signs into the map etc.. - if you got runes you always find a way to spend them - variety of weapons: this is also sth I want to point out: you are faced with a huge amount of a great choice of weapons. There are over 300 weapons spread across 32 categories. Not all of them are useful and ofc most of them are useful more or less to a certain build, but you can pretty easily respec your char (which is limited) to try out different builds. I had a lot of fun experimenting with it, until I reached the point where every build I tested came to more or less the same dmg output just in different colors. So far that all sounds very fun you might say and wonder where that negative criticism derives from. Well, now I will share the drawbacks of that game and they will become more and more significant the longer the game lasts: - first of all the open world: this is an empty and hollow world with no real background living behind it or living behind the inhabitants of the world. It´s more like you travel from one diorama to the next. When you reach a certain trigger point that diorama sets in motion. This becomes even worse since the two first areas are very similiar to each other and very boring. The way you uncover this world is better than in most open world games, yes, since you dont have your map cluttered with items, but still its a shallow world - Questdesign: this is also a huge problem. FromSoft stayed with their established formular of stumbling into NPCs which then give you cryptic instructions (well a bit less cryptic than in former games, but still very cryptic). Then you are left up with trying to figure out where to find this NPC next. Only problem is, since this game is open world and these NPCs sometimes travel to locations you already have been, you might never find them again. Also if you reach certain areas before you met this NPC you will miss the entire questline. Since I want to see as much content as possible and not that guy who plays a huge open world game a second time, I was lot reading where to find all these NPCs, which I think is not fun anymore at a certain point. Also the quests also lead to the same fate for their protagonists. - Dungeons: and here I am not speaking of these level-like dungeons but of the smaller dungeons which are all around in this world. There are four or five types of dungeons which are all build very similiar and follow the same formular. At the end you will always find a boss or chest with some loot. They get boring very quickly and feel like a classical filler of a too big open world. In most dungeons you also find the same enemy types which even more make them boring. - enemy variety: yes you read it right. I praised the variety further above, but its just the overall variety. So here are more dffetnt types then i.e. Dark Souls 3. But the longer the game lasts the lesser the variation gets, since in new areas are all the same enemies just in different combninations. They also just have more dmg output and a higher healt bar, which make progress seem pale because you wonder why this enemy takes so much more hits than he needed two areas before. Also, some stroy-unique bosses get reused, which make them feel less unique. I dont have a problem with mini-boss reusage if it fits the scenario, but story important characters reused breaks the immersion and the meaning. - Bosss-fights: Speaking of bosses, the boss-fights are some of the weakest parts of the game. Either you are most of the time overpowered for the average mini or dungeon bosses or you run into annoying boss fights which have the following problems: the bosses spam aggressively their attacks with no stamina constraints. They use input reading which means they don't react to what you do, they react the moment you press a button, before your action has even started. This also becomes relevant when they use their huge wind up to delay their attacks. If you cant stand the tensions and press the dodge button they turn towards you and strike their attack just in that moment. These wind-ups mess up dodge timing and ruins the rythm of the fight, which also becomes very unnatural since you dont react to what the enemy does but more try to guess when his delayed will finally come down to react. - Upgrading: I said I had a lot of fun experimenting with weapons, which is true, but there is also a caveat to the system. Upgrading material is scarce, you can find items which allow you to buy these materials at a special merchant, but grinding for upgrade material can become tedious. But its neccassary, since if you change your build you will need your new weapons at the same level as your weapons you had before, because otherwise you wont deal enough damage. - Bonfires: this is one of the biggest problems, which is a result of an open world. There are bonfires everywhere. The problem that encompasses this design is, that there is no real tension if you die, no real meaning for shortcuts. The amount here is ridiculous. There are some areas where bonfire placement is scarce and they are great for that, but overall it breaks the mechanics for a soulslike. - Music: the music is lackluster. Music playing in different area is just some annoying ambience rattle, which gets nerve-racking pretty quickly. The music of boss-fights is mostly very uninspired and just gets better towards the end. Only good titel here is the main screen music in my opinion. If you wanna here good background music which is fitting for each area you should try out Tainted Grail: Fall of Avalon, which does a formidable work in this aspect. - PVP: this is a double-edged sowrd, but as so many of these criticims it becomes worse the longer the game lasts: you cant play in a relaxing coop, because if you do, you will always almost instantly get invaded. Either you fight some hardcore-super-pros which will kill you instantly, what will be almost the best outcome, because there is a bonfre nearby and you can go on. But often you get invaders which will hide somewhere or runaway if they realize they cant win. Thats a problem because invading closes the area and you cant leave until invader or you is deafeated. From my almost 200 hrs you can easily discount 40-50 hrs of being invaded and need to find or follow invader and then regroup with teammember. Because if you die you have to summon your friend again, which often doesnt work to disconnects, then you need to restart the game - so after hundreds of invasions where you actually dont fight - no fun! So after all I would not recommend the game to anyone who has the inner commitment to fully complete a game (as I do) because it becomes more and more a chore. 78 / 100

Elden Ring is, in my opinion, one of the best art directed games ever made. Every location in the world feels carefully designed, with breathtaking landscapes, unique architecture, and a visual style that constantly makes you stop and look around. The world of the Lands Between feels mysterious, beautiful, and sometimes haunting, which makes exploring it incredibly rewarding. The story is also surprisingly captivating. Instead of telling everything directly, the game lets you uncover its lore piece by piece through characters, environments, and items. This makes the world feel deep and ancient, and it encourages players to truly pay attention to what is happening around them. Overall, Elden Ring sets a new standard for art direction, world building, and gameplay in modern games. It is an unforgettable experience that stands above most other games in its genre.

Farron Woods feels like a forest, when it's one larger open area. In the Lands Between, there is no elision. Mt. Gelmir is as big as a volcano would be. The Royal Capital is a fully fleshed out city. The scale here is immense and amazing. Because of the scale of the map, the game captures this incredible feeling of adventure. There's entertainment to be had riding around the countryside and seeing what lies over the next hill. I found plenty of environmental storytelling and side objectives by simply traveling around. There is so much to and also so much to do. The game is a remarkable achievement.

To preface this, I put over 120 hours into this game in 2022 on console. I love this game. However, I don't recommend this game on PC. It was not designed for PC. The game/animations are max 60 frames (or it will break the combat systems, a massive pitfall of FromSoftware game design), and the game has limited settings available to configure the game correctly for a PC level of experience. The default vsync function does not work, the game resolution breaks completely if you try to play it while you have more than one monitor connected, and you can't click off the game screen even when it's in windowed mode. There are so many issues with the PC port of this game it genuinely ruins the experience. I paid good money for both the base game and the DLC, I should not have to be troubleshooting workarounds to fix basic functions of the game. This is a souls game, therefore it has a level of difficulty that's unmatched by any other game. BUT, on top of the actual gameplay difficulty, the developers couldn't be bothered to finish certain functions of the game so that they work properly. The lock on system is a prime example of this. It is nearly impossible to lock on to the target you want to hit. You'll be locked onto an enemy, and another will attack you from another direction that you can clearly see coming, but you can't do anything about it because you're frantically cycling through locking on all other enemies before you reach the one that you need to hit in that moment. Game difficulty is a lazy excuse for an incomplete game. It should be difficult but feel good to play. This is not the case for this game on PC. A complete game should never be at a point where you have to do actual research before your every move to make sure you are not breaking questlines. Unfortunately, you can break questlines permanently in this game. You can't just save the game manually before doing something and reload if it destroys your whole playthrough. The only way to save the game is by saving AND exiting. Beautiful and maddening game. If you haven't played a Dark Souls type game before, just be prepared: you will die. A lot. It's part of the gameplay mechanic. You die, you respawn, you try again. And eventually you either win or give up. Visually very impressive and creative. Gameplay mechanics could use some work, as the sprawling open-world map makes it difficult to understand where you are, what quest you are on (hint: there is no quest tracking at all), or where to go next. A lot of the game is rewarding discovery, but at a certain point, that begins to feel more like a chore than a game. Sometimes it's a simple thing like forgetting to cycle through all dialogue options with a NPC, which you may not know about since it frequently ends the dialogue chain until you start it anew and realize they have more to stay. Only once they start to repeat themselves have to exhausted all options. The real winning formula here is the mix of beautiful graphics, creative enemy design, and fight mechanics. Learning how the fight mechanics works can be frustrating, and learning to dodge and parry at the right time can really have you question your sanity. It's not logical fighting by any means -- you are fighting giant creatures and dragons and monsters that are 10-50 times your size, yet all you need to do is hack away at their legs or feet and that is usually enough to bring them down. Dodging into an attack is often rewarded here, which is unusual. In my head, this would just end up getting myself into worse position, but in Elden Ring, it has almost the opposite effect. Learning to roll into an enemy/boss rather than away from them takes effort if you have spent most fighting games doing the opposite. It's a 4 year old game at this point (released in 2022), but it is still very entertaining and enjoyable. It does become redundant, and eventually you no longer want to fight most of the creatures. Then it just becomes a run to the boss fights. Replayability seems fairly decent. All in all, a worthwhile purchase.

IF YOU ARE INTENT ON BUYING ELDEN RING, DO NOT BUY IT ON PC While I believe that Elden Ring stands as one of the greatest games of all time, I cannot and will not give this a positive review. I first experienced Elden Ring on my Xbox and played through all the main content and DLC content. Revisiting this game on PC a few years later, I have completed the optional content I missed. With my context out of the way, this game on PC is abysmal. (I have a Nvidia GTX 3060TI, and I run at 25-30fps) My current computer can run every game I have downloaded with max settings. Elden Ring, Dark Souls 3, and Sekiro all suffer severe performance issues. Charging nearly 100 dollars for ER and its DLC to run at 30 fps and locked to 60hz refresh is lazy developer work. On release, ER had issues running on PC, and the release of the DLC didn't address any concerns for the PC crowd's inability to experience ER. While I understand that this may be the cause of their engine not being able to run games on computer, much less millions of different builds and kinds of computers, nearly a decade of lazy developer optimization for TripleAAA games is ridiculous. I am going as far to say as it is unplayable. You must buy a console if you wish to play this game. IF YOU ARE INTENT ON BUYING ELDEN RING, DO NOT BUY IT ON PC

I have played this game a lot, both with and without mods. I'll be blunt: it's a good game overall, but it has a lot of things dragging it down. Some say it's a 10/10 game, but I disagree. First of all, the biggest issue with this game, is input reading. Enemies and bosses don't react to what you do, they react the moment you press a button, before your action has even started. The enemy in Fort Gael is a good example: I try to shoot it with a crossbow, but it evade the moment I press the button, wether I'm aiming at it or not. This is dumb. -1 point. Next is wind-up attacks and tracking: a lot of bosses and enemies have ridiculous wind-ups that mess up dodge timing and ruins the rythm of the fight. And if you try to reposition to avoid it completely, they will simply turn around 180 degrees and hit you with that attack anyway. This is cheap, not difficoult. -1 point. Then there is the game balance: it feels like they spent less than 10 minuttes to balance this game. In a lot of late game areas, enemies are just basic scrubs that do nothing, while a mid game area might have enemies that will utterly destroy you regardless of stats and defence. Bosses also do WAYYYY too much damage in proportion to how often they attack and how long their combos are. They get to kill me in 2-3 hits while being able to chain 3-7 attacks in a row, while I'm lucky to land 1 single hit before they jump away from me and just stare at me from the other side of the area. This is utterly stupid. -2 points. Next is the ability to respec, upgrade weapons, and change builds: this is hopeless.... the game is incredibly stingy with upgrade materials, and even if you obtain the bellbearings, the mats get increasingly expensive. You need a total of 12 of each basic smithingstone to max a weapon, from lvl 1 stones to lvl 9 stones. And lvl 8 stones cost 30 000 runes a piece, just to give an example. This discourages experimentation in a game with over 100 weapons. Respecing is also limited, as there is a fixed amount of larval tears you can obtain in a single playthrough. This can hardlock you to stick with the same build through the whole game. -2 points. Now we are down to 4/10. Now lets add the good things: The world is big, with lots of things to discover around every corner. Everything from weapons, mats and spells, to catacombs, castles and dungeons. Exploration is very rewarding. +2 points. Buildvariaty: if we look away from the horrible upgrade system, there is a lot of different ways to build your character. You can go pure meele, or pure spell/incantation builds, or heavily focus on status buildup, or make a combination of either of them, and much more. +1 point. Encounters: there are many npcs to stumble upon in this game, most of wich leads to new side quests or detours, or even new areas. Some are missable, wich can lead to missing out on certain questlines or items, but this isn't really a problem. The npcs of this game are fairly interesting, and some will even fight alongside you at certain bosses if you summon them. +1 point. Now we are at 8/10. There is a lot more that drag this game both up and down, but these are my takes. Personally I give the game a 7/10. It's an overall good game, especially with certain mods, but it can be really frustrating at times, and I can't really think of anyone I would ever recommend this game to. I had my fun, along with much frustration. Edit: Steam doesn't ask if the game is good, Steam ask if I would recommend it. I would not, unless it is with mods.

I have never played a Souls-like game before. I've seen countless hours of gameplay of all 3 Dark Souls, and some of Elden Ring, but have never played them myself. The sheer, absolute scale of the open world. The intriguing, mysterious story and characters, and actions that matter. The "figure it out" mindset of throwing you off the deep end. The insanely choreographed boss encounters and powerful, epic soundtrack combine to push you to the edge of your seat. I had chills multiple times from some of the boss introductions alone. I spent hours just wandering, getting lost in the world that seems to never, ever end. There are new enemies with new movesets up until the end of the game. You are kept on your toes CONSTANTLY. This is, without a doubt, a 10/10 game and I wish there was a higher rating I could give. Miyazaki and George R.R. Martin have created an absolute, flawless masterpiece. I wish I could experience it again for the first time.

Look, I'm bitter, but my save data was just corrupted after 470+ hours of playtime. (It's probably closer to about 400 hours, as there were several points where I just had to step away for a while when the game was running.) The fact that the lost save data can happen feels a bit ludicrous, especially when other players have experienced the same thing and cite a.) fully manual attempts to recover and b.) very low probability of success in recovery. (Yes, I tried several things, and, no, none were successful. Also, no, I don't use any mods.) I had started a second character, and that character was my first time going through the DLC. I'm getting kicked out of playing just before I got to experience the last couple of bosses -- the really big ones for the story that would finally test my character and play. It's all pretty devastating, and it's enough so that I'm willing to just go ahead and leave a negative review for the fact that I could have had this deeply unsatisfying conclusion at any point after being many hours into the game. The game needs better save management so that this doesn't happen. The game itself crashed during the DLC several times and always yelled at me when I logged back in, and now I would have to start over on hundreds of hours worth of work if I wanted to see this through. That, to me, with even just a 1% chance of happening, is a pretty bad thing to let happen to many paying players. You want to know about the game itself? It's very Fromsoft, and it has an absolute ton of things going for it. That said, on a per-hour-of-play basis, it's below any Dark Souls title or Sekiro for me. You're getting a ton if you get the game, but you're also getting some baggage and the risk of losing your save like I did.

10/10 – Nearly 1,000 Hours Across Platforms I don’t throw this around lightly: this is one of the best games I’ve ever played. Across multiple platforms, I’ve accumulated nearly 1,000 hours in Elden Ring. My first playthrough alone was around 170 hours. Later runs went over 200. Most recently, I completed a 3-hour NG+2 speedrun to finish every achievement. A game does not hold your attention for 1,000 hours unless it’s doing something special. The World The Lands Between is one of the most rewarding open worlds in gaming. It doesn’t hold your hand. It doesn’t flood your map with meaningless icons. It lets you explore naturally. Every region feels distinct. Limgrave feels like discovery. Caelid feels oppressive. Leyndell feels earned. Exploration isn’t filler — it’s progression. On my first run, I explored everything. Every cave. Every boss. Every hidden path. And even hundreds of hours later, I was still discovering things I had missed. Combat & Build Variety The build depth is absurd. Lightning, faith, bleed, frost, magic, strength, dex — almost anything is viable if you understand the mechanics. I’ve experimented with high-damage lightning builds, buff stacking setups, hybrid stat spreads, and Ash of War nukes just to push damage numbers as far as possible. The game rewards experimentation. It rewards knowledge. It rewards mastery. Watching your character evolve from struggling through early bosses to routing NG+ cycles efficiently feels incredible. Difficulty & Freedom The difficulty is challenging but fair — and more importantly, flexible. If something feels impossible, you can leave. Level up. Change builds. Explore somewhere else. The game respects your time and your decisions. By NG+2, I wasn’t just surviving bosses — I was executing clean runs. That progression feels earned, not handed to you. Replay Value This is where the game truly stands out. It transforms depending on how you approach it: First run: exploration and survival. Second run: optimization. Later runs: experimentation. Endgame: speed and efficiency. I went from a 170-hour immersive first playthrough to a 3-hour NG+2 clear. That kind of growth doesn’t happen unless the game systems are deep and well-designed. Very few games evolve with the player like this. Final Verdict This became my first fully completed achievement game — not because I forced myself to finish it, but because I genuinely didn’t want to stop playing. If a game can give you nearly 1,000 hours of enjoyment across multiple platforms and still make you want to start “just one more run,” that’s not just a good game. That’s a masterpiece. Nearly 1,000 hours later, and I’d still press “New Game” again without hesitation.

Elden Ring is a modern classic. I do think the game is good, but I just think there is WAY too much to do. I felt very overwhelmed with stuff that I could do or get. While I was playing I didn't really find it that fun, I felt like I was just slamming my character against a boss over and over until I managed to hit the perfect run. I mean, that's what souls games are known for. Tough bosses. But here it just didn't really click. If I do decided to replay Elden Ring, I'll probably do things a bit different. In terms of achievements. They were alright. I did find the "collect all things" achievements to be quite tedious. The boss achivements on the other hand were the main show. I enjoyed the bosses, but only to a certain point. My favourite boss that I fought was suprisingly, Dragonlord Placidusax. I think that was the only fight I really enjoyed out of all of them tbh. Of course the hardest achievment was Shardbearer Malenia. So hard in fact that I gave up and got someone else to do it. That is my only regret really. Not doing that boss. But I was tired of Elden Ring at that point and just wanted to get it done. Overall, Elden Ring is a good game. I may have played it wrong, I may have not enjoyed it as much as I thought I would. But it didn't leave a bad taste in my mouth. Only regret. I will come back and beat Malenia, Blade of Miquella. But that will be for future me to decide. 7/10

This is my first fromsoftware game that i have tried and it is really nice game with many gimmicks and mechanics. The world is beautiful and one of the most detailed worlds that I have seen in a game. The open-world is really vast with many quirks. The boss fights are very well crafted and rememberable. The one thing that I really like about this game is that you have the ability to choose, how difficult the base game is. Some people like it and some don't, but you can cheese or choose a very difficult path - it is up to you. There are things that I don't like, like the poor lore delivery - it is very hard to understand, what is happening lore-wise in the world. Maybe it is just me, but it is very easy to get lost and get annoyed in the world as the openness of it makes it hard to navigate without guides. This might sound like a contradiction, but the openness makes it awesome and annoying at the same time. A friendly advise, If you want a fun challenge, please, don't use the mimic tear - it is overpowered and boring. Also, try the multiplayer with friends - it is even better with them.

Masterpiece. Early on there's a bit of a learning curve, and a few times you'll get hardstuck. Eventually you'll get the hang of how everything works, and then you can kiss dozens of hours goodbye as the game does not take the foot off the pedal. The interiors and architectural layouts make no practical sense at times, but it's all designed with video game logic in mind. Dripping in atmosphere throughout. The art team did something special here. Exploration is rewarded on such a minute level - every corner or ledge or alternate path rewards something major, it's impressive a game of this scope can deliver surprises consistently. Towards the end, when you get to the snowy area you're somewhat grateful the later zones are a little smaller and less content-dense. Combat, once you get used to the rules, is a fun dance of swing and dodge timings, and never gets stale. Towards the end you start deleting everything pretty quickly but even the later zones' trash mobs are not to be trifled with. You can cheese pretty much any encounter if you wish - you'll get there anyway once you've spent enough runes and points on leveling. Game is GOATed for a reason, no cap.

Elden Ring ring is a mostly good game. I say "mostly" because one of the things that the game puts a heavy emphasis on is also one of its serious downfalls. That being the bosses. [b]Pretty much every dragon boss is a copy and paste of the last with a different status effect.[/b] It really makes dragons feel like more of an inconvenience because you'll get good at fighting them by your second or third dragon boss. They should be way more threatening and keep you on your toes with mixed up movesets. Instead, they become old very quick. (this doesn't only apply to dragons, however they make for a great example) [b]Elden Ring also has some of the worst implementations of duo bosses I've seen in the series.[/b] Duo bosses' attacks don't compliment eachother whatsoever, they're too independent to the point where it's like you're fighting two boss battles at the same time instead of a single 2v1 battle. The constant rushing of some bosses in this game really doesn't help either. I'll use Valiant Gargoyles as an example: One of their attacks is an AoE that does both instant damage and poison build up, which is fine. We've seen attacks like that hundreds of time before. Where the issue lies though is that you're sometimes put in a situation where this AoE attack is near unavoidable because the second Gargoyle wants to get up your backside CONSTANTLY, which leads you to being stuck in a poison AoE whilst also try dodge wild swings from another enemy. You're pretty much guranteed to take damage and you just have to take it. That's not a "git gud" moment, that's just poor boss design. [b]Some boss strings are so quick they're almost impossible to dodge completely.[/b] This wouldn't be an issue if dodging the first attack of a string would give you an improved opportunity to evade the rest of said string, but with some bosses that isn't the case. The player's movement doesn't match the speed of some of the flurries thrown at you. Luckily, this is a pretty uncommon occurrence and so it doesn't affect the majority of bosses, but it is still a very clear issue with balancing in this game... [b]With all that being said, Elden Ring is still a very fun experience.[/b] Moving to an open world map offers for a lot more exploration and secrets that previous souls games. There's a whole bunch of NPCs to interact with and side quests to complete, which will keep you occupied for hours. There's a huge range of weapons and spells to find throughout your playthrough which really adds to the freedom of stylising your builds. I do have other critiques and complaints about this game but it'll turn this into a much longer review than I'd like to make it. And if you're someone who has already played Elden Ring and hasn't given the Dark Souls series a try yet, I highly recommend you give it a shot. It's a much more linear and more hardcore experience than Elden Ring but it makes beating it all the more satisfying.

[h2]Elden Ring is a great game, yet with glaring issues when you scratch the surface! Oh thee, lowly Tarnished...[/h2] Elden Ring was my first Souls game, yet I've seen playthroughs of the Dark Souls games, so I was pretty aware of what to expect when I started playing. Struggle... struggle... and yet more struggle. My aim was to do a blind playthrough, but I quickly decided to check out some "non-spoiler" guides to actually enjoy the game. Overall I did have a great time, yet at times the game was insanely frustrating and unfair, which was to be expected. The game is wellmade, yet has some glaring issues... [h3]Positives:[/h3] 1. The combat: Overall a great feeling when you manage to progress through parts of the game or killing a hard boss that you've been struggling on. There's a lot to learn and master, which improves your performance over time. Just get to grinding! 2. Builds: Anything and everything can work on any build, some things are obviously better (even broken) than others. You can choose yourself if you want to play with them and cheese bosses. 3. Difficulty "settings": Being able to play with OP builds/weapons, summons (spirit ashes) increased my enjoyment by a lot! I would've needed probably around 200-300 hrs to finish the game without them. Wiping on bosses for 100+ wipes is simply not enjoyable for me, but hey if you like that, go for it! "Unless you kill the boss on first try without summons and being full-naked with no weapons, then it's not a legit kill!", just touch grass lol! 4. Exploration & The Aesthetics: The Open World is simply amazing. I spent the first ten hours just exploring Limgrave (1st zone) and bonking around. It was great and I kept finding new secrets all the time. [h3]The negatives:[/h3] 1. Reused assets: There's simply *too much* in the game. Side content such as catacombs, mines, mobs etc are just copy+pasted in several locations. The first few "secrets" are hype to discover, but finding the roughly same layout of catacombs with the same boss after 50+ hrs is simply not fun. I think the game would've been better with a smaller and more compacted design (fewer unique bosses/zones), with a smaller map. 2. Controls: The mount (Torrent) is amazing, but the [b]mount controls on PC are HORRIBLE![/b] I can't count the amount of times I've died due to the goat simply jumping off the map, even if my input was the opposite way... Not to mention the JP-path to the [b]Frenzied Flame in the severs... I spent like 30 mins and 20+ deaths trying to get down there, because my character randomly kept overshooting/moving on landing etc[/b] 3. "Punishing gameplay": The difficulty of the game is FINE and Souls games are supposed to be challenging and punishing. To a degree I would even say that they are supposed to "waste your time", until you "git gud". However... there are a lot of elements that are simply unfair. Many aspects (maps, bosses, mobs) are deliberatly designed to make you ragequit. I don't mind the challenge, but it should at least be a "even playing field", where you can learn. 4. The tryhard community: Holy... reading the input of parts of the Souls community makes me question my life choices. Can you just let people play the game THE WAY THEY WANT. If you want to play it as a "no-hit, naked, no ashes"-playthrough, then do so. Stop bothering people who use spirit ashes, summons etc. You can enjoy the game the way you want, and others are entitled to the same... [h3]Overall a very solid game. Punishing & challenging, yet very enjoyable. Would strongly recommend, even though its apparant flaws![/h3]

I love it when multiple aspects of a game combine together to form a cohesive whole that exceeds the sum of its parts. Elden Ring, unfortunately, failed do that for me. And while I don't want to not recommend a game I had a lot of fun playing, there are just too many seemingly small irksome factors here that compound to produce a somewhat tedious experience for me where every time I'm about to enter a boss arena, I shudder at the thought of having to spend the next hour or two (or four) grinding that boss. Keep in mind that I'm no expert at this game, obviously; I've yet to beat R+EB & M (I'm sure everyone understands who I'm referring to). I simply did not have the heart to continue playing Elden Ring and this review serves as my closure so that I don't keep ruminating over it afterwards. As I stated before, I have many "minor" gripes with this game. [spoiler] [h2]1. The Gear Upgrade System[/h2] Let's start with an easy one. Elden Ring, is significantly more open than previous games. It has a bunch of cool weapons, spells, incantations and items to enable further exploration and every time I see a new exciting looking item, I want to try it out immediately and to this end, ER does have a re-spec system. But in classic FromSoft fashion, it is quite limited. I can only re-spec my character if I have a larval tear in my inventory. So, every time I want to change my build after finding a new item or in response to a boss, I need to go take a massive detour and try to find larval tears on my own, or look up the wiki and go on a much smaller detour. You can guess my preference. Not only that, after the re-spec, I also need to upgrade my new shiny weapon/staff/seal so that it does not do terrible damage, which means, you guessed it, more massive detours (or wiki-powered smaller detours). I just wish that ER had the following two QoL upgrades in order to incentivize exploration, if at least for the first playthrough (I know that during subsequent playthroughs, players either look up or cook up a build and beeline towards the items they want while ignoring everything else). [list] [*][b]Free re-specs[/b], similar to games like Divinity Original Sin 2. [*][b]Smithing stone transfer[/b]: If I am to re-spec my character, chances are my previous fully upgraded weapon is now completely unusable anyway. So why not just let me transfer the +X upgrade to my new weapon. Of course, if I have two +25 (or +10) weapons and I want a +25 seal on top of that, I [i]have[/i] to farm, but exchanging one +25 weapon for another +25 weapon does not feel "unfair" to me at all. If I lose the ability/desire to use a certain weapon, having it rot in my inventory while I have to either find more stones or farm more runes to buy stones feels tedious. [/list] [h2]2. Enemies[/h2] [h3]2.1. Design[/h3] To me souls games live or die by their enemies. These games are not the most flashy/combo-driven and have relatively simple weapon movesets so most of the fun comes from fighting interesting enemies. But enemies in ER just have ridiculous physical form and movesets. Some of the most annoying enemies are either massive and have hitboxes that greatly exceed the dodge window or are so ridiculously fast that they attack non-stop and constantly hitstun. Allow me to list out some [b]large[/b] enemies that have what feels like a million health and also do a million damage. And then some ridiculously fast/multi hit enemies like rats, the blob with a million arms that has a wild combo, Grafted Scions, black-knife assassins and the insect guys that shoot the 100 needles also fit this mold. And then, in classic Souls fashion, there are enemies that cast insta-kill clouds. [h3]Placement and Scaling[/h3] Outside of some enemies being inherently annoying, their placement and scaling, especially in late game areas, feels to me as if I'm supposed to avoid them altogether. In the mountaintops, the only enemies I found were giant crows, giant t-rex dogs, giant hands, rune bears and so forth. Catacombs now have the giant stone dogs as normal enemies. The Zamur heros are also just normal enemies now. The haligtree branches also has those massive trumpet bubble guys. Not to mention the giant ants in Ainsel that do a ton of damage. On top of this ridiculous placement, the damage they deal is also outrageous. One strike from any of these enemies does like 50-75% of my health bar at 50 vigor. Some kill in one hit or one hitstun combo. Fighting one such enemy takes like 2-3 charges of my flask on a good day which quickly gets tedious. [h2]3. Bosses and Rhythm[/h2] ER has good bosses, outside of the obviously annoying ones. But I can't help but notice that every boss has an unstoppable flurry of 5-7 piece combos paired with a highly off putting rhythm. ER almost feels like a turn based game to me where the boss does a 7 hit combo while I dodge, then I get like two seconds to counter-attack wherein if I am not in the exact place to strike back, I lose that opportunity. Even staggered bosses require stamina to reposte, so while I stand around recharging my stamina for one second, the boss has already recovered. The rhythm of the fight also just seems to demand rote memorization. I can't seem to extrapolate the rhythm or tempo of the whole fight by sampling a handful of random moves in my first few attempts. I just feel like every move is uniquely timed to catch rolls and dish out maximum punishment. Unless I can just out damage the boss, and there are builds capable of doing that, I just feel like I have to experience every single move first hand over the course of 2-3 hours before I can finally make any progress. This has been a real bummer for me, especially in the case of Rhadann (Starscourge), Maliketh, Godfrey, Malenia and Mogh (sewer and palace). The attacks these bosses do seems almost randomized where sometimes the exact same combo ends after 3 hits and other times is immediately followed up by another combo basically obliterating my punish window, punishing me instead for daring to attack after what felt like (and was in 60% of the cases) the final hit of the combo. After this happens a couple times, I am just afraid to go in again, what if there are more follow up hits? After like 20 attempts of failing to make heads or tails of the fight and making zero, I am forced watch a YouTube guide breaking down every single move and possible follow up which I then internalize and beat the boss in the next 5 attempts. This does not feel fun to me, it feels like I'm learning an instrument that I can't even play a song in. Just for illustration, the rhythm of these fights feels something like this: one . . . two . . . . . . . . three FOUR . . five orr, maybe like this: . . . . one TWO THREE . . four . . . . . . five or perhaps: . . one TWO . . . . three FOUR or most likely, all of the above in a single fight, where every single move has a distinct rhythm and the rhythm of one chain of combos simply does not apply to another. I could go on but I am literally hitting the character limit. [/spoiler] [h2]Conclusion[/h2] I really want to like ER. Heck, if I persisted, I could probably beat both M and R+EB in due time but I just couldn't bring myself plough on; it does not feel rewarding for me to do so. This is also, in part, because the DLC seems to exaggerate the exact same things that I've disliked about the base game. Maybe I can come back to it in 6 months and enjoy it again in the way I have enjoyed the earlier parts of ER but for the time being I feel like I'm done.

I have always been in love with the Souls-like genre, and this game is probably the closest thing to a perfect souls game. The combat feels phenomenal; the bosses are really cool and unique, but they can get stale when you encounter some of them in the open world multiple times(referring mostly to the side bosses). The multiplayer aspect of the game is, I would say, done pretty well, even though it can feel unbalanced sometimes compared to its predecessor, Dark Souls 3. Story-wise, it is also a lot simpler compared to other FromSoftware games, with the exception of Sekiro. For that reason, I would argue it loses the charm that the other games had, and because of this, it’s not my favorite from the Soulsborne series (that spot still belongs to Dark Souls 1). In conclusion, I would rate this game a 9.5/10—it’s a must-play for any Souls-like enjoyer.

At first I thought this is too hard for me (Tree sentinel) then I realised that the game is as hard or easy as you want it to be as a player by creating specific builds and even being completely over powered if you wanted to be. from there I researched builds, and set off on my journey to collect the items id need for my build to help give me an easier time in the game. I travelled into end(ish) game areas early on, speeding through on my steed, gathering talismans, weapons, map pieces, golden seeds, levelling up my stats. bypassing many of the games enemies entirely, now reading this you may think well that's not really playing the game properly, and I would agree, however though by doing this I learned something... I learned what actually makes this game so special, for me, at that point in time anyway, and that is the WORLD, it is phenomenally designed, beautiful, creepy, dark, mysterious, I had no idea about any of the plot at this point... but that didn't matter I was engulfed by the majesty of the world. Elden Ring to jedna z tych gier, które jeszcze przed premierą zostały wyniesione na piedestał. Produkcja studia FromSoftware, twórców serii Dark Souls, była zapowiadana jako rozwinięcie znanej formuły w otwartym świecie. Efekt końcowy jest jednak bardziej złożony. To gra z wieloma świetnymi pomysłami, ale jednocześnie z wyraźnymi problemami projektowymi, które często wpływają na komfort rozgrywki. System rozwoju postaci Jednym z największych atutów gry jest ogromna różnorodność buildów. Gracz może rozwijać postać na wiele sposobów, od klasycznego wojownika z ciężką bronią, przez szybkie buildy zręcznościowe, aż po potężne postacie oparte na magii. System rozwoju daje dużą swobodę i zachęca do eksperymentowania. Problem pojawia się jednak w trakcie rozgrywki. Dość często okazuje się, że build, który wcześniej działał bardzo dobrze, nagle przestaje być skuteczny. W pewnym momencie trafiamy na ścianę i przeciwnicy lub bossowie zaczynają być wyraźnie trudniejsi dla konkretnego stylu gry. W efekcie gracz zamiast rozwijać postać według własnej wizji zaczyna dostosowywać się do wymagań konkretnych walk. Oprawa wizualna i świat gry Pod względem artystycznym gra prezentuje się znakomicie. Świat jest ogromny, różnorodny i pełen charakterystycznych lokacji, a każdy region ma swój klimat i wizualną tożsamość. Na uwagę zasługuje również historia świata współtworzona przez George R. R. Martin. Lore jest ciekawy i intrygujący, choć duża część fabuły pozostaje ukryta w opisach przedmiotów i fragmentach dialogów. Dla jednych jest to element budujący tajemnicę świata, dla innych bariera w odbiorze historii. Problemy z kamerą Największą wadą gry jest kamera. To właśnie tutaj pojawia się najwięcej sytuacji prowadzących do frustracji. Podczas walki z przeciwnikiem można zablokować kamerę na celu. W teorii ma to pomagać w śledzeniu przeciwnika, ale w praktyce często prowadzi do chaosu. Kamera potrafi się gubić, nagle zmieniać pozycję albo ustawiać pod dziwnym kątem. W efekcie gracz nie widzi ani ataków przeciwnika, ani czasami nawet własnej postaci. Problem szczególnie nasila się przy dużych przeciwnikach. Kamera potrafi wtedy ustawić się tak blisko modelu bossa, że trudno ocenić sytuację na ekranie. Próba grania bez blokady celu również nie rozwiązuje problemu, ponieważ kamera nadal potrafi poruszać się samoczynnie i nie zawsze pozostaje tam, gdzie gracz chciałby ją ustawić. W praktyce oznacza to, że część zgonów nie wynika z błędu gracza ani z poziomu trudności walki, lecz z problemów technicznych i projektowych. Powtarzalność przeciwników i bossów Kolejną wadą jest design przeciwników oraz powtarzalność wielu walk. W wielu miejscach widać wyraźne użycie metody kopiuj i wklej. Boss, z którym wcześniej stoczyliśmy efektowną walkę, później pojawia się jako zwykły przeciwnik w innej lokacji. Osłabia to poczucie wyjątkowości starć i sprawia, że niektóre momenty przestają być tak znaczące, jak powinny. Walki bywają widowiskowe, ale to nie zawsze oznacza, że są dobrze zaprojektowane. Niektóre starcia sprawiają wrażenie mocno oskryptowanych. Czasami wygląda to tak, jakby można je było przejść sensownie tylko jednym konkretnym stylem gry, ponieważ inne podejścia są znacznie trudniejsze. Podejście do nowych graczy Gra nie szanuje również graczy, którzy wcześniej nie mieli styczności z tytułami typu Souls. W wielu momentach zakłada się, że gracz już zna mechaniki charakterystyczne dla tego gatunku. Systemy gry są słabo tłumaczone i wiele rzeczy trzeba odkrywać metodą prób i błędów. Popularność marki w dużej mierze opiera się na opinii o jej wyjątkowej trudności. W praktyce jednak spora część tej trudności wynika z problemów projektowych. Nieczytelność walki, problemy z kamerą czy niespójne decyzje designerskie sprawiają, że gra bywa wymagająca nie dlatego, że przeciwnicy są świetnie zaprojektowani, ale dlatego, że niektóre elementy gry utrudniają komfortowe granie. System punktów odrodzenia Dobrym przykładem niespójnego designu jest system punktów odrodzenia. Czasami ognisko znajduje się dosłownie przed areną bossa, a dodatkowo mamy jeszcze statuę, która pozwala odrodzić się jeszcze bliżej. W innych sytuacjach po każdej śmierci trzeba pokonywać długą drogę z ogniska do bramy bossa. Przy trudniejszych przeciwnikach, takich jak Malenia, Blade of Miquella, oznacza to, że spora część czasu nie jest poświęcona samej walce. Zamiast tego gracz biegnie z powrotem do areny i ponownie nakłada buffy przed starciem. W efekcie nawet jedna czwarta czasu spędzonego przy bossie może polegać po prostu na powtarzaniu tej samej drogi. Podsumowanie Elden Ring jest produkcją pełną kontrastów. Z jednej strony oferuje piękny świat, ciekawy lore i ogromne możliwości budowania postaci. Z drugiej strony cierpi na wyraźne problemy projektowe, takie jak praca kamery, powtarzalność przeciwników czy niespójne rozwiązania w designie walk. Nie jest to zła gra, ale zdecydowanie nie jest też tak bezbłędna, jak sugerują niektóre opinie. Część graczy wynosi ją na piedestał głównie ze względu na renomę studia FromSoftware, a niekoniecznie przez faktyczną jakość wszystkich elementów gry. To tytuł, który potrafi zachwycić wizją świata, ale jednocześnie momentami potrafi też bardzo frustrować.

My first dodge-based souls/souls-like game, I found the game overall great (I still prefer parry-based systems like sekiro/lies of p). By far the best aspect is the open world exploration and subtle worldbuilding, but I would've enjoyed to see more of a narrative/story. The environments are gorgeous and the game runs well on PC. The music is good too, although not much was memorable. Unfortunately, I knew of some of the bosses and a couple areas from social media (like sword woman, blood man, first couple major bosses, and final boss), but the exploration was still top tier, as most areas I have not seen. This game is the game to play if you are looking for exploration. Another pro is the gameplay; the game feels snappy and responsive, very cool enemy designs, and it is overall satisfying to play. There are also some cons. The main, unavoidable one is having an open world souls game, as that makes some areas you explore "out of order" easier or harder than "intended". For example, I followed the main quest for a little, then I went back to the starting region and found the rest of that region really easy. Similarly, since there are so many extra places and things to do to earn souls, I got to a high enough level starting at the midgame that I could beat every boss in one or two attempts, and a lot of the endgame bosses also became too easy aside from malenia (beat blood man, and the final few bosses all in 1 or 2 attempts). There were no exceptionally difficult bosses, as I only had 3 bosses take around 2 hours (malenia, 1st tree sentinel, and a black blade kindred), but I think it is hard to make an exceptionally difficult boss because of the open world nature of the game. The other primary con I had was the parkour/jumping was janky, which was sometimes frustrating. Overall, if you like exploration and some challenge, this is the game for you (or you could use summons to make it easier). However, because of the open world, many of the bosses will end up being too easy if you choose to explore a lot. If you are looking for a challenging souls game, you can get that as long as you choose not to level up as much, otherwise the main draw of the game is exploration.

What else can I say other than that this game is a modern classic. I love how open ended and expansive the game is with there being so many options on how to tackle the humongous world. I've done multiple playthroughs of this game on different platforms and each one always leads to new discoveries and challenges. From spirit ash summons, swappable ashes of war/special attacks, the wonderous physick, new weapon and spell types, and multiple accessible areas of varying difficulty at the start, the game is yours to customize to your taste with no need for traditional difficulty options. Those who want an easier time with magic and the like will also have to do a lot more exploring which makes it feel much more like you have earned your power instead of gaining power by just getting a bunch of money and making a number go up (and before you ask, yes my first playthrough was done with a no summon, no buff, pure strength melee run with the bastard sword so I think I've earned my right to have fun). The game also hides many large areas behind side content, hidden walls, and quest lines which is a double edged sword since it can mean you find hours of new content on repeat playthroughs, but at the same time it means that many useful items for builds may never be found if you don't look in the right places or use a guide. My main problem with the game is you'll encounter the same couple bosses (many of which become normal enemies) over the course of the game and that lots of the side areas have copy pasted layouts, gimmicks, and enemies (although much of it is designed with some intentionality which I will take any day over the god forsaken chalice dungeons of Bloodborne). I'd highly recommend anyone who plays to pace themselves and to vary up what side content they engage with or you'll be in for quite a few boring hours. After the first playthrough, making a new build can also be less interesting as the game just becomes a checklist to get whatever you want for a certain loadout. My last problem off the top of my head is that multiplayer has been gutted quite a bit with what would traditionally be covenants in the souls games now being reduced to questlines and player invasions only happening to players with summons. The "covenants" in the game are also quite meaningless since you can just join every faction you come across freely with no penalty or rivalry between them, losing much of the identity and focus of what was in the souls games. Overall, although the game isn't absolutely perfect I still think that the quality shines through and it is worth at least one playthrough, if not more.

Elden Ring is, quite simply, a masterpiece and easily a 10/10 experience in my book. It stands as one of the most complete and ambitious action RPGs ever created and firmly sits in my personal top 10 games of all time. The most immediate achievement Elden Ring delivers is its open world design. The Lands Between feel vast, mysterious, and endlessly explorable without ever relying on traditional map markers or hand-holding. Discovery happens naturally through curiosity, whether stumbling upon hidden dungeons, unexpected bosses, or entire underground regions that feel like secrets waiting to be uncovered. Exploration consistently rewards players with meaningful encounters, gear, lore, or progression opportunities, making nearly every direction feel worth investigating. Combat builds upon the refined mechanics seen in previous FromSoftware titles while expanding player freedom dramatically. The variety of weapons, Ashes of War, spells, summons, and build paths allows players to craft highly personalized playstyles. Whether leaning into melee mastery, magic dominance, hybrid experimentation, or unconventional approaches, Elden Ring supports creativity in ways that feel empowering rather than restrictive. Boss design is another major highlight. The game features some of the best encounters FromSoftware has ever produced, blending spectacle, mechanical challenge, and strong thematic presence. Many fights feel like climactic moments that reflect the world’s mythology and decay, creating victories that are both mechanically satisfying and narratively meaningful. The lore and worldbuilding are equally exceptional. Elden Ring presents a layered mythos filled with fallen demigods, fractured powers, and cosmic influences that players gradually piece together through exploration, dialogue, and item descriptions. This approach preserves the studio’s signature interpretive storytelling while scaling it to match the game’s massive world. Atmosphere and art direction further elevate the experience. Every region carries a distinct identity, from golden plains to scarlet wastelands and haunting eternal cities. The visual variety ensures that the world rarely feels repetitive despite its size, maintaining a constant sense of wonder and discovery. In terms of flaws, there are very few that significantly impact the experience. Crafting stands out as the most noticeable limitation. While it functions as a useful supplementary system, many players can progress comfortably without relying heavily on it. As a mechanic, it feels like it had potential for deeper integration into gameplay loops, but its current implementation often makes it optional rather than essential. Even with that minor criticism, Elden Ring succeeds on nearly every level. Its world design, combat depth, boss encounters, lore, and atmosphere come together to form an experience that feels both expansive and cohesive. It captures the sense of adventure and discovery that defines the best RPGs while maintaining the challenge and identity that FromSoftware is known for. Overall, Elden Ring is a landmark title that represents the peak of modern action RPG design. With unforgettable exploration, some of the studio’s strongest bosses, and deeply compelling lore, it stands as an easy recommendation and a game that will likely be remembered as one of the defining releases of its generation.

The experience of Elden Ring is impressive in scale but underwhelming in variety. The open world looks magnificent, yet exploration often yields repetitive encounters and predictable rewards. Combat is precise but rigid swing, dodge, repeat with only marginal differences between weapons and little evolution in mechanics over time. Boss fights provide challenge, though many rely on memorization rather than strategic depth, making victories feel like endurance tests. The narrative atmosphere is strong but distant. Lore is delivered cryptically, requiring significant interpretation, which can enrich immersion but also reduce emotional engagement. Smaller design issues clunky menus and sparse system explanations add friction. I liked aspects of it, particularly the art direction and moments of discovery, but the overall experience feels mechanically stagnant. It is polished and competent, yet rarely transcends its core loop or delivers sustained innovation. But the fire giant is pretty s3xy so 10/10

A recent return to Elden Ring finally helped me understand what so many players have been praising for years. After multiple past attempts where the magic just didn’t click, this latest playthrough opened my eyes to how remarkable the game truly is. The world is stunning, with sweeping vistas, intricate ruins, and atmospheric lighting that make every region feel alive. The sound design elevates that sense of place even further—haunting ambient tracks, thunderous boss themes, and crisp combat audio all work together to pull you deeper into the Lands Between. The combat is where everything really came together for me. It’s challenging, sometimes brutally so, but it’s also deliberate, responsive, and endlessly rewarding once the rhythm sets in. What made the difficulty feel more manageable this time was embracing both player summons and spirit ashes. They don’t trivialize the game, but they smooth out the rough edges enough to let the brilliance of the encounters shine through instead of feeling like a wall. After finally “getting it,” I can confidently say Elden Ring is an exceptional experience—one that rewards persistence with moments of awe, triumph, and discovery. 9.5/10.

It took me three attempts to get into this game and I’m glad I kept trying. It’s a masterpiece through and through. Don’t be put off if this is your first Soulslike like it was mine. Whether you’re experienced with the genre or not, you’re going to die a lot. Just note that every death is a lesson and there’s always something to learn from it. Apart from deaths to fall damage. You’ll keep thinking you’ll survive the fall, and you know what? You won’t know until you try. Boss fights will have you questioning what you did to deserve the beating you’re about to receive, but when you finally get them down it’s such a rewarding feeling. My main piece of advice is that you have got to play this game blind. The game is absolutely huge and with its DLC it’s bigger than you could ever imagine. It just keeps going, and going, and going. You are never going to do or find everything in your first run unless you’re studying a guide from day one. Since the game is so focused on exploration and in a way, creating your own journey, you’re robbing yourself of the experience if your first playthrough is through someone else’s eyes. So don’t worry about seeing everything. Keep your first run organic, and then if you really take to the game you can run it back in NG+ and clean up what you missed. The game is breathtaking to look at, and every scene really does feel like a painting. The music is insane and some of the boss OST tracks go so hard to the point where you'll be too busy getting hyped up and you'll forget you're about to die. The story is dark and heartbreaking, although unfortunately unless you read the description of every single item in the game, a lot of the story is going to fly under the radar. Don’t be afraid to listen to some YouTube videos where people dive deep into the lore. I fully recommend VaatiVidya’s lore videos. Just be careful about diving too deep into the lore too early as you may spoil some revelations. The Shadow of the Erdtree DLC basically feels like Elden Ring 2 due to the sheer size of its content. It also does a really good job of recreating the experience of playing the game for the first time, as you’ll go in thinking you’re prepared and quickly learn that all those levels you grinded in the base game mean nothing here. Get used to dying again. 10/10. Turtles are dogs. You owe all the Lobsters money. I'm going to play the game again and still fall for every trapped chest because I suck.

An amazing artistic work with cool exploration, but the worst gameplay ever put in a AAA game. 1. There's no pause button. Immediately that's just unacceptable to not have a basic game feature such as pausing. Also you can't open an check your map if there's an enemy nearby. Why? I'm trying to navigate and there are basically always enemies nearby. This is just annoying and there's no reason for it. 2. Multiplayer system requires in-game resources which need to be repeatedly used if someone dies. This is pointless. 3. Combat is slow, clunky, unresponsive, insufferable, and unfortunately a big part of the game. Playing as a mage, your character takes so long to cast a spell you're just going to get hit doing it. Your spells rely on guzzling infinite potions, but your character also takes so long to drink a potion that you're also going to get hit doing that. There's also a lock-on feature since there's no actual cross-hairs to aim spells, but your character can't actually aim straight. You can "lock on" to an enemy, and your character will just miss anyway, burning more of your magic meter in the process through no control of your own. I swear, Skyrim of all games had better magic use than this because you could actually just aim magic yourself. On top of this, your spells have an absolutely pitiful range. You could throw a rock farther than you could cast a spell. Also the spells don't aim where you're aiming, they aim where your body direction is pointing. Speaking of guzzling potions. You can get away with not having to drink health potions if you're good enough since you can mostly dodge damage outside of some attacks that just fill the whole screen, however for magic you just need to. You will also need to select spells to use. Both of these require you to use the game's cycling menu. Normal games would have some sort of wheel you pull up to select an item or spell. Instead, the developers make you cycle through spells and potions in a one-way selection scroll by pressing up or down on your D-Pad. So you also have to frantically manage an unintuitive and clunky spell and potions selection system amidst the slow and clumsy character gameplay. Your character can "dodge", but is so slothful even with a lighter load that it's a good second between pressing the button and him rolling as if you're playing a laggy online game. This is fairly integral to the game, and so having so central a mechanic be so slow, and also not actionable if you're drinking a potion for example, is completely insane and against any sort of common sense. You would think if the character had any sense of self-preservation whatsoever they would supercede drinking a potion with rolling and moving out of the way of an incoming attack. Not so. Our stupid hero has an IQ of a lemming and zero regard for his own life, and so if you try to hit that dodge button while drinking a potion or performing an action, nothing will happen. The devs programmed the character to simply be stupid and you have little control over what he does moment to moment. You almost need to think of it as a turn based game rather than an action game, and lock in your actions in a queue far ahead of time, like playing chess by mail. Compare this to something like DOOM. You have fast attack power, intuitive aiming, responsive movement. Combat actions are entirely in your hands in other better games, not arguing with an in-game avatar to do what it's told. Playing this game and its controls feel so disconnected it's as if I'm yelling at the character what to do and he's a bit hard of hearing so only registers it a second or so after. This is just what we'd call basic unresponsive controls in any other game and it's not really charming or excusable here just because the art is nice. 4. The game's "difficulty" is pretty much just based on levelling and enemies having bigger numbers than your numbers, and the above described incompetent controls. The "action" of the "action RPG" is better served if you're running melee, because with magic you are hard locked to the amount of meter you have to trade into damage dealt. It's a math equation more than any sort of action. 5. I swear, I thought we were done with garbage cameras in games, but this one if you use the targeting system (there is no other way to actually aim) the camera absolutely freaks out so you can't see anything if you're close to the enemy you're targeting in many cases, especially with big bosses. 6. The final boss is pathetic. The first stage is easy, the second just runs away from you the entire time. It's not even really a boss fight so much as a marathon simulator. Doesn't matter if you're magic or melee, your magic has no range so you'll have to be running after it either way. It's extremely anticlimactic, especially after there were a couple of cool bosses right before leading up to it. The boss you fight right before the final boss should have been the final boss, felt like a much more intense battle. Overall it's like a beautiful woman with a nightmare personality. The game is gorgeous to look at, and then absolutely unbearable to actually interact with. At best combat just becomes boring and repetitive while having to slog through the controls. Instead the game shines most when exploring, and is like pulling teeth when you have to actually play it.

Elden Ring is beautiful, creative, and very rewarding when you’re exploring and learning the world. That’s what makes it special. But the invasion mechanic completely breaks that experience for me. For me, the game is at its best when it feels like this: exploring a dangerous world, learning enemy patterns, discovering secrets, slowly getting better through practice. That is the experience I signed up for, and I love it. But invasions suddenly throw in a completely different kind of game. You go from learning the world and fighting designed enemies to dealing with another player who is often much more experienced in PvP and built specifically for it. It feels less like a challenge you can learn from and more like someone interrupting your session. I don’t mind difficulty. I mind unfairness and interruption. If invasions were separate/optional in a clearer way, this would be an easy positive review from me.

[h1]Aah, I knew you'd come...[/h1] Welcome brave Tarnished, welcome indeed. The Lands Between await! [h2]What is this Elden Ring game then?[/h2] Well... It's a Souls game, no doubt you've heard things like "Souls like" thrown around to describe many other games, but what does it mean? It means that you're in for an adventure like no other. You see, a Souls game (starting with the first Dark Souls) doesn't hold your hand... It doesn't have big exclamation points for quest NPC's, it doesn't give you a path to follow and it doesn't forgive you when you decide to wander into an area you're technically not yet meant to be, but hey, there's ways around that... It's not a game where you can start fresh and just clobber everything, you'll be the one getting clobbered, over & over... And even IF you take your time (which I REALLY recommend you do!) you'll still die. A lot. Elden ring is the latest From Software Souls game (and it's expansion), Nightrein being a sidetrack from that as that's more a co-op roguelike Souls game. [h1]Is this a game for you?[/h1] As I said before: A Souls game isn't for someone looking for an easy cosy game... It's a brutal environment, where just about everything is out to kill you (and will easily do so)... So why does anyone play this then, I hear you ask? Because the adventure is so damn good... Take your time, explore every nook & cranny (and even then you'll miss things), try different strategies and invest proper time. I guarantee you, you'll love your time in The Lands Between... [h1]The nitty gritty[/h1] The game looks great, it just does... It's dark, eary and generally feels harsh at first, unwelcoming even but as you spend more & more time in The Lands Between you'll find yourself starting to really appreciate the environment (Well, I do, except for Caelid, what a horrid place...). Sound & music is good as well, can't fault it... Controls feel good, but I HIGHLY recommend playing using a controller! You can play it with mouse & keyboard, but I found that to be a very annoying thing to do... Gameplay wise then... It's a Souls game by FromSoftware, what do you think? From exploring the vast world to running through caves, it just feels good to move around... And the combat? Well... [h1]Yes, the combat[/h1] Wether you're a ranged magic player, or a melee player, or a combination of it all, the combat is another aspect of any Souls game that will try & test your patience... Not because the mechanics aren't good, but because it's a Souls game... Dodge, parry, jump, roll are essential to your survival and are EXTREMELY rewarding to do when you've finally taken down a big foe that has been stopping you... [h1]Conclusion[/h1] I grew to love this game so much... When I first bought it, I played for a bit and then left it be... But later one I become more & more drawn to it... I'm currently about 13 hours into a new playthrough, taking it slow and there's just so much to do, to explore... I highly recommend Elden Ring (and it's expansion, although I haven't reach it yet) to anyone looking for a game where they can spend HOURS and HOURS adventuring, exploring The Lands Between!
