I recently re-played Dark Souls 1 and 3, and then started Elden Ring - I can't help but notice a couple of things so flagrant: Every FromSoft game (except Sekiro, I didn't play that) was hard, but not for the sake of being hard. Bosses had purpose in Dark Souls games. They filled the bottom of the lore of almost every single boss, even the unimportant looking optional ones. In Elden Ring, even though the story and the world is quite exciting, they f*cked it up by filling the world with the same bosses, mini-bosses and makeshift looking mobs everywhere. They made a huge and beautiful open-world just to fill it with Godskins, Tree Sentinels and Gargoyles. They may have the lore behind why they're everywhere, but it's sickening me that I have to kill the same f*cking gargoyle with the same f*cking moveset for the 7th time throughout my playthrough, just because George R.R. Martin couldn't figure out how to connect that part of the story. Oh, the regular Gargoyle isn't enough? Let's put 2 of them there and make them attack the player simultaneously just because we ran out of ideas to design an actual, smart boss to put there. [spoiler]The "Godskin Duo" isn't a duo either, don't trust the game - never.[/spoiler] The game's clearly against you, that's not a secret and has always been like that, but Elden Ring has the d*ck moves I thought only Dark Souls 2 could've pulled. Again; the game's filled with many cheap tricks and traps to kill you - totally ruining the bit of fun I've been having throughout the game. Also, I never had this much dependence on community guides and wikis of the game IN ANY GAME that I've ever played, and I've played the Dark Souls series. You literally have times that you have to find your way via wiki, just to progress in the main storyline. In no game I was frustrated this much because no matter how much you level your character up, you're never enough. The game basically never rewards the player. You never get "strong". It's just an 100 hour long suffer-fest. Not only these, but also the game fails to tell its story so much that I wasn't able to find my "main way" for the main storyline until about 40-45 hours - and when I found, I still couldn't continue from there because I was too weak to continue the main story, even though I spent about 3-5 hours of those 40-45 hours just to grind mindlessly... So yeah, the game makes sure you don't catch up with the content in the main story as well, it pushes you to "go out and explore the mysteries of the world that Miyazaki has built!". That's the way they romanticize failing to explain the story to the player. I believe why Elden Ring's praised this much is because it plays its marketing cards to the new players instead of the existing Souls players - having George R.R. Martin for the lore is a proof of that. They don't know how deep and beautiful the Dark Souls were, so it was easy to fill the world with meaningless things with unworthy awards and recycling bosses again and again, just to say "we made an huge open-world for you". I can't blame, the world is really beautiful - but that's about it for Elden Ring. Literally everything else was more enjoyable when they were simpler in Dark Souls. Darkeater Midir was the hardest boss I've ever fought in a Souls game. It took me about 2 weeks to level up my character, learn sorceries and learn the moveset of Midir properly to kill it. I never complained for a second of that journey. But I find myself complaining about Elden Ring quite often, even on very simple enemies. Not because it's hard, but because it's quite a low quality experience that I have to fight the sh*t I stepped on 60 hours ago. All and all, Elden Ring is a good game, maybe a great one even, but it's quite a bad FromSoftware game I would say. It's never fair - not that it promises that but the Soulslike genre used to be fair before. You can't simply enjoy this game, you have to be a nerd about it. The difference with before is; you could enjoy Dark Souls because you felt the power as you're going through the story in those games. This... This is a great and exciting world that is very stretched, borderline never ending and quite bloated, in which you're never "the stronger one". This kind of feels like the 17th season of your favorite TV show because it milks the money out of people. It was an experience for sure - one that I wish I never had and wouldn't recommend to anybody. [h1]5/10[/h1]

Discount not my playtime, I have journeyed from the realms of Sony in order to traverse the lands between and write this review. While I could talk for a while about this game, I think I'll keep things short and sweet. Elden Ring is probably my most replayed game aside from Dark Souls 3, and so with that comes an obvious bias towards the more fast paced direction Fromsoft went with their later entries. Elden Ring follows in this new direction, which may understandably not be to some people's preference. However, Elden Ring offers players a bountiful amount of weapons to choose from and switch between. Variety is the spice of life they say! And that's this game's greatest strength and weakness: Variety. There are a variety of options for builds, weapons, and where you can go in this world. So much of it is amazing, but there are also portions of this game that are correctly labeled as repetitive and bland. But there's always the choice to do something else, something that is genuinely cool or rewarding not far away. Or maybe far enough away to warrant an expedition! This game has its' flaws and its' combat will not be to everyone's liking, but I think this is one of the best games ever made and you'd be doing yourself a favor to at least check it out.

Another classic from Fromsoft themselves. The expansive world and ability to take the game as you please lets even the worst players (myself) feel powerful and fulfilled. 9/10 Fighting is smooth and fluid. As someone who has only played the first Dark Souls, I don't feel clogged or stuck when running through enemies or taking on bosses. Alongside this is the ability to level up attributes like dex and endurance that make your character able to move in a freeing state. It makes the player feel like they are truly on their way to be the Elden Lord with status and prestige. This next bit is a huge skill issue: there is obviously Fromsoft jank. Enemy placements are often random. Getting jumped by an enemy on the other side of a wall is not fun. It is not good game design. It's dumb and stupid and I should not be punished for walking. Getting jumped by multiple enemies and getting stun locked or hit with madness is not fun. The random ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ is what takes the most time to complete and makes the playtime from the intended 30+ hours to 100+ hours. Tangent over, this game is really great. The polish of the open world and gameplay flow is genre-defining and will continue to be the blueprint of massive games over the years. A masterpiece with a touch of masochism

Elden Ring is genuinely one of the best gaming experiences I’ve had — and it was also my first Soulsborne / first FromSoftware game. Before starting, everyone kept telling me it was brutally hard and frustrating, but honestly it didn’t feel that way to me. What makes Elden Ring special is that it doesn’t just say “get good or quit.” It gives you options. If something feels too tough, you can explore somewhere else, level up, upgrade your gear, change your build, use Ashes of War, spells, summons — and come back stronger. For almost every boss there’s some strategy that works, and that feeling of adapting and finally winning is incredibly satisfying. Once you get stronger, the game opens up even more. You can experiment with different weapons and completely different playstyles, and it still feels fresh. I also loved the fast travel system — it keeps the pacing smooth and prevents the open world from becoming boring or time-wasting. The freedom you have in this game is amazing, the world is full of surprises, and it absolutely feels worth the price. Highly recommended, even if you’ve never played a FromSoftware game before

This was my first souls-like game, and first truly difficult game for that matter. I'm giving this a positive review, but there are many things holding me in the threshold between "love" and "obsessed". [h1] Positives (in no particular order): [/h1] [h3] - Amazing worldbuilding. [/h3] The world feels alive and it feels like it would exist without the player. It does a great job of making you feel small and helpless, causing you to treat every enemy with respect and plan ahead, instead of just rushing in and spamming. Because of this, it really made me use my brain, something I don't usually do in my day to day life. [h3] - Fantastic enemy design. [/h3] Each enemy has something different to offer, while also staying predictable. One of my favorite parts of this game is entering a boss arena for the first time, not knowing what to expect, with a hare trigger finger on the roll button. I love the first few tries of memorizing their move-sets, looking for damage and heal windows, and getting over the anxiety of a new enemy. [h3] - Gorgeous visuals. [/h3] I will talk more about the [i] graphics [/i] in the negative part, since... there definitely are some issues, but the way the world is laid out, I remember being awestruck when I stepped in to limgrave for the first time, and seeing the entire world ascending in a spiral in front of me. There are plenty of beautiful views, and each region is easily told apart from its visuals. [h3] - Insane amount of spells and weapons. [/h3] I am absolutely blown away by the amount of spells and weapons in this game. Some may be much more viable than others, but it really just has something for everyone. (see negatives for more) [h3] - Easy to climb over the brick wall. [/h3] I have never once raged at this game (says a lot, I suck at games), because there's always the option to go explore and level up to better match your foe. If you're REALLY stuck, (looking at you, Maliketh...) you have the options of spirit summoning, co-op summoning to just get you through. [h3] - Great control scheme. [/h3] (Not sure about KBM, I only played on controller) It was a huge learning curve, but I think it couldn't be any better. Anyone who complains, try to think of a better way to fit 50 or so options onto a gamepad. [h3] - Story and writing. [/h3] While I haven't fully dove in to the lore yet, I find the world to be extremely intriguing. Going back to my first point, it has a way of making you feel insignificant, forcing your way in to the history of the world. The characters and NPC's are whimiscal and mysterious, grabbing my curiosity and making me want to do their sidequests. (more about these in the negatives) [h1] Negatives (ordered from severe to neglegable): [/h1] [h3] - Horrible performance. [/h3] I have a Ryzen 7 7800x3d and an RTX 5080, and I still get horrendous stutters, and in areas like Farum Azula, I can barely manage to get over 50fps. The only way to stop these stutters is to turn off raytracing and turn on windowed borderless, which for one, makes shadows look horrendous, and second, disables HDR entirely. [h3] - 60fps cap. [/h3] Do I even have to explain? its 2026. What the heck man. Don't get me wrong, it's fine when you're playing on controller, but still, its jittery and rough whenever you move the camera. Its also tough when you're facing an enemy with very quick move-sets. [h3] - Inconsistent graphics. [/h3] There is terrible artifacting in the screen spaced reflections, and in shadows as well. I'm not sure why they relied on screen space data for shadows, but it looks terrible, causing a white glow in the grass around my character. which brings me to another point. Why have ray tracing without ray traced reflections and global illumination? Indoor and underground scenes look extremely lackluster, and there are soooo many lighting bugs. [h3] - Empty world after Limgrave / no incentive to explore. [/h3] When I first began playing, I found the world to be rich, and full of possible exploration, but that quickly came to a halt when I got in to Liurnia and further. It's not that there's nothing to explore, it's that 9/10 times, you end up getting an item that you'll never use for your build, or just an entirely useless weapon. Also, I got so so tired of the cycle of, "caves and catacombs, catacombs and caves, oop, a tunnel, oh back to a catacomb, and then a cave." They're all more or less the same, and get repetitive to explore. There are absolutely some out-liars, but speaking in general here. The open world aspect of exploration stays fun up until Altus, where the world is full of enemies that will one-shot you off your horse, and swarm you to death. I preferred how in the previous regions, you could just run past the open world enemies, and only kill them if you want the runes. [h3] - Quests. [/h3] Say skill issue all you want, but I found the quests to be very confusing and drawn out. Ride to point A, kill this thing, take said thing to point B, talk to so and so, do a portion of the main story then return, oops you're locked out of another quest. Now I'm not saying there should be map markers and yellow paint, but I think some of the quests could have been made much clearer. [h3] - All build variations feel more or less the same. [/h3] I tried many different builds in my first playthrough, taking full advantage of every larval tear I found to find what I liked, and I found the different builds to be very lackluster. My favorites were a strength build with Radahn's swords, and a Moonveil build, but even then, both were still the same playstyle when you really look in to it. I did also try using magic, and it seemed awesome, but just wasn't for me. Overall, the positives outweigh the negatives ten fold, but there are so many things that should have been patched in the first year, or even with the DLC release. What matters the most however, is that I had LOADS of fun on my first playthrough, and will be trying all the other soulslike games soon. I would go so far as to say it's worth the full price. Overall, 9.5/10, it would get a 10/10 from me if they fixed the performance. [h2]Introduction:[/h2] At the time of writing this, I am 25 hours into my playthrough. I've tried the game before, but it didn't really stick. I can't remember why. This time though, it's really really hitting me. I was having a real life struggle and there was a parallel. The only Souls game I've finished before is Sekiro, so that may dictate some opinions. It's a bit early for a review, so let's call this an [h2]impressions:[/h2] I'm getting my driver's license late in life, and just going behind the wheel is giving me anxiety. And I was wondering why I was feeling this way, so that I could do something to combat the anxiousness. And The Tree Sentinel really gave me a similar sensation. I knew he wasn't that tough of a mini-boss. He was basically the first boss of the game, the tutorial boss, the easiest, tiniest boss, but I was having trouble with it. I had even beat him before when I first tried the game, and some lingering muscle memory was there; I thought I could predict his movements simply. I didn't understand why driving was giving me anxiety, so many people in the world do it, so it can't be that stressful. But it was for me. I did the take-a-break maneuver since it didn't seem like I was getting anywhere with the boss, and almost immediately after I put down the controller, I realized something. I was trying to balance firing spells at it, and melee attacking, while my wolves attacked it. To put it simply, too much was going on. I recalled how I normally played Souls games. I started two-handing my sword and put aside all thoughts of Spirit Ashes and magic arrows and went back to basics; dodge and stab, and I killed him in around 3 tries. I was so stuck on one way of doing things that I could not see another. I had heard or felt that I knew the game was easier with spellcasting and summons, but in that specific case, where my fundamentals were so rusty, the very opposite was true for me. The game had an appresive air for I want to say the first couple hours. I wasn't really enjoying it. I felt like I was either running away from everything or running into everything. It all felt panicked and stressful. It didn't' feel like how a game is supposed to feel - fun. It didn't feel like how everyone talked about the game - with an air of casual disregard. And then I started looking up builds. I'd always loved the feeling of synergies and minmaxing in other RPGs. And that changed game for me. I know the sense of discovery, of finding things for yourself is paramount in this sort of game's enjoyment, but getting that one item, that one powerful early game staff changed everything for me. I also began leveling my health because of how important I read it was. Now I too walked around the game with the casual swagger that I imagined everyone else did. The world changed completely for me. Frustration was no longer lurking behind every corner, but opportunity. I was no longer scared to explore. I could finally take my time instead of feeling rushed. I began trying out different weapons for the fun of it even if they weren't as strong or as reliable as my starting sword which I had upgraded. I felt like I finally understood the game, what it offered, and how other's got enjoyment out of it. As of writing this, I can't stop playing the game. I think about it whenever I'm not playing it. I can't remember the last time I was so engrossed in a game. As for the story, I have little to no idea what's going on, but I get the feeling that that's something I'll only understand after my second playthrough. The periods between the story being so long since I'm really exploring every corner that I can. [b]10/10[/b]

[b]General verdict:[/b] Elden Ring is the most beautiful game ever made and currently sits at #1 on my list, with The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim in second place like a proud but slightly confused uncle. [b]This is the most video game, game ever made.[/b] Not “cinematic experience,” not “interactive movie,” not “press X to feel emotions.” No. This is pure, concentrated VIDEO GAME. You go somewhere → something horrible happens → you get stronger → you come back → you commit violence with confidence. Repeat until you accidentally become a god. I finished the base game at around 110 hours — not because it had to take that long, but because I was vibing, sightseeing, and treating the Lands Between like a medieval vacation spot with occasional murder. I absolutely could’ve finished faster, but why rush when every hill hides a cave, every cave hides trauma, and every piece of scenery looks like a desktop wallpaper? And even then, I still missed a TON of stuff. Started NG+ and immediately discovered areas and bosses I somehow walked past like an NPC with no dialogue options. Exploration in this game isn’t just rewarded, it’s aggressively encouraged. The map whispers “go over there :)” and then over there is either: 1. a legendary weapon 2. a lore revelation that rewires your brain 3. a guy named something like “Ulcerated Tree Spirit Who Ate God” 4. or a chest that teleports you to Brazil (Caelid) Every time you say “I’ll just check that one thing,” congratulations, it’s now 3 AM. The lore is absolute peak. Not spoon-fed, not dumped in your lap — you have to assemble it like IKEA furniture but with depression and cosmic horror. Voice acting? Incredible. Cutscenes? Cinema. NPCs? Either tragic icons, cryptic weirdos, or people who will absolutely die if you blink wrong during their questline. If you’re new to Soulslikes: yes, it will beat you up, take your lunch money, and call you maidenless. But it’s fair. Mostly. The real trick is leveling up, learning attack patterns, and accepting that panic-rolling is a lifestyle, not a mistake. Also the build variety is insane. Want to be a holy knight? Done. Edgy bleed goblin? Easy. Wizard with nuclear capabilities? Absolutely. Naked guy with a stick and trust issues? The game fully supports your bad decisions. [b]Final thoughts:[/b] This game made me feel awe, triumph, terror, confusion, grief, and the primal urge to fight trees. It is art. It is suffering. It is a horse that can double-jump. 10/10 would get psychologically evaluated and physically molested by a boss again.

Some games you finish. Some games you shelve. And then there's Elden Ring — the game that lives in your head rent-free long after the credits roll, quietly pulling you back every single time. I've tried to articulate what makes this game special. I've drafted paragraphs in my mind, rehearsed arguments about the level design, the atmosphere, the sheer audacity of its open world. But every time I sit down to put it into words, all that comes out is this: "After all this time, the game I keep coming back to is this. Forever." And maybe that says more than any structured critique ever could. The Lands Between isn't just a map — it's a world that rewards curiosity in ways few games even attempt. Every crumbling ruin hides something. Every horizon begs to be reached. FromSoftware built a place that feels ancient and alive at the same time, and no matter how many times you ride through Limgrave or descend into the depths beneath the capital, there's always something you missed. The combat is punishing, sure. But it's also deeply fair in a way that makes every victory feel earned and every death feel like a lesson. Whether you're a colossal greatsword enjoyer or a sorcery-slinging glass cannon, the game respects your choices and challenges you to master them. But what truly sets Elden Ring apart isn't any single system or mechanic. It's the pull. That inexplicable gravity that draws you back months or even years later. You'll be playing something else entirely and suddenly think: I wonder what a new build would feel like. I wonder what I missed in that one cave. I wonder if I can finally beat Malenia without summoning. And just like that, you're back. Again. There are games you recommend. There are games you love. And then there's the rare game that simply becomes part of you. Elden Ring is that game. 10/10 — not because it's flawless, but because nothing else feels like home the way this does.

A 10/10 Would Get Emotionally Damaged Again I bought Elden Ring thinking I was going to be a brave warrior. I am not a brave warrior. I am a professional “YOU DIED” screen collector. This game gently places you into a beautiful open world and says, “Go anywhere!” What it really means is, “Go anywhere and get folded like a lawn chair.” Every enemy is legally allowed to disrespect you. Even goats. Especially goats. The bosses? Oh, they don’t fight you. They perform interpretive dance routines that end with you being launched into the stratosphere. I once rolled 47 times in a row just to get hit anyway. Apparently, panic-rolling is not a viable life strategy. Character creation? Incredible. You can craft a majestic hero… who will immediately get bonked by a guy named something like “Sir Stabs-a-Lot, Devourer of Hope.” The open world is stunning. Truly breathtaking. I’ve never admired scenery so much while running for my life. Combat feels amazing though. When you finally beat a boss after 63 attempts, you ascend. You are no longer human. You are a being fueled purely by spite and caffeine. 10/10 game. Would question my self-worth again.

It is a good game for many reasons : The overworld is insanely big, so big that I still lose myself in places that i've never encountered even after 220 hours. Also, the gamestyle is really good and the lore is absolutely incredible. Bosses are well made and it gives a good time playing. Cons: The side-quests have almost no help, you don't know where to go or what to do most of the time which could be hard for players to figure out what to do. Also, there is a lot of bosses that repeat, even in the DLC which I think is a lack of originality. Though, I recommend because this game gave a experience that I did not experience for a very long time while playing a game!

"Would you recommend" absolutely, no questions asked. Personally this is my third favourite game. Story-wise, it is somewhat deep but nothing too emotional. Has an insane amount of replayability. Took me 72 hours to beat the game for the first time, and now I wanna get every other ending.

Elden Ring is nothing short of a masterpiece! At last, we have a game that feels like a genuine experience, not just another cash grab. It immerses you in a sprawling, vibrant world brimming with endless possibilities. The control system is remarkably intuitive, making it easy to dive right in. The combat mechanics are not just well-designed; they are exhilarating, creating a sense of thrill with every encounter. What truly sets Elden Ring apart is its brilliantly crafted open world, which encourages exploration and discovery at every turn. Even though I never identified as a Dark Souls fan, my heart has undeniably been captured by Elden Ring. It does everything right and has rekindled that nostalgic feeling of my childhood, reminiscent of playing Hellfire on the Mega Drive. Those were truly golden times! If you're looking for a game that offers depth, excitement, and a world to truly lose yourself in, look no further. Elden Ring is an unforgettable adventure waiting to be experienced!
As someone who has obtained every achievement, I can safely say that this is by far the best game I have ever played. 100/10

I'm not qualified to give a review yet, but as someone who's played the Dark Souls series and more, this is certainly one of my favorite games of all time. They've done such an incredible job taking the worlds that they'd built and scaling it up into a modern, no holds barred, truly free roam game with so much to explore, the only thing that gets repetitive is the dying. There will be dying.

What an epic journey from start to finish! This is how open world games should be. This game proves you don't need a massive narrative, countless npcs or quests for a game to be fun to explore. The game's challenge is also another thing that makes it more interesting for the player to progress and all the more satisfying when he overcomes it. A few gripes here and there especially for completionists like myself. For instance, missing features that help you explore everything the game has to offer without roaming around endlessly especially after beating it or attending a 2nd playthrough. Missable quests, items etc that do require multiple playthroughts. Things like that are just personal nitpicking and an actual positive for others.

Easier verison of DarkSoul, yet still challenging, very rewarding if you get good at it. Best story (in my opinion) of FromSoftware games, game is fairly optimized over the years, usually goes on sale. Buy it at any price and it worth every single cents.

This game ruined my life, after becoming a dex, blood build, everyone hates me, my wife left me, she took everything, when I try to get a job, they refuse, and ban me from the vicinity. The only reason my life keeps on going is because of me finding validation in 2d characters, I am a failure. 10/10, must play.

Uhm, so at this point of time, I have played roughly 250 hours and haven't finished my FIRST playthrough yet. AND NO, IT'S NOT BECAUSE I SUCK AT THIS GAME! There is just so much to explore and tbh it's fun to stray away from your initial goal and get lost in your ADHD that takes you to overpowered areas too soon. But that's the thing I love about this game that represents Fromsoft's core message: Do whatever the heck you want. There's nobody here that forces you to follow a certain route, in fact, there are so many routes that you might get onto another by sheer accident and without noticing it. Tons of things and lore to explore and for someone like me who's a completionist, this is a godsend. YOU decide how long a playthrough can become and I absolutely love this type of freedom. Slash the maidens, ride a troll (or vice-versa, up to you) but the important part is to have fun in misery. Because you will die. In case you were wondering, just saying.

Holy Hell! Just play the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game already, Elden Ring is an absolute masterpiece! For my first soulslike game, I couldn't have asked for a better experience, and I also had no idea what kind of experience this was even going to be so, all I could do was brace myself for peak. And ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ was it peak. To begin, I always have a soft spot for unique video game artstyles, even before playing this game I couldn't help but appreciate how insanely cool the design and look of the Lands Between are. Every single area in this world is perfectly positioned and hand crafted to give you the most cinematic and beautiful experience possible, I wont spoil what areas and where, but these visuals and how they were presented had my jaw drop too many times to count. The next closest thing to the artstyle that first really captured my attention was the music. Whether it was peacefully riding through golden pastures or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ diamonds in the hardest boss fights I've every played through the music raised the bar and kept surpassing it every single time. I think there is a separation between video game music I would listen to outside of a game compared to while I'm playing it though, and although literally more than half of the songs here are masterpieces in their own right, for me the music nestles itself neatly in the latter category. Finally, the gameplay. Having never touched a soulslike property in my life, it was very difficult, almost unfairly so. But this was the one and only thing I was definitely expecting going into the game, and looking back on my experience as a whole, I don't think there has been any game in recent memory that has made me feel this personally rewarded after persevering time and time again. This was the biggest factor in keeping me going through the whole game and its DLC, knowing how good it would feel to finally come out on top and to say 'I did that thing that was super hard' lol. Between the absolutely stunning visual audio landscapes, the insanely tough but rewarding gameplay, and how much fun I had going through it with one of my best friends, the whole experience has cemented itself in my top three games of all time, and I only hope that you may find it just as fun as well, 11/10.

Elden Ring. Oh Elden Ring, my very first Fromsoft game. Hold my heart, but also please stop crushing it between your fingers. This game has some of the coolest, biggest, most insane stuff Fromsoft has ever done. It also has some of the worst they have done, and lots of people like to look over that. Despite how awesome the designs of the bosses are, so many of them are broken by two of Elden Ring's supposed "successes." The open world in this game is very, very unique and delivers a lot of enjoyment, but it also commonly has the player fight bosses both underleveled and overleveled, with little idea of which spot he she go to next or if he is even in the right spot to begin with. The next success that is actually a detriment I would argue, is the desire to make Elden Ring so "difficult." Tons of bosses have very poorly telegraphed attacks, delay attacks that hold for comical lengths, high health bars, crazy damage and crazy speed. Average players, and some above average players, have no chance of keeping up with them, and so have to rely on summons and the bell bearings or whatever, or even cheese tactics, to defeat a lot of the bosses in this game. For those who enjoy using those, its fine. For some, myself included, it dilutes the impact of a boss if I have to get someone else to fight it for me or if I have to use freezing pots to make a certain boss stop in the middle of an attack that is simply impossible to dodge unless you do extensive research. If you, as a developer see that you have to add something to the game that puts a barrier between the boss in the player just to make it fair on the player, maybe you need to make the bosses less unfair instead. Last complaint, because that was a lot, but the last several hours of this game are very rocky. The snow area is empty, boring, and chalked full with repeat enemies. The Haligtree is a labyrinth with old dark souls level design mixed with Elden Ring's fast paced enemies. Doesn't work very well. Overall, the ending of this game does not live up to the hype and expectations set by the first half of the game. All of that being said, it's still awesome. A single playthrough of Elden Ring will change how you look at video games forever, and if you can get through it, then you can get through anything. Highly recommend, but take it in bite sized chunks. If you want to get into the Fromsoft series easier, I would personally start with Dark Souls 3. Good luck, and don't you dare go hollow.

Playing Elden Ring is like watching your favorite food truck become a restaurant chain. More options, more locations, a more accessible experience. But what did we lose along the way? [hr][/hr] Let me preface this by saying if you really enjoy souls games, just go ahead and buy this, you're going to have a great time, even if there are faults. I think Elden Ring is actually a really fun time, but it seems to be weighed down by its open world nature. Fromsoft as a developer have always been a masterclass in creating tight enclosed spaces that connect to each other in really fun ways, and overall just beautiful labyrinthian "playgrounds". Similar to something like Breath of the Wild, taking an "open-zone" or more linear series and turning it into an open world game really takes away from that hand crafted feel. You definitely lose a lot of that tight focus, and more deliberate feeling exploration. In Elden Ring there are a lot of hand crafted fun set pieces, but moving between them is not as pleasurable as past games. The actual open world areas are pretty drab, wide open, and it becomes tedious as you progress through each area. I find my mind drifting away from the game as I am running through the open world on my horse. On to more important things: Maybe the retention pond and cavern system I have built up under the local kindergarten, or my collection of framed Swedish Fish. I think Fromsoft up until Elden Ring had a clear design philosophy. Create a tight but not necessarily linear experience, that the player can explore and get lost in. Hand place our bosses, items, and enemies, exactly where they need to be. This is exactly what has gotten lost in translation during the switch to open world. Horsing around fields and swamps takes away that hand crafted feel. I exit one of the many evergaols, or castles, or little villages, and my eyes immediately start to roll as I realize I now have to play through the Ubisoft portion of the game, before I can get back into those tightly designed areas. If you are a Fromsoft Truther™ you are going to enjoy this, period. But at the end of the day, I can't shake the feeling we certainly lost a little of that early Dark Souls Magic.

Elden Ring was my first proper Souls-style game, and I’ll be honest. I was this close to refunding it. At the beginning, I didn’t understand how it worked. There were no clear quest markers, no hand-holding, enemies hit hard, and bosses felt impossible. It didn’t play like other games I was used to. I thought maybe it just wasn’t for me. But instead of quitting, I gave it a chance. Slowly, I began to understand the combat. I learned that panic rolling gets you killed. Knowing when to step in or back off matters. I learned that the game doesn’t reward aggression without patience. Beat all main bosses, including Malenia, was one of the most satisfying feelings I’ve ever had in gaming. No excuses. Just focus, timing, and growth. Discovering hidden fights like Dragonlord Placidusax made the world feel alive and mysterious. When I finally sat on the throne, it wasn’t just relief I felt. It was pride, knowing I had earned it. Right now, as I write this, I honestly feel emotional. I didn’t even want to finish the game, because I wasn’t ready to say goodbye to the journey. That’s how powerful and beautiful this masterpiece truly is. It challenges you. It frustrates you. It makes you doubt yourself. And then it rewards you with growth. The game doesn’t get easier. You get better. What an unforgettable journey.

Generational game. Be prepared to die... a lot. [b]+[/b] Massive and beautifully crafted open world. One of, if not the best fantasy worlds ever made. George R. R. Martin advising the devs on the world and story makes perfect sense now. [b]+[/b] Incredible music that is very immersive, epic and cinematic. Pieces in Leyndell and Malenia theme are my favorites. [b]+[/b] Combat feels great and boss encounters are quite diverse and interesting. Every major enemy is simply epic. For others, horse meta is a good break from sweaty fights. ;) [b]+[/b] The whole experience is extremely rewarding, especially if you are new to souls games. I have never played any of them before and it never appealed to me due to their notorious difficulty. However, I decided to give Elden Ring a go and I gotta say, there is nothing more empowering than starting weak and getting your ass handed to you by nearly everything that moves, and then conquering this massive world. [b]+[/b] Optimization is great. RTX 4070 Super pulled consistent 60 FPS at 4K native (no DLSS) on highest settings (no RT). There were some stutters at one point that went away eventually, which I suspect was due to either drivers or another brilliant Windows update. [b]-[/b] Catacombs (optional content) feel repetitive and often times not really worth doing. A few of them have really good and important rewards but they are not distinguished in any way from generic ones. [b]-[/b] Crafting system is meh. I have gathered many recipe books but I still had reagents that weren't attached to any recipe and many recipes are simply redundant and don't provide any substantial benefit. Some reagents that are very useful are too scarse. [b]-[/b] Late-game balance is really bad. At some point there is spike in difficulty for no apparent reason even though your character is very high level. [b]-[/b] There are areas in the game designed to ♥♥♥♥ with you for no reason but I guess that's part of the identity of FromSoftware games. [b]+/-[/b] Placidusax, which is an optional and a bit of a hidden boss is arguably the best fight in the game and can be easily missed. [b]+/-[/b] I feel like exploration isn't always rewarded accordingly. [b]+/-[/b] The story is a bit hard to follow and there is no journal, quest log or books to find in the open world to read up on the lore. Instead, you have to remember the dialogues and quests and for the lore, you need to read the item (armor, weapons etc.) descriptions to understand the mystical world around you.

Good game in general, but the difficulty is all artificial. The actual mechanics are not hard whatsoever, the only difficulty that they put in the game is delayed attacks in an attempt to throw you off, but every single enemy has delayed attacks that look completely unnatural and buggy at times. And it's not just an enemy holding their stance until they can reach you with their weapon, they run up to you and don't swing until they literally touch your body so you can't accurately predict the attack, which in turn makes the enemy roll-catch you 9/10 times. That does not take skill to learn, that takes luck and legit immediate reaction. There are corner enemies everywhere that you cannot do anything to bait out, they are hard coded to not react unless you pass in front of them, making throwables absolutely useless for distractions/flushing them out (which in turn, makes throwables completely useless in the overall game because they suck for damage). The only way you can do anything against enemies that are super tucked into a corner without having to risk the buggy AI is having an AOE spell that goes through walls, and you hope it reaches while their weapons go through the wall to hit you somehow. It's also an open world game that punishes you for exploring by way of locking you out of countless quests and items with no prior warning or even interaction whatsoever, which in my opinion is just a way to inflate the amount of people who continue into NG+ so they can go back and get stuff that shouldn't have been locked in the first place. There is barely a quest system, and it's extremely barebones and lazy, not to mention buggy at times, which again, in turn inflates NG+ numbers so that people can hopefully do the quest that bugged out on them. This game runs on hype and depends on fans who dismiss any kind of criticism as "you're bad". Those people are the reason the DLC was as shallow as it was, and why FromSoft has such an awful relationship with their community. They change what they want, when they want with no regard for the community. For example, they changed the menus to be sluggish and slower and refused to revert it despite community-wide backlash all in the name of fixing an unrelated bug. They pigeonhole players into going with a magic or bleed build, because any other build is mid at best and they nerf any other weapon that is even remotely good into complete uselessness. The only good bosses in the DLC that actually have cool mechanics and no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ delayed attacks are killed in a minute or two because they have so little health, all while providing absolutely no story whatsoever. We went through the entire expansion just to be told something that we have known since the game's release. The only well-made boss in the game is Bayle, his attacks aren't delayed, you can tell when he's charging up an attack, you can differentiate between his attacks, and his fight is difficult enough to be satisfying to learn and he has enough health for the fight to actually feel like a fight. Compare that to a buggy fight like Godskin Duo, which FromSoft has of course refused to address the awful geometry of the room, which makes a mechanic completely unavoidable at times whenever the boss feels like rolling over the broken pillars. The scariest and most toe-curling part of the game is hiding behind a broken pillar and hoping the Noble doesn't run you over. Them endlessly reusing bosses and movesets aside, the fact that the Godskin Duo fight even made it into the game in the first place shows they are just constantly searching for ways to make the game difficult and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ instead of just designing a fight properly and incorporating the difficulty into the mechanics themselves. Make the mechanics harder, fix bugs in the fights and the geometry of multiple fights, and give players freedom to make their own viable build without having to resort to mods to buff certain things to be useable in the first place. That cool looking spell that you get for killing Radahn and Miquella? Complete trash, because it's holy damage and holy has always been trash. It hurts your eyes more than the enemies. I would love to make a build surrounding such a visually appealing spell, but it would become a challenge run just by using the spell. Divine power channeled into a mini nuke will tickle a wolf, but if you kill some vulgar shrimp lover in the middle of a swamp, you get one of the best weapons in the game, which is just a downgraded version of another best weapon in the game, which you find off a random corpse in a dark corner. All that being said, I would say the game overall is fun. For me, the fun is exploring and getting overpowered so that I don't have to deal with all the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, though some of it is just unavoidable. I would say that I wish they would make armor better and more of a help than a hinderance, but it is widely agreed that Fashion Souls is more important than stats, and I completely agree. I'm a moon mage dressed in black with the hat and mask of someone who turned people into puppets. I look badass. Another prop I will give FromSoft is that they made a LOT of different ways to do stuff. Challenge runs will open your eyes to this. Can't jump? Use one of the ashes of war that makes you jump. There are multiple ways to get to certain important locations, many of which let you get to the locations earlier than you usually would which is extremely important in my eyes in order to prevent doing the same thing. The bell bearings are really nice so that you don't have to waste time grinding most of the materials in the game. All I can hope is that FromSoft takes the good from this game, and then builds even more good on top of it while keeping in touch with their community.

Pros This game offers a huge variety of weapon builds, making it great for players who love playing with different weapons. Cons Many legendary weapons are hidden in corners of the world. Without a guide, they’re very hard to be found. The game’s guidance is quite poor. In the starting area, you basically have no idea what you’re supposed to do. If you just follow the Sites of Grace, it becomes a typical Souls-like experience. But if you use a guide such as reddit or youtube to quickly locate legendary weapons, then it stops being a Souls-like exploration game and becomes more of a “power trip” game. However, with a guide, you’ll also get spoiled a lot, which takes away the joy of discovery. BTW, many of the town/city maps and dungeons in this game are extremely confusing, and without video walkthroughs, it’s easy to get lost. Summary This game is best suited for players who have plenty of time and enjoy exploring on their own; or for players who have limit time or don’t care about the story, use reddit/youtube guides to quickly grab your ideal weapons, and experience all the content.

This is my second playthrough (1st was on PS) and I have to say this is the most incredible game I have ever played. The difficulty: The first 10 hours I hated it, but pushed through to learn how to fight the most basic enemies. Every boss was a personal challenge to overcome. And despite being intimated at first, this is what I loved the most - the challenge! The second run it was just me and my brick hammer against all the bosses. Therefore, the difficulty is arbitrary - you can make it easier or harder for yourself by using various tools in the game. You can use summons, buffs, consumables, or you can be a crazy person and beat the game at level 1! The world building: This game studio knows how to build a world worth exploring. Every nook and cranny will have a hidden item or at least a view you can adore. Truly, the world is epic and expands beyond your initial idea of it. Dungeons have puzzles, secrets and tricks that you will make you feel dumb at first, this is how good it is. Replayability: Even after 2 playthroughs, I don't think I have explored everything, and there is still so much to learn in terms of combat possibilities. Some bosses are still challenging, even though I know most of their moves.

If you're looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if you're looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place. Ingredients: 1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter 2. 1/2 cup white sugar 3. 1/2 cup brown sugar 4. 1/4 cup water 5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon 6. 1 pinch salt 7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced 8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie Directions: 1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C). 2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside. 3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices. 4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal. 5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust. 6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I wish I could like this game more, God knows I tried. It is very reminiscent of the way Morrowind made me feel many moons ago. It doesn't hold your hard, it encourages exploration, it encourages experimentation, the open world and world building are absolutely incredible, and it is overall extremely interesting. That said, just about everything else is insanely underwhelming. Obviously the game is insanely unfair towards the player. It isn't a hard game, it is an unfair game. Some people really like the feeling of accomplishment from beating their head against the wall for hours until it finally breaks, and I'm definitely not against a challenge, but what doesn't feel rewarding is defeating a boss because you got lucky. And sure, some things are worth suffering through for the reward, except there really isn't any reward other than saying you did it. There is clearly lore and some semblance of a story here, but there is absolutely no coherent storyline or characters for me to feel invested in whatsoever, which makes the idea of working through yet another insanely cheap and unfair boss encounter all the more uninteresting. I've played for over 65 hours this point and couldn't tell you why I'm doing anything in the game other than I guess because it's my destiny to do so or something? The insane thing is I'm actually the kind of player to go and explore and try to read and interact with everything I can. I will interact with every NPC and exhaust every dialogue trying to learn more about worlds like this that are very interesting, but there quite literally isn't a narrative at all. The combat feels pretty generic and uninteresting, like a more hardcore version of Skyrim. What is disappointing is I felt this way around 5 hours into the game but decided I would give it the good ole college try, but here I am at 65+ hours feeling the exact same. If you like the genre, you'll probably enjoy this. If you're okay with an insanely unfair challenge, give it a go. If you're looking for a truly wonderful open world experience with interesting boss fights, you'll easily get dozens of hours out of this game. If you're looking for a game with depth to really draw you into its world and immerse you, then this isn't it. It was fun working through some castles while watching videos on my second monitor. Definitely feels insanely overhyped. I'd probably give it a 6.5/10. If you like open worlds, RPG games, and aren't averse to challenge, maybe give it a try especially if its on sale. The real crime is if you don't play the game, you really aren't missing out on anything. No one is ever going to say "Whaaat, you didn't play Elden Ring!?"

I bought Elden Ring thinking I was good at video games. Within the first hour, a man on a golden horse beat that confidence out of me like it owed him money. That was my official welcome to the Lands Between—a beautiful world where everything is stronger than you, including wildlife and gravity. Death isn’t a rare mistake in this game. It’s part of the daily routine. I’ve died heroically to dragons and embarrassingly to basic soldiers with torches. Every time I get a boss down to a tiny sliver of health, I get greedy, go for “one more hit,” and immediately regret my entire existence. The game punishes panic, impatience, and overconfidence—which unfortunately are my three main personality traits while gaming. And yet… I can’t stop playing. Because when you finally beat that boss who’s been ruining your evening, the feeling is unmatched. Your hands are shaking, your heart’s racing, and you just sit there thinking, “I actually did it.” No hand-holding, no easy wins—just pure, earned victory. It’s frustrating. It’s brutal. It will test your patience and possibly your controller’s durability. But it’s also one of the most rewarding and addictive games I’ve ever played. 10/10. Would get humbled again.

The highs and the lows that this beautiful game provided me is unlike any other game I have played. Elden Ring was my first entry into the Souls series, so the learning curve was quite difficult for me to overcome compared to veterans of this series. After my first two runs taught me that I was being to harsh on myself with every mistake and life. So in my most recent playthrough I casted that mindset aside, noting that every mistake that I made in each life were happening less and less. This is a game that rewards patience and gradual growth, which made accomplishments and milestones all the more rewarding. On my most recent playthrough, I fought the Tree sentinel over 50 times. I refused to move on and level up, because I wanted to prove to myself that I can learn from every prior life. So with every life, I started to notice that I was doing better than the last time, chipping away at their health further and further. There were lives where I did worse than I had before, but I didn't let that deter me one bit, for I must persevere and embody the indomitable will of man. Every attack that he threw at me became a new addition to my mental repertoire, making me wiser than I was in my previous life. The last life was flawless for the first three quarters of their life. Bloodied and battered, the knight was able to land a devasting blow onto me. This didn't phase me one bit for I knew in that moment panic would be my down fall, recalling the many times where I was panic dodging into my demise. So I stood there, swinging my wooden club at their steed, causing them to be staggered, and allowing me to hit him with a critical blow onto his head. I knew I couldn't finish him off right away and on top of that the next hit that he lands on me will lead to my demise. So I backed off, waiting for him to charge at me. My heart was beating so fast in this moment, yet mentally I was locked in. As I predicted, the tree sentinel and his trusty steed started to gallop towards me at full speed. I dodge rolled past him, and immediately use the last charge of my flask to cure my aching wounds. They then turn back around, trying to use the same exact charge on me. I realize in this moment I need to clear the distance after they plow through, so I started to walk backwards. They're right on top of me in this moment, yet I have done this old song and dance with them over 50 times, dodging past them as the knight swings his halberd. I turn around at a full sprint with my wooden club, like a caveman cornering their prey. As soon as I approach them, the knight swings at me with full force into the ground, only to miss and plunge their halberd into the ground. This was my moment, one, two, three swings of the club fiercely strikes against the metal armor of the horse, the health bar nearing zero. My breathing was getting faster and faster, I was beginning to lose my composure, for I was to kill the being that caused me pain and suffering for the last three hours. The knight got his halberd loose from the ground to make a desperate swipe at me, hitting me square in the chest. A millisecond of panic flashed within my skull and my heart dropped as soon at the hit connected. In my past lives, I would've dodged rolled away in pure panic. Nay, my training and suffering caused me to snap back, for I must complete my directive of slaying the sentinel of trees. I realized that I saw this attack patter many a times before, I was hit by the end of a combo, meaning after this he needed to recharge for his next attack. I stood my ground, bonk, bonk, BONK!!! The knight and his beast slumped over forward dissipating into ashes as the words ENEMY FELLED filled my screen. In this moment, I was in pure disbelief. "I... I.. I did it?!" Jaw agape, heart beating rapidly, dopamine flooding my receptors. "I DID IT!!!" A tidy sum of runes lined my pocket, I must go back to the grace to level up my level one character. As I was looking over the attributes thinking of what build I wanted to go for this run, a poignant feeling arose within me. I hated the tree sentinel when I was fighting him... why did I feel respect for him right now? As I explored that thought, I came to understand that despite being my biggest enemy for the past three hours, he was also my mentor, preparing me for what horrors lie beyond his grove. I held myself back for the tree sentinel, refusing to level up while playing as the wretch. I defeated this great being with the bare minimum... how am I going to fare now that I can level up and equip better gear? It was like Rock Lee taking off his training weights in his fight against Garaa. The true beauty of this game is that you didn't have to do what I did, you can mix and match weapons, armor, and items that suit your playstyle the best. After all it is a single player game, no one but you can judge how you play the game. If you want to play with the mimic tear and use a cheesy magic, do it! Having fun is what really matters, right? Also how are you going to appreciate this amazing story if you cannot progress? This game will always hold a special place in my heart. The writers of this game created a world that takes a lot of inspiration from many fantasy series and refined and perfected it into this masterpiece. The programmers created a really challenging and unforgiving game that greatly rewards those whom are patient enough to learn it. Those coming hand in hand with one another captured a feeling I haven't felt since I was a child playing games. Triple A developers and studios need to realize that throwing a near impossible amount of money at a project won't make masterpieces like they once did. This mindset leads to unfinished, unpolished, and generally terrible games that are released far too early all because they wanted to turn a profit sooner than later. FromSoft realized that a majority of gamers would rather wait a couple years longer for a finished product, all amazing art takes time, right? TLDR: Mechanically fun, visually stunning, cohesive story that can be played at your own pace, amazing music, one of the hardest games I've played yet very rewarding when surpassing hurdles. 10/10

This has become one of my favorite games of all time. I just played a session where a lot of things finally clicked for me. I’ve been at conflict with myself on whenever to rate this game as positive or negative. But considering this is AAA title and GOTY holder - Based on my experience with the game I’ve decided to be a little bit more harsh in reviewing this based on the title of the game, and thus it’s negative. It will be a little lengthy - to put a negative stick into what a lot of people treasure i’ll need to describe it properly. I’ve beat the game like the other 22% of players lol. Elden ring is not my first souls like experience, I have played Code Vein and Lords of the fallen before, but it’s my first experience with From Software games - as a pioneer in the genre, and widely praised for their design - I expected a lot. You might say a ♥♥♥♥ eater only knows how ♥♥♥♥ tastes like, well if Elden Ring is a donut, then it might look like Donut but it still tastes like ♥♥♥♥. I know the game does not really have any difficulty settings officially - but my friend who is a fan of the series provided me with feedback that magic is basically what you call easy mode in this game, and so I’ve ventured on the adventure with this game as a warrior. The game start harsh for a new player you being lore dumped with new lore about new world and then thrown into tutorial area where you can experience for the first time horrible control design of FromSoftware - I’ve been told it was even worse in their first games, but what ♥♥♥♥♥♥ though it’s good idea to put sprint on holding B on pad, and jump on A - sprint jump requires you to bend your thumb to some weird angles and then hope you are doing it correct - there are countless other examples in gaming where this was done better - you can’t rebind - like the friend said - “get used to it” - and that seems like the motto of this game tbh. Anyway, the tutorial is to smash or get smashed - I was smashed. The first time you see the world - it is truly magical - I can see the care and attention put into the world design - you are instantly encouraged to explore the world. Too bad the world does not have much to offer. Let me explain. The Elden Ring story is a main quest which involves 13 bosses, every other boss is optional and the story is tied to main bosses. Dialogues, lore dumps, interesting bits - all tied to the main story. Now what about side content - There are some side quests in a old school type where you don’t have a marker of where to go or what to do - which are something you do for npc you find in the world, for example carrying a message to the father of daughter to the fort he is stationed at, you get some lore bits for that - that’s nice. But what about the rest of the world? Dungeons? Smaller bosses - like Erdtree Avatars? - Nah, not even ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ notes. Don’t get me wrong - the main quest is great - I enjoyed it - It was great - I don’t have anything wrong to slap there - but the main story is not the whole game, and that’s what I am essentially reviewing. Almost every dungeon is the same thing - enter, avoid traps, find levers, unlock doors - kill the boss and leave. No story about why this boss is here, is this a prison? Who was held here? Who was the boss, why was he here? There is literally nothing about it - almost every location is just a location with no ties to the massive canvas of beautiful world you are in. I am sucker for good story, and I love discovering bits about lore - when they are presented to me in an enjoyable way - I don’t want to bother with navigating this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ UI of an inventory that they didn’t bother to change since DS1 to view description of items and read the lore about items - that’s moronic design. To understand the world of Elden RIng you either need to know someone who loves the world and spend time getting to know it a little better like my friend, watch a youtube lore videos or maybe read a book - anything other than main story quest - I dunno maybe if you look hard enough you will find some. Speaking of DS1 - combat is ass. Now the boss fights are amazing, I love design, the animations are flashy and visual, they are dancing on the field - no complaints - other than Dragons - but nobody likes dragon fights from what I heard. You, the player, have the most wooden animation possible - I have cross referenced the animations and they are exactly the same animations they’ve used in DS1 - no changes at all, every class dodges the same, every class attacks the same. One handed animation looks like it's from Minecraft. The special skills have some flash - some work done - I can see those apart from previous games - that means developers actually worked on them instead of coping and pasting it from previous games like movement, dodges and basic attacks. Most games I played when they used previous animations they were used as a base and then refined upon, not in Elden Ring - GOTY btw. The magic looks cool, the magic weapons look cool - but I was told it's an easy mode - Don’t use magic I was told - You will get bored quick, well I am bored anyways. Combat gets so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dull after a while, that you are hoping that at least story will prevent you from falling asleep. But like I’ve mentioned before when you are exploring - forget about the story you won’t get anything. While the world is amazingly pretty, for the most part it’s empty - Hey is that ruined tower atop of the cliff? I wonder what’s there, a bunch of trash mobs, 1 elite and a few golden runes scattered on the ground and few plants. So just some ruins like most of the ruins and locations you find in the world - there is nothing special about it, definitely not a story that would set it apart, or I dunno a small dialogue for the present Monster when they idle. Nah. The RNG loot in Single Player experience is just retarded - Hey that Cuckoo Knight looks cool I wonder if I can get his armor, you can after 50 kills or more if your RNG is ♥♥♥♥. At the very ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ least the inventory weight is only counted on what you are wearing not the stash you are hoarding, that would get annoying pretty quick to teleport to round table to sell another 10 pair of boots because you are over-encumbered. Now the PVP - I wouldn’t review if it wasn’t forced on you. I know it is some kind of tradition from FromSoftware games, that you can invade other players' worlds and kill them for trash loot. I been told by my friend that it operates on vengeance basic, a new player is invaded by heavy sweat that puts 3000 hours in this game, is easily outskilled and killed, and when they eventually get good stuff and level they proceed to do the same to another new player, and circle of vengeance is closed. I saw there is an arena for the players to PVP in, but most of the players apparently do not want to be matched against same level players - they could lose, that’s not as fun as bullying low levels. There is no cool loot for these encounters for either invader or the one being invaded, so they just do it for pure pleasure of bullying the weak. You cannot out-yourself from PVP, it's hard locked as enabled, the only way to avoid it is to play offline. Also another fun note - If you disable anti-cheat and start cheating, the game is too retarded to detect that the client has disabled anti-cheat and will still allow players to invade you. So the anti-cheat is so retarded that it will prevent you from cheating, but it won’t prevent you from matching with a cheater without anti-cheat. I am just leaving it here as another fun point on why PVP is pointless in this game. The Game of The Year - I expected such a game to be set apart from the competition - after all it claimed the title at the top - but me it’s 5/10 or 6/10 if being generous, It’s really mediocre, and there are rip-offs who offer more condensed package rather than pretty open and empty world. The art, music, visuals might be GOTY worthy but the actual content - definitely not.

Elden Ring is not here to guide you. It throws you into its world — and waits to see if you survive. The world is massive, open, and hauntingly quiet. Nothing is explained, nothing is guaranteed, and every path can lead to death. That’s exactly what makes it one of the strongest gaming experiences ever. You don’t play because you have to — you play because you want to understand what happened here. Combat is brutal, fair, and addictive. Every boss is a lesson. Every death has meaning. And when you finally succeed, the reward is worth every failure. The game teaches patience, awareness, and respect — it doesn’t forgive, but it rewards. The story isn’t told through words, but through atmosphere, environments, and subtle clues. You don’t read it — you feel it. And the deeper you go, the harder it pulls you in. This game isn’t for everyone. But if you’re looking for something that breaks you… and then lets you grow, Elden Ring is a masterpiece.

Elden Ring is the perfect game for parents. Let me explain: 1. It is always auto-saving, so less chance of losing progress when your gaming window closes (expectedly or unexpectedly). You can do a lot in a little bit of time. 2. The plentiful bonfires respect your limited gaming time. 3. The game is large enough to deliver very good value for the amount of time you likely have to play it. 4. Really great opportunity for role playing expression with character creation and build variety. 5. Barely any cutscenes, and the ones that are there are like ~30 seconds. 6. Really well-optimized at this point and can run on a lot of hardware (3 kids and no money kinda rigs or no kids and 3 money kinda rigs). 7. Great challenge that isn't too cheesy so you don't feel like you're wasting your limited gaming time, but also feels rewarding (yes, even PCR). 8. Stakes of Marika eliminate stupidly painful runbacks. Elden Ring is now my favorite game of all time. Partly because I became a dad right when it came out and these things helped me enjoy it, but it's also just a solid experience. It's got some real magic to it.

It's a From Software game which as a result inherits many of the good mechanics from the Dark Souls series and forms a great base for gameplay however it is ruined by the addition of the needless open world design. The world feels empty and did not make new game plus enjoyable through its repetitive dungeons and reuse of bosses as common enemies. The disuse of previous linear and interconnected design of Dark Souls negatively impacted the game's travelling and discourages normal traversal of the world in favour of the fast travel system. The PvP scene is very lively albeit highly over tuned, power-stancing certain weapons such as great spears deals far too much damage, in addition, many spells and weapons seem far too powerful comparatively to the rest of the roster leading to fights being repetitive. Whilst some weapon such as rivers of blood received a rightful nerf, it seems to have inherent balance issues. The boss fights in this game whilst visually stunning, relies heavily on delayed attacks intertwined with normal attacks or attacks requiring the player to stay in a safe zone or risk an instant death, an example being Malenia. Not every boss displays these attack types however it seems that, from the base roster, and the new DLC, that From Software has favoured such boss designs over the conventional ones found in previous games such as Bloodborne or Dark Souls. The community's common response of "Git Gud" focuses on the difficulty rather than inherent boss design, ignoring that memorising attack patterns can be done by anyone and a person who did successfully beat a boss may have criticisms of its design nonetheless. TLDR: Game STINKS

Elden Ring delivers an amazing experience with a beautiful open world full of stunning environments that constantly encourage exploration. The main bosses stand out with well-designed movesets that are challenging and rewarding, and the huge variety of weapons and build options allows for a lot of playstyle freedom. One of the game’s biggest strengths is its flexible difficulty. You can make the game easier by leveling up, fighting weaker bosses, and optimizing your build, or go for a hardcore experience by limiting leveling and facing the challenge head-on. On the downside, quests are often too vague, making it easy to get lost, and the story can feel confusing without digging deeply into the lore. Some bosses are also repeated too often, and facing the same boss multiple times (sometimes 3–4 times) can reduce the impact of those encounters. Additionally, there is a lot of traveling to reach certain locations. Even with these flaws, Elden Ring is an outstanding game and absolutely worth playing.

Elden Ring (202 Hours Later) – A Professional Sufferer’s Review After sinking 202 hours into Elden Ring and finally beating it with the Frenzied Flame ending (yes, I’m one of the elite 16.2% of Tarnished who chose to burn literally everything), I can confidently say: This game did not just humble me— It filed the paperwork, notarized it, and sent it via express delivery. Difficulty: Imagine taking an exam you didn’t study for. Now imagine the exam is alive, 30 feet tall, has multiple phases, and screams at you. That’s Elden Ring. Every victory feels earned. Every death feels personally insulting. Exploration: FromSoftware created the most beautiful open world ever— and then populated it exclusively with creatures that hate you. Combat: Roll. Die. Roll. Die again. Try a new weapon. Die with that too. Learn. Adapt. Overcome. Or don’t—and emotionally disintegrate like I did during Malenia. Frenzied Flame Ending: Choosing to become the Lord of Chaos was not a decision. It was a lifestyle. After 202 hours I no longer wanted to save the world— I wanted to set it on fire and clock out early. Final Verdict: A masterpiece forged from equal parts pain and glory. It will break you, rebuild you, and then break you again for fun. 10/10 would get steamrolled by a boss and still say “One more try.”

I noticed there was a lack of genuine criticism, so here is everything I don't like about Elden Ring I have sunk so so many hours in Elden Ring on both console and PC. I first bought the game when it came out and played it day one. I enjoyed Elden Ring during my first playthrough, but given time and multiple replays my opinion has drifted greatly since then. The world in Elden Ring is disgustingly empty or full of not so rewarding challenges and it doesn't get enough slack. I huge talking point near launch was the 100 bosses and that sounds great on paper, however 80% if not more are just repeats of usually not even good bosses to begin with. One experience I remember in particular is Morne Castle. Morne Castle is one of the legacy Dungeons in the game (areas which are more linear) probably one of my favorites in the game too. You work your way through this castle and fight a fairly cool boss at the end, only to fight the same boss again, and again... and then as a common enemy. It really takes away from the first experience on top of feeling lazy. The enemy variety gets very weak not even halfway through the game, and starts to make little sense as to why they are placed where they are. And don't forget the endless amount of copy and paste catacombs, caves, and encampments. On a new playthrough I would skip all side content and only do the essentials unless there was a specific item/weapon I wanted to use. One more final point is the lack of interesting NPCs in Elden Ring when compared to the other Souls games that Fromsoft has created. All of the endings for NPCs are usually very underwhelming/they end abruptly. Near the end game enemies and bosses alike do so much damage that if you want to avoid getting one shot, you need 60 Vigor. In DS3 about 27 vigor is all you need for both the base game and DLC. To put it short (and add some tiny mentions) 1. Too many junk/repeat of junk bosses (82% of base game is repeats, 73% if you buy DLC) 2. Unrewarding exploration 3. Boring/Repetitive points of interests (Caves, Catacombs etc.) 4. Too much walking/riding to point A to B with not enough interesting AND rewarding points on the way 5. Crafting is either pointless or too annoying to farm resources for 6. Endgame enemies/bosses do too much damage while being spongy 7. Builds don't feel very different from one another 8. AOE attacks/hitboxes way bigger than they should be (Side note, Online has and has had a huge hacking problem) I've been playing the game through a mod called "Reforged" and have been enjoying it the game that way. Reforged alters combat greatly, changes balancing of weapons, adds many QoL changes, and so much more that I could never go back to base game. All of this isn't to say the base game is terrible. If you are the type to only do one run of a game and are not a completionist then you will probably finish this game and write it off as a solid experience. But too many people refuse to criticize the game and the community of Fromsoft doesn't take kindly to anything that isn't glaze. I've seen people get clowned on for simply saying "I wish this boss was a little different" or "Anyone else think the open world is kind of empty?". It is one of the most hostile fan bases I have ever seen.
