[h1] The Great Disappointment [/h1] Game that was supposed to be great was shattered, but by whom? and why? Elden Ring, from all the fanfare and praise I heard about this game, I truly expected something special, one of best games of all time was finally in front of me, although I'm few years late to the party, and if it wasn't so hyped this would probably be a positive review. The patented FromSoft gameplay still works, you roll and then you hit(in second phase you cant hit on that timing anymore, find a new one bro), base of gameplay is as engaging as ever, but seemingly nobody bothered to fix issues that were already present in Dark Souls before, instead prioritizing adding new ones. [h2] The Open Nothing [/h2] One of the biggest changes from this title to previous ones FromSoft made is the inclusion of open world. So what did this bring to old formula? There's some stunning views in game, landmarks, like Eldentree on majority of land or Mohgwyn Palace from down below under second sky of Siofra River are very beautiful and stand out through your exploration. Thats about all pluses of it. One of things i realized after playing Elden Ring for about 20 hours is how extremely dull the exploration is. Main content might as well been a better linear game with better area transitions than ones that we sometimes have in open world. To punish you for exploring there's quite a few giant archers/catapults/other ranged ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that gets old after two encounters, with archers being by far the worst. Locations that you can stumble upon randomly that supposed to reward you for exploring are three main things - ruins, catacombs and mines. All of them are an exercise in ctrl+c and ctrl+v pressing in editor, you did one of them - you pretty much know rest of them: - Ruins are mostly small and just different placements of same textures with some staircase downwards leading to a chest, only differential is enemies of region. - Mines are an exercise in moving same assets around and pretending you did something new, with mini-boss you probably already fought at end as a "reward", maybe if you're lucky you will get loot useful for your build from that. Even worse is that sometimes u actually NEED to go to mines to collect stones to upgrade your weapon, and they are certainly not good enough to ever go there more than once. - Especially offensive for me were catacombs, FromSoft wanted players to see them so much they even put statues lighting the way towards them scattered around the map, after you follow the blue light you will find... something similar to Ayleid Ruins from Oblivion(yes your main exploration target is about same as in RPG from 2006 that ran on xbox 360). Not only they all look the same and only difference is layout, but they also feature traps-cliche galore just like Todd wanted it. [h2] The sparce good and the vast ugly [/h2] The standout of Miyazaki's modus operandi always was and will be one thing - boss fights. Elden Ring has about 200 bosses, and that roster also suffers heavily from disease of copypastetonis. Dragons are the worst of that world by far - not only are they all basically same, they are also plan and simple unfun, with AOE attacks either right under boss while you're trying to fight it, or after a little bit of flying in air always aiming at one side. These flying critters are mostly just waste of time, defeat one on your horseback and forget about them for rest of game(or until game forces you to fight more). Around 30 out of 200 bosses are even worth actually talking about, and its truly a mixed bag. From heights of well designed fights like Godfrey, Godwyn and Godrick that make you realize that it was worth paying George R. R. Martin big bucks to come up with these names or first ever FromSoft gimmick boss that actually works brilliantly - God-Devouring Serpent. To straight up piles of hot garbage like ALL DRAGONS, Valiant Gargoyle, Godskin Duo and Crucible Knights, hopefully one day they will realize that putting two enemies that don't work together at all is not the best idea, and circling around them for 2 minutes to isolate one is not a fun challenge at all. However that's not what pained me most, the worst bosses of Elden Ring are the almost great bosses that for some reason got worse. Hardest challenge of game is Malenia(Blade of Miquella btw), with her smooth and interesting combos making a thrilling experience... up to the point she uses Waterfowl and you don't want to see that fight again. Or you can spend hours on boss just to learn one attack and realize that you're trying to dodge camera circling around, not attack itself. Or the long awaited and teased battle on top of Pantheon against Mohg, where just when you start having fun with it, up to point he randomly covers entire arena with AOE attack from sky, that stays on ground to ♥♥♥♥ you over for quite a while, until you learn that for some reason you're supposed to dodge it into attack and stay next to boss that is doing AOE splatter damage from sky, not away from it, which visually and logically makes 0 sense. Or you fight against also very nice and dynamic Radagon, and awaiting to experience second phase you are greeted by one of worst bosses of the game. Elden Beast is glorified dragon-like boss, a boss that you need constantly run towards and get right under, just to get hit by attack you couldn't even see... because you need to be right under boss to hit it in first place, sadly FromSoft haven't figured out a way to zoom out camera for these fights just yet. [h2] The everso bad [/h2] While we're at camera, why is locking in still randomly breaking when boss is behind some column or other piece of geometry, just like it used to from way back in first Dark Souls? And when you try to lock in again you randomly look forward and get hit by attack you can't see anymore cause you're looking at nearby scenery for some reason. Why there's random pieces of geometry scattered around boss arena to begin with, that will randomly ♥♥♥♥ up your movement? Why bosses and mobs attacks still go through walls like they exist only for player character? Why can't game remember that i used to two hand this weapon when i switch back to it? Why I can remember only two tracks from entire game's OST? Why I'm forced to single-hand weapon near blacksmith where I'd actually like to see what upgrades I'm spending resources is doing, making numbers in UI entirely useless if I'm two-handing said weapon? Why are all grab attacks getting a random 1m of extra range of animation even thought visually it looks like they shouldn't get you. Visual clarity and just general logic of some rolls is iffy sometimes, only way to understand which direction game actually wants you to roll is trial and error, not your eyes quite a few times. Why are poison swamps and their alternatives still in game? How exactly standing around for minutes to wait for status effect meter to empty is fun or interesting? Why are some bosses(especially Malenia) not doing anything for 40 seconds and if you try to attack them first you get punished? Surely you can use same code that makes them attack you after input reading your heal to speed it up a bit. [h2] The sad conclusion [/h2] It's fitting i mentioned Oblivion already, Bethesda used to be kings of open world RPGs, with nobody to even touch their throne, that was so successful they refused to improve anything and used their everbigger fame and oldtime glory to make more games. Sadly for me it looks like without a wake up call FromSoft are heading down similar path, this is their Skyrim, wide as ocean, deep as a puddle, with enough good things to still be a great experience, but if things continue like this in a few games we might end up with their Starfield. The more and more aggressively annoying fanbase deflecting every criticism with "get good" is not doing them favors either. This game could have been so much more than it is right now and its truly saddening

[h1] One of the greatest and highest-quality games ever made. [/h1] I’ve been putting this game off for a long time because, honestly, I’m not a big fan of open-world games. Too many of them feel bloated, repetitive, and filled with busywork and i get lost and frustrate easily. Elden Ring is different. This is open-world done right. The map is massive, but it never feels like lazy copy-paste filler. Every region feels distinct: different enemies, different bosses, different environments, and different challenges. Exploration is constantly rewarded—whether it’s a powerful weapon, a new spell, a hidden dungeon, or lore that makes you stop and think. You’re not just wandering for the sake of it; the game respects your time and curiosity. Elden Ring doesn’t rely on cutting-edge, photorealistic graphics—and it doesn’t need to. The art direction is absolutely stunning. There were multiple moments where I literally put the controller down just to stare at the scenery. This game is living proof that art direction > realism every single time. The character and boss designs are incredible. Every major boss feels unique, intimidating, and straight-up badass. Add in the phenomenal soundtrack, and every boss fight feels like an epic event. Even when you’re getting absolutely destroyed, you can’t help but appreciate how cool everything looks and sounds. The combat is easily the best part of the game. The combat is deep, satisfying, and insanely flexible. There are countless ways to play: different classes, builds, weapons, spells, and playstyles. This gives the game ridiculous replay value—you could finish it multiple times and still feel like you’re playing something new. Boss fights are intense and memorable, but also frustrating as hell—sometimes in the funniest way. Some bosses will start an attack, stall for what feels like 20 years (just like my government), and then drop it on you the moment you least expect it. Painful? Yes. Memorable? Absolutely. I’m not going to sugarcoat it: this game is hard. That said, it’s more forgiving than other Souls games thanks to mechanics like spirit summons and co-op options. The difficulty feels challenging rather than unfair, and the game gives you tools to overcome obstacles—if you’re willing to experiment and adapt. The story is dark, mysterious, and incredibly alluring—but it won’t hold your hand. There are no 20-minute cinematics explaining everything, no quest logs telling you exactly where to go. If you don’t pay attention to NPC dialogue, item descriptions, and environmental clues, you will get lost. The narrative is told in fragments, pieced together by the player. It’s written by Hidetaka Miyazaki and George R. R. Martin, so expect heavy themes of decay, tragedy, and a world on the brink of collapse. If you want a straightforward, cinematic story, this isn’t it—but if you enjoy deep lore and worldbuilding, it’s one of the best in modern gaming. [h1] Final Thoughts [/h1] If you have the patience of a saint and the curiosity of a cat, buy this game. If you value your blood pressure, maybe think twice. But skipping Elden Ring means missing out on one of the most ambitious, rewarding, and unforgettable gaming experiences ever made.

This is my first Souls-like game, so I’m leaving comments open in case someone wants to share their perspective or maybe spark my interest in the genre again. That said, I genuinely don’t see the appeal. I played fairly deep into the game, far enough to defeat major bosses, slay something massive, and set something important on fire (no spoilers). So this isn’t a surface level take. Story: There barely is a story. What’s there feels vague and disconnected, more like a sequence of boss fights than a narrative. Lore exists, sure, but it’s buried so deeply that it never felt engaging or motivating to me. I never felt invested in what I was doing or why. Is it the genre? Like racing games where lore and story is not the point? Combat: It’s… fine. Rarely exciting. The biggest issue is rewards: you’re showered with an overwhelming number of weapons, most of which feel completely pointless. Beating around 95% of bosses gives you nothing meaningful, which is a big problem when the game is essentially a boss-rush experience. Progress often feels hollow. Setting: The world is technically open, but it feels lifeless. There are almost no people, no real villages, no towns just ruins and enemies. Exploration didn’t feel rewarding or immersive, it felt empty. An open world should invite curiosity, not make you feel alone in a dead museum. Overall I don’t understand the obsession. For me, Elden Ring feels more like endurance than enjoyment and I will not be returning to the genre again... Maybe for that Napoleon era game.

"Long and hard didst thou fight. Tarnished Warrior. Spurned by the grace of gold. Be assured, the Elden Ring resteth close at hand." Elden Ring is an exceptional entry in the Soulslike genre and one of the best executions of its formula to date. It’s demanding and opaque, but far more approachable than earlier titles, making it a strong—if still challenging—entry point for newcomers willing to engage with its systems. I waited until a second playthrough to review it, and it genuinely may be one of the greatest games ever made. That said, meaningful criticism is often dismissed with “get good,” which does the game no favors. The story and worldbuilding are genuinely interesting, but deliberately esoteric. Lore is fragmented, subtle, and easy to miss if you don’t already know what to look for. It can feel scattered and opaque, but that’s very much how these games operate—and for many players, that mystery is part of the appeal. Brief note for new players: ranged magic builds are extremely powerful but hard to set up without deep game knowledge; melee builds are easier to start with, but significantly harder to master in practice.

Love this game. I hadn't played any of the souls games before getting Elden Ring, and I feel like it's a perfect introduction to the series/genre. There's just enough tutorial and guidance to give the player the tools needed to progress but it's still vague and difficult enough to maintain the challenging nature these types of games are known for. I've played a lot and it's been really fun and motivating to improve at the game. Now, with just over 200 hours, I've gone from not knowing that the roll was a dodge to getting close on my first no-hit run and I'm still loving it. The DLC, Shadow of the Erdtree, is much closer to some of the other souls games in nature. It's significantly more difficult than the base game, and much more confusing to piece together the narrative and even figure out where you need to go. There were several major areas and bosses that I completely missed my first time playing through the DLC, whereas I found almost all of them in the base game even with no souls experience. All in all, I'd give the game a solid 8/10. I'm taking one point off because perfect games don't exist, and another because there are a few annoying aspects of some of the major boss fights. They aren't difficulty problems so much as they are things that just make the experience of fighting those bosses less enjoyable than they could be (i.e. Godskin Duo's inconsistent AI, the fire physics, Divine Beast Dancing Lion's existence...), so other people may think differently.

Optimization is horrendous, I have a 5070ti and a 7800X3D and still the game regularly freezes, one building in Leyndell is particularly bad with an estimated average of 0.25 FPS, regardless of graphical settings, if it wasn't possible to skip it the game would've been incompletable. Edit: Optimization is not the issue, rather it's a bad PC-port, not G-sync compatible, not compatible with hz over 60, not compatible with VRR, not compatible with logitech g-hub, etc. Disabling these features/processes and switching v-sync to application controlled solved all of these issues for me. Being a bad port also explains why the Options are extremely limited, something so easy such as re-binding the map button isn't allowed, no option regarding lock-on at all, only X-box glyphs, etc. Lazy or inept. All of the classic FromSoft bugs and jank are present, attacks going through walls / obstacles, clipping around shields etc. Most enemies have clearly not been designed for an open-world with variable terrain in mind, meaning they get stuck on or in terrain a lot, even the ones that can fly, the dragons are particularly egregious. I feel like the majority of enemy attacks blatantly track you now, there are very few enemies you can out position any more, and since the shields can only be reliably used against weak enemies that means you're going to be I-frame rolling in most boss fights since many of them can one-shot you if you don't, resulting in them all feeling very samey, even before addressing the staggering number of repeats. Torrent's double jump not being able to prevent fall damage is one of the worst game design decisions in living memory, objectively.

Elden Ring + Shadow of the Erdtree was my first Souls game and I wasn’t fully prepared for either the combat or the storytelling. I went in with guidance from an experienced player, and looking back, I probably should’ve kept a death counter. Frustrating at times, but also a clear marker of progress as those deaths slowly became fewer. The world design is visually stunning. I had multiple moments of cresting a hill and just stopping to take it all in. Sometimes breathtakingly beautiful (notably for me, Limgrave, Liurnia, Gravesite Plains), other times deeply unsettling (horrid and grotesque Caelid). The underground areas, especially Nokron and Nokstella, felt other-worldly and remain some of my favorite locations in the game. Boss designs are massive and intimidating, making each fight feel truly epic. The music complements this perfectly: choral, gothic, and atmospheric when needed, then swelling into dramatic orchestral scores during combat without overwhelming the scenery. Cons - Story is obscure and difficult to follow (I had expected more cnematic cutscenes similar to that of the beginning sequence introducing the world, but it only happened like that at beginning). So, if you’re looking for a clearer or more accessable narrative, this probably isn’t the game for you. That said, it didn’t hurt my enjoyment much, since my focus was learning combat and exploring the world. - Wish there were an option to replay cutscenes (some moments I wanted to really re-visit) Overall, Elden Ring (and its DLC) delivered an incredible sense of escapism. Between the hauntingly beautiful world, immersive music, and colossal bosses that tested my persistence, it was a rewarding experience.

long overdue, 4 year gap review. played on release on ps5 originally people who say "this game ruined other games for me" or "this is the best game ever" are clearly new players with no frame of reference, or worse, fanboys. this game, by comparison to others, sucks, mainly because the bosses suck. i don't think i've ever seen so much negative discussion around a fromsoft game since ds2. and that's telling. sure, people may have their issues with the others. ds1 is janky, ds3 is too linear, etc. etc. but that's pretty much where the negativity ends. outside of ds2, it's rare to see people discussing the fundamental flaws of the designers so regularly...elden ring is the complete opposite and i don't think that's because of the audience it reached. you have long-time vets pretty much all saying the same thing about elden ring and i'm more inclined to believe someone who's played the other games ad nauseum (like myself) than a new player riding the hype train. (see what i mean by the hype train?) the open world is pretty to look but...what else? it's just a ubisoft open world without map markers and a few interesting secrets. if that makes it greatest open world of all time...yeah, i won't say anymore. as a long-time fan who's been rotating these games for the past 5 years or so...elden ring is a disappointment in almost every way. bland open world with (some) good legacy dungeons (stormveil, shadowkeep, leyndell). copy/paste ds3 combat with sekiro's jump but with overall worse bosses than ds3. there are some good ones in there, just not many (cough, just YT "elden ring bosses" no added bias like "good" or "bad" and see what comes up) yeah, not sure what there is to like about this one when you take the rose-tinted glasses off. it pretty much takes everything from all the other games and doesn't have it's own identity while diluting what made the original games so special - tight level design and consistent combat. you get that with regular enemies...some...but bosses? overall horrible. it's a fromsoft game and the world is pretty i guess so maybe that's why people froth at the mouth. oh, and the mentality of "miyazaki can do no wrong" "it's supposed to be this way" "git gud" ya know, braindead talk

Playing Elden Ring as an Intellect build completely changes the mechanical experience, and it’s incredibly satisfying. Combat shifts from melee pacing to high-stakes spellcasting, where timing, positioning, and resource management dominate. Spells hit hard, but each cast requires careful spacing, FP management, and awareness of enemy attack windows, turning every encounter into a tactical puzzle. Sorceries, catalysts, and buffs feel distinct and meaningful. Selecting the right spells for range, crowd control, or single-target burst is crucial, and experimentation with combos like Glintstone Barrage followed by swift melee or ranged backup is highly rewarding. Spellcasting is not just powerful — it’s a mechanical system that encourages creativity and adaptability. Movement and positioning are critical. Intellect builds rely on kiting enemies, reading attack patterns, and controlling engagement distances. Dodging and rolling aren’t optional; they’re key tools to survive while channeling high-damage sorceries. Mount combat also opens interesting tactical options, letting you cast and reposition simultaneously in open-world encounters. Resource and cooldown management adds depth. FP consumption, catalyst upgrades, and buff durations create constant decisions about when to commit, retreat, or change tactics. Even boss fights feel like complex mechanical challenges, rewarding smart spell rotation, precise timing, and environmental awareness. Elden Ring’s RPG systems shine for magic builds. Gear, talismans, and Ashes of War all meaningfully impact your playstyle, letting Intellect characters feel powerful without breaking combat balance. Every fight, exploration moment, and encounter is a test of skill and strategy, making victories feel earned. 10/10 — precise, tactical, and mechanically brilliant for spellcasters.

[h1] Its alright, I guess [/h1] Fresh off the back of getting all achievements for Dark Souls 3 & Dark Souls Remastered (I've also completed and loved Sekiro), I decided to give Elden Ring a crack. Elden Ring is arguably the culmination of lofty developer ambitions, twinned with game design trends of the time. A classic Dark Souls game (big dungeons, unforgiving combat, vague narrative and beautiful world design), but bigger and better, with an open world, teeming with optional content and areas to explore. You play as 'Insert Name Here', who's a generic nobody, in a world that is uncaring. Along the way, to your vague goal, you meet various NPC's, conquer large dungeons and multiple mini-dungeons/tombs and get your bootay handed to you on many an occasion. Do you play melee warrior, ranged mage, or something in between? The choice is yours. It still won't help you 'git gud'! I absolutely adore the world itself. It's beautiful, with some great setpieces (Stormveil & Raya Lucaria), a great soundtrack, and great variety in enemies and how you build your character. There's a good variety in bosses too. The soundtrack is really really great too, as with all Souls games. Where I think this falls apart, is the open world. I don't think it adds anything, and coupled with the many many smaller dungeons scattered across the lands, I feel it causes the game to lose pace. I decided to clear all dungeons and kill all bosses (including mini-dungeons), getting every item available, which no doubt led to fatigue, and influenced my opinion on this, as I wanted to make sure I experienced everything the game had to offer. I think the inclusion of a vast open world, works against the game and is very much a product of design trends at the time. What it does well, is the large, sprawling dungeons (classic style), along with music, area design and world building. I did however decide to skip the DLC, as I was so burned out at the end of NG, I didn't want more of the same. I found that fun did return, once I was steam rolling NG+2 and NG+3, blitzing my way to the end and focusing on core objectives, having all the items I needed to just ignore optional areas/smaller dungeons altogether, and this ignoring all optional content, reminded me of why I liked previous games. It felt tighter, easier to get around, without the open world padding. Each to their own, but I was disappointed by this, but then again, I was also disappointed by Breath of the Wild, because of how samey the mini-dungeons were, bar one or two which actually did something to differentiate themselves. [h2] Summary [/h2] [h3] Pros [/h3] - World building - Music - Clean and responsive combat - Multiple ways to build and play your character - Lots to do - Rani [h3] Cons [/h3] - Mini-dungeons feel repetitive and uninspired - Traversing the open world gets really boring, really fast - Invisible Scarabs - Feels like there's too much to do, it's easy to lose track of key objectives [h2] Final Verdict - 7/10 - Good Game [/h2] This game is really worth a look at, if you're in need of another SoulsBourne title, and love open world games (e.g. Breath of the wild). If you don't like open world games, that is a major detracting factor, which will annoy you. So much of what there is great, but it's the middling areas in between, which feel like unnecessary padding, which work to its detriment. At 120 hours I really really wanted to love it, and gave it enough of my time to win me over, and went to great lengths to complete everything, but it just never clicked, and I think the open world is the reason. I'd rank this 45th best Souls game that I've completed (for me), with my order of Best > Worst games being Sekiro > Demons Souls > Dark Souls Remastered > Dark Souls 3 > Elden Ring.

Elden Ring is a rare masterpiece of open-world design that prioritizes discovery over mindless map markers. It offers a sense of scale and atmosphere that few other games can match. It is a demanding experience that requires patience and resilience, but the reward is a profound sense of accomplishment and a journey through one of the most imaginative landscapes in digital history. If you are looking for a game that respects your intellegience and rewards curiosity, Elden Ring is a perfect choice. 10/10 ( no ai was used for this review )

It's a great experience. The combat, which I always thought at a glance looked a little boring, is in fact some of the most satisfying combat I've ever played. The variety of weapons are great, and they really feel good to use. I feel like anyone who wants to play a spell slinging, hack and slash game, anyone who ever dreamt of being a Merlin, or King Arthur, any dark, grim, knightly fantasy needs to play it. The enemies and bosses look wonderful. I'm not going to go too much into the good, you'll know it as soon as you start playing, and I think you should. I'm going to go through some bullet points of the bad, so that some people understand them. -Some of the bosses are hard, simply for the sake of hard. Don't matter how big they are, they'll be able to move better than you, throw out more attacks faster and more often than you. It's not all bad, it can just get tiring after enough of them. -The world is fairly massive, which is great, however, the verticality of it can get frustrating as can be. You'll see so many places, that look so close, but are so very hard to reach. When you start wanting to explore all of the Volcano Manor area of the map, you'll really understand what I'm talking about. Many hours were spent just figuring out, how I could get to places. -This is both a positive and a negative. The game is completely open world. There is no journal or quests in the modern way we know them. This game is more related to the games of long long ago where if you want to know and understand the story, you're really going to have to pay attention and remember things, and I've found on a first play through, when you're so busy trying just to survive, and figure out how to get where, that it can be hard to do, so a lot of the time, I had a really vague idea on what was going on, who hated who, who loved who, and the reasons why. Not with everything and everyone, but enough for it to be kind of sad. -My biggest complaint and let down, is the ending I got, and I'm sure the others, are God awful. Short, open to interpritation, which makes me wonder if even learning all the lore is really worth it given the ending. It really irks me because of how much challenge, and how many hours you're going to drop into this game to be given next to nothing at the end of it. I mean that whole heartedly, next to nothing. That said, I don't regret a minute of my playtime. The world is worth exploring, and the fights are worth fighting. The gameplay is fantastic, and it's presented something I hope future games emulate, just improve upon.

This is easily the worst game in the entire Souls series by far. It's trashy, lazy developing. Collision boxes versus hit boxes are absolute garbage. You can clip through enemies' models because your character is literally making contact, yet your strikes will not hit. This is obvious on ANY large enemy, but particularly obvious on any troll. Clipping? Your enemies will clip through walls. You cannot do the same. If you are not on perfectly level ground with your enemies, attacks will miss entirely. Parrying is a useless movement in this game - don't waste your time with it. There is an absurd amount of in-game input lag that has nothing to do with button release mechanics or hardware and oftentimes inputs won't just be delayed, but often missed entirely. I own the entire series, some on multiple platforms, and will not be purchasing another at this point.

5/5 stars Elden Ring is special. I feel like FromSoft has been building up to this game since the first release of Dark Souls, possibly longer. This game is extremely well made and stunning in every sense of the word. I can talk about how beautiful the world is, how amazing the story is, how fine tuned and gratifying the combat is, how much fun it is to explore but I know you have heard that all before. As someone who has played DS1, DS3 and Bloodborne I am used to some of the basic knowledge of how these games work. It is tricky though, because this game falls victim to one of the sharpest learning curves out there. It is difficult to call this a negative because I feel that this is part of what makes this game so special. I am a firm believer that this game would not work in a world without the internet. I feel like the meta of searching how to do some niche thing and finding an entire community of passionate people enjoying the game is part of the experience itself. Talking with your friends who have played it and explaining different tactics, gear, secrets and more is part of the fun. This game is not friendly, and I am not referring to the fact that it is "hard", but that it intentionally does not guide the player in any way. Yes there is a tutorial but most of the games mechanics are not explained in any way and just left for the players to experiment and find themselves. I spent my first 30 hours in the game when it first came out not understanding how Ashes of War worked. Not until I picked the game up again and started over recently did I start to understand how the combat worked fully. I think the best example of this is the story of Elden Ring itself. A player can play hundreds of hours of the game and not understand a single thing of what's going on. Not understanding what NPCs are talking about, not understanding the overarching plot, maybe they dont even understand who Michela is (the key character in the story). Not until I started watching lore videos did I start piecing everything together and start to appreciate the impact someone like George RR Martin had on the creation of this game. Everything is not there to serve you, it just is. I think this is kind of magical in a way, breathing a sense of life into the world, as if it has always been there and you are just a passerby of this breathing beautiful world. This is how all of the mechanics in the game feel, from the exploration to the combat to the obtuse side quests. Its tricky because if it was executed in any other way I would say this is just bad design but I believe it is the intentional fun of it. They want you to research, they want you to learn. By the time you finish Elden Ring for the first time, if you start all over from a new save you will undoubtedly be a better player because you have taken the time to learn and understand how the game works, not just because your end game character is level 150+. This game is not for the causal player, and I am not saying that to gatekeep, I am saying that because I don't think you will be able to enjoy Elden Ring in any casual way, you absolutely have to “lock in”. It's funny to see when people are in the middle of their first playthrough because I have seen it basically take over their consciousness, once it starts, it works its way into your brain and it's hard to not stop thinking about it. I know that happened to me. If you are willing to give Elden Ring your time and energy, you will not regret it. It is absolutely fantastic.

This game was my first souls-like ever. It introduce a genre of games that I never would've thought to pick up. Now, over 300 hours later (and somehow convincing my wife to play it with me via Seamless Co-Op), it's safe to say that this was the best investment in a game I could've ever made. If this is your first "Souls" game, Elden Ring is hard. But you know, so is life. It teaches you a valuable lesson without you ever having to get off your chair: it's not a matter of IF your reach your goals, it's WHEN and HOW. My first attempt at this game, it took me ~70 hours, and that's relying HEAVILY on the wiki for anything quest or location related. My second playthrough? 30 flat, and that still with exploration and taking things at my pace. My point is: it's a learning curve, and it's worth the struggle. I then took it upon myself to beat every Dark Souls game to see the progression of how Elden Ring came to be, and dare I say after beating all of them, Elden Ring is truly FromSoft's greatest work. FromSoft took everything lacking in the DS franchise and completely put it on its head. DO NOT SAY THIS GAME ISN'T FOR YOU. It is. It is for anyone who has any semblance of interest in fantasy/action/RPG. Just because you died 30 times and are bashing your head against the wall (I've been there a lot), it doesn't mean you're bad. It just means it wasn't time for you yet.

On top of that, it's very easy to lock yourself out of a questline because of an accident or by simply exploring too much (example: finding and killing rykard before finishing the volcano manor quests). 3. I think its important to know exactly how much % something is increased or decreased to properly build my character and understand the value of an item.

Honnestly, i didn't like this game at all. I'm a quite invested RPG player, BG3 is my fav game of all time so i might be opiniated, but my time is cyberpunk was not really a good time. I see what the game wants to propose, i see what it wants to do, where it wants me to go, what it wants me to feels, etc. But i really feel like it's not polish well enough to have the impact it wants. I think the best exemple for that is in the begining (spoiler ahead): [spoiler] For me, the best example of that is Jacky's death. Tbh, seing him died did not make me feel... anything? Like i see how my character feels, i see how i am suppose to feel, but from my point of view? Like, i did not know that guy, i had a single mission with him (+ the failed one but it's peanuts), i saw him for one cutscene and some small talk, but i was not really able to developp anything with him. He dies too soon, i did not get to know him before it happend. Like for exemple, Alfira death was far more impactfull in bg3 just because i was able to really connect with her in a previous scene, to share something with her. In comparison Jacky is just a random PNJ important in my character story. To give another comparison, i felt more thing with Delamain questline because we had more "shared story" as a player and PNJ (not lorewise) [/spoiler] And sadly the game is like that with everything. (another spoil:) [spoiler] Evelyn Parker quest was like that too, i did not really know her more than that, and her s****** was just "empty" of emotion. TBH when i got the called, i was just a bit upset that she did that just after i saved her [/spoiler] I feel like the quests, narratives, relationship etc are really empty. It really misses substance, impact. Some missions try to bring that with, like, no action at all, only dialogue, but even those are just a bit heavy and not really interesting. Sometimes i'm just there waiting for the discussion to finish because it lacks something. Maybe i'm too harsh because i'm used to Baldur's Gate in depth dialogue, but even with more tolerance it really feels like you have absolutly no impact in the game narratives, you are following a path, a rail, and watching a show you are not a part but just a spectator of. Also the open world was not really interesting. I appreciate the cyberpsycho questlines but other than that... Contracts are always the same, just basic infiltration/combat sequence. Secondary quest are mostly classic and even a bit stupid sometimes, like that time i had to reload my save because my line choise during a dialogue gave me a stupid resolution to a stupid quest (the barman's wife's "affair" quest if you want to know). Combat are not really an issue, even in hard difficulty, and sneaky built are SO STUPIDLY STRONG that the game has to nerf you with "unsneakable" PNJ so you can't roll on all the games with it. The skills trees are really uneven. Some skill are really interesting and impactfull, while other feels like useless (like what are those lvl 20 shinobi skills?? I did not felt reward for my farming. Also, some skill are only oriented on ONE SPECIFIC cyber équipement or gameplay, so for a RPG it really limits what you can do with your character. Driving is AWFULL, roads feel like full of soap. Also the map really feels more like an empty grid with box to tic than like a persistant environment with events and life out of the player intervention. So yeah, if you like RPG with a great deal of narration, i would not recommand this game. Agains maybe it's just me, but i really didn't get the thing. I hope this help my fellow RPG enjoyer, and have a nice day!

So yeah, this game is essentially "what if GTA5 were an FPS, but in a cyberpunk world and with heavy RPG elements". You want that, you find nothing better than this. Personally I regret buying it, and wish I could still refund it. I put the game off for many, many years (bought it years after the Ultimate Edition was released), and I should have known better what was the reason for that: lack of interest.

Don’t get me wrong, this game is still really buggy at times, but it is absolutely night and day from launch. CDPR really managed to delta the hell out of this game. The best part about this game, and what has been nova since the very beginning, is the story and lore. I genuinely cannot explain how attached I got to Night City and the people in it. There’s so much depth packed into the world that even random side content feels important instead of feeling like filler gigs. Few games have made me sit there after the credits like ‘♥♥♥♥… what now?’ but Cyberpunk absolutely did. The characters, the atmosphere, the music, the constant feeling that you’re just another gonk trying to survive in a city that couldn’t give less of a ♥♥♥♥ about you… it all sticks with you. What really stuck with me is how the game refuses to give you a perfect ending. Every path leaves you with some kind of loss, regret, or emptiness. It sounds depressing as ♥♥♥♥, but it makes the world feel real. Night City chews people up and spits them back out, and the game never lets you forget that. There’s no happy ending in Night City… just different ways to survive it. And honestly? That’s what makes the story so preem.

It's been a while since I've played this game, but I figured I'd finally leave a review for it since one's been pending for a while. This game was honestly always a good game. It may have had a rough start due to bugs and performance issues, but the core storyline and gameplay, as well as the more interesting questlines you can follow, were always there. Then with all the QoL changes and the complete overhaul they did to the perk system, it became much more refined and enjoyable to play since you now had a variety of builds and perks you could experiment with. I think one of my favorite things about the game was the story and characters. Every character has an interesting and expressive personality, including your own as expressed through the voice acting (I personally prefer Male V's voice direction). Everyone feels fleshed out and like they actually have a growing relationship to you the more you interact with them. The main story itself feels very personal and high stakes, though some of that is admittedly ruined by the open world nature of the game since you can just dally along however long you want. As the meme goes, "Anything but meeting Hanako at Embers" lol. Even so, I think it manages to portray a nice drama about the meaningfulness of life, self-determination, and even hope in a world that seems determined to grind you down. The environment is effective in portraying just how degenerate and trashy (literally, even) Night City really is, which helps in creating this sense of "contamination" and a desire to separate yourself and rise above it. Also, the music. The music in this game kicks ass, and I still listen to some of my favorite tracks on my Spotify every so often. I'd say my only real complaint with the game is the lack of being able to clearly show yourself as cybernetically enhanced, such as by having clearly mechanical limbs or metallic embellishments like a Kano-style red eye. I was also never too fond of any of the romance options, but it was nice that I never felt forced to pursue any of them from what I can remember.

This game is wide as an ocean, shallow as a puddle. It's good, but people keep overrating this game. The endings fit the settings theme and it's very cinematic. The shooting is mediocre, character creation is not really that engaging, the "choices" you make don't really matter all that much, on both a micro and macro level, and EVERY single mechanic is very surface level. Jack of all traits, master of none. It's also just a god awful RPG. Like to the point that it being described as that feels like false advertising. There's literally no "roleplaying" in this game beyond picking dialogue options. The backgrounds hardly matter beyond how you meet your character's first friend. Shooting is boring, driving is awful, the cybernetics aren't that interesting of a system. (Deus Ex and even 'Cruelty Squad' do it better! Which is embarrassing for a game that was in development for this long.) I've tried my best to care for the characters, but I kind of just don't. You hardly get to know each other, and you don't really "work" with another beyond the individual missions. Your "friends" are not plot relevant at all, beyond Panam for Act 1 and the finale. The "ending" of the game is probably what 'saves' this game at all, as it resonates so thematically with the nihilistic world that it almost convinces you the story was actually good, and not boring meaningless filler for 80% of it. You are so absurdly powerful in this game - both mechanically and storywise that it kind of makes all mission "planning" a bit boring and annoying. Why even do all of this if I can just kill everything that moves? Phantom Liberty is a little bit better about this but it's still not really enough. The themes and story is so annoyingly nihilistic, and to make it worse it comes from a pretty decently sized studio with a huge budget behind it. Oh, I'm sure a corporation would be HAPPY to promote a game where capitalism is some magical all consuming force that enslaves the planet and cannot be stopped by literally any means possible. Solutions? To capitalism? Well the writer doesn't want you to think about that, they just want you to bask in how miserable everyone is! It's individualist slop that I can't tell is out of ignorance or out of malice for the world. The anime just saved this game's ass insanely badly. It's THE "hype moments and aura" game. If you like that, play this game. If you want an actually good story with good gameplay?? Hope that maybe the sequel will be actually good.

This game is a total dumpster fire. I cant believe how many reviews sing it any praises, beyond it looks good. Visuals are the only thing CP2077 has going for it. The world is shallow and derivative, with little to no reason to go anywhere or see anything in particular. Not counting the fact that when you are inspired to check something out, there is ZERO interactability. Very little to actually DO in night city, except vibe. The cutscenes are all drawn out, basically just Visual Novel style, except the characters are paper thin. Seriously, it's like the writers here don't even understand basic humanity, or how people interact together. Characters feel stiff and lifeless, without real human depth, just an edgy facade with a subtle implication of substance. Story pacing is all over the place. There's moments of intrigue, ruined by ♥♥♥♥♥♥ dialogue or some ubelievably thin character aspect; cool cars scene ruined by on the rails action, generally inconsistent action will pull you out of the scene over and over in a playthrough. Not to mention the driving feels terrible. Nothing like a cool looking veneer on a slippery brick to get around NC with. When you do get somewhere with 'something to do' you're basically just killing everyone on site for the plot. Guns are weak and clunky, melee feels inorganic and unrealistic, and hacking is just not that fun, not to mention they don't reward stealth play very much, if at all, thanks to enemies being omniscient or totally blind. My biggest gripe with the game is one I almost never see mentioned: Almost every single story line, quest story, side quest, some characters and locations are Straight up RIPOFFS, from ACTUAL GOOD media. They ripped the name from a whole genre, confusing newbies into the scene, trying to force themselves into the discussion around the genre, when CDPR haven't even really contributed in that realm; its very disingenuous, and speaks to their philosophy as a company. Go check out any foundational cyberpunk media, and see how many tropes CP2077 straight ripped off from actual good writers and creators. Everything voodoo/AI ghost in the machine/ sentient AI using peons to escape, etc. are total 1:1 rips from William Gibson's Neuromancer trilogy. The only reason this game wasn't a MASSIVE flop is because braindead CONSUMERS ate up Witcher 3, and cant be honest with themselves, that this game is no anywhere near that level. Honestly hate this game, and I will NOT purchase anything CDPR does in the future.

I would argue that the opening of the game is maybe a little excessively vulgar. Maybe that's the point: desensitize everyone to this new world as quickly as possible so the banality of it at a point isn't shocking whatsoever. Regardless of whether that was fully intentional, I do think the gameplay of the opening, at least, is by far the weakest stretch of the game, even if it isn't particularly bad. Nevertheless, the game looks beautiful, plays well, and has a solid enough story. Even if its themes and world as a whole are largely derivative of more original works (but, at the same time, it's difficult to do anything in a cyberpunk universe without taking from Neuromancer and Ghost in the Shell and the like), the execution is largely there. I will say that V isn't a particularly memorable protagonist (maybe that's a maleV thing, or maybe he hasn't grown on me like Commander Shepard did). However, the world feels well lived in, the quests feel largely comprehensive, and it's ultimately just plain fun to play.

It's come a long way since release. The graphics are great, better optimized, and the bugs are more quirky than game breaking. The DLC Phantom Liberty really helps to flush the game out with content. It can be a little bit of a lore dump at times, but once the world opens up you'll be clearing the map of points of interests and quests, progressing and growing your character. I've played with all of the talent trees and builds at this point and they're all fun and viable in their own ways. You used to be able to re-work your attributes for in game currency, but now you can only do that once. The game then only allows you to re-work your talents, but your attributes are fixed. I find this to be a strange design choice, as it would be infinitely more fun to set your builds at your base (apartment) and experiment as you enjoy the story and events. The combat is fun. You feel super powerful, but on the higher difficulties the enemies can drop you super fast. The driving is also much improved from launch. If you want a first person action game with RPG progression systems and a dystopian story with a fully fleshed out open world, this is a must play.

I honestly loved playing Cyberpunk 2077. Night City feels absolutely alive — every street, every neon sign, every random conversation makes the world feel real and immersive. It’s one of those games where you can just walk around for hours and still find something interesting. What surprised me the most was how good the story is. I got genuinely attached to the characters, especially Johnny Silverhand. The game mixes action, emotional moments, and dark humor really well, and some of the side missions were honestly better than entire storylines in other games. The gameplay is super fun too because you can approach things however you want. One minute I was sneaking around hacking cameras, the next I was running in with a katana like a complete maniac. The freedom to build your character your own way makes the experience feel personal. And visually? The game is gorgeous. At night, with the rain, neon lights, and music playing in the background, it feels like you’re inside a sci-fi movie. The soundtrack deserves a lot of credit too because it perfectly matches the atmosphere. The game had a rough launch, but after all the updates it has become something really special. Now it feels polished, immersive, and genuinely memorable. For me, Cyberpunk 2077 ended up being one of those games that stays in your head long after you finish it.

You can never get enough of this world. Right off the bat, go experience the game.. just go and play and experience the miriad of stories and characters it hides inside this marvelously crafted world. Storytelling is apt for the genre and the effort it puts into the choices and outcomes for the quests is breathtaking to say the least. They don't do it for just the main questline (if you can figure out which one is the main story by half way mark that is), they consistently do it for even side quests which is amazing. You may not have the emotional connect with the side quests as you might expect from a Witcher 3 fanatic but that's okay. In this world where the line blurs between humanity and machines and where emotion is a data chip, it is expected that you take the deaths in a monotonous tone and it doesn't affect us much, no matter how much depth the characters might have. But given that there are stories that hits you and you will not see it coming. To do that level of immersion in this hopeless city in itself is a great achievement. Now coming to the world building. The world is a living breathing city. Each corner and alleys have something to tell. Each district has a unique style. Each have their faction and a history. And the people you meet there, well they add more to the world. And they entangle well with the missions where you have the choice to go which route you wanna go. I once tried climbing an impossible sky scraper just to avoid paying 50 eddies and guess what, I was greeted with the only scissor lift mechanism in the entire game. And to think they have an option to enter the building via the garden at the top floor is an icing on the cake. Brilliant game design, that I felt so satisfied with each different way I try to enter a building for the missions. I could give a 10 outta 10 just for that. But there is more, the abilities not only add to your combat prowess but also how you could potentially do the mission without much turmoil as it lets you interact with the buildings in 3 different ways atleast. Combat was sluggish at the beginning or so I thought until I discovered how to equip the cyberwares. Oh boy then started the real combat. As of now, I haven't yet experienced two different playstyles. Netrunner plus SMG fun. The possibilities are many whether you go with a Katana with the reflex tree, or you go stealth with throwable knifes with a cool build. Cyberpunk boiled down to bones is an upgraded version of GTA, full stop. For quests, instead of doing yoga or goofing off at a port doing nothing for hours like in GTA, you will have the most insane side quests AND get paid for it. Just to give a glimpse into what that could mean - you pick up an AI pistol off a dead guy in a shady alley and it makes you kill 50 people with it while it talks to you, you drive a creepy clown to a specific burrito vending machine (found everywhere in the city btw) only for him to kill the people standing in front of it for no reason, you eat Chinese food from a stand with a Japanese man and he calls it ♥♥♥♥ to the chef’s face, you use a light machine gun to mow down a homeless camp while they charge you, you have a street fight with a guy and take away his car in front of his pregnant girlfriend (dw tho, it makes sense and he ends up better off), the list just goes on. How is the game though? Overall it runs amazing and have had no major issues. One crash an hour in or something when I blew up 8 cars at the same time by accident (dropped a grenade when I went to change weapons into a car pile up). Never had an issue again. The city is beautiful, the quests are awesome, the game takes way over 100 hours to complete, the city and surrounding badlands is huge map wise (yes, you get fast travel points everywhere), the cars are fun, the clothing is awesome, the choices during conversations will require a few playthroughs (just bought the game for my main account so haven't finished the nomad one yet), the physics make sense, and the save button is the most used thing you will ever use (very very useful for going back if you screw up a convo or fight). For the story, it is a must play. Anything wrong with it? Yeah, nothing major but "stuff happens" sometimes. You could be on a hill trying to spawn in your car after a quest and it may explode on another car (nothing happens it's just annoying because you need to respawn it - ps it is NOT common), a quest could get stuck if you go into a cutscene and you weren't standing in the place they told you to be in (just reload last save, takes 4 seconds), people speaking can sometimes overlap (NPC 1 finishing their sentence and NPC 2 starts talking on the last word or something), loot can get stuck on bodies that you can't dispose of or loot, that kind of stuff. Most importantly, does it impact the gameplay? 100% no, it just "happens" and you reload and move on. Why the pos recommendation? The story and character development is worth it, full stop. Once you start, you can't put the game down because you want to complete the 270+ missions they have available. There is a LOT to do lol. ^ With all the above said, any negatives? Yeah, this game is way too into LGBT stuff. One character that you do street races with added in randomly that they were trans for 0 reason (you can't tell at all btw, knowing the fact added nothing to the gameplay) and then they suddenly had a personality shift to get revenge on their partner's killer mid race despite the dude dying fair and square. Made 0 sense and was forced. You could also talk about this girl that has the EXACT same romance lines as if you were a woman (because she's apparently gay) and you don't find that out until the last quest where she leaves the city. The lines were double dipped and the devs were lazy there 100%. As a straight male, she just shuts you down out of left field. Last major character was this cop you did quests with. The game gives you an option to start a gay relationship with the guy, keep him as a friend, or leave entirely all in the same conversation prompt. Does the game force you to be gay or bi or whatever? Def NOT, but you will have the "option" to if you wanted it. Wish there was a feature to turn on a "straight male" mode to avoid it altogether but I guess they want night city to truly feel degenerate and without morals. "No happy endings" right? It does not impact your gameplay, it just makes it slightly annoying to see. I am totally hyperfocusing on this despite it not even being 1% of the game because it could have been perfect with an option to let you avoid all that stuff. Right, enough said about that. Cyberpunk is worth every dollar and you should dive right into night city choom. Thanks for reading and God bless.

We are all aware of this game's horrible launch state, but with 2.0, the Phantom Liberty DLC and subsequent updates, I believe CDPR has turned that launch disaster into what it was always meant to be, that being one of the greatest games in recent memory. Something I'd happily call this generation's New Vegas. Pros: - Incredible worldbuilding through lifepaths. I would recommend a new player starting with Nomad but Corpo is my favorite - Well-written and complex characters that feel like actual people with everyone hiding at least something under the surface, no matter how insignificant they may be to the story - Great story with a well-handled approach to many complex themes along with emotional hard-hitting moments (Especially Phantom Liberty) - Incredible amounts of replayability, that can be owed to rewarding, deliberate and varied buildcrafting (especially on higher difficulties), satisfying gameplay, multiple endings, and of course, mod support (I have way more hours on the GOG version dw) - Great soundtrack - Fashion potential is off the charts, especially with mods Cons (if I really have to nitpick): - Some jank is still to be found if you look for it - The open world sometimes feels a bit lifeless, but you'll be too busy doing gigs to care Lol - The first ten levels or so are pretty slow to do, especially on harder difficulties (despite which I can still absolutely recommend them regardless) - Some guns are straight up useless for 80% of players, which ends up diluting gunplay a lot more than it should Despite some minor flaws, I'd still say this game has 100% earned its roses now.

[h1]Cyberpunk 2077: A game that everyone must try[/h1] The graphics: Nowadays a game like this is hard to find, it remains within a small select group of games that I and many others would consider near perfect. And here's the reasons why: Starting with the obvious, the graphics. Cyberpunk boasts some of the greatest looking visuals within gaming as a whole as it takes full usage of the neo-lit world. It truly immerses you into the position of V as you're put into this ginormous worst-case scenario world. It is also openly used as NVIDIAs golden goose for gaming visuals, as it's spoon fed the newest features such as higher frame gen and the exclusive path tracing which I am lucky enough to try. And it is nothing less than breath-taking. The story: CDPR is known for they deal with their stories, as primarily seen within how they adapted The Witcher. Similarly Cyberpunk 2077 is merely adding onto the Cyberpunk world created by Mike Pondsmith, and it does it more than enough justice. The story perfectly resonates with the main source material and is able to encapsulate you into it immediately. After the heist and with V's slowly deteriorating health it was able to make you feel true sympathy for both V and those around you. It makes you feel for characters and at times it really feels like you're sharing their misfortune. And with the decision-based story (albeit sometimes it doesn't make full use of it) it allows for you to carve your own path within Night City. Overall no game is without its flaws. For instance, the NPC depth could have definitely been further worked upon as sometimes the walking animations can feel out of place and their reactions uncanny and unrealistic. Furthermore, the bugs. Now I remember the horror movie that was Cyberpunk on release, and they did indeed build upon this game from the ground up. But sometimes I do find myself encountering a few bugs that really feel like they shouldn't still exist within the game's current state. Cyberpunk holds a special place within my heart as both the base game and DLC allow for CDPR to show the true extent to what they can do with games. I hope this review either convinces you to buy the game or at least makes you aware of Cyberpunk 2077's greatness.

Cyberpunk is a really good game. It is considered a reference on multiple fronts which combined result in a highly entertaining experience. If you get the chance, buy it and play it. Cyberpunk is an ambitious project in terms of scope and technical capabilities. Despite its rough start, it's undeniable this is one of the most good looking game there was when it came out, and the dimension of the project is not something that many studios would dare to tackle for an entirely new IP. I'm happy they did and we should give them credit that they took it to the end, to ensure its mostly failed launch was just a light stain on their track record. This game was designed with realism in mind and it will pull everything out of your graphics card to make it happen. At the same time, it is still somehow flexible to be able to run on something as restricted as a steam deck. It's impressive. If you have the necessary hardware, your eyes will feast. It's a game from 2020 but still used as a tech demo reference in 2026. That's saying something. I feel the Cyberpunk can be best described as a linear game built on top of a massive (open?) world. Yes, you can take quests in mostly assorted order but you do feel they're all leading to the same outcome. Your decisions don't shape the world, you're just following the pre-destined path, but this path is highly entertaining. To be fair to the devs, open world games are tough. It's hard to get them right. Most just end up being too sprawling with little substance (looking at your Starfield) and struggle with pacing. In Cyberpunk, the devs decided to use this massive maps to sprinkle curated experiences all over the places: the quests, the gigs, the NYCP arrests, etc... All in all, making sure in every region, that there was at least something interesting happening there once. It's not a game where the world on its own has the built-in dynamics to entertain you by itself, but CD PROJECT RED left plenty to do everywhere. I personally loved the gigs, secondary to the plot, because it provides that kind of experience you get with Hitman: "here's a constrained location and goal, there are multiple ways to fulfill the goal, go and have fun". The NYCP arrests were a bit more trash tier casual events for me. I didn't really connect with them and I failed to see their appeal. The world building and design this project did is amazing and they just deserve praise. The weapon systems are interesting; the way gameplay changes based on the implants you decide to install on your character is peak. The implant and skill system is solid and built to ensure that only your imagination is the limit in deciding how you want to play this game: in your face bruiser, long range assassin, sneaky cyber-runner, a combination of the previous, etc. There are more combinations than the time you'll have to play them. Phantom Liberty is DLC done right. The DLC has its own review page but this doesn't subtract from the value it added to the experience, although you can't help but to feel that they are detached. The way it intertwines with the main story is superficial. To be fair, it would technically very hard to have it any other way. Regarding music and soundtrack: I remember spending hours driving to the radios in GTA 3 and Vice City. That was no longer the case in Cyberpunk. I mostly kept the radio quiet and can't really pinpoint why. Maybe I just got old, the samples I got from the radio didn't really connect on the first listens and then I just ended up turning off the radio. Or maybe it's a sign that in general I didn't feel them appealing enough, despite the random sampling. I know there are at least 2 or 3 banger tracks, that I felt welt placed, some of them during key dialogs that really helped to shape the mood. In the places it really mattered, the score was there and provided the necessary lift. However the passive listening experience (radio) was not the best. Maybe it's just the reality of Night City of being very self-imposing with its piercing ads and obnoxious jingles. There was nothing I really disliked in this game. Only things that I would not mind the see changed into the next iteration of Cyberpunk 2077, if that ever ends up being a thing: 1. V's personality was extremely bland. I picked a corpo path and the way V spoke just sounded often like a low education gangster. This dissonance between personality and background killed immersion. 2. I would like to see the design philosophy behinds the gigs more present even in the main quest. Right now everything is absolutely scripted. One way in, one way out. I feel "The Last Of Us" showed us there's is flexibility for having both. If you have level designers on your team that can develop maps like the gigs, I'm sure these can still flow into your main quest. 3. I felt sad the gigs never really tied properly with the world lore. The story is baked-in and its not reactive to decisions you took in some of these gigs. It's a great game. Be ready to commit some time to it :)

I've been gameing for more than 30 years. And this game surely takes place in the list of the best I've ever played. Verty fruitful and exciting. Passed it 2 times, 40-50 hours of juice. When I say "characters", I also mean their model, animations, voicing and so on. Including the character that you play for. The style of everything in the game is a 100% hit. Including advs, signboards and so on, my respect to the designers and story authors. + Action. There is a lot of action. Yes, this is real 3-D action game, where you can set the difficult challending enough for you. Shooting, fighting, moving, all the stuff. Driving from the first-player-view is also implemented quite well. + Mechanics. There are several ways to evolve and become more dangerous. I played 2 times and 2 totally different combat experience. And I know at least 2 more ways. The cyber-related options and mechanics are implemented in an interesting and well-played ways (on of my game completions done with cybernetics maxed). + The level/map. Yes, the city and its outskirts are rather huge, their design, road net, fast travel map - all looks and works quite fine. There are main story lines, additional story lines, separate missions and additional engagement, enough things to take care about. + Graphics. I'm not the most demanding player but I'd call this nice. Rather huge map with seamless traveling across by foot/car or fast-travel with short loading. I did just a pair of key remappings but the whole interface worked well for me, maybe some minor improvements could be done but really not that important. - There are still some bugs. Non of them prevented me from progressing stories neither crashed the game so they are quite minor. Mostly related to some transport. I heard the the amount of bugs was greater in the beginning. TLDR: Having never played it before this, I don't have bad memories of a broken and unplayable game. Instead I was able to go in almost completely blind and enjoyed the game a lot. The game actually surprised me quite a bit, as I was expecting a bland or shallow game (entirely due to residual internet disdain that I was exposed to), but in truth the story was great and had a lot of fun moments. The actual gameplay is really fun and more dynamic than something like Skyrim or Fallout, which are the closest games I've played to this sort of thing. Mixing fast movements with quickhacks and fun abilities makes this game really good in and out of combat. Katanas especially... those felt really fun to parry bullets with. The driving is SO fun in this game, which is good because they love to do sidequests that involve a LOT of back and forth. Even playing on the standard difficulty I felt super overpowered for most of the game, which resulting in clearing enemy hideouts really quickly. That almost meant I spent even more time driving, which I was able to enjoy. It's especially fun when you save up enough money to get a car with tons of health and built-in machine guns, purely to cause mischief. The game has some flaws here and there, but they're pretty minor gripes. Most of them involve slow elevators, and the fact that your character flashes you every time you change gear. Outside of that, I enjoyed the game enough that I immediately went and watched Cyberpunk Edgerunners after finishing this game, and was sad when there weren't any more quests to do. Highly recommend this if your computer has the specs to run it.

To me, Cyberpunk is a modern iteration of some of the overall themes and tone of the original Fallout. Cyberpunk is a game about you against the world a true uphill battle where there is no possible way of winning. The world is built around you losing, and you know that. V knows that. But we keep fighting; we have to. While Fallout 1 leans into a pulp vibe and focuses more on racial themes and the failed foundations of social Darwinism, Cyberpunk focuses on the crushing aspects of late-stage capitalism, where the sky is filled with ads and the only way to make a living is by getting yourself killed. The system is built to destroy you, to isolate you so what is your answer? How do you keep yourself alive? You build connections, you live your life, and you fall in love.

Where to even start. I've loved cyberpunk as a genre since I first read Ghostrunner as a kid, and Mike Pondsmith really did something special. Cyberpunk 2077 isn't the best game in the world, I wouldn't even go as far to say its the best game in my steam library, but it is special. There are not enough words in the universe to describe how I feel about this game in any reasonable amount of time. There is nothing I could say about this game that could convince you to play it more than other people likely have already.

Easily the best AAA game I played in the last ten years, and probably one of the best action RPG and open-world game too. Didn't finish the main story yet, nor played the DLC, though the story and narration is solid. The choices feel interesting and impactful. The city really feel alive, dangerous, and overall represent well the ultra capitalist corporation-dominated dystopia its supposed to be. The universe is interesting with a lot of detail and fluff being present in the game. Encountered very few bugs during my playthrough for now. Playing a stealth build with some support netrunning is really fun, feel like HITMAN but with a giant open-world and plenty of interesting zone to explore different approach. For instance some areas of the cities offer a great environnement for outdoor long-range snipper shots, while other are more compact and enclosed, perfect for infiltration. I like how the game use its setup to offer levels with verticality, and a really good amount of plausible physics, move and tools to make the most out of them. On the negative side, the progression curve is a little weird, in particular in Very hard difficulty but not only. Basically, it's really hard at the beginning, but suddently after the 20 first levels everything feel quite easy and less challenging. The voice acting and dialogue are quite inequal, the protagonist for instance has sometime quite unsufferable edgelord lines which does not really feel in-character or fitting the condition they are facing. They are sometimes way too phlegmatic for the stuff happening around them. Otherwise the most important NPC are way better, with strong identity, struggles, goals, development during the story and various way of dealing with what's happening. You can easily feel attached (or repulsed) to them. Overall the tone remain quite edgy, sometimes boomer-esque, but that fit the Cyberpunk universe, which is so maximalist it becomes really goofy at some times, lightyears away from the very serious and eerie neo-noir aesthetic of Blade Runner or the first Deus Ex and its never ending socio-political schemes and conspirations. That is not a problem at all, just don't expect any profound political or metaphysical meditation from this game because it will not deliver that. Though, I think the setup (and the game !) is really good at exploring the unheimlich/unhomely aspect of cybernetics due to how common it is in the universe and the first-person perspective.

TL;DR: For the majority of my time, the game was actively fighting against my playstyle. Both in terms of gameplay (locking me into dogtown for hours) and narrative (V constantly acting and speaking in ways that don't match my choices) IMO, you either have a silent protagonist with player agency OR a narrated protagonist with a fixed story. As V keeps acting and speaking in a way that only matches a specific 'canonical' character. It's very immersion breaking if you try to go off the path. The sidequest were infinitely more emotionally engaging than the main story. As they were more condensed, had more likable characters and were less cluttered with "choices". Cyberpunk 2077 isn’t just a game. And Edgerunners isn’t just an anime. Both present a futuristic world full of chrome, violence, and massive corporations… but at its core, it reflects something very real: real life. Today, people often burn themselves out chasing ambition, money, status, or validation. In Night City, it happens through cyberware and implants. In real life, it happens in quieter, less neon-lit ways—but it still destroys people just the same. David Martinez wanted to prove his worth to the world. V just wanted to survive in a system that was already stacked against them. And honestly, how many people today are living versions of that same struggle? Cyberpunk constantly reminds us that when ambition goes blind, it stops motivating and starts consuming you instead. People stop living for themselves and start chasing something that may never fill the emptiness. And that’s what makes this universe so special: behind the neon lights, intense action, and the absolutely unhinged amount of chaos (and yes, NSFW energy) in Night City, there are real lessons about humanity, loneliness, love, trauma, and the price of trying to “win” in a broken world. There are no perfect endings in Night City. Just like there are rarely perfect endings in real life. But people still love, still dream, and still fight anyway. And maybe that’s the real message of Cyberpunk. (Also, half the city definitely needs therapy… and the other half needs to log off for a bit.)

Cyberpunk 2077 Review:- After playing for around 16 hours, I can honestly say this game surprised me in a very good way. When I started GTA 5, I mostly treated it like an open-world sandbox. I enjoyed driving, causing chaos, and exploring, but I was never deeply invested in the story. Cyberpunk 2077 feels completely different to me. In Cyberpunk, I am not just treating it as an open-world game — I am treating it as an open-world story-based choice matters game. The storyline is genuinely great and emotional. Some moments actually hit hard emotionally, and the characters feel memorable. What I love the most is that my choices actually matter. I feel like the story changes depending on what I choose, and that makes me think before making decisions. It makes me more attached to the world and characters. The gameplay is also really fun: ✔ Cool cars and bikes to drive ✔ Great action (not too hard, not too easy — balanced difficulty) ✔ Amazing world design ✔ Freedom to do many things But the biggest difference compared to GTA or many other open-world games for me is hacking. I absolutely love that I can use intelligence and strategy instead of just shooting enemies. Hacking enemies, using quickhacks, scanning, and planning attacks makes combat feel unique and smart. Honestly, after 16 hours, I understand why people love this game so much. It feels immersive, emotional, and gives me freedom while still making me care about the story. Highly recommended if you love story-driven games where your choices matter.
