Petit préambule : je rédige cette critique après deux runs complets (DLC compris) effectués début 2026. Cyberpunk 2077 a fait couler beaucoup d'encre et suscité beaucoup d'attente suite à sa présentation à l'E3 et la diffusion de multiples trailers alléchants. Lorsqu'il est sorti, de nombreux bugs et des finitions bâclées ont fait les choux gras de la presse et enflammé les réseaux sociaux. Pourquoi me sens-je obligé de faire ce rappel des évènements passés ? Tout simplement car on peut constater qu'en 2026, après de nombreux patchs et une v2 salutaire, Cyberpunk 2077 me paraît être pleinement à la hauteur des promesses faites à son annonce. D'abord, ce qui saute aux yeux, littéralement, c'est la beauté et la cohérence graphique du jeu. Il n'y a pas un recoin du jeu ou l'on ne sente pas le boulot et l'amour des artistes de CD Projekt. La moindre affiche, le plus petit bout de ruelle, le couloir d'immeuble le plus banal témoignent tous d'un sens du détail admirable. La partie graphique est également magnifiée par une surcouche technique bien musclée qui à grand renfort de ray tracing (ou path tracing) produit des ambiances lumineuses et colorées qui renforcent l'atmosphère des lieux. Ensuite, on est frappé par l'habillage sonore extrêmement touffu du jeu. Les longues promenades pédestres que l'on fait en jeu permettent de se sentir plongé dans cet univers grâce à de multiples couches de sons: des conversations, des jingles de pub, la circulation aérienne et automobile, des fusillades... Tout cela renforce l'immersion. Quant à l'ambiance musicale, elle est particulièrement soignée. Les nombreuses pistes musicales dispensées par les multiples radios thématiques sont toutes excellentes et raccord avec l'univers du jeu. La bande originale n'est pas en reste avec de nombreux morceaux illustrant efficacement les différentes phases du jeu. Le scénario nous met dans les chaussures d'un mercenaire débutant qui va au fil de ses aventures acquérir un statut légendaire jusqu'à un dénouement final qui ne manquera pas de vous surprendre ( plusieurs fins sont possibles, mais il n'y a pas de happy end à Night City). Toutes les missions, des principales aux secondaires, bénéficient d'un niveau d'écriture très élevé : il y a toujours des situations intéressantes, des personnages intrigants, des pans de lore à découvrir. Les dialogues sont particulièrement vivants et n'interrompent jamais le flow du jeu. Les choix du joueur ont des impacts appréciables sur le déroulé des échanges verbaux. Mention spéciale aux choix de dialogues liés aux compétences ou background du personnage principal qui apportent vraiment une variété bienvenue lors de multiples runs. Enfin le gameplay est vraiment satisfaisant. Les fusillades sont toujours excellentes, avec de nombreuses combinaisons possibles entre les armes, leurs modificateurs et les compétences du personnage. Les capacités de hacking permettent vraiment d'enrichir l'approche tactique: utilisation des caméras de surveillance, explosion à distance d'éléments du décor, suicide des ennemis, affection contagieuse, cécité, surdité... La boîte à outils du joueur est très garnie et il n'appartient qu'à lui de se constituer son petit panier sur mesure d'armes, d' améliorations cybernétiques et de hackings. Différents builds sont ainsi possibles, du ninja adepte des armes blanches au gros bourrin spécialiste des explosifs et du shotgun en passant par le hacker adepte des armes aux munitions téléguidées. Il n'y a pas un build qui n'apporte pas son lot de surprises bienvenues ce qui apporte une rejouabilité bienvenue. Vous l'aurez compris, Cyberpunk 2077 est un jeu fantastique. Ce n'est pas les quelques bugs (jamais bloquants) ou les plantages (évitez le fast travel) persistant encore aujourd'hui qui vont vous empêcher d'apprécier ce qui est aujourd'hui à mes yeux l'un des plus grands monuments du jeu vidéo AAA moderne.

"The Greatest Comeback in Gaming History" It is 2026, and I can finally say that Cyberpunk 2077 is the game we were promised back in 2020—and then some. If you were holding off because of the launch drama, the "Redemption Arc" is officially complete. This is now a mandatory experience for anyone who loves RPGs or immersive sims. Night City & Atmosphere The city itself is the main character. It is the most dense, visually stunning, and atmospheric open world ever built. Now that the technical issues are ironed out and PS5 Pro/high-end PC support has peaked, walking through the neon-soaked streets of Japantown or the lawless slums of Dogtown is breathtaking. It finally feels "alive." Build Variety & Combat (The RPG Core) The 2.0 and 2.1 overhauls changed everything. Combat isn't just about shooting; it's about Synergy: The Cyberdeck/Netrunner Build: You can clear entire rooms without firing a shot by jumping from camera to camera, uploading quickhacks. The "Sandevistan" Ninja: Using slow-mo tech to deflect bullets with a katana feels incredible. The Synergy: Just like a good TD game, you can mix and match. Combine poison-tipped knives with hacks that spread on death, or use high-explosive arms with perks that make you immune to your own blasts. The skill trees are finally deep enough to reward creative playstyles. Phantom Liberty & Story The Phantom Liberty expansion is the gold standard for DLC. It adds a spy-thriller vibe with Idris Elba that is arguably better than the main quest. The writing is mature, the choices actually feel heavy, and the emotional payoff is brutal in the best way possible. Performance Note Unlike the early days, the game is now remarkably stable. It's no longer a "resource hog" for no reason; the optimization is top-tier. Even on mid-range hardware, you can get a smooth, beautiful experience. Pros: Impeccable Storytelling: Top-tier voice acting and cinematic direction. True Build Freedom: Every perk feels like it adds a new way to play. Visual Masterpiece: Still the benchmark for "Next Gen" graphics in 2026. Cons: Initial Grind: The first few hours have a lot of dialogue and setup (though the payoff is worth it). Driving: While improved, the vehicle physics can still feel a bit "floaty" compared to dedicated racing games. Final Verdict Night City eventually wins, but the journey to the top is the best 100+ hours you can spend in a digital world. Don't skip this one.

I finally put real time into Cyberpunk 2077, and honestly—it’s a completely different game compared to launch. The biggest thing that stands out is how immersive Night City feels. The world is packed with detail, and just driving or walking around makes it feel alive. Between the lighting, sound design, and overall atmosphere, it’s one of the best-looking open-world games out right now. Gameplay-wise, there’s a ton of freedom. You can go full gunner, stealth, hacking, or mix everything together. The combat feels smooth now, and the skill trees actually let you build your character how you want. Gunplay has weight to it, and cyberware upgrades make a big difference. Story is where the game really shines. The main story pulls you in, and the side missions aren’t just filler—they’re actually worth doing. Some of them hit just as hard as the main storyline. Performance has improved a lot too. It’s way more stable now, and most of the bugs that killed the game at launch are gone. It finally feels like the game that was originally promised. That said, it’s not perfect. NPCs can still feel a little lifeless at times, and some systems don’t go as deep as you’d expect for a game this big. But overall, those issues don’t ruin the experience. Final Verdict: Cyberpunk 2077 went from a disaster at launch to one of the best RPGs you can play right now. If you skipped it before, it’s absolutely worth picking up. Rating: 8.5/10

I honestly don't think I can recommend this, at least not to players that have the same mindset that I do when it comes to playing a game that you invest this much time into only to be blue balled with the ending. It felt like your entire journey as V was cheapened into some pre-determined outcome and you were just along for the ride. I felt like I didn't really have a satisfying outcome with The Sun. It didn't make any sense. Didn't give you any closure. Everything went to hell and back and left you feeling just hollow and numb to it all. And then the build up (if you can even call it that) was so flat and ill prepared that it just made the ending make no sense at all. maybe it was just that ending, but I clocked that from the moment you accept the Hanako Embers quest until you can get through all the "ending extras"? You're at just under 2 hours of actual time between points. I'm not wanting to spend 2 hours in the hopes that I 'get a better ending, because this one sucked royally'. That's not how I really operate. So if you're like me and you're hoping for "yeah. Let's go have a satisfying ending"? You don't have high chances of that happening, sadly. Prepare yourself for it, because the game will let you down if you at least end up with The Sun for an ending. I enjoyed going through everything and I would also recommend to finish up everything in Phantom Liberty before going to the Embers quest: because you "can't go back afterwards", you can just simply "repeat and try again". I won't go into the game since so many reviews have already been written and there's not much I can add that hasn't already been said. I have played this around 1500 hours on PS5, so instead I just want to compare on how this runs on my Macbook Pro laptop. Some specs: 16" MacBook Pro November 2024 CPU: Apple M4 Pro (14 CPU cores, 20 GPU cores) Memory: 48GB unified memory (combined RAM and VRAM) Disk: 512GB Apple SSD Disk space used: 89.9 GB Resolution: 1728x1080 fullscreen Controller: PS5 DualSense I'm running this frame locked at 60 fps, high graphics settings, ray tracing off. I have my Steam library on a very fast Samsung external SSD (USB 3.2, 10 Gb/s) because Apple charges ridiculous prices for more disk space, so I'm not sure if this helps or hurts. So how does it run and how does it compare to the PS5? I run it frame locked at 60 fps because I don't see the need to run any higher and it's rock solid at that rate. If I unlock the frame rate, the benchmark gives me 71 fps average, so not much difference. Ray tracing doesn't seem to add much to the graphics, but that could be because my eyes are shot. Turning ray tracing on sends the frame rate in the benchmark all over the place from a high of 112 to a low of 41 with a 61 fps average. Compared to my experience with the game on PS5, the game loads slightly faster and the draw distance is much better. Pop-in was very noticeable on PS5 and though it's not completely gone, it's much better. The game is also very stable on MacOS. I think I've had maybe 4 or 5 crashes over 300 hours, but a couple of those were probably caused when the SSD intermittently disconnected. As for thermals, let me put it this way: I haven't burned my thighs. The laptop gets warm, but never uncomfortably hot and fan noise is barely noticeable. I normally run off of the AC adapter, but sometimes the MagSafe connector falls off and I don't notice. Unplugged, it'll be about 1-2 hours before I see a battery low warning or the frame rate goes to hell. So if you have a Mac and wonder whether it can play this? Well, I can't say how well it runs on lower end Macs, but it helps to have one of the higher-end CPU's and lots of RAM. If you short on SSD, get a fast external and problem solved.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a very good game with a lot of personality and an incredible atmosphere. Night City is genuinely one of the most impressive open worlds ever made, both visually and artistically. Even on older hardware, the game runs surprisingly well after all the updates and optimization work. The story is strong, the main characters are well written, and the game allows for decent roleplay and replayability similar to The Witcher 3, your V can feel quite personal depending on your choices and attitude. Gameplay-wise, the game has great potential, although some systems can feel clunky and overcomplicated, especially progression and stats management. Boss fights are probably one of the weakest parts of the game: several of them feel poorly balanced or frustrating rather than genuinely challenging. The difficulty balancing also has a Skyrim-like problem. If you start on a high difficulty, the early game can feel unnecessarily punishing, but if you stay on Normal later on, your character eventually becomes overpowered and destroys almost everything too easily. One thing that deserves more praise is the driving. After the patches, driving in Cyberpunk became genuinely enjoyable, and honestly, some vehicles feel better to control than in certain games that are entirely focused on driving mechanics. Overall, despite some frustrating design choices, Cyberpunk 2077 became a beautiful, memorable, and technically impressive RPG that is absolutely worth playing.

One of the best games ever made, for a lot of reasons. 1. The Story - Masterfully done, never a dull moment when it comes to the plot of this game. The twists and turns will have you hooked and desperate to play that next story mission. 2. The World - I believe this game accurately depicts a version of Mike Pondsmith's Cyberpunk. While a few small details are perhaps missing, cyberpunk fans will love this game. - THERE IS SO MUCH DETAIL. Everytime you play this game again you find something new, and it really shows just how much work the devs put in when building the world. - You never run out of stuff to do. Even when you complete all the side quests and side content for this game, you can still find things tucked away in the nooks and crannies for you to explore. 3. The Combat - THRE IS INFINITE BUILD POTENTIAL IN THIS GAME. Whether you min max. or play a generalist, pretty much any build you can think of will be viable, and it always makes me want to go back and start over completely to try something new. You wanna play a tank that absorbs bullets and smashes gonks? You can do that. You wanna play a stealthy hacker that kills majority of enemies before combat even starts? You can do that. You want to be a total badass with a pistol and crazy movement? You can do that. You want to be a tank, hacker, and total badass? You. Can. Do. That. - The actual combat and gunplay in this game is soooooo unique. There's so many differentt ways to play. You can utilize cover and hit and run tactics with a stealthy build. You can bring a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ SWORD to a gunfight and utilzie crazy movement mechanics and hack away at gonks. You can do none of that, stare at people, and fry their brains before they can even unholster their weapon. Wanna be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ cyber ninja with swords, throwing knives, and flys from enemy to enemy? DO IT. You wanna casually walk down enemies with a shotgun and (litterally) rip and tear through enemies like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ doom guy?? DO IT. - All in all, never a dull moment in this game when it comes to shooting people, or cutting them open... 4. The Progression System - As stated before, this game has INFINTE BUILD POTENTIAL, and my favorite progression system of all time. Leveling up in this game feels sooooooooo goooood. A single perk can change the entire way you play, and once you start getting a lot of perks, you can start killing a lot of gonks, with the master level perks turning you into a total cyberpunk. - The attribute system is perfect. Opening certain areas or doing certian things in dialogue sometimes requires a certain amount of attribute points, litterally affecting your personality in game, which is CRAZY. 5. The Side Content - All of the gigs are unique and are well put together. All of them have some story element that is interesting and sometimes funny, and a lot of times ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up, which is the cyberpunk way. I never feel bored when doing the side quests, ESPECIALLY in the Phantom Liberty Expansion, where everything is turned up to the max. This game had a terrible launch, and it's a realy shame, because this game could've had the potential to surpass super big games like GTA. This game has improved so, so so much. I would reccomend the game to everyone, worth every single dollar 10 times over.

[i] “Let us go then, you and I, When the evening is spread out against the sky…” [/i] CDPR managed to create a world that’s perhaps one of, if not the most immersive world I’ve ever experienced in video games. Night City genuinely feels lived-in, and it’s full of places to explore, characters to meet, and things to do. The story narrative is gripping and hits on a unique, personal level. Your relationship with V and how you manage to endure and survive with them is a dramatic projection of our lives and how we find ourselves in situations that force us to question our own identities and what we stand for. That along with the more dark, mature themes, such as corporate colonialism and the fall of society - which I find rarely explored in video games especially with this level of depth. As for gameplay mechanics, you’re in complete control over choosing your playstyle and building your own perk tree - RPG textbook. There’s a wide variety of weapons, cyberware, quickhacks, clothing items and even vehicles that will fit your style and help you progress through the game. Though, some people are still claiming it’s clunky and unplayable, even after all these fixes. I’d absolutely suggest not listening to them. In fact, don’t go out with them. Might as well consider cutting ties with them. Sure, a game with this sheer magnitude and scope is prone to have a few flaws or even a bumpy launch, but that doesn’t take away from the overall experience it has to offer. Bottom line is, there’s something for everyone in Cyberpunk 2077. It will take you down a path full of wonders. You’ll find yourself in a strange place faced with questions. [i] Where do we go now? [/i] is a reflection in your rear-view mirror and the answer lies in the next stop. The best thing I can tell you is to experience it yourself and become fully immersed in its world. Even after beating it a couple dozen times and unlocking that sweet 100%, I'm still cruising around the city blasting [b] Samurai [/b] over the radio and finding things I’ve never seen before. [i] NEVER FADE AWAY [/i]

Absolute Cinema! Cyberpunk 2077 is a neon drenched body in a Capitalistic Dystopian world. The way V (one of the best written protagonist) tries to be a legend in a city that only cares about blood, money and sex is nothing sort of an epic in itself. And While the RPG gameplay at it's core gives you everything you need to enjoy this colored world. The actual soul of the game resides in the characters. From Johnny Silverhand to minor tells and encounter, all to make this world more lived in. It is a beautiful game with a beautiful DLC where every choice has a consequence but not in "Detroit become human" way but more like what you, as a player, feel way. But it is not perfect, The most weakest point of the game itself is Romance section. While om witcher 3, even with minor scenes, Yen and Triss had an impactful presence. Even Shani was indirectly a great character. Here we have four choices, best being Judy and Panam. Now they are complex characters that you feel like, you wish to know about, Yet their questlines are small, interactions are quick and as soon as their stories completes. The rest of the game, they became a hollow shell of their previous self. And then Game pushes you to meet with them every day, Yet they act like NPCs left there with few commands to follow. So I wish in the next game they work on all the characters more where you can have few but more impactful interactions with them. So at the end, It is a triumph of storytelling, A magnificent world of bad endings and intimate but cynical soul. As one of the greatest game of these times, I highly recommend it.

First time playing Cyberpunk? Buy it, install it, and prepare to go on a trip. This game blends stealth, technical, and even guns blazing gameplay incredibly well. I ran around pinging "Short Circuit" on everyone on Normal Difficulty, but the game REALLY got fleshed out when I went on the harder difficulties. Still, I recommend "Normal" if it's your first time as a merc in Night City. Go ham. Returning to Cyberpunk? Reinstall it, and play it on "Hard" or "VERY HARD". Mods optional but recommended. Like your other "build" games like Fallout, the higher the difficulty the more important it is to spec into a build. It makes progression feel significantly better as your cyberware really does build up, and the game WILL kick your butt until you reach that stage. Become a Netrunner that kills before anyone else sees you, or a Desperado from Metal Gear Rising with some heavy & sharp Mantis Blades. For example, I set out for a "Gorilla Arms" build and at first I had to draw out Cyberpsychos from their den so I could run them over with my car. I went from just grabbing whatever gun could make me that money I needed for those sweet new implants to going full Donkey Kong on some mad fools, throwing their comrades around like barrels off a crimson girder. Either way, be ready to hit the big leagues, choom. And be sure to pay back Victor.

PERSONALLY however I found this game hits a point where many elements I prize in a game: discovery, leveling up, upgrading, enemies hit a plateau, somewhere about 50% through the game. You start to see a limit to the guns/builds, a repetition in the enemy engagements, a been there done that to the quests, so on and so forth. I come from traditional Borderlands/Fallout/Skyrim esque open world plays where it felt like there were no matter how many times or long you've played, the game can find a way to surprise you. Not CP2077. I also found the emotional hook of the game quite shallow. I wasn't particularly invested in any characters' plight, least of all my own. The romancable characters were okay, rather one-note, and with limited interactions so if you wanted the immersion of V leaning on them for relief or escapism, you don't very far. By the final 90% of the game I found myself quick-tabbing through all the dialogue of the game in general. As far as actual game function goes, seems as of 2026 the majority of the bugs are gone. Ironically in the first 5 minutes of cinematic some chars were T-posing, but other than that, everything seemed to work the way it was supposed to. Only 2-3 times over 80+ hours of play did I have to reload a game since an NPC wasn't moving to the next checkpoint. I'm glad I played it through to see what all the hubaloo was about. Would not replay and give me a year or two and I probably won't remember much about it.

[h1]One of the best stories I've ever lived through[/h1] For once, no decision felt 100% right. The narrative speaks to you personally and it reflects your own ambitions and ideals as a person. Felt good finally seeing the game polished enought to enjoy it properly, even though there are minor flaws, the gameplay is amazing and worthy of an RPG, no combat felt dull independently of the build choice. The worldbuilding is beyond belief, few games made me feel that immersed. Hard to have a story-driven singleplayer game to keep me actively obsessed for 300+ hours. SPOILERS AHEAD (my takes) [spoiler] It was extremly interesting having my own take/perspective of the situation being respected the entire time. I felt like a man living with borrowed time (from Jackie) and trying to make the most of it. The actualization of late stage capitalism was amazing to witness as well, I just can't express how much I liked the parallel stories and how they turned out in different runs. My last one as Male Corpo V was the one that satisfied me the most. Accepting that there are things we cannot change and trying to make the best of it was an interesting experience. Having Judy not suffer the Clouds massacre and leaving (becoming actually happy in the end), even if it meant leaving it all to the Tyger Claws. Having to kill Reed (loyal soldier, would've died like that sooner or later) to give a second chance to Songbird even after her betrail (I couldn't help but to feel sorry for her, an animal trying to survive, just like us). Alena having her "spy retirement" to Monte Carlo (nice post card). Giving Johnny his revival of his old days of glory (Samurai perfomance, Rogue romance), becoming friends with the very own thing that is killing you. Panam romance (the Jackie toast on the campfire was what made me change to Male V and replay the whole game just to get with her). The small gig stories and side missions made the game feel so alive and complete. Narratively, The Star ending was my favourite. In life, we struggle to find a sense of belonging, personally, I've found it in people I love and choose as family. Conections make it all worth it, independently of where you are. Maybe there are happy endings in Night City.[/spoiler]

Growing up I always wanted to play an open-world game that felt convincing enough, that I could really get into character. For me, Cyberpunk 2077 is the first time I truly experienced that. I know not everyone loves how combat feels, but to me, the story richness and atmosphere is the strength of the game. I enjoy driving to my destinations, getting distracted by things and listening to the radio; I enjoy the slow passage of time and pretty to-scale map distances -- they make the world and my time playing feel "full". I'm not an FPS gamer, and I struggle with shooting games but to me, combat feels manageable at the Hard difficulty, and there are many ways to approach each scenario you may land yourself in, which really helps me not feel railroaded at any given point, and contributes to the game as a roleplaying experience. If this type of reasoning makes sense to you, get the game. You'll probably enjoy it as much as I did.

This is (currently) my favourite game of all time,possibly even favourite piece of media. I had the oppurtunity to play it around when it released, but i chose not to get it after hearing all the bad reviews about it. After watching edgerunners (twice), i decided id try the game, not expecting the best experience ever since i'd heard some still recent reports of the game being buggy, but still try it. I was pretty underwhelmed with the starting missions, and thought that i felt very underpowered at the start, but after doing more missions and getting to the heist, it felt like i was getting stronger. I LOVE that, it adds an actual sense of progression and not just the same "oh you get stronger items throughout the main story and eventually become some unkillable overpowered beast thats so overpowered it makes the game not fun " ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that most other games use. It's not just the items you have getting stronger, its your character, and you as the player understanding the combat more. I also cant tell you how much i love the fact you dont even have to do the main missions to get stronger. You can do any missions rather than just the story ones. This game also has one of the best stories ive experienced. I genuinely felt connected to all the characters in the game as if i'd known them personally for years. I think jackies death might've been the first time i've genuinely cried of sadness at a game. Even for a character we knew for such a little amount of time compared to other characters, he still felt like he had so much story to him, going from someone who held us gunpoint in a stolen car, to our best friend in a matter of days. It wasn't just jackie either, Evelyn's death was so unexpected that i was actually sitting there speechless like i'd been informed someone i knew had died. Even characters that i didnt really like still felt like they had so much depth in them. Characters like kirk, who i met at the start and thought was this ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of a guy, also had some good sides. And even his death felt strong. Even saul, who i barely spoke to, but heard from panam that he was a bit of a ♥♥♥♥, His death still felt strong. what im trying to get at here, is that i think the characters are so well written and made that they felt like real people. I think the best example of the characters feeling like real people is definitely Johnny Silverhand. He went from this douchebag who didnt give a ♥♥♥♥ about V, and would actively try to kill them, to being casual with them, to one of the most important people in V's life. Even as a engram, it felt like he was a real person there with us. The whole story arc where johnny was trying to fix broken ties with his old friends was such a good detail. I also love how johnny tells the story of his arasaka raid like it was this great attack that went so well but was eventually ended by adam smasher, and how everyone knew of johnny as a legend, but in reality, it didnt go as well as he said, and smasher barely even acknowledges johnny in the ending. It really shows how no matter what happens, no one will truly be remembered forever in night city. "Goodbye V, Never stop fightin'"

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best games ever made. The story is truly unique and you really feel for the characters. The voice actors did a fantastic job especially male V. While some prefer the female performance, I found the male voice to be incredibly intimidating and impactful. The gameplay is top-notch. You can play differently every single run, and even repeating a build never feels boring. However, even with the freedom of the skill tree, some dialogue options or outcomes are blocked by the level cap. Even with mods, you can’t max out everything, which is one of the game's few downsides. Night City feels unique. Even without the random world events found in games like Red Dead Redemption 2, the side gigs provide plenty of content, offering at least 40 hours of playtime on a first run. The endings are also stellar; each one is distinct and worth experiencing. The romance options feel genuine because they require significant investment unlike The Witcher 3, where some encounters feel more random. Furthermore, the Phantom Liberty DLC improves on the base game's missions significantly. It’s clear CDPR wanted to create the best expansion possible. If you have a decent rig, this game is absolutely worth buying. It remains one of the best-looking titles on the market and a staple for hardware benchmarks. 10/10

So far I've been really enjoying this game. [h3] Story and setting [/h3] I've been positively surprised by the quality of the story and setting. I thought it might just feel like a mindless Nvidia GPU ad, but I feel like it has heart. I love the inspiration it's taking and showing from works such as those of William Gibson, Ghost in the Shell, Akira, the Matrix and Mad Max. As a fan of the cyberpunk genre this game really doesn't disappoint. You see familiar things everywhere and it really makes my heart sing. There are easter eggs related to other franchises, [spoiler] such as Portal [/spoiler], as well. You have futuristic vehicles, computer-controlled robot spiders, people entering "the net" or even being digitized. Futuristic weapons, AI and robot people. Japanese tradition mixed with future tech. Everything you'd expect from a cyberpunk epic. It's very nice. I love Night City, it feels like a place set in the future. It's a sprawling city, where technology is always present. You see flying vehicles glide across the sky and holographic ads everywhere. The mega corporations dominate the scene with their huge buildings, not to mention how they dominate politically. So you feel the tension and dynamics between the crime-ridden streets, the police department, military, street gangs and corporate affiliates. I love the characters. You have the super sweet Jackie Welles who invades your heart and all the love you see within his family. You meet street criminals, desert nomads, corporate people, netrunners, etc. All with their own personalities and desires. So I'd say the story feels immersive. I love how people make you a part of their lives, asking for help when they need it, inviting you to funerals when someone died, asking to talk when they're feeling down. It's fun to see what people have going on and to be a part of it. You're also often given dialogue options and it does give you a sense of agency although it's unclear to me how big of a difference the choices make. [h3] Graphics and performance [/h3] I run the game with the RT medium setting at 1440p with FSR 2 set to Quality. But with RT shadows turned off. FPS vary depending on scene, most of the time laying around 50-60 fps. Sometimes it's over 60 too. While riding a vehicle it's typically 40-50 fps. I'm sad that I can't have RT reflections on, I feel like it would make a big difference visually, but it pulls my fps down to the 30s. :'( Maybe some day I'll upgrade my gpu and experience that. Personally I'm pleased with the performance, but I'm not very sensitive to fps. I can be really bothered by poor 1% frames but I feel like in this game the framerate is pretty steady at all times. Even if it drops a bit lower, at least it's steady instead of having sudden drops or jitter or anything like that. Graphically it looks great too. Sometimes I feel the uncanny valley of something looking photo-realistic, but typically you can tell it's a game. The lighting looks really good in my opinion. You can also tell the artists went all out putting lights and volumetric fog everywhere to add to the ambiance. I think it works. Bars and clubs feel atmospheric in their own futuristic way. [h3] Sound design and music [/h3] Speaking of atmosphere, the sound design is phenomenal. Right as the game is loading you hear these futuristic, digital-sounding noises that really set the tone. Then in the main menu you get a similarly futuristic atmospheric track and you already feel like you're being transported to another time, where people have robotic enhancements and have brain computer interfaces that they use to connect to the internet. Or at least I feel that way. The sonic atmosphere on the streets of night city feel like you're really in a futuristic town. You hear the people and cars, music from nearby restaurants, ads constantly blaring and the sound of flying cars buzzing somewhere above you. I love the music in the game. It's super nice to ride to the next mission while watching the scenery and listening to the radio in your car or bike. I also love the music during fights, it's high-adrenaline, pumping future music that really gets your heart pumping. [h3] Gameplay and mechanics [/h3] For me this game had a bit of a learning curve. It has you go through a bit of a tutorial in the beginning and to be honest the gameplay felt pretty intimidating for me. I did not understand how to be stealthy and get around or neutralize targets without being seen. So for quite a while I'd just get spotted, even in stealth missions, and end up in a big firefight. For quite a while I'd put off playing this because I felt intimidated and like I wasn't good enough. The game doesn't hold your hand just as much as some other games do. There can be more than one approach to finishing your objective and the game doesn't fail you for being spotted. But over time I started to figure it out. It often does guide you through its design, even though I didn't notice it at first. Now I'm glad it doesn't hold your hand and gives you freedom to deal with things how you want. I also had to swallow my pride and accept using the quicksave and -load function. It's just a lot more fun that way. It frickin sucks to be spotted and blast your way through a stealth mission and feel like you messed up. Sometimes that happens because I expected something to work differently than it does in the game. For example in one mission you're looking for stached money in a casino. Even going near the door leading to the second floor suddenly triggers an all out gunfight from the guards. How was I supposed to know that would happen? But when you do manage to sneak around unnoticed and take care of guards silently, it's very satisfying. It's also actually not too difficult which feels nice. Sometimes MGS felt too difficult for me personally, this feels more like something I can handle. I also felt intimidated by the abundance of menus. You have skills and perks, equipment you can wear, crafting, enhancements and consumables. It can feel overwhelming. But it's fun to learn new perks and see how it gives you new abilities to use when sneaking and fighting. Anyway, I haven't finished the story yet and I don't know how far along I am. But so far I've been thoroughly enjoying it and am playing a bit every day. I love the variety in the missions you get and how you can at least seemingly decide how to relate to missions and different people. Too bad the story will end at some point, but I am looking forward to how it all ends. Wonder if it has multiple endings... Guess we'll see. :)

Cyberpunk 2077 is a game that borders on greatness but ultimately fails to achieve it. Nevertheless, I truly believe that everyone should experience this game at least once in their life. A truly unique experience that only CD Project Red could have produced [Performance and Optimization] In its initial release, Cyberpunk was lambasted for its poor performance and optimization, as well as being riddled with bugs. In the current year however, Cyberpunk 2077 is a feast for the eyes and runs phenomenally. Additionally, in my current 47 hours of gameplay, I have only observed a single bug. This complete turnaround speaks to the dedication of CD Project Red towards their fanbase and they should be commended for taking the criticism and actively working to make the game better. [Story and Environment] Cyberpunk is often touted as an action role-playing game set in an expansive open world. While this can serve as an apt description for the game, in practice. this description falls apart. The main story and many of the side jobs attached to primary characters for the most part, are extremely well done, with amazing writing, voice acting and animations that bring everything together in a neat package. Problems with the story arise whereby the player is presented with a multitude of choices and methods to complete given missions. However, there are no consequences for any player actions and to this extent, your choices ultimately don't matter. Night city is an expansive, visual spectacle but there is practically nothing to do in the city. If you go into this game expecting to have random NPC missions, dialogue and activities such as in Fallout or Elder Scrolls you would be greatly disappointed. NPCs on the streets are basically non-interactable with the majority having only single lines of dialogue. Missions are given via phone call, so all the game's important characters will just contact you to do missions as long as you attain the relevant level and street cred. As such, outside of finding collectibles and completing missions for steam achievements, there is ZERO incentive to explore Night City. [Gameplay and Systems] Gameplay is extremely fun with a variety of upgrades, weapons and vehicles that all feel great to use and experiment with. The game's systems are a bit complex at the start, but as you continue through the story and the open world, they are integrated seamlessly. The game's cyberware upgrades in the beginning are substantial but as you go further up the tree, they become mostly minor stat upgrades with no substantial effect on gameplay.

Cyberpunk changed the way I think about games. Firstly, the storytelling is astounding; you have the power to decide dialogues (I would like to highlight this). Each decision you make is based on your behavior, such as story path (Nomad, Street Kid, Corpo) and attributes (Body, Reflexes, Cool, Intelligence, Technical Ability, and Relic). Despite the freedom, there is no massive impact on the narrative; however, you can know more about the characters or quests just by asking. Each life path has a different beginning and choices of dialogue. It means that a "Street Kid" could be more of a hustler due to knowledge of local gangs, fixers, and slang. A "Nomad" is the outsider; you are a traveler who lives in the Badlands with your clan, the Bakkers or Aldecaldos. In addition, you are an expert in repairing machinery, fixing cars, and securing resources—kind of a smuggler. As a "Corpo," you are in charge of a huge company that controls the majority of society's sectors. Consequently, your choices result in tiny gifts or different quest lines. Furthermore, Night City has a bunch of things to do, such as gigs, police scanners, side quests, secrets, car races, and so on. Likewise, the city is gorgeous; each corner is extremely well-designed. Each neighborhood is well-developed, from the richest to the poorest, and their NPCs' outfits too. In addition, we notice gang fights, car pursuits, and spots dominated by them. It's always a pleasure riding to the North, South, or Badlands to appreciate the colors, either during the day or night, within opposing seasons. Nevertheless, facing gang spots provides you with substantial resource gains to spend on whatever you want—for instance, clothes, weapons, cars, or apartments. Moreover, the core attributes are split into Body (fortitude), Reflex (agility/dash), Intelligence (hacking), Technical (explosives), and Cool (stealth). You are in charge of your playstyle. In summary, CD Projekt Red built a game with originality and identity. A quick tip: if you want to get 100% achievements, the time will probably be around 100h+.

To be honest the only thing I have against the game itself is the performance of the game on common hardware at its time of release. After years of patches the game has been purged of most of the bugs but the performance was never really brought to the level that makes it truly accessible. In regards to the gameplay and the story, well it works I guess but the years of marketing presented a product that has turned out to be less of an RPG and more of a Far Cry style open world shooter. In demos we were presented with a story that would be defined by non linear progression and player autonomy that would rival and ultimately supersede previous RPGs such as Fallout: New Vegas. Instead what we ended up with was an on rails system more like Fallout: 3, where your given illusions of freedom that ultimately course correct you back to the destined path. One of the main themes of the game is the idea of fate, a lack of control over the world, and the daunting seemingly unstoppable institutions and mechanisms that your powerless to do anything against but instead of the main story addressing those themes in any meaningful way the story just focusses on what I can only describe as Vs "shenanigans", a series of quests that might as well be side quest's as they all turn out to be inconsequential and barely related to the main story. The DLC is the shining example of this where for some reason V is asked to save the president of the United States by infiltrating a city controlled by a paramilitary organization. Upon learning that you HAVE to save the president upon starting the questline for some arbitrary reason or else she kills you I decided the best and most reasonable course of action was to just run away from this strange call for help from a person I've never heard of and go back to doing laundry for Takemura or something like that. This is really the only type of dilemma you see in this games quests, either you do something or you don't and everyone dies, or literally nothing happens and the story continues like nothing happened. The president dying literally has no impact on the games ending or world as with most other major quests in this game, not because they wouldn't have an impact to some degree but because CD project red just it just too lazy to present those consequences in subtle or meaningful ways, just like Bethesda I guess. Anyways besides that Refused did a good job portraying Samurai, Keanu Reeves did a great job voice acting Johnny Silver hand, and if your looking for a Far Cry style shooter then here you go. Buy on sale, don't buy the DLC, dont watch Edgerunners, pirate before you buy it if your concerned about performance.

Cyberpunk 2077 feels like a true masterpiece. Every action you take and every ending you reach never gives V a truly happy conclusion. No matter what you choose, there’s always a sacrifice—power, soul, or even the people around you. That’s what makes the experience so impactful. CD Projekt Red created a world where I didn’t just play the story—I felt it and got completely immersed in it. Every decision carries weight, and every ending stays with you. Truly a masterpiece.

I went into this not really knowing what to expect, but by the end I can say I’d recommend it, especially if you’re into near-future sci-fi with light RPG elements. What stuck with me most wasn’t the combat or even the world at first. It was the characters, and how much of them is only revealed through the endings. There isn’t a clean, perfect resolution waiting for you. Every ending I reached left me feeling at least a little conflicted, and that feels intentional. The game leans into themes of sacrifice and justice, even more so in the DLC, and the different conclusions do a great job of reframing what you thought you knew about people. Seeing those different sides is where a lot of the replayability comes from. The characters themselves have more depth than they initially let on. Motivations aren’t spelled out, and your understanding of people shifts the more time you spend with them. That was especially true for some of the DLC characters. I found my opinions changing as I saw more of their perspective. Johnny Silverhand is probably the best example of this. He starts off feeling one-dimensional, almost like a stereotype, but that impression doesn’t hold. The more you learn about his past, and especially if you take the time to engage with optional conversations, you start to see the regrets and reasoning behind who he is. He became a much more empathetic character than I expected. The world itself feels immersive, and a big part of that comes from those hidden motivations. It feels like people have their own agendas, whether you fully understand them or not. Gameplay-wise, I liked how flexible things felt. You can approach situations however you want, whether that’s stealth, direct combat, or using quickhacks alongside either. I started off playing it safe, sneaking around with a silenced pistol and relying on quickhacks. Over time, I shifted into a more aggressive style, running in with mantis blades. That change didn’t just feel mechanical. It felt like a natural progression for my character. Going from someone unknown to someone with a reputation, maybe even infamous, fit well with the world. If I had to point out a downside, driving can feel inconsistent. I had trouble judging corners at times, though that might just be on me. Overall, I’d recommend it. It’s not perfect, but if you enjoy strong character writing and morally complex choices, there’s a lot here to appreciate. Achievements achieved at time of review: 57/57

Секс, кибер-люди и рок-н-ролл. Игра очень сильная в плане сюжета и затянула с головой на несколько дней. Было прикольно и интересно проходить её на разные концовки. В первый раз я только изучал этот мир, поэтому пришел к финалу за корпоратов. Думал, что на этом всё, но потом решил пойти на другую концовку и уничтожить «Арасаку». Во время второго прохождения стало еще веселее: игра ощущалась гораздо динамичнее, я начал активно выполнять другие миссии и закрыл ветки Панам, Джуди и Джонни. При повторном прохождении было сложнее выбирать варианты ответов в диалогах, так как понимание, что они реально влияют на отношение персонажей к тебе. Единственный раз, когда я пошел наперекор это квест с гонками от Клэр. Я решил поехать к финишу вместо того, чтобы убивать типочка который убил ее "мужа". Честно говоря, изначально, увидев флаг на её машине, вообще не особо хотел с ней ездить. После моего выбора она перестала со мной общаться, но мне было на это пофиг. По геймплею: тут всё решают пушки и импланты (двойной прыжок и киберимплант на замедление времени это мастхэв). Евродоллары фармятся элементарно — просто собираешь оружие и продаешь в почтоматах. Ближе к концу, когда ты уже сильно прокачан, деньги копятся сами собой, потому что с врагов падает куча легендарок, которые стоят очень дорого. В итоге я вышел на концовку с Панам, и оно того стоило. Единственное, чего хотелось бы чтобы Сол и другие ребята из Альдекальдо остались живы, а то к финалу мы приходим всего вчетвером. После этого мы остаемся без Джонни и покидаем Найт-Сити. Очень понравились видеосообщения в титрах: Джуди, Виктор, Мама Уэллс, Мисти и Митч искренне рады тому, что ты выбрался из этого города. Моя оценка — 9/10. Есть легкое ощущение, что игре всё же чего-то немного не хватает, но эмоции она дарит отличные. И возможно в будущем пройду на остальные концовки и приобрету DLC.

In 2026, this is still one of the best looking games on the market. With massive strides post-release on UI updates, bug fixes, physics engines, and optimization, this should be the gold standard for a modern-day RPG. It addresses very adult themes through its side missions, makes you question the impacts of corporate greed, and delivers powerful political messages in a way that feels grounded without hitting you over the head with it. CDPR delivers an RPG experience with their best combat system to date, and immersion that rivals Red Dead Redemption 2.

When I went into 2077, I never would have thought I would end up so attached to both its world and characters, especially since I knew a large amount of the story beforehand. The majority of the games characters, especially those in the DLC, left a significant lasting impact on me. For a long while I felt the game wouldn't live up the emotional intensity Edgerunners delivered, but the DLC subverted this completely, as well as certain points in the base game. The performances and writing of so many characters in 2077 completely blew me away, the most notable characters in this regard would be Silverhand, Songbird, and Reed. The general gameplay and side content was always remarkably fun, so much so that even on my second playthrough I felt driven to complete it all again. The game is still moderately buggy, though this never detracted from the game and often made for funny and memorable moments. I would recommend this game without a doubt, as well as its flawless DLC, the experience overall is easily a 10/10.

When installing the game again for maybe my 9th or 10th playthrough, I realised I am long overdue with this review. Have played probably 2-3x the time logged on Steam(didn't always bother to launch Steam when launching the game through modmanager)... This is simply the best story focused RPG of the last decade or more. The story, characters and universe is just superb, and the city is an amazing place to explore. The gameplay is fun and varied, to the point where you can build and roleplay vastly different characters. And speaking of different characters, it is wonderful to replay, as doing things different will open up loads of hidden reactions and changes to things. Every part of the game is interwoven with everything else, so even thousands of hours in, you will still find new details or connections you never realised before. Like often you will realise that seemingly separate events like a bigger side mission, a smaller side mission, one or more open-world events, and various hidden little notes all spread out over the entire map and across hundreds of hours are actually connected through events or characters. There are also a bunch of different endings that you can choose from based on how you want to roleplay your character. Definitely recommend everyone interested in great story-telling give this game a chance.

Many updates later, I have so much to say about this game. Cyberpunk 2077 holds a special place among the games I have played. Every aspect of this game plays towards an experience that is emotion-driven. The environments, the dialogue, the soundtrack, the characters and story immerse you in a hopeless reality, one where you're ruled by corporations and greed, and there isn't a thing you can do about it. But underneath this, this story gets to the heart of what it means to be human in a world of cybernetic implants and mind-killing constructs. Are you truly yourself? Where do you end and someone else begins? Gameplay is overall very fun and engaging. Improvements in the most recent overhauls make it even more so. The refined leveling system is far more expansive than previously, making builds viable and rewarding. If you held understandable doubts due to poor reception upon release, heavy improvements have remedied many initial issues and the game itself feels much more alive and dynamic.

This is hands-down the best game I have ever played. Steam only shows around 100+ hours for me, but that's just part of the story—trust me, I've sunk way more time into it. I played hundreds of hours on GOG (easily 300+ across multiple playthroughs), plus a solid chunk on PS5 as well. Night City has become my second home, and I keep coming back to it even years later. Before diving into the actual review, I want to address the elephant in the room: I was one of those players who jumped in at launch back in 2020. The game had issues—there was even one game-breaking bug that forced me to restart a section—but I could already see the incredible potential buried underneath. Fast-forward to today, and Cyberpunk 2077 has completely redeemed itself. Thanks to years of massive updates (especially the game-changing 2.0 overhaul and beyond), the Phantom Liberty expansion, and ongoing polish, it now delivers on nearly every promise CD Projekt RED made. It's no longer the buggy mess some remember—it's a polished, immersive masterpiece that feels alive in ways few games ever achieve. One of the things that keeps pulling me back is how many favorite moments this game has given me. The storytelling is exceptional across the board. The main campaign is a gripping, emotional rollercoaster about identity, mortality, and survival in a brutal dystopia—your relationship with Johnny Silverhand (brilliantly voiced by Keanu Reeves) alone is one of the most compelling dynamics I've experienced in gaming. The side quests and gigs aren't filler; many of them rival the quality of the main story, with heartbreaking twists, moral dilemmas, and unexpected depth. And then there's Phantom Liberty—the DLC feels like a premium spy-thriller packed into Night City, introducing Dogtown as a brand-new, gritty district full of intrigue, new characters, and high-stakes choices. Every playthrough reveals new layers, and the multiple endings still hit hard. The world and atmosphere are simply unmatched. Night City is a neon-drenched beast—crowded, chaotic, and overflowing with personality. The streets pulse with life: holographic ads screaming for attention, flying cars zooming overhead, street vendors hawking cyberware, and random encounters that make the city feel dangerous and unpredictable. Sure, NPCs don't have hyper-detailed 24-hour routines like in Red Dead Redemption 2, but honestly, I never missed that. Why would I want to tail a random stranger just to watch them grab a coffee or go home? The density of interesting individuals you can interact with more than makes up for it—fixers, mercenaries, netrunners, and everyday citizens all have their own stories if you take the time to listen. Visually, Cyberpunk 2077 still stands at the top of the mountain in 2026. The graphics are breathtaking, especially with Path Tracing enabled (if your hardware can handle it). The way light bounces realistically off wet streets, chrome implants, and rain-slicked surfaces creates an unparalleled sense of immersion. Reflections, shadows, and global illumination look so natural that it often feels like you're watching a high-budget sci-fi movie rather than playing a game. Even without max settings, the art direction, character models, and environmental detail hold up incredibly well. Driving through the city at night with the radio blasting is pure atmosphere porn. The characters—both major and minor—are fantastically written. V feels like your character, but the supporting cast steals the show. Panam, Judy, Kerry, River, Takemura, and so many others feel like real people with their own motivations, flaws, and arcs. You'll want to help them, romance them, or just hang out and talk. The voice acting and facial animations are top-tier, making every conversation feel meaningful. Building relationships (platonic or romantic) adds huge replay value, as different lifepaths and choices lead to wildly different interactions. Gameplay-wise, the experience is pretty much flawless once you embrace what the game is: a deep first-person RPG, not a pure shooter. Yes, the gunplay is satisfying and highly customizable— you can go full netrunner, stealthy blade assassin, tanky shotgun psycho, or anything in between thanks to the excellent skill trees and cyberware system. The 2.0 updates massively improved combat, police AI, vehicle handling, and progression, making builds feel impactful and fun. Exploration rewards curiosity, with hidden gigs, cyberpsycho sightings, and endless loot. That said, if you're expecting something like Call of Duty with RPG elements tacked on, you might need a slight mindset shift— this is a role-playing game first, where your choices, attributes, and playstyle shape everything. In the end, Cyberpunk 2077 isn't perfect (no game is), but its strengths far outweigh any minor nitpicks. The music, sound design, and overall vibe are addictive. I've lost count of how many times I've just driven around aimlessly, taking in the sights and listening to the radio. If you gave the game a chance at launch and bounced off, or if you're new to it in 2026—do yourself a favor and dive in now, ideally with the Ultimate Edition that includes Phantom Liberty. This is the version of Night City we were always promised. Story/Narrative — 10/10 Graphics — 10/10 Gameplay — 9.5/10 Atmosphere — 10/10 Sound Design — 10/10 Overall — 9.9/10 Also, Sasha Grey is a radio host. :D

A very strange beast of a game that will have been received very differently based on exactly when you got around to experiencing it, and to this day still serving as a cautionary tale for why no one should ever pre-order anything with how disastrous the game was on-release after nearly a decade of anticipation, *and* coming off the dramatic success of 'The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt'. The mismanagement was hellish enough behind the scenes for CDPR staff to bounce off the project at multiple points and to go form their own studios - such as Rebel Wolves, working on 'Blood of Dawnwalker' - and the released product so unfinished and janky that it required multiple soft re-launches (ala the 1.6 and 2.0 updates respectively) to bring the game closer to the promised state alluded to in the barrage of incredibly atmospheric and hype-accelerance that was the suberbly-made marketing, trailers that *still* serve to masterfully convey the tone and aesthetic of the ttrpg's setting. The years of messy development and contentious reception behind it, what's here after the additions of the 'Phantom Liberty' DLC and the broad changes of the 2.0 patch have smoothed-over and consolidated systems is a solid, massive, action-RPG (that unfortunately emphasized more 'action' than 'RPG' elements after many updates simplified and overhauled the nature of the weapon, armor, and perk systems) that, if nothing else, nails the atmosphere of its setting and the blood-and-chrome aesthetic of the ttrpg it's based on (and was even dragged into the Edgrunners anime more or less without any change to its visual language or OST). Even on-release, environments of Night City's urban dystopia and the surrounding desert landscapes were hyper-detailed, complicated to navigate, and readily screenshot-able, with an above-and-beyond soundtrack that remains probably the best-made component of the game and an easy resource for use in soundscaping a game of the ttrpg. If you're looking for RPG 'crunch' rather than vibes, the story is unfortunately more or less linear in the same way CDPR's 'The Witcher' games are, and the gameplay won't have much to sell you on mechanically, though there remains distinction and build-variety among the options of gunplay, melee, and netrunning. If you don't mind the concession of moreso 'being along for a ride' rather than something closer to playing a direct adaptation of the Cyberpunk: RED tabletop ruleset, then Cyberpunk 2077 is a masterclass in delivering on the tone and worldbuilding of the property it's based on; this finally 'finished' version showing the promise of what a less-erratically-developed sequel in the portions of the setting 'Phantom Liberty' hints at could look like.

6 years later and the game is still a buggy mess. Had quite a few bugs were corpses would clip through the map and a lot of the time the map just doesn't load properly whilst driving and you will just either have to wait a good 30 seconds for it to load the road you are driving on or you will fall through the map infinitely. Now for the actual game itself, combat is really fast paced. Which is both good and bad. Good because it's not boring but bad because you can be killed before you can even turn around. Some quests and dialogue options just take away any player agency at all. Such as the quest where you let Johnny have control for a bit. It also forces you character to have had only straight relationships which is kinda dumb. You also have a surprising lack of control over what your character looks like. I really expected a much more in depth character customisation. Quite a few times you would get detected or in police trouble using quickhacks when there is absolutely no way they would know where you are or that it was you that hacked it. (e.g. self destruct hacks on cars or remote control on cars) It was quite annoying. At this point I haven't finished the game but the bugs have been getting steadily more common and I'm not even sure I can or will finish it. I really hoped for better after 6 years of this game being out.

Personally, as someone who never knew anything Cyberpunk related until playing this game, it made me invested and hooked into learning more about the overall lore of the world outside of playing. The uniqueness of the entire setting of Cyberpunk dystopia is an enjoyable playground to have in 2077. The amount of power that you have over the way your character (V) is portrayed with a skillset that matches your playstyle is one of the most enjoyable experiences I've had in gaming. Starting off with barely being able to win a fistfight, to quite literally having gorilla arms attached to your character that lets you beat an entire gang hideout with your fists. Or, maybe you're more interested in a stealth profile with sniper rifles and hacking into anyone with cyberware in the game. There are just so many ways that you can enjoy this title from a gameplay perspective and even a graphical standpoint. It's one of the most beautiful games you can play on modern PC's, with probably the best usage of Ray Tracing in any current video game that makes 3000-4000+ series of Nvidia cards reach their actual potential. Photo mode was a welcome addition to capturing some of the best vistas or atmospheres that you can find in the lively Nightcity. Without getting into any spoilers, my only disappointment with the game that never was addressed was the lack of influence your background actually gives your character throughout the game. Sure, you'll be prompted with some dialogue that your background allows you to answer differently or find a way around skillchecks, but in terms of consistent missions or things that allow you to "roleplay" your V to potential simply are non existent. Act One of the game should've been more focused on your actual background and should've been longer overall so players could experience the importance of their background. Despite that flaw, I cannot find many others with the game at this point. You play it and get lost for hours at a time from how much nightcity sucks you in. Everytime you finish a mission or a bounty, you'll tell yourself "just one more" and before you know it, it's midnight. The impressive audio rivals games like GTA V and some modern FPS with quality that goes above and beyond. I would recommend this game to anyone at full price, especially on sale, and find yourself an RPG that lives up to the standard set by games like Skyrim over a decade ago. The post-game support (even adding an expansion) shows the TLC that the devs had for reaching their vision for the game. I'm happy to say they redeemed themselves and Cyberpunk from it's horrendous launch.

The worst part about Cyberpunk 2077, is that at some point it ends. And that you'll never experience another open world RPG like it. This game is genuinely prophetic in its depiction of a futuristic dystopian hellscape of a society. It was depressing to me enough that I genuinely was put off from playing it at first. But at the same time, as a game the bulk of its story is incredibly character focused, and that's really what balances a lot of the dystopian hopelessness. The glimmers of hope that shine throughout this game serve as a reminder that even in the face of the constant dehumanization that is forced upon us; through the staggering amount of narcissism that is embedded into so many foundational levels of our society. It's in our best interest to cut through as much of the noise as possible, and try as best we can to connect with each other. In a system so ruthlessly dehumanizing, solidarity is all we have. One of the most incredible video games I've ever played. Genuinely a work of art; a must play.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a stunning achievement in open-world RPG gaming. Night City is one of the most breathtaking, densely detailed game worlds ever created — every neon-lit alley and towering megabuilding feels alive and purposeful. The story is gripping, emotional, and full of unforgettable characters (Johnny Silverhand is an all-timer). The writing tackles heavy themes with surprising nuance, and the side quests are some of the best in the genre — many rival the main storyline in quality. Combat is slick and versatile, letting you hack, shoot, sneak, or slash your way through encounters however you see fit. The RPG progression is deeply satisfying, and the Phantom Liberty expansion elevates everything even further. If you bounced off it at launch, now is the time to come back. CD Projekt Red transformed this game into the experience it was always meant to be.

A masterpiece. I've played it twice, once a few years ago after it was patched to playability, then just recently. The second time around hit harder, which is difficult in my book, because there are few surprises in a replayed game. It's impact on me is in part due to the state of the U.S. and the world in general. When an impassioned Johnny Silverhand explains his hatred of the corpos and the sytem, that they're paved over farms, and taken the people's clean water to build countless data centers, I felt it like a punch to the gut. How quickly things have changed in the real world to reflect the dark future portrayed in Cyberpunk. My advice: don't look up what choices you should make,; don't spoiler to see which are deemed the 'right ones' by internet strangers you haven't met. You can look those up later. Play organically, making choices that feel right to you as a player. Enjoy the ride. Lean into the pain. I promise you, it's worth it. Fallout 4, Diablo 2, and the Elder Scrolls games have always been my top all-time games. Without a doubt, after my 100-hour, second playthrough, my number one is Cyberpunk 2077.

Of course I enjoyed CP2077, but I almost want to give it a negative rating to emphasize why I think it's merely a "really good" game as opposed to an "incredible" one. The storyline was a highlight (compelling and with choices that mattered), but there is very little mechanically in the game that hasn't been done before: GTA4/5 defined the standard for open worlds decades ago, and any mainline RPG has similar depth for character choices, skill trees, progression etc. So, does CP2077 differentiate with an immersive world that is truly novel? For me, not really. The map is expansive with some incredible artwork, but can feel samey within any given district. The characters, while memorable, are ultimately formulaic. The voice acting was surprisingly lacking in places (male V sounds like he's reading out instructions for a dishwasher). Towards the latter stages of the game, the combat starts to feel mundane due to a lack of enemy diversity. Despite playing with the latest patch (April 2026), the game is still super buggy: floating world items, stuttering animations, glitching quests, CTDs (all of which are perhaps to be expected for a game of this scale, but still no less annoying). I enjoyed my play-through, but don't see a reason to replay any time soon!

Not necessarily a bad game. It tries to include too many features and ends up shallow and bloated. This extends for the contradiction of "open-world ARPG" and a strict narrative structure. Any open-world content is low-quality and purposeless. Writing of the main plot is extremely shallow and leans more into interpersonal drama instead of using the greater elements of the world to push the story along, but this second part is subjective. Most "RPG mechanics" and systems wind up unimpactful due to power creep, and the ability for more unique playstyle is absent (i.e. most tech weapons are handguns, so you are forced into specing into "cool" stats if you are also specing into "technical" stats). Cyberpunk 2077 tries to do too many things and live up to hype and player count, and they then wind up as mid, AAA slop and another ARPG that does not live up to the genre. Not a bad game, some major flaws objectively, and many subjective flaws if you share my preferences. Would have been better as a linear world with more fleshed out narrative (more than interpersonal drama) and more fleshed out systems and mechanics (especially since it is the cyberpunk genre).

Played the game on Hard, Corpo netrunner with Phantom Liberty DLC on patch 2.3. The game was pretty stable for me except when there was smoke or excessive shrubberies then there was noticeable frame drops. Compared to most Action CRPGs it's pretty top tier, your choices in the story matter and the moment to moment action is fun too especially the leg upgrades enhancing movement abilities, I think build diversity is in a fine place for the main story which leads me to my main criticism of the game. The game is simply too big, has too much content, too many missions for it's mechanics to last through your playthrough. I feel like your builds will be done by level 40 and every thing else is just icing on the cake but leads me to feel I have nothing to look forward too after 30 hours unless you skip the side missions, which I feel are where the game shines best, but it leads me to feel the majority of the game is side content. I also feel my 120 hour playthrough was mostly used on transit going from one mission to the next, the DLC is slightly more compact and I enjoyed that level design much more, Frankly I just don't enjoy driving around compared to charge or double jumping. If you look at the map most of it is empty road for driving on, lots of open world games are filled with these negative spaces to pad it out and make the game feel bigger. I recently played the original Deus Ex and I think the level sizes and length of the story match the character progression routes. If CDPR made a Deus Ex game it would be amazing.

The bad: -Personnal but it took a long time to get into. Great game once I did. -Bugs: Not a lot of bugs but got 2 during bosses that made them stuck wich is an imersion killer. -Difficulty: I don't know if it is possible but enemy scaling would but nice even if just a bit. At the end you are way too strong. I know you can change difficulty mid game but still. - Driving a car is so bad. Use the bikes. - the NPCs reaction in the world are not so great. The Good: -The world is really good. If you dont look to closely to NPC it feels alive and very well designed. -The story and the relationships are great. So I'll most certainly boot it up again and play different endings and finish some of the sidequest. I had to edit the review the next day to add this. It is one hell of a good game. Overview: Cyberpunk 2077 is an ambitious open-world RPG set in a futuristic city (Night City). It delivers an incredibly immersive experience with strong storytelling and visuals—but it has also been criticized for technical issues and some underdeveloped gameplay systems. Pros 1. Immersive Open World Night City is widely praised as one of the most detailed and atmospheric game worlds ever created. Dense environments, strong world-building, and tons of side activities make it feel alive. 2. Stunning Graphics Incredible visuals, especially on high-end PCs with ray tracing. Lighting, reflections, and character detail are top-tier. 3. Strong Story & Characters Excellent writing and memorable characters enhance the narrative. Side quests are often as engaging as the main story. 4. Flexible Gameplay & Builds Multiple playstyles (stealth, hacking, combat) give players freedom. Deep RPG systems allow for character customization. 5. Voice Acting & Presentation High-quality voice acting and cinematic storytelling elevate immersion. Cons 1. Bugs & Technical Issues (especially at launch) Frequent glitches, crashes, and performance problems were heavily criticized. While many fixes have been released, reputation damage still lingers. 2. Some Gameplay Systems Feel Incomplete Melee combat and certain mechanics feel underdeveloped or “half-baked.” Balancing issues between different playstyles. 3. Main Story Length The main campaign is shorter than expected for an RPG of this scale. 4. Limited Impact of Choices Dialogue and choices don’t always significantly affect the world or story outcomes. 5. NPC & World Interaction Limitations Some players feel NPCs lack depth or realism compared to the environment. Final Verdict Rating: 9/10 If you want a deep, story-driven RPG with amazing visuals, this is a great pick. If you care most about polished gameplay systems and perfect performance, it may still feel inconsistent in places. Bottom line: Cyberpunk 2077 is a flawed but highly enjoyable game—one that delivers unforgettable moments, even if it doesn’t fully live up to its original hype. Highly replayable.

Cyberpunk 2077 is easily the best game I have ever felt. It is a pure masterpiece that will stick with me forever. The developers clearly poured their entire lives into this and the result is an insane emotional gauntlet. This isn't just a game you play for the action you play it for a story so intense that you’ll find yourself staring at the screen for several minutes paralyzed trying to decide what to do next because ngl the choices are really hard to choose. The beauty of this world is staggering. I’ve lost count of how many times I just stopped driving or stood on a balcony staring at the buildings and the lighting just to soak in the atmosphere. Every single character has their own deep story and unique design. Tbh most games out there straight up lack this kind of perfect balance. And by balance I mean the story and the world-building and the fighting styles all coming together not just one thing. You can switch from ghosting everyone in stealth to going full-on combat mode whenever you want and the game handles both perfectly. Phantom Liberty pack: Listen you MUST buy the DLC. It is the absolute gem of the experience. You’re basically missing the soul of the game if you don’t have it. From the second you finish the Voodoo Boys mission and get that first mysterious call the stakes hit a level I didn't think was possible. Best DLC ever made no cap. dlc pack:[SPOILERS] The journey from the Voodoo Boys to the surgery is a masterclass in tension. The betrayal part is what actually breaks you fr. Whether you turn on Songbird or Reed it feels like a physical weight on your chest. You aren't just picking a path you are betraying someone who trusted you and the guilt is real. Not to mention that second massive choice later on—deciding whether to still send Songbird to the moon or give her up after the insane shock that she played you the whole time. The genius of the writing is that the consequences don't always hit you immediately. Sometimes you discover the true cost of your choices hours later. The Endings: The endings aren't just win or lose screens. They are deep philosophical questions. There is a huge debate where many say the best ending is sacrificing yourself for Johnny. I kind of agree imo but it’s a heavy price. You can also choose to live out your 6 months with hope, which as a Nomad means everything since clan comes first. But for me the surgery ending is easily the most depressing. You get exactly what you wanted—to survive—but lose everything that made you V. Going from a legendary merc to getting tossed down stairs by random thugs is a brutal reality check. It proves every miracle has a price, leaving you with a hollow bittersweet feeling forever. There is no perfect ending here. Pro tip save the game before the point of no return so you can experience all these crazy conclusions. Overall Rating: 10/10

After 515 hours, Night City is a permanent headspace. It’s the ritual of a 3:00 AM Sandevistan-fuelled slaughter followed by the sensory overload of **Afterlife’s** neon grime. You’ve mastered the lethal choreography of high-tier chrome, yet the real pull remains that atmospheric hostility—the way the strobe lights in **Totentanz** blur with the city’s indifference. It’s a masterful, terminal simulation where the high-octane violence and sleek, corporate cynicism collide. Even with the ticking narrative clock, the "live fast, die young" nightlife and visceral combat make this digital dystopia an inescapable, post-human mood. Absolute peak immersion.

The game has its flaws, but it's an incredible game. It not only respects the original TRPG but also does the genre justice completely. It's fun to play, Night City is an amazing map to explore, the main story is just okay, but the characters and the world more than make up for it. One of the game's downsides is that it leaves you wanting more. The game tackles its themes in a very simple and effective way, leaving just enough room for you to fill in with your imagination. Like its city, the game immerses you in this beautiful but completely bleak and dystopian world where the challenge isn't saving the world, but saving yourself, not letting it change you and turn you into something you're not, or not letting it dehumanize you, and despite everything, trying to do the right thing. Phantom Liberty is wonderful; it grabs you from the start and doesn't let go. It has all the game's strengths, but multiplied, leaving you devastated but satisfied if you got the good ending.
