Ok, where do I even begin... This game is an absolute masterpiece. - Story 10/10 (RIP everyone) - Gameplay 9/10 (only hand to hand combat is clunky, the rest is fantastic) - Graphics 10/10 - Music 10/10 - Voice Acting / Motion Capture 10/10 - DLC 10/10 (I'd recommend buying the DLC since the beginning) I'm doing this review at almost 160 hours, this includes main story + DLC + all the side quests in the game + all the endings (excluding "(Don't Fear) The Reaper", more on this later). You do not need to spend that amount of time to complete the game, you can probably 100% in 120 if you don't do side quests and if you actually only use a single play-style (more on this soon). Key points to remember: - Male V vs Female V, there is a lot of discussion here. I chose male V, it felt like it worked better with Johnny, romance with Panam is great and it makes more sense to me for Aldecaldos ending (The Star). - Whenever playing you don't need a guide for anything imo, BUT, please CHECK A GUIDE for "Chippin' In", the dialog decisions will lock you out of the ending "(Don't Fear) The Reaper". This happened to me, and given that I did that at around 40 hours, I wasn't gonna restart the game when I was already in 100+. I'll have to use mods if I want to play that that ending without replaying the whole game. - Another tip would be when you find the weapon Skippy it will ask you to choose between "Stone Cold Killer Mode" or "Puppy Loving Pacifist Mode", choose the puppy-loving mode, this will get you the best rewards long term. - There are many other decisions I could suggest my opinion, but honestly, play the game and make mistakes. - You can't max out all specs and attributes in the game (not without mods), so make sure you pick according with your play style. I screw up the first time around and I had to use my "Reset Attributes" (there is only 1) to accommodate what I wanted for the rest of the game. - Max level in the game is level 50, unless you get the DLC, which allows you to go up to level 60. This also comes with more attribute and perk points, so buy the DLC before you reach level 50. - Play the endings whenever you want, right after the ending, it basically brings you back before to the point of no return, and you can continue playing any other missions you want, so might be worth just experimenting and having fun. - You don't need to upgrade your Cyberware all the time, it goes from Tier 1 to Tier 5+ (or 5++ with DLC), I'd say to upgrade once mid game around level 30, and then just wait until you are around level 50 to get everything at Tier 5+ and be absolutely broken. - Quickhacks (Netrunner build) are broken if you max them out, so it's everything else. But I found that the best option for most endings is going with the Sadevistan build, it's just a great help to avoid damage and to inflict it too. Berserk build is my least favorite option, it's cool, just not as cool. - Depending on the DLC choices you make and the ending you choose, you might be able to get certain weapon. Best loot overall are in the "King of Pentacles" ending, but imo, the most best ending is "King of Wands". Only thing missing for me is NG+ where I can keep all my loot and just level up until I am the most overpowered character ever with every attribute and perk (even though it already feels like that without maxing out everything!) PS: Worst main ending is by far "The Devil", and for the DLC I'd say "King of Swords" PS2: I was able to use commands to be able to play the secret ending "(Don't Fear) The Reaper", and I gotta say, if you are choosing Temperance or The Sun as your favorite endings, this path is better, imo. Also, more challenging since your max health drops as time passes, which is awesome.

Cyberpunk 2077 has turned out to be one of the most immersive and rewarding games I’ve played on Steam. Going in, I had heard mixed opinions, but my personal experience has been overwhelmingly positive—and honestly, it exceeded my expectations. The first thing that stands out is the world itself. Night City feels alive in a way few open-world games manage to achieve. From the neon-lit streets to the dense urban design, every district has its own personality. Simply walking or driving around can be an experience on its own, with constant details, side activities, and random encounters making the world feel dynamic. The story is another highlight. It’s engaging, emotional, and filled with meaningful choices that actually feel impactful. The characters are well-written and memorable, and the narrative does a great job of pulling you into its futuristic setting. It’s not just about action—there’s depth, moral ambiguity, and plenty of moments that stick with you even after you log off. Gameplay-wise, the flexibility is impressive. Whether you prefer stealth, hacking, or going in guns blazing, the game gives you the freedom to shape your own playstyle. The skill system and upgrades allow for a lot of experimentation, which keeps things fresh over time. Visually, the game looks stunning, especially on a well-optimized setup. Lighting, reflections, and overall atmosphere contribute heavily to the immersion. Performance on Steam has also been smooth for me, with noticeable improvements compared to earlier versions of the game. Overall, I’m genuinely satisfied with my purchase. Cyberpunk 2077 delivers a rich open-world experience, strong storytelling, and enjoyable gameplay mechanics. It’s a game that’s easy to get lost in, and one I’d definitely recommend to anyone looking for a deep and visually impressive RPG.

I’ve played quite a few RPGs in my time—some on Steam, some on Xbox, and others on older PC setups. After putting what I’d consider a solid amount of time into this game, I can confidently say it’s more than deserving of all the praise it gets. The story and characters you encounter are incredibly strong, but the real magic happens when you fully lean into the world—immersing yourself in the side quests along the way. Do that, and you’ll find a narrative that’s not only engaging, but almost effortless to get lost in. Before you know it, you’re deeply invested—maybe even dangerously attached—to the people you meet. The icing on the cake is just how much depth the game continues to gain through its updates. From a gameplay perspective, it’s easy to fall back into old habits with your usual playstyle, but there’s a surprising amount of depth in how you can approach nearly every quest. Outcomes can vary in subtle ways or shift dramatically depending on your choices, which keeps things feeling fresh and meaningful. Visually, the game looks great—and with mods, it can look even better. Personally, I ran into very few issues—maybe one or two—and they were quickly resolved with a simple restart or minor setting adjustment. Overall, it’s just a great game that somehow manages to get even better once you finish it and dive into Phantom Liberty.

Cyberpunk 2077 is not really about becoming the best mercenary in Night City. It is about personhood under siege. It is science fiction, but only by degree. People are already flattened into profiles, performances, labour value, social image, sexual currency, and marketable identity. Cyberpunk 2077 just pushes that process until it becomes impossible to ignore. Its cruelest idea is simple: you are born hoping to become someone real, and the world immediately starts negotiating what parts of you it can own. Johnny Silverhand is what makes that idea personal. He is rage, regret, defiance, and the voice that refuses to let compromise feel normal. The part of you that would rather burn than disappear quietly into something obedient and useful. The journey is about trying to stay a person in a world that wants a product. And even then, it still leaves room for one stubborn answer: No.

This game pisses me off. This [i]should[/i] be a masterpiece, if not for one egregious flaw. The combat is terrible, specifically the enemy AI. NPCs are Skyrim levels of stupid, and difficulty means bigger health bar. That is genuinely what 90% of combat encounters in vanilla offer you. There is no dynamism to all but a few select boss encounters. By the time I started getting tier 4 weapons I was basically just god, running around instantly ending everyone as I saw fit; and I played the entire campaign on hard. The combat is so ass it actually dissuaded me from exploring. Typically in games like this I like to explore every nook and cranny I can find, but in this one I thought what is the point? I'm just going to instantly end any fight I get into and the rewards are meaningless crafting supplies I already have 10,000 of and have never needed to use ever. Everything else about this game is amazing. The soundtrack, the city, the visuals, the driving (the only game to make me avoid using fast travel because driving around is really just that fun), all of it is great, except for the archaic Gamebryo-ass NPC AI. There are a lot of other nitpicks I could get into but none of it is as game-breaking as the terrible combat system. There are so many cool quickhacks and weapons you can use and none of it matters because you just gun down everyone instantly. I ended up skipping the DLC because I was so bored of the same combat over and over and over. All of that being said, there is still plenty of enjoyment to get out of this game, it just disappoints me that they screwed up such a fundamental aspect of gameplay so badly that it kind of ruined the game for me. Worth it on a heavy discount, but anything more and I'd say wait. You're not missing out on a whole lot besides atmosphere and story, even if they are the best atmosphere and story I've experienced in an FPS.

I decided to wait a while after the initial release to let the developers fix the launch issues and give them some time to polish the game (yep, 5 years). Yet, all these years later, I’m still running into various glitches that are definitely not "gameplay features" or "implant malfunctions." - [b]visual glitches[/b]: blinking shadows, dissolving cars, Path Tracing issues with strobing lights, and jittering textures. - [b]soft-locks[/b]: several bugs in different quests that force you to restart from the last checkpoint. I really wish there was an option to save while in elevators or during scripted scenes, but alas. By the way, this isn’t an RPG in the classical sense. I mean, it’s a bad sign when the dialogue system in Fallout 4 is fundamentally better (which is hilarious in itself). This is a [i] "new school" RPG[/i], where the role-playing element is mostly limited to picking your skill tree. That said, the game does have a decent and, at times, high-octane story (even if it is mostly "on rails" and follows a character who consistently makes stupid decisions). It also boasts a great soundtrack (I’m talking about the original score, not the radio stations) and, of course, Keanu Reeves.

Tried playing this again for the first time in over two years. Couldn't recall why I hadn't played more than the first couple of story beats. Figured it was probably due to a mix of busy with work and busy playing other games. So I go on Nexus, setup a collection of mods, and proceed to get into the game. Or so I thought. Right after the first conversation with Jackie, I realized what the stumbling block was that prompted me to spend time on other games. When not in a vehicle, you're stuck in first person. No options for Third Person. So I grit my teeth and go search for a mod that provides Third Person view, should be something out there yea?> ... Well, there is. Kind of. There's a set of mods on Nexus that do exactly that. Both buggy as all hell. Animations don't play right, sometimes crash to desktop, often character will be bald when first loading into a scene or room, as the game isn't accustomed to having to load your hair, the list goes on. And you DO need both of those mods. One provides the ... "Framework" we'll call it, for having Third Person, the other tries to fix the various animation issues created by playing a game meant to be only in First Person - in Third Person. I don't blame those modders though for not gift wrapping me a perfect fix for this. They're creating that stuff on their own time, and presumably doing the best they can. But it's been over 5 years. CDPR could certainly have corrected this failing. And hey, it's ok if you don't see it as a failing. You can choose to be wrong and disagree with me on this. No hurt feelings. Cept for the fact that players accepting this kind of nonsense just means more of it is likely down the line. There in lies the problem. It's an RPG, I do not get the all encompasses desire some jackals have for First Person. It works for shooters though. I guess. For some people. But more than that, I detest game devs that eliminate choice for players. Being able to choose my own keybinds is important, but being able to toggle between First Person & Third Person should be a given. Being able to pan out away from my character, should be a given. It certainly is in many RPG games over the years. For Cyberpunk I don't know if this was a hardline choice from the folks at CDPR to force players to experience their game a certain way, or just ineptitude. CDPR does a lot of great stuff, and props to them for dragging this game out of the buggy mess that it was at release. But refusal to implement a Third Person option in their RPG turns what might otherwise be enjoyable hours of gaming into a sloppy mess I'd rather not waste time with. So, great game, yadda yadda, and I do recommend it, with the caveat that you should avoid it if you don't enjoy first person perspective. For $60, gamers deserve better. [Edit] Soon as I post my review, the games trailer starts playing, and I'm struck by the ironic idiocy that they show "Your" character's face, in trailers, in game you actually design your look. Why? You won't be showing up in any mirrors. In fact if you pick up a body to move it, and walk past a reflective surface, the dead body will be floating as you don't have a proper model cause why would you need one? No need to display you in mirrors etc. BUT you took the time to give your character a face at creation. Perhaps you get to glimpse yourself in cut scenes or when you get in/out of a vehicle, who cares? That's a fraction of the time you play and honestly if I'm not pausing to look at a my character I certainly don't care what the plethora of NPCs think about it. I'd say well played CDPR, but that'd just be silly.

Oh my GOD I love cyberpunk 2077 so much. The world is amazing and full of depth, every nook and cranny is full of life in some way and the setting is unlike anything I've seen before. I know CDPR usually has good writing but even so these characters can be amazing. Everyone has their own level of depth and feels like a real person. The plot is phenomenal; my favorite kind of story is one that can genuinely make you feel something, and this game does that. Just the vibe (so to speak) at times is palpable-feelings of helplessness, of being lost, of feeling like everything is out of control or that you're just another bug under the greater world's shoe. Emotions stick with you for a long time-the ones cyberpunk's storyline made me experience have. I absolutely love the combat-it kicks ass. There are so many unique weapon types with perks and cyberware that make gameplay a whole buffet of choices for how you want to approach any given situation. Play behind cover with medium-long range weapons? Strategically utilize quickhacks to debuff or damage enemies? Stealth through it with camo and silent weapons? Speed blitz through an entire scavenger outpost with a sword? There's a little something for everyone. What I don't see nearly enough appreciation for is the soundtrack. Combat tracks are amazing and give so much tension and flare to everything; the radio is full of stations and the number of unlikable tracks fitting on one hand. Cyberpunk is my favorite RPG-open world or not-of all time, and I would go as far as to say it's in my top 5, maybe even top 3 favorite games of all time. Whether it will be for you I can't say, but it would be a disservice to yourself not to try it.

I went into Cyberpunk pretty excited, but the beginning honestly threw me off more than I expected. Right away you’re hit with a ton of characters calling you... a lot of dialogue and its not always clear whos who or why it matters yet. It felt overwhelming and confusing early on. Looking back I think I played it the wrong way at first because I rushed the main story. This really isnt a game youre supposed to blow through. Its way better when you slow down and explore. The main story didnt fully land for me either. Theres a lot of talking and dialogue choices but not much action if you just go mission to mission and a lot of the responses didn’t feel like what I actually wanted to say. Things only really started to click for me near the end of the Takemura and Hanako storyline, which felt like weird pacing since I was just starting to understand the mechanics when the game was basically over. On top of that, I was pretty disappointed that after finishing the final mission it just loads you back before the ending. Once I started digging into side content, my opinion improved a lot. The side gigs and NCPD activities are honestly where the game shines for me. There are a ton of them and you can approach each one in completely different ways depending on your build. The gameplay really opens up once you invest in skills, especially mobility. I found myself running and scaling buildings instead of driving most of the time. Driving does feel clunky at first but you do get used to it. The hacking system is one of the best parts of the game and really sells the futuristic feel. It opens up a ton of creative ways to approach encounters. Throwing knives especially surprised me with how strong they are, and once I leaned into that it made you feel like a ninja. One of my favorite moments was setting up a full stealth chain where I hacked into cameras to ping enemies, used distractions like generators and a ferris wheel to turn them around, then moved across rooftops landing throwing knife headshots one by one. Even the chaos side of things is fun, like getting max wanted level and hacking enemies to turn on each other. The world itself is one of the best parts of the game. You can just be walking around and see cops arresting people or fighting gangs and it actually feels alive. The map and tracking system is really clean and easy to use, especially being able to mark multiple objectives and follow different routes. The only downside is that it keeps defaulting back to the main story after you finish the game. I wish there was a simple way to turn that off or fully deselect it, because it will keep tracking the final mission with the yellow route. There were a few times I wasn’t paying attention and thought I was heading toward a side activity, only to end up back at the point where you meet Hanako at Embers. Once you go in, you’re locked into the ending again, which gets pretty frustrating... Weapon variety is great and honestly reminded me of Borderlands but better, with a wide range from common to legendary and solid customization options. Performance wise it ran really well for me on an i9 9900k and 2080 Ti at 1440p on high settings with no ray tracing, averaging around 115–150 fps. There were still some bugs especially in the main story where a few bosses glitched out and got stuck but I didnt run into nearly as many issues in side content. Overall the game has a really immersive world and strong gameplay systems but the main story pacing and heavy focus on dull dialogue held it back for me. If you take your time with it instead of rushing like I did the first time, chances are you are going to love it.

The most non-plussed 50 hours of my life. I don't even know where the time went. The entire game feels like a half-remembered dream. Let me start with the most obvious implication on gameplay: the user interface. It is so overloaded with numbers and colors and flashing icons. It never feels familiar. I'm 50 hours into the game and trying to remember what button gets me to exit a car. When combat happens there are so many bars and statuses and timers and whatever else... I have no idea what is going on. All of this obscures the fact that pretty much every encounter I take out an SMG, empty it into a dude, and he dies. If take too much damage, I dash around a corner and press the heal button. I don't say this to be reductive. I say this to say: for all the complex user interface decisions, it's not a complicated game mechanically. The next most-immediate part of the experience is the story. Maybe more specifically the lore. I felt like I was drowning for the prologue. To the game's credit, this isn't really an important part of the game. It doesn't really start until Keanu Reeves shows up and after that it is mostly coherent. I think the peak was in the desert with Panam and her crew where there was a fairly straight forward story with some personals takes. A little bit of the Arasaka storyline with that one due who helps you. That made sense to me. Immediately after that... I have no idea what happened. I'm on the literal last mission -- where it tells you "this is the point of no return" -- and I have no idea what is happening in this story. What drove me to review this game — after 50 hours and slowly going through it for more than a year — was the unbelievably insulting side quest design. This extends to Phantom Liberty too. Every side quest — and I really mean EVERY SINGLE SIDE QUEST — is not designed to be played, it is designed to be watched. This game has more than 10-20 hours of standing there while someone talks at you. It is unbelievable how boring this game can be. I have been agonizing finishing this game. There was a part of me that enjoyed it enough to buy the expansion and make it through 50 hours worth of content. Then at some point I must have ran out of the game and all that was left was cut scenes and dialogue. I have attempted to play this game 4 times over the past 4 weeks. All 4 sessions were 1 hour to 90 minutes of watching characters talk at me. And it's not even interesting! It's not science fiction concepts. It's not moral quandaries. It's not interesting characters. It's just YAPPING. Talking and talking and talking and talking. I've had a rocky relatiomship with this game. I bought it on release day and it was in such a bad state I uninstalled it and never picked it up again for 4 years. I finally got back into it in late December 2024 and over the course of 2025 I logged the hours you see here now. At some point, I couldn't do it anymore. I've stretched this out over several months now but I've accepted I have gotten all the value there is in this game. It is so unbelievably boring.

Cyberpunk 2077: A dystopian future masterpiece I really can't understate how phenomenal an experience this game is, and having just finished my 2nd playthrough this time with the Phantom Liberty DLC (which was incredible), I have a whole new appreciation for the storytelling and universe of Cyberpunk. The first time around, I was a Street Kid V who leaned more towards a balanced persona with my dialogue options, whereas this time I played a much colder Corpo V. Same story, totally different perspectives. It's amazing just how much depth and gravity your choices end up making throughout your journey, I'll definitely be picking this back up to try a 3rd run as Nomad V. Unlike how quickly I move on from other games, I actually need some time off to process the choices I made, and the outcome I got as a self-serving Corpo Merc who accomplished his ultimate goal of surviving, but lost pretty much everything in the process. Cyberpunk 2077 is a game that pulls you into the story like nothing else, and if anything exists as a spiritual successor to the like of Fallout New Vegas. From a gameplay perspective, I've experimented with different builds, weapons, and cyberware, and never felt bored no matter which areas I specialized in. I think it's fair to say some skill trees got more love and attention than others, but the ability to blend them together into something new will keep you curious and invested for quite a while. This game really gives you the freedom to step into your own persona as portrayed by V, and depending on which direction you go, you'll get very different results. From a lore perspective, this game is so realistic it makes me feel uncomfortable at times, thinking about what could await humanity in the future with Rogue AIs, cyberspace, the integration of cybernetics into the human body, and the inevitable corporatization of society. It's almost as if nations and countries don't even really matter anymore, just the corps that fight for control over them. It makes you feel incredibly small when you take in the totality of things going on within the cyberpunk timeline. Your companion throughout the game Johnny Silverhand is a layer cake of selfish and noble personality traits that end up manifesting in very thought provoking ways. He's someone that you'd instinctively dislike, yet you come to understand him and his motivations on a much deeper level, and realize that nothing is ever that simple. What you choose to make of the time you get spend with him is what makes his presence so unforgettable. He can be your best friend, or your worst enemy, depending on your point of view. Keanu Reeves may be criticized for always just playing another version of himself in movies, but I felt he really did stand out as Johnny Silverhand, and gave an incredible performance. Not to glaze a celebrity, but had it not been for Keanu, I don't think I would have grown to like Johnny at all, and that deserves recognition. As for criticisms, I don't have many. Yes there were a few small things that I felt could have been executed better, like some of the relationships of the friends you meet along the way. I would have liked to have more time getting to know Jackie, as it felt like I got a case of whiplash from that montage of doing gigs with him. A longer prologue exploring the early days of the different types of V would have made for a smoother transition to the life he gets pulled into after the events of Konpeki Plaza. Also iterating a bit further with some of the friend/love interests would have been interesting, as some of them felt a bit short or half-baked. Not bad, just not totally satisfying at times. I felt the clothing options in this game could have been better, but luckily there are mods to address that, which I only really used 1 to do. The vehicles and driving also aren't great at times depending on your ride, but it does get better after some time behind the wheel. I appreciate how difficult driving in first person is, and if you actually try, it adds another layer of immersion to the game. The weapons are really cool, and there is a pretty good variety, but more customization options would have been welcome, like different mods or paint jobs, cyberware etc. Depending on your playstyle and preferences, you'll have plenty to work with. The game did have a rough start due to bugs in it's early days (which I wasn't around for), and I think some of those small bugs do still exist within the engine. Strange behavior or random occurrences from NPCs and vehicles glitching out, mostly harmless and sometimes funny, but also immersion breaking. The frequency of glitches I noticed wasn't nearly enough to frustrate me or ruin the experience. Overall, I would give this game a solid 9.5 out of 10 with Phantom Liberty. A damn-near flawless masterpiece with very little to complain about, and so, so much more to offer than the vast majority of other titles being released these days. The base game alone was incredible, but with the DLC is just kicks it up a notch to a truly phenomenal experience. If you haven't played this game, you're missing out, choom.

I waited to write this review to let time pass, observe mechanical updates, and distance myself from real-world events I experienced during my first playthrough. My conclusions remain unchanged. I played on release via Stadia (logging around 600 hours, bug-free) and later transitioned to Steam with the expansion. If you are looking for a highly structured, immersive world where you can exist as a single character, this game delivers. But beneath the surface, it is a heavy, uncompromising examination of autonomy, mental health, and the ethical cost of survival. ## Fair content warning: ## This review contains spoilers and discusses severe mental health issues and suicide. ## THE WORLD AND THE ATMOSPHERE As someone who grew up in the 80s, the retro-future aesthetic resonates well with me. The environmental design — ranging from corporate skyscrapers to neon-lit, trash-filled alleys — balances surface splendour with the tragedy of an unforgiving dystopia. The soundscape is very good, and the OST remains in my regular rotation. I particularly liked the diegetic inclusion of music through radios, speakers, etc. It feels natural. The developers successfully created a graphically believable universe with its own distinct clothing, colloquialisms, and professions. On the downside, I wish they had done something like the procedural, emergent roleplay of games like *Daggerfall*. The city is dense, but the NPCs lack complex schedules or interactions. Most of the world is setting, and there are few things (or people!) you can interact with. It was a satisfying (but frustrating) realization to find out you could actually confess yourself in the absolution vending machines. There is also a distinct tension — and this is a crucial issue — between exploring the world and the main quest. The narrative insists V is dying rapidly, urging you to rush. It makes absolute sense, but doing so deprives you of exploring the setting. But if you suspend the dissonance this urgency creates, the lore and visual storytelling are highly detailed. ## GAMEPLAY AND MECHANICS The gunplay and movement mechanics are satisfying, offering varied approaches: fast-paced reflexes, time-dilating cyberware, or real-time quickhacks. The combat functions well, accommodating everything from stealth to direct assault. However, the RPG elements lack structural consequence. The reputation system is shallow: working for one gang should logically anger others, and aiding the police should make you a target in the underworld. This all could lead tor restricting access to certain resources or quests based on alliances, and would foster replayability. Similarly, the game allows complete character respecs. I value games where you can make your own choices, but choices must have some degree of consequence, and this applies also to character creation and development. A system where choices have permanence — where mastering hacking precludes being a swordmaster, for instance — would ground the experience. The game also omits cyberpsychosis as a gameplay mechanic for the player. Lore dictates that heavy bodily modification risks mental breakdown, yet the game imposes no such penalty on V. This is ironic because cyberpsychosis is hardly forgotten in these modern iterations of the setting: the entire Edgerunners series runs on it. It is also (in the TTRPG) a very important mechanic to limit the possibilitites of expanding your own character or respeccing it. These issues I am critiquing are not a problem for Cyberpunk 2077 only — this plague is an AAA development philosophy hesitant to lock players out of content, but in doing so, robs them of actual consequence to their actions. ## NARRATIVE, MENTAL HEALTH, AND ENDINGS Yet, apart from my appreciation of its lore and aesthetics, where the game holds the most value for me is in its somber handling of psychological trauma and survival. I have seen other players too credit this game's themes with helping them process dark times in their own lives, and looking at the quests, one can imagine why. The game repeatedly forces engagement with autonomy and personhood: The Delamain Arc requires permanent choices regarding a fractured AI's perception of reality. Brendan is vending machine treated as corporate property — he insists he is not sentient, yet acts as if he is, raising practical questions about the definition of personhood. Lizzy Wizzy is clearly suffering from cyberpsychosis, but also facing the horror of having her mind tampered with by a partner. Barry's story is an approach to depression from a darkly humorous angle, but delivers a grim look at how mental health struggles are ignored by peers. Cyberpsycho sightings themselves, on which I haven't seen much comment, are excuses for boss fights, ok. But if you look through them, they are tragedies. The one titled 'Family Matters' hit very hard, with one woman struggling to help her sister, and ultimately losing her husband and even her life to it. People often cite that the main narrative is 'V is dying', but that isn't accurate: the body can survive. V is facing her mind being rewritten by the Relic, and that is a much more horrible reality. I think the game does a good job at presenting this, both subtly and explicitly: V's dialogue options and actions (like smoking) begin to mirror Johnny Silverhand, and Johnny's own arc shifts as he realizes this, moving from hostility to empathy. You are fading away, and the game acknowledges the terror of that process. ## CONTENT WARNING: SUICIDE DISCUSSION During my first playthrough, I was dealing with the immediate aftermath of a suicide attempt by someone close to me. I interrupted the attempt, but witnessing their intense pain left me grappling with whether I did them a disservice. I prioritize personal autonomy, and intervening felt like an intrusion on their ultimate choice, even if it stemmed from a compromised mental state. Processing the game through that lens influenced how I saw the final choices. Players often view the endings as a way to «win» but, to me, they were a calculation of whom I was willing to sacrifice. Asking the Nomads for help gets many of them killed to buy you time. Siding with Rogue gets her killed. Siding with Arasaka surrenders both your mind and Johny's to them. The secret «solo» ending requires the mass murder of corporate guards who are ultimately just working people. Under this light, the suicide ending seems the cleanest, most ethical option. It respects the autonomy and safety of everyone else. You prioritize your friends' lives above your survival, deciding not to drag them into your self-destruction. Johnny respects the choice. Your friends will call in the credits, grieving and cursing you, but the structural fact remains: you did not force anyone else to pay the price for your life. ## CONCLUSION I acknowledge my experience with this game comes from a very specific, difficult place in my life, which colored my perception. Mechanically, it has flaws and missed opportunities for deeper RPG consequences. However, it captures the genre's aesthetic accurately and delivers a solid narrative. If you are willing to engage with its themes of autonomy, mental health, and the systemic cost of survival, I think it offers a dense, worthwhile experience.

7/10, A flawed work of art that deserves recognition…After completing all life paths and getting all achievements, this is by far one of the most hauntingly beautiful games I’ve ever played. In a game that seems to have more loot than Skyrim. There's no pressure to pick up everything that falls on the ground (though you may miss some iconic loot if you’re not careful). It’s a game that takes itself a bit too seriously at times and shares the same kind of bleak atmosphere that GTA 4 has but with a lot more neon and much better graphics. A lot of characters like Johnny and Takemura are surprisingly funny at times as neither can seem to comprehend the size of their own egos. Whilst the game pushes a strong narrative that Corpos are the worst thing to ever exist, there also seems to be a somewhat subtle narrative that the AI in this world could potentially be worse and far more catastrophic than its human creators. Unfortunately, it never digs deep enough to give you a much bigger perspective of what this could mean besides some hints from characters like So mi, Alt and Mr blue eyes. Outside of that there is also references to the dangers of the ocean which seem to be controlled by AI. Its possible that CDPR could just be laying the groundwork for the sequel with Mr Blue Eyes potentially being an antagonist in the next game, though nothing seems to be confirmed yet at the time of this review. Gameplay This is where the game starts losing points, for an FPS it feels very safe. Much in the same way that Bethesda sacrificed depth for accessibility to those new to the genre in the world of Skyrim. CDPR has done this with a first-person shooter, having played the likes of Wolfenstein and the Metro games, the FPS aspect is unbearably easy for me, even on higher difficulties. The game gives you more money and guns than you know what to do with, I had over a 100k eddies by the time I did the Arasaka heist with Jackie (This was on my first playthrough). Despite these issues, the overall atmosphere of the game was compelling enough to try different lifepaths and builds. Customization Another reason why I’m only giving this a 7/10 is that It’s a game that seems to contradict itself at times. It surrounds you with a wide variety of npcs whilst limiting the player customization without mods. Some of the npcs barely look human due to how chromed out they are and it was surprising that I could not achieve the same sort of look for V. Car customization is also limited as you can only buy a certain amount colour designs for your car, the cap on this feature makes no sense. The Phantom Liberty This is arguably the best DLC CDPR have ever produced and gives you an insight into what the base game could have felt like if it spent more time in the oven instead of rushing into a buggy release (which thankfully I skipped). The relic skill tree was a nice touch and it should have been in the base game really (similar to the unique perk tree from dragon age inquisition). Having said that the DLC is still worth it for its price, if you’re new to this DLC, the roads in dog town are terrible and I recommend getting yourself a bike for smoother navigation (I went for the custom bike in the base game which is easy to miss). Songbird is a tragic yet manipulative character and her complexity is what makes this DLC so interesting, Reed is basically just a NUSA Takemura. He is blinded by loyalty to something that doesn’t really care about him but his loyalty is somewhat admirable nonetheless, even if its misplaced. The gameplay isn’t that much different from the base game in terms of combat but the new chrome, perk tree and different weapons add some flavour along with the story. the black market and the contracts from Mr Hands are a nice touch and add a bit more moral ambiguity to the side quests compared to those in the base game. Overall It’s a great RPG that’s worth playing, but if you want a less beginner friendly FPS and you don’t care much for the story and atmosphere of this game then it may not be for you. If you view this game as a work of art that can be interacted with and more importantly if you treat Johnny as more of a comedian that makes perfectly timed commentary on what you’re doing. You will find that this game has a lot to offer (I also recommend the Johnny and Rogue ending at least once as its just pure comedy). The Don’t Fear the reaper ending was surprisingly easy for those with more experience in FPS like me, even on higher difficulties, though I still highly recommended it. (This may not be the case if you go in with terrible weapons and chrome obviously.) Despite some of its flaws, it really is worth it just for the atmosphere and experience alone.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those rare games that feels as much like an experience as it does a story. Set in the sprawling, neon-soaked Night City, it drops you into a world that’s chaotic, beautiful, and deeply immersive. From the moment you step into the shoes of V, the game pulls you into a narrative filled with ambition, identity, and the cost of chasing dreams in a broken system. What really stands out is the world-building. Night City isn’t just a backdrop—it feels alive. Every district has its own personality, from the polished corporate towers to the gritty back alleys. The attention to detail is incredible, and it rewards exploration in a way few open-world games do. The story is another highlight. With strong performances—especially from Keanu Reeves as Johnny Silverhand—the game delivers emotional weight alongside its action. Your choices matter, shaping not just the ending but how characters perceive you along the way. Gameplay-wise, Cyberpunk 2077 offers a lot of freedom. Whether you prefer stealth, hacking, or going in guns blazing, the game supports multiple playstyles. The RPG elements, including skill trees and cybernetic upgrades, let you tailor V to your liking. While the game had a rough launch, it has since been significantly improved with updates and expansions, making it far more stable and polished. Today, it stands as a testament to how much a game can evolve post-release. Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 is a bold, visually stunning, and emotionally engaging game that’s absolutely worth playing—especially now.

Cyberpunk 2077 (2020) СЮЖЕТ: Ну… поехали. Вопреки общему мнению, что сюжет Cyberpunk 2077 лучше Ведьмака 3, что он мрачнее и глубже — я не согласен. И перед тем как меня начнут закидывать гнилыми помидорами (а пока что, кому бы я это ни сказал, именно так и делали), я поясню свою позицию. Мне очень нравится общая идея игры с цифровым бессмертием и дилеммой «лучше умереть в лучах славы, чем прожить долгую и скучную жизнь». К ним претензий нет. Наоборот, столкнувшись с этими концепциями, я сразу понял — они продали мне игру. Проблема сюжета не в общей идее, а в том, КАК она раскрывается. CDPR создали историю мечты, но у них не хватило времени, а потом желания грамотно её распределить по всей сюжетной линии. В итоге мы имеем безумное вступление, концовки и пара увлекательных квестов, а в остальном скучно и неинтересно. Я не совру, если скажу, что Cyberpunk 2077 — это лучший сюжет у CDPR. Уровень постановки катсцен и звукорежиссуры — пик индустрии. Но я так же не совру, что сюжет Ведьмака 3 вызвал у меня намного бóльшую вовлечённость. Мир Ведьмака разнообразнее и насыщеннее. Каждая история цепляла больше. Да, идея Ведьмака 3 (поиск родственника) — являлась дурным тоном не то, что сейчас, а уже тогда, но за счёт сильной RPG-составляющей, проработки мира, развилок и живых персонажей они отвели глаз от банальной мотивации Геральта так, что вы бы даже не задумались. А что Cyberpunk? У «неонового города» есть оригинальная идея, неплохие персонажи (до Ведьмака не дотягивают) и абсолютно ебанутая постановка, но больше ничего. У красивейшей синтетической кожи нет скелета и имплантов. И не забывайте: в «RPG будущего» ваши варианты ответа, происхождение, способ прохождения миссий не влияет… ни… на… что. Это позор. CDPR, подарившие нам одну из лучших RPG всех времён, не смогли сделать… RPG?) Да, в общей концепции Cyberpunk укладывает «Дикую охоту» на лопатки, но разрабам будто не хватило времени и сил раскрыть её до конца. ГЕЙМПЛЕЙ: Я НЕ УМЕЮ ИГРАТЬ В РПГ. Практически везде я отыгрываю один билд — Гатса в играх про мечи или танка в стрелялках. Я знаю, это высшая форма игровой импотенции, но я ничего не могу с этим поделать. В Киберпанк я зашёл с той же проблемой, но все же решил качать всё понемногу и все попробовать. Геймплей не впечатлял первые часов 20–30. Унылая стрельба, кастомизация оружия из 2015 года, аркадный транспорт, полицейские погони, которые при съезде в поле сразу исчезают. Спасали только вопросики, сайт-квесты и заказы, а когда это единственное, что достойно похвалы значит с игрой что-то не так. Но тут главное не ошибиться. Ведь дело в моём стиле игры. Я качал всё равномерно, а значит прокачка шла долго, а навыки, которые я открывал первое время были либо бесполезным говном, либо абсолютно дефолтнымиперками. Барьер в 20–30 часов — момент, когда заканчиваются унылые навыки и начинается самая маковка. Стоит ли говорить, как я был удивлен, когда обнаружил что мой лутер-шутер превратился сначала в ULTRAKILL, а потом чуть ли не в DOOM Eternal. А когда я увидел видосы в тиктоке с геймплеем ниндзя, нетраннера, милишника — я натурально охуел. ОКАЗЫВАЕТСЯ, я играл в Киберпанк неправильно. Стоило скинуть все очки в одну ветку — и я сразу почувствовал вкус игры. Да, стоковая стрельба и мувмент невыразительные, боты тупорылые, как призраки из Пакмана. Но перетерпите первые пару часов, выберите ветку и качайте её, уверяю – геймплей удивит. Единственное, чего не хватало (хотя бы как суперредкого события), — киберпсихоза. Через лор и персонажей нам говорят: если напихивать себя хромом с ног до головы, то ты сойдёшь с ума. На мой взгляд, возможность превращения в киберпсиха было бы в духе киберпанка. Я понимаю, CDPR не до этого, но хотя бы минимальные изменения реплик или сбои биочипа не только в катсценах. Это добавило бы в погружении ЗВУК И ВИЗУАЛ: Музыка разочаровала. Помимо заглавной темы, трейлер-темы и темы Джонни — ничего. Пресное радио, слабый звук оружия. Русская локализация — ужас. Позвать блогеров на озвучку… ебанный бобанный… Вместо актёров — нормисные блогеры, которые не понимают, что делать. Отсутствие интонации, неуместный или выдавленный мат, нет актёрского образования. Самое смешное: даже Кирк Сойер (Поперечный) звучит лучше, чем Ви. По визуалу буду краток. Графика, дизайн — наравне с RDR 2, а то и лучше. Не постесняюсь сказать, что Cyberpunk 2077 - одна из самых красивых игр в индустрии. Единственное, чего не хватило в визуале – это малое количество жести. Игра сразу была заявлена как 18+. И вроде кровь, кишки и голые сиськи на месте, но явно меньше, чем задумывалось. RoN (2023) показывает абсолютный ♥♥♥♥♥♥ на экране и поднимает спорные темы. За что его разрабам регулярно прилетает, чувствуется что «полякам» не хочется таких же проблем. Однако я считаю, что если бы игра вышла с таким же количеством жести, как планировалось, то игре бы это пошло лишь в плюс. ТЕХНИЧЕСКАЯ ЧАСТЬ: Честно говоря, могло быть и лучше. Критические баги залатали (встретил1–2 за всю игру), незначительные баги есть, но немного. Проблемы с хитбоксами и регистрациями. Раздражает враньё про оптимизацию. ИГРА ОЧЕНЬ ТРЕБОВАТЕЛЬНАЯ. Когда в Найт-Сити ночь и ты едешь в Japan Town за неончиком — при любом железе 25–30 кадров, оператива и проц в нули, а потом вылет. О вылетах: это раковая опухоль игры. Я люблю делать скрины в играх. Однако если вы смотрели мои скрины в CP 2077 — того, что мы подразумеваем под киберпанком, там нет. И не стоит думать, что я такая нетакуська и мне не нравилось происходящее на экране, наоборот, первые 5 часов я ходил с отпавшей челюстью. Дело в том, что игра вылетала, когда я хотел сфоткать небо, вывески или неон. Причём иногда выдавала ебанный синий экран. Ну это же уровень Таркова! Я думал, что проблема в драйверах они и правда были староватые, однако НИЧЕГО НЕ ПОМЕНЯЛОСЬ. Движок проклят. Ведьмаки тоже тяжело релизились, но это переплюнуло всё. ИТОГ: Cyberpunk 2077 — очень противоречивая игра. С одной стороны, хороший геймплей, невероятная графика, спорный, но скорее хороший сюжет. С другой — отсутствие RPG-элементов, тонны вырезанного контента, отвратительное техническое состояние на релизе и спорное сейчас, на мой взгляд скучнейшее DLC. Cyberpunk должен был стать игрой мечты CD Projekt, но долгая разработка, амбициозность и самоуверенность не дали игре стать той, которой она заслуживает быть. Многие говорят, что CDPR учтут ошибки в сиквеле. Но выйдет ли он? Будущее киберпанка на плечах DLC к Ведьмаку 3 и Ведьмака 4. В Cyberpunk 2077 у CD Project был карт-бланш на свинство — фанаты готовы были принять любую ошибку. Примут ли сейчас? Сомневаюсь. Cyberpunk 2077 — это действительно хорошая игра, которая заставила меня поменять мнение о ней. Уверен, я ещё вернусь в неё и игра мне скорее понравилась. Однако то, какой она должна была стать, расстраивает намного больше, чем радует то, какой она вышла. Cyberpunk 2077 — 7/10

I have a very tumultuous relationship with this game. Touted as one of the greatest rpgs of the modern day, as well as having a significant impact on the revitalization of the cyberpunk genre within mainstream pop culture, Cyberpunk 2077 felt inescapable. All that being said, CD Projekt Red’s The Witcher III failed to fully resonate with me, so I never bought into the hype for their shiny new game, nor did I experience the crushing disappointment of its damn near unplayable state at launch. Years removed from its horrific launch, with countless updates, a DLC, and a hearty recommendation from a dear friend, I finally gave it a try. After playing it for damn near 100 hours and fully completing every achievement, did it live up to the hype? If you want the TL;DR answer, I recommend the game well enough. If you want the long answer, keep reading. First of all, it’s a lot. I think I failed to recognize the sheer scope of the game when I first started playing it. Like, they really did make a colossal dystopian metropolis for you to explore, with an entire ecosystem and flow to it that makes sense. From a purely artistic standpoint, the game is a resounding achievement. The art direction, music, and voice acting here are genuinely A1, and speak to an immense amount of passion and confidence in the developer’s vision. It’s no wonder the game captured so many people based on its visuals alone, as the game is capable of creating sequences you can’t help but look upon in awe. I only wish they placed more attention on the game’s RPG mechanics. Have you ever played Fallout 4? “Fun game, terrible RPG” is the tagline many associate with it, as it abandoned much of the player agency native to the Fallout series in favor of a more limited, linear style of storytelling, with major choices being relegated to ♥♥♥♥ like “who do you want to blow up” at the end of the game. I actually quite like Fallout 4, but I think the criticisms against it as a narrative RPG are undeniable, save for the wonderful Far Harbor DLC. I think far and away the worst aspect of it is its insistence on offering you meaningless choices. You will see “Yes, Sarcastic (Yes), No (yes but later), More Info” for damn near every conversation in the game. I think it really speaks to how vapid the dialogue options are when the developers themselves don’t even tell you what you’re actually gonna say, instead choosing to condense the intent into three and a half laughable ways of saying yes. Now, why am I bringing all this up for a review on Cyberpunk 2077? Well, I honestly see quite a lot of similarity between the two! More specifically, I am ASTOUNDED that people give Fallout 4 so much flak for its poor RPG mechanics when Cyberpunk 2077 fares even worse as a narrative RPG! The game opens with a seemingly vital decision: your background. Are you a nomad living on the fringes of society? A gang member trying to get by in the seedy underbelly of Night City? Or a corpo, a part of the upper echelon of society, callously trampling on any and all beneath you? An interesting selection! I chose Nomad, and got a fun opening sequence of getting into Night City through a job to transport a real, living iguana. This set me down the path of forming a bond of friendship with the guy who hired me, acting as my leading narrative thread through Night City. Awesome! I wonder how drastically this would’ve changed if I chose corpo or gang member? Spoilers! Not at all, or at least, not in a way that actually matters. No matter what fun opening sequence you get, you will ALWAYS befriend Jackie, who will ALWAYS prompt the Arasaka heist, which will ALWAYS end the exact same way. Learning this opened my eyes to the true nature of Cyberpunk 2077: this is not an RPG; this is a futuristic Grand Theft Auto. The game, like Fallout 4, is confused. Is it an open-ended game about impacting the world through your choices? Or is it a carefully-constructed roller coaster through a campaign the devs planned out piece by piece? It tries to be both, much to the detriment of each half. The developers have constructed a well-built, engaging campaign for you to play through, yet they also want the game to be a narrative RPG where your choices matter. There are many complicated aspects that go into this game being a weak RPG, in my opinion, but there are two fundamental ones that harm the experience most severely. First problem: voiced protagonist. This was a problem in Fallout 4, and it’s a problem here. I play RPGs to imagine what decisions I’d make in fantastical, unrealistic situations, and, yes, roleplay in them. That goes out the window when a wholly new voice is attached to them. Multiple times, I’d pick a dialogue option I read to be more reasonable or calm, only for V to shout them out aggressively, completely altering the flow of the conversation in a way that was unintended by me, the player. Also, this single choice has a profoundly negative effect on replayability. If I want to replay the game trying to roleplay as a corpo-loving jackass, guess what? He’s gonna have the exact same voice as my nomad character. Not only does this game not allow you to make meaningful decisions, it doesn’t even give you the courtesy of having what little decisions you CAN make even superficially feel different. This is further compounded by the second problem: not showing the full dialogue option. Again, just like in Fallout 4, Cyberpunk 2077 makes the baffling decision to not show the full dialogue option before you choose it. Numerous times, I’d pick an option I read one way, only for the FULL line to come off the complete opposite way, prompting a very annoyed reload. I have to imagine this was done to reduce the amount of reading players would have to do, but I want to read! I want to know the full context of what I’m gonna say in this game where, supposedly, what I say impacts the world! The truth is, a vast majority of what you say is flavor text, with actual decisions being relegated to the end of the game, once the developers know you’ve thoroughly enjoyed their roller coaster. You can choose how the ride ends, and you can do so in spectacular fashion, but everything up to that point is premeditated. It’s disappointing, and can lead to some genuinely infuriating narrative moments. Take the Voodoo Boys mission, for example. Placide has made it abundantly clear that you, an outsider, are worth nothing to them beyond this single job that mutually benefits both parties, so it comes as no surprise that Voodoo Boys betray you. I chose to trust Placide during the mission, and when I was betrayed, I thought it was awesome! It made perfect sense for them to cut out this loose end tracing them back to the job, and I was excited to now go back to their hideout and have to fight them to get what I want! Except, that’s not what happens. You step outside the mall, where two of Placide’s goons are waiting for you. They call Placide, informing him you survived. I assumed I was too slow to kill them, and you could prevent them from calling Placide if you’re fast enough, but, no, they’re immortal! They even offer to DRIVE you to Placide, after which, you have a sheepish conversation where Placide goes “erm… what the scallop?” and then Brigitte shows up and continues like nothing happened. I ended up reloading the save and siding with the Netwatch guy, and you know what changed? NOTHING. Johnny makes fun of you for choosing this option, almost like the devs laughing at you for expecting player impact in their narrative RPG, the two guys Placide sent still drive you back, and then you have the SAME conversation with Placide, only now, he’s a little upset. Hell, you can even PUNCH Placide, only for Brigitte to interrupt the conversation the exact. same. way. Why even give me the option when it’s ultimately meaningless? I waited ages to get this game after seeing the debacle of the launch. I can confidently say though, that the game is nearly unrecognizable as a buggy beast. I'll grant it's crashed once over 60 hours and had maybe 5-6 moment's of freezing that it recovered from. But overall runs solidly, no major issues. Which is to completely switch to what surprised me the most about the game- the writing is seriously good. I haven't cared this much about side characters in a while. I've described the game as a cross over between skyrim and GTAV, which isn't really fair to the writing of any of those 3. The quests in this game unapologetically hit on heavy topics, say their piece (usually also presented beautifully), and make you sit with it. It leaves me wanting more. Makes me consider the role of the rpg so much more. It's frankly criminal that a game whose characters have obviously been built with nothing short of love to have fallen by the wayside. Like, if you're a lit major, it won't rock your world- but to everybody else it's an easy contender for top 10 or so in its class. Literally perfect game? No. Do I have complaints and things I'd tweak? Yeah. Do I advise anyone with a mere shred of hope in their heart for the good of humanity under crushing conditions give this game a whirl? YES.

Very good game. I 100%’d it and had a great time with it. The graphics are amazing, the soundtrack is great, and Night City is easily one of the best parts of the game. The worldbuilding is excellent and the city really does feel alive. Path Tracing in particular looked incredible, and this was definitely one of the first times I was genuinely taken aback by how far video game graphics have come. Driving down the highway at night with all the neon lights everywhere while it was raining, seeing all the reflections on the road, was honestly something to behold. I played with DLSS Quality and Frame Generation and had no complaints there, other than my PC turning into an oven half the time lol. I also really liked how memorable a lot of the side missions were. One minute you’re getting involved in some religious cult sacrifice, and the next you’re talking to a friendly vending machine. Stuff like that made the game stand out and kept it interesting the whole way through. I did run into some glitches during my playthrough, but nothing even close to how bad it was at launch. The driving is also something that took me a little time to get used to because a lot of the cars felt weirdly floaty, almost like GTA IV floaty driving. It was not a huge deal, just something I had to adjust to. I was also a little disappointed by the radio stations since there were only one or two songs I actually liked. I also really wish there was a third-person option outside of driving, but I do understand why the devs wanted the full experience to be in first person. Still, it was nice being able to drive in third person, so I’m glad that was at least an option. Overall though, this game has a ton of content and is absolutely worth playing. I also highly recommend getting Phantom Liberty because it’s easily one of the best DLCs out there. If you like open world games, cyberpunk settings, multiple endings, and choices that actually matter then this is a no brainer. Easily one of the top 10 single-player games I’ve played.

Night City feels alive now, especially after all the updates. This is the version the game should’ve been at launch, and it’s honestly one of my favorite games at this point. Playing as V, you begin to notice parallels all around. The cyberware, the gigs, and the fixers are more than just gameplay systems. The combat feels good, builds are actually fun to use, and there’s enough variety to keep things interesting. The characters and side jobs do a lot of the heavy lifting, way more than the main story at times. If you loved Edgerunners, this game becomes more than just an RPG; it turns into an extension of that emotional experience. If you played the game first, the anime adds a layer of meaning that makes a second playthrough even more impactful. If you’ve seen Edgerunners, you’ll get more out of it. If not, it’s still an amazing game. Welcome to Night City. Just don’t expect a happy ending.

Like a lot of people, I bought this game early on and put it down fairly quickly, deciding I'd come back to it after some patches fixed the myriad of bugs. I actually ended up forgetting about it and moved on to other things, only coming back to it recently when I saw the drama surrounding the VR mod. As an Oculus owner, I thought I should grab the mod before its gone and give it another try - as it turns out its been over 5 years since I had uninstalled the game awaiting a patch. The game on its own in flat I'm sure would be great, but in VR, it is honestly a masterpiece or close to it. Definitely the best VR experience I have had to date. Experiencing life in Night City in VR is really something. In VR, you can really appreciate the level of detail the developers put in to the world. Sometimes to get to missions I would simply walk or take the metro, just so I could experience and explore the city fully. Generally in a game like this, I would only drive. In addition to the world detail you can take in through VR, the story and emotions within it hit harder to. The game is well written, and the voice actors do an excellent job with their line delivery - but in VR, it enhanced even more. In the dog eat dog world of Night City, there are some tough choices, and I found myself thinking about them long after after I put down the headset. Looking the characters in the eyes while events you put in to motion start to unfold, also carries a lot more impact in VR as well. All in all, I really enjoyed this game. I hope the legal and community attention the VR mod got gets CDPR to have native VR support for the next game in this universe. In order to play the game in VR on my rig, I used a variation (a bit lower) of the Hardware Unboxed optimized settings. It is a resource hog, but even on lower settings it still looks great in VR.

I have played this game periodically since it was first released and I admit, it filled a gap in genres that I needed. This game has such depth - the story line, the choices, the customizability. The graphics are beautiful. The NPCs are people you sincerely grow to care about. And you can taste the fall of civilization in every image. The depravity, the hopelessness. The projects. People dying on the streets near crowds. The killers and the mad. It grabs you viscerally. But the endings? I took a wrong turn one night in dialog and my character made a decision that erased all other futures. After400+s of hours on her, it was shocking. The credits started to roll and I burst out crying. I haven't played since. That ending was so well done, with other characters giving emotional vignettes. I am still upset about it. That moment is stark across my mind, even over a year later. I suspect I could reverse the outcome if I tried, but the emotional scarring is deep. This is one of maybe 5 titles I can say that hit that deep. The best thing I can say is that the game is still a masterpiece, even for all that I cannot play it anymore.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those rare gaming experiences you don't come across often. I didn't play it at launch. I waited, took my time and man, it was worth it. Even now, after playing it on GeForce Now, PS5 and PC, I am still enjoing every minute of it. The game takes a little time fully open up, so be patient. But once it does, it builds a world that completely pulls you in. Night City isn't just a city, it's a experience. Visually, the game is on another level. Even after hundreds of hours, it still manages to impress. I dare to argue, you won't find any other game that delivers this level of detail and atmosphere, especially if you are running it on high-end settings with ray tracing. The game isn't just a visual showcase though - the storytelling is what will really stay with youl. The characters, the tone, the way everything connects... it leaves a lasting impact. The only real downside is that it raises your standards. After this, very few games hit the same level. Huge respect to the developers and everyone involved. This is a game I will keep coming back to.

Considering its shaky, turbulent and, at times, broken start in late 2020, early 2021, you'd be well justified to write Cyberpunk off as all hype; a AAA game completely failing to live up to its potential. How things can radically change with the eb and flow of time. In this case, entirely for the better. For someone who grew up with and was moulded by narratively driven behemoths, the likes of Metal Gear Solid, Mass Effect and Fallout, Cyberpunk is well and truly shoulder-to-shoulder with the absolute best. Everything from the world building to the aesthetics, the ambience to the choices, both pivotal or otherwise, all come together seamlessly to build a fully immersive RPG experience that may well linger with you long after you've completed the game. So many of the characters are remarkably realistic; relatable, flawed, conflicted, haunted by their pasts and each having their own individual motives driving them to their fate... including you, V. Cyberpunk isn't your typical surface-level RPG. It makes you painfully aware of the fact that every choice, both of yours as well as those around you, has a cost... not just within the world of Cyberpunk but in life as well. Some choices cost too much. Some will cost your freedom but some may set you free. I can't stress enough that, although the base game on it's own is incredible, it is genuinely incomplete without Phantom Liberty. Still not sure? Watch the music video for Phantom Liberty by Dawid Podsiadło. It's so outstanding that it belongs in a Bond movie. No joke, it is truly breath-taking. Finally, you will almost certainly feel bittersweet once the story is over. If, like me, you're something of a completionist with RPGs and you want to finish Cyberpunk 2077 in the best possible way, save "The Star" ending for last. Trust me.

Cyberpunk 2077 had one the roughest launches in recent memory. Unfinished, buggy, hated. Deservedly so. Today? It's an absolute powerhouse. Edgerunners broke me and made me crave more of Night City. After swearing off the dumpster fire, I dove back in after a few years. It was absolutely worth it. Night City is absurd, alive, and dripping with personality. The slang, the culture, the overwhelming feeling of dystopia - it all clicks and works flawlessly. It screams a perfect parallel to a world ran by unsatiated corporations, a world that could exist in an alternate reality. The story was crafted with such care and attention to detail. Relationships hit hard. Motivations rest in morally grey areas and every character has justification that feel real. Your own choices have weight and the consequences hit like a freight train. Johnny Silverhand is a dope mf and a standout. V and Johnny clash, argue, and evolve together. Sometimes you hate him, sometimes you respect him. That's the point. He's a poignant reminder of what this world is and what happens when you fight the corporations. Combat is insanely crispy and chaotic. Apogee Sandevistan + Byakko with a sneaky throwing knife was unhinged and so much fun. Not to mention, the movement felt buttery. I found myself scaling every possible skyscraper and pushing the limits of what the game would allow. (Incase you're curious, Mega Buildings are the only skyscrapers with solid, climbable assets through and through) The story of Phantom Liberty lives up to the standards already set by the main game. Dogtown is fine, but the story slaps. Every ending is justified and only further reveals the twisted and pervasive nature of Night City. Cyberpunk went from a disappointing laughingstock to legend. $60 in 2026 is still worth every cent. Night City will grab you by the throat, drag your through hell, and refuse to let go.

Despite all the crap I am going to say about it- I simply love this game. This game is throughout quite an immersive and fun experience, that is ocasionally ruined a little bit with the hicups caused by some tedious issues. The story, while it explores tropes that are typical to this genre - it does it quite well. Colorful (maybe too much during daytime) yet dark, near altfuture, urban dystopia. Society indulged, obsessed and drained both with consumerism and sex. Uploading the very soul to the net. Exploring the topics of afterlife, leaving a mark in the world, identity and fighting with the system. Characters are well written, they fit in perfectly and so does the dialogue. There is a lot of memorable quests and peeps, especially among the main cast. I love both Johnny's and V's characters, their relationship and how they interact with eachother. Kudos to English female V voice actress, her performance was amazing. Graphically it is stunning. The lights, effects, sounds, atmosphere, weapons, buildings and especially car models - all of this builds up the world almost flawlessly. Night City does look and feel authentic. The music is spot on, both in the game's soundtrack and it's radio track selection - they literally did a 10/10 job here, especially with the Samurai bits. But... Sadly this whole immersive experience can be broken by the bugs that persisted in this game over the years. You can spot civilians phasing through walls, multiple car models being stuck on top of or inside each other, enemies shooting you through some walls, animations/scripted events not playing correctly or at all. One of the more annoying bugs that I remember from when I first played the game ~5 years ago was "clown boots" - the game loops the sound of the crushing bottles as your footsteps when you first walk on them in specific area during the Evelyn questline and it doesn't stop unless you restart the game... Luckily I didn't run into anything that was game breaking or soft locking my progress. The game also flatlined like two times for me. Yet it is still disappointing seeing that those old issues weren't fixed, despite devs supporting the game and pushing new updates over the years. Bugs are very rare, yet they are there. It also feels that the further you go from the start of the game, there is less of them. AI could also be better as it is very basic. Civilian behaviour feels mostly like an "A" than an "I". On top of everything the police is not a threat at all. You can lose a tail in mere seconds and it feels like they are not even interested in chasing you. Whats also a bit wild is that pedestrians tend to jump under your wheels for no reason, as if they were trying to avoid your vehicle... in the wrong direction.., even if you were not a threat to them to begin with. And then, there is a Sinnerman quest - an absolute joke... I would still strongly recommend getting this game. It's not without its flaws, but it is truly a great experience. It also does hold a replayability value with the build variety, some choices you make during the story and it has a mod support. Just keep in mind that you will eventually encounter bugs that will make the world of the game less believable to you. Would bomb Saka tower again tho.

Do you like big, open-world games and bleak, dystopian science fiction films? Do you like good storylines where decisions affect the outcomes? Do you like to spend a lot of time killing people and driving/racing many vehicles with very different handling characteristics? Are you into body modifications, nudity, sex scenes and extreme profanity? Do you want to lose weeks of your life in a deeply immersive environment that keeps bringing you back for more? If so, you've found the right game. Blending elements of Blade Runner, Mad Max (game and movies), Brazil, GTA, Fallout, Read Dead Redemption it is a visual treat from start to finish. You'll need a fairly decent PC if you want to have all the graphics settings maxed out but it's definitely worth it. The storylines are good and most of the main characters are well-developed and interesting enough to make you care about their survival. There were a few minor glitches evident in my first play through (e.g. candles burning under water and cops spawning out of thin air) but most seem to have been fixed in subsequent patches. The Phantom Liberty expansion adds a few hours of gameplay and more variety to the storytelling and is a worthy addition to the main game. Explore vast areas and experience many different settings, each with their own clans and vibes. Gameplay varies from relaxed and serene to full on madness, so there's something for everyone. Well, not everyone. With sex, nudity, violence, drugs and a lot of very strong language, this is a game best played when there are no young kids around. If you value your job and/or family time, you may want to set the alarm on your phone to drag you back into the real world every now and then. I played this on a Windows PC using an Xbox controller and that worked fine, although the controls could sometimes be a little fiddly. I have completed it twice, exploring different storylines and experiencing two very different endings. After 188 hours in the game I'm ready to play something else for while, but I will revisit this in the future. It's absolutely brilliant and highly addictive. 9/10. It lost a point for the occasionally frustrating controls.

I was a few years late to this game so I missed the car crash launch. It actually ran really well for me, albeit on GeForce Now because the graphics were well beyond my elderly rig. I absolutely loved the setting - Night CIty feels so alive in all of its seedy, dystopian glory - the gunplay, stealth and hacking elements of gameplay as strong and above all, the characterisation, branching storylines and worldbuilding are really compelling. There are a few features that I would really have liked to see - like car customisation and V's origin story actually mattering beyond a few dialogue options here and there. The biggest issue for me though is how the stories all end; I was expecting it to end GTA/Witcher 3 style so that once the main story is done you are free to just noodle around the world, find all the hidden stuff and finish the many, many side quests that feel too small to bother with because the main story is so urgent. Unfortunately, CDPR didn't go for that and (no spoilers) whatever happens you just get teleported back to the beginning of the final section of the main quest. It's a real shame because the game is so immersive that it feels immersion-breaking to stop and do all the trivial stuff on the way. And the DLC doesn't correct that either. The game is still a great game, but it would've had considerably more longevity had CDPR retained a properly open post-endgame experience.

This is a tough one to rate. Trying this 5 years after release, with hardware that allows me to experience it in path traced glory on a 4K OLED monitor, I did initially enjoy the novelty of looking at those neons at night and the way light bounces off of of high resolution skin textures. However, the game makes me feel awfully empty, and the world while big, is barren, with very little that can be done in it that isn't a subset of repetitive actions. Combined with the dystopian setting, and the game being pretty big, playing it feels.. lonely for the lack of a better term. I'm a sucker for large open world games and great graphics, so on paper this was supposed to be a win. But I find myself just not enjoying playing with it, not enjoying interacting with the world in its extremely limited capacity, or the few unique characters that last beyond specific missions. Despite 5 years passing since launch, I still fell through the ground for the game to crash hours into my playthrough. Despite those same 5 years passing, and there being some more cars, weapons, it feels like the content added is fairly mundate, adding inconsequential type of novelty. I was able to make the world a bit more interesting with mods, as 5 years allowed the community to produce quite a bit. And while the most ambitious can add some things to do, they can't address the fundamental issue of how uninterractable and barren the world feels. The negative rating isn't a reflection of the bugs or technical prowess of the developers, which they have demonstrated. The game looks good and generally plays at a C+ reliability level. Totally acceptable if the game was actually fun. But most of it is doing the same few things slightly differently dozens of times. The big city serves little purpose beyond providing a distance you need to drive between places where you do those things. Interesting things happen just during finite missions, and then they end, and the world is unexciting again. If something happens, it's usually a one-time scripted event where you just watch it. There is a whole lot of filler to make the city appear like a city-ish, but you can't do anything with it. And it leads to an experience that isn't particularly fun, and it isn't as enjoyable as the other large open world games that either add interactivity, or at least introduce pleasant worlds to make up for it. I don't hate this game - I felt indifferent and slightly more negative with each hour spent in the game feeling like more and more of a waste of time on something that didn't feel fun, and I will likely not complete the story, as it feels like too much commitment to something that surprisingly doesn't spark joy.

It's OK. Yes the graphics are fire, yes Night City is dense. Combat is fine - you won't get your souls kick here, but it's not bad. I guess I was expecting it to be more distinct from typical RPGs (beyond the aesthetics, which are great). What I found was a very polished standard RPG wrapped up in a few standout ideas that weren't fully realized. The voice acting is good. Panam and Judy feel like real people I actually wanted to do things for, which helps the immersion. But, then you can 'hack' a fuel container to explode because it's on the internet for some reason. Oh, and every combat encounter will have near a dozen of those fuel containers sitting around for reasons. Loot is abundant. Overwhelmingly so. Most of it is junk. Driving is iffy... better on a bike (this is the part I liked best) since there are no windshield frames to block your vision. You can listen to your radio and cruise (peak vibes), but if you do it regularly you will see that there is like no traffic - certain nothing like big city traffic - and you need to keep watching the minimap to know where to go instead of the road or the cityscape. Not bad. If you like skill-tree RPGs with many mini enemy camps, abundance low quality loot, and tons of side quests this will definitely be a great fit! I was expecting something else tho, and I guess that may be on me.
