Cyberpunk 2077 on PC is almost a masterpiece. First off, the visuals are absolutely stunning. Night City looks insane—especially on a good PC. The lighting, reflections, and overall detail make the world feel alive and immersive. Gameplay feels just right. It’s not overly complex, but it gives you enough freedom to play how you want—stealth, aggressive, or a mix of both. It stays fun without becoming frustrating. The story is solid. Not mind-blowing, but definitely not bad either. It keeps you engaged, and the characters and choices make it worth playing through. One thing to note—progression can feel grindy. If you really want to level up and unlock the best upgrades, you’ll need to put in the time. Combat? No major complaints. Gunplay feels good, skills are fun to use, and overall it’s satisfying. Bugs still exist, but nothing too game-breaking (at least in my experience). You’ll notice them here and there. Overall, despite a few flaws, Cyberpunk 2077 delivers a fantastic experience. If you’ve got the hardware, it’s definitely worth playing.

[b]Note:[/b] Didn’t play much vanilla. I mostly used a visually upgraded + QoL-rich mod pack. [h1]PROs:[/h1] ✅ Large and unique world ✅ Plenty of lore from various sources ✅ Great modding community ✅ Visuals can be amazing with modding ✅ Lots of small details and collectibles in the world ✅ Solid OST ✅ Lots of viable playstyles ✅ Plenty of fun easter eggs to find ✅ Driving system felt pretty good (even though I probably had mods improving it) ✅ Panam ;) [h1]CONs:[/h1] ❌ Still a lot of bugs even with mods that fix various issues ❌ Broken HDR (needs a mod to fix) ❌ Vanilla lacks a lot of QoL features ❌ Heavily relies on ray tracing for a lot of its beauty (world is filled with screens and reflective surfaces, especially indoor clubs and city centers) ❌ Maxed difficulty still feels pretty casual ❌ A lot of side missions became way too samey (go in, do the thing, go out) [h1]Comments:[/h1] Another disclaimer: I didn’t even finish the main story, so my thoughts are based on a limited playthrough. Sadly, I lost interest pretty quickly because most sessions started feeling very forced. Long story short — this game just wasn’t for me. Cyberpunk worlds are usually packed with drugs, sex, low morals, heavy violence, ugly augmented people and chaos. (which I don't mind if done in a way I enjoy it) This game does an excellent job diving deep into that theme with insane amounts of detail, a huge world, and tons of lore. Still, I’d rather play Skyrim. If you enjoy FPS/RPGs in a Cyberpunk setting, it delivers a great world with lots of build variety and many ways to approach objectives. There are endless stories and characters to discover. However, even though many characters have deep background lore, I didn’t find most of them likeable. Almost every character I met I genuinely didn’t care about. Silverhand was entertaining at the start thanks to his crazy personality and Keanu’s voice, but he quickly became an annoying, deluded, self-righteous punk. His speeches turned moronic fast. Visually the base game looks decent, but you need a bunch of mods (plus ray tracing in certain areas) to get that real “wow” eyegasm. Combat felt oddly easy for the most part. My stealth + power sniper build didn’t help with that easy feeling — I could just snipe everyone through walls from outside the building when I didn’t feel like sneaking. In the end I was mostly doing checkbox hunting from point A to B and felt more exhausted than excited. Driving around the city was genuinely nice though. I gave this game a shot mainly because I really loved the Cyberpunk Edgerunners anime. In the end, the lore, the characters, and the overall feel wasn't simply my cup of tea. It’s definitely a good game (aside from the jank and bugs), it just wasn’t the right fit for me. Short comment: I started playing Cyberpunk 2077 at the end of 2025. The game is very enjoyable, however there is a lot of room for improvements. The dark world in the game is very tragic, but also a good warning for possible future. I would honestly score the game as strong 9/10 (Modded) and 7/10 (without any mods). Huge thank you for CDPR for making ability to create mods, as they really help with minor inconveniences that Cyberpunk 2077 has. My take on the game details: Gameplay: 10/10 Graphics: 9/10 Performance: 8/10 Mechanics: 7/10 Main game finish time: ~ 340h (All gigs, all ncpd, cyberpsychos, exploration, main story (Temperance) + PhantomLiberty DLC (King of Wands)) Mods I used: Skip intro, Lizzy Braindances, Enhanced Romances, change of color for arms cyberware - we can say all are cosmetic, not changing gameplay. Detailed description(Contains spoilers): Very interesting dark world scenario in possible near future. Multiple warnings and truths about possible dark scenarios with usage of AI, big corporations and people just trying to survive. It is still hard to believe that our MC dies no matter what, but the whole road to death of V is very interesting. The world is corrupted, twisted and basically all residents of Night City are evil, with maybe very few exceptions(like River, seems he was one of very few that actually were not bad). When it comes to gameplay - it is really cool. Multiple interesting aspects, details, fun interactions. Multiple options for most of gigs. Fun action gameplay with a nice scenery to it. Graphically the game is pretty nice, with only some drawbacks, but it is for sure one of highest standards. When it comes to performance, the game has hiccups on my 12GB RTX2060 dual by Palit. Of course for enjoyment of gameplay I turned off unnecessary things like DLSS, raytracing and rendered native. Nonetheless with native rendering it was working fine with around 70fps, with AI frame generation using AMD FSR it reaches target that was interesting me of 120fps at most times, however as it is with frame gen - sometimes it creates artefacts. I wish the performance would be good enough to last at 100-120fps without AI frame generation, but nowadays engines it's quite hard to achieve. Game mechanics are pretty interesting and very likeable, with some exceptions. I really hoped that clothes and "legendary" items would prevail, but now I can see that the system lacked a lot of options and Damage over time was not actually implemented as long-time damage over time I always seek in games. Level scaling for statistic check is quite terrible in my opinion and should never be implemented. Overall I enjoyed the game, had a lot of fun with it and might come back to it to finish with other endings some time, try out new builds, enjoy graphics and sing pon pon ♥♥♥♥. This game surely is one of a kind and honestly I am glad I did not play it at launch time, as I would not enjoy it as much. A lot as I see has changed, most of it for good - maybe except for some pre 2.0 mechanics. Tragic story in tragic city with tragic people and tragic outcomes, crime is everywhere, AI takes over the world behind the scenes, corporations treat people like crap, government treats people like crap, it is very relatable to Real Life 2026 and this game shows a good warning on what direction might all of this take. That's all from me, see you around, chooms!

TLDR: Play if you want to experience the power fantasy of a professional mercenary fighting for their life in a bleak dystopia, with an amazing story that has some pacing issues In this game you play as V, a mercenary who lives in a dystopian hellhole that is Night City, whose attempt at becoming a legend lands them in a whole lot of trouble. Your job is to fix that. The story is actually really well told, and you experience it entirely from the first person perspective and they put a lot of work into making it feel as immersive as possible. The writing of characters makes them sound like actual people, the factions feel believable and the slang actually feels natural instead of tacked on. The world, as mentioned, is pretty damn bleak. Rampant capitalism has made most people miserable and everyone tries to find a way to cope. The game does actually do a great job at hammering that point home, sometimes a bit hamfisted, but often in pretty subtle ways. The first time I realized my apartment had a mandatory adscreen in the middle of the living area it started to feel a lot less like a home, and nobody will even comment on that. And of course violence, drug abuse and sexual exploitation is everywhere. There is however the issue that this world is also very "set". You are not going to fix that (spoilers I guess), fine, but you are also going to have very little to no impact at all. Tons of side quests give you all sorts of decisions to make with interesting moral questions to ponder, but rarely does this have any affect but a slightly different quest reward or an angry voice call afterwards because things ended in tragedy - there are no happy endings in Night City - that it feels like a follow up was missing or you are playing an abandoned storyline. Outside of quests, if you start running people over you might trigger the police in a GTA style star system of escalations, but remain undetected for a minute and things turn back to normal. Similiarly, you can gun down a group of thugs belonging to a big gang and nobody ever will care about that, with the gang behaving just as before towards you. So this game is more about the powerfantasy of the moment to moment gameplay. And my God is that well done. You can play all sorts of drastically different builds, like a hacker that infiltrates hideouts and triggers the grenades carried by every enemy, some shotgun wearing juggernaut that guns everything down, or a cyber ninja who parries bullets. The game lets you try everything out to find your perfect build, and if you know what you are doing your late game V is going to feel like a demigod of Night City. Before you buy though, there is one big issue, bigger even than the non-responsive world. At the release of the game, that would have been the technical state, but nowadays CDPR managed to fix it that it runs mostly stable - still, save when possible. Now, the main issue is the pacing. The game is structured to work with quest chains, where the main story paths, the excellent DLC story and important side stories (like the ones of Vs allies) get tons of quests, and each finished one triggers the start of the next. That works like every RPG ever. What is different that the beginning of the follow up quest often happens after a certain amount of time. So you will crash through a gang hideout, extract some data, send that to Vs friend, they will say that this will take some time to look through and they will message you once they have something. You can do something else in the meantime, and granted, you always have a full quest log, your phone constantly gets bombarded with new quests to take. The issue is if you found what you were doing really interesting and would like to continue that questline. So you wait 24 ingame hours. You wait another 24. You do another gig or five. You look up the wiki and read that the next quest step should trigger roughly 24 hours later, but at this point it has been an ingame week. This gets frustrating, because there seem to be triggers for quest updates, but they only update one quest per update, so you are at the mercy of RNGesus that you can continue the quest chain you found interesting. There also seems to be some priority with the main quest chains, which makes sense, but also means you only get to see some cool side content you would have liked to see earlier only after the main questlines have been exhausted until the point of no return. Which usually happens in the first third of my runs. A certain character is waiting a long time in the Embers, tell you that. This issue with the quest progression triggers has no clear answer. You'll find all kinds of theories on what triggers progression online, from restarts, to specific elevators to take, to just standing still next to water for 5 minutes. The Mechanicus ain't got ♥♥♥♥ on the Cyberpunk community when it comes to esoteric tech solutions. Still, if you can deal with the fact that some quest chains will just have an inconsistent pacing, you are rewarded with an amazing - if depressing - story, superb gameplay and overall a unique cyberpunk experience.

Honestly, I never review games. But given the amount of hours I've spent within Night City, I feel almost obligated. I played since launch, and personally I had no bugs throughout the entire playthrough, I finished the game, that was that. I thoroughly enjoyed my time and thought that would be the end of it. Well, I was wrong. It ended up being a complete masterpiece in my book. Graphics wise, I have - by modern standards - a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pc with a 1650 (I love you really). However, how a game this beautiful, diverse, vertical and detailed runs so well on medium settings is beyond me. It ran okay on launch and has since only gotten more stable. The soundtrack in this game is insane. I'm not really referring to the songs on the radio, though I think they're pretty damn good too, but the ambient soundtrack is brilliant. If I ever put the Spotify playlist on, all of those songs have emotional nostalgic weight attached to them, because they play at such traumatic in-game events. Also I really enjoy the combat music, gets me super hyped. On the topic of combat, I recall when the game released some reviewers not enjoying it. While I believe in 'to each their own' I couldn't really understand it. For me the gunfights are extremely satisfying, especially handguns, with most all weapons feeling really *punchy* when you fire. Melee has seen a massive improvement since launch and is as fun as the gunfights. However, I could never let go of my quickhack deck for a melee something more melee focused like a sandevistan, as I feel you're missing out on a massive aspect of the combat by not using them (quickhacks). Anyways, combat = awesome. Story - what can I say. Story is phenomenal. Even in instances where the choices don't necessarily matter, you really think about what you want to say carefully. I honestly think the forced first person perspective really enhances this feeling of weight and immersion that you'd lose out on with the third-person so many are clamouring for (though I think it could be cool, first person really works well). By the end of the story, when making the final few decisions, I really sat with myself to consider what I thought was morally right, and as very few games have done that, it gets top marks in my book. Also the DLC credits roll had me feeling all types of complex feelings about it. I think since launch the devs did some good work towards immersion. Initially there wasn't a lot you could necessarily do to engage with the world, but they've since added in some stuff like being able to go to the bar and have a drink (animated). Do I think there could be more? Absolutely. Mods fixed that for me, added loads of immersion spots, being able to lean, sit, smoke, drink anywhere. For this I simply can't rate it too highly, as if it were great already I wouldn't have sought mods to fix it. I suppose I should go into more detail as I already mentioned it, but yes, mods are pretty great for this game. Don't get me wrong, it's not competing with a bethesda title for the types of game changing/overhauls mods, but Cyberpunk has some pretty great ones. A lot of the gameplay ones I used altered things very slightly, as I felt the gameplay was already great and I had no real desire to change anything about that, except for adding in survival aspects like eating, drinking, sleeping and nerve (which gives you tremors/ptsd). Plenty of gooner mods too (a lot actually), but I think you'll find whatever mod you would probably want (except the third person mod, that's still super janky). The performances of all actors are all solid. The weakest performance for me is Keanu Reaves, but I've never thought he was a particularly good actor. However, he grows on you, and he for sure has some great moments and monologues. One thing I noticed on my second playthrough that I did not appreciate enough the first time I played was the body language. This is where I think third person would take away from the performances. With your little optical eyes, you can zoom in at will, and you start to notice during conversations with NPCs their body language is as good as the vocals. Honestly can't think of another game that's done it this well. Maybe RDR2? But the difference here is there's never a set cutscene. It's all first-person, all the way through, the interaction with a random NPC will be as cinematic as the most climatic moments, but it just works so well due to the performances (and the script I suppose). Last comment is the fashion aspect. It's good. I enjoyed it. Especially when they removed the classic RPG "wear the things with the highest stats" so you end up looking ridiculous. Also it didn't make a lot of sense that in a universe with cyberwear, completely cybernetic bodies, that the real defining from gunfire is a hi-vis vest. Really not sure what else to say. I like the shooting, I like the soundtrack, I like the story, I like the city, I like I can enhance the whole experience with minimal mods, and photomode (which I mentioning only now) is very well done. 10/10

I have roughly 80~ hours on this game, coming from PS4 before moving everything over to PC. There are only a handful of bugs, but compared to 1.8.3 to current? It's so, so much better. The gameplay is much smoother and runs so much better. But that's not what I want to talk about. When I first started playing this game a couple months ago, my first impression, upon completing the game, was that it lacked in the story. Going in, I was expecting anti-consumerism and anti-capitalism/corporation themes, and they are indeed there, but not the fore front. I finished the game, complained about it to my girlfriend, then came back and played a few more times, getting a few more endings. That's when I realized what the game is also trying to point out. Yeah, yeah, consumerism narrative or whatever, but I don't mean that, I mean V, your player. Post prologue, V has everything ripped from them. Closest friend, they had trust taken and broken, they died and came back and now are stuck with a rockerboy terrorist in their head that's trying to take over their body. The game has an artificial timer for this, but this is important to mention, the gameplay not forcing this timer is probably the most important to me. As you go through Night City, completing jobs, finding friends, partners, even developing your relations with Johnny, it all sets in, "you're on borrowed time, how will you spend it?" One ending, which I can barely consider it an ending as it is very abrupt (with the player's choice), you see everyone you met, rubbed shoulders with or were acquainted. Depending on the romance option you chose, they could be furious or broken. Friends torn inside, wishing things were different. Another ending, just, give in. Let the corporation win and what becomes of you? You abondoned everything you loved and had. In a sense, betrayal. This is coming from a girl who came out of a really bad drug addiction and is just getting out of frequent suicide ideation. On surface level, this game asks, "what makes you human," but digging deeper, paying attention to your playthrough, you're asked, "if you're on limited time, you die next week, what do you do? Do you pretend things are fine? Prolong your life at the expense of others and the experiences around you, or do you leave everything behind, abandon it all; leaving behind scars, damaging the people you built community with?" This game has many problems but its story isn't one of them. This game made me change my perception of what life is. From being nihilistic, hateful, I turned the spotlight and, sure some things didn't change but, my approach to life changed. There are a lot of things I could glaze this game for, a lot of themes I could beg and beg to become a reality. But the change that did happen, within me, I accept. This is a really, really great game. 20-50 hours per save gives you everything you need to experience this game in all aspects and I could not recommend it enough.

[h2]Look at my play time. I write this review with utmost confidence and personal experience. No BS included[/h2] [h1] TL;DR - Just play it [/h1] I played this game not long after its original release. Bugs, crashes and all. I still enjoyed it. The story was so different from anything I had played before, and the different builds I could use drew me in deeper. After diving deep into Cyberpunk 2077 and Phantom Liberty, I can confidently say this is one of best RPG experiences created. And with it's bad release, and fantastic comeback - that should be enough for you. [h2] Story [/h2] The story is nothing short of phenomenal. What starts as a tale of survival, quickly evolves into a deeply personal journey filled with moral dilemmas, unforgettable characters, and choices that genuinely matter and change the outcome of the story. The narrative grabs you early and never lets go. It’s layered, mature, and constantly evolving based on your choices. Phantom Liberty elevates this even further with a spy-thriller twist that feels intense, unpredictable, and emotionally grounded. It injects a tense espionage storyline that perfectly complements the base game’s themes of identity and control. It throws you into a horror-type scenario that keeps your heart pumping towards the end, or throws you into emotional despair. Did you, or did you not make the correct decision? Johnny Silverhand starts off as an abrasive, self-centered arse. He is loud, reckless, and seemingly impossible to trust. He constantly clashes with you, challenges your decisions, and feels more like a curse than a companion. But as the story unfolds, layers begin to peel back. You see his regrets, his failures, and the ideals buried beneath all that anger. By the end, depending on your choices, Johnny can transform into something genuinely meaningful: a loyal ally, a voice of hard-earned wisdom, and even a friend. That evolution - from intolerable to unforgettable - is one of the most compelling character arcs in the game. Night City itself is a masterpiece. It deserves its own spotlight. The world isn’t just big - it’s feels alive for the most part. Every district tells its own story through architecture, culture, and the people who inhabit it. Every alleyway, megabuilding, and neon-lit street corner feels handcrafted with lore and purpose. The world building is insanely detailed. From corporate power struggles to street-level desperation, making it feel like a real, breathing dystopia. Not to mention the views. I pressed F12 so many damn times in this city. [h2] Graphics [/h2] Visually, the game is stunning. The neon-soaked skyline, dense crowds, and dynamic lighting create a level of atmosphere that few games can match. Reflective rain-soaked streets, to the glow of holographic ads cutting through the night. The game delivers a consistently cinematic experience. Whether you’re cruising through the city at night or exploring its darker corners, it’s consistently breathtaking. [h2] Gameplay [/h2] Gameplay wise, the freedom is incredible. You can approach situations however you want - guns blazing, swords slashing, stealthy hacking, or something in between. The build variety is where the game truly shines: netrunners, cyber-enhanced melee monsters, precision snipers - each playstyle feels distinct and viable. Experimenting with different builds keeps the experience fresh even after dozens of hours. Don't forget about the mods, either. I sunk an extra 500+ hours with mods added alone. [h2] Endings - where your decisions matter [/h2] And then there are the endings. There’s no single “right” conclusion - just consequences shaped by your decisions throughout the game. None of them feel like an afterthought. Each ending feels meaningful, emotional, reinforcing the themes of identity, choice, and sacrifice. Cyberpunk 2077, especially with Phantom Liberty, has become the game it was always meant to be - and then some. It took some time for Projekt CD RED to live up to their promises for this game, but behold true beauty as of today. Definitely in my top 3 games of all time. [u]If you are looking for a crazy fun OP build, I'd recommend a Militech Sandevistan build with the Byakko katana (obtained through doing all of Wakako's gigs) with perks in deflect, dashing and everything relating to the Sandevistan. Funnest build I've made[/u] Absolutely worth your time and money. Absolutely

I think so much discussion at release focused on what a steaming pile of trash this game's code was that it distracted from both the good and the bad. As I finally visit this game with a complete playthrough well over 5 years later, with I suppose a good chunk of the problems fixed, I can weigh in objectively having never played this game at release time. First, this game is still horrifically buggy. People who say that the problems have been fixed are grading this on a curve versus the original release. Leaving the room where I flatlined the voodoo guy via the blackwall, I would, for example, be frozen in place while crouching and scope focused while stepping on a bit of conduit on the floor. That simple movement is still unsolved in some cases is glaring. I'm not going to go through all the bugs, just that this is still at a point that the problems are completely immersion breaking and required me to redo from saves many times. Secondly, Keanu Reeves is a horrifically unsuited for his role here. It was a cheap and tawdry way to promote the game to cast him as Johnny. Keanu excels when he can play someone who is completely overcome by awe (The Matrix) or a stoned idiot (Bill and Ted). These are some of my favorite movies. I don't hate him as an actor. But let's face it, he should be typecasted into a very specific kind of role which is not Johnny. Keanu Reeves cannot play an emotionally stagnant revolutionary displaced decades into the future. This role is much too nuanced for him, and his voice bits come off as overread and contrived in the manner of a high school theater production. It's embarrassing. This comes off to me as cheap PR that compromises the work. Which is sad, because there are many characters here that are so well acted and could have created a timeless emotive experience that was beloved as Skyrim, but they are overshadowed by Johnny's piss-poor dialogue reading. Anyways, the game is good enough. Play it.

This is, hands down, one of the best things I've ever played. It's got a huge, complex setting that's brilliantly and beautifully realized. It's got a story that stays engaging from start to finish. It's got characters so deep and well written that you actually end up caring about them. The player-character builds are astonishing. On my second playthrough I played a sort of cyber-ninja, all souped up to the point I could clear a room with just a katana and some throwing knives before anybody knew what was happening. It was genuinely an incredible experience. But here's one word of warning: don't try to be a jack-of-all-trades. This character system hugely rewards specialization, and specialized characters are so much fun that it's worth playing again and again just to have those different experiences across different specializations. That, and each playthrough is like a blast of nostalgia, and you get to see all those people and places you've missed. It ain't real life, but it'll do in a pinch. I rate this as one of the true masterpieces of gaming. Don't miss it.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best games of all time. It’s genre-defining in both its aesthetic and its story. As an ARPG with a full capital A. it gives you an immense amount of playstyle freedom in its action. You can be a stealthy rogue hacking everything, or a ruthless tank taking hits like it’s breakfast cereal. Or everything in between. That’s where the gameplay really shines, the sheer amount of customization in how your character works. It’s an RPG that becomes an immersive sim in its depth. This is tied together with one of the best stories in video games, especially for a game with a fully customizable main character. My V felt like a real extension of me, and I got so invested in the story because of the choices V gets put through. That's set alongside not just one of the best main characters in all of video games, but one of the best secondary leads too, Johnny Silverhand, played brilliantly by Keanu Reeves. But don't sleep on the rest of the cast either. close friends who genuinely feel like they care about V. To ambiguous fixers and morally grey but necessary allies. The world itself is stunning. It’s one of the best-looking games out there. There is not a single shot of the skyline that looks bad. It does cost your PC some performance, it's not a light game to run, but it runs well enough, even with full path tracing. The raw graphics are made even better by the art style, which the game nails to a T. Cyberpunk's aesthetic has never looked this realized. Everything, from cars and clothes, to buildings and weapons, fits perfectly. As a total experience of walking through a cyberpunk world, nothing beats Cyberpunk 2077. I really recommend this game. I know the launch game had heavy criticism, and a lot has changed since then. Updates have improved it massively, and the Phantom Liberty DLC is a must-play, adding an amazing side story. It's grown into a game that defines its genre, puts CDPR among the best game developers in the world, and creates a world I simply won't forget. A truly amazing game.

The Redemption of Night City (With Cavéats) I’ve been here since the beginning, and while Cyberpunk 2077 will be studied as a remarkable turnaround, we shouldn't forget that it launched two years too early. CD Projekt Red arguably got a "free pass" for a state they knew wasn't ready, but the current version of the game is finally something remarkable. The Good The World: Night City is visually outstanding. It is easily one of the most detailed environments ever put in a game, and it’s easy to get lost in the atmosphere. Build Variety: Spec-ing your character is a total joy. The game truly allows you to play how you want, making it incredibly approachable regardless of your preferred playstyle. Masterful Side Quests: Some of the darker, gloomier side stories are the best parts of the game. They are masterfully written and stand as great stories in their own right. Combat: Whether you're hacking or shooting, the combat loop is genuinely fun. The Bad The Writing: While the characters are mostly great, the dialogue can often be "cringe." V feels somewhat bland as a protagonist, and the character creation system still feels like it lacks meaningful impact. Navigation: As beautiful as the map is, it just isn’t fun to navigate. Its scale is impressive, but getting from point A to point B often feels like a chore. The "Arasaka" Irony: There is a lot of deserved love for the game now, but let's not forget the corporate decisions behind the launch. In the end, CDPR acted a lot like the megacorps they satirize. Verdict It’s not a solid 5/5, but the story and the sheer detail of the world keep me coming back. It is a must-play for the atmosphere alone, even if the "soul" of the protagonist and the dialogue occasionally miss the mark

This is a highly overrated game, essentially sci-fi GTA but worse. I bought this game because I read reviews and comments that described it as an open world RPG; some people commented that it is "like a science fiction Skyrim." I spent 4 hours creating my character and going through the tutorial stage; after I got into the world and saw this game for what it really is it was already too late to get a refund (denied twice). So I played it some more to give it a chance. This game is NOT an RPG. You are a pre-determined character that is just walking through a pre-set story on rails with a few possible different game endings. In one case I rescued an annoying monk from a gang who was going to give him cyberware against his wishes. I killed the gang to rescue him, and then he insults me saying I am worse than the gang members because I killed them. I immediately tried to kill him for insulting me like that, but the game wouldn't let me! I don't think this character is tied to a later quest, the game just refused to let me kill him because the game wants to force its morality onto you. The game is constantly pushing its moral message at you, your contacts always whine about you killing criminals and scum. Some cyber-freak could kill 20 people and then I go deal with him and he attacks me and I kill him. Then, my contact cries about it and harangues me. If this was an RPG, then I would be able to kill that stupid monk and I would just do missions for a different contact that appreciated my abilities. But this is not an RPG - you don't create your own identity, you don't make a character or even pick a name. You have hit points, you get to pick your appearance and you get to pick skills from a skill tree - that is not what it means to be a role playing game. The world is boring and repetitive. It's just a sprawling city of closed doors with nothing behind them (well, you can't even open most doors or buildings), except a few areas that are defined for the mission objectives.

While the world build was gorgeous and took a toll on my pretty good GPU, this game heavily relies on it while ignoring a basic timeline for all of its quests. It feels more like a sandbox game where youre allowed to complete gigs however you want instead of experiencing the urge that the main quest desired to show, mainly the MC not having enough time to live. Another thing that i dont understand is while the DLC gives us an alternate ending, i really dislike it when I had to load an older save file just to complete the original last main story quest. I also find that the main story quests are shorter than the DLC quests which is a bit weird because im used to playing story based games where the DLC is just an extension of the story, not a separate ending. Another thing that disappointed me was the fight against Adam smasher, maybe it was just my settings or me being accidentally to strong, but Ive had way harder gigs at the beginning than the fight against the infamous big boss who looked AMAZING in the anime. Its an alright game but by far not worth it to name it your favourite game. I just wish there was more story and cool fight scenes and not just me trying to find something to do in the game before meeting Hanako at Embers. The DLC is definitely necessary if you want to enjoy this world more, because the original game alone is too little. I reccommend this game simply to just see it for yourself and enjoy the beautiful world, not because the story is big or immersive.

Cyberpunk 2077 is an ambitious and unforgettable journey into a futuristic world that pushes the boundaries of open-world storytelling. Despite having faced a rocky launch, the game has grown into something truly special thanks to constant updates, improvements, and expansions that transformed the experience into one of the most immersive RPGs of this generation. From the very beginning, Cyberpunk 2077 impresses with its richly detailed setting: Night City. This vibrant megacity feels alive, unpredictable, and layered with stories waiting to be discovered on every corner. The world design is outstanding neon lights, towering skyscrapers, hidden back-alleys, bustling marketplaces, and diverse districts all contribute to an atmosphere that truly makes you feel like you’re living inside a cyberpunk dystopia. The narrative is one of the game’s biggest strengths. The story is deep, emotional, and filled with intriguing characters. Every major decision you make has weight — whether it’s how you handle a mission, how you approach a conversation, or how you shape your own version of V. There are moments of humor, moments of heartbreak, and moments of sheer intensity that make the entire arc unforgettable. Characters like Jackie, Johnny Silverhand, and Panam are memorable, and their personal journeys enhance the game’s emotional impact. Combat is dynamic, fluid, and highly customizable. Whether you prefer going in guns blazing, using stealth tactics, hacking enemies from the shadows, or crafting your own cyber-build, the game encourages different playstyles and rewards creativity. The cyberware system adds an extra layer of depth upgrading your abilities and modding gear feels incredibly satisfying, and it gives players a real sense of progression and personalization. Even years after release, Cyberpunk 2077 continues to impress with its visuals and performance on PC. With powerful hardware, the game looks striking detailed character models, particle effects, lighting, reflections, and atmospheric weather all contribute to making Night City feel breathtaking and alive. Night City’s ambient soundscape and soundtrack only deepen immersion, making nighttime runs through the streets unforgettable. Side content in Cyberpunk 2077 is also worth exploring. From small gigs to long-form quests, you’ll find a variety of stories that can surprise, entertain, and even challenge you sometimes even more than the main storyline. There’s always something interesting around the corner, and many of the side missions feel like fully fleshed out mini-stories. Cyberpunk 2077 is not just a game it’s an experience. It blends narrative depth, freedom of choice, stunning world design, and intense gameplay into a package that’s bold, thought-provoking, and incredibly engaging. If you enjoy games that let you dive into a rich story, customize your playstyle, and explore a huge, detailed world at your own pace, this title delivers on all fronts. It’s a testament to how far immersive RPG design has come.

Once again got it as a gift from a good friend, but it was a plan to get it either case as it is an amazing game. The review will be for both the base game and the Phantom liberty DLC, based on multiple playthroughs and exploring. First of all I will mention my setup as for this game that is really important and it gives more prospective, processor i7-12700K, 32GB DDR5 @6000 CL30, nvidia 5060 TI 16GB, installed on a nvme drive. The game was run on 1440p with DLSS 4.5 forced with path tracing enabled and frame generation x3 for most runs. [h3]Positives:[/h3] [list] [*]Well we have to start with the visuals, this game is extremely stunning with the visuals, on the first playthrough you will spend more time looking around than actually playing the game, it really dominates visually, especially with path tracing. [*]Attention to detail, you are going to notice it all over the place, especially small details that you would not expect. [*]The audio is the next thing that is also up there, and here the top place is for the prime example on how great it comes out when you get great voice actors, not to mention that the ingame radio has awesome songs, and the battle music really fits the whole atmosphere. [*]RPG elements are well made and balanced, you do get a bit overpowered but it fits the game lore perfectly. [*]Variety of weapons to use and there is something we haven't seen in other games, netrunning abilities, it adds a unique way of playing. [*]Map is big, with tons of things to do and explore, with many distinguish spots that look apart from each so you can feel that now you are in the different place. [*]A lot of vehicles to traverse the vast map, even though you have fast travel, you can use the auto driver feature to enjoy the scenery. [*]Many factions that are different in their looks, talk and way they react to you, each fixed in their own block with some overlaps. [*]And do not let me started with how many different unique characters you are going to meet in game, many are complex characters with twists. [*]Keanu Reeves - do I need to say more?! [*]Idris Elba - not as much bonding on the screen as Johnny, but he filled the role pretty good. [*]Story is great, it has all you need, ups, downs, twists, comedy, annoyances, rage, culminations, etc... it is nice that some choices do matter on the story. [*]You want to play guns blazing?! No one is stopping you, oh you prefer stealth, go ahead it is optimized for it, netrunning it more your thing?! Well you will be able to make some superb combos. I want to say, you can play any way you like there is no limit and the game is not hindering you if you do not play a meta build. [*]The game is extremely well optimized for fast pace movement and slow motion. [*]Multiple endings, each one being different and unique in it's nature, and the main thing that was a surprise, as I cannot recall the last game that had this, once you get to the ending you get to play a bit more afterwards to have that proper feeling that you reached the end. [*]I feel like this needs to be mentioned, as they are one of the proper good ones, the developers are CD project RED. [*]Modding!!! This is done pretty good, with full support on how to get into modding, so if you want to tinker around and learn to code a bit, it can be done, but it is easier to go on Nexus mods, and just download the ones that you like the most, more than 10000 mods available. ps You do need a an account there but it is free and fast to create. [*]There is a character creation, it has fairly good options to create unique looks. [*]Great option from the developers, you can enable mature filter and it will hide certain scenes and characters will have at least underwear, this is really good as without this you would not be able to stream on youtube for example many parts of the story for example. There is also an option to remove songs from the radio that are copyrighted. [*]Optimized for DLSS, FSR, XeSS, choose whichever based on which video card you have, you lose a bit of quality that you will not notice unless you are looking for it hard and in return you will gain a nice boost in fps ( depends from system to system and the ingame settings you are using ). [/list] [h3]Negatives:[/h3] [list] [*]It still has issues, none of these are game breaking in a sense that you cannot fix all of them by either restarting the game or reloading a save game. I did get 2 game crashes as there is still a memory leak issue, happens mostly if you teleport many many times in quick successions and once when I overdid it with forcing the mod to spawn more police. Sometimes your dashing will put you through the floor, sometimes kerenzikov will not work. [*]Have to mention this, there is a one big inconsistency with the story that bothers me, without spoiling it, you will figure it out once you replay it. [*]As mentioned above, attention to detail is always a double edged sword, if you add some things and then fail to make others that are expected to be working, not work... is jus disappointing. [*]Even though there is plenty of weapons to play with, it felt poorly optimized for this masterpiece, simple example once you find the one iconic that fits your play style that is the only thing you will use for, in some cases, 90% of the game. Weapon modding is also simplified, compared to how cyberware was done, this felt like -lets just add this as an option. Prime example - why give me a silencer for an AR or SMG, if you cannot use it as a stealth weapon, to hear it a bit less? To have a cooler sound when you shoot? [*]Takedowns could have been done better to add more variety. [*]You do get to create your own character, visually I mean, but it felt more of just being there as an option that leads nowhere as you do not get to see yourself at all, except at the endings. [*]This is a personal opinion based on very hard difficulty, but it is a bit biased as the playthroughs were consecutive, the fighting becomes boring because you do become too overpowered soon, especially if you explore around, it does fit the lore. I had to give myself additional tasks to make it interesting. [*]Some of the mods would be better if they were part of the game to begin with, once you add some of them you do not want to play it without them anymore. This is not a negative per say but more of a notice. [/list] [h1]VERDICT 9/10[/h1] Definitely a big [b]YES[/b]on this one, and by this one I mean both the main game and the phantom liberty, the DLC is a must, it not only adds to the levels and skills, but enriches the story on it's own, you do get a great storyception there that fits perfectly with the main game. If you want a futuristic GTA like game with a great story and awesome characters, that lets you play however you like playing without punishing you for it, this is the game for you then. The story is rich and filled with everything you would like to see, if you were watching a movie, but here you play the main protagonist. This might be a spoiler but hopefully not a big one, for me personally, I liked that there is no happy end, that is a such a great curve ball from many other games, and it fits the whole futuristic grim dystopia. Should you get this game if you cannot run ray tracing or path tracing? -YES, you should, the game is visually stunning even without those enabled, and yes being able to run either adds more to the visuals, but it is not that you are missing chunks of the game. If you need videos on how the game worked, looked, how the mods fit, look and work, you can check some of the videos on my profile, be warned for spoilers as they are part of playthroughs.

5+ years on from one of the most historically disastrous launches, Cyberpunk 2077 has become an experience that captivates and immerses the player in a world where nothing truly feels impossible. Not only is Night City itself one of the most fun game worlds I've ever explored, but the characters and gameplay possibilities therein give the game a sense of personality that keeps me wanting to come back and uncover every nook and cranny of it. I finished my first playthrough of CP2077 in a week and started a new one almost immediately - that alone should speak to how captivating the world here truly feels. This is not a game you play for only 30 minutes at a time. The game world is so immersive, in fact, that while fast travel is an option, I'd sooner jump into a car and drive from point A to point B than use a fast travel point. And I can't say the same about a lot of other open-world games I've played. Anyway, as far as the gameplay is concerned, it's heaps of fun overall. Being on my second playthrough at the time of writing this review, I've only barely scratched the surface as far as the build options at your disposal are concerned, and I'm looking forward to experimenting with many more different builds - I'm especially eager to try out a build that's less focused on direct combat. Now that isn't to say that the combat is bad - quite the opposite, in fact. It's all sorts of satisfying, especially once you settle into a set of perks and cyberware that synergize with your weapon(s) of choice. Prime example: blades + Berserk = *chef's kiss*. Now the game does still have some intermittent issues - NPCs are proper idiots sometimes, models and textures have trouble loading, the game might crash outright - but in my experience, game-breaking bugs have been very few and far between all things considered. CDPR definitely did their best to improve the game post-launch, and improve it they did. It's arguably the redemption arc of the decade, and they have my utmost respect for it. In the relatively short time I've actually been playing it, CP2077 has already become one of my all-time favorites, and I expect it to be no surprise why that is the case.

Three years ago, this game was a disaster, but today, after the 2.0 update and the Phantom Liberty expansion, it is a completely different product with great mechanics and a GOAT atmosphere. If you quit because of bugs back in 2020, now is the perfect time to come back. The new skill trees finally allow for real specialization because every point you spend actually changes how you move or fight, rather than just adding a tiny damage bonus. This makes every battle satisfying, whether you use a katana or hacking. The new cyberware system also limits how much gear you can install, which forces you to plan carefully since every choice has real consequences for your stats. Night City is immersive with its neon lights, and the new Dogtown area is even better than the original districts because it is more detailed and packed with content, so it no longer feels empty. The story in Phantom Liberty feels like a political thriller with complex characters like Solomon Reed and Songbird, making every moral choice difficult and heavy. The improved AI and new police system make the city feel alive, as it now reacts to your actions in a logical and challenging way. On the other hand, driving is still not great because cars slide too much, which is frustrating during fast chases. Also, some side activities can feel repetitive after many hours. Despite these small flaws, the graphics look amazing with path tracing, and the deep story makes this one of the best action RPGs on the market, so it is definitely worth buying the full bundle.

There are few times in my life where I play a videogame that feels like it was made for me. Like some time traveller went back in time and made this game to show me something. SPOILERS AHEAD [spoiler] The moment of epiphany came when I was doing the quest to find all of Delemain's vehicles. The 2nd part of the questline. Now I thought this was going to be some random completion quest, and at one point I even got so lost inside the air ducts of the facility I needed to look up a video to get me to the next room. When I got there, I was completely expecting to just kill the splinter personalities of Delemain and fix him, after all he'd been so good to me for the whole game. Saving my life, helping me get around, rewarding me for finding his splinter personalities; and that moment when I was driving into the slums and I heard GladOS on the phone I just burst out laughing because it, apart from the absurdity, brought back memories of Portal. Delemain's questline had been so memorable and I was so glad it was the first sidequest chain I did. So when I went into the reactor room, Johnny stopped me right before I got to the console. "Stop you idiot, you're gonna end up killing living beings!" (not verbatum) I stopped for a moment to think, well sure they MIGHT be sentient, but if so then so is Delemain, who is dying right now. Johnny then acquainted the situation to being a cab driver asking me to kill his kids, which made me think about it. The splinter personalities were calling Delemain prime their father, and with how realistic Delemain was, I would've believed that he himself could be a sentient cyber-lifeform. This caused a mental conflict that I didnt expect from this random sidequest I chose out of the 12 other options. Johnny and I talked for abit and then left me with the option. I couldn't pass the skill check to compress the personalities into Delemain's code, meaning my only options were to A: Reset Delemain and possibly kill 8 people, or shoot the core and... what? I didnt know what breaking the core would do. Might kill him? Might free them? Might kill them all? I had no idea. This confliction was overloading my irl brain and I started thinking erratically, worried I would make the wrong decision in the long run, till eventually I just shot it. I didnt think at all I just shot the damn thing. Boom, the whole room goes dark. I am now hearing demonic screeching and roars from outside of the room. My first thought was "Oh ♥♥♥♥ what kind of demon did I just release on this world." So when I ran upstairs to see Delemain's children driving around saying that they were free, I was pleasantly surprised. I asked Johnny what he thought happened to Del, and he told me one of the car stayed. The music kicks in and I slowly walk down to the car, already mind blown by the ending timing, scene, and just aura of the whole moment. I walk down to the car and get in to find Delemain inside, but not exactly, more like a new copy, completely reset. This moment brought me back to a youtube audiobook I listened to a LONG time ago, "What if The Enclave Survived in Fallout 76? - Episode 3 by The Omega Initiative". That story had a similar premise involving an AI dying but giving a smaller, reborn version of himself life as he dies. Not being reborn, but a whole other lifeform created. Now I had really only played Bethesda games so I was DEF not expecting this fckin sidequest to be this good, so when the car told me to "Drive V" right as the chorus of the background song started, my jaw was left agape. Completely brain melted levels of stunned. I had to literally step away from the computer and just take a breather for a minute cuz I had NEVER seen anything like this happen for an optional, easily missable SIDEQUEST. I had to quickly go to work for a couple hours afterwards. When I got back I started thinking again about the story. Just how blown away I was. Skyrim, Fallout 3 and Fallout 4 never did anything like this. Then when I was in the shower, pondering the story meaning, as one does in the shower, as showers are known to give a +10 buff to intelligence and philosophy; I realized what the story meant. I have 22 hours in the game, I have only completed the Delemain quest, the Tarot card quest, and the Main tutorial up to meeting with Takemura. And yet in this moment I think I understood what the main character's story is. At least, this far in. Cyberpunk's main character isn't V. It isn't Johnny. It's you. The player. When V was shot, he died, even by the doctor's accounts. Johnny himself has already died. His soul left this realm decades ago. Instead, what happened was this being, this form, capable of life existed, at a point where no one really inhabited it. This being (the main character) held the memories, body, and emotions of V, while also accessed and interfaced with the memories and personality of Johnny. Quite literally, two dead guys in his head, not 1. V's body is dressed up with mechanical and cybernetic parts already, to the point he's practically more machine than man when it comes to the physical, so perhaps it could be like Delemain's situation. Delemain was being bombarded by his splinter personalities, fighting for control and to be free of him. V is being bombarded by Johnny, fighting for control and to be free of him. Doesn't seem that far different. So what I propose is thus, The main character is both V and Johnny, this new being born of the death of V and generated by the memories, personality, everything of both V and Johnny. The perspective of Johnny being the one invading the mind of the main character isnt accurate, Johnny IS the main character, the same was V is, the same way Delemain's GladOS car is still Delemain, the same way Excelsior(the newborn car) is still Delemain. The story isnt about Johnny slowly eating away at V's mind and taking control. It's about YOU, the player, this new being born into this world, living with the experiences of both V and Johnny. You are both of them. You are like Excelsior. Learning to live a life as both Johnny and V. The perception of Johnny taking control is just you adapting and understanding a different side of you, same as V. I mean think about it, there's definitelly been times where you've meant to say something ingame and it came out WAY different than expected. A residual of V's memories, his way of speech, his personality. On the other hand, you have Johnny, slowly integrating, being understood, becoming more you the way someone growing up becomes themselves, not over forcing it, but over slowly growing and learning what you want to be. The story is about YOU, the player, given a life in the world, with the memories of V and Johnny, and the body of V, choosing what you will do. You have two tarot cards you can't get from the connected quest, I assume because they are later in the story. The Devil and Judgement. Misty explains that these cards are on your "path to discover" and are not required to complete her quest. In Cyberpunk 2077, the Judgment tarot card represents critical reflection, ultimate consequences, and finality. It symbolizes reaping what you've sown, acting as a reflection of the player's choices and the end of V's journey. The story is about YOU, and your decisions. It's about what YOU will do in this world. What life you want to make. What choices you want to make. Resetting Delemain, or shooting the core. [/spoiler] I am amazed by this game. It's truly something else. I am so excited to get back to playing after finishing this review. 10/10 worth the money and time investment. Great game, instantly one of my favorites

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of those games that went from being a complete mess to something actually worth your time. I didn’t touch it at launch for obvious reasons, and honestly that was the right move. Playing it now, especially after the 2.0 update, it finally feels like the game they were trying to sell back then. First thing, Night City carries the entire experience. The atmosphere, lighting, and overall vibe are insane. It’s one of the few games where just walking or driving around feels worth it. The world design is doing most of the heavy lifting here, which lines up with what a lot of people say: great presentation, everything else ranges from solid to just okay. ([reddit.com][1]) The story is actually strong. Characters like Johnny and the side questlines are where the game peaks. Some of the side missions are better than the main story, which isn’t something I expected. It’s immersive when it works, and it pulls you in way more than most open-world games. Gameplay is where it’s mixed. Gunplay feels good now, builds are way better after the overhaul, and there’s actual freedom in how you play. But the AI is still questionable at times, and the open world can feel a bit shallow once you look past the visuals. That criticism hasn’t really gone away since release. ([Steam Community][2]) Performance-wise, it depends on your setup. If you’ve got a decent PC, it runs fine now. Bugs still exist, but nothing like before. Back then it was borderline unplayable for some people, now it’s just occasional weirdness. ([reddit.com][3]) Overall, this is basically a “what could’ve been” game that still ended up good anyway. If you ignore the original hype and just take it for what it is, it’s a really solid RPG with insane visuals and a memorable story. Not perfect, not revolutionary, but definitely worth playing in its current state. Do expect it to be the greatest open world ever made.

This game truly is a masterpiece in every regard. It made me see things from new perspectives. The story is flawless, really letting anyone get the ending they want while still staying true to the idea that there’s “no happy ending in Night City.” I love this game. It’s by far my favorite I’ve ever played, and I’ve even earned the platinum trophy in Dark Souls 1–3 (random flex, by the way). Putting hours into this game feels like investing in yourself, as you dive into the intense, deeply layered stories of every character and fall in love with their journeys. This game will always hold a place in my heart, but what do I know? I’m just a random choom.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of my favorite games of all time, and in its current state I absolutely recommend it. I also want to be fair about it, because pretending the launch disaster never happened would be dishonest. It released in a horrible state, especially on older consoles, and it deserved criticism for that. But judging the game as it exists now, this thing is excellent. What kept winning me over was the sheer feel of it. Night City still looks absurdly good. The lighting is ridiculous, the atmosphere carries almost every scene, and even years later this game still has moments where you just stop and stare at the environment. It is not just technically pretty, it has style, mood, and identity everywhere. Few games sell a place this well. The other big strength is that the game is just fun to play when your build comes online. Cyberpunk absolutely nails the power fantasy. Once you get some real chrome installed and your build starts working the way you want, combat becomes a blast. Slow-mo, shotguns, LMGs, cyberware, explosions, chaos, all of it feels great. I spent a lot of this run doing side content simply because moving through the world and deleting enemies was enjoyable on its own. Story-wise, I think it is very strong, especially in the character writing. The game has a lot more texture than people give it credit for. Even side gigs often have enough personality, weirdness, tragedy, or moral grime to make them memorable. Phantom Liberty in particular is outstanding. I think it is the best content in the game. It feels tighter, meaner, and more focused, with some great spy-thriller energy layered on top of the base game’s drama. I do still have a few complaints. The game can still be janky. I ran into weird NPC behavior, some visual glitches, odd physics, and the occasional quest jolt. Nothing here ruined the experience for me, but the game still has rough edges. The driving is also inconsistent. Some cars feel amazing, some feel like boats with wheels. And the main story’s urgency can clash with the open-world design, because the narrative tells you your life is collapsing right now while the game also wants you to go do fifty side jobs and boxing matches. Still, the good outweighs the bad by a mile. Cyberpunk 2077 now feels like the game people wanted it to be in the first place: gorgeous, stylish, mechanically fun, full of personality, and backed by genuinely strong story content. It is not flawless, but it is absolutely worth playing, and Phantom Liberty only makes that more true.

Many years ago, I first stepped into Night City on my PS4 when Cyberpunk 2077 launched. Like many players at the time, my experience was… mixed. I ended up getting bored with the main story and dropped the game before even making it to the Arasaka Tower raid with Jackie. Fast forward to the start of 2026, and I decided to return to Night City and give Cyberpunk 2077 another real chance. This time, I committed to finishing the journey. I played through the entire main story and even completed the Phantom Liberty DLC. And after finally experiencing everything the game has to offer… I’m honestly blown away. But at the same time, I’m also a little disappointed. Main Story: For this playthrough, I started as a Nomad instead of a Corpo like I did the first time around—and right away the beginning of the game felt much better. The intro felt more natural and grounded, and it pulled me into the world in a way that my first playthrough never quite did. Once I made it past the Arasaka Tower raid—the exact point where I stopped playing years ago—the story really started to hook me. Things began escalating quickly, and the game introduced several important and memorable characters. One of Cyberpunk 2077’s biggest strengths is easily its characters. The people you meet throughout the story genuinely feel real. The dialogue, the facial animations, the body language—everything works together to make interactions feel believable. Experiencing all of it through a first-person perspective adds another layer of immersion that very few games manage to pull off this well. However, despite those strengths, the pacing of the story sometimes became a problem for me. There were stretches where things slowed down quite a bit, and during those moments I actually found myself dreading returning to the game. Still, I knew I wanted to push through and see the story to the end. Around the 30-hour mark, something changed. The story started to grab me again—especially Johnny Silverhand’s storyline. His character became increasingly fascinating, and many of the side quests tied to him were some of the most interesting moments in the entire game. Side stories involving Judy, River, and Johnny also surprised me. They pulled me deeper into the world of Cyberpunk and added emotional weight that the main story alone didn’t always deliver. That said, I didn’t complete every side quest the game had to offer. Normally, in a game like this, I would try to do everything. But Cyberpunk has a massive amount of side content, and while some of it is fantastic, a lot of it felt like filler to me. If I ever return to Cyberpunk 2077 again, I’ll probably take the time to explore more of those side missions. But during this playthrough, I wanted to stay focused on finishing the main story. And when I finally reached the ending, I experienced one of the most surprising moments in the entire game. The final cutscene before the credits—where I left Night City with the Aldecaldos and Panam in the tank—felt like a genuine “out-of-body” moment. For the entire game, you experience everything strictly through first-person perspective, including most cutscenes. So suddenly seeing your character in third person at the end was honestly shocking in the best way possible. It was a powerful moment, and it made the ending feel very personal. At the same time though, the ending also felt a little… incomplete. Not in a bad way necessarily, but in a way that left me feeling like there was still more story left to tell. More adventures that could still happen in this world. And that’s exactly why I immediately jumped into the Phantom Liberty DLC after finishing the main game. Because honestly… I found myself wanting more. Phantom Liberty DLC: The Phantom Liberty DLC Kicks off with a BANG and hooked me way quicker than the main story ever did. It ties directly into the main story as well, giving the story new and important plot points and expanding upon the "lore" and knowledge we already know about. The characters Solomon Reed, President Myer and Songbird are already interesting characters and at the start of the DLC, don't need much development or explanation. Dogtown is another important character of it's own, adding a more run down element of Night City. But Dogtown isn't just run down either, it has some hidden Gem's like the rest of Night City that are truly just beautiful! I have not completed the Phantom Liberty DLC in full yet as it is time to make some room for Crimson Desert - but I will be back to finish it soon! I will edit this once I complete it! Final Comments: Overall, Cyberpunk 2077 has many highs, and a few lows (mainly story pacing) but the game is honestly a must play for anyone who enjoys a good story, and a great RPG. I must also say CD Project Red, you're team killed it with fixing all the bugs and turning the world of Cyberpunk 2077 into something amazing. Rating: 8.6/10 | Great

TLDR: This is a great game but a weak RPG. Cyberpunk’s incredible narrative, enhanced by its DLC, is undoubtedly worth playing, or at least trying. There’s a lot to say about this game’s launch and subsequent redemption, but from someone who played it through multiple endings before 2.0, most of the best parts of the game were always there, if not just more accessible now. The story is great, tense and complex with interesting characters that pulls you along all the while you as V build your rep by taking on fun, if not short, gigs throughout Night City. There’s some tastes of meaningful choice in the main story (and moreso in the DLC) but outside of that there’s little room for you to actually express yourself in this world, especially with how predetermined some aspects of your character are. Even basic features of expression like clothing, looks, and vehicles are seriously limited by a lot of modern RPG standards. More than that, one playthrough of the game’s main narratives will lead you through most of the game’s side content, with about 5 non-repeatable hours of “postgame content” (exclusively in the DLC). Sure, there’s always the other endings, but after that what are you left with? With how full Night City is I’m shocked by how dead the moment to moment exploration is. Night City is crowded, but hardly alive. It may be heretical to say, but outside of CD Projekt’s incredible curated content the transitory gameplay could be swapped with Starfield’s exploration. Its still well worth the money, ESPECIALLY recommended on sale, and mods can fill some of that empty space I’m dissatisfied with, but every so often I’ll stare wistfully at its icon before jumping in just to look at a cleared map and log out.

[h2]Main-Game[/h2] [h2]Intro[/h2] After the disaster that was the launch, I finally decided to play Cyberpunk 2077 and let me tell you, the game made a comeback. With new positive reviews, and recommendations I decided to give it a go. Which let me tell you, it was well worth the wait, and the reason for waiting was because I knew the game was gonna take a long time to finish. But now that I'm done, let me tell you what I think. [h2] Freedom [/h2] One of the best parts of the game is most definitely the freedom, most RPG games nowadays only give you like three solid choices when it comes to dialogue, or sometimes only two way's that you can go about things, or just two major choices. But in Cyberpunk all that's removed, instead what you get is a variety of things to choose from, I'm talking about 4 different lines of dialogue on almost every interaction, 9 endings, multiple ways of doing missions and with the manual save being an option you can also re-load a save and see how your choices turns out. [h2] Builds [/h2] In some RPG games once you commit to a build then that's it. There's no going back or if there is, you have to reach a certain level or get X or Y amount of items in order to "respec" or "re-build" your character....However in this game, you can literally pick and choose your build and play around with what you got. Whenever you want, meaning if you get bored of a build or if you feel like your investment was crap. Then just "undo" your skill investment and put it into something else or if you want to just try something new then you are free to do so whenever you want at any time. [h2]Writing/Characters[/h2] When it comes to characters or writing in this game, it honestly fits in so well. You actually care for the character's and what they want to achieve, the writing isn't cringe-worthy or predictable. There's dynamic, chemistry, growth, and character. All these elements and things that make the writing and character develop in such a way that feel's like real life or a movie. Plus there are lore-dumps everywhere meaning if you ever want to know more about Cyberpunk, then you can read everything you have collected in your pause menu. [h2]Gripe[/h2] The only complaint I have about this game is honestly the lack of color, customization, and vehicles. For clothes Idc how much copium you have to inhale, but there isn't a lot of choices to pick and choose from with the odd colors, and the ugly shoes/pants. However Cyberpunk defenders will just look at this and say "But there is, you just have to look for it." But they are flatly wrong, my character was supposed to have a green theme, and the amount of bright neon green I could find was worrisome not to mention the fact that some combinations make the males look like clowns. For the customization, same thing. The game gives you apartments, and car's, but you are extremely limited on what you can design. You can change some pictures in your apartment's, but you can't reorganize furniture or add different things and change the headlights on a car....but somehow you can't add different types of engines, window tint's, rims, exhaust pipes or basic decal, even though there's already cool NPC vehicles that have some of these things. Funny enough though, there's an entire studio picture-mode set with lot's of gimmick's and way's to take pictures. Last but not least, the driving in this game is so f****** s*** that they need to re-work the physics behind driving and instead need to remove races if the driving was this bad. Because last time I checked from playing Gran Turismo, Need For Speed, Driving Sims, and just real life driving experience....cars don't slip and slide on asphalt, dirt, sand or cement like they are on ice. Especially the way they do in Cyberpunk. And again for those who want to defend the driving in this game, you are full of s***, never driven a car or you are just straight-up coping. [h3]Good[/h3] - Character Development - Writing - Freedom - Build(s) Flexibility - Multiple Endings - Radio Station ;) [h3]Bad[/h3] - Vehicles - Bothersome Glitches [h3]Story Overall: 8.5/10[/h3] [h3]Game Overall: 9/10[/h3] [h2] Phantom Liberty [/h2] When it comes to the DLC for cyberpunk, at this point just get it. The entire DLC makes the entire game look like a downgrade, that's how good it really is. Plus the ending cutscenes literally look like something out of a movie, with visuals being extremely cool. [h3]Good[/h3] - Major Upgrade From The First [h3]Bad[/h3] - None [h3]Story Overall: 9.5/10[/h3] [h3]Game Overall: 9/10[/h3]

While it's not without its glitches, Cyberpunk 2077 remains a rich source of fast-paced combat, highly immersive world-building, and splendid sci-fi scenery. It’s all the more impressive when viewed through the lens of a VR mod. Even with all of that modded VR performance jank, Cyberpunk has frankly unbeatable atmosphere. I found myself RP-walking through the markets, stopping to overhear strangers’ conversations and take in the cityscape. In a genre where “open” usually means miles of barren wilderness, Night City is a definitive deviation that feels dense, alive, and brimming with possibilities. Cyberpunk has got to have one of the strongest prologues I can think of. It excellently brings you into the world, teaches you about the culture of Night City, and sets up a motive for the rest of the expansive game. Although, the time-sensitive nature of the main conflict does rather fail to match the amount of time that the game lets you faff about. This is an unoriginal critique and honestly kind of an unavoidable side effect of this being a video game, but it really stood out to a player who wanted to see as much of the world as possible. Even though the quality of side quests did vary, the majority of them really stood out. There are some truly unforgettable stories to play through here. They offered so much insight into this fleshed-out world. Every significant character you meet through these stories has a place in this dystopian world, and the actions you perform for/with them consistently lead in intriguing directions. Player choice isn’t a big part of Cyberpunk, but there’s enough of it to give you a good sense of agency that further draws you into the setting. Combat throughout the game was a huge highlight. All your futuristic firearms and cybernetic abilities feel great to use. Your cyberpunk guns all click, slide, and go boom satisfyingly. Your superhuman mods let you perform various feats of badassery. Even stealth, the bane of pacing and scourge of open-world games, provides you with plenty of options for going unnoticed or getting the jump on encounters. There are loads of playstyles/weapons/powers to experiment with. The skill trees always had something that was catching my eye. Finding the various stylish “iconic” weapons always enticed me and had me reanalyzing my build. As you accumulate more violent options, you do become pretty overpowered, which slightly undermines the tactical decision-making of combat. Still, it’s a great sci-fi power fantasy that parallels the unstoppable reputation you gain as an up-and-coming legend. There’s a lot to enjoy about Cyberpunk 2077 now that it's long-since grown out of its infamously mucky release. Very few parts of the game are worth avoiding. However, if I could overhaul one thing, it would be the driving. It's not hideous, just sensitive and slippery as hell. Operating any vehicle using a keyboard is not recommended. Even the AutoDrive feature has pretty serious limits. Fast traveling can get you most places, but I found the few high-speed vehicle segments to be the least controllable moments. Open-world games are becoming a more tiresome affair for me in recent years, yet Cyberpunk managed to fully capture my attention. If you’re like me and can only stomach, like, two open-world games a year, you should make Cyberpunk a priority on that list. You won’t regret it, especially if you’ve got the hardware to run it in VR. [i](Oh, and grab the DLC if you find yourself enjoying the game. That story isn’t worth missing either.)[/i]
