A short disclaimer first: I never tried to play this back when it first released so I approached it without the same bad taste in the mouth a lot of people had after the launch fiasco. What I got is a pretty solid game that still has some rough edges but it mostly works and it's been fun to play and experience. [h2]Gameplay[/h2] It's one of those games I'd describe as "GTA-likes", in that you navigate a sandboxy open world, often with vehicles, and do various violent and otherwise shady activities around it. There are some RPG mechanics, to a slightly greater extent than usual in the genre - you get several stats and skill trees to unlock stuff in to tailor the experience to how you want to play the game. The effective differences in how missions play out based on your playstyle are often mostly cosmetic, but sometimes it can pay off to go the stealthy route for example. The gunplay is reasonably satisfying and you're frequently given ways to use the environment to your advantage or get an edge by using skills, I found it pretty fun. I kinda wish the loot system was dialled down a little though. You're constantly getting new weapons, usually with only minor differences in stats and I don't like having to pause the game every couple minutes to analyse if the new gun is 0.9% better than my current one. I'd rather have scarce upgrades that actually mean something. [h2]Audiovisuals[/h2] The game looks nice, and I appreciate how customisable the graphics are so you really don't need a cutting edge computer to play it. I just wish there were more character creation options, but alas. The music is pretty good and includes a couple of tracks made specifically for the game - and I mean "normal" songs that play on the radio, not the usual ambient or orchestral stuff usually written for OSTs. There's no one radio station where I like every single song, so that's a bit sad but not unusual, I'm a picky bastard. [h2]Story & plot[/h2] The main plot thread is shockingly short, as in I unlocked the final mission around the time I thought "okay, we're probably like halfway into Act 2 by now, right?". That said, there's a TON of optional content and a lot of it actually ties into the main story and influences how it all ends. So you [i]can[/i] rush through the game in just a couple hours, but getting the full experience is a different story and I definitely recommend it. There are several endings and it's one of those games where (some of) your choices actually have a lasting impact. It's rarely clear who you can/should trust and it often feels like there really is no good solution to a given problem and even after you've made a decision it's not always obvious if it was a good one. I like games that aren't afraid to do that. Several NPCs have long rich quest lines that help you get to know them, tie into the central plot at least in some way (or at least play a world-building role) and you can even romance them. The choice of who you can and cannot romance is dependent on your sex (or perhaps your pronouns, I haven't tried mismatching the two), that actually feels real as opposed to the increasingly common "lol everyone is bi because we don't want to disappoint anyone" approach. That last point is indicative of a broader tendency, in that the world rarely (if ever) feels like it's actively pandering to me, the player. I like that, it feels more real. [hr][/hr] So yeah, I consider this a pretty good game overall. Definitely recommended if you like GTA style games and/or cyberpunk aesthetics and/or interesting stories with believable characters. The DLC is worth it too.

Even years after release, the game still has some issues. I played it on SteamOS using a Legion Go, and overall it was beautiful and ran surprisingly well, though I still encountered a few small bugs here and there. One thing that bothered me sometimes is how the game creates the illusion of choice but occasionally pushes you toward certain outcomes. That said, the Corpo ending, which was the path I followed in my first playthrough, was incredibly powerful. The final hour of the game was so emotional that I almost cried. In the end, that last stretch made the whole journey worth it. My advice to new players: push through the first act. It’s honestly the slowest and most boring part of the game. Once you meet Keanu Reeves’ character (Johnny Silverhand), the story really takes off and becomes an amazing ride. The whole storyline involving Panam was easily one of the highlights for me. I do wish the Corpo path had been explored more deeply. Aside from the opening office sequence, I would have loved to see more corporate intrigue and stronger consequences tied to those choices. Maybe that’s something we’ll see expanded if there’s ever a sequel. Now I’m moving on to the Phantom Liberty DLC, and I’m curious to see what improvements and new experiences it brings.

Pros: - Great story - Beautify Graphics - Game play is solid. Weapons and customization options feel amazing. Cons: - Main protagonist can't seem to get the sand out of his vagina no matter what you do or how many people you murder. - You barely really get to play the game there is so much story. You can mess around in act 2 though. - Illusion of narrative choice. Your choices make absolutely no difference. The story is the story and it's a railroad. - Illusion of build diversity. There really aren't many different ways to play the game. They give an illusion of being able to do what ever you want, but there is really only 5 or 6 different builds (Stealthy assassin, Netrunner, Bruiser, Melee Specialist, Sniper, and maybe one more). The game is great, but it gives a lot of illusion of choice. There is really only one way to play the game and it will force you to play it that way. For example, say you want to be a stealthy assassin. They'll let you sneak your way to the objective, then the game will skrew you be either alerting everyone (through a scripted event) to your presence or giving you an objective that makes it impossible to sneak out (escort this damsel in distress). Say you wan to be a bad @$$ Netrunner, too bad the game sent a boss that is immune to your hacks. And on and on. Again, great game. I see why people like it. Hell, why some people love it. The game designer did "try" to make every problem have multiple solutions, but their attention to detail was lacking at a frustrating rate. This is a weird one. As proved by the hours played, I've finished the game along with the Phantom Liberty DLC, but have no desire to play it again. First, the pros: Gameplay and voice acting is good, and I experienced no issues with the performance. Many of the systems are enjoyable, especially the driving, combat, and hacking, and there truly are many ways to play this game. I had some issues of taste with some crafting system in that it feels pretty shallow and the weapons you can make are not as interesting or powerful as the drops. Now, the reason for my negative review: the theme and setting. This game's setting is absolutely disgusting. I fully understand that this is supposed to be social commentary on the nihilism, greed, consumerism, lasciviousness and techno-obsession of the modern world, but the experience of playing through all that left me feeling gross. I kept waiting for some kind of heart in the game that would make me care more about the characters, and while the main conflict V ultimately faces is (kind of) interesting, and the choices you have to make do have impact, it still all against this backdrop of hopelessness, moral relativism, and grime that feels so depressing. If you enjoy that sort of experience, go ahead and play this. The game is well designed and does what it tries to do quite well. I just won't recommend the feeling. I felt similarly about What Remains of Edith Finch, another modern, highly rated game whose story left me feeling as if I'd just spent way too long in a modern art museum looking at, at best, some screwed up interpretation of beauty, and at worst, an intentional display of ugliness.

I started playing Cyberpunk 2077 expecting a stylish futuristic RPG with a good story and lots of action. And while it definitely delivers on those things, what surprised me the most was how much the game makes you think about your choices. In many games, decisions feel simple. You usually know which option is the “good” one and which one is the “bad” one. In Cyberpunk 2077 it rarely works like that. A lot of the time you read the dialogue options and honestly don’t know what the best decision is. You sit there thinking about the situation, the characters involved, and what might happen next. Sometimes every option feels risky in its own way. What makes it even more interesting is that the consequences don’t always show up immediately. You might make a decision and then continue playing for hours before realizing that something later in the story happened because of that earlier choice. When that happens, it really makes you reflect on what you did. There were moments when I spent several minutes just staring at the dialogue options, thinking so much that my head almost started to hurt. The world itself is also one of the strongest parts of the game. Night City feels alive, full of different districts, characters, and small details that make the environment believable. The atmosphere, the neon lights, the music, and the overall cyberpunk aesthetic make exploring the city really enjoyable. Sometimes just walking or driving around the city can be fun on its own. The characters are another highlight. Many of them feel well written and realistic, with their own personalities, problems, and motivations. Because of that, the choices you make in conversations feel even more important. You start caring about what happens to these characters, which makes the story much more engaging. The gameplay itself is also quite flexible. You can approach situations in different ways depending on your playstyle. Some players prefer stealth, others go for direct combat, and the game allows you to experiment with different builds and abilities. Of course, the game isn’t perfect. Sometimes there can still be small bugs, and a few mechanics could feel a bit more polished. But overall, the experience is still very strong, especially because of the story, the atmosphere, and the meaningful choices. For me personally, Cyberpunk 2077 is a game that really stands out because it constantly makes you think about your decisions and their consequences. It’s not just about completing missions, it’s about being part of the story and shaping how it unfolds. [h3] My rating: 10/10 [/h3]

I love this game with every cell of my body. Not just because I love the cyberpunk genre, but because of its story and characters. I always end up coming back to replay it and I never get tired, even knowing everything that happens. This game was there for me during the worst moments of my life and helped me immensely by making me forget my problems, even if only temporarily. The friendship that V and Johnny form as the story progresses is beautiful to see. A rockstar surrounded by people he considered 'friends' and fans who couldn't even stand to be in the same room as him yet V was there, putting up with his madness and nonsense 24/7, always listening and talking to him like a true friend. V could have taken the pills to get rid of Johnny temporarily at any time but chose to keep him there, which makes their bond feel truly genuine. The story is obviously one of the highlights. Seeing V go from just a random mercenary wanting the good life in Night City to a person desperate to survive having to help others to try and save themselves. Even if 'helping someone just to save yourself' sounds selfish, V doesn't just save them; they build real bonds. The gameplay is also super fun, letting you experiment with many different builds. If you want to go 'guns blazing,' you can; if you want to play as a hacker, being a terrifying Netrunner to the NPCs, go right ahead. The game offers a great diversity of builds without forcing you into a single playstyle. The side quests and quests, in general, are also excellent. To me, the best side quests are the ones featuring Johnny’s commentary because it adds an 'extra spice' to them, and the main quests are simply incredible. The endings are also amazing, especially 'Temperance' and 'The Star.' SPOILERS***>>** Personally, the 'Temperance' ending is and always will be my favorite. V sacrificing themselves at the end and going beyond the Blackwall with Alt Cunningham so Johnny can have a second chance at life giving him the opportunity to make different choices is exactly what I feel V would do after everything they went through together. You can clearly see Johnny actively making the most of this second chance. It’s a 'sad' ending, so to speak, but I still find it beautiful: Johnny visiting V’s grave one last time, leaving the bullet necklace, and leaving Night City by bus to finally move on, thanking V for the second chance. Now, 'The Star' ending features V becoming part of the Aldecaldos nomad family, whom they helped so much during the campaign. When they said they would help V no matter what, they weren't kidding. Raiding Arasaka Tower with the nomads feels like a suicide mission, yet they don't give up, choosing to go to the end with V even if it costs them their lives which is exactly what happens. After the chaos of the raid and returning to their body, V and the Aldecaldos decide to leave Night City to search for a cure. This ending gives a bit more hope that the protagonist might survive after everything, but it's left open-ended. Many consider this the best ending of Cyberpunk 2077, and I don't blame them; it makes total sense to choose it. Anyway, I'm just rambling about how much I love this game! :P

# Pros - Visuals & Atmosphere - Characters & Story - Tarrot theme - Panam's ass # Overview I got duped when I saw this on sale and saw steam reviews that said this was "one of the best RPGs/games ever made"... Not true, save your time and money. Cyberpunk was obviously built by 100 different teams that ran out of time & money, they tried to glue it together at the end and they forgot to add the "game" part. It's basically an interactive movie as the game is 80% dialog, 10% shooting down a hallway, 10% driving. I think they spent too much of the budget on holywood actors. # Gameplay - There's no challenge at all. I beat the game on Hard with a level 1 silenced pistol, I could one shot 80% of enemies. I didn't have to interact with cyberware, crafting or item upgrades at all really. - Choices and interations have no consiquences, it's not really an RPG. - Items suck, 5% increased reload speed, Tier 5 components, great - Half baked mechanics that don't matter: - Crafting - Stamina - Stealth - Non lethal/lethal Take downs - Hiding bodies - Shooting while driving (think I used it twice just to see what it did) - Hacking mini game for quickhacking components - 1st person only is an issue. I had a bug on my first ending, where I thought I woke up as Jonny but I was actually V. I didn't know what was happening and it made no sense. Kind of ruined the playthrough. Lots of reports of the same bug online. There were also times that finishing a quest had unequipped my clothes, so I was running around the city naked with no idea cause it's 1st person only. It's a shame that a game that looks this good is so shallow and boring to play. Honestly, I'm glad to be done with it.

If you like technical achievements over a good story, vibrant situations, complex puzzles, exciting moments, emotive music and atmosphere, characters and plot twists that make you cry, then this game IS for you. But if you, like me, are more on the emotional side than the technical bells & whistles, maybe you should pass on this game. Or in other words: -Are you a fan of GTA games? Then go for it. -Are you a fan of NieR: Automata? Then don't.

First and foremost, Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the best games I've played when it comes to worldbuilding and immersion. Every aspect of the game - from advertisements on billboards, to npc dialogue, to fancy street crossing indicators - work together to create a truly cohesive, fleshed out universe. The main storyline is great, with a few alternate paths depending on the decisions you make, although it can be pretty short if you ignore all the sidequests. Speaking of sidequests: some can be a little repetitive (I personally don't mind the "kill everyone and grab an item" quests since combat is pretty fun, but I could see it get boring for some people), however there are also a number of very unique ones which provide a more detailed dive into different aspects of night city. Combat might seem basic at first, but as you unlock more perks and cyberware options, you'll discover a variety of different playstyles which you can mix and match depending on your preferences. Upgrading your preferred playstyle is also a lot more than just seeing numbers go up, many perks and cyberware add completely new capabilities over the course of your run, so that by late game you might have half a dozen or more abilities to keep track of (or you can spec into simpler playstyles that don't require you to actively manage them). Visually, Cyberpunk lives up to it's reputation of being one of the best looking games made to this day. Not every model is perfect, and there have been a few times when a bad one stands out, but overall the combination of both size and fidelity is very impressive. The soundtrack is excellent. Cyberpunk features a huge variety of music from different genres with both the main composer, and tons of third party artists. The in game radio has over 100 songs total. I'm not sure I can put it on the same pedestal as doom or halo, but you could make an argument for it.

Beautiful and engaging. If you're looking for a new game to get hooked on, this is it. From the breathtaking crowded city to the fields of dust, Cyberpunk 2077 is packed with immersive details, extensive quests, and enough decisions to allow for multiple playthroughs. I also highly recommend the Phantom Liberty DLC to add a large chunk of playtime to your playthrough. It took me a little under 90 hours to beat the game, complete Phantom Liberty, complete (almost) all side quests, and experience a couple endings. Additionally, the game runs great on my system with DLSS and FG with ray tracing. I did experience the occasional crash, so make sure to quick save every once in a while. You can catch the game + DLC on sale for $40, but it's (probably) worth every enny even full price.

Having played through this game at least 6 times, I'd say I've seen what this game has to offer, and it is good. For a game that really screwed up it's launch, it has come a long way, especially after Cyberpunk 2.0 and Phantom Liberty. While it may have had a rough start, even under all the bugs and performance issues, there was still a great game under the grime. Not every game can say the same. This is a great open world game with some really fun quests, and great gameplay. The gameplay was good but flawed before 2.0, but after the 2.0 update, the gameplay has been refined into a fine wine. It is fun being a cyber ninja chopping everyone in sight to pieces, being a netrunner wizard melting the brains of everyone on the battlefield with but a glance, Or being an assassin blowing the brains out of everyone you come across. The RPG mechanics backing up your playstyle are amazing, and the cyberware is awesome. You can become the ultimate killing machine and it is sublime. Story wise, the main quest in this game is amazing, like honestly, the story of V while a tragic one, is a great one. I've seen every ending, and they are all really cool to reach. The "companion" characters and the other major side content are also really great. In the base game, the gigs from fixers are okay, a lot of them are pretty basic shooting galleries. But in Phantom Liberty, the gigs are amazing, they have full stories with interesting characters and interesting and hard choices to make. But also exploring night city is just a blast. There might be a fast travel system, but honestly I almost never use it because driving around night city, dodging traffic at 150mph is super fun, especially with the fine tuning they have done to vehicles, also there are a stupid amount of awesome looking cars, and while you can buy cars, you get plenty of cool ones doing side quests too for free. My two main complaints for this game are. My first major gripe is that the life paths are very underwhelming, especially in the base game, aside from one extra quest and some special lines of dialog here and there, it really doesn't matter. In fairness, CDPR recognized that as a flaw, and in Phantom Liberty you do actually get a few special options based on what lifepath you have in quests. My second main complaint is the lack of interactivity and simulation of interactions with the gangs, or more specifically reputation systems with the various factions. Except for a few specific circumstances, your actions don't really have an effect on the gangs of night city, even though you've mowed down hundreds, if not thousands, of them by the end of the game. I would say that expands to more world interactivity in general, and life sim elements that I wish the game had more of, or deeper interactions. There are a handful of mods that move to address this, but they can only go so far without new voice lines, especially for example, romance interactions with the 4 companion characters. So for the sequel, I hope CDPR adds a lot more world interactivity, and life sim elements. Not to the point of say survival, but just to help you feel really immersed in the world. In other words, I want more stuff in the game that isn't just "go and kill everyone here". I suppose it made sense for V as a mercenary, but still.

Cyberpunk 2077 with Phantom Liberty isn’t just a game, it’s a first‑person midlife crisis with ray tracing and way too many cool jackets. Night City is the only place where you can be a broke merc, a glitchy rockstar, and an unlicensed therapist for traumatized NPCs all in the same side quest. You log in to “do one quick gig” and somehow end up knee‑deep in corpo conspiracies, brain surgery, and philosophical arguments with the voice in your head. Builds range from anime katana monster to cyber‑wizard hacker to “I put points everywhere and now people just evaporate when I look at them funny.” Every fight is either a flawless John Wick montage or you screaming, over‑healing, and throwing grenades at your own feet. Phantom Liberty is basically Season 2 of the story: darker, sharper, and with just the right amount of Idris Elba judging your life choices. Dogtown feels like a compressed warzone where every quest starts simple and ends with you staring at the screen, wondering if you accidentally picked the bad ending again. Cyberpunk 2077 now is the game where you boot it up to change your outfit, then realize it’s 3 AM, you’ve finished another ending, and your screenshot folder has doubled in size.

Cyberpunk is truly a once in a lifetime game. I didn't play it when it first came out, so I experienced the game as it is now. And ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it blew me away. It's an absolutely gorgeous game, and the city feels alive. There are people everywhere, not just walking around but seemingly actually living their lives. I drive to every destination I have because I enjoy just existing within the city so much. The story is amazing, the NPCs are memorable and deep, and even the side missions are amazing. They go from silly things like a man whose peepee is burning to genuine and unsettling injustices done against others that make you sit and think about how terrible people can be. It balances humor and dark themes effortlessly. I love this world so much. I avoided ending the game for maybe 30 hours or so just because I didn't want it to end, only to find out that the game is kind and allows you to keep playing even if you end it. The choices you face, especially at the end, feel heavy and hard. Even the happiest of endings feels bittersweet, and that's okay because the story is so good that it makes sense. It tackles its darkest themes with grace but without holding back. I also love that V really has a personality - you're controlling her, yes, and you do make decisions, but you're playing AS her. She's a deep character full of flaws and grit and hope and emotion. I love the NPCs who become her friends in the game too. I also just enjoyed the gameplay. Hacking is fun, sniping is fun, running and gunning is fun, throwing knives is FUN (my favorite playstyle personally). As you level up you slowly feel more powerful, but not so much so that you'd never struggle. Driving is fun with the right vehicles (the handling on some is rough, but once you find the right ones you're cruising). The amount of character customization is amazing too. But at the core of it, Cyberpunk is just one of a kind. There's nothing like it. No other open-world game comes close to the depth of its world, the importance of its themes, its writing, its art. I've played so many single player games and none made me feel the way that Cyberpunk has. I would do anything to play this game again for the first time - I cannot recommend it enough.

--- Personal Thoughts --- An incredibly enjoyable open-world RPG looter-shooter experience; The base game provides a palpable power fantasy, and does so by making it exceedingly easy to create an extremely powerful character from messing around with the build & cyberware system. As such, don't expect a challenge. Even on some of the harder difficulties, I wager most people will be able to get through the game with relative ease. By far the strongest part of the game is the environment & story itself. Night City is a vivid, striking cyberpunk dystopia riddled with bright neon literally everywhere. The constant firefights happening as you drive through the city, the various gigs you can get, even the random calls you can get from important NPC's that start entire questlines helps sell that this is a city where things are actively moving and happening. The only real criticism with regards to that is a certain time-limited aspect of the narrative that clashes with what is, ostensibly, an unlimited amount of time to engage in the endless amount of side quests throughout the game. --- Additional Thoughts on Phantom Liberty --- Easily one of the most impressive DLC's for a game I've seen so far. It's a step up in terms of voice acting, difficulty balancing, and narrative. The DLC area is incredibly interesting, the characters are complex and compelling, and there are some scenarios in the game that genuinely had my adrenaline pumping. It was never truly unforgiving, but the step up in overall difficulty definitely helped sell a lot of the narrative beats within the DLC (something that the main game, unfortunately, suffers a little from). --- Overall Thoughts on the Game --- *Very* good game. I'd probably put it as it exists right now at around an 8.5/10. Highly recommended if you're into looter shooters with RPG mechanics. Good story and strong environment design. Pick up the main game and DLC if you can afford it, and *definitely* pick it up on a good sale.

I almost never played Cyberpunk 2077. And honestly, that would’ve been a tragedy. When the first trailers dropped, I was instantly sold. I love the cyberpunk genre, and with both Blade Runner films among my all-time favorites, this looked like my dream game. Neon lights, dystopian megacities, chrome, it looked like the whole package. Then launch day happened. Reviews showed a buggy, unfinished mess, and my hype flatlined. Fast forward a few years, after watching Cyberpunk: Edgerunners (and emotionally recovering), I checked back in and realized CD Projekt Red had actually turned things around. So near the end of 2025, when the game and Phantom Liberty DLC went on sale, I finally jacked into Night City. The prologue hooked me immediately, but Act 2 is where the game really got its hooks in. A few side jobs deep, wandering the streets at 2-3 a.m., and I was completely locked in. Night City is one of the most immersive worlds I’ve experienced in a game from the atmosphere, characters, the stories and tiny details hidden in gigs and side quests… it all just hits different. And then there’s Phantom Liberty DLC... No spoilers, but choom it’s nova. Instead of just adding more content, it somehow levels the whole experience up. Is it perfect? Not quite. There are still occasional bugs like cars sometimes getting stuck or behaving weirdly, NPCs clipping through you, that sort of thing. The difficulty can also feel a bit easy even on harder settings, which is why I eventually installed a few mods to spice things up which in turn brought more flatlining(but thats on me for getting too chromed up) . And if you're expecting top-tier NPC interaction? Sorry, choom. Most Night City locals are just ambient bodies in the city’s braindance. But once you’re immersed in the city, those issues barely matter. The base game alone sits around an 8.5–9/10 for me. With Phantom Liberty tho? Easy 10/10. Right now, it’s easily my favorite game of all time. Preem game. Worth every eddie. Buy it, choom. Don’t be a gonk.

If you’ve ever wondered what it would be like to live inside a neon-soaked fever dream where everyone has a cybernetic arm, a questionable moral compass, and at least three unresolved emotional issues, Cyberpunk 2077 is the game for you. Set in the chaotic playground of Night City, the game drops you into a world where corporations run everything, the streets are full of chrome-plated chaos, and somehow the most dangerous thing you’ll encounter is still your own bad decision making. You play as V, a mercenary trying to climb the city’s ladder of power, fame, and very expensive jackets. Night City itself is the real star. It’s ridiculously detailed — a place where you can admire glowing skyscrapers, overhear bizarre conversations, and accidentally run over a pedestrian while trying to answer a phone call from Keanu Reeves living in your brain. Speaking of Keanu, Johnny Silverhand might be the only video game character capable of insulting you, encouraging you, and questioning your life choices all at the same time. The gameplay gives you freedom to approach missions however you want: stealthy hacker, guns-blazing maniac, or the person who spends 20 minutes sneaking around only to panic and throw a grenade at the wrong moment. The RPG elements are deep enough that you can build a character who feels truly yours… even if that character specializes in solving every problem with a shotgun. Yes, the game had a famously rocky launch. Early versions contained enough bugs to qualify as a wildlife preserve. But after years of updates and improvements, Cyberpunk 2077 now feels like the game it was always trying to be: ambitious, immersive, and occasionally absurd in the best way. At its heart, Cyberpunk 2077 is a story about identity, technology, ambition, and what it means to be human in a world where people replace half their organs with machinery but still can’t figure out their relationships. Also, there’s a mission where you crucify a guy for a braindance recording. So… it really runs the full emotional spectrum. Final Verdict: Cyberpunk 2077 is messy, beautiful, weird, occasionally profound, and sometimes unintentionally hilarious — kind of like the future itself. If you enjoy deep stories, chaotic open worlds, and Keanu Reeves calling you a legend while you crash a stolen motorcycle into a hotdog stand, Night City is absolutely worth the trip. Rating: 9/10 — Would absolutely install illegal cyberware again.

Cyberpunk 2077: Phantom Liberty is the best Action Film I’ve ever played. People often ask me, Apple, “what happens when you take a team of engineers that build fleets and have them make a ship in a bottle?” To that I’d say “What a weird and specific question about something I don’t know anything about.” but after that I’d say, “You’d get one of the densest, best paced experiences out there. Nooks in every cranny and a billion crannies to find.” Cyberpunk 2077 exists in three phases. The first are all the base quests and experiences. The game at launch. It’s good. It has its flaws, but that’s to be expected and has largely been forgotten. It was uncharted territory on a scale no one could prepare for. Undercooked. Highlight: John Matrix is stuck in your head. The second is all the further, free base-game updates. These are phenomenal. They are interesting. They flesh out the world. They aren’t afraid to stray from the beaten path in order to tell absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stories. Peak speculative sci-fi. If phase one is undercooked, this phase lets it rest, cooking under its own heat and making it a perfectly juicy steak. Highlight: You crucify Jesus. Phase Three. That’s Phantom Liberty. Let me give you the elevator pitch. “The President is coming home from the Moon, but is shot down by Paramilitant Tax Dodgers. You need to save her with the help of a The World’s Greatest Nerd’s Astral Projection and Knuckles the Echidna” This expansion shows absolute mastery over the game and its world, putting into action every lesson learnt by the devs up to this point. The quests are perfect examples of moral dilemmas in a dog-eat-dog-world seperate to our own. It places you in a new world, and asks you to see how you would adapt to the problems within. Highlight: I haven’t done laundry in a week and a half.

Lack of archaeological and whole-genome diversity data has restricted current knowledge of the evolutionary history of donkeys. With the advancement of science and technology, the discovery of archaeological evidence, the development of molecular genetics, and the improvement of whole-genome sequencing technology, the in-depth understanding of the origin and domestication of donkeys has been enhanced, however. Given the lack of systematic research, the present study carefully screened and collected multiple academic papers and books, journals, and literature on donkeys over the past 15 years. The origin and domestication of donkeys are reviewed in this paper from the aspects of basic information, cultural origin, bioarcheology, mitochondrial and chromosomal microsatellite sequences, and whole-genome sequence comparison. It also highlights and reviews genome assembly technology, by assembling the genome of an individual organism and comparing it with related sample genomes, which can be used to produce more accurate results through big data statistics, analysis, and computational correlation models. Background: The donkey industry in the world and especially in China is developing rapidly, and donkey farming is transforming gradually from the family farming model to large-scale, intensive, and integrated industrial operations, which could ensure the stability of product quality and quantity. However, theoretical research on donkey breeding and its technical development lags far behind that of other livestock, thereby limiting its industrial development. This review provides holistic information for the donkey industry and researchers, that could promote theoretical research, genomic selection (GS), and reproductive management of the donkey population.

The biggest negative point about this game would probably be the lack of roleplaying elements. It is visually impressive and everything is consistently presented but ultimately there are not many choices that you get to make during the game. Furthermore, this is not an RPG like Skyrim - the experience feels very controlled and curated through quests and cutscenes. This means that you can't really get immersed and feel like you are actually living in the world. One example is that at the start of the game, you have an apartment with a computer. If you read your email on the computer, you will see that you have an email from the landlord complaining about missed rent. But this is just window dressing - there is no way to pay the landlord nor are there any future repercussions. I don't think CDPR intended to make a game more like Skyrim (as the Witcher 3 is similar in some aspects). However, as I look at the world they created I can't help but feel like there was a missed opportunity to create something more.

Cyberpunk 2077 isn’t just a game… it’s an experience that sticks with you long after you log out of Night City. From the moment I stepped into those neon-soaked streets, I felt like I was living inside a futuristic dream — beautiful, chaotic, and sometimes painfully real. The city feels alive in a way very few games manage. Every alley, every billboard, every random conversation makes you feel like you’re part of something bigger. But what really hit me wasn’t just the visuals — it was the stories. The characters feel incredibly human. Some moments made me laugh, some made me angry, and a few genuinely made me sit there in silence thinking about the choices I made. It’s rare for a game to make you feel that way. Night City is brutal, flashy, and broken… yet strangely beautiful. And somehow, in all that chrome and chaos, you still find moments of humanity — friendship, loyalty, loss, hope. Sure, the game had a rough start, but looking at it today, it’s clear how much love and effort went into building this world. When the credits rolled, I didn’t just feel like I finished a game… I felt like I lived a story. Cyberpunk 2077 reminded me why I love video games in the first place — because sometimes they’re not just entertainment… they’re unforgettable journeys. 🌆💔✨

I guess this game does not require more recommendations since it has redeemed itself since release, and now it has become a benchmark for many gamers to test their rigs. But I will approach this from a different angle because I actually played and finished this game in 2020-2021 when it was first released. Back then, it was riddled with bugs, yet I really enjoyed the story. I love the cyberpunk genre, and Neuromancer is one of my favorite books. Surprisingly, even though the game had major issues, I personally did not run into many problems, and I was using the GOG version. Recently, when it was on sale, I bought it again on Steam with zero expectations, and I am positively surprised by how much they have changed. They have almost completely overhauled the endings and added many more options to the game. I am not even talking about the bunch of other features they added, such as customizable cars and more. The 2.0 update clearly turned this game around. The game is not only far more polished right now, it is also much more compelling in terms of story. So if you heard bad things after the game’s release, just ignore them and give it a go. This game is really fun to play for people who are into the genre. Of course, if you do not like the genre, do not expect this to be like Grand Theft Auto just because both have cars and cities. This game is nothing like GTA, and it is not trying to be that anymore either. tldr; If you are a fan of the cyberpunk genre and are looking for a fun game with an excellent story, go ahead and give it a try.

Cyberpunk 2077 7 / 10 (good, I recommend it for players that like action games with RPG elements). The Positive: * Excellent voice acting; * Very good characters; * Very good graphics and art direction; * Very beautiful Night City; * Good main story and good story for the most important side quests; * Good overall lore of earth and humankind in this alternative dark future; * Good performance and stability; * Good soundtrack and sound in effects and ambience; * Good character customization for ‘’builds’’ and gameplay style (but mainly for fighting); * Good character customization for body and clothes (but almost useless since we mainly play as FPS); * The way V interacts in 1st person with the characters is well done, very immersive and cool for us players. It’s done in a ‘’cinematic’’ way when we are in control or not; * Very good decision to let the players achieve different endings without having to reset the game entirely. The Neutral: * Mediocre gameplay at fighting and exploring. Mediocre action and ‘’adventure’’; * Considerable part of the minor side quests are repetitive and uninspired; * Mediocre police mechanics; * Mediocre population mechanics; * The main quest is too short. I liked it much more than the side quests, but it ended when I wanted more of it; * Night City is beautiful and huge, but it lacks depth in its routine and main services/infrastructure. The Negative: * The game would be better if it had an alternative solid 3rd person mode, especially because it’s a cyberpunk game with good options for visual customization, just aesthetic or linked to body improvements… It’s a shame a locked 1st person mode to a very customizable V in a dark future where customization is a huge part of human culture. That’s not enough the motorcycle 3rd person camera; * The RPG mechanical elements linked to V’s roleplaying and choices-consequences are weak; * V’s origins are poorly linked to V’s journey; * I couldn’t feel Night City as a real living metropolis; * CDPR lies and many broken promises about game features, easily noted even playing at March/2026. CONCLUSION: * Cyberpunk 2077 is a good game, worth my time and money.

Most bugs have been ironed out since launch. There are occasional glitches but it's quite rare (hardly 1 every 10h). The skilltree offers good build variety, which has improved a lot since launch, although some builds require a hefty amount of perk points to be effective. Respec is cheap. I highly encourage players to try investing in different skills and see what fits them most. The main quest is alright, but not as engaging as one would expect. However some great sidequests (such as Dream On and The Hunt) make up for it. Phantom Liberty has a better structure, good plot, and also unlocks alternate endings to the main game's storyline. I highly suggest using a few mods to increase difficulty, mute the damn background sound in the menus, and Night City Alive to increase gang activity. Played the game through on normal difficulty, completed the main questline. Only buy if you're willing to set aside the story and play it only as a video game, not a narrative. The story pushes you as if there's a very critical thing that has to be done as soon as possible, but you have to ignore that if you want to experience most of the game content. As such, it must be considered as an action game, and not an RPG. Character choices in quests and dialog really don't matter and have no appreciable effect. It would have really been improved by dropping the open world aspect and gone for a more linear experience. Also, the level-ups are disappointing. There's no real effects from increasing your stats other than some meaningless skill checks for optional doors or conversations. You can easily beat the game with just some random guns you find along the way, so even the whole cyberware system can be ignored. Therefore, the difficulty level is a slider that adjusts how much busy work you need to do to finish the game. At least the voice acting is great. If you get this, it's for the aesthetic and not for the content.

Great game, I've played a few times (PS4 and PC) and would highly recommend, but to me it has a pretty major problem. My issue with this was that I personally never liked the story or the character you play as (both male and female versions). The main motivation of the protagonist is to run from death so desperately, but they're a mercenary, and it just feels silly that they can kill a thousand people and get shot constantly but then later have panic attacks about their impending death. This is in stark contrast to the developer's previous masterpiece The Witcher 3, where the protagonist is motivated to save someone he loves and is not afraid to kill everyone on her trail and die in order to do so. That simple concept makes the game more fun, but in Cyberpunk they're simply a gun for hire who wants to be a legend but is their time is running out. That doesn't resonate with me at all. That is not to say that there are not moments of pretty powerful story-telling. Some quests/subplots are beautifully and poetically crafted and hit pretty hard emotionally, but the main story never did that for me because I just could not care about my character. For the positives, I think most everything else is very well-done. The gameplay is extremely unique, varied, and fun, and everything/everywhere is visually stunning. Those alone make this an excellent game that I will always recommend—very fun gameplay that doesn't get old, and it's beautiful to look at, but for me the story is just a little lackluster. But it looks like most people don't share my opinion, so hopefully you may find something about the story that resonates with you. Last thing— Phantom Liberty DLC: fun little expansion but still the same unlikable character and weak story.

This game has a big open world with lots of npcs everywhere doing their own thing and honestly one of the most immersive, "Real" feeling worlds out there. It was a bit too much for me in some ways, just the time spent alone was insane for a single player game, not a flaw for some but for me, it means a lot of time was "wasted" running around and it feels like I only saw about 60-70% of what the game had to offer, what with all the other endings and all the choices you can make. I feel a bit sad to not be able to see everything in a game but it's simply not worth the time to play another round. Things like gigs and npcd missions were designed to just waste time unless you're VERY interested in lore and random goings on in night city, but luckily they're not in your quest log and can be ignored easily. I played on hard but honestly, the difficulty felt at best normal, especially once you get some levels and implants/cyberware, ultimately I was able to just run around not giving a crap about what weapon I used, hiding to avoid getting shot or anything else, just walking around shooting everyone, even bosses were far too easy, so I can just imagine how easy it'd be on a lower difficulty. I don't particularly care for dfficulty anymore as I do not want to waste time on dying hundreds of times but at the same time it kind of ruins the gameplay when things are so easy you simply don't need to even try. To the very end, I was left clueless about the crafting system and upgrading iconic weapons if you even can and most other parts. Only the ripperdoc part and upgrading my cyberware to the max and using the talent tree was done. Using attachmets for weapons were poorly explained and crafting stuff weren't pushed in the slightest. I felt no need or desire to utilize any system in the game, which makes these systems a big waste of time. It was more than easy to just use random dropped weapons or job weapons and change them with new ones when there's a better one dropped. I feel it's a big waste when there's no real incentive whatsoever to craft things. Looting things also felt like a waste of time, needless filler, because all it did was give you some extra pocket change and materials. Why is there even food in the game and various other junk that didn't seem to provide any signficiant benefit? I'm not eating random crap for small boosts and wasting time in the menu for that when it's completely unnecessary. Hacking was fun but aslo felt useless most of the time unless you want to roleplay. Gaining skill points in certain things like body to get new dialogue choices never seemed to affect the outcome in any real way. I also really, really want to question the choice of only giving you two slots for quick actions, one grenade/extra action slot and one for healing items. Especially the extra one/grenade one. I had a bunch of different grenades but never got to use any of them, only using the cyberware projectiles. Why wasn't there a quick switch at least? A way to throw grenades in addition to using arm projectiles? So many questionable decisions. Buying houses and cars were also mere filler for people who enjoy grinding, there was no incentive to buy anything in general except cyberware. I'd say a lot in this game is poorly designed even if it's still a huge and rather impressive game world with a good story. Like they took too big a challenge and couldn't properly tie everything together. I hated the endings, to be honest, pretty much all of them. Seems that's the point, like no ending can truly be a great one. I quite enjoy immersing myself as the protagonist and not being able to get a satisfying ending made me a bit frustrated and honestly somewhat sad towards the end, it's all so melancholic and pretentiously dramatic, some people get off on that, I don't in the slightest. I want a good ending for myself even if everyone else has to burn for it, sadly even that wasn't really an option here. I don't particularly think it's good game design to not leave ANY good endings to cater to my crowd when there are so many endings to be had. I don't mean some kind of flowers and rainbows ending where night city becomes day city, all the drug addicts and people are enlightened and become buddhists, the corps become moral pillars that try to better humanity and no one dies anymore as everyone transcends their mortal shell and lives on forever in joy and harmony, I just mean an ending where the PROTAGONIST gets a relatively happy ending, like putting johnny in another body and somehow solving your own issue and living a good, full life even if it has to be on the grave of a lot of other people as only the winners get to live a good life in night city... Phantom liberty was the best part of the game. It felt much better put together, perhaps because it also took place in a much smaller area and had a more solid, put together and rapid quest line? It was better written and just more interesting, although I didn't like the ending there either, just too melodramatic for my taste. I do not regret buying the game, it was a pretty fun experience, it just takes itself too seriously with some poor design choices. It's definitely one of the best games in modern times, even if I would personally prefer a lot of other games to this as it's not really my cup of tea, though cool. Oh, and I'm real happy to finally be done. Was getting real sick and freaking tired of all the crashes, sometimes even locking me out from continuing until I lowered the resolution to 1080p. The game crashed on average every hour I'd say, sometimes it'd crash every 15 minutes, sometimes 30 minutes, sometimes it'd run for a few hours but every single day when I played this, it'd crash at least 3 times. Worst was 20 times. Seriously annoying, I think I wasted about 5 hours easily just trying to get back into the game after crashes, maybe more, especially if you include troubleshooting, so maybe 10 hours. Happy to finally have played the game I heard so much about, even if a lot of it was because it was a buggy mess. I still laugh thinking about reed in phantom liberty skipping like a girl in a flower field while pushing a garbage bag in front of him towards an elevator and finally the bag exploded as he, the whole time, talked in an extremely serious voice. Wish I had recorded it.

Cyberpunk 2077 is a beautiful game. Visually, artistically, and atmospherically, it is one of the most impressive open-world titles I’ve played. Let me be clear — the story itself is good, but not something extraordinary. It’s not a once-in-a-generation narrative experience like Red Dead Redemption 2. It doesn’t aim for that emotional depth. However, what it does, it does exceptionally well in its own way. Night City feels real. Not just big — but alive. Driving around the city at night, with the neon lights reflecting off wet streets, traffic moving naturally, ambient conversations happening in the background — it genuinely feels immersive. Sometimes I would just drive around without a mission, purely to take in the atmosphere. I know the game had a very rough launch. Performance issues, bugs, poor optimization — it was widely criticized at release. But I played it after the 2.0 update, and the experience was completely different. The overhaul improved the mechanics, systems, and overall polish significantly. Technically, I played with path tracing enabled along with DLSS Frame Generation (2x), and the visual experience was phenomenal. The lighting, reflections, and shadows transform the city into something next level. Every gunfight felt cinematic. Speaking of combat — the Adam Smasher fight was absolutely top tier. The intensity, the destruction, and the final moment when he goes down — especially the explosion and overall presentation — were executed perfectly. It felt earned. Cyberpunk 2077 may not have the deepest story ever told in gaming, but as a complete package — visuals, atmosphere, combat, and world design — it is exceptional. It has carved its own identity. If you’re playing it post-2.0, you’re getting the game as it was meant to be experienced. A flawed launch, but an outstanding comeback.

One of the best games ever. Seriously. When it first launched, I played it on a friend’s PC. There were a lot of bugs back then — but honestly, they never stopped me from enjoying the game. The core experience was already strong. And now? It’s been massively improved, polished, expanded — it feels like a completely different level of quality. The world-building is incredible. Night City feels alive, layered, immersive. The characters are all compelling in their own way. The overall design — environments, fashion, UI, everything — is just cool. And the soundtrack? Absolutely great. Morro Rock Radio always fits the vibe perfectly. As someone who mostly plays story-driven games, I did have some mixed feelings about the romance options for female V. It sometimes felt like the partners get very attached very quickly. I personally prefer something more balanced — that’s why I actually like the dynamic with Panam (even though you can’t romance her as female V in the base game). She feels like a fully independent character with her own life and priorities. I just wish there was a bit more variety in relationship dynamics — maybe more shared activities, more different emotional tones. Everyone has their own preferences, of course, but for me the romance paths for female V felt a bit too centered on intense attachment. That said — everything else? I loved it. Leveling up is fun. Experimenting with builds is fun. Exploring is fun. The story hits hard. I 2077% recommend playing this game. And trust me — you won’t finish it just once.

Amazing game, there really isn't another game like it which is very disappointing. This review may look negative but trust me there is far more positives to outweigh the negatives I list To start, I'd highly recommend installing the "New Game+" mod from Nexus, as this game does not have a new game plus mechanic. I would also like to warn you that when it comes to missions in this game, they are chronologically awful. They use mission tokens that can be received only after finishing select missions, however these tokens are not directly tied to said missions so you may not receive the next part of a quest line for like 3 in game days. There is a mod that allows you to force the mission token so you don't have to be waiting hours on end. The mods name is Content Token Activator The story and sub stories are amazing, my only issues with it are: 1) Lack of expansive content: This is not to say the game does not have a lot of content, there's a decent amount of missions, however none of the missions really stand out to you, none of them I really found myself enjoying (aside from the relationship questlines). There isn't a lot to any of the questlines for that matter and once you finish them there really isn't anything to do. Ideally most players would want a lot more content or at least the have the community provided with better mod tools so the players can continue to expand the game. 2) Lack of difficulty: The games really easy, even on it's hardest difficulties. This is all I really have to say about this and I'd definitely recommend adding some form of combat or enemy overhaul mod. 3) Lack of creativity: The game itself is a creative masterpiece, however when it comes down to combat/enemies/missions nothing really feels unique. All of the enemies have the same attack patterns, mechanics, etc. The missions are pretty predictable and all feel the same just with slight twists. There's no real sense of urgency with any of the missions and they're mostly all just "kill this group of people" type missions. Would have definitely been nicer to see a more extensive set of quests and game mechanics. P.S: The driving mechanic is kinda clunky I don't think much time was put into it ---- The entire CP2077 community share the same sentiment with wanting more content for this game which we unfortunately will not be getting as CDPR have started working on the next Cyberpunk game. They have stated that when they started working on CP2077 that this is not the game they intended on making, however I'm glad they did because it's truly a masterpiece. This being said, this is and likely forever will be my favourite game (unless the second game is even better) and I highly recommend it because it's definitely an experience.

Cyberpunk 2077: A Neon-Drenched Masterpiece It is a rare and beautiful thing in the gaming industry when a title not only redeems itself but completely eclipses its original promises. Playing Cyberpunk 2077 in 2026 is an entirely different experience than it was at its initial launch. Through relentless patching, sweeping system overhauls, and the masterful Phantom Liberty expansion, CD Projekt Red has forged one of the most immersive, breathtaking open-world action RPGs of this generation. Cyberpunk 2077 is an absolute must-play experience today. A City Like No Other Night City is arguably the main character of the game, and it stands as a marvel of virtual architecture and atmosphere. Unmatched Immersion: From the towering, rain-slicked corporate skyscrapers of Corpo Plaza to the dusty, sun-baked badlands outside the city limits, the world feels incredibly dense and alive. You can spend hours simply cruising the streets, listening to the meticulously curated radio stations. Granular Detail: Continuous updates—right up to the latest 2.3 patch—have introduced fully functioning transit systems, AutoDrive features, and expanded weather dynamics like acid rain and sandstorms. The neon-lit alleys, shifting crowd densities, and towering megabuildings make this one of the most believable dystopian settings ever crafted. Deep, Rewarding Gameplay The core gameplay loop has been completely rebuilt since launch, evolving into a phenomenally satisfying sandbox of destruction, hacking, and stealth. Total Freedom in Combat: You are not locked into a single playstyle. You can be a hyper-mobile cyber-ninja deflecting bullets with a katana, a hulking solo with Gorilla Arms tearing heavy machine guns off their turrets, or a netrunner frying enemies’ cyberware from the shadows without ever drawing a weapon. Meaningful Progression: The overhauled perk and cyberware systems ensure that every skill point you spend fundamentally changes how you approach encounters. Installing "chrome" at a Ripperdoc actually feels impactful, balancing your immense new powers against the limits of your character's physical capacity. Narrative Brilliance Where the game truly cements its legacy is in its writing, voice acting, and intricate quest design. Emotional Resonance: V’s desperate fight for survival, complicated by the digital ghost of rockerboy-terrorist Johnny Silverhand (played brilliantly by Keanu Reeves), is deeply gripping. The companions you meet—like Panam, Judy, and River—feel incredibly human, flawed, and memorable. The Spy-Thriller Peak: The Phantom Liberty expansion elevates the storytelling to new heights. It introduces Dogtown, a ruined, walled-off district, and delivers a tense, espionage-driven storyline featuring Idris Elba. Furthermore, the game's side gigs rarely feel like filler; they are rich, tangled moral dilemmas that force you to make tough, lasting choices. The Verdict Cyberpunk 2077 is a triumph of persistence, artistic direction, and creative vision. It manages to balance high-octane, visceral action with quiet, introspective moments exploring identity, extreme corporate greed, and the commodification of the human body. Whether you are experiencing it on a high-end PC or through the impressively optimized modern console versions, it is a stunning, deeply rewarding RPG that fully delivers on the fantasy of being an edgerunner trying to become a legend.

And every moment is chock full of moments as you rise to the status of legend within Night City, the sprawling, chaotic, alive maze of roads that it is. Story: It's good, Keanu Reeves really is 1 of the biggest highlights of this game honestly as he sticks with you throughout the entire damn thing. Gameplay: With so many choices to make and ways to approach combat, I can see why people enjoy replaying this game a lot. Once in a while, a bright star shines in the gaming firmament, gifting us with a gem like Cyberpunk 2077. I haven't seen such a well-made game in a very long time—and I've seen a lot. Yes, I was late to the party and can't say much about the bugs that were reported at release. But in its current state, the game is a steroid-fueled rollercoaster ride. Pure cinematic magic. I love the execution and the sheer audacity that CD Projekt Red has shown with this game. The legend is woven slowly and lovingly, only to mercilessly throw the player back into the cyberpunk setting at the next opportunity. The German voice acting features many well-known and truly great voices, which immediately gave me a big-screen feel. And I'm sure my next playthrough in English will be just as captivating. I still have a few achievements to unlock. The modding community has showered the game with love because the possibilities are wide open – replayability and fun have always been the primary focus, rather than monetization. Let's see if the sequel maintains these qualities and – I sincerely hope so – includes an online mode. 11 out of 10 – not because it's flawless or perfect, but because it tells a story that stands out so wonderfully from the bland uniformity so common today.

Want to stab people from a mile away with throwing knives along with stealth? Have at it. Want to handle LMGs like they're regular rifles and slam hundreds of rounds into people, shredding them to bits? ♥♥♥♥ it, why not? Maybe you're more into hacking their miserable brain and uploading 40PB of furry art or some ♥♥♥♥ into their neurons? The world (and their brains) is (are?) your oyster(s). I'd have heavily not recommended this game years ago, but in the state it is, it's *extremely* hard not to recommend it. I mean I played the ♥♥♥♥ out of it in multiple story paths and builds. Playing Cyberpunk 2077 felt like stepping into a city that never truly lets you breathe. From the moment I started, there was this constant sense of tension — like everything around me was bigger, louder, and more dangerous than I was. Night City isn’t just a setting; it feels oppressive, seductive, and strangely beautiful all at once. What struck me the most was how personal everything felt. Conversations didn’t feel like simple dialogue options — they felt loaded. Some choices left me sitting there for a second, actually thinking about the consequences. There were moments of chaos and gunfire, sure, but the quiet scenes hit just as hard. Driving alone at night with the neon lights reflecting on the streets gave me this strange mix of loneliness and freedom. Combat felt satisfying in different ways depending on how I approached it. Sometimes I went in loud and reckless, and other times I slowed down, hacked cameras, and watched everything unfold from the shadows. That freedom made every encounter feel like my own story instead of a scripted sequence. What really stayed with me, though, was the atmosphere. The music, the lights, the crowds, the small details in random alleyways — it all builds this world that feels alive but also decaying. There’s glamour on the surface, but underneath it all, there’s desperation. And the more I played, the more I felt like I was becoming part of that machine. It’s one of those experiences that pulls you in slowly. The longer I stayed in Night City, the harder it was to leave.

When I first played this game in May of 2016, the only thing anyone would say was that it was an amazing, outstanding game and I needed to put down whatever I was doing and give it a go. I absolutely hated it. I went through over 2 years of in-game time before uninstalling it out of frustration, wondering how anyone got ahead in this game with so little help, and I had made almost no progress due to being grossly uninformed about how to play the game. There are no in-game gui tutorials or mechanical explanations of anything in the entire game, and you are very much dropped into the thick of it, up a certain creek without an oar. Townspeople seem arbitrarily cold, dismissive, and harsh until you remember that you are a stranger in a town of no more than 40, and they don't really have much to say to you to start with. Your tools suck. You went from being an office worker to a farmhand, so your stamina sucks. You have almost no starting capital. Seed is expensive, and working the farm is hard work. You'll find that in the first week, you barely have the energy to turn over a frighteningly small amount of soil, plant seeds, and water your crops, much less talk to anybody and get on their good side. Your seeds routinely die at the season's turn, and you will need to start your farm plot over. You need to turn around your farm from a rotting cabin in an overgrown and refuse filled starting area to an economic powerhouse and pillar of community. How do you do it? I'll give you a secret that I wish I had when I had started. THIS IS A WIKI GAME. You will miss out on a lot of information and mechanics if you don't have someone to tell you or walk you through getting on your feet. Exploration is rewarded, and there are a LOT of secrets and niche to-do lists that can easily escape your notice in your already difficult routine. Answers are hard to come by, but there is literally no time pressure. You could make like SCP-7179 and play this game for an extraordinarily long time before finding something new and interesting. There's a lot to love, so I would encourage people to either play unaware or look up answers to their standard of enjoyment. If it's grown stale, you could well be missing something. Give it a chance, do not be afraid to look up answers, whether they be townspeople's routines, their favorite gifts, what they do on certain days, where to get items (and when!), and the nuances of various game mechanics. Unfortunately, one of the most helpful ways to approach the game is to get a mental head-start by watching someone else play it, either in tutorial fashion online or getting your wife to walk you through it. This is not my preferred way to induct myself into games, but I enjoy the game anyway. I now have the Perfection achievement, and I plan on doing so again in my newly modded version. It's daunting, it's big, and as of writing it's all for a very respectable price. One of the means by which I judge a game as being "worth my time" is whether it can meet a bare minimum of 1 hour of enjoyment per dollar USD that I spent on it. I've achieved that milestone by an order of magnitude, and I likely will twice over, as have many other people. Give it a chance, and don't give up like I did all those years ago.

Stardew Valley is my favorite game. It finds the perfect balance between compelling stakes and peaceful routine. There's so much versatility and so many areas to focus on, yet it never feels like you're missing out on something. The day/season/year system is the perfect pace. The combat feels balanced. The fishing mechanic is one of the best in any game. Of course the farming is simple and meditative. For a game with a set map, it still feels exciting to explore every corner. There are minigames, puzzles, and events that keep the game fresh. Secrets to find. The decorating aspect and customization options feel immensely underrated. The characters and story give a soul to a game that already feels full of life. The music and art are endearing and complement the atmosphere very well. There is consistently more to the game than meets the eye. In addition to all of this, I think the main thing that made me keep playing was the sense of progression. No matter what my goal was at the time, it always felt like I was making progress. There's always a small, medium, and large goal to work toward. If any one of them begin to feel stale, you can shift your focus without moving backward. Advancing in any scope feels rewarding. From a more external perspective, it has an extensive and well-organized wiki. It has great mod support and plenty of tools and trackers to support unmodded gameplay. The updates never detract from the game, and if anything they feel natural and integrate very well into the existing content. The gameplay is smooth and the performance is good. It's worth the price and then some. Stardew Valley is so much more than a farming sim. Stardew is great if you like grinding. It's great if you like to play casually. It's fun if you like collecting, and satisfying if you're a completionist. It's structured if you like to plan things out, and flexible if you're a more free-form player. It's equally as good a singleplayer as it is a multiplayer game. There is not a single area in which it doesn't exceed my expectations.

As someone who usually gravitates toward indie strategy and simulation games like RimWorld, Songs of Syx, and thousands of hours of Sid Meier’s Civilization IV with the Realism Invictus mod, Stardew Valley really doesn’t fit the normal mold of games I typically play. However, this game is nothing short of a masterpiece. ConcernedApe is an absolute mad genius. The guy is a folk hero who has elevated indie gaming to an entirely new level, and Stardew Valley truly sits at the summit of the genre. The gameplay loop is incredible. The “just one more day” problem is very real — you keep telling yourself you’ll stop after tomorrow, then suddenly you want to finish the season, unlock the next upgrade, complete one more bundle, build one more shed, or see what happens next. There is always another goal, another progression point, and another thing to look forward to. What’s most impressive is how deceptively deep the game is. At first glance it looks simple and relaxing, but underneath is one of the most addictive and rewarding gameplay systems I’ve experienced in years. If you’ve ever thought about trying Stardew Valley and haven’t yet, you are genuinely missing out. I know I was. This game deserves every bit of praise it receives. Buy it now and don’t think twice about it.

[h2] Gameplay [/h2] Stardew Valley is a 2D farming game but it is not just about the farm. You can fish, forage around the map, raise animals and go into mines for resources. During this process, you can build relationships with local residents and join town festivals. There is no limit in the game but you unlock new areas step by step. You progress by completing tasks in the main story, improving your farm and getting closer to NPCs. [h2] Graphics [/h2] Stardew Valley is a 2D pixel game. The file size is very small and even a potato computer can run it. If you do not like pixel art, the graphics might bother you. However, you can enjoy the game with its cute pixel style. [h2] Audio [/h2] The game has unique sounds and very sweet music. I think the nature sounds are great. The wind and the sound of falling leaves in Autumn are my favorites. When Winter comes, everything becomes quiet. They put a lot of effort into the audio and it fits this kind of game perfectly. [h2] Storytelling [/h2] In the story, we take over a farm in Stardew Valley that belonged to our grandfather. We start the game by leaving the capitalist world and the "Joja" company because we are tired of that life. We dedicate ourselves to nature and farming. We meet other people in the valley, build relationships and witness some fantasy events. You can even choose a partner and get married. The story always focuses on themes of friendship and nature. [h2] Difficulty [/h2] The game is mostly easy but has some challenging parts. You need to fight monsters in the mines to get metal ores, which has a decent difficulty. The main challenge is planning your farm and crops to make enough money. You can run out of cash, but you can always catch up in the following years. Just remember that you cannot grow crops in winter.

Ludonarrative dissonance is a term used to describe the conflict between a game's story and its mechanics/gameplay. In the case of Stardew Valley, I have nothing but praise for the gameplay loops and design, blending almost every single possible element of classic games like Harvest Moon and Rune Factory into deep and fairly beginner-friendly farming experience with only a few minor exceptions. However, of all of Stardew Valley's flaws, I believe the greatest to be the aforementioned ludonarrative dissonance. Community building, anti-corporate sentiment, appreciation for a small-town lifestyle, and a return to simple living are prominently featured themes of the game, but basically every player ends up turning their own slice of small town heaven into an automated money printer that's filled to the brim with ways to get richer and richer. The game tells you to live a simple life, but so much of what you do in game is designed to increase the efficiency and output of your farm. That isn't to say that I believe the game is designed poorly, since I don't believe that at all. Rather, this is just a commentary on how people play games and constantly push the boundaries towards their logical extremes. After all, it's nice to have a farm with 80 green bean plants that you have to water every day by hand, but why settle for that when you can just do a little mining and have those 80 plants automatically watered by sprinklers? And once you have those sprinklers, why not make a few more? And so on, until you're planting 1678 Ancient Fruit on your farm to harvest a total of 15k fruit by the end of Fall and cycling through dehydrators, kegs, and casks to earn a roundabout figure of 22,665,000 for that calendar year. Fantastic game. Highly recommend.

Stardew Valley will always have a permanent place in my heart—and honestly, in our story. My (now soon-to-be husband) and I had just started dating in early 2020 when the world shut down. Like so many people, we suddenly found ourselves separated with no real way to see each other in person. What we did have, though, was time—and Stardew Valley. What started as a simple way to pass the time turned into something so much more. We played on every platform we could get our hands on, building farm after farm, learning each other’s quirks through how we played—who handled crops, who mined, who forgot to water things (me). Those countless hours weren’t just gaming sessions—they were our dates, our quality time, our way of staying connected when everything else felt uncertain. Since then, we’ve started new farms, made new memories, and even got to experience Symphony of Seasons together, which felt like such a full-circle moment. It reminded me just how much this game has meant to us. I genuinely believe that Stardew Valley helped build the foundation of our relationship during a time when we needed it most. It gave us a space to laugh, work together, and just be together when we physically couldn’t. For that, it will always be more than just a game to me. It’s a piece of our love story.

I've been playing Stardew Valley since my cousin showed it to me in the summer of 2020. I initially played on the Nintendo Switch and immediately fell in love with the game. I had never really been much of a gamer outside of Mario Kart and Mario Party (games you typically play with other people) but it was so easy to get lost in the world that ConcernedApe created. After figuring out the mechanics of how to play, it didn't take long for me to sink hours into the game. When it came time for my cousin to leave the state, my husband bought me my own copy to play and I ended up racking up 600 hours before I managed to save enough for my own PC. (POV: I'm the girl that spent $1400 on a PC that can run huge games just so I could play modded Stardew Valley 😂😂) It's so much more than a farming simulator! This game has so much wrapped up in it and I honestly couldn't recommend it enough. There's farming, fishing, mining, and so much more! You can take care of farm animals and pets, you can start your own brewery/winery, you can get married! (Marriage is also inclusive-sometimes mentioned in dialogue when you're in a same-sex relationship!) The NPCs and their stories are so well done and fun to play through, the quests constantly give you something new to do, not to mention that Eric is constantly working on the game to add more things to it! I'm so excited for the 1.7 update to see what he adds along with how he writes both Sandy and Clint's stories! This game is incredible and so fun to play solo and/or with others! There's so many shenanigans to get up to with others (text signs are often used in my co-ops😂😂) All in all I just really love this game and I've bought many of my friends their own copy via Steam's gifting option! It's a wonderful game and I cannot recommend it enough 💛 Also note: This is a top down view game, so if you struggle with motion sickness from 1st person games like me (ex: minecraft/peak/repo/fps/vrchat) this game won't trigger that nausea!
