Genuielly the coziest game I've played in a long time. For me, someone with major ADHD, it does take me keeping a list on my phone so that I can stay on track, but its such an amazing game, its so much fun, the graphics are amazing, and its just over so much fun. For me, I love the marriage graphics as well, everytime I got for Harvey, he is the sweetest! I also really like the range of quests and characters, it helps the game be more immersive. Some games I've played have minimal quests and its easy and quick, but this challenges you, it also gives you a big range of time to finish it all. I also love how you can choose what you like to do most, mining, foraging, fishing, farming, completing quests, getting full hearts with everyone, etc. ANYWAYS, I love the games and totally recommend it to someone who likes cozy games but also likes a bit of range and challenge. TIPS IF YOU BOUGHT THE GAME: - Go to the cindersap forest every Friday and Sunday with money, towards the pink tree/secret forrest there is a cart that can help you finish the community center/help you buy things. - Check the Stardew Valley WIKI for help, it has info on everything, from Fish to Foraging to Characters. - If you friend certain characters they will send you things in the mail (I can't remember the characters but look it up on google or youtube) - Cooking Lady is on the TV every Wednesday (Re-Run) and Sunday. She teaches you new recipes and can really help - If you're going into the mines, pack high energy foods, you will get lower energy and not be able to finish automatically. - Giving presents on characters birthdays majorly boosts friendship points - Finish the community center earlier on, it may not seem important but trust me, it is, it unlocks a lot of important/helpful quests (Like Willy's Boat) and finishing bundles helps a lot (Like with the greenhouse, minecarts, bus to the desert, the quarry, etc.)

Stardew Valley is a perfect game because it works regardless of the kind of person you are: A. You are a person who wants to relax and have a nice, cozy experience watering some crops, raising some animals, fishing, making friends, and exploring caves. Stardew Valley puts no pressure on you to have anything done by a certain date, so you are free to do whatever you want each day and work towards one goal at a time if you want to. B. You're a hardcore optimizer who wants to unlock the late game as early as possible, so you min-max every single day, calculating ROI and profit/day, even arguing online as to why parsnips are actually one of the best early game crops and cauliflower is massively overrated. You view each season not as a change of pace or scenery, but as a clock where X, Y, Z, and W all need to be finished before the season ends. This game isn't a relaxing, cozy farm simulator, it's a machine needing to be optimized to make sweet sweet money. I'm a B type, and I know plenty of my friends are A types. If either of those sound appealing to you, there's never been a better time to play than right now.

Stardew Valley is one of those games you start casually and suddenly lose hours to. It is a farming sim at its core, but there is so much more to it. You build your farm, form relationships, explore mines, fish, and slowly become part of the town. The freedom to play at your own pace is what makes it so special. The pixel art and music are charming, and the game has a really relaxing, comforting vibe. It is easy to get into but has a surprising amount of depth if you want to optimise everything. There is not really a downside unless you are looking for fast paced gameplay. It is meant to be slow and chill. Overall, it is one of the best indie games ever made and easily worth your time. Highly Recommended.

I've been meaning to write this for a while, because as you can see, I have 101 hours played in this game. That alone should tell you how good the game is, lol. After all, if you didn't like the game, why play that long, right? Anyways! This game has so much too it, that it's almost overwhelming (but in a good way). There's never nothing to do, and I don't ever feel bored while playing it. While gardening is a good portion of it, you can also fish and go mining, and collect things to sell or keep. The aesthetic of the game is very pleasing, and the music is perfect and fits the game nicely. I find a lot of the time that I play Stardew, that I can relax and have a good time. But it also has lots of difficulty too. Like you have to know what items are worth more to sell, where to find everything, and when going to a mine, you have to keep track of your health or you may die! Not only that, you also have to focus on energy, too, which can be depleted by most things you do in-game. This makes it more fun, and spices things up. It also helps those who want something more intense to do! You can also own animals, as well as pets, and have bonds with them! This is another great feature as it makes things feel more personal and customized. Let alone the fact you can get married and have kids, too! The game makes you feel like you're a part of a community, and these aspects (along with the others mentioned), just makes it feel more rewarding and satisfying. This is a game where you don't even need mods to enjoy (though there are some amazing ones that I'm sure would make it even better), and while there are some frustrating things--such as the days going so quick--it doesn't dampen the fun you can have in this game. Overall, with all that I mentioned (and the stuff I didn't), this game is very worth giving a shot!

Stardew Valley is, by far, the best game in existence. It's such a rare occurrence to find a game that does everything so well. You can engage in farming, fishing, mining, battling monsters, building friendships, decorating your land, and simply chilling to the music at your leisure. There is no stress or outside pressure; it's strictly up to you how you want to play. What makes this game so exceptional is how relaxing it is the end of a long day. As a game, it is an escape. The soundtrack is soothing, the art is simple yet beautiful, and the town feels like it's alive. You've grown to care about each character, their backstories, and even their most mundane daily activities. And the best part? You won't ever get bored. There's always something new for you to do or achieve, whether upgrading your land, finishing collections, or arranging your farm just so. Hours pass by in what feels like seconds. This is more than a video game, this is both comfort and nostalgia, along with having fun rolled together in one. If you haven't experienced this yet, then you're missing out!

Couple things: 1) This game is awesome. From the first in-game day I was hooked. (unlike those Legendary fish unfortunately, but that comes with time and patience.) 2) Please remember to eat, sleep, and use the bathroom regularly while playing this game. (This goes for the human you AS WELL as your in-game avatar... although I don't even have a concept of how going to the bathroom would work in Stardew Valley) It's very engrossing, so much so it can feel like you've built a whole life, a whole world in here. However -- you have not, and you should probably get some fresh air, call a friend, and take your Zoloft. 3) Beware of the Maple Syrup bear. I'm pretty sure that's just Clint dressed up as a bear to mooch maple syrup off of you. Just be safe out there. 4) In my first playthrough I made the dumb mistake of not crafting as many kegs as I could and also giving away the first prismatic shard I ever got. And buying only chickens for your coops. Save money and buy pigs. Also get auto-petters with max luck in the Skull Caverns. Or give your animals some delicious yum yum blue grass or regular and plant it around. USE FIBER SEEDS BETWEEN SEASONS THEY GROW IN WINTER. Also do not make all of your tree seeds into field snacks and eat them. You will want those trees. Sell some of the valuable stuff too. Smoke some largemouth bass. 5) OP TIP -- fishing. Fishing in this game is lowkey goated. If you get good at the minigame you can make so much money and quickly. Once you get to Mr. Qi's Walnut room get the challenge bait, get two cork bobbers on as your tackles, make seafoam pudding with Qi seasoning, which I call Qi-salt -- get it? like sea salt? -- anyways. Also max out your fishing skill early obviously, and choose the Angler profession. You can catch multiple Legend II fish per day with the Extended Family Quest from Mr. Qi. If you get Iridium Legend II fish, save one and smoke the rest to make 42000g per fish with the Artisan profession. Don't forget to put some of them into ponds for really great profit from their aged roe. Don't put a high quality fish into a pond though, or it will lose its value if you try to fish it out. 6) The spouses are fine. I usually marry Abigail or Hailey but Emily is seriously underrated. Alex gets way too much hate imo. But I always play as the male farmer so I guess that's privilege speaking. Honestly they're all so tiring sometimes and the little kids are so irritating. I like when you can rocket throw them into the air like a ballistic missile but that's about all the fun you'll have. Meh. If you ask me, get Krobus to move in with you. We should also have the option to marry or become roomies with Dwarf. I love Dwarf so much. Is it too much to ask that I move into the mines? 7) We should be able to upgrade cabins without multiplayer in the game. I want to have a ton of places to decorate and I play Stardew solo most of the time (there was that one time with that one loooong gone situationship but that file is somewhere in hell with the lava eels, I'm sure. I think I trauma bonded with this game. Bygones will be bygones but the echoes in my memory will haunt me forever). 8) The Dangerous Skull Caverns is awesome for mining radioactive ore. Max luck + (lucky ring + iridium band) + (napalm + slime charmer) + (qi seasoning + lucky lunch) + (+1 ore per vein buff from Dwarf Statue) + staircases + (ginger ale/triple shot espresso + qi seasoning) + Statue of Blessings = Radioactive Ore-a Farming (see what I did there? Ore-a? Aura? Eh? Eh? Please feed me to a Serpent.) 9) If you don't have life elixir just eat a lot of carrots or summer squash. 10) Make sure you put tappers on enough oak trees. You can never have enough of the sticky stuff (oak resin, get your mind out of the gutter). Also maple syrup for beehives. 11) Slime hutches are not worth it. Do them once and never again. 12) Gil should be a friendable character. 13) For a lot of profit, short term, Starfruit is the answer. For long term steady and replenishable profit, ancient fruit wins every single time. 14) I hate the little squids in the Dangerous mines. They are nothing but trouble. It would redeem them slightly if you could capture one and put a hat on it. ConcernedApe? You'll consider this for the 1.8 Update maybe? 15) Seed makers are a game changer once you unlock them. It beats having to go to Pierre every time for overpriced BS. 16) Don't ignore dehydrators, especially for medium high value fruits (like pineapples) and mushrooms especially. 17) Jade farming from Crystalariums is OP for staircases. Love me a good staircase. 18) Name your animals after item codes when you get them from Marnie. You can change the name back later and you get free stuff. 19) Enrichers are not that helpful. Pressure nozzles are much better. Ultimately use Deluxe Retaining soil for the most yield (it's just a lot of crafting). 20) If you have a lot of Qi gems buy a bunch of hoppers and a deconstructor and get a ton of radioactive bars from deconstructing the ore. Plant a ton of mossy seeds to get moss which is very important and one of the most difficult resources to have enough of in game. The Fairy or Parrot Egg are the best trinkets in game. Put the Frog Eggs in an aquarium. Sell the other trinkets or throw them out to make more space in your inventories. They don't stack. Take advantage of the Desert Festival to get Magic Rock Candy. Use a staircase in Mayor Lewis' bedroom to get to a dark maze and at the end of it, get his Purple "shorts". Then use them on any tackle of which you wish to preserve the quality. Then use Emily's Sewing machine to tailor them and wear them around Lewis and Marnie to troll them. Put the extra ones in the town's soup at the Luau. Buy rare seeds from the Traveling cart and grow iridium or gold Sweet Gem Berries for fun. Feed the Trash bear. Beat Abigail at the Egg Hunt every. Single. Time. Put jukeboxes in the barns/coops so your animals have something to listen to as they quietly wait out their inevitable existence. Be free. Have fun. Relax by sorting things. I don't know. There's a lot to do and I haven't even scratched the surface.

The way this game allows you to set your own pace -- from one extreme of maximising efficiency to the other of strolling through town and talking to villagers (or standing outside their door grasping a gift you're ready to throw at them the second it opens) -- is so flawlessly executed that I tip my hat to ConcernedApe. You can tell he poured his heart and soul into this game; it has so much warmth and personality, and I truly find it such a comfort each time I play it, whether alone or with friends. In the annals of rustic diversion and pastoral delight, there existeth a singular creation of notable charm and quiet profundity, known unto the modern age as Stardew Valley. This electronic contrivance, though fashioned in an era of advanced artifices, doth summon the spirit of simpler times, wherein the labours of the field and the fellowship of a close-knit village did form the essence of a life well-lived. It is with due reverence and studied contemplation that one may examine the manifold virtues of this most commendable game. At its commencement, the participant is cast as an inheritor of neglected lands, once tended with care, yet now fallen into disrepair. This inheritance, bestowed by a departed grandsire, doth serve as both burden and opportunity. The soil lieth fallow, the structures crumbleth, and yet within such decay resideth the promise of renewal. Thus beginneth the noble endeavour of cultivation, whereby the player must, through diligence and foresight, restore vitality unto the land. The act of husbandry, though simple in its outward appearance, revealeth itself to be of intricate design. Seeds must be chosen with wisdom, for each season bringeth forth its own bounty and demandeth its own sacrifices. The tilling of earth, the watering of crops, and the eventual harvest thereof are tasks that, whilst repetitive, instil a curious satisfaction. Therein lieth a reflection of life itself, wherein persistence and patience yield fruits most gratifying. Yet Stardew Valley is not solely a tale of soil and seed. It is, in equal measure, a study of community and human connexion. The village, quaint and unassuming, is inhabited by a diverse assembly of souls, each possessed of distinct character and temperament. Through acts of kindness, the offering of gifts, and the simple courtesy of conversation, bonds may be forged. Friendships blossom, rivalries soften, and, in some instances, love itself may take root. The passage of time within this world is marked by the turning of seasons, each bearing its own visage and atmosphere. Spring awakeneth the land with gentle rains and budding life; summer bestoweth warmth and abundance; autumn painteth the fields in hues of gold and crimson; and winter bringeth a hush of snow and introspection. This cyclical nature imparteth a rhythm that governeth all endeavours, urging the player to plan with care and to cherish each fleeting moment. Moreover, the game extendeth its diversions beyond the confines of agriculture. The adventurous spirit may descend into caverns, wherein lurketh both treasure and peril. Fishing in tranquil waters, foraging in the wilderness, and crafting implements of utility further enrich the experience. Such variety ensureth that monotony findeth no lasting foothold, and that each day presenteth new choices and possibilities. Of particular note is the aesthetic presentation of Stardew Valley, which employeth a style both modest and evocative. The visual form, rendered in pixels, doth nonetheless convey a richness of detail and emotion. The music, gentle and melodious, accompanieth the player’s journey with a grace that stirreth the heart. Together, these elements createth an atmosphere of serenity seldom matched in works of its kind. One must also commend the spirit in which this game was brought into being. It standeth as a testament to the vision and perseverance of its creator, who, through singular effort, hath fashioned a work of enduring appeal. Such dedication is mirrored in the experience itself, wherein the player is likewise encouraged to invest time and care into the shaping of their virtual existence. In contemplation of all these facets, it becometh evident that Stardew Valley is more than mere pastime. It is an ode to the virtues of simplicity, a meditation upon labour and reward, and a celebration of community. In an age oft consumed by haste and distraction, it offereth a gentle reminder of the joys to be found in patience, in routine, and in the quiet cultivation of one’s surroundings. Thus, in conclusion, one may assert with confidence that Stardew Valley is indeed a game of uncommon merit. Its harmonious blending of mechanics, aesthetics, and thematic depth rendereth it worthy of both admiration and enduring regard. Whosoever seeketh solace in a world of gentle endeavour and heartfelt connexion would do well to partake in its offerings, for therein lieth an experience both enriching and profoundly agreeable.

I played this game a lot on my Switch, I guess handheld is just for me! But let me tell ya something, this game is beautiful, it brings back a lot of nostalgic game play when it comes to cozy gaming. It has endless, quests to work on, but most of all it is ENDLESS. Its a cozy game! What can I say? You are going to find yourself trying to make coin, to provide for your expansion in your home, to make upgrades such as fishing poles, axe, and steel pick, not to mention provide for your farm animals. You also get lost in structuring how your farm will look, such as your crops, if you wanna grow some parsnips, or grow a beautiful tulip flower garden. All in the while, you make sure to socialize with everyone, learn what gifts they want, and let me tell ya some of them are the most pickiest SOB's I ever met (hahahaa but its cool its like a quest!) One person will like that you handed them over a purple crystal such as an Amythest quartz, and one person will absolutely hate it! Its fun to learn these characters and what kind of gifts they like in order to be closer with them. get you some chickens though, they are cute AF, I love feeding them and collecting their eggs. Eventually you get to have more farm animals, you even get started off with a farm pet of your choice whether it is a cat, or a dog + giving you a choice from different breeds. OH don't forget the dungeons, you get to explore those too! There are many levels, to discover different loot that will boost your fight power, and skills. Also when you first start you get to choose what map ya want, and thats just the cherry on top. Different terrains? THATS A WIN! I like the beach, you get to find washed up crates, the spooky map is fun too! Creatures appear at night, makes you feel like your in Silent hill where ya got a curfew HAHAH. Anyways, if you want immersive game play that is endless, and at your own leisure GET you this game.

Stardew valley is a near perfect farming sim game, I'd give it 9/10. The graphic style and soundtrack are my favourite out of the other popular farming sim games that I've seen, and the intro that shows your character escaping the rush of modern life to live on the farm can really resonate. There are so many different aspects and systems to this game that it makes you feel like whatever you're doing, you're always making progress or money for your farm. There's a huge variety of crops, plants and trees to grow and harvest, animals to look after and fish to catch which you can of course sell but also use for cooking a huge variety of meals. One of the games goals it to cook them all, other goals that yield great rewards including catching every fish and selling one of every item in the game, giving completionists something to strive for. One thing I would like to state though is that this game is not "relaxing", despite it's appearance and what some people may say. In the early game you will be rushing around to accomplish your tasks each day before bedtime or before you run out of stamina, and in the mid to late game there are some difficult areas with tough enemies that require a lot of preparation to navigate. I don't mind this, but this game may not be what some people are looking for because of this. The rushing around diminishes as you progress through the game thankfully, as you become faster, unlock fast travel and special items for teleportation. That's not why I gave 9/10 instead of 10/10 though. The reason for this is because of the relationships system, I feel it doesn't hold up to the other main systems of the game in terms of quality and rewards. I feel like the relationship system would be a lot better if it was less one-sided. Relationships are of course optional, but the gifts and rewards you get aren't really worthwhile for the amount of gifts you have to give and the money it costs to get married and have children. It would be great if each marriage candidate could bring something unique to the farm to help you. For example Maru could build gadgets that help you farm more efficiently since she's into tech and inventions. It would also be better if there were more ways to increase the heart metre for the characters. Currently I believe the only way to do this outside of a few specific quests is by giving gifts and talking to them, but it would be cool if you could take people out on dates, bond over farming activities and play games with your children. My criticisms of the relationship system aside, this game is a near perfect farming sim and is worth it even at full price for the amount great content available.

Tldr; Wiki-game. Look up everything. Punishes your ignorance rather than rewarding your curiosity. Frustrating rather than relaxing. Induces "fear of missing out" while pressing deadlines over your head. I would recommend the game due to the general fun there is, but it feels like a game you’re supposed to have a wiki next to you to enjoy, despite me trying to avoid that until I get too tired of the pressing ingame deadlines and dates to keep up with to have more than just watering my crops. Simply put- there’s too many "gotcha, try again next year" moments and small annoyances to make this game relaxing and not just annoying to play. Want an example? A small assignment, get 20 copper ore. Earlier assignments allow you to use items you found before, but for this specific job you can’t use the 80 copper ore you had mined before. You need NEW copper ore. Could’ve been worded better or been very explicit rather than "bring 20 copper ore". Another example? Giving villagers gifts is a pain in the ass too. They don’t like a gift? They’ll take it anyway, say "I hate it! Don’t give me gifts!" like a toddler having a tantrum and practically speaking, throw it on the ground to spite you rather than to say no thanks and refuse it. Why can’t I straight up slap the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ after that level of disrespect? The relaxing baby game feels more like a drama town simulator. Also, long term saves will not make much sense because the villagers will never change or age. Another, different criticism is about villagers never bothering to initiate conversation with you- except for business owners trying to sell you ♥♥♥♥. "Come buy new seeds! Buy my furniture!" I like Willy at least. That guy gives you a free fishing rod and just shares with you his love for fishing. The villagers are realistic in a sense, but moreso boring and the lack of interaction makes not only the characters feel shallow but the social game as well, as they will only say the same lines everyday. Like I get it, Penny works as a teacher, Shane works a depressing job at Joja and hates you and so on- they will never bother to get to know you, they only care if you, the new guy showers them in gifts they specifically like (which you would never find out about without trial and error, hence the wikipedia game label)

Let me start by saying that Stardew Valley has firmly placed itself in the Top 3 of my favorite games of all time. I do take breaks from time to time, but I ALWAYS end up coming back to start a new farm and try out something I haven't done before in other playthroughs. I'll start out by going over some dislikes I have, all be it very few, then we can move on to the good stuff. Dislikes: 1. Clint. Look I know it's a meme to hate on this guy, but it does come from reason. There is something about his personality that just comes across, to me, as a whiney man baby, that just doesn't sit right with me. His constant obsession with Emily, as an adult, is weird. Its like an elementary school kid having a crush, as an adult its just weird. Then, what is this guy's hours. He closes at 4pm. What else does he have to do all day? He literally does nothing besides a blacksmith, which is a huge part of the game, yet this dude closes at 4pm. 2. Harvey/The Clinic. I understand the need for this location from a gameplay perspective and a in-world perspective, but same issue as Clint but worse....what on earth are these hours. I feel like I NEVER interact with the clinic yet Harvey AND Maru work there. Every time I ever see Harvey he's just standing around not even in the clinic and Maru isn't even behind the desk 50% of the time. On top of that its only open from like 11am-3pm. Why? It doesn't help that Harvey as a character is so dull and boring. I wish there was more of a purpose for The Clinic as a whole. 3. Some of the Farm choices. This is a very small nitpick, but some of the farm types I find to be confusing on why I would ever choose them. Hilltop is significantly smaller than any other farm in map size but also WAY less space to even build or farm in. Its a cool idea for a farm, I just wish it had more room to breathe. The Wilderness farm is also a weird one to me, mostly because there's an option in game to turn on or off Monster Spawns on any Farm type. Likes: 1. The Progression. I've never played a game with a progression system as satisfying. Throughout all the types of skills, the slow burn of tiering up weapons and gaining XP in each skill to become more efficient, I don't know its just super satisfying. 2. The Characters(as a whole). The sheer amount of character lore and growth and amount of interactions and dialogue, its stunning someone came up with all of this and has it all work together so well. I will never begin to understand the Dark Magic that Concerned Ape was able to conjure to map out this many NPC's individual schedules that are ALL dependent on what season, character progression, weather, etc. Its emaculate. 3. The Art style. This game is the king of 2D Pixel Art. Everything about the way this game looks is just iconic. As a Pixel Artist myself, its so fun to see all the ways things are made to look like, from the shaping to the shading, etc. 4. Gameplay Variety. A lot of the time with games like this, players are mostly locked into a certain playstyle. However, with Stardew, you can be a casual gamer who's just trying to play the game as it comes. You could be an absolute chad and minmax the entire game. You can even play it entirely as a dating sim game with the NPCs. There's so many ways to play the game, which add to its replayability. Conclusion(for now): As of the time of this review, I have admittedly, not had the ability to explore much of Ginger Island, so I can not speak on that edition to the game. However I have watched my wife play through a lot of it, and I can say its impressive how much extra has been added to the point it feels like a whole seperate game that most companies would be charging full price for, and its just a free update. Overall, I think any type of gamer or even non-gamer, should give this game a try. I have recommended this game to a bunch of people over the years, that come from different walks of life, and I have yet to find someone who didn't have a blast playing this game in whatever capacity they had played it. If you have EVER considered trying the game, just get it. Don't wait for a sale or anything, its worth every bit of the cost and more. We still get FREE major content updates. Stardew Valley is a gold standard for farming sims. It’s got that perfect "just one more day" vibe that works whether you want to chill out or go full try-hard with your farm's efficiency. You start with a beat-up plot of land and build it back up by farming, fishing, and mining. The best part is how all those chores actually feel connected and rewarding. Even the combat is fun. It’s got this retro Zelda feel when you’re diving into the mines for loot. The story hits home too. You play as a tired corpo slave who ditches the corpo life for chill farm life, eventually choosing between saving the local community or letting a big corporation take over. The NPCs aren't just cardboard cutouts either. They’ve got real depth and deal with heavy, relatable stuff, which makes befriending or romancing them feel way more meaningful. Plus, the whole thing looks like a gorgeous 16-bit dream and has a soundtrack that’s absolute fire.

[h2] The gold Standard of Cozy Gaming [/h2] ​It is genuinely mind-blowing to think that Stardew Valley was created by just one person. When you compare it to other titles—which I won't name—that stay stuck in Early Access for years despite having entire studios behind them, Eric Barone’s achievement is even more impressive. This isn't just a farming sim; it is a labor of love that has become the definitive blueprint for what a "cozy game" should be. ​The beauty of Stardew is that the pacing is entirely up to you. You can play it as a chill, relaxing escape where you just enjoy the scenery, or you can go full "hard-grind" mode and try to complete the Community Center challenge in a single year. Whether you want to min-max your profits or just spend your days fishing, the game never forces a specific playstyle on you. With the variety of seasons, festivals, unique crops, and hidden secrets, there is always something new to discover. You are never limited to just farming; you can be a miner, a combat specialist, or a master socialite. ​Especially after the massive 1.6 update, the endgame and progression feel unmatched. There is a deeply satisfying arc to going from a struggling farmer who uses all their energy just watering a few parsnips, to becoming the "Overlord of Stardew Valley" with automated systems and total freedom. You can customize your farm to your exact liking, maximize your millions, or simply focus on building your dream life—getting married, having kids, and becoming the heart of the town. ​Honestly, it’s a massive time sink where the "just one more day" feeling hits harder than almost any other game I’ve played. It’s a masterpiece on every platform, and while it’s incredible solo, it’s especially fun if you have a group of friends to run the farm with. If you haven't played this yet, you are missing out on one of the greatest gaming experiences ever made.

At first, Stardew Valley feels simple. You clear weeds. You water parsnips. You pass out at 2:00 AM because you misjudged how far the mines are from your house. Then something shifts. You start planning crop rotations in your head while doing dishes. You calculate optimal keg layouts instead of sleeping. You develop emotional attachments to pixel chickens. The gameplay loop — farm, mine, fish, befriend, upgrade — is deceptively tight. Every day is short enough to feel urgent but long enough to feel meaningful. And before you know it, you have 150+ hours of gameplay :))

I have poured more hours into Stardew Valley than I can honestly count, and not once did it feel wasted. The first time I arrived in Pelican Town, it felt small and almost insignificant. A run-down farm, a handful of townsfolk, a few parsnip seeds in the ground, but that is the quiet brilliance of it. You build everything from almost nothing. You clear the land one stone at a time (maybe a little too difficult for a beginner). You watch the seasons turn. You begin to recognise the music that plays on a rainy morning in spring. Slowly, that tiny patch of land becomes yours. What makes this game so important to me is how it shields you from the harshness of real life without pretending problems do not exist. When the outside world feels overwhelming, Stardew is there to protect you with its coziness. Wake up. Water crops. Check on the animals. Maybe head to the mines. Maybe just fish until sunset. There is comfort in that routine. The relationships are another reason Stardew Valley stays with me. The villagers are not just quest dispensers; they struggle with loneliness, depression, expectations, alcoholism and family pressure. Their stories unfold slowly and earning their trust feels like an accomplishment. I also love how the game respects different playstyles. You can optimise every tile of your farm and chase profit, or you can grow flowers, decorate and take it slow. You can focus on friendships. You can disappear into the caves. There is no single correct path and that freedom makes every play session enjoyable. Stardew Valley It is a place I go when I need to breathe and I know I will keep coming back to that valley for years to come. Thank you ConcernedApe for creating such a masterpiece and for helping so many humans through their struggles with your game! P.S. If you picked the Joja route, shame on you! There is no other way to see this T_T!

Happy 10th Anniversary, Stardew Valley. It’s hard to believe this is my sixth year playing this game. I don’t know if you’ll ever see this, ConcernedApe, but I need to say it anyway. Thank you for saving my life. Over the past six years, during countless moments when I felt like I couldn’t go on, when I wanted to disappear, your game healed me. It gave me warmth, strength, and a sense of connection. When I was disappointed in the world and in myself, Stardew Valley accepted me. It gave me belonging. It gave me a home. I saw myself in the villagers of Pelican Town, their loneliness, confusion, quiet pressure, and small hopes mirrored my own. The music comforted me through breakdowns more times than I can count. It calmed the parts of me that wanted to vanish. Sometimes I watch your interviews. Hearing you talk about the pressure, the self-doubt, the anxiety, and the perfectionism you faced while creating this game made me feel less alone. When I was writing my PhD dissertation and drowning in my own doubt, I felt understood. Your pure love for what you created reminded me that doing one thing with sincerity and idealism still has meaning. Because of you, I truly understood what games can be. They can cross time and space and reach a desperate soul. I have graduated with my PhD, but new challenges have followed. I immigrated to a new country. The language, the culture, and the life here are all unfamiliar. Even the PhD degree I worked so hard for sometimes feels like it has no place here. I feel like I have lost my ability and am even afraid to go out and face people and the world. I trapped myself in my room day by day. I miss my family and friends on the other side of the earth. I feel lonely again. So I opened Stardew Valley once more. I started a new save file, just like my real life, beginning from nothing and slowly rebuilding. I know Pelican Town will flourish again. I know I’ll go from stranger to family with its villagers. Maybe that means I will build a home here too, one day. Little by little. Season by season. That is what I hope for. And I’m still trying. Thank you, ConcernedApe. I don’t think my gratitude will ever fit into words. I really wish that one day I could tell you this in person. Thank you for showing the world that loving something purely, and doing it with your whole heart, is enough to give it meaning. Stardew Valley, thank you for the joy and hope you have given me. I believe you’ve saved countless people like me. Happy 10th anniversary. Here’s to twenty, thirty, forty more years. 🌱

Now that I've spent a few years in the Valley, I'm ready to share my thoughts. I have to admit, this game did not immediately grab me. I spent a lot of time trying to figure out how things worked since it doesn't tell you anything, and I even wondered if I should get a refund and just go back to Story Of Seasons: Trio Of Towns. But I spent so much time looking things up on the wiki while playing that I passed the 2 hour mark. So I kept pressing on. I tried things and made mistakes because I knew nothing. I contributed forage to the potluck soup and ruined everyone's day. I took my time and decided not to hurry about completing anything. Whatever didn't happen this year, there was next year. I still haven't finished the community center because there's one thing I still need for one bundle. (On that note, how stupid is it that I can't retrieve hay from the silo or the hopper if the feeding bench is full? I can always retrieve fodder in SoS. I should always be able to access all my resources!) Also, it kind of annoys me that using the seed maker isn't very straightforward - I never know how many seeds it will make, and sometimes I get wild seeds or something, and I just lost a crop I could have sold or used. In SoS I can make seeds from anything in my storage, one to one, and ask for a specific amount. Much more reliable than deciding whether to play seed lotto or just go buy more. Sprinklers are a lifesaver, though. Even making money is more nuanced here. In SoS I can use high quality ingredients to cook dishes to sell, and I'm raking in millions. Here I'm running around processing all sorts of things and bringing in a few thousand a day, and apparently cooking or processing some items will actually lose money. I'm still figuring out what is actually profitable, and how to scale it to make it worth it. Over time, though, I started to see the appeal. The story is simple and sweet, just right. The art is adorable, and the music is calming. There's always something to do, and it's open ended enough that you can grind hard or take it slow, specialize or be a Jack/Janet of all trades. The NPCs are kind of bland and I often forget to talk to them, but that's NPCs for you. They have made me laugh a few times, though. (I found out where the purple shorts are...) It's getting a little better as I bribe them with gifts, but I feel like SoS often has characters with more personality from the get go. On a related note, I'll probably be staying single. I do appreciate that my horse stays put when I dismount - my horse in SoS always wanders off, LOL. And having a dinosaur in my livestock is pretty unique. Livestock that let themselves in and out is much easier than in SoS where I literally have to push them in or out or carry them. The fishing, though... I hate that fishing mini game. Hate it. I tried it all spring and lost so many fish and finally said heck with it. For the first time, I modded a game and I took that sucker out. Don't miss it at all. SoS doesn't waste my time like this. I also added a mod so I can actually see what things are worth before I ship them. How am I supposed to know what's profitable or not if I don't know the price of anything? Another thing this game won't tell you, at least not for free. It turns out there's a book you have to buy for that feature. Nope. Again, SoS gives you this basic information right from the start without any extra steps. As I enter my third year, I'm still finding things to explore, and there are more surprises, which is great. This game really leans into exploration - it expects you to just jump in and try things, and will wait around until you discover everything on your own. I think an optional tutorial could be useful for first time players who just want to know how the heck basic farming works, something like a bookshelf in the house they can consult if they want, and players who hate hand holding or are starting their 20th farm can safely ignore it. Having the wiki pulled up on your phone is a must while playing, at least for me, but it is an extra step. Overall though, I see now why this game is so popular. It's truly a sandbox where you can go in almost any direction, and I can see myself trying different kinds of farms in the future. Maybe even joining Joja Mart just to see what happens. It does start pretty slow, but that's how it is with farming games. If you keep showing up, you get rewarded, and it looks like there is still more to be unlocked. That being said, sometimes I miss my SoS farm and go there instead. But Stardew Valley is an excellent offering on the farming sim menu, even if it does take longer to chew sometimes.

The game looks simple at first. Just farming, right? But it’s so much deeper than that. The only criticism I had was addressed years ago, as when I first tried the game on release I totally fell in love with it, and then was apalled at the back-then gender-locked and heteronormative parts of game events and mechanics. These have since been updated to be more inclusive, so if you as a woman want to be friends with or date one of the many endearing women in the valley, you will no longer be forced to play a man's role during events and cutscenes. Likewise, the modding community has added options that allow you to tailor your personal experience to your preferences, including aro/ace, purely platonic or polyamourous solutions to the relationship dilemma.

tldr: THE cozy farming sim that is worth every single cent and will give you hundreds, even thousands of enjoyable hours [h3] ¸,ø¤º°`°º¤ø¤º°`°º¤ø,¸¸,ø¤º°`°º¤ø¤º°`°º¤ø,¸¸,ø¤º°`°º¤ø¤º°`°º¤ø,¸¸,ø¤º°`°º¤ø¤º°`°º¤ø,¸¸,ø¤º°`°º¤ø¤º°`°º¤ø,¸ [/h3] Now, for those who like reading long ass reviews [b] (no spoilers) [/b] : Be me in 2017. Freshly in university and meeting other big gaming fans. So far, I have only really played Pokémon or other creature collector games, or straight up JRPGs like Dragon Quest. I have never really played Farming Sims, or Simulators over all, maybe a bit Sims and Animal Crossing New World for the DS when I was very young Then my friend recommends me this game for the Switch, that she just hasn't been able to put down. Stardew Valley. I like the art style but I am not really convinced. This isn't the type of game I usually play. But I trusted her and bought the game for my Switch (at the time it even was on sale and costed like...5€ or smth?). Skip forward a whole week and there I am sitting in my lecture, not being able to put down my Switch and completely focusing on my farm. Stardew Valley started my love for farming simulators. Here on Steam I have roughly 200h (at the point of this review) and on my Switch around 150h. In the meantime I have checked out a whole lot of different Cozy Farming Sims but I always come back to Stardew. The artstyle, the music and the gameplay overall just keep me hooked and even 9 years later, I will always recommend this game to someone, who never heard of it or is hesitant to play it. [h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ BUGS ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3] In the day and age, were buggy and unplayable games come out, this game never disappoints. In my whole 9 years, I have never encountered a game breaking bug, neither on Switch, nor here on PC. I am sure I have seen a few smaller bugs here and there but I honestly can't remember. Also, whenever a new Update comes out, it will be fully functional and playable. No unplayable state or making existing systems worse. It is sad that this is something that needs to be mentioned nowadays but it is part of why I still love this game to this day. [h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ PC REQUIREMENTS ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3] This game runs on the biggest potato PCs and shouldn't cause any major issues or frame drops. My beefy PC nowadays can run the game without a sweat and roughly 8 years ago, when I bought Stardew Valley for my PC back then, that wouldn't be really able to run a lot of modern games, I never experienced any stutters. [h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ PRICE & PLAYTIME ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3] In my personal opinion, the 14€ for this game are more than worth it. If you are big into Farming Sims, you will easily reach over 100 hours (or 1000), so 14€ for a one time purchase? No brainer. In case you don't have enough money, the game does go on Sale pretty often and I think you can easily get it for half the price or less. And in the case that you will get bored and think that there should be more content? Just look into the Modding Community and your playtime will easily double or triple, OR there are so many stupid challenges people have done over the years, that maybe something tickles your fancy [h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ AUDIO ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3] Absolutely beautiful pieces. I have studied for various exams just listening to the soundtrack and it's just such a comfy vibe. Music always fits the season/situation, except maybe the mines but I still like the calmer vibe of the songs in there, it makes the mine runs just a nice experience. [h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ GRAPHICS ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3] Nice pixel art style that has captured my heart. Personally I really love the villager portraits, they way no one looks the same and isn't just straight up perfect. Filled with enough details but also a very unique and charming fantastical look. [h3] ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ GAMEPLAY ~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^~^ [/h3] The gameplay. The bread and butter of every cozy farming sim. The loop is fairly simple. You wake up at 6am and can do whatever you want until preferably 12am, or at the latest 2am. You can fish, grow veggies, take care of your farm animal, clean up your farm, hang out with the villagers, do a mine run or just run around the village exploring. There are a lot of small details and other things you can do but I don't want to spoil these, since I think that they will be a nice and pleasant surprise. Just know, that the game can go deeper than you may think at first. Really, you can play the game however you want and in the speed you want. If you are a min-maxer, there are tons of ways on how to optimize your farm and get a lot of money as quickly as possible. If you just want to vibe, make your farm look pretty and take it easy, you can also just do that. There are a bunch of customization features available and if you look up farms online, you can see how many possibilities there are to make your farm and house look absolutely stunning. The overarching story isn't really a lot of content and you will see it all during a normal run normally. Where most of the story is, is in the heart events. Personally I think every villager is worth getting to max hearts, because everyone is nice and charming, having their own unique quirks (except maybe one but oh well). Still there are certain goals that you can work towards but you aren't forced to do it. Over the years, more and more goals got added and they will help you to get deeper into certain parts of the gameplay features. Difficulty wise I would say, that it's overall a very easy game but you do need to understand the core mechanics, like keeping track of your crops and not letting them wilt. Some friends of mine struggled with the fishing minigame, while I didn't have any problems at all and would even say that it's one of my favourite mini fishing games ever. It will get easier tho, when you get better equipment. It can be hard to keep track of all the villagers and where they are at certain points in the game. Most people just look it up online, just wait until they naturally meet them or have learned over time where to look for certain NPCs. I can see why some QoL features might be wanted for new players, that I don't necessarily need (for example a tracker on the map to see where each NPC is at the moment) but fear not. The Stardew Modding Community is big and even if you (sadly) can't just install the mods over Steam, there are a lot useful guides online on how to set things up to start your modded Stardew journey. Have fun farming! I’ll be honest — for a long time, Stardew Valley was a game I kept at arm’s length. Not because of the mechanics, and not because of the art style, but because of my experiences around parts of the community. It left a bad taste before I ever planted my first parsnip. Then a friend dropped the game in my lap and told me to try it for myself. No discourse. No debates. Just the game. I’m glad they did. Somewhere between my first harvest and my first winter, I realized something uncomfortable: I wasn’t just enjoying Stardew Valley — I was completely absorbed by it. It scratched the exact same itch Harvest Moon left behind years ago. The slow seasonal rhythm, the steady growth of the farm, the quiet routine of tending crops and building relationships — it all works with a kind of deliberate calm that’s increasingly rare. Stardew Valley, at its heart, is exactly what it looks like: a warm, thoughtful farming escape. It understands pacing. It respects the player’s time. And the sheer fact that this was built largely by one developer gives the whole project an extra layer of respect. There’s care in the details here, and it shows. If this review were based purely on the game itself, it would be an easy recommendation. However — and this is where my earlier hesitation came from — the surrounding discourse in some corners can feel oddly intense for such a gentle game. I’ve seen: Romance debates get surprisingly heated Playstyle and even moral choices picked apart and policed Character preferences treated like personality tests And, at times, NPCs discussed with a level of personal projection that can feel a bit much To be clear, none of that is the game’s fault. Every large, passionate community develops its own strong currents, and Stardew Valley is no exception. But for players on the outside looking in, it can create an intimidating first impression that doesn’t really reflect the quiet, personal experience the game itself delivers. That contrast is what surprised me most. Because once you step away from the noise and just sit with the game, what you find is something genuinely special: a patient, comforting loop that rewards consistency, curiosity, and a bit of long-term planning. It filled a space I didn’t realize was still empty. Part of me walked in expecting to dislike this game on principle. Part of me almost wanted to. But it would feel wrong to condemn a genuinely well-crafted project for the behavior of its loudest fans. Stardew Valley stands on its own merits — and those merits are strong. Bottom line: If you’ve been hesitant because of the surrounding discourse, do yourself a favor and try the game anyway. The farm is much quieter than the conversation around it — and in this case, that quiet is exactly where the magic lives.

Happy 10 years Stardew Valley! I first played this game very close to release and have loved it ever since. I have two separate 100% save files and have every single achievement. I play each and every update when they arrive and experience everything that's new. I have a blast every time. This nails just about everything you'd want in an immersive pixel art farming game, from the gameplay, skills, crops, exploration, customization, furniture, to the art style, music, sound design, and dialogue. The sheer amount of content in this game will keep you entertained for days on end. It's also just a pleasant, relaxing experience when you want to just take it easy and forget your troubles. As an avid collector in video games, it hits all the right spots. All the upgrades you make and the progression you get through hard work and patience is extremely satisfying. Achieving perfection requires you to explore every inch the game has to offer. Perfection is quite a prestigious journey, and I would suggest anyone who is a fan of this game to try it at least once if they haven't already. I've shared but a fraction of what I enjoy about this game, but I'm sure enough has been said by others, considering at the time of this review, Stardew Valley is the 2nd highest rated game on Steam, right behind Portal 2. It also consistently reaches around 80,000–100,000+ concurrent players every single day. So if you ever needed a scope on just how much of a juggernaut this game is, there you have it. Stardew Valley is genuinely one of my favorite video games ever made, and it has been such an honor to have been around for a good majority of its time. I've seen it grow in many ways and I can tell it has been treated with the utmost passion and care. To everyone who worked on this game, I cannot thank you enough. The impact it has made on me is inexpressible and ConcernedApe has my full support in his next project.

Stardew Valley is a game for a very particular time. It's not that the game is for a specific person, but a time in every person's life that it kind of hits and makes sense. I got this game ages ago on a crazy steam sale, probably a winter sale, I booted it up and didn't get the appeal. I had Terraria and it did all the things I liked better. The mining, exploration, and combat were much better in Terraria. At the time those were the features that I was drawn to in the game, though ofc I love farming in general, I tend to gravitate to that sort of thing in Minecraft and other titles because I find it peaceful. Needless to say I didn't play the game long, I didn't really get the hype and ethos that believers have for this game. However I think the place that ConcernedApe was in when making the game is the perfect example of when to play Stardew. He labored over the game while out of a job and dealing with a lot. I hit some hard times and found myself with a large bank of freetime and was trying to comb through my bloated steam library when I came back across the title. If you spend a little time with the game it will draw you in. Building a cozy little farm and managing the local townfolk and filling out your fishing portfolio between delving deeper into the mines becomes second nature. Once you get into the flow, the world vanishes and it's just Stardew. It's a wonderful little title that is perfect for what it's trying to be. It's a great little indy game that I think everyone should pick up. And I ask only that even if you dislike the game, leave it in your library and circle back to it. It will pay off in a big way. TL:DR - Stardew is for you, the only question is if now is the time.

Stardew Valley offers a wide range of activities such as farming, gathering resources, expanding your business, fishing, exploring, getting married, having kids, and decorating your house. Yet none of these systems are overly layered or mechanically complex. Even the skills you level up retain their simplicity from beginning to end, which I see as a major strength because it keeps the game accessible to any player. Visually, it is vibrant and full of small details that bring the world to life. The seasons dramatically shift the color palette and the town’s atmosphere, and while the main premise is simple, the characters’ backstories explore themes such as family abandonment, depression, alcoholism, introversion, and not belonging. What I enjoy most is the methodical, relaxing rhythm of tending my farm. The variety of seasonal crops, their planting and harvesting times, the range of animal products, and the different ways to process them create a steady sense of challenge as production grows and management becomes more demanding. Since the game tracks everything I have harvested, crafted, and sold, there is strong incentive to diversify rather than settle into repetition, especially if you are a completionist. Even when routine sets in, each new day feels full of quiet possibilities, small goals, and relationships waiting to deepen.

If you're looking for a chill, cozy farming game with character stories and some dating, this is for you. If you want to go fast, you can go fast, and if you want to go slow, you can go slow, it's truly for every playstyle.

Calling this game a cozy farming sim, while accurate, is a highly reductive view of the game. The game is plenty cozy and has a *lot* of flavor, charm, and story hooks to keep you invested if that's your jam, and the game's progression mechanics are unobtrusive to that, while remaining enjoyable. But it is *not* a fully stress free experience, and is better off for it. There's only so much you can do in a day, both because you only have so much time to do things, and because you need to wait for days to pass for things to progress. Deciding what to do in a day is a major question mark for a lot of the game, and has ramifications for any activity you want to do. Shops open and close, Crops take days to grow, crops and animals need to be tended to daily, and many progression upgrades are about saving time, giving you more time with which to do other things. And it's not just farming and all day. Spend hours fishing up a catch or mining through monster infested caves, or engaging with any number of this games other systems to sink your teeth into. And all of these systems push you to try out other ones with the items you get, so you won't be grinding something out for very long unless you actually want to, making the game refreshingly engaging. The game's main objectives usually require 1 of many, rather than many of 1 anyway, so grinding is usually not the way to progress, which is a good thing. Not to mention this game runs deep with social mechanics. They aren't obtrusive if you don't like them, but the game's full effect involves getting to know a wide cast of well written characters, and becoming a trusted and liked member of this small town. And nobody is everything they seem to be at first glance. It's awesome. Also, doing all of this has tangible benefits to nudge you in the direction of the cool story bits you actually want to see, so you will never feel too lost for who to spend your limited time with. You need these people regardless, for many reasons, and they need you, so might as well get to know 'em! I love it, there's a reason it's so damn popular. A $15 game that's a more complete and content packed experience than most $60 AAA games. Give it a shot if you can.

I've been playing Stardew since it first came out (along with trying many other games along the way, but I always wind up coming back to Stardew). I noticed one review mentioned it was for all players/audience (except Grandma). Well, I am a great-grandma and I still love the game! I have about 2,660 hours in it and I always come back to it because other games tire me after a time. I'm free to make up different scenarios to play. I usually don't like pixel games, but this one isn't overdone...sprites are easy to see what they are without stressing the eyes. I like that the people and animals are realistic in looks and personalities, not faded, washed out, odd-looking, blown up like balloons, or people looking like animals of some type (cutesy games). I like that the game has land/town/water/stores/mines/etc. that are easily accessible, not hidden at all. I hate running into awkward, dead-end spaces, too many hills, or towns on multiple levels that you constantly get lost in. I will say that I never could manage to get into the second part of the game though...I got stuck and couldn't figure out how. Also, I've only played in the main mine; I don't like the others. I'm not a 'completionist' either. So ALL of my time has been spent on the main island and I'm STILL not tired of it...and this is with NO MODS. I'm forever grateful to the developer for this game for my entertainment! If I live a few more years I'll probably be a great-great grandma and STILL playing Stardew!!! Note: I've spent many years playing multi-player games too, from the first one that came online and almost every one that came out after that until a few years ago. But Stardew is my favorite overall. I'd like to see a good new farming game, but they all fall short somehow. Long live Stardew Valley!

I started Stardew Valley expecting a simple farming simulator, but it quickly became something much more meaningful. There’s something incredibly satisfying about restoring a small, run-down farm and slowly shaping it into your own peaceful space. What I love most is the freedom. The characters feel surprisingly real, and their small stories add a lot of warmth to the experience. The game has a calm, cozy atmosphere, yet there’s always something new to discover. It’s relaxing without being boring and detailed without feeling overwhelming — just a genuinely charming and heartfelt game.

You can feel the love, effort, and admiration put into this game as you play it. It is filled with unique and diverse characters, each with their own specific charm, and probably thousands of unique interactions between Zag and the supporting characters. I've played this game for 140 hours as of writing this, and I don't think I've even gotten close to having every possible interaction within the game. The storyline is great - it develops with the characters, changes as you grow closer with the cast, and ends in a very satisfactory and rewarding way. The combat, encounters, and bosses are well balanced, each testing your skill, abilities, and patience as you fight your way out of Hades to the surface. The game even gives you the option to adjust the difficulty level in-game once you beat it properly. As someone who absolutely loves well-written and in-depth stories and characters, as well as Greek mythology and history, I absolutely adore this game. 1000/10, I think everyone should play through this game at least once.

But the combat has that same nasty skill ceiling as CS. You start trash, then suddenly you’re chaining dashes and boons like it’s a clutch 1v5. Except the enemy is your dead uncle and he’s got better aim. The writing is actually funny. Dry, sharp, no cringe. Greek gods talking ♥♥♥♥ to each other while you die for the 47th time. Somehow you end up learning random mythology facts without it feeling like homework. Only real downside: my right thumb is wrecked. 10/10.

Hades is a roguelite action game built around Zagreus, the son of Hades, as he repeatedly attempts to escape the Underworld. On paper, it follows a familiar run-based structure, but what makes it exceptional is how every failed escape feels meaningful. Instead of treating death as a reset, the game turns it into progression, storytelling, character development, and motivation to try again. The combat is fast, responsive, and endlessly satisfying. Each weapon feels distinct, and the Boons from Olympian gods constantly reshape how a run plays out. One attempt might revolve around lightning-fast melee aggression, while another becomes a ranged build focused on poison, deflection, or critical damage. The game encourages experimentation without making failure feel punishing, and its balance is strong enough that almost every build can become viable with the right choices. What truly elevates Hades is how seamlessly it blends gameplay and narrative. Characters remember your attempts, comment on your progress, and evolve over time through conversations, gifts, and side stories. The writing is sharp, funny, emotional, and remarkably consistent. Even after dozens of runs, there is still new dialogue to uncover, which makes the Underworld feel alive rather than repetitive. Progression is excellent. Permanent upgrades, weapon aspects, keepsakes, house renovations, and relationship systems all give you reasons to keep playing beyond simply reaching the surface. The game constantly rewards effort in small but meaningful ways, creating one of the most addictive loops in the genre. Even when a run goes badly, you usually come away with resources, knowledge, or new story moments. The presentation is outstanding. The art style is bold and expressive, the soundtrack is incredible, and the voice acting gives every character personality. From the House of Hades to the chaos of combat, every part of the game feels polished and intentional. It is stylish without sacrificing readability, which is especially important in such a fast-paced game. There are very few real weaknesses. Some late-game progression can become grindy, especially when chasing specific upgrades or story resolutions, and repeated areas naturally lose a little surprise over time. But these are minor issues in a game that remains engaging far longer than most roguelites. [hr][/hr] [b]Highlights:[/b] [list] [*]Fast, precise, and highly satisfying combat [*]Excellent weapon variety and build experimentation [*]Brilliant integration of roguelite structure and storytelling [*]Memorable characters with consistently strong writing [*]Rewarding progression that makes every run feel worthwhile [*]Outstanding art direction, music, and voice acting [*]Late-game progression can become slightly grindy [/list] [hr][/hr] [b]TL;DR:[/b] Hades is a near-perfect roguelite that combines sharp combat, meaningful progression, and exceptional storytelling into one of the most polished games in the genre. Every failed run still feels rewarding, every character adds personality, and every system works together to keep the experience fresh, addictive, and memorable.

My first roguelike, or roguelite, (but who cares lol), and what a way to start. I fell in love with the game almost immediately. The colorful art style, the character designs, the voice acting that perfectly captured each character's personality, it all won me over straight away. Speaking of the characters, they are all incredibly likeable, and that was a huge part of why I enjoyed the game so much. I never felt frustrated by a failed run because it meant heading back to talk to them, learning more about them, and slowly building those relationships. They're actually the reason I kept playing even after the credits rolled. I just wanted to spend more time with them. The gameplay helped a lot too, of course. It was perfect for me. The sheer variety of possible builds, (favorites being the cannon and Zeus' boons), made every run feel fresh, and after nearly 100 hours I still wasn't tired of it. That says a lot. The music is stunning, especially the credits track. As for the story, I'd say it's the game's weakest point, though not because it's bad, just not quite at the same level as everything else, which really speaks to the overall quality of the game. What I did love, though, was how it was told. With each run, each failure, you'd learn a little more, and the desire to escape kept growing alongside it. In that sense, the gameplay and the story fed into each other perfectly, and honestly, what more could you ask for? Hades made me want to play every game Supergiant has ever made, which says everything about how much I loved their work. And I will definitely be playing Hades 2, which looks every bit as fantastic as the first. 28h22 to finish it 95h10 for the platinum trophy 99h40 total 10/10

A friendship simulator with the Live Die Repeat twist. The art, the music, the gameplay all are amazing. A perfect handheld game. Not a huge fan of the rogue-like nature — since locations and enemies are same-ish, beating the story makes it all too familiar over time. As a greek mythology nerd, I was interested in the story and it’s great. What’s not great — I will not experience it in full since the delivery is based on a dialogue queue. One exchange between characters is permitted per run and it’s more or less random. It’s not possible to talk to a character two times in a row. To get the entire story, the “friendship” comes into play where all characters must be given gifts. Given that character appearances are also random, it might take dozens of hours of grinding to progress everything to completion. I understand that it was done to provide the motivation for subsequent runs but to spend 50 hours to get 10 minutes of dialogue (combined)? Not for me. From what I’ve heard, Hades 2 focuses on the gameplay even more than Hades 1 so I’m not even going to check it out. Can recommend but be warned that the story progresses via grinding and that’s the nature of the game.

I've just now finished trying a playthrough with every weapon type, so I guess I can leave a review. I thought I would enjoy this game a lot. I have played Diablo 3 at a pretty high level, for probably thousands of hours (so similar gameplay type), and I've beaten Rogue Legacy 1 and 2 (so, similar "rogue-lite"-ish loop), and also beaten Dead Cells on ng+1 and maybe +2. Specifically I have even done the huge grind in RL2 to do all of the secret postgame bosses, and have done the same on RL1. But frankly I can only tolerate this game (barely) while I'm also watching a Youtube video in another monitor. It's so bloody boring to sit there and have to grind all the way up to where I was at previously EVERY SINGLE RUN. This game would benefit a lot from cutting repetition down by letting you start out in a zone you let off at previously. There's already going to be a penalty because you won't have any of the powerups gained earlier. Specifically, the 3rd boss (which I'm getting to fairly consistently) is just such a massive step up from the previous ones, and apparently they will randomly throw alternate versions of the first two bosses at you as well. This ♥♥♥♥ just takes too long. It's boring. There's not enough variations in room or enemy types. Some enemies are just plain terrible if you don't have the right boons, and each run just takes way too long. The time vs enjoyment tradeoff is just not there for me. I can't even see myself trying to get better at this game, because it's not like the enemies have any fun or complex mechanics. Most of their attacks are pretty basic. I'm mostly just mindlessly grinding to each boss, where I might or might not get completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ because I barely get to practice them at all (and even less the alt forms). So, I don't get the hype behind this. I might try playing more sometime, but at the moment I don't recommend it personally. Somehow not my thing despite the fact that in every way it should be. Rogue Legacy 1/2 felt much better to play because I could just return and retry bosses when I failed, and thus I could feel myself getting better with every attempt, and every run of a biome. Here? Not really. I found myself getting more bored with every run. I REALLY... REALLY hate games where they just insert mechanics JUST to waste time like this so you'll play longer. RL1/2 let you cut out anything you didn't want, in exchange for some downsides. This game? Haven't seen anything. I guess you could just check "God mode" and then walk over to where you were previously before actually starting to play, but even this would still waste a lot of time.

The only things I would complain about are the sometimes hard-to-understand fights due to so much stuff happening, and the fact that the only way to unlock the final ending is to defeat the final boss 10 times, which felt a bit too much to me. I played this game years ago on Nintendo Switch, but I didn’t get very far and definitely didn’t manage to escape. With the Steam version on PC, I was a bit worried whether keyboard and mouse would help — and they definitely did. The game has a beautiful art style, great visuals, an excellent soundtrack, and fantastic voice acting. That said, it still falls into a category of games that aren’t entirely for me. Roguelike/roguelite games have never really been my thing. Even though your character gradually improves with each escape attempt and item progression helps a lot, I only managed to escape once after roughly 12 hours. On the other hand, the way the game handles its story is incredible. Even after so many deaths, the characters around you keep delivering new dialogue. The story slowly unfolds and reveals more and more about the world and its characters. The gameplay encourages you to experiment with different weapons and playstyles. Everyone will find something that suits them. The boons — and there are hundreds of them — are fun, but I personally struggled with combining them effectively. I approached the game quite casually, which is probably why I only escaped once after 12 hours, and the story is far from over. Fans of roguelike/lite games can easily add +1 to my score. The game is genuinely well made — it’s just not for everyone. Rating: 7/10

This is a phenomemal game no doubt...but, I do have some issues, however personal they might be. Art is absolutely gorgeous, and the characters..dear god they're sooo good. Gameplay is great for like a run a day, two at most, but I gotta say, and it is very subjective, I am not that big of a fan of it, and I find it rather dull after some time. The general loop as well unfortunately, especially with the fact that after the first succesfull attempt, you have officially seen the entire map and all the characters. Rest of the story and side activities is just pure repetition, which isn't super bad, but it sure is a slight problem for me. However my biggest issue has got to be the RNG, and I don't mean the gameplay one, I mean the story one. Some quests are far too reliant on it. The fact that an important story-related dialogue has the same chance of showing up as a random throwaway line is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ joke, and it is clear to me that it is made for pure padding. It makes no sense story-wise too, cos you have this crucial message that one character tells you to deliver to another, and when you do find them, they just spit some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ about a completely unrelated topic, cos you basically lost the lottery. It is espacially infuriating when that character happens to only spawn in a location (and even that isn't guaranteed) that takes about 15-20 minutes to get to per run. It is ridicoulous, I have to say it. It also leads to the situation where some characters start a certain storyline, and then they abandon it cos the queue doesn't line up for tens of hours, only to out of nowhere continue it when you have made such progress with certain characters that it hardly makes sense for the storyline to continue. I think that while the gameplay undeniably need this level of RNG, it should have NEVER been implemented for the story and side stories, cos it just ruins them, All that whining aside, Hades is a fantastic game, and I did love it (for the most part). Can recommend no doubt.

This is the kind of game that will make you play again and again. I have played other roguelites before but this is one of the best games let alone action-roguelite out there. You will never feel tired of playing, I played over 90 hours of this game and can confidentaly say that I never felt bored once. Plot- As the name suggests, the game is based on Greek mythology and the God fof the Dead Hades' house i.e. the underworld. Hades' son is on a quest to escape from the underworld to reach the surface and is repeatedly stopped by his own father. Story- I won't spoil much but this is one of the best written games I have played. There is a sense of urgency to escape while you interact with several characters and form deep bonds with them, learning their past and sharing gifts. There are more than a 1000 lines of dialogue for each character I assume which makes every conversation different and keeps the gameplay fresh. Gameplay- This is not an easy game and you will die a lot in the beginning. It takes an average of around 80-100 attempts to complete the game (with all the achivements of course), and may take more if you don't follow any guide. The controls are smooth but you will have to practice with a lot of different weapons and abilities and it will take time. Art- Hades has a very distict and beautiful art style. Each and every element of the game is ridiculously polished and if you are into art, this is a must play. The environments are designed very well and I really appreciate all the art choices the devs made. Music- I think it is the most undervalued aspect of the game because it is my favourite part of the game. Every zone has a different vibe and music intensifies as you reach to the end. The heavy metal riffs really suit the game and the music gives me Prince of Persia Warrior Within vibes, but there is much much more than just metal riffs. If you are into game soundtracks, do listen to the soundtracks (they can be accessed for free on about any streaming platform). Overall, I'd say it is a must buy for those who are interested even in the slightest. The game goes on sale once or twice a year and you can get it then but it is well worth the actual price.
