[h1]Hades[/h1] [h3]Overwhelmingly Repetitive and Overpraised Roguelite[/h3] [h3]Not worth trying[/h3] Hades is one of the worst slow-paced roguelites in the genre, it requires a lot of grinding to progress through a story that honestly doesn’t feel worth watching, since it’s a very average coming-of-age escape narrative set in a Greek mythology world from a fairly superficial perspective, taking a lot of awkward artistic and historical liberties. Personally, I think this title has been praised for the same wrong reasons. In reality It has a terrible progression system that feels monotonous and slow, colorful but incredibly flat visuals that affect gameplay readability, and an uninteresting story filled with too many side characters and subplots, making the story endlessly boring. [h3]Gameplay[/h3] As I mentioned before, the game is pretty repetitive and demands far too much time just to make a little progress. From the very beginning, it’s hard to reach the next area due to the poor starting equipment of our character, with limited abilities, terrible damage output and a mediocre health pool that barely gives any room to make mistakes and learn enemy attack patterns. It’s a very tedious game to learn, and the early difficulty walls feel unfair because you basically won’t have any truly useful upgrades to help you out unless you keep grinding resources, loss after loss. The game only becomes genuinely fun once you have enough upgrades to at least get through each area and actually experiment with different gods’ boons and synergies without constantly having to restart a run. Combat feels good overall, it’s fast and smooth with melee weapons. However, other options like the bow or the gunrail feel clunky and frustratingly slow, especially for a game with such fast enemies and close environments. On the other hand, the relationship system is slow and inconsistent, since it requires a lot of interactions just to complete a single storyline with a side character whose presence is, in some cases, low and often feels insignificant. [h3]Art and World Design[/h3] The game has a very vibrant visual style for its assets, characters and enemies. However, this artistic decision often gets in the way during combat. This title has a serious visual hierarchy problem. Most of its elements within the same scene share the exact same line quality and very similar color values, combined with an exaggerated lighting system that makes shadows and depth harder to read. As a result, many environmental obstacles feel flat and oversimplified, and it’s common to bump into them because of how poorly they blend into the environment. And then there’s the character design. Honestly, I think it was handled in a very poor artistic way, trying to justify their depiction under the excuse of a “reinterpretation” of Greek mythology by one of the developers, based on the idea that the Greek gods are not necessarily ethnically Greek. This is blatantly wrong and dishonest. It's pretty obvious that Greek gods are portrayed according to the ancient Greek canon standards, not foreign ones that have nothing to do with the culture they are trying to portray. [h3]Music and Sound effects[/h3] The soundtrack is energetic and playful, it’s genuinely enjoyable, and it’s easily one of the game’s strongest aspects. It’s the only aspect that actually integrates Greek culture well into the game using its typical instruments and melodies along with more modern arrangements.

Short version: In theory, Hades offers endless replayability; in practice, it requires it. Long version: I have very mixed feelings about this game, and I hate that I don't like it more than I do. Let's start with the positive. The combat is fantastic and feels amazing. It's snappy and varied and it feels weighty. There's arena hazards, traps, and destructible cover that affects the player as well as enemies, which makes positioning vital and allows for interesting strategies. Bosses are hard at first but when you master them, they become very manageable. The God boon system is compact enough to allow for synergy while still being varied enough to promote experimentation. I also like the art direction and the fact that all areas are vastly unique and engaging. Last but certainly not least: the music is phenomenal. All of this praise is well-earned, and I do get the overwhelmingly positive Steam rating. But there's a few negative points as well. Let's start with the final boss. My oh my did it take me long to defeat him. He is a huge step up from anything you have previously fought. Now, usually I'm all for difficult bosses (big souls fan, here). But in this game, a run back to the final boss can easily take 45 minutes or more. That means that getting to learn his move set and dodge properly is a lengthy endeavour. I got to the point where I breezed through the entire game, only to be killed by the final boss and having to do it all again, simply because I haven't been able to experiment with his attacks enough. Yes, that's a skill issue, but it's also a game design issue if playing the run up to the boss becomes a chore. I found myself being bored more than being frustrated by or excited about the final boss. And when I did beat him, I was hit with a very anti climactic "end". I won't spoil details, here, though. The game doesn't actually end there, and to get any sort of progress, you have to play through the entire game again and again and again. Now, that wouldn't have been a bad thing if I hadn't already been doing that and already got bored. Okay, the game does offer some additional rules that you can choose from to make replays different, but they just boil down to: buff enemies or debuff yourself. And that gets old pretty quickly. There was one setting where you can introduce new mechanics for the bosses, which was good for some variety when you first try that out, but the options just weren't enough to keep additional runs more interesting. I think that if the challenge runs had included more profound changes to arenas, enemies, bosses, my own weapons, that it would have made the game worth playing after this point. Still, as a good little gamer, I wanted to know how the story would end and pressed on and pushed through the slog and got to the very "end". But even then, the ending was boring and had no impact. It offered no catharsis, no profound meaning, and nothing "cool" either. It just kind of went: "Yeah, well, uh, good, I guess! Now, get back to it!" and then told me to continue playing. I didn't. I had had enough. And that's really what bothers me about this game, because the gameplay loop, the progression, the world, the design, almost everything is stellar. It just wears out its welcome and fades like the chorus of a song. And that's what really pains me, because I want to like this game. I want to recommend it, because there's so much to like about it. And I'm glad that so many people (almost 300k at the time of writing) enjoyed it so much to leave a positive review. For me, though, it just doesn't prove its own premise. In theory, Hades offers endless replayability; in practice, it requires it. I'm going back to Bastion.

Whilst I think this is the best of the Supergiant games, I still think it is very lacking and not a patch on the best 80s and 90s 2D action games. I'll definitely give it credit for the fact that its combat is fast and satisfying. I wouldn't necessarily call it good, because it has other issues, but in isolation the feel of it is good. And I'll also give it credit for a really cool story and some really cool characters. All the gods that they include here come with a lot of personality, and I really like that aspect of it. But it's a typical grind-to-win modern game. This isn't about skill, this is just about repetitively doing the same mash and dash over and over to you level up enough to press on. The more you play, the more you unlock, the easier things get. It's that traditional old cycle that I find stupidly boring and insulting to anyone who wants a genuine challenge in an action gam. This isn't like a Wonderboy game where powering up is because you've cleverly discovered something, this is just button bash, button bash, button bash until off your pop. And what makes it feel worse is just it's so repetitive in general. Same enemies appear over and over again, with only three and a half dungeon floors that you're playing in a similar order every single time with little variety. More disappointingly is the fact that there's not really much to the build varieties ether. Everything's kind of just a stat upgrade, which, again, emphasizes that just grind-to-win mentality. I mean, I stop and think about it, and this is even more archaic than said 80s and 90s games. Like, if you were to play something like Smash TV, when you clear the first stage, you've cleared the first stage. You kill the first boss, that's it, you move on to your next section. Hades has you do all that again. Like I say, baffling that this has been so highly praised.

Well, first of all, let me say that the game is godlike *wink wink*. No, seriously, the game is fricking amazing and I highly recommend it to anyone. The "On the Coast" scene and soundtrack is just 11/10 and the OST (especially the NPC songs) in this game is just breathtaking. You literally stop in your tracks just to listen. Now, with the above being said, unfortunately, the game isn't perfect (what really is?) and it does have flaws: The biggest and most common issue most people encounter, which, also doesn't make any sort of sense to me for a product, is that A LOT of the game content (story, dialogue, side quests, NPCs etc.) is gated/gate locked behind a wall of grind atop a mountain of RNG (and a very poorly designed RNG if I'm being completely honest; the devs have a weird definition of time and the fun factor gamers/people expect from their product). I particularly think that NPC dialogue being chosen and given at random (even when going through their respective quest) is just nonsensical. Thus, I HIGHLY recommend the use of at least a couple of addons/mods to alleviate some of the major issue this game has and just overall increase it's enjoyment after doing a couple of runs to get yourself familiar with the game and its mechanics. I would also add that doing some suicide runs (just killing yourself after accomplishing your goal) to get certain NPC dialogue or choices to trigger and actually being able to properly complete the story and side quests is HIGHLY encouraged (otherwise you're gonna waste huge amounts of time on RNG that is just gonna disappoint you and will probably/eventually frustate you enough that you'll just abandon the game completely). I must say, after playing Hades 2, you can certainly see the QoL improvements they added to it compared to the first game, even if it's still basically plagued by the exact same issues. Still, all in all, I still think Hades is in a lot of ways better than Hades 2, tho Hades 2 also has its perks and a very enjoyable (and at least, more balance, in a way) gameplay, combat and farm/grind. I am happy to say that after playing Hades 2 (which is also an amazing game), I was hyped and entertained enough that I had to play through Hades again, and properly finish it and explore and enjoy all the content as much as possible. So I definitely recommend giving both games a buy/try, in whatever order. This game is just amazing and I gotta give a round of applause for the studio that made it. Cheers!

Hades is one of those games that need no introduction, it has claimed it's place in history as the best rouge-lites ever made, and whilst I don't know if it ranks that highly on my list purely as a rouge-lite, it does place highly as just a fantastic, well made game that everyone should try, this is the perfect gateway into the genre and has already introduced millions. What Hades does better than games like slay the spire, risk of rain and dead cells is that it puts narrative at the forefront, with an incredible ensemble of characters that are memorable with excellent voice acting and an eye watering amount of dialogue. Hades succeeds in pulling in even people who don't play rouge-lites due to the way it handles death, even if you die in the first room multiple times it's likely characters will have new dialogue. The game takes the edge of death and makes it less of a punishment and more a narrative tool. So how's gameplay? Well very good to be blunt. In essence this game is similar to diablo, in which it's a top down rpg in which you hack and slash your way through various dungeons all with greek mythology serving as the backdrop. You pick powers from different gods, using a variety of interesting weapons and fight hordes of enemies only to die and do it all again. Combat is incredibly fast and fluid with the build variety being quite staggering. The more you play the more the game hands out new systems which keeps the repetitive nature of the game fresh. Story, music, presentation are all top quality. As mentioned the amount of dialogue is insane but it would mean nothing if the voice acting sucked or if the story was uninteresting. Thankfully this is a game that delivers on all fronts, characters are memorable, the main character zagreus is enduring and the titular Hades is intimidating. I think my only issue is the fact that some areas and bosses do get quite samey and build variety whilst varied does start falling into the meta trap when you just want to start smashing out clears. For pure rouge-lite I'd always lean towards dead cells but for the simple experience of a good game, hades is unmatched. In short Hades is fantastic, that one of a kind game that has bridged the gap for a genre that was quite niche and brought it into the mainstream, hades has been an incredible gane bringing in many to the genre and has gone on to show the narrative power only games can achieve.

I have heard about this game and how good it was for the last 5 years or so, but I never really was too big into the top down beat em up gameplay that the game's spiritual predecessor "Transistor" had and am not really into beat em ups in general. I do like roguelikes, but Hades never really felt like it was the type of game I would like. It felt like a Hollow Knight in that way, a great game in a genre I'm not really into (platformers). As such, I slept on it. I slept on it for years. And then it went on sale and steam recommended it to me. I had a few extra bucks in my wallet so I went ahead and grabbed it. Why not? I've heard endless praise, maybe it'll be good. Worse case scenario I refund it in an hour. I didn't sleep that night. I only played Hades. This might be my favorite roguelike ever made. And the beat em up playstyle doesn't even factor against it. The gameplay is that good. The story is so flawlessly woven into the looping mechanics of the game, that it doesn't even make resetting and dying feel like a failure, but rather progression of the story. Do you know how hard it is to make failure FEEL like progression in a game where you have to beat it in one shot? Dying is never frustrating. Worst it ever got out of me was a "Aww, I almost had him!" Dying literally feels like part of the story progression. There was always more to look forward to when you got back home. More conversations, more things to unlock, more things to play with. I'm only 11 hours in, but this is going to be a game that I come back to again and again. This game has found a home with me. And unlike Zagreus, it won't be leaving any time soon.

Hades is a great game full of interesting lore and a unique take on Greek Mythology. Hades was my first time properly getting into a roguelike, and honestly, it completely sold me on the genre. I didn’t know what to expect going in, but the way the game is designed just makes everything click. Dying never feels frustrating — if anything, it feels like part of the progression. Every run teaches you something new, gives you better upgrades, or pushes the story forward in a really satisfying way. The gameplay is insanely smooth. Combat is fast, responsive, and just feels good. Each weapon plays differently, and the variety of builds you can create with boons keeps every run feeling fresh. You can play aggressively, play safe, experiment — it all works, and that flexibility makes it hard to put down. What really surprised me is how strong the story is. I wasn’t expecting a roguelike to have this much personality and depth. The characters are all memorable, the voice acting is top-tier, and the way the narrative unfolds over multiple runs is honestly impressive. It gives you a reason to keep going beyond just “one more run.” Visually, the game looks amazing. The art style is clean and vibrant, and everything from character design to environments just stands out. The soundtrack also deserves a mention — it fits the pace of the game perfectly and really adds to the intensity of each run. For a first roguelike experience, Hades couldn’t have been better. It’s one of those games that just hooks you without trying too hard. Easy to pick up, hard to stop playing, and genuinely one of the most enjoyable and unique games I’ve played in a long time.

This game has rewritten the book on the roguelite genre, delivering an unprecedented level of depth, quality, and what can only be called genius-level presentation. Despite being the company's first game and lacking a massive budget—something many companies cannot even manage with one—they have achieved the highest possible quality. Whether you love the genre or not, this is a game everyone should try at least once. The game cracked the code for combining roguelike mechanics with story. They have managed something no one has ever done before: story progression through death. In this genre, you are likely to die a lot and come back with different builds and strategies, but they went further by progressing the story with each and every death. What you killed before you died, what killed you in your last run, or whom you encountered—everything matters. Truly a masterpiece.

I'm reviewing way after it's hayday, so bare that in mind: It's fun. It's a fun 'die and retry' rogue-like, though the rougelike elements are very mild. There are a few run-modifiers that feel like they make the game way too easy, quite a lot that feel inconsequential, and dying isn't always your own fault. I've had rooms where it'll surround you with 6x armoured unblockable spellcasters that murder your great run instantly, and erratic damage application from bosses. Generally it works well, but there are moment's where it will kill a run in a way that feels similar to a child throwing a toy out of the pram. The combat feels quite messy. Basically you have to spam dodge constantly and there is an element of timing there, but you are basically constantly pressing dodge and not doing so is a death sentence, unless you're a very high level player I suspect. Sometimes though, as a result, it can feel like a very awesome and chaotic desperate battle. Also the art is very nice, characters are pretty great, though I'd say the 'relationship' mechanic with all the characters is only skin deep and doesn't really come into play much from what I've seen so far. Overall a firmly enjoyable game. I still think now, as I did when it released, that it's quite confusing that it was so well received, but I think I know why, and its' the same reason a lot of games have been in recent years; it looks really nice. Looking at Hollow Knight and Dart Souls, it's not just that these are all beautiful games, but that there's some life and backstory to the worlds. They're 'full worlds' and you can really root around in them. Maybe it's just that. The gameplay itself is ok, I don't think it was every that amazing, and more often I'm annoyed at dying to an enemy I wasn't given time to learn, than I'm delighted at how fun a fight was.

This was my first proper roguelite experience and I always thought the genre isn't for me, but damn did Hades proof me wrong! I love how this game which is repetitious by its nature doesn't feel repetitious at all, because of the massive build variety through the different weapons, the many boons and Daedalus hammers you get to choose from. You don't know with which build you'll end up in a run but it's almost guaranteed to be be fun and different from the previous one. The VA, OST, and art is also very nice and expressive. EDIT: I've been playing the game for 100% achievements after finishing the story and I had to add one point of criticism to my review which sadly took out a lot of fun of the last 20ish hours I played the game. Completing the last quests is heavily reliant on getting good RNG with encounters in the runs, with feels insane to me and is frankly speaking bad game design. [b] 4/7 - Beginner-friendly roguelite that basically anyone can get into [/b] You can clear the game in few hours, since a succesful run takes roughly ~30 minutes to complete. The game has a surprising breadth of dialogue and character responses to how you cleared / died in the dungeon, which makes for a satisfying tertiary loop for the first 10 hours or so. While the build possibilites are many, making the secondary loop interesting, they mostly boil down to combining passives to do DPS in the background, while the actual powerups that change weapon handling and thus the primary loop of the game are few and far between. If you're not completely braindead, there is no "bad" RNG, and most runs provide viable build opportunities. This makes the primary loop rather tedious, as the small selection of weapons/enemies/arenas play the exact same until 10-20 minutes into your run. Music is nothing to write home about which is not-so-good since you listen to the same tracks over and over, but visuals and character designs are charming. The game is very podcast-able after you exhaust the tertiary loop as a result.

Nothing more can really be said about Hades; I have nothing new to add. Everyone knows it's an incredible game. Undoubtedly one of the best I've ever played. Supergiant Games are in a class of their own amongst both indie and AAA studios when it comes to delivering quality. Beautiful, immediately recognisable art style showcased through awesome character designs and environments, killer soundtrack, fun, in-depth, and extremely satisfying combat and gameplay, and excellent roguelike/roguelite mechanics. Its iconic cast of characters are made even better and truly brought to life through the incredible voice acting and the game's impressive and uniquely intricate dialogue system. The best interpretation of Greek mythology in gaming, or, arguably, in any medium. Whilst the core combat gameplay itself is great and could be enough for some, I think Hades is at its best when you engage with everything it has to offer, and try to do all that you can (e.g. completing character quests, unlocking weapon variants, etc.). Hades is a consistently reliable source of fun and is such an easy game to fall in love with. This is a must-play for everyone. [h2] S-Tier !!! ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ 10/10 [/h2] [h1] There is no escape. The combat is extremely responsive and satisfying, and even for someone not usually strong in action games, it feels learnable and rewarding over time. If you like 2.5D games and haven’t played Hades yet… what are you even doing? You play as Zagreus, prince of the Underworld, whose main goal is simple: leave. The problem? The Underworld has a strict “no exit” policy, and it enforces it by absolutely wrecking you every single time. The loop sounds rough: fight through Tartarus, Asphodel, Elysium, and the Temple of Styx → get obliterated → wake up back home → pretend that went better than it did. But it quickly becomes addictive. Every run makes you stronger, gives you new abilities, and unlocks more story. Losing never feels like wasted time—just aggressive character development. The story is way deeper than expected. Zagreus is trying to find his mom, Persephone, while dealing with Hades, who clearly majored in “emotional communication is optional.” What starts as a simple escape turns into a really well-written family drama with actual payoff. Meanwhile, the Olympian gods are handing you powers like: “Here, take this. Don’t ask questions. Go cause problems.” The 2.5D visuals are gorgeous, the combat is smooth as butter, and the voice acting is ridiculously good across the board. Final verdict: You will die. A lot. You will get better. Slowly. You will say “last run” and absolutely not mean it. And somehow… you’ll keep coming back for more.

Fifty runs later, my screen is a blinding explosion of lightning boons, arrows, and purple lasers. I am mashing every button. I am moving at the speed of light. Am I winning? Am I dying? Has my brain melted? I have absolutely no idea, but the room is clear and I got a pomegranate. 9/10. Deducting one point because my dad needs therapy and my thumbs need physical therapy. 100% would blindly button-mash my way out of hell again. Pet the dog.

Yet somehow, this one shows up like, “Oh you thought you escaped? Cute.” And suddenly I’m 47 runs deep, emotionally attached to a floating head that insults me, and arguing with a god about my work ethic. First off, this game feels illegal in how polished it is. Like, the developers and QA really knew what they were doing. The PM clearly ran flawless retrospectives, and the UAT testers’ feedback actually mattered. Somewhere out there is a Jira board that achieved enlightenment. It seems like this game delivers on multiple levels: Gameplay: Addictive. Not “just one more run,” but “oops it’s 2 AM and I’m negotiating with my alarm clock.” Combat: Fast, smooth, and somehow makes button mashing feel like a deliberate art form. Progression: You die. A lot. But instead of rage-quitting, you’re like, “Ah yes, I have learned nothing. Let’s go again immediately.” Storyline: Surprisingly good. Like, “why am I emotionally invested in Greek family drama?” good. Speaking of story—the character you play (Zagreus, aka “Professional Son Disappointment”) is hilarious and witty. Every time he dies—and he WILL die—he strolls back into the House like he just got back from Costco. Meanwhile, his dad is basically the CEO of Toxic Management™, and their conversations feel like annual performance reviews from hell. Literally. The soundtrack? Eerie and enchanting. It’s the kind of music that makes you feel powerful while simultaneously reminding you that you are, in fact, getting absolutely wrecked by a butterfly with anger issues. The mobs and bosses are all top notch. Each one has personality, style, and a personal vendetta against your hopes and dreams. You’ll go from “I’ve got this!” to “I have made a terrible mistake” in about 3 seconds flat. Now, the storyline does get a bit cringey near the end of a run. There are moments where you’re like, “Wow, this is deep,” immediately followed by, “Okay but did we need that much emotional vulnerability right before I got flattened?” But it does have meaning… eventually… probably… after your 83rd attempt. Also: You can pet the dog. 10/10 Game of the Year. Every character is either incredibly attractive, deeply mysterious, or both. I don’t trust it. The game rewards you for dying, which is great because I am extremely talented at that. Final verdict: Hades is what happens when a game respects your time, your intelligence, and your inevitable failure—all at once. It’s beautiful, brutal, and somehow comforting in a “welcome back, loser” kind of way. Would I recommend it? Absolutely. Will it consume your life? Also absolutely. Will you escape? Absolutely not tied in a knot.

The Bottom Line: A 9/10 roguelite for people who normally hate roguelites. It completely eliminates the frustration of dying by weaving every death directly into a phenomenal, constantly progressing story. The "Crunch" (Mechanics & Combat): Typically, run-based games feel like smashing your head against a brick wall, but Hades is different. The combat is incredibly tight, and testing yourself against the different weapons keeps the mechanical loop fresh. The genius of the game is its progression system—even when you inevitably die, you return to the hub with resources to permanently upgrade your stats. You never feel like a run was a waste of time. The "Flow" (Pacing & Narrative): This is where the game truly shines. Death isn't just a reset; it's the mechanism that pushes the story forward. The characters are exceptionally well-written, and interacting with them—whether it's giving them Ambrosia to build friendships or just listening to their banter—makes returning to the hub after a death something to actually look forward to. The only drawback: Once you finally reach the true end of the story, the motivation plummets. Without the narrative pushing you forward, the core loop eventually begins to feel repetitive and tiring, leaving little reason to do runs "just for fun." The Setup (Hardware & Controls): Unsurprisingly, this game is an absolute must-play on the Steam Deck. The fast-paced, run-based nature makes it perfect for quick handheld sessions.

I don't get the hype of this game. Is it bad. No. Is it good. At first, yes, but it gets old and repetitive very quickly. Unlike most roguelike games that offer a massive variety of levels, enemies, and bosses... Hades offers 3 basic levels: Tartarus, Asphodel, and Elysium (unsure on spelling, didn't care enough to double-check lol). That's it. You repeat the same 3 over, and over, and over, and over. At the end of each are the exact same bosses, maybe with some slight differences, but they're still the same: 1. Same 3 furies. Cosmetically different and each have their own variety of move sets and attacks, but still very similar. 2. A bone hydra. Boss #2 NEVER changes, with the exception of a few different attacks. 3. I have yet to see a different boss at the end of level 3. Did I complete the game? No. Could there be more. Yes. But how long does that take? I've been playing 30 hours and it's the same thing constantly. I can switch up my weapons, gain different abilities, and unlock new furniture at the home base, but that's about it. What I dislike... 1. The dialogue isn't great and most conversations are pointless. The story is basic (Zagreus wants to leave The Underworld)... aside from that, most conversations are dull. 2. Every single time you pick up a power, that corresponding God just has to say something LOL Again, more pointless dialogue here. 3. Repetitive levels, enemies and weapons. Yes, you have a variety of weapons you can switch between, plus upgrade them to act different... but no # of weapons makes the same levels, enemies and bosses entertaining. 4. Very grindy, and with no side levels, enemies or bosses... it gets boring quick. 5. Did I mention you have the same THREE levels, THREE bosses, and enemy variation per level? LOL I just find it hard to give this a thumbs up and understand WHY it's so popular when you have roguelikes like Dead Cells... with a vast amount of levels, paths, weapons, items, enemies, bosses, endings, DLC, power ups, and content that blows this game (and most roguelikes) out of the water. Yet, somehow, Hades with it's massive lack of content and boring, uncreative story sits at Overwhelmingly Positive. I don't get the hype. I'm writing this review because after 30 hours, I'm officially bored and done playing. Maybe Hades 2 offers a lot more, but after this game, I likely won't buy the sequel. There are just far better roguelikes out there. But who am I? I'm the 1% that actually dislikes this overhyped game. Buy it. Try it. Maybe you'll like it. Just know your money is likely better spent on another roguelike.

you leave and every run feels like the same run but not the same run but also exactly the same run in a way that doesn’t cancel itself out but stacks on top of itself like memory that refuses to settle you die and you die and you die but it doesn’t feel like failure it feels like the system confirming that you are participating correctly and each death is not an end but a continuation disguised as interruption and every return to the house feels like progress even when nothing has progressed except your familiarity with the repetition which itself becomes a form of progression that replaces actual progression the combat is fast but also predetermined in a way that only becomes visible after you’ve already reacted and everything feels responsive but also inevitable like you are making choices that were already aligned with outcomes you haven’t reached yet and when you win it feels earned but also pre-approved as if the system allowed that version of you to exist just long enough to escape the gods speak to you constantly and it feels like guidance but also surveillance like they are not helping you escape but observing how you try and adjusting what you are allowed to become based on how you fail and succeed and fail again and their voices repeat but not exactly repeat they evolve slightly but remain trapped in the same conversational orbit like they also cannot leave whatever structure this is the upgrades accumulate but not linearly they fold into each other and create versions of yourself that feel stronger but also more temporary because every build disappears and reappears as a memory of something that worked once and might never work again and this uncertainty becomes the core of the experience because you are not building a character you are approximating one over and over and over the story progresses but only if you repeat enough times for it to notice you and even then it doesn’t move forward it unfolds sideways revealing fragments that were already there but locked behind your willingness to continue participating in the loop and the loop and the loop and the loop which starts to feel less like a mechanic and more like the actual subject of the game i stopped playing but it didn’t feel like stopping it felt like exiting a cycle that did not require my exit to continue and i could still sense the structure of it still (I promise this is not a case of someone playing for 5 minutes and deciding to leave a mean review lmao. I played Hades on a different version). Gods. I remember playing Hades for the first time on my birthday. I also remember it being the first game that ever got me to care about fighting mechanics. How to stack doom tick or what sort of aspect is good for crits. I-frames. Actually learning movement instead of stumbling around like in other games haha. It's so good you guys. The story. The voice acting. The characters! Oh the characters. I will scroll through dialogue wikis at least every 3 months give or take. The character implications of trial chambers? Themes of family disfunction? Blurred relational lines? Hades has it all wtf. Also, it's a small thing, but Hades lets you romance multiple people at a time. It even encourages you to do so. It's just so unique to see that in a game, and it really made sense for the characters too. Another small thing, I adore how strong the theming is. I was talking to a friend, and we were like, if Hades is about fixing relationships and love and coming together, leaving home (The Iliad?) then Hades II is The Odyssey (letting go and literally going home). No idea if this was intentional or not, but I would not be surprised if it was. As someone who doesn't game much, Hades has long been my single favourite game. I also adored how much care they put into it. Dionysus and Zagreus pretending they are one deity, because in some sources they are. Adaptions are hard to get right, but I will forever unapologetically love Hades because it cares. It researched, it had reasons for leaving some things out and adding other things in. There are so many loveable characters, and the dialogue system is something else. Highly recommend researching how they did that if you're interested in game design. And the art. My goodness. Sooo many talented people I recognise worked on this game and it SHOWS. Am honestly shocked there's not an artbook, even though there's not much developmental art. Tbh I know Hades fans would buy a 4 page artbook. Loved looking at the development of this game too. And after years or refusing to, maybe I'll relearn this ISOMETRIC GAME on the KBM version here on Steam. Ahhhh or not. Well, Transistor wasn't too bad for the few hours I played on KBM.

The ending was wonderful and was written in a way that justifies its replayability in a cohesive way. However, after having played it's sequel Hades 2, it's hard getting used to the movement of the original again, particularly without the option to sprint AND dash.

Absolutely incredible game. It's fast-paced and always keeping you on your toes. Plus the Pact of Punishment allows you to bump up the difficulty and be rewarded for it after you've gotten skilled at the game. The characters are a joy to interact with too. Lots of style and personality went into the game, and you can feel it. I can also appreciate the Ancient Greek Mythology knowledge used here. It's something I've always enjoyed reading about, and this really makes it come to life. Only complaint I have for the game is that it's hard to replay the game. The story progresses via deaths, so you're EXPECTED to die a certain number of times to reach certain plot points and conversations. This works fantastically on a first playthrough, where you feel like the characters are actually interacting with your progression. However, on a replay, if you make it all the way to one of the final areas of the game on one of your first runs, you skip a lot of fun dialogue, and conversations might reference previous interactions that hadn't happened yet due to your unexpected skill. In summary... get this game. You'll like it.

I would like to preface by asserting that Hades is a 9/10. Hades is a 9/10 in the sense that I believe Resident Evil 2 Remake, Prey (2016), Neon White, DOOM (2016), Cuphead are a 9/10. These games are flawless, yet they lack the innovation, unique factor, or emotion connection that push a game to a masterpiece. Hades does not do dungeon crawler as well as Enter the Gungeon, does not have the depth of combat as Transistor, does not have the so many unique things of Pyre. Balancing that makes sense in the story means less possible BS, but also less interesting and funny builds that make runs memorable like those of Gungeon. Ease of replayablity inevitably reveals the meta aspects that harm what makes Supergiants' previous game journeys so special and connected emotionally; the way Hades contextuallise the repeated replays is very smart yes, but not good enough. However, it is supremely impressive that Hades can get so much right in so many aspects. Hades is Supergiants' most approachable and evidently most successful game when it was released. Although I believe the game is in no way pandering, during the mission to chisel its jack of all trades Hades, Supergiants also carved away the chagrin (fancy way of saying BS) needed to make it truly one of a kind.

Now, just because I decided to not recommend, does not mean that it's a bad game, it's just, a game for those, who like roguelite and roeguelike games. I never played this type of game before, so initially, it was fun, but as I progressed through the gameplay that fun slowly became to boredom, because, essentially, you repeat ad nauseam everything until you successfully defeat the end boss (and, if I'm not mistaken, you have to do that ten times in order to see the real ending). The gameplay revolves around you doing a gauntlet of monsters until you get to the boss of that area. Each attempt to escape is sort of unique, but sort of not really. At first, you are very weak and will not go far, but as you progress, you receive materials to spec-out your passive skills. However, if you are anything like me, just turn the God Mode on, and on top of that your character will be getting stronger with each failed attempt (less squishy). And here's what I don't like and why I don't recommend it for anyone who does not like roguelites and roguelikes. When you die, you loose all of your active upgrades (boons). Let's say, you got a very good RNG and managed to even go to the final boss of the game; and your active skills that run were top notch. Unfortunately, you died, and you lost all those active skills. You no longer have them, and you have to rely on the game's RNG again to maybe give you what you want for your build to succeed. I don't like that. Aside from God Mode, runs in my opinion are simply luck and RNG based, because, honestly, some boons just flat out suck for your playstyle, so you are left to grind away the same thing over and over again in order to defeat the final boss. Nope. I tried it. Played it for 14 hours give or take. Went up to the final boss a couple of times, but... nah, this game is not for me.

Hades is one of the best roguelike/roguelite out there. The story is great, the art style is stunning, and the gameplay itself is really engaging. The character designs look incredible. This game got me into the roguelike genre. Overall, this game is a masterpiece.

This game is basically digital "cocaine". It gives you an adrenaline rush and makes you completely obsessed with doing just one more run. You sit down to play, and suddenly hours have passed without you even realizing. It's honestly a bit dangerous. For what it wants to be, the game is perfect. It's incredibly fun, no two runs are the same, and you never really get bored because you're always trying to get stronger with different builds. The combat and animations are super smooth. The dialogue between the gods is genuinely funny and interesting, and the art direction is just clean and fits the vibe perfectly. The soundtrack is also great, it really gets you pumped for the fights. Personally, I decided to stop after beating the game once. I know there's a "true ending" if you keep going, but I proved to myself I could finish it, and I'm usually not the type to replay games anyway. As a roguelike, it's a solid 9/10, I really don't think there's anything better out there right now (besides Hades 2? We will see haha). But for me, the gameplay loop eventually gets a bit monotonous and I just don't have the motivation to beat it multiple times. If you're looking for instant dopamine, I highly recommend it. Just set a timer so you don't forget to live your life. I finished it in under 15 hours, but I played it continuously for 2-3 days straight haha.

You'll be replaying the same levels, enemies and bosses. Some people love it and I say fair play to them. This is my first ever roguelite and I heard Hades was good introduction into the genre, and I have to say, this game and genre is definitely not for me. I like metroidvanias and don't mind the backtracking some of those games have, but in those you get to chose your path somewhat, and you can avoid enemies, whereas in this, you're forced to clear each room and defeat each boss. I wish I liked this genre as there seems to be a lot of great choice but unfortunately this is a hard pass for me.

[h3]A Review of Hades, [i]as Overheard Somewhere in the House of Hades[/i][/h3] [b]Zagreus:[/b] So apparently, Father, mortals have been writing [i]reviews[/i] about my attempts to escape. [b]Hades:[/b] Reviews? About your repeated failures? How touching. We usually just call that “routine”. [b]Zagreus:[/b] Well, according to them, the combat is “incredibly fluid”. [b]Athena:[/b] A reasonable observation. When guided by wisdom and strategy, your movements display admirable precision. Particularly when my blessings are involved. [b]Zeus:[/b] Precision is fine, niece, but what the mortals really enjoy is spectacle! Nothing spices up a battle like a proper thunderbolt. When Zagreus channels my power, the Underworld becomes quite electrifying. [b]Dionysus:[/b] Oh please, Uncle. Lightning is flashy, sure, but mortals adore a bit of chaos. A dash of divine hangover, a splash of poison, and suddenly every run turns into a delightful mess. [b]Zagreus:[/b] They actually call that “build synergy”. [b]Hades:[/b] I call it [i]reckless improvisation[/i]. [b]Nyx:[/b] And yet each attempt brings him further than the last. Progress, even through failure, can be a powerful thing. [b]Zagreus:[/b] That’s something the reviewers seem to love. Every time I die – which happens a lot, by the way – there’s more dialogue, more story, more … well, life here in the House. [b]Athena:[/b] An elegant structure. Advancement through persistence rather than simple victory. [b]Zeus:[/b] And through lightning. Don’t forget the lightning. [b]Dionysus:[/b] And good company after a run. [b]Zagreus:[/b] Another thing they mention: every escape attempt feels different. Different weapons, different blessings, different combinations of powers. [b]Hades:[/b] Randomness. [b]Zagreus:[/b] Possibility. [b]Nyx:[/b] Destiny unfolding in fragments. [b]Zagreus:[/b] Exactly. Mortals say the art is beautiful, the music unforgettable, and the fights feel like a dance – fast, dangerous, but strangely graceful. [b]Hades:[/b] A dance that always ends with you back in my House. [b]Zagreus:[/b] For now. [b]Zeus:[/b] Well then, if the mortals insist on a review, let’s give them one. [b]Athena:[/b] “Hades” is a game of skill, strategy, and relentless improvement. [b]Dionysus:[/b] A game where every run becomes a new kind of chaos. [b]Nyx:[/b] A game where failure is merely another step in the story. [b]Hades:[/b] And a game that proves no one truly escapes the Underworld. [b]Zagreus:[/b] … I’m still working on that part. [i]Zagreus picks up his weapon.[/i] [b]Zagreus:[/b] Well then. One more run!

Hades is a wonderful, punchy, stylish experience that has yet to be equaled in its space by its competitors or its successors. It's a roguelite where the controls don't feel compromised in some way, where the experience doesn't feel Sisyphean (pun intended), and the whole experience feels rich right from the start. The difficulty is tuned excellently, offering an accessibly challenging normal route with loads of difficulty modifiers available either by beating your first run, or starting a save file in "Hell Mode". My spent time with Hades across PC and Playstation has felt rewarding in a way that many others in the genre simply fail to capture, as it feels more directly tied to my skill with the game, rather than depending on favourable RNG. The artistic aesthetic is razor-sharp, everything feels integrated and connected, the use of solid shapes over any real alpha blending doing a lot of heavy lifting and it is executed masterfully. The colour palette is a joy to look at from start to finish (Tartarus is my personal favourite zone to look at), evoking clear feeling and identity in each map, able to tell a story even without the narrator. The story feels worthwhile and interesting, with Zagreus experiencing a pretty full character arc as he makes connections with other characters throughout the game. There's something to be said about the title sweeping the uncomfortable aspects of the stories the game borrows from under the rug, but that's a task suited for someone more educated in that area than I. The last aspect of note I'll add is the sound design. This game feels full-bodied in an auditory sense that even AAA titles fall down on a lot. There's a wonderful range of treble and bass, and the volume attenuation is dramatic and clear, giving you a great sense of where you are in relation to what's around you. (Reviewer also plays on Playstation)

Weapon varients, attacks, boons(perks) synergizing with one another are just the standard for any roguelike game so I'm not sure why it's being praised so much here. The mechanics are simple and easy to understand but this also makes the gameplay lack depth. Its the standard gameplay loop of attack attack attack dodge, repeat. The story... is uninteresting. I'm a huge greek mythology fan but I feel like the knowledge actually made the story less enjoyable to me. The way a lot of characters is portrayed is simply standard and boring. I think anyone who's read Percy jackson or similar would agree. Stuff like Hades being portrayed as "overworked" good guy might have been a subversion years ago, but its now extremely standard in modern media. The heat system is badly designed. I enjoy chasing higher difficulties in games, but the problem is higher heat is more difficult not because of adding depth of gameplay but simply limiting your options. Time limits, standard more enemy hp, attack, movement, spawn rate etc etc. The worst ones are the ones that add boss movesets and remove perk choices. The boss movesets could have been so much more interesting but for all of them it just ends up being more large AOE attacks that you avoid with no counterplay. The removing boon choices is a baffling decision for a game which relies on boons synergizing. In higher difficulties your run depends way more on luck than any skill, whether the game gives you boons that synergize or 3 completely useless ones. There's no motivation to push higher difficulties if your run is dependent on something out of your control. Hades is just... unremarkable to me. If you enjoy it, good for you, but it seems to just be a standard run of the mill roguelike imo.

[h1]“One more run.” That’s the dangerous promise Hades makes to you, and somehow it keeps delivering every single time.[/h1] At first glance, Hades looks like a stylish roguelike built around fast combat and Greek mythology. Spend a few hours with it, though, and it quickly becomes clear that Supergiant Games has created something far more special. This is one of those rare games where every system works together so smoothly that the whole experience becomes almost impossible to put down. Combat is the first thing that grabs your attention. It’s fast, responsive and incredibly satisfying, with a constant flow of weapons, powers and divine upgrades that allow each run to feel a little different. Whether you’re experimenting with a new weapon or stacking blessings from the Olympian gods, the build variety encourages creativity and keeps every escape attempt fresh. Even after dozens of runs, the gameplay rarely feels repetitive because the systems are designed to constantly surprise you and the dialogues almost never repeat.. What truly elevates Hades above many other roguelikes is how well the narrative fits into that gameplay loop. Instead of treating failure as a simple restart, the game embraces it. Every return to the House of Hades brings new dialogue, new character interactions and new pieces of story. I have 124h into Hades, and the dialogues didnt repeat once. The cast is full of personality, from the charming Zagreus to the many gods, allies and rivals you meet along the way. Conversations feel natural, often funny and occasionally emotional, turning what could have been a simple action game into something much more memorable. The presentation deserves just as much praise. The art direction is stunning, full of bold colors and striking character designs that reinterpret Greek mythology in a way that feels both fresh and timeless. Add to that an incredible soundtrack and excellent voice acting, and the entire world feels alive in a way that many games struggle to achieve. Perhaps the most impressive part of Hades is how accessible it is. Even players who normally shy away from roguelikes may find themselves hooked thanks to the steady sense of progression and the way the story keeps rewarding persistence. Each attempt feels meaningful, whether you make it a few rooms further or uncover another piece of the larger narrative. By the time you finally break through the many layers of the underworld, you realize something surprising. The real magic of Hades is not just escaping once, it’s wanting to come back and do it all over again. Few games balance action, storytelling and replayability this well, and the result is an experience that feels endlessly rewarding. Simply put, Hades is one of the finest roguelikes ever made, and easily one of the standout games of its generation. A dream and a wish I like to make to Supergiant Games: Greek mythology is fully embraced here. How about some new "Hades" game but an "Odin" or "Anubis" instead? This game with Nordic mythology would be a blast. Or a game with Egyptian mythology, a concept with a lot of interesting gods just like the Greek Pantheon and rarely used in the gaming industry. Please make it happen. <3

I finally reached the complete story ending. I might go back for some of the side stories, but they are not a priority for me. It took seventy runs to get there, and on the final attempt I was so tired of redoing everything that I turned on God Mode for the first time. I thought I had several more runs ahead of me and I was simply over it. At this point I am only missing five diamonds and some ambrosia for side stories, but the bounties are punishing enough that I am not rushing to finish them. Before anything else, yes, I do recommend this game. The review may sound negative because the frustrations are fresh, but Hades is still a strong example of the roguelike genre. The weapons feel distinct, the upgrades can be satisfying, and the core gameplay loop is solid. I am starting with the negatives because they hit me the hardest. Cons RNG and Build Control The biggest issue for me is the RNG and how it is implemented. One run with the gun (a weapon I already disliked but needed for diamonds and ambrosia) gave me nothing but Darkness, Keys, and stores. The only boons I saw were from Chaos and whatever I could buy near the end. That run is what pushed me to turn on God Mode. It felt like the game itself was trying to beat me. Roguelikes always rely on RNG, but in Hades it determines whether enemies are mildly annoying or unstoppable. You will see people say things like “Just use this build,” but you can easily go a dozen runs without seeing a single boon from the god that build requires. Even when you do get the right god, the skills offered may be useless for your weapon. Artemis is a good example. Her call is great and her arrow rain passive is fantastic, but getting a massive dash attack bonus on a weapon that has no dash attack is pointless. Some weapons also block cast mechanics, yet you can end up with nothing but cast related boons. It is a roguelike, so randomness is expected, but the balance here can feel as punishing as Noita. In many games you have a base playstyle and the buffs enhance it. In Hades the RNG decides whether you can even kill the mobs in a given room or whether you are burning through all your revives because you simply cannot hit anything. Enemy Design and Room Layout Certain enemies feel unfair rather than challenging. The large carts that never stop unless you deal enough damage and the small carts that swarm and explode are frustrating. The flying casters that drift off the map so you cannot hit them at all are even worse. When your only option is to run to the edge of the arena, run back, hit them once, and repeat, something has gone wrong. If I pick a weapon with no cast ability, the game should not generate entire rooms full of enemies that can only be safely handled with cast abilities. That combination feels like a design oversight rather than a difficulty spike. Movement Speed and Dash Limitations Some runs left me with no movement or dash upgrades from Hermes. When that happens, avoiding attacks from Hades or the Minotaur becomes nearly impossible. You can see the attack coming, but your dash simply does not travel far enough to escape it. This is a situation where RNG should be optional rather than mandatory. You need either a ranged weapon or a strong dash, and when the game refuses to offer either, the fight becomes unfair. Pros Core Gameplay When the RNG cooperates, the game feels fantastic. The weapons support a variety of playstyles including hit and run, stand and fight, and even something close to stealth. The base mechanics are fun on their own, and when the boons line up, the game can feel like a power fantasy. One of my favorite runs involved a cast that bounced repeatedly between enemies, slamming poison mobs into walls until they melted. It was hilarious and satisfying. I only saw that combination once in seventy runs, but it was memorable. Art and World Design The art direction is incredible. I often wished I could zoom in and explore the environments without enemies. An in game art book or a free roam mode would be amazing. Even after seventy runs, I still appreciated the visual design. Music and Sound The music is good overall. I did not care for the final song, but the soundtrack and sound effects are strong. Story and Characters The story is decent, though like many modern narratives it could be resolved with a single honest conversation. The side stories are more interesting to me because they explore characters with deep mythological backgrounds. I only wish the story were easier to access without repeating the same run so many times with increasing difficulty. Controls Responsiveness depends heavily on weapon choice and RNG, but the controls themselves are snappy and precise. Final Thoughts I would give Hades a solid seven out of ten. I liked the main character and I am glad I finally reached the true ending, though I wish the requirements were cut in half for that ending. I will see how Hades 2 improves on the formula. The game often goes on sale for around six dollars, and at that price it is an absolute steal. You will get your hours, your immersion, and your money’s worth. Despite the frustrations, I have no regrets about playing it, even if it took me years to finally commit to finishing it

[h1] Backlog Review Nr. 11: Hades [/h1] (Completed) I have had Hades in my catalogue for quite a while, because I'm usually not a huge fan of the genre and the setting of greek mythology is uninteresting to me for the most part. However, I'm glad to say, this game ranks high among the best roguelikes I've ever played, and I will definitely put more time into it as time goes on. Hades is a game that just oozes love and passion out of every nook and cranny. The character designs are so incredibly epic, the gameplay is responsive and polished and is accompanied by a loop that get's you hooked almost instantly. Not only that, the artstyle is stellar and truly one-of-a-kind; sometimes I just want to stay and [i] look[/i] at the stages before moving onto the next. The fluidity of every scenery and animation definitely have an entrancing quality to it and add a lot to the overall feel of the game. Another huge plus is how truly arcade-y the game feels. You can finish a run in 30 minutes, and if that happens to be too long there is still the option to save within a stage. Considering I have a lot of catching up to do with my studies, this game came at just the right time. The weapons themselves provide just enough variety to keep every run and every build you get feel fresh and exciting, and experimenting feels rewarding aswell. The main gripe is that the progression seemingly comes to a halt at some point. The upgrades you get are either tediously grindy or lackluster, and in a lot of cases, they're both. At some point the power creep has most upgrades feel a lot less meaningful the further you go, which makes grinding the game after beating the final boss for the first time somewhat pointless. As stated, this game I will definitely return to as time goes on. It's been ages since I was this hooked to a game, and I'll definitely check out Hades II in the future!

Hell yeah. I'd heard about this game years ago, but for some reason didn't think I'd like it. Just not a gameplay genre I typically like (top-down rogue-like whatever else it is), but after finally trying it, I'm pleasantly surprised. Honestly what impressed me the most about this game is how well the gameplay mechanics *make sense* and fit in with the lore. For example, you're *expected* to die. A lot. So it isn't immersion breaking or rage quit inducing. Another prominent example is that even once you beat the game, it gives you a reason to beat it again and again after that, in a way that makes sense with the story. It's not just those two examples though, it's everything, it all just fits so well. The voice acting is also *very* good. Not just quality, but also quantity: there's quite a large diversity of voicelines for specific situations. And of course the gameplay is sufficiently fun. Very repeatable, though after a while I do just start hoping for a few specific power-ups from the RNG, and favor just a couple weapons, though on that note, the weapons *are* fairly balanced, with very different playstyles, so that's cool. The difficulty is also *highly* customizable. Great art, great music. The list goes on. Overall just a very well-made game with great attention to detail, and appealing to a wide audience.

The most impressive thing about Hades for me is how naturally the story progresses, evolves, and persists through each run. At its core it's a regular rogue-like where you start a run, finish it (win or die), then start a new run, but the story and dialogue are so seamlessly woven into this structure that it always feels like a cohesive and monolithic journey across all the runs. There's A LOT of dialogue, I did 50+ runs and I ran out of unique lines with only maybe a couple of characters, and even then the generic things that they said varied from run to run. The characters also have a lot of conditional dialogue, as in they often react to your equipment, boons, past interactions with themselves or other characters, etc. Then there's the main hub in between runs, the House of Hades, where there's also a lot of quests and interesting interactions with different characters. The story itself isn't genius or anything, but it's definitely engaging enough, and the dialogue is very well written, has nice humor and a lot of flavor overall. It's fully voiced and the voice acting is good. On the gameplay side it's sort of like Bastion but better. Diversity is great, at the start of the run you can select a weapon which all play and feel very different, and then there's lots of boon combinations that you can get during the run. Combat is a lot of fun, it's fast paced and fluid, and the boss battles are great. Soundtrack is very good and complements the game's other aspects extremely well, but I think Bastion and Transistor had catchier OST overall. All in all, not counting Hades II because I haven't played it yet, this is Supergiant's best work by far, and by a large margin at that.

The soundtrack ♥♥♥♥♥, the voice acting is entirely cinematic, the ending and the epilogue don't quite feel like goodbye, so staying for a couple more runs to complete the remaining achievements doesn't feel bad. Lots of games about the Living could only wish to be able to breathe nearly as much life force into the audience as this game about the Dead does.

Highly Recommended This game is extremely addictive. I will talk about my experience playing it on the Steam Deck, which in my opinion is one of the best ways to enjoy it. Why the game works so well: • Perfect for short or long sessions It is great to start a run and, if you need to stop playing, you can simply put the Steam Deck to sleep and continue later exactly where you left off. • Very satisfying progression Each run depends on luck, but also on your previous experience. Over time you start recognizing which ability combinations and builds work best for your playstyle, which makes every run feel more strategic. • Challenging but not frustrating The game is difficult, but losing a run never feels overly frustrating. Instead, it motivates you to try again with a better strategy. • Great characters and mythology The characters from Greek mythology have personalities that match their myths very well. The way they talk and interact with you changes as you build affinity with them by giving gifts, which is a really nice touch. Final thoughts This game is absolutely worth picking up if you want something to enjoy casually or if you want the challenge of trying to platinum the game, which will definitely not be easy. I started from scratch recently and am reminded of the things I found annoying. I mentioned builds already, but also conversation progression. Sometimes characters who should have something to say have nothing to say. Sometimes they have so much to say that the thing you want them to do in order to progression a story/quest takes far too many runs. Other times they just aren't there (or like the 3 that are outside of the house, you don't get their room to show up). Progression itself is slow especially when there aren't differing areas. Would've been cool if there was something like two different versions of asphodel(could also happen with the other areas, but only asphodel has mentioned to have looked entirely different in the past) and/or some sort of zone randomization with proper scaling so I could get something like Styx first then end up in Elysium second and so on. Could be something where you can have Chaos warp the areas into a differing order. Could've also done something similar with randomized enemy spawns and enemies spawning outside of their normal environment(LMFAO ROR/2). Things you get from Hermes feel like they should just be character growth QOL similar to the Mirror of Night or something you buy from him before you start each run for something like gemstones or his own currency. You should be able to buy rerolls from the Well of Charon. Unlocking the last weapon aspects are a little ridiculous in their requirements to even figure out if you would actually like them or not. Dark Thirst is a Trap. The main story speed is actually fine, its everything else after that. Companions not existing for a long time, the majority of keepsakes being useless never to be used again after you've maxed them for that save file/achievement. Some boons requiring so many of their respective gods to actually work (POSEIDON) you begin to entirely avoid them altogether. I don't understand why this game got it so good when it as a roguelike gameplay wise it is less than mid. I queued this back up again to see if I would want to play Hades 2 for any reason, but I most likely won't. I've may have been spoiled by Enter the Gungeon being as good as it was as a roguelike. Probably head back to dead cells to reclaim what I've lost once I've cleared up what I wanted to here on this game. What a phenomenal game! My gripes are pretty minor, enough so that I don't feel they necessarily warrant being placed in this review. But I did, and now I'm looking to budget some time to play the sequel. It is readily apparent how much thought and work went into this game to make it so incredible!

The game has such great mechanics and combat, especially once you find the style of fighting that really fits for you, as it gives you a plethora of options and tools to explore and experiment with. The music and all of the environments you roll through are incredibly beautiful. And. Man. All of the designs. I mentioned the environments already but the character designs, the designs for the weaponry, for the flourishes surrounding attacks and abilities as you fight, for little collectibles and items, even for something like the menu are so detailed and wonderful to look at. I appreciate the way this game tackles and represents Greek Mythology. The gods and goddesses, and even the heroes of old that also are present in the game, all feel fairly portrayed and really seem to fit with how they are in their myths, neither good nor bad but just… beings with flaws and strengths like the rest of us. There’s still some creative liberties taken with how things are portrayed in the Underworld, specifically with the environments and some of the enemies, but it still manages to feel really fun and entertaining regardless. Hades is still an antagonist, a role I feel he's unfairly thrown into in a lot of media, but it feels a lot more fair and understandable with him being a dad to your player character, who is currently going through a rebellious period. Truly this was just a joy of a game and is definitely worth checking out. Roguelikes tend to be hard for people not already a fan of them to get into, but I hear that it's an easier task with this game than other titles, and it does try and make it more accessible to people who might struggle with the gameplay but are interested in experiencing the story.

In short: Hades is a great game and a mediocre Rogue-like. there are a lot of issues with the game, many of them addressed in the sequel. However, this is still a very good game and well worth your time. You will have your favorite gods, and I suggest gravitating towards them and sticking to them, because my least favorite runs were the ones in which I tried to experiment or when I was trying to check off something for the list of prophecies that function as ways to gather resources for your upgrades. and the scarcity of resources for upgrades and the limited ways to accrue them is a whole other can of beans Should you play Hades? Yes. The Supergiant charm is here, the story of a troubled family is well written, but if you want a rogue-like you will sink your teeth in for countless hours? Maybe this will scratch some itch, but you can be better served elsewhere.

Greek myth is unique in the sense that it has infinite unique interpretations, themes, and stories. Anyone can take the Ancient Greek mythos and spin just about any tale they desire, using the very tools of the Fates themselves. The sheer amount of dialogue and minor interactions has never made a land of the dead feel so alive, every minor action you can take has some kind of reaction or comment from at least one character, besides minor quips, I have not seen a single repeated dialogue between any two characters after 60 hours of gameplay and at least that many runs. Oh, and the soundtrack, an absolute gift from the gods! I don't think I have ever had a big of an [i]oh ♥♥♥♥[\i] moment than when I struck the final blow on the final boss only for the baseline to kick in as he stood back up and that health bar filled all the way back up for phase two. I could do little more than panic as he proceeded to give me an all-expenses-paid, first-class, food-and-drink-included trip right back down to the house of Hades. One thing: definitely make sure you have at least 30 minutes for each run, I started one thinking I would lose in about 15 minutes and ended up making it all the way and finding the credits at about midnight before my 9am class the next day. I do recommend playing this game first if you're going to play Hades 2, although not necessary, I feel like the story of the second game makes a lot more sense when given the context of this game. Supergiant games absolutely cooked, now I'm going to go beat Hades 2...

[h1] 9/10 - God-like Roguelike [/h1] [b] There is no escape - from this peak experience! [/b] I originally played this for a few hours years ago but the Elysium heroes were gatekeeping me with a big skill issue and I swiftly dropped the game... I am SO glad I returned and 100%'d it now! [hr][/hr][h2] Gameplay [/h2] Some of the finest roguelite gameplay of all time with a great selection of weapons, aspects that change each weapon's feel, and of course the roguelike boons from the gods - some amazing boons with each god offering different specialties - as well as being able to combine some together for powerful duo boons! Very fun hack and slash combat letting you combine variety of moves together, basic attacks, specials, casts, dashes and calls. Hades is that rare roguelike where failure never feels like punishment, only progress wearing a different mask. Every escape attempt from the Underworld sharpens your skill, deepens relationships, and peels back another layer of a world that somehow grows warmer the more time you spend dying in it. Combat is razor sharp and endlessly expressive. Each weapon completely reshapes how you fight, and the Olympian boons layer on synergies that can turn a cautious run into a screen clearing power fantasy. Few games make experimentation this thrilling or make you feel this clever when a build suddenly clicks. What truly elevates Hades is its storytelling. Instead of pausing the action for narrative, it threads character arcs through repetition itself, conversations evolve, bonds deepen, and even the gods feel reactive to your journey. Zagreus’s rebellion becomes less about escape and more about belonging. It’s stylish, addictive, surprisingly heartfelt, and polished to an almost absurd degree. Hades doesn’t just perfect the roguelike formula, it redefines it, proving that a game built on endless repetition can still move forward emotionally. A modern classic, and one of the clearest examples of indie ambition executed flawlessly.

I don't enjoy this game because of big design flaws in my opinion, but hear me out! The core of roguelites is to get excited for new unlocks that make your journey either easier or different in a substential way. Hades fails to do that to some degree. - You get some sort of trinket (= keepsake) that buffs you. You unlock more keepsakes over time by gifting special items to different characters. You can make these keepsakes stronger by wearing them on your runs and killing monsters. Ok cool stuff! However, only two keepsakes make sense when you start to play, because they are far superior to everything else. One that gives you flat more life and one that resurrects you. As you wanna survive as long as possible, you don't need 10 % more damage or some more gold or gimmicks. Maybe when you are super buffed and high level, other keepsakes are worth to pick up, but it's basically a mechanic to ignore for the first 20+ hours ingame. I'm not even interested to unlock the remaining ones. Being able to only ever use one keepsake at a time feels like wasted potential too. - Then you also unlock new main weapons over time, however they all play VERY similar. A shield, a sword, a bow? Doesn't really matter. You wanna smash your buttons and be in constant movement to not get hit by enemies anway. - Your meta progression is a mirror that lets you enhance certain stats, mainly life and damage related. You have to spend currency you earn in your runs to do so. This makes you stronger and therefore your runs last longer, it just feels rather boring. - Then there are "quests" called prophecies that usually take many runs to fulfill. The rewards feel rather poor regarding the huge time investment. - The "story" is cut and distributed between NPCs and your runs. Every run you can walk up to an NPC and get two lines of text, rinse repeat. The voice acting is great, but I can't remember what a person told me 10 hours ago already, when we started the conversation. It feels very forced too, because you need certain voice lines from certain characters to get [spoiler]special upgrades of your weapons[/spoiler]. So you really wanna talk to everyone after each run to make this happen faster. Because again, 2 voice lines at a time to progress the relationship and story. - I already mentioned that the weapons all feel very similar to play. This is also due to the god powers that enhance your attacks feel extremely similar and - sorry to say - unimaginative. One adds knowback, the other chance to crit and so on. All the same for every weapon. - By the time you have a special god ability ready in a fight, the fight is basically over already, because you need to charge it up by fighting mosters. These would be somewhat cool abilities but then again, happens rarely enough to use them, not to forget you first need to even unlock them each run to begin with. - That brings me to my second last point, which is the often horrible - because seemingly random - choices you get between rooms to upgrade your attacks. I had runs where I didn't get the offer to upgrade my main attack. Sure other attacks are stronger therefore but I can't always use them. - The codex is lackluster as you need to face bosses and monsters many, many times to complete the entry and information. You get no reward for doing so, it's lore only. Now some good things I really enjoyed: + Boss fights changing over time, so it's not the same fight over and over again and adds some challenge is a real cool addition! + Being able to choose the rewards depending on the rooms you fight during your runs is great! + The art style and voice acting are amazing, same goes for the Greek mythology setting for this game! As you can see, there are a lot of negatives and only some positives so I can't recommend the game. You might see things differently, especially if you are not familiar with this genre. I love the developer and their other games, so hopefully I can enjoy their future creations again.
