​Hades is one of those rare games that manages to make the act of dying feel like a reward rather than a failure. The "addiction" is real because the game perfectly balances high-stakes action with a narrative that only moves forward when you fall. It features some of the best voice acting and storytelling I’ve encountered, where every character in the House of Hades feels like a living, breathing person with their own grudges and evolving relationships. You don't just keep playing to see the next boss; you keep playing to see what Megaera or Achilles has to say to you after your latest failed attempt. ​The combat system and progression are where the game truly shines, offering a journey that makes you feel your growth as a player. At the beginning, you feel completely outmatched, struggling to even clear the first area or put a dent in the first boss. However, through a deep system of permanent upgrades and weapon mastery, you eventually transform into a true underworld overlord. Unlike many other titles in the roguelite genre that rely on automatic shooting or passive gameplay, Hades is built on a highly interactive and kinetic combat system. With a variety of weapons to choose from, you are always in the driver's seat, making every dash and strike feel purposeful. ​The variety of builds and ability combinations is staggering, ensuring that no two runs ever feel the same. Each god from the Olympian pantheon offers a distinct set of boons that feel powerful and satisfying to execute. Furthermore, the game offers a brilliant scalable difficulty system through the "Heat" mechanic, allowing you to tailor the challenge even more and spice things up. ​For those playing on the Steam Deck, the experience is flawless. It is easily one of the best-optimized games for the handheld, running with a buttery smooth 90Hz refresh rate on the OLED model. The controls feel native and incredibly responsive, and the battery life is impressive, giving you over six hours of playtime on a single charge. It is the ultimate "pick-up-and-play" experience for someone looking to chip away at a massive game while on the go. ​However, there are a few things to consider if you are worried about repetition. While the ability combinations are almost endless, the core gameplay loop can start to feel repetitive since you are clearing the same four themed areas over and over again. Additionally, reaching the "true" ending is a significant grind. You have to successfully escape a specific number of times to see the conclusion of Zagreus’s story, which might feel like a barrier for players who want to move quickly through their backlog or get bored easiluly. That said, the quality of the journey is so high that for most, the grind is well worth the effort.

ꨄ My rating: 10/10 ꨄ Pros: - The artstyle is very unique, featuring lots of different artworks of many different deities from the Greek Mythology, ranging from the Olympian deities to Chthonic gods and many more. The camera also features a top-down, isometric view of the main character: Zagreus. - The gameplay despite being "repetitive" since its a roguelite game, feels very refreshing and I've genuinely never gotten bored of this game while playing, nor have I ever felt like something was a chore (besides the damn achievement regarding a specific musical instrument...). It features lots of different weapons with different "aspects" which are alternative forms with different movesets, and each run is unique since the gods that show up to empower you are random until a pool is made for the gods that will reappear during the same run. - The story was surprisingly good. Didn't really have a massive plot twist but it also didn't need one for the story to be as engaging as it is. - Replayability is also featured in a very creative way as it actually is explained in-game why Zagreus has to constantly beat the game, adding to the immersion of the game. - Soundtrack is incredible, definitely one of the games which I went as far as looking up its OST to listen to randomly. Cons: - The only con I can think of is that some weapon aspects are clearly much better than others unless you fully upgrade them, and some gods are clearly stronger than others, limiting a little which aspects works with certain gods and vice versa, something that is massively improved on in Hades 2.

If you’ve ever wanted to disappoint your dad repeatedly but in a stylish, emotionally supportive way Hades has you covered. From the first time I dashed out of the House of Hades in Hades, I knew I was in trouble. Not “oh no, I might lose” trouble. I mean “I will absolutely lose 47 times and enjoy every second of it” trouble. You play as Zagreus, son of literal God of the Underworld, and your main hobby is trying to leave. Your father, Hades, is not thrilled about this. Family therapy? No. Weaponized bureaucracy and fire-spewing doom monsters? Yes. The combat is buttery smooth. Every weapon feels distinct, every dash makes you feel like a mythological figure with a caffeine addiction, and every boon from the Olympian gods turns you into a progressively more chaotic blender of destruction. One run you’re zapping everything with lightning like a budget Zeus. The next, you’re critting so hard the enemies probably reconsider their life choices in the afterlife. And the dialogue? Unreal. I have never failed so many times in a game and felt so emotionally supported. Every death comes with new voice lines, new lore, new sass. The characters somehow manage to roast you and encourage you at the same time. It’s like dying is part of the customer rewards program. Visually, it’s gorgeous. The art style is bold, colorful, and dramatic in a “yes, this is the Underworld, but make it fashion” kind of way. Every region feels distinct, every boss fight feels theatrical, and somehow even lava looks aesthetically pleasing. And can we talk about the bosses? They’re tough, they’re dramatic, and they absolutely love monologuing before ruining your day. But when you finally beat one after getting obliterated multiple times? Pure serotonin. What really makes Hades special is that losing never feels bad. You’re always progressing. Always unlocking something. Always getting a little stronger. It’s the only game where dying feels productive. In summary: Hades is fast, funny, brutally challenging, weirdly wholesome, and dangerously addictive. It turns repeated failure into a lifestyle choice and somehow makes it glamorous. 10/10 would attempt to escape the Underworld again. Sorry, Dad.

Context: I've played this game for about 3 days. I've beaten the final boss once. I've gotten to the stage immediately before the final boss with three weapon types. I've gotten access, (I believe), to all the core upgrade mechanics, and upgraded a fair number of things in the mirror specifically to max, Overall, this is a fun experience. I'm a mostly pretty casual gamer, and I worried a bit that this game would be too difficult for me, but if you level your attributes aggressively you can at least beat it once, just. Mechanically I think it's a pretty solid experience. If I had some general nitpicks it would be that: 1) Enemies level somewhat to match your upgrades, with progressively more difficult ones slowly rolling out. And while, yes, that provides more variety, it's a little too close to complete parity. EG, it sort of feels like a treadmill you're making no real progress on. It could actually be argued the game is easier to beat in the window where you've got a few key upgrades, but before you've really finished leveling, since certain of the higher level enemies that show up in the last level are quite annoying. The result is that the enemies around you will consistently be able to tank, truly, an annoying number of hits, most of the time. You *do* feel like you're getting more powerful if you squint, but it's awfully muted. 2) Relatedly, the biggest felt effect was honestly from death defiance. Most other upgrades besides health were tinkering at the margins. The spongey enemies mean most of your survivability is down to your ability to kite, by jumping in, hitting, and jumping out, without getting hit. Encounters are simultaneously very hard and very easy, in that there's basically no question what to do most of the time, but it's just a question of if you can pull off nipping in, biting, and running away, 400 consecutive times without getting hit enough to lose a critical amount of health. Literally, health and revives just let you spin the roulette wheel longer and that's what makes the difference. 3) Certain enemy types are *considerably* harder to kill with weapons that confine you to close range, especially in the third and fourth stage, because the enemies are both more resistant to attack and more dangerous to even be near. Most games would compensate by making ranged weapons weaker and melee weapons stronger. I honestly couldn't tell if they were doing this. I consulted the wiki and if anything I think there's a slight bias towards the weapons with longer range having more damage, albeit that *might* be balanced by attack speed. What I can confidently assert is that my main attack almost always felt badly under-leveled with every weapon, even if I focused on it, which is odd. It may be that I haven't leveled up my probability of getting higher levels of boon enough, so I'm getting common-tier boons that are relatively weak. 4) Related point: I expected the different weapon options to be more in the vein of, hey, here are choices for different playstyles. In practice a couple of them are hard counters to the most important challenges in the game, and the rest aren't. There is definitely a best choice in my opinion, pretty much regardless of who you are, and there's another that you get that's a close second. A couple of the weapons are borderline suicidal to use on certain bosses, or at least, your kiting and multitasking games had better be on point. 5) Speaking of bosses-- boss difficulty is all over the shop. The most dangerous boss out of all of them is the third boss and it's not even close. There's an event that you can get that makes the third boss arena a little easier but it's still honestly where most of my runs ended. The last boss is actually less difficult, and if we're judging by the criteria of death defiance charges burned, pretty much on par with the hardest variant of the *first* boss. The rest of the first boss variants are the next most difficult. And the least difficult boss was consistently the second boss. I think across all my runs I've had a run end with the second boss exactly once, and it was specifically because I'd drawn into the hardest variant of the first boss, my boons were not particularly helpful against her, and I played unusually badly around traps, so she kicked my ever living tail. *Even then*, I got close. Okay, that's a lot of critique. What's good? 1) Despite being relatively grindy, it does balance the grind with a generally hectic tone. Put another way, you don't get bored because you still feel a lot of tension trying to stay one step ahead. If anything fatigue was a bigger problem than boredom. I had to pause to work out a hand cramp a few times. 2) The game has a very forgiving dodge mechanic, so you can actually finish certain encounters, even kind of long, bullet-Hell style encounters, without getting hit, if you're fast and a little bit lucky. And there are a few ways to claw yourself back from the brink once you know the game. I think the run I finally won with was one where I came within just a few points of death in the third stage and clawed it back semi-miraculously with a couple of good draws (not totally sure, because I've done that more than once). 3) The game rewards paying attention-- learning what things cost, what boons are offered by whom, etc. At the beginning your choices will be mostly random, but within a couple of hours you'll be plotting a strategic route and doing risk-reward calculations. This effect is augmented by troves, a couple of types of which can rescue a run that's teetering if you perform well. 4) The game does a really good job of feeding new content to you gradually over an extended period of time, so the game always feels a little bit fresh (or at least, for the first 20-odd hours it does). 5) The production quality is just fantastic. Artwork is excellent and distinctive. Voicework does a great job giving all the characters a unique feel and it really helps get you invested. There are a LOT of unique interactions and voice lines. At 20-odd hours in I still haven't run into any repeats that I can think of. The music is mostly pretty solid if occasionally a little bit oddly modern-sounding (given the setting) but nothing too jarring. The writing is above average and there are cute little interchanges between tons of characters that make the world feel alive. The overall plot is also above average and does a good job of justifying the mechanics of the game, without excessive contrivance, at almost every turn. ------------------------- TL;DR and final verdict: typically when I'm trying to evaluate if a game is going to be worthwhile I figure I want to get at least an hour of entertainment per dollar invested. I'm not *quite* there yet but I'm pretty close. I'm overall happy with my purchase and would enthusiastically recommend it to a friend. I do think there are some balance issues, which at times threaten to make the game too grindy or frustrating. But the game has other mechanics that give it just enough give not to have this issue quite take it under, and when you factor in the fact that there's clearly a lot of heart and effort put into the audiovisual quality, the game ends up having a certain charm that forgives a lot of it's annoyances. And all this is coming from a person who is not exactly an MLG pro. You probably won't regret purchasing it.

This game is a reminder for myself to not buy a game just because it looks good (in this case fantastic) and because of the hype. Let me start with the good stuff. That is obviously the visuals. Hades is a really stunning game with its distinct graphical style that just looks incredibly good. Along with visuals, I have to say that the characters, dialogues and voice acting is top notch as well. Makes me wish this game was a visual novel. Oh well. And I guess I can mention audio as a positive as well. So, what went wrong? The core of the game, the combat system, is just painfully awful. It's not bad in the first part of the Hell, but it starts appearing in the second and just sucks in the third one: There is just constantly something or somebody going after you. You are constantly dashing, trying to avoid various traps while attempting to defeat enemies. At some point you have 2 or 3 enemies with better armour, a God's projectile that can't be destroyed going after you awfully long, projectiles from statues that cannot be destroyed and you try to avoid all of that while also avoiding the traps on the floor. The enemies are not really interesting and defeating them is not exactly satisfying. After almost 9 hours, the best moment was I uninstalled the game. Hades 2 looks great, but this time I won't make the same mistake.

Incredible amount of variety, very fun fast-paced combat, a good story with unexpectedly well-written characters, a gorgeous art style and character designs supported by an amazing soundtrack. Each run feels completely different thanks to Boons and weapons, their forms, and how much they have to offer. As someone who isn’t a big fan of the roguelike/roguelite genre, I am amazed by this game. Almost flawless, other than a few minor issues: The Epilogue felt a bit underwhelming, I would have loved to see interaction between the Gods of Olympus and the Underworld. Some storylines/rapport take too long to progress, most of which are required to get the Epilogue, and some of them also unlock weapon forms and companions, having them a bit earlier would have been better. The main bosses could have been better, they definitely need more movesets and changes in different runs, though you can make them more fun thanks to the Pact, which also keeps the game fresh with some gameplay changes, it isn't enough for me. Still, these points do not change the fact that this game is absolutely amazing and a must-play, especially if you like Greek mythology and satisfying, fast-paced combat.

I have had this game on my radar since its release, but only recently did I actually play it, and oh boy. I loved it! For a fan of Greek mythology this game was a treat. Unlike many other dungeon crawlers which go rather light on the story, in Hades 1 the story is without a doubt its strongest part. The game is set after Kora, Demeter's daughter, had been kidnapped by Hades. It's must have been a while since then, as Zag is in his early twenties, but Demeter hasn't yet reconciled with the Olympians or contacted her daughter. I love it! It's a fantastic adaptation of that myth and focusing on Zagreus' point of view is a genius idea. If you know Greek mythology well you will be able to recognize how genius the writing is. Most of gods and goddesses interactions with each other is exactly what I imagined it would be. The gameplay is very solid and the controls are easy to learn and use. There are a lot of different boons, keepsakes, weapons to try and mix together and see what sticks. What I really like about this game is how some boons are completely worthless when using one weapon and then they excel when combined with the other. This game is pretty much perfect in my eyes. Sure there might be some things that could be explored especially gameplay wise, but that's what sequels are for, right? 10/10

I finished dozens of games and Hades is one of the best I've ever played! Not many games fascinate me enough to play it all day and all night for a week straight, I did 130 hours in 8 days :| :D It's a great mix of strategy, action and RPG with the right amount of challenge. Boss fights have a lot of things going on: bombs exploding + laser beams, it can be stressful in the beginning when you don't know what's going on. Progress feels very fluid for the first 75% of the game (100 hours) but then it turns into a bit of a grind. Only <5% of players reach that point and it took me further 50-75 hours to get 100% achievements. Achievs are very intuitive and well designed, I didn't even have to look them up (except the last one). They come naturally as you progress through the game and don't require any RNG or super skill. After finishing the main story, I just played for fun whilst trying new builds and gathering bounties, not for the sake of achievements. My spoiler-free tips for new players: - Do not choose Hell Mode, it will only make things needlessly difficult. Game is challenging enough and you can always make it harder later. - You will die a lot at the start, everybody does, game is designed for that so don't be discouraged. With every attempt you will grow in power but your skills, knowledge and experience will also improve. - If you are struggling, force [spoiler]Athena's Dash[/spoiler] boon and pick extra Dashes from Mirror/Hermes, it will greatly improve your survivability. You may also enable a God Mode in settings until you get a deeper understanding of combat. It takes many hours to learn how to dodge various attacks or how to clear difficult rooms. - I used ChatGPT to guide me through this game spoiler-free and it was pretty good though sometimes it would gie me some outdated info, from an earlier patch I assume. When reading forums or watching YT you often get info you didn't ask for like the best builds, which you may want to discover yourself. Typical answer to how/why something did not unlock yet is to just keep playing and in most cases I unlocked it a few runs (or rather deaths) later. - Try every weapon, pick one/two aspects you enjoy, level it up, master it. Do a quick search if your chosen aspect is any good on high Heat because you can't easily switch them. I had the easiest time with with [spoiler]Zag Shield[/spoiler] and I recommend maxing this one first. All non-Zag [spoiler]bow/rail/shield[/spoiler] aspects are very strong, versatile, consistent and offer unique playstyles but require a lot of Titan Blood and some game/build knowledge to pull off. [spoiler]Fists/Sword[/spoiler] are very easy to use but I found them boring, I would avoid investing in a [spoiler]Spear[/spoiler]. You need to [spoiler]spend 5 Blood on non-Zagreus aspects among all weapons[/spoiler] to start unlocking hidden aspects. - Unlock Contractor upgrades that will enhance your runs first (main tab). Once you buy everything important, keep about 5 Diamonds, 300 Gems, 15 Keys and 10 Nectar in reserve in case of quests/trade opportunities, cosmetics can wait (they won't improve your win rate). In retrospect I would avoid limited-time-offers except for 500 Darkness and Gems/Darkness/Keys for something else. - Fishing is about reaction time (how fast you click after they bite), you need very good reflexes to catch rare fish but remember that fourth bait bite is always a catch. Good fishing guide can be bound on Wiki. - Choose 6 gods and feed them Nectar in mid-game if you want to go through the story asap (always choose Artemis+Zeus). Optional friendships you may want to prioritize: [spoiler]Meg > Than > Dusa > Skelly[/spoiler] - There are 2 hammers + 2 Hermes in every run with a 50/50 chance of getting a third (Anvil) in the last shop. You can skip them if there is Chaos/boon you really want, they will re-appear later. - Supposedly controller is better for movement/melee, keyboard for casting/ranged. I had no issue with mouse+KB after the initial feasting on traps/lava. You need to pay a close attention to everything because new systems unlock with very little notification, examples include: - Charon middle room (not the one before the boss) can spawn [spoiler]a lootable object behind him[/spoiler]. - Mirror gets another set of very powerful talents (you switch between dark and green). - After many interactions with Sisyphus, you can [spoiler]talk to Bouldy[/spoiler]. Save scumming tip: [spoiler]you can re-roll (!) room reward as long as you didn't fish yet, just quit and resume :)[/spoiler] I'm still unlocking new dialogues after nearly 100 clears and long after finishing Codex, Fates etc., e.g. try wearing Tooth keepsake during your first Hermes boon (typically in Asphodel).

Rogue-likes aren't generally my thing. But this one looked interesting, and I loved the stylized designs (and, ya know, all those positive reviews). Bought it. Played it. And promptly [b]dumped[/b] it. [i]"Dude, what is this? No meaningful progression. Same boss over and over again. Ain't got time for that!"[/i] So, I laid this game to rest. Or so I thought. 5 years later, Hades 2 comes out, and I've just finished Silksong and a few other titles I absolutely loved. [i]"Wait.. I have the first Hades. Hmm..."[/i] So, I get back into the game, and after a few runs, I finally understand. There's a moment where you "get" this game. It's like that Cat Transcendence vid on YT. I finally see the light, "what I'm supposed to do" becomes apparent. I proceed to "do that which I must do" and the game is suddenly [b]super[/b] fun. [DISCLAIMER] And no, I'm not talking "looked up outdated OP build on YT and follow it" type of stuff. No, no. You see... the whole time, I was trying to WIN. I was trying to make it to the "End Of The Game". That's not what you're supposed to do. You're supposed to LEARN the game, LEARN the mechanics, LEARN the boons, LEARN what works with what. LEARN the different weapons. LEARN the Gods. Because once you have those down, winning is just a bonus that comes pretty easily. So yup, great game. Great story. Great mechanics. As soon as I get my Hades fill, I'm moving on to the next one!

Hades is a masterclass in roguelite mechanics, where every system works together to create combat that’s fast, fluid, and endlessly satisfying — and progression that feels meaningful even in defeat. Combat is tight and responsive. Every weapon type has a distinct feel, timing, and range: from rapid spear jabs to heavy hammer swings to magical blasts. Movement isn’t an afterthought — dashing, positioning, and spacing are core to survival, and mastering when to dash away versus when to stay aggressive is mechanically rich and rewarding. The boon system is phenomenal. Each run offers random but thematically linked upgrades from gods like Zeus, Athena, or Dionysus. Boons don’t just buff numbers — they change how your abilities behave, letting players create wildly different builds run to run. Synergies between boons (like a Zeus chain lightning plus Artemis crit boosts) feel deeply satisfying and strategically potent. Weapon aspects and deliverance upgrades give long‑term build depth. Every time you unlock a new aspect or upgrade path, it permanently expands mechanical options, letting you shape a playstyle that matches your approach — burst, sustain, status effects, etc. Enemy design reinforces mechanical engagement. Patterns are clear but challenging, forcing you to read tells, anticipate attacks, and react with mechanics you’ve practiced. Mini‑bosses and boss fights act as mechanical checkpoints, testing mastery of movement, dash usage, and boon synergies. Progression loop is elegantly tied to choice and failure. Even when you fall, you earn resources that unlock new boons, weapons, or stats, which mechanically alters future runs. This creates a sense of forward momentum that’s rare in roguelites. Every run feels distinct, every decision — from boon pick to dash timing — has real impact, and the combat loop keeps you learning and adapting. 10/10 — precise, deep, and incredibly rewarding roguelite mechanics.

Let's see. A singleplayer roguelite game that's balanced and has a variety of builds driven by both chance and choice. With a storyline. The storyline borrows heavily from Ancient Greek lore but then gets creative in not playing it straight. With nicely shaped NPC personalities for that social-interaction itch even nerds sometimes want to scratch. With stylish 2D graphics (Elysium fields FTW) that runs well on budget PCs. Seems to be stable, too; zero problems so far with my generally glitchy Radeon Vega 11. With lots of voiceover that's not gotten repetitive after 18h of escape attempts. Where you can save in the middle of a run and go do something IRL. And sometimes available at a huge discount. 10 burning skulls out of 10.

[h3]A bit repetitive game...[/h3] Okay, jokes aside - this is one of the greatest roguelites I have played (sorry yeah, [spoiler]Balatro[/spoiler] exists and nothing can be better). I love how this game core idea, plot and story fuses so well with an actual gameplay. You die? That makes sense, because you are trying to escape from hell, so of course you'll start there. You get stronger? Of course, because gods are trying to help you. I am amazed by how natural it feels to play it, there are almost zero gaming conventions in this game. Every small thing makes total sense in this universe, and the game genre perfectly fits the story. [h3]But I don't like roguelikes![/h3] That's also an important point here. You see, what keeps me engaged is the meta-progression element. As you grow stronger, you are able to go further. This is what I like, this is not full-scale roguelike, there is a change. But after I have completed the attempt to escape, and after I have completed my progression, the game feels...just repetitive? I know that I won't be able to be stronger, but I am forced to do the same thing 9 more times on even higher difficulty, or using the weapon that I just don't like. This is the place when the game became truly "repetitive" for me. Progression done, so there is just some kind of late-game challenges left. And that feels rather tiring. Again, great game, just 22 hrs was enough to engage with the most fun parts. I'm not the guy who will spent 100+ hrs more, I'd rather explore something else entirely.

[u][b]-Quick Review-[/b][/u] Hades is a lesson in patience and persistence. It’s lining up the “Skill”, “Luck”, and “Experience” circles in a Venn diagram. If you’ve got more skill and luck, you’ll make progress faster. If you’ve got more luck and experience, you can compensate for skills or natural aptitude. And if you’ve got no luck, you can still grind your way to success with developing skills and getting experience playing the game (Best of all as you grind you’ll level up skills which literally improve you luck, so even an poor unlucky soul like me can get some of that luck-o-matic-magic). Hades is a Roguelite Action RPG developed by Super Giant Games and released in 2020; I’ve loved everything about Hades, from its music to its gameplay, to its voice acting, to its theming and art style, and I can easily recommend the game to pretty much anyone! I had been busy working on other games, and suddenly I noticed a good Sale for Hades, and I told my wife “Hey, this is a must buy game”. Then I promptly started streaming it on Twitch. While everyone is over there having fun playing Hades 2, I’m back here playing Hades 1 …and living my best life! [u][b]Review Video:[/b][/u] If you don't like reading, or are curious about watching gameplay check out my video here: https://youtu.be/s3fZnFaEHvw [u][b]-Detailed breakdown review-[/b][/u] [b]Story:[/b] The story just tosses you right in. You’re playing as Zagreus the son of Hades, as he attempts to escape the various layers of the underworld and make it to the surface. Zagreus will fight his way through Tartarus, Asphodel, Elysium, and the Temple of Styx. In all likelihood your first run will be unsuccessful… correction; it would be incredible and unbelievable to successfully escape on your first run with zero experience in the game. Expect to fail, expect to fail a lot. But after every run you’ll return to the Hall of Hades to get dialogue and exposition from the narrator and various colorful characters to fill in the background of who Zagreus is, and why he’s hellbent on getting to the surface. I intentionally want to avoid talking about specific story details because uncovering the story bit by bit is another extremely rewarding experience from your subsequent playthroughs. The important story detail to remember is this: even when I failed an attempt, I went back to the beginning and had new character interactions, new stuff to unlock, and a fresh run with a fresh change to try mixing different boons and upgrades together to see what kind of smorgasbord-soup I could cook up. Hades’ story kept my attention the whole time, sure it’s disappointing when I lose on a run that I was so certain I was going to succeed! But after a loss I’d just dust myself off and give it another try, again, and again. And the pay off after you successfully fight your way through the game to get to the end… was one of the most dopamine-rewarding experiences I’ve had in a long time. And then you restart from the beginning again! I needed to take a break after that first one because I wasn’t emotionally ready to do it all over again to get more story. But as a word of encouragement: remember Zagreus gets more and more upgrades to help make the successful escape attempts more and more likely. https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3582640942 [b]Gameplay:[/b] Hades is played from an isometric view and has some hack and slash inspired combat elements to it. You have a Primary attack which is your basic damage dealing move, A Secondary Attack called a “Cast” which is unique and changes with different god’s boons and is limited in how many “cast” points you have, each weapon also has a Special Attack which will change drastically based on the weapon, and lastly there’s also a Dash move to quickly side step attacks, jump through barriers, and you can also attack while dashing! My first experience playing Hades was clearing the first set of levels until promptly being destroyed by the first boss. Then went back to the Hall of Hades and spent my darkness to get permanent upgrades, unlocked new weapons with my keys, and then dived right back into it with another escape attempt… I continued to fight to get to back to that boss and dying to it several times until I got a good run where I beat the boss, then rinse and repeat on the next zone fighting my way out of the underworld until after 24 hours total gametime and roughly 35 attempts, I got my first successful escape! The underworld is said to be in constant flux, and chambers will move around so each time you play you’ll encounter different chambers from the last time you visited. You’ll find chambers which reward you darkness, coins, keys, god boons, skill levels, the Hammer Artifact which improves your weapon somehow, and more. You walk into a chamber, clear it of hostile NPC’s, pick up the reward, and move on to the next chamber (sometimes you also get a choice of which chamber you want to go to next, that’s how you make your “build”). As usual for this game, just when you get used to running from chamber to chamber, you’ll get a new upgrade and now you gotta look for the shiny gold vases. Just when I got comfortable with a boss the boss changes slightly and gets new attacks… Hades just keeps incrementally adding new stuff. It's truly amazing how well paced everything is! https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3620098581 [b]Conclusion:[/b] As I said at the start of this review: I can easily recommend Hades to pretty much anyone! Hades is one of the best games I’ve ever played. I’d absolutely put it on my top 10 list if I made top 10 lists. There hasn’t been any game Supergiant has put out that I haven’t loved, but Hades has blown me away, the story was engaging, the gameplay was compelling and enjoyable, I will be playing the music from the game for the rest of my life, and as bonus points Hades has extremely good replay value and lots of ways to add extra challenge to the game! If you haven’t played Hades yet, you should absolutely give it a shot. I'm confident you’ll agree with me on how great this game is.

Hades, the game not the mythos, but also the mythos, is an action-packed "god-like roguelike" that absolutely lives up to its own hype. It is a rich and fulfilling experience that will challenge you at every turn. Every moment, from your first run to your most recent is captured and documented for later review. Review your mind and muscles do. Every run, you get a bit better. Every death means something. Then, you have that run, that moment. that chance. I don't like roguelikes that much. I find them to be repetitive and often uninteresting. Progress can get stale, the gameplay loop can get a bit too rng dependent, and generally many roguelikes don't have super outstanding stories. Hades is different. After many, many recommendations and the purchase of a Steam Deck, I bought it and threw myself into the game. I found that the game was repetitive, in an interesting way. The lore and story tie death into it closely giving your losses meaning and your failures purpose. My progress was careful and calculated. Each death happened a bit further out, and runs weren't taking that long. I actively wanted to pursue the goal, because I simply had to surpass my previous record. I needed to clear that wall. Each boon made my runs different, unique, but always powerful. Very, very few of them were not beneficial to my success. And even in the end, my escape run had some throw aways. Hades is not my exception, nor is it my expectation for roguelikes I play going forward. It is simply the game that succeeded in capturing my interest with the genre. Simply put, Hades is fun. It is an absolutely exhilarating game that held my interest because I was truly enjoying my time with it. And I will continue to do so as there is more to do and see. There were tremendous highs and some devastating lows. Neither of which are in regards to game quality, just pure emotion felt while doing runs. Hades is beautifully made and the team behind it is truly one of a kind. My journey with Hades has been more than just with the game. I've grown to love Supergiant and their philosophy behind games. They have a tremendous amount of respect for their audience, the industry, the creative process, and themselves. They have earned my respect in a way that very few studios have. I am tremendously excited to play Hades 2 and fall deeper down the rabbit hole. Oh yeah that's right this is a game review/recommendation. uhhhhhh Hades is a remarkable roguelike experience. If you are a fan of roguelikes or beat em' up dungeon crawlers, then you will likely enjoy Hades. My top recommendation is to those who are entranced by the art and general style of the game. The music, designs, writing, and pure execution are all on a different level here. If you appreciate games as art, then you may come to adore Hades. The gameplay is really fun and the progression system really makes you feel like your efforts are rewarded properly. Absolutely try this one out if you're interested. It is likely going to enter into my top 10 games of all time.

TLDR: Well-made game with great art-style, soundtrack and smooth gameplay. I found the gameplay shallow and repetitive the more I played, however. Would recommend if goes on a large sale but probably not at full price. Hades has a great art-style, with really nice voice attacking. It feels smooth to play and has a main story. The 6 main weapons feel good to use and have a few different playstyles between them. But I feel bored of this game already. For me, the game felt too simple, with not much synergy in builds. As others have pointed out, most boons (the buffs you get each run), mostly just give either flat +damage or damage multipliers. Although you can stack these, different God boons will replace each other, so I can't stack interesting passives together it feels. There are some cool unique things like Calls which can rarely rely on multiple Gods, but besides this it feels like each playthrough is just finding either a flat damage or percentage damage boon and upgrading it as much as you can (depending on your choice of weapon). I think the game was easy to beat for the first time, and completing it on more heat feels tedious (although I will most likely try to beat on 32 heat due to a deal with a friend). Although the story was at times interesting, it felt tedious going back and forth to learn more each time, with many deaths required for each individual NPC (of which there are many) to get items to progress story. It has gotten to the point where I no longer really care about any of the characters, and am just rushing to start each run. Throughout the game there are many permanent upgrades (hence rogue-lite) which improve your odds of beating the game. They mainly permanently increase rarity or give you more revives upon death, nothing crazy. They cost a unique currency which you earn in your runs which you spend when you die. Overall I have no problems with this system, besides the fact that it is extremely cheap. I never once prioritised this currency over something else in my run and would instantly max it out each time I was able to. Some of the upgrades (such as the revive) felt very strong, but are worth more currency so I believe this is fair. While I am lacking a lot of the keepsakes (a unique item you equip for your run, although you can change it after a major boss), they do not feel very impactful and won't change the gameplay much. They mainly serve to affect RNG in a particular direction from my experience. I have no problem with this either, but combined these facts make the gameplay feel repetitive, but not in the way that I have liked in other games like Dead Cells. I really wish there was a "meh" rating on steam, it feels weird to leave a positive or negative review for this as I think there are many good qualities, I just found the game boring quickly. I think there are other games in the genre which would be better to play first, but if you have already played them then I would maybe recommend this game.

Hades is nothing short of a masterpiece, a game that redefines what a roguelike can be by seamlessly blending relentless action, profound storytelling, and emotional depth. From the very first run, the game hooks you with its fluid, twitch-based combat, where every weapon—be it the spear, bow, or colossal fists—feels distinct and satisfying to wield. But what truly sets Hades apart is its unparalleled narrative integration: each death isn’t a setback, but a step forward in a rich, evolving story. The characters—Zagreus, his family, and the gods of Olympus—are vividly written, voiced with charisma, and grow with you through countless runs. The art direction is stunning, the soundtrack is legendary, and the randomly generated dungeons ensure no two runs feel the same. With deep progression systems, meaningful relationships to build with gods and underworld figures, and a world that feels alive and reactive, Hades turns repetition into a joy. It’s a game that rewards patience, strategy, and curiosity—perfect for both newcomers and veterans. Whether you're chasing a perfect run or simply savoring the next piece of lore, Hades delivers an experience that’s as emotionally resonant as it is thrilling. At its core, it’s not just a game—it’s a must-play triumph of design, heart, and innovation.

I'm not a roguelike/lite fan, Dead Cells, Binding of Isaac, Windsblown, etc... never stuck with me. That is until I have played this game. It certainly lived up to the hype, even captivating a non-fan like me. I got my first successful escape attempt at the 14th run. After numerous close calls with [REDACTED], with me over-exerting, dying when the boss's health only having a sliver of it left, I finally had my first successful run. Now usually with other roguelike games, I put down the games after one singular successful run, done deal. Not with this game, no. What kept me coming back was the absolutely phenomenal story, characters' writing and execution. The voice acting and direction are absolute top-notch, Zagreus has me completely charmed by his niceness and politeness to everyone he meets, and straight to-the-point personality. Furthermore, the gods' distinctive interactions with each other and personalities are also very interesting to observe. Onto the gameplay, at first glance you might think the game encourages fast-paced, high octane gameplay. However, keeping yourself collected, and keeping things at your own pace is a much better way of doing things, learning enemies' patterns, kiting them around the stage while making use of all your abilities you accumulated in an efficient manner. The variety of builds that you can do is abundant, and the game does not overwhelm you with said mechanics all in one go. The game introduces them one by one as you play and die, so it feels natural to progress the game without feeling bloated or blasted by walls of texts. Additionally, another reason why I might like this game is because the encounters or rooms were hand-crafted, not procedurally-generated. Only the orders of the encounters are randomized and you never know what type of encounters that you will get. There is another similarly designed roguelike game called Mosa Lina, which is also one of my favorite games of all time. All in all, if this game can convince someone like me to repeatedly play a roguelike, it's a really good game in my book, a masterpiece even. As of this review, when I first finished my run yesterday, I went on to finish 4 more successful runs with different weapons each time and 2 more successful runs today. There is an incentive for me to come back for just one more run, but I won't spoil it. *wink* Go buy this game, support these developers, they absolutely deserve your hard-earned money.

By the time you are at the Champion fight you will notice that you start getting hit more and more for reasons that just did not occur on the lower floors. If you pay attention you may even find that one attack from a hostile will actually damage you multiple times in the same frame, resulting in a mass loss of hp. It starts to become incredibly frustrating trying to iron out the post campaign quests and loop through the pact for all of the above reasons and so I cannot recommend this game. After more play, there is DEFINITE input lag on the hades fight, it is bad enough that again. The choreographed spear lunges hit regardless of whether you dodge before or after cue, I have been monster hit three different times by a single move for a total of 120+ hp, and Aegis does not track to the mouse well. Clearing any difficulty over pact 5 becomes a mess and dont even get me started on how the gameplay suffers adding even more mobs to rooms. Still do not reccommend. Be PREPARED for the game to make you dodge the complete WRONG direction despite you only holding one input key. Be PREPARED for it to move you exactly into the move you were trying to avoid. Like Magic card drafting (I can just imagine the developers sitting down with an enormous white board and figuring out the thousands of synergies possible - it's insane how well it all works together), it's amazing the types of combos you can naturally come up with on the fly in this action roguelike. Sure, you could try to plan for certain combinations, and that becomes more likely/possible the more permanent upgrades you get (like the ones that permanently increase your likelihood of getting rare upgrades), but there is still an element of random chance that can derail your "deck", but this random chance also pushes/encourages you to try out boons (an upgrade you get each time you complete a room) you may not have otherwise tried for your build. This feeds into an incredibly satisfying gameplay/feedback loop of discovering new play styles you may never have even considered. I thought the weapons that were essentially boxing gloves were the dumbest weapons and saved them for last to beat the game with, but after I unlocked the "Aspect of Zeus" which allowed me to generate a magnetic pull whenever i used an uppercut (effectively drawing enemies directly into my fists) and then stacking various attack multiplier's on top of that, I absolutely blazed through my run, beating my previous best time by 10 minutes (for comparison, on average a successful run lasts about 35 minutes) Finished playing this years ago but felt compelled to post my review after finding it scrawled down in an old word doc lol.

Basically takes the strengths from Supergiants' previous games and puts it into a fun roguelike. It's a little hard to explain but it just feels snappy and good to control. Each of the weapons feel distinct from each other and combined with all the upgrades and boons and you have a lot of room for experimentation and build variety. I was ready to move on by the time I got to the credits. The first reason is because of the way the main story wrapped up itself neatly enough; to where I was fine not seeing anything extra. Secondly, I was just getting burned out of doing runs in general. Just not quite enough variety there for my tastes and the game can be quite the grind for all the resources you'll want. Obviously, I don't regret my time with the game. From the story, characters, music, art style, there's a lot to love here. I'm definitely in the minority of people who don't quite love this game as much as most people seem to. I definitely got my money's worth either way.

Recommended Hades is one of the best roguelikes/roguelites ever made (call it whatever you want, it’s the one that makes everyone else look lazy). The pacing and progression are basically perfect: every run feels meaningful, failures still push you forward, and the game has that rare “one more run” energy that turns into “wait, why is it 3AM?”. The setting and tone are fantastic, stylish, sharp, and genuinely funny. Greek mythology has never felt this alive… or this willing to roast you after you die for the 47th time. The real magic is how varied the gameplay stays. With the amount of weapons and aspects, runs don’t blur together, you’re constantly experimenting, adapting, and discovering new combos. It’s a roguelike that actually respects your time and your brain. If I had to nitpick, I’d say some Olympian boons could be better balanced or more consistently exciting, a few picks feel clearly stronger or more “auto-take” than others. But that’s a small complaint in a game that’s basically a masterclass in design. And the music… the music is divine. Not “good for a game” good, just straight-up great. Every track hits, and the vibe is so strong it feels like the soundtrack is carrying you out of the Underworld by sheer willpower. Hades isn’t just excellent. It’s the game other roguelikes should study before they’re allowed to leave the house. Pros Perfect pacing + meta progression Huge variety thanks to weapons/aspects Fantastic writing, humor, and worldbuilding God-tier soundtrack Cons Some boons could be tuned/balanced better

(Ignore my hour count, I played mostly on PS4) Hades is a roguelike that handles its narrative in a unique way. It's full of characters both in your home base and in the levels themselves that will talk to you once per run, with dialogue that comments on new things you've accomplished or unlocked. It also has a story that progresses over time, though it's less about raw plot and more about knowing the world and characters. The real selling point is the sheer amount of voiced dialogue. It's actually ridiculous. You will be hearing new voiced lines from like 20 different characters every run, up to like a hundred hours.

An absolute masterclass in both narrative story telling and the roguelike genre. Now all of that being said, buy it anyway. ♥♥♥♥♥♥ at combat? Buy it anyway. Don't usually enjoy roguelikes? Buy it anyway. Not interested in mythology? Buy it anyway. This game is such a seamless experience that grows along side you. I cannot imagine how much work went into ensuring that regardless of skill, speed, or interest, Hades is still a complete, satisfying experience for anyone who touches it. You can absolutely feel the love and care that went into this game, and I highly encourage anyone reading this to set aside their previous notions of what constitutes a game that is "up your alley", and try Hades anyway.

Hades tackles the rogue-like genre with astonishing grace - motivating players to complete all of it's 80 hours of content with enthusiasm. I recently returned to the game after putting it down around release. Happy to say, the second go around was even more rewarding. Once you master the loop, and choose a favorite weapon, gameplay narrows a bit - but the exploration feels good up to that point. The achievements felt like a natural extension of the core game elements. Some of the more challenging rewards are locked behind Cthonic companions, and big swings of RNG. I was able to reach 100% after 85 runs on the dot. A sequel is now available, which I will play in due time. Curious to see how another 80 hours of this style of gameplay could really expand on the formula. Action: 8/10 Style: 7/10 Achievements: 8/10

[h1]Ελληνική Αξιολόγηση / English Review Below[/h1] [i]This review is bilingual. Scroll down for the English version.[/i] [h2]ΕΛΛΗΝΙΚΑ[/h2] [b]Recommended[/b] Θετική [b]Περίληψη:[/b] Το Hades είναι ένας εξαιρετικός τίτλος που καταφέρνει να συνδυάσει την αισθητική με το ουσιαστικό βάθος στο gameplay. Είναι το πρώτο παιχνίδι του είδους roguelike που κατάφερε πραγματικά να με κερδίσει. [b]Αισθητική και Παρουσίαση:[/b] - Η τέχνη του παιχνιδιού είναι τέλεια, με πανέμορφα "cartoon" γραφικά που υποστηρίζουν μια εξαιρετική αισθητική. - Η απόδοση της ελληνικής μυθολογίας είναι άψογη, εμπλουτισμένη με ωραίο χιούμορ. - Η δουλειά που έχει γίνει στις φωνές (voice acting) και στη μουσική είναι κορυφαίου επιπέδου. [b]Gameplay και Μηχανισμοί:[/b] Το gameplay είναι πολύ ευχάριστο. Ένα από τα μεγαλύτερα πλεονεκτήματα του παιχνιδιού είναι ότι δεν απαιτεί από τον παίκτη να μάθει απέξω άπειρους συνδυασμούς κουμπιών για να αυξήσει το damage του. Αυτό σου δίνει την ελευθερία να γίνεσαι καλύτερος οργανικά, χωρίς το παιχνίδι να σε αναγκάζει σε στείρα αποστήθιση combos, κάτι το οποίο με απωθεί από άλλα αντίστοιχα παιχνίδια. [b]Το αρνητικό:[/b] Το μοναδικό μελανό σημείο είναι ότι στην αρχή το παιχνίδι δεν εξηγεί ξεκάθαρα τη λειτουργία των διαφόρων currencies (νομισμάτων/πόρων). Χρειάζεται χρόνος για να καταλάβεις τι ακριβώς να περιμένεις από το κάθε είδος currency που συλλέγεις. --- [h2]ENGLISH[/h2] [b]Recommended:[/b] [b]Summary:[/b] Hades is a masterpiece of art and design, and notably the first roguelike title that has ever truly won me over. [b]Art and Aesthetics:[/b] - The art style is perfect, featuring beautiful cartoon-style graphics and a fantastic overall aesthetic. - The depiction of Greek mythology is wonderful and cleverly infused with great humor. - Both the voice acting and the musical score are of exceptional quality. [b]Gameplay Mechanics:[/b] The gameplay experience is highly rewarding. A major positive is that it doesn't rely on infinite button combinations to scale your damage. You don't feel forced to memorize complex sequences just to improve, which makes the progression feel much more natural, less tedious and which has kept me off similar titles in the past. [b]The Flaw:[/b] If there is one negative, it is that the game fails to clearly explain the various currencies at the start. It isn't immediately obvious how each one functions or what kind of rewards/utility to expect from them during the early stages of the game. [b]Verdict:[/b] An accessible and stylish roguelike that respects the player's time.

🕹️ Hades | ⭐ Highly Recommended | ⏱ ~50h played === TL;DR === 🧠 A roguelite action-RPG masterpiece with fast, fluid combat, endless build variety, and a story that unfolds across multiple runs — death is fun, progression is rewarding, and every attempt feels fresh. === What this game is === 📖 Hades casts you as Zagreus, son of Hades, attempting to escape the Underworld. Each run pits you against randomized rooms, traps, monsters, and bosses while you collect upgrades, god-given boons, and permanent meta-progression. The narrative and relationships with gods and Underworld denizens grow with every death, making failure feel meaningful. If you like challenging, replayable action-RPGs with story depth and rich character interactions, this is a must-play. === Gameplay === 🎮 Core loop: fight → collect upgrades/boons → die → improve Zagreus → repeat. Combat is tight, precise, and highly customizable. Choose from six weapons, dozens of god boons, and hundreds of upgrade combinations. Player freedom is high: weapon choice, boons, upgrades, and dungeon paths all matter. Randomized rooms and events ensure each run feels new, while meta-progression ensures even failure advances your progress. === What it does well === ✨ Combat: Fast, responsive, versatile; synergies between weapons and boons feel powerful and rewarding. 🎶 Soundtrack: Darren Korb delivers one of the best video game soundtracks of the decade. 🧩 Progression & replayability: Meta-upgrades, keepsakes, and god boons make each run feel meaningful. 👥 Story & characters: Funny, heartfelt, and revealed gradually. Voice acting and dialogue bring the Underworld to life. 🎨 Presentation: Smooth framerate, vibrant art, and detailed animations enhance every fight. === Where it falls short === ⚠ Some repetition in rooms and bosses, inevitable in a roguelite. ⚠ Story delivery mostly via portraits and text rather than cinematic sequences. === Replayability === 🔁 Extremely high — randomized layouts, builds, god boons, and evolving story fragments make every run unique. === Who should play === ✅ Fans of roguelites and action-RPGs ✅ Players who enjoy mastering combat systems and builds ✅ Anyone who appreciates deep character interactions and narrative 🚫 Players who dislike dying repeatedly 🚫 Players seeking purely linear, story-first experiences === Technical & value === 🛠 Performance: Smooth and stable on all tested hardware 🎮 Controls/UI: Excellent with both controller and keyboard/mouse 💰 Length: ~20–30h for main story; 50+h for full progression/endgame ✅ Value: Exceptional — a masterpiece worth every penny === Final verdict === 🏁 Hades is a masterclass in combat, progression, and narrative design. Every run is exciting, every death teaches, and every discovery feels rewarding. One of the best action-RPGs and roguelites ever made — failure has never been this fun.

If you need a break from your dad, you will probably find it easier than Zagreus, who battles through a parade of numbskulls, gorgons, soul catchers, and more, with endless reinforcements sent his way in his hellish quest to escape the Underworld. Hades turns this premise into one of the most satisfying gameplay loops ever made. Combat is fast, precise, and constantly reshaped by the Olympian gods, who function like a deeply dysfunctional support network. They intervene with lightning, hangovers, and, on rare occasions, better fishing odds. The experience is dangerously good at convincing you that you are improving. Death is not failure here, but rather it is how the story talks back. Every return to the House of Hades unlocks new dialogue, new character beats, and fresh commentary on your increasingly complicated family situation. The writing is sharp, and the music makes every bad decision feel truly heroic. Hades does not ask you to win. It asks you to try again, slightly wiser, slightly stronger, and absolutely convinced this time will be different.

It is currently January 15th, 2026. I have had Hades in my library since January 5th, 2026. I currently have 53.5 hours on record. Actual review: Yeah it's great. You probably didn't need me to tell you that. [list] [*]The dialogue and story are masterful. The characters feel alive—as much as that word applies to some. They react to seemingly the player's every move. Even generic lines are numerous enough that you likely won't see one repeated for a while. [*]The voice acting is stellar, contributing just as much to the life of the characters as the dialogue itself. [*]Runs are just long enough to be satisfying, and just short enough to create the "one more run..." feeling that makes roguelikes/lites so addictive. [*]Meta-progression is impactful, but doesn't trivialize the game. Especially as someone new-ish to dungeon crawlers like this, I found that the pace of upgrades was just enough to still demand skill development from me, while also easing the difficulty of progression as I went. [*]Bouldy is in it. Can't get that awesome Bouldy belief anywhere else. [/list] In conclusion, if someone is somehow still on the fence about this game, pick it up.

Graphics and artstyle good. Voice acting superb. But gameplay is the pain in the ass. First two worlds is alright, Traps and magma are super annoying, but a couple of playthrough then it is not a problem. The only few encounters are super annoying are foom full of wretches with multi spread shot in Tartarus and Asphodel, which is literally bullet hell. Everything is fine then suddenly they throw you in a tiny room possible with enemies constantly fire shot that spread out everywhere. It is even annoying than the big brimstone which actually really slow and easier to deal with. Asphodel, the worst encounter beside the full wretches room is the falling boulder + medusa shooting at you. It is not really harder than the other encounter, it's just that you have to move a lot otherwise you will be stoned and the boulder just fall on top of you. The other one you can just throw cast or special in between dash, but this one is really bored because you move more than you attack. Now the final one to talk about is Elysium. Not Styx, because i rather fight in this area than the previous. The poison is super annoying yes but if you have tons of damage which most likely you do then it is super fast. You just gonna have to minimize damage taken. Elysium on the other hand is a borefest. Not because it is uninteresting, but the all the enemies are basically just a huge sponge. Armor, resurrection, it takes super long to kill. You deal zero damage to them, they have ton of dashes, almost instant attack animation, deal crap ton of damage with a single swipe. Their lances are tiny but somehow have triple and quadruple range compare to the weapon length. Same thing with swipe attack radius. Instead of dodge your range attack with left and right or some pattern, they just randomly move around. And when they lock on to you, they sudden dash 0 to 100 at you. Same thing the boss. It basically is a spongefest. The minotaur is whatever, it just soak up whatever damage you have, pretty predictable attack pattern. But the fight is super long when you fight two sponge at one, so you bound to get hit at some points, it just the matter of minimize damage taken. The spear throwing guy, i don't even bother to remember his name. Super punchable face with that smirk, don't know his actual lore probably an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the same with his ingame character. Gamplay wise, ♥♥♥♥ this guy. Immune to front damage, if you get close, immediately swipe and sometime charge at you. Elysium, least favorite world. Hades is actually more tolerable than the other two. Has two phase sure, summon minion sure, annoying damage ring and deadly laser, yes. But at least he leaves you some breathing room, some preparation time between attack. The bull bros just charge at you constantly. Now for the gameplay progression. I think encounters feels imbalance. Some room you just slide through no problem, some suddenly spike up and it's not even a mini boss. It just some room layout is really bad for you with certain enemy. Lastly, i don't like the meta progression in this game. It is build upon an idea that if you die enough time and collect enough power up and resources, you eventually beat the game. I don't like this as the core design. Other games, even though they some what have this where subsequent runs will be easier, but you can win without those. Hades feels very dependent on the upgrades and new weapon unlock. It is very much built in the game. Much of the room reward are not boon but stuffs used after the run over to upgrade next run. It is like the game telling if you die enough, you eventually get there. These should be collect only after the run over, and based on your performance on the run or some quest, objective, things like that, instead of be given as room reward. Which provide no benefits to the current run. As for the build, i never feel like i had a crazy run or some really good that even if you lost, you have a good time, maybe i've done some or everything wrong. But every run feels like only slight different from the others. Compared to other like The Binding of Issac, Slay the Spire, to name a few, i sometime have worst run and best run ever, feel very refreshing. Beating a run in this game is like, thanks god it is over. Not looking forward to do another

Hades caught me faster than I would have liked. The gameplay feels really good, everything is smooth, direct and has that dangerous ‘just one more run’ effect. Before you know it, three hours have gone by and you briefly wonder what you were actually planning to do with your life. What really surprised me was the story. I didn't expect it to be so good in this genre and to really keep you hooked. The dialogue and characters give the game a lot of personality and make you want to keep going even after you die. Added to this is the great variety. There are several weapons, all of which play differently, and the many possible combinations mean that no two runs feel the same. With the different builds, the game stays fresh and motivates you to keep trying again and again. The bottom line is that Hades does a lot of things right. It feels high-quality throughout, makes good use of its genre and manages to neatly combine gameplay, story and variety. Highly recommended.

Hades: Exceptionally Polished, But One Clear Was Enough (For Me) Recommended? Yes, but with clear caveats. Hades is the first roguelike that I have properly played through and completed. After finishing it, I completely understand why it is so highly regarded. The art direction is strong, the combat is demanding, and the overall system design is deep and cohesive. That said, I also came to a clear personal conclusion: for me, Hades is a game that only needed to be completed once. This is not a criticism of its quality, but rather a reflection of how well (or not) its core structure aligns with my own gaming preferences. 1. Presentation & Platform Fit One of Hades’ biggest strengths is how well it fits handheld play. I bought the game a long time ago but never started it. With Hades II releasing and receiving similar praise, and with a Steam Deck in hand, this felt like the right moment to finally play it. That decision paid off. The 2D visuals look excellent on a handheld screen, performance is stable, and there’s no reliance on large displays or heavy graphical detail. It’s easy to pick up and play a run anytime. Visually and technically, Hades is almost ideal for the Steam Deck. The overall feel reminded me of Diablo II from my childhood, but with far greater emphasis on timing, positioning, and mechanical execution. This is not a mindless hack-and-slash — it demands attention and skill. 2. Gameplay Systems & Combat Mechanically, Hades is very well designed. Each weapon has multiple upgrade paths, Olympian boons allow for a wide range of builds, and enemies require different approaches. Every run forces you to commit to a playstyle and adapt as the build evolves. My first successful escape took 30 attempts. The build that carried me through focused on area damage and armor breaking: rapid-fire attacks upgraded into armor-piercing shotgun bursts, grenade-style AOE damage, Dionysus-enhanced cast attacks for shield control and damage-over-time, and Hermes boons providing speed and defensive buffs after dashing. When all these systems finally clicked together and I defeated Hades, the sense of achievement was absolutely real. There is no question that the game rewards mastery and understanding of its systems. 3. Characters, Writing & Tone The character and art design are standout elements. Despite being fully 2D, both the Olympian gods and the Underworld cast have strong visual identities and clear personalities. Voice acting across the board is solid. However, I personally struggled with the tone of the protagonist, Zagreus. His relaxed, playful, almost modern delivery often felt like a contemporary person role-playing a mythological figure. Since the story ultimately revolves around family reconciliation and emotional closure, I would have preferred a more serious, fatalistic tone, something closer to games like Darksiders, which would have made it easier for me to emotionally invest. This is subjective, but it significantly shaped my experience. 4. World Structure & Narrative Design One element I genuinely appreciated was the game’s inverted progression. Instead of starting in the human world and descending into the Underworld, Hades begins in the realm of the dead and pushes upward. You fight through the depths, pass through fire-filled regions and arenas, confront Hades himself, and finally reach the surface world to reunite with Persephone. Zagreus seeing sunlight for the first time is a memorable moment. Conceptually, it’s interesting that many figures who would normally be framed as ultimate villains are instead familiar faces, colleagues, or reluctant allies. Nearly every character, from the Olympians to Thanatos, Skelly, Chaos, and Charon, helps Zagreus in some way, even when it initially feels like opposition. The gift system reinforces this interconnected world and works well thematically. 5. Where It Ultimately Lost Me Despite all of this polish, Hades cannot escape the fundamental nature of the roguelike structure: heavy repetition and extensive reuse of content. Roguelikes rely on randomness, unlocks, and gradual narrative layering to justify repetition. While Hades executes this formula extremely well, it does not change the fact that each escape attempt feels broadly similar at its core. In other genres, repeated reuse of content would likely be criticized; in roguelikes, it is accepted as part of the design philosophy. For me, that repetition became the limiting factor. Although new dialogue and story fragments unlock over time, I was not particularly invested in consuming them, and the text-heavy presentation is not the type of immersive storytelling I personally enjoy. My preferences lean toward exploration, cinematic presentation, and strong role-playing elements, games like Cyberpunk 2077, Red Dead Redemption, or Fallout. Hades does not aim to provide that kind of experience, and that’s fine. I don’t oppose grinding as a concept, but I believe grinding needs context. In multiplayer games, repetition is paired with human interaction, unpredictability, and competition. In single-player games, repeatedly running the same structure holds far less appeal for me. After one successful escape, I felt I had experienced most of what Hades wanted to offer. 6. Final Thoughts Hades is a high-quality game with a very clearly defined target audience. If you enjoy 2D comic-style visuals, deep roguelike systems, and mastering mechanics through repeated runs, this could easily be a 10/10 experience. For me, however, its internal structure does not align with how I enjoy games. I’m glad I played it, and I respect its craftsmanship, but I don’t feel compelled to keep escaping over and over again. Score: 8/10

Hades is the rare masterpiece that takes the "roguelike" genre—notoriously known for being a cycle of brutal failure and frustration—and turns it into a warm, addictive family drama about a son who just wants to visit his mom. You play as Zagreus, the Prince of the Underworld, who is desperately trying to claw his way out of hell. Every time you die, you aren't just "resetting"; you’re being spat back into the House of Hades to gossip with your step-mom Nyx, pet your three-headed dog Cerberus, and get snidely roasted by your dad, the God of the Dead himself. The combat is an isometric ballet of pure, kinetic energy. You start each run with one of six legendary weapons—like a shield that would make Captain America jealous or a spear that feels like a lightning bolt—and as you move through the rooms, your Olympian aunts and uncles (Zeus, Athena, Poseidon, etc.) offer you "Boons." These upgrades stack in ridiculous ways, turning your simple dash into a tidal wave or your arrows into homing drunk-missiles. I found that the "God Mode" setting is a stroke of genius—it grants you a small permanent resistance to damage every time you die, ensuring that even if you aren't a pro-gamer, you can eventually see the end of this incredible story without the gameplay becoming a brick wall. What truly elevates Hades above its peers is the writing. There are thousands of lines of unique dialogue; characters remember how you died, what weapons you were using, and even who you’re currently flirting with. It’s a "dating sim" buried inside a high-octane dungeon crawler. The art style is a vibrant, painterly tribute to Greek mythology, and the soundtrack is a heavy-metal-meets-lyre-plucking banger that makes every boss fight feel like a legendary event. It’s the kind of game where "just one more run" isn't a suggestion—it’s an inevitability because you genuinely care about whether or not Orpheus and Eurydice ever get back together. 10/10. It is a flawless blend of narrative and mechanics. It’s the only game where dying feels like a reward because it means you finally get to go home and see your friends again. Grab a boon, pet the dog, and tell your father you're moving out—one floor at a time.

If you’re hesitating on this one, stop overthinking it and just buy it. I normally bounce off roguelike games pretty fast, but Hades somehow kept pulling me back in. Pretty hard, which is fine. Took about 16 hours to actually finish a run, mostly because I forgot to buy more revivals for runs. If you like completely random roguelites, this one's for you. Can't recommend for one reason though: no rerolls. The game has 9 "gods" that give out boons, which are basically ability upgrades/modifications. The way these gods come to you is completely random. The boons they give is completely random. There are a total of 157 boons in this game, which means that there's no way to "make" a build during a run, the only way is to stumble upon one. That combined with some mechanics (mainly deflect) being stupidly OP makes the game feel too RNG. Dying is obviously fine, and a big part of why I love roguelikes and -lites, but most runs here feel like there's no chance of going all the way even if you know what you're aiming for. The art and gameplay are fantastic otherwise. Dialogue is fine, even if 50% if it ended up being "my mom, my dad, your mom, your dad" in different words.

In a gaming landscape where many players struggle to finish their games, Hades stands as an absolute exception. Where so many titles — even great ones — end up abandoned due to lack of time or interest, this game manages to captivate relentlessly, to the point of being devoured with passion and left behind with genuine regret. At its core is a fast-paced action roguelike built around quick runs through four procedurally generated zones. Each attempt blends weapons, aspects, upgrades, difficulty modifiers, and especially divine boons, creating a staggering variety of builds. With 6 weapons and their 4 aspects, dozens of godly powers, keepsakes, passive upgrades, and companions, the possibilities feel nearly endless. Despite a limited pool of enemies and environments, no two runs ever feel the same. Combat is smooth, readable, and explosive, with every hit delivering immediate satisfaction. The dash mechanic is perfectly tuned, allowing you to stay in control even in the middle of chaos. Visually, the game is vibrant and clean, driven by superb animations and a striking art direction. The music and voice acting further elevate the immersion. What truly sets Hades apart, however, is its exceptional storytelling, seamlessly woven into the gameplay. The cycle of death and resurrection is fully justified within the narrative, turning every failure into meaningful progression. Characters are aware of the protagonist’s immortality, reacting to your attempts and commenting on your progress. The dialogue pool is massive, varied, and rarely repeats — even after dozens of hours. The world feels cohesive, alive, and deeply engaging, with each return home bringing new scenes, conversations, and discoveries. The result is a polished, generous, and incredibly addictive experience. Whether you enjoy melee, ranged combat, experimentation, or narrative depth, Hades always has something to offer. Many consider it one of the best roguelikes ever made — if not one of the finest single-player games of recent years. 🎯 Summary Hades isn’t just a great game — it’s a standout work that redefines its genre, teaches mythology while entertaining, and manages to be accessible, deep, elegant, and immensely fun all at once. An absolute must-have.

This game has one of the best combinations of story and gameplay I have ever seen. The act of trying to escape the underworld while repeatedly failing miserably results in a feeling that you really are in sync with Zagreus as the player. The sheer amount of dialog paired with inventive gameplay and mechanics make this game feel larger in scope than most modern AAA titles, which is a feat considering how limited the actual gameplay loop is. The character performances and overall story are wonderful, packed with many surprises. I do have some mild criticism, though take it with a shaker of salt as these are more personal gripes than anything objective. For starters, this game is exhausting. The progression can be glacial (especially if you are an untalented gamer like me) and the game is far too stingy with loot. This wouldn't be too bad if loot was not tied so closely to progression. Thankfully, I found some mods that alleviated this issue, greatly enhancing my enjoyment and made me feel the game respected my time more. On another note, the main quest is phenomenal but the side quests could have used more time in the oven. It takes too much back and forth at a miserable pace to build character relationships or satisfy vague requirements to unlock something. Also, this really is just personal tastes but I would liked the romances to be a bit more, well, romantic. They kind of just lead to the characters understanding each other a little better and then proceeding to get freaky. I would have preferred maybe something a bit sweeter and more vanilla romance wise, but I realize that might be an unreasonable request for a rouge-like set in the underworld. This game has kind of drained me, but in the best way possible. It will probably be quite awhile before I attempt the game's sequel, but I know I will enjoy it when I get there. I generally recommend this game to most people who have played games for awhile, though for very casual players this may be daunting. To those who love difficult games or rouge likes, this is a must play.
