Intro/Context: Just beat Hades for the first time. I've tried other roguelikes before but wanted to try the most popular one after building my confidence. I did a playthrough of Hades sometime in 2025, but wasn't having fun with any roguelikes and not taking the time to actually learn them. Thought I'd give it a proper go in 2026 since getting my Deck and I want to see how it'd look on an OLED. Also got this game on sale during the Winter Sale in 2025, and it goes on sale a lot so worth waiting for. Good: - Even though game is 5 years old, graphics hold up really well and look good on the Deck OLED - They just throw you in the game and get you to explore, but it's not difficult to understand the controls - Themes with lore is cool and well written for the Greek Mythology - Ran well on my Steam Deck and can run on low settings with no affect to performance (can go as low as 7-8 TDP and I was using the Steam Deck Vulkan version as suggested by the developers but DirectX version still worked with no issues for me) - Once you get the ball rolling with upgrades, skills etc... then it gets easier so don't be disheartened like me - Lot's of replayability for speed runners, completionists, and everyone - Literally a weapon selection for every playstyle - Even after you beat the final boss there's more lore that gives you reason to play to discover and get endgame content - Side characters/gods have cool designs and voice acting in this game is strong - You're incentivised well throughout the game for upgrades, improving - Minibosses were challenging and has a learning curve that felt rewarding to learn - Enemies had good variety and felt balanced - Combos you can build out are so broad so you'll truly never have the same run and you can build so many cool builds Bad: - Nothing really (seems like they've thought through everything) - Might be very critical for me but I do think some of the areas were quite small and could do with just a little bit of room (but most room designs were still well designed and this is not the case for all rooms though) Final/Conclusion: This is a great game to see if you'd like Roguelike's, is easy to get into and is worth the buy if you're debating whether or not to get Hades 2 (which I will be doing now). Time honestly went by so much and the game IS beatable and just needs a little bit of strategy to it. I feel more confident in exploring other roguelikes now and have found another fun genre for me to explore. Shoutout to Supergiant Games for making a great game! Score: 9.75/10

This game is absolutely incredible. I got it at a deep discount, but having played it I can confidently say it's worth full price if you can afford it. I had only very limited and basic knowledge of Greek mythology going in (courtesy of a month-long phase in elementary school) but it was not a detriment. The game presents it's world in a way that is enjoyable to play regardless of how much background knowledge you already have on the topic. The gameplay itself is great. I played on Steam Deck, and my biggest complaint was battery life (which is much improved in Hades II, I've found!) The controls are intuitive and easy to learn. I was hesitant to play the game for years because real-time combat tends to be an issue for me—I lack coordination skills and usually end up pressing random buttons until I die or fail when there are time-based game mechanics like fast-paced combat. But in Hades, pressing random buttons until you die—or win—is a part of the experience. The game also doesn't penalize you in any way for using God Mode, which isn't as overpowered as it sounds, and in fact I got extra dialogue when I turned it on! I actually was able to play the game for about an hour before deciding to use God Mode (a damage reduction buff that increases slightly every time you die) and it really didn't make much of a difference at first. It DID make the game more enjoyable, and I suspect I would have gotten frustrated at some points had I not turned it on. For me with my coordination, God Mode took the game from "punishingly hard" to "challenging but still fun", and I suspect for people more seasoned with this type of game, it might take the challenge away for them. But I greatly appreciate it's inclusion as an accessibility option. The meta-progression in this game is especially good. Before playing, I'd been looking for a satisfying progression experience in a game for a few months, but nothing I played really scratched that itch until Hades. I especially liked unlocking all the Infernal Arms and trying out the different weapons. I eventually settled on the spear as my main weapon, and had a ton of fun fine-tuning the build with it in each run. There's just enough randomness—and ways to influence that randomness—that even when /trying/ to get the same build each time, things were still fresh and interesting each run. The main story of the game was really good too, and I love the idea of a story-driven rouguelite so much, and I'm very glad it works so well. Overall, this game is a 9.5/10. Points off for only being able to play for a couple hours at a time on Steam Deck instead of doing runs until my eyes fall out, as I wanted to every time I had to put the game down to charge the Deck. And finally, just a note: the voice acting in this game is PHENOMENAL. I'm not usually a big fan of voice acting in games because it doesn't tend to be great and can break my immersion. But this game is like playing an action anime with an ancient Greek setting, and I don't even like anime. It's that good. If you made it this far, one last thing. Megaera is the best character in this game and I will accept no arguments. I love her and I love this game, and I can't wait to finish the sequel so I can leave a review on that one too <3

I tried this game because I love Greek mythology and rogue-likes. It delivered on both fronts and more! The characters all have unique and vibrant personalities, and the amount of funny dialogue between Zagreus and the other characters (including the narrator) always made me chuckle. The gameplay loop has yet to be boring for me. I've "beaten" the game (murdered a certain relative) thrice, and still want to play, if not for the gameplay, for the characters and story. I wasn't expecting a game about the layers of hell in Greek mythology where you play as the prince of the underworld to be very lighthearted and funny, while still having major emotional impacts land. Zagreus is a delightful protagonist, and is quippy without being annoying and undermining the severity of the situation. All of the lore is revealed in a way that is easy to grasp and remember. I love how all the Boons can have different effects depending on which ones you already have and how they interact with your weapon upgrades. The trinkets that you get from the first heart with each character essentially allow for quests or goals you can complete along the way, allowing for easy buildcrafting. My favorite thing to do is using a weapon that seems like it would fit a particular god, then using their trinket to collect their specific boons and making it a single god run. It doesn't always work, but I like being able to set a goal like that and not just go on aimlessly and manage with what I randomly get. Although, that can be fun to. This game has become one of, if not my absolute, favorite very quickly. I freaking adore Skelly. Protect Skelly. I freaking despise that one chamber in Asphodel with the witch circle. Instant death. Wonderful game! Excited to play the second one! After I extract every last drop of content from this delightful masterpiece first, of course.

have around 200 hours in Hades, and I’m still far from finished. I’ve even lost a save once or twice and still came back, which says enough on its own. I don’t usually play roguelikes; I’m more into builders and RPGs. Hades still managed to pull me in hard. The core loop is repetitive by design, but in a good way: every run makes you better as a player. Progress isn’t just stats or unlocks, it’s skill and familiarity, and the game is forgiving enough that casual players can take it slow. Combat feels tight and satisfying. I personally prefer ranged weapons like the bow and gun, but the game pushes you to rotate weapons and improve across the board. That can be mildly annoying at times, but it also prevents stagnation. Boon and build variety stays fresh even after dozens of hours. Difficulty is well handled. You can play on easy settings or ramp things up significantly with Heat, which is one of the better post-clear systems I’ve seen. It gives runs a purpose long after your first escape. The art style is excellent and carries a lot of personality. Music and sound design are solid, though not the main draw for me. Dialogue changes over time and supports the repetition theme well, even if I personally skip a lot of it. Humor lands consistently. Also: you can pet the dog. Controls on keyboard and mouse are straightforward and intuitive. I didn’t experience in-game technical issues, though I did lose a save early on due to PC problems and had to restart. Overall, if you don’t mind repetition and enjoy a grind that actively rewards player improvement, this is an easy recommendation. I still return to it now and then, which is rare for me. Pros - Extremely polished core gameplay loop - Strong art style and humor - Flexible difficulty with meaningful endgame modifiers - High replay value Cons - Forced weapon rotation can be annoying - Not for players who dislike repetition

The combat system is elegant, and there are many, many different builds, using different weapons each with different aspects to choose, so you won't be running out of ways to play soon. Completing your first run is only scratching the surface of what this game has to offer, as later on you can vastly increase the difficulty in many different ways of your own choosing. As a roguelite, there is permanent progression that significantly increases your strength and will keep players motivated if they're struggling. The learning curve is refined and highly rewarding from my experience. This game makes you feel very weak at first, then very powerful, and then weak again when you turn up the heat. This cycle can continue for a LONG TIME. The skill ceiling is high, and there are ways to reduce the RNG aspects a lot, but much of the fun comes from having to adapt to unexpected/unwanted situations the game throws you into, and seeing if you can still come out on top. My only complaint about the gameplay is how there are some weapon aspects and boons which are essentially unusable at higher difficulties, while others are somewhat overpowered by default, but the overall balance is decent. I have found fun and viable ways to play with every weapon, and make use of most boons the gods give you. The story is engaging, and all the characters have distinct personalities which you can pursue by gifting nectar. Hades does a great job bringing Greek mythology to life here, while sprinkling in tasteful humor and details which diverge from the traditional mythology. Finally, the visuals, voice acting, and music bring everything together. This is one of the most polished games I have played, and the best part is, there is a sequel if you just can't get enough of Hades 1!

What I love most about Hades is the atmosphere. Every run feels drenched in mood... the voice acting, the art, the way the characters react to your success and your failures. Even when you die, the world keeps moving. Nobody scolds you for it. The game just says, “Cool, let’s talk about what happened,” and then gently pushes you back out the door. The music deserves its own praise. Darren Korb absolutely nailed it. The soundtrack makes every fight feel urgent and mythic without ever being exhausting. It ramps you up when it needs to and fades back when you’re catching your breath. It’s the kind of music that sticks in your head long after you’ve put the controller down. And maybe my favorite thing: Hades makes it okay to fail a run every now and then. Dying isn’t punishment... it’s progress. You unlock new dialogue, deepen relationships, and come back stronger. That design choice takes the pressure off and turns frustration into motivation. You’re never wasting time; you’re always learning something or unlocking something. Hades is challenging, stylish, and strangely comforting for a game about fighting your way out of the underworld. It respects your time, your effort, and your failures.. and that’s why it’s so easy to love.

This is my first Supergiant game, but Hades is a great time. I feel like this is both a great gateway into the roguelite genre and a great game on its own. It heavily relies on meta-progression and runs can feel static at times, but the game has sheer quality in its writing, gameplay, and mechanics to help remedy many potential issues. Additionally, the meta-progression isn't something that carries you to the finish line. It helps greatly. However, both player skill and meta-progression need to climb at a parallel rate to actually beat a run. If the player makes too many mistakes, you won't be given many handouts to carry you across the finish line. Also, if the game is overall too easy for roguelite experienced players, the heat system provides many varied challenges to add back any missed sense of challenge On top of the great gameplay, Hades is one of the few roguelites with compelling writing and characters. Its setting and established rules provide an almost perfect avenue to explore what the underworld is like and how it affects the immortal characters within. There are so many interactions that queue themselves up after failed or beaten runs. The amount of dialogue written AND fully voiced is staggering. If you love the gameplay and writing, you can spend nearly 100+ hours until you've seen almost everything Most importantly, the story of Hades is a very sweet and down-to-earth tale of fostering and maintaining relationships in an unfortunate situation. Zagrius is the perfect main character for a story like this, and when you have friends and family like he does, maybe hell isn't so bad after all...

[h3][b]Worth the Hype After All [/b][/h3] I put off Hades for a long time. I’d tried Bastion years ago after it was recommended to me and gave it a few honest attempts, but it just never clicked. Because of that, I assumed Hades wouldn’t be for me either. Although I still avoided any online content and spoilers entirely, just in case I’d changed my mind in the future. At first, Hades was easy to pick up and hard to put down. Going in completely blind made the early hours especially fun since everything felt fresh and surprising. It took me around 20 runs to really get into the flow of things and start consistently reaching the later areas. That’s also around when the game started to feel grindy for me though. Not in a bad way, but in a way that clashed with how I personally like to play. I enjoy roguelikes conceptually, but they aren’t my favourite genre, and that definitely shaped my experience. Around this point, I shifted into optimisation mode, trying to find a reliable build I could use to push through. On my 30th run exactly, I beat the final boss, which felt great, but then I realised that was only the beginning of the Hades experience. Once the endgame systems opened up, the grind really kicked in. Some builds felt dramatically stronger than others, and while that’s partly on me and my skill level, it pushed me toward finding something consistent rather than experimenting. Dionysus’ Drunken Strike paired with the bow quickly became my go-to, and I stuck with variations of that setup for most of my clears. It worked so well, but by the end it started to feel really repetitive after having forced the build so many times. I believe that repetition feeling came mostly from my own approach though since doing the same fights over and over with the exact same kit is bound to get a bit tiresome. I was rushing to finish Hades so I could move on to Hades 2 before the holidays ended, and I think the game would’ve benefitted from a slower, more casual playstyle while experimenting a lot more with different weapons and abilities. Even so, I still had a really great time. What really stood out to me was how well everything was integrated conceptually. The mechanics, progression systems, and repeated deaths all make sense within the world and story. From a design and immersion standpoint, it’s some of the best I’ve seen. The art direction was easily a highlight as well. Gameplay-wise, it’s solid across the board. Not every weapon or build clicked for me, but the core combat always felt good. I also ended up playing across both PC and Switch while travelling, and the experience was super seamless. Different control setups even changed which weapons I preferred, which was nice. The story and characters were another strong point. It can be a bit goofy at times, but in a way that fits the tone. Every character felt relatively distinct, and interacting with them was enjoyable, I was really surprised at how much variety of dialogue there was to the game too. Despite the amount of hours I'd played, I hadn't exhausted all the dialogue options with each of the characters yet. It also left me with a genuine interest in Greek mythology again, I really liked how the lore was used and woven into the experience. I don’t really have anything bad to say about Hades. It’s an excellent game. My only real drawbacks came down to rushing it and the genre not fully being my thing. Even with that, I can easily recommend it to just about anyone. It’s great value for money, rewarding without being overwhelming, and gives you plenty of room to experiment. [h3][b]Personal Overall Experience: 7/10 – Good[/b][/h3] [i]~ Updated based on how my memories and fondness for the game have aged.[/i]

I was never a big fan of losing huge chunks of progress and having to play everything again, our time is precious, i get bored easily etc etc. Enter Hades a rogue like that you have to play multiple - hundreds of runs in order to grasp the concept of the game and explore the story, dialogues, extra challenges and so on. Hades knows how to appeal to the player since every time you die or later start to win/escape you unlock more of the story, weapons and abilities to keep things fresh and exciting. I ended up completing everything even stuff that did not matter for the achievements and i also did most of the pacts of punishment ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ which was fun for a while. I gotta say though that last achievement with the maxing all keepsakes was cruel and evil, i had to play music from my playlist in the background so as to push through it. Both Clair Obscur and Hades 1 made me appreciate two genres i had never thought of trying out and i ended up loving both of those games. That doesn't mean that i will be playing either turn based rpgs or rogue like games regularly since they still definitely aren't my cup of tea, but i've learnt to keep an eye out for gems like those and let me tell you after i take a long break i will be coming back for Hades 2 later this year with a new appetite. I recommend this game either on a sale or full price since it is pretty cheap and has a lot of content - it is a rather deceptively lengthy game as long as you wish to experience the true ending and most of the features provided.
Great game. Enjoyed the fact that there are multiple weapons to play with so you can build your own style.
Pros meta-progression. Cons story delivery relies too heavily. conversations disrupt sharp action tempo. dialogue skip and selection confirm use the same button.
Great art, engaging battle. Just nice to play, also the difficulty (for me a casual gamer) is just perfect, not too Dark Soul and not too "just do nothing but you'll win". Love it!

This game is all about progression, story and gameplay wise. Despite some ocasional dips (from which you have to crawl from, just like Zagreus crawls from the Underworld), you are promptly hooked again by a relationship you can foster, a problem you can solve in the house of Hades or a new strategy you can take to obliterate the stages more quickly. I am 43 hours in and there are still aspects of the game I haven't even touched yet. If those dips don't become chasms going forward, this games has proven to be one of the greatest.

I am a 45 yo father, probably one of the oldest people playing this game. I am a single father to my Son, who is 14 now. My son got this game for Easter in 2025 from his uncle, so we installed it on his computer and he started playing. By the end of the week he had 24 hours on this game. This was horrible for me, as it was already hard for me to find ways to spend time with my son, as he is always out with his friends or just watching YouTube. So i decided to make a Steam account and get this game to see if I could maybe play alongside him. I loaded into the game, picked my character and world and started playing but I was stuck on what you where supposed to do. I asked my Son for help and he hosted a game for me to join. I loved it as it was the best time I had spent with my Son since my wife had died. This game has ever since brought me and my son closer again and now we actually spend time together outside the house together as well. This game reminded me that there's fun to be had in everything, and it has brought both me and my Son many happy memories.

Finally got around to playing it after all these years. It's no wonder it's highly awarded. Supergiant was able to distill the combat from Bastion, add the spice of Transistor, and give it their unique style of art and storytelling for a really great and well-rounded title. The premise is slightly familiar for most people being no stranger to mythology so I had my doubts that they'd follow through on an interesting story but it turned out to be interesting enough to keep me chasing the narrative. Combat is fast and button-mashy and the game does a great job of making you feel powerful quickly. Some powers just aren't very good and I wish more effort had been put into making every 'build' feel equally interesting but overall I find the system enjoyable. Truly a 10/10 game that many people love and comes at a great price point on sale.

Rogue-ish games feel bad because your personal skill at the game is only a small factor among many that determine the success of any given run. This game is no different. It feels like my progression is chained to the RNG of the game. The design of acquiring incremental permanent upgrades also lends itself to the idea that I'm stuck with a slow pace of progression that the developers arbitrarily decided upon. Rather than progressing further into game by becoming more proficient at the gameplay, it feels like the developers intend for me to play x number of runs to build resources to carry myself. That, or I need to play x number of runs until I get lucky RNG for an OP build. I'm not saying that your level of skill won't help you in this game. I am saying that the level of skill required to progress significantly without relying on farming runs to either build resources for permanent upgrades OR to search for good RNG is not reasonable to attain. You will not get good enough at this game to carry yourself on skill without having already put in the time to farm the arbitrary amount that the developers intended you to farm. Having to rely on that RNG for a good run, and in the process having so many runs end because your RNG wasn't good enough, sucks. I want to like this game, but I do not.
The art direction, the playstyle, the music, the story, the rich amount of dialogue... one of my favourite games hands down. If you like roguelikes, this one is one of the best I've played.

My main complaint is that it's hard to learn the optimal strat to play this game. The further you go, the higher the stakes become so you don't really have a lot of time to slow things down and observe how exactly the various enemies function and learn the best way to deal with them. It also doesn't help that the in-game codex contains only lore. While I do appreciate lore as much as the next guy, I'd appreciate having a description of how each enemy functions. The end result of this is that the gameplay eventually becomes smashing a bunch of keyboard buttons and hoping that you win the fight.

Too fast, poor controls, and an art style that makes it hard to judge where attacks are and where safe spots are. Great game overall if these things do not bother you, and a very beautiful art style, but I have tried several time to enjoy Hades and I do not. I consider a similar game, Sworn, to be much better. Maybe I'm just getting old.

Okay first of all... I was not ready to have to start over when I die. I was in disbelief thinking all I needed to do was reach a checkpoint. Nope. Start over. That's been tough to adjust to considering I am practically new to this style of game. Turns out it's a whole genre. But I have to say... dying and interacting with the central hob after every failure is something I truly look forward to. The characters and the art are amazing. I have only ever made it to the 25th dungeon and still trying to escape hades realm. Overall I think this is a great introduction to this genre and I am loving the game.

well here's my hades review after 6ish hours. i don't know how to feel about it. it doesn't really feel like it's a good roguelite. in something like the binding of isaac, you'll pick up your first item and on first glance, it's abysmal ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, you're like wtf is this and you'll sulk about it for the next 15 minutes, and then your next item will interact with it in a weird way and you'll be like wtf this is kind of good and then your next item will take it to a new level and through something you couldn't possibly predict, your build is now awesome and unique. while in a different stat based game like diablo, you are mostly looking at how you can stack the most amount of multiplicative modifiers in the most scenarios. you'll find an item that makes your fire attacks deal 400% more damage against frozen enemies, and then your entire build will pivot towards freezing enemies before shooting fireballs or w/e, and you add and add and add onto these until you have some weird kooky build that's probably nowhere near meta, but it's fun and you made it yourself. hades has me feeling like i'm at the end of a diablo build, where no longer am i interested in what could be behind the next boon, but rather i'm just looking for a bigger number on my existing boon, just like how endgame diablo is trying to find the exact same pants you're wearing now, but with a bigger number. i just wish there was more. it disappointed me that one attack boon will replace another attack boon, and the only boons you could stack were simple number boons. i would've loved being able to stack boons that created interesting effects. like what if merging a doom boon and a hangover boon created a timebomb, where after a hit, if you specifically DIDN'T hit them until the hangover wore off, a bomb would be armed and you have to hit again to detonate it, which would deal a lot of damage and if it doesn't kill, the cycle repeats, you know? let me merge a zeus and dionysus attack and get lightning that spreads poison or something, like do something that makes me go "wow". because finding something that works and then just stacking levels is boring to me. it's why i don't really find risk of rain super replayable. and the keepsakes or w/e they're called initially interested me, but from what i can tell, it mostly exists not to radically alter builds, but to manipulate RNG, which makes me think the "end-game" is just going to be manipulate RNG to get the exact build you want, and if you can't get it, pivot to one or two alternate builds that work with your boon and that's it. idk. i think it's a bad omen if this entire time i've constantly been asking "is this it? am i missing something?" my last few minor gripes are just stuff like visibility issues. there's often so much ♥♥♥♥ on the screen that half the time it feels like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ when i take damage because i just couldn't see what is going on. so yeah idk, it makes me sad that i can't get into something that others clearly enjoy, but i just can't see a reason why i should keep playing. it feels like hades has already played its hand, and i don't see dropping a couple extra meta-progression mechanics on my head fixing anything. sadge. maybe next time i'll play with god mode turned on so i can ignore the painfully dull buildcrafting and just do my best to enjoy the story. idk.

When I first ran through this game back in 2020, it took me 29 attempts to actually complete a run. When I decided to kill time by playing again a few days ago, it only took me 19. What I'm trying to say is that the game is good. It's STILL good. If you were considering getting into Hades II, I would assume that you should play this first, although I don't know much about the sequel other than what I've seen on the steam page. Still, the combat, builds, and story have enough meat on them to last a while, ranging from a few full days to several years, depending on how you count my experience. Just know that if you suck, it's going to take a while. Word to the wise? Try and get the aegis as fast as possible. It completely trivializes most encounters if you know how to move the shield in between you and whatever's trying to kill you. And once you got the hang of the shield, you'll start to notice the attack patterns of the bosses, and once you got those down, you should have enough ability to dodge most attacks with the other weapons. But I don't need to tell you that.

Gorgeous game with great voice acting. My only complaints, as a rogue like enjoyer the actual mechanics of the game are more on the minimal side. The game play felt quickly repetitive after 20 runs. I had to uninstall this game, take a few months off, and come back to it so I had some freshness to have motivation to beat it. Maybe I'll do the same with finishing the heats.

I’ve attempted to escape the Underworld many times, and I can confidently say Hades is the most stylish, violent, and emotionally complicated way to do it. Every run ends in either heroic progress or humiliating death, usually followed by my father pretending he’s not impressed. The combat is fast, flashy, and deeply satisfying especially when a god blesses you mid-fight and then immediately starts judging your life choices. What really makes this whole ordeal worth repeating is everyone I keep running into between deaths. Gods argue, friends gossip, enemies monologue, and somehow every conversation feels new no matter how many times I’ve died. The music slaps, the art is divine (literally), and failure is not only expected but encouraged... apparently it builds character. All told, if you enjoy sharp dialogue, perfect combat flow, and dying repeatedly for personal growth, I’d say Hades is absolutely to die for. Now if you’ll excuse me, I have somewhere I’m not allowed to be.

One of my favorite games of all time. Favorite adaptation of Greek mythology across all forms of fiction brilliant, beautiful story with incredible gameplay. I love this game and will always come back to it.

A must play only for the dialogues between the characters. Rich story. Funny moments. Nice combat and enough weapon and power combinations to make a lot of runs unique. Always new stuff happening even after 100 hours.

Hades is probably the best rougelite you'll find around. It perfectly blends gameplay with story and never really takes you out of being immersed into its world. Every run upgrade is a talk with a god, every NPC you meet is a chance to tell a story and when you die, you return to the underworld as if everything you just experienced was canon in the story. I also loved every character - Supergiantgames are just so talented at this stuff. It probably also helps that the fast paced gameplay is really intense and fun, that the music is masterful, that the art is gorgeous and that the voice acting is absolutely perfect. An extra bonus is also that all achievements are pretty fun to get and before i knew it, i had them all. THAT BEING SAID: If you hate fast paced games, this game probably isn't for you. You press the dodge button constantly in Hades and some things are hard to dodge. Go play this awesome game and PLEASE do it before you play Hades 2! Hades 2 has slightly better gameplay but a slightly worse story. Returning to Hades after Hades 2 will probably feel a little odd and playing them in order will tell the story better. Both games are about as good as each other anyway.

I have owned this game for years now, but it is until now that I have become addicted to it. Turns out taking the game seriously and trying to beat it really make the difference. If you just take it as a light session game like I did for years, the game is fun for a while and then you might drop it. However, once you play with intention and really sink your teeth into what it offers, it becomes a whole different experience. I never knew how much customization and progression it offers until I really made an effort to make it further. The game has sick art style, great characters, great voice acting and a story that makes a lot of sense within the context of a rogue lite. Gameplay is great also. I have only ever played it with keyboard and mouse but a friend tells me it was great on controller as well. Please try to make it to the point where you unlock all the weapons so you find your favorite. I love to cycle through all of them now, but for a while all I played was the sword and not only do I suck with it, it made the game so repetitive and boring. Anyways, this game is great and for its price I don't even think it is a risk to just get it and try it out. There's a reason why it was nominated at so many awards when it came out and why it has so many great reviews. I don't remember the last time I wanted to get better at a game and I'm surprised by how strong I feel about wanting to beat it (more so now that the sequel is out).
very fun to play, game is luck based because of boons, fun yes but most runs will not go past the first stage because you get bad boons. would recommend to other people, great story.

Never really clicked with any of the other isometric/top down action roguelikes but this one is different. The writing is stellar and the story is compelling and well paced so it is absolutely helping to keep me hooked. Outside of the runs the 'House of Hades' is an awesome way to tie progression of both your character's power and the story into the gameplay rather than menuing and cutscenes. Game play when you're in a run feels incredibly satisfying due to the level of challenge but not too difficult that I am feeling walled off from actually feeling like I am progressing like I am on for example the binding of isaac or gungeon for not being good enough. I attribute this to the power-scaling progression that carries between runs but isn't too overpowered either. Sure you'll end up breezing through the early chambers of Tartarus with upgrades and skill but the game will have you using your brain by the first major boss of almost every run unless you get lucky with boons. Right after my first session I made sure to pick up all of the supergiant games on this sale because this level of attention to detail and care in all of the design here is hard to come by nowadays.

As a long-time fan of Supergiant's work, I have no good excuse for why it took me this long to play Hades. I can only add to the chorus to confirm that it's excellent - a masterclass in both writing and action-feel. Ultimately, it's the combination of these two things that makes it an all-time great. See, the roguelike formula is so likely to be repellent to so many: The repetition can feel arduous. Why would I want to repeat large sections of a game, when I could play another action game that allows me to journey through new environments and new enemies? Hades answers as all roguelikes do: Because mastery is its own reward. But that's not a simple lesson to learn, and so Hades softens the blow with its exceptional character work. It is easy to accept death in Hades, when each of those frustrating moments is immediatley followed by a new morsel of plot. Yes, there were perhaps times where I felt as if this was coming out to slowly, where I said to myself "no, I think I'm almost done here, I don't actually want to do another run so why am I still playing? Is the story really going to be worth it?" But it is very much worth it: Each new bit of dialogue funny, or charming, or intruiging. Every time a character I hadn't seen in a while showed up, I was eager to see what they had to say this time - and there is a real sense that they're following along with your journey - that they're reacting to your choices - and that all of this is leading up to a real and genuine narrative conclusion (which it does, quite successfully). The game could have been considerably more clunky, and I likely still would have pushed through it just to see the characters unfold with each successive run... For the most part at least. I do think that pursuing the epilogue can drag a little for those who aren't thrilled with the challenge of the action itself. But even then, it's likely that if you change up the way you play, a little more story will eek out along the way. Each weapon, too, is a new treasure handed down to you from Supergiant. Picking up each one causes a moment of "no, really? They can't be letting me get away with *this*?" And if that empowerment were not enough, there is a carefully measured approach to stat growth - so that as you get better at the game, it also becomes mechanically easier to beat. Until, of course, you start increasing the difficult to pull yourself back down to earth. But only if you want to. None of that is required to see the story through, making it an incredibly approachable game when compared to its rogue-ish peers. My first successful run in Hades is, without a doubt, a top 10 #gamingmoment. Unless you truly hate action games, Hades will have something for you, and it will likely delight.

I avoided playing this game for ages because I wasn't sure if it was something that I'd like. When I booted this game up, I immediately recognised the art style, and released that these devs also made transistor, which I enjoyed the story of, but I really disliked the combat. I'm also not usually a fan of isometric games, or hack-and-slash games, or story heavy games. All that being said, I think that this isometric, hack-and-slash, story heavy game is absolutely phenomenal, genuinely a masterpiece This game is a roguelite where you play Zagreus, son of Hades, and your goal is to escape the underworld. In order to do this you fight through 4 levels: Tartarus, Asphodel, Elysium and the Temple of Styx, with each area becoming progressively harder and having a boss that you need to beat in order to progress to the next level Things I thought were great: [list] [*] [b]Contextualised game mechanics[/b] - I really enjoy when games are able to do this. Usually there's a gulf between the gameplay and the story. Like you can play something like last of us, which is all about trying to survive, but then if you die you go back to the checkpoint. This is necessary for the game to be a game, but obviously doesn't make sense in the story. With Hades though, every mechanic is actually part of the story. Why do you keep coming back to life? Because you're immortal. Why are the rooms random every run? The underworld is constantly shifting to make escape impossible. How do your powers get upgraded? They're blessed from the olympian gods (your relatives). How does Zagreus start back at the house every time? Because he dies and the pool of styx, where everything that dies ends up, is in the house of Hades. [spoiler]Why does Zagreus need to keep trying to escape after he succeeds? Because he can't survive outside of the underworld for very long.[/spoiler] It may seem like a small detail, but I think it really makes the game feel much more solid and well put together, especially as these things are even mentioned in the dialogue, it's pretty cool [*] [b]Story[/b] - As I've said above I don't like story heavy games much, but I really enjoyed the story here. Every character felt unique and grounded, the voice acting was incredible, the side quests were all enjoyable. The epilogue I could take it or leave it, but the rest of it was really good. The only time I really skipped dialogue was after I'd finished the epilogue. I'm not sure that I heard a line of repeated dialogue in the 100 hours I played, it's genuinely incredibly impressive how they managed to do that [*] [b]Gameplay[/b] - Incredibly fun and satisfying. It's definitely challenging, and occasionally it crossed over into the point of frustration, but I would say that happened quite rarely, so I think overall, it's good. You have 6 infernal arms (weapons) that you can pick from, each with a very different play style. Not only that but you can also get aspects which will modify the weapons fairly substantially. For example, the spear, Varatha, has the aspect of Achilles which means after you throw it you can dash to where it lands, which the normal spear doesn't have the ability to do. Stuff like this keeps the gameplay very interesting and diverse. On top of that you have stuff like keepsakes, boons, duo boons, legendary boons, etc. Which all modify the runs quite a lot, so each run feels pretty different which makes it enjoyable to keep playing [*] [b]Quest cadence[/b] - A very interesting choice, but one I really quite enjoyed. Basically, you can only talk to a character for 1 conversation per run, so if you want to advance a quest you have to do runs to advance it. I quite like this because it felt a bit more like natural conversation than some other games where you just go through the dialogue as fast as possible. It was quite a nice change [*] [b]Meta-progression[/b] - This one will probably split the roguelite fans, but some roguelites seem to opt for meta-progression and some don't. Some games like Haste, Enter the gungeon, or even slay the spire, you don't upgrade your character in substantial ways between runs, it's mostly down to the luck and the items on each run. Hades is the total opposite where you have tons of ways of making yourself more powerful and even adding in deterministic boons to your runs. There's literally an ability which gives you an extra life, and if that's upgraded to the max and you have the lucky tooth, then it means that you can get like 5 lives on a run, which is obviously hugely impactful. I personally really like this. Between the keepsakes, the abilities, [spoiler]the cthonic companions,[/spoiler] the infernal arms, the contractor table, etc. It becomes difficult to lose before the 3rd area at a certain stage, which is quite nice [/list] Stuff that wasn't so great: [list] [*] [b]Quest cadence[/b] - Although I did enjoy this, it got to a point with some side quests where I felt like it got a bit grindy, because I was having to do runs just to push forward quests which wasn't super great [*] [b]Bugs[/b] - I seemed to get quite a few bugs and issues while playing. For example there was one that was super common where I would attack (with coronacht, the bow) and then move the stick in the opposite direction and dash and it would dash me in the same direction that I fired, which was pretty annoying. An even worse bug I got using coronacht was sometimes the direction would just get stuck, no matter where I tried to aim the stick on my controller, the aim was just locked at a certain angle and I wasn't able to move it. I'm not sure what fixed it, usually running around in circles for a bit or firing a shot or something like that it would make it go back to normal, but it was pretty frustrating. That one was less common, it happened maybe like 6 or 7 times in the 100 hours, but yeah still not great. I was using proton on linux with a PS5 controller if that factors in at all? [*] [b]Enemies[/b] - Some of the enemies were pretty frustrating to be honest, specifically I'm thinking of the flame wheels (little chariots) in Elysium, the shield warriors in Elysium, even [spoiler]Theseus[/spoiler] is quite a pain to deal with. Same with the satyrs, there's not much fun either, but it's never too bad, it's just that they can be pretty frustrating at points [/list] I would say overall though this game was a lot of fun, I would easily give it a 9/10, and again, I thought I was not going to enjoy the game much at all Really good!

Pros: Great animations. Nice voice acting too. Most isometric games don't even have voicing at all but this one does and they did a good job with it. It can be a little silly or cartoonish at times, but it's clearly a kid game so it works out just fine. Cons: Doesn't truly support ultrawide resolutions. It adds borders to the edges of the screen since it's designed just to be a 16x9 game. That surprised me since the game isn't that old. Not much of a tutorial. It dumps you into a fight with virtually no explanation as to why you are fighting nor how to do the different attack types. I eventually checked the controls and saw stuff that I hadn't used yet so I got it figured out. It will eventually run you through a combat tutorial but only after you've died the first time. It also doesn't explain what the symbols mean. So if you choose a reward and it's between two different symbols, there is no clue as to what they are or what they do. You just have to learn as you go. Overall: This is not a game for me but it is not a bad game, it's actually well done for what it is. If you like a solid action isometric title and don't mind repetition then you will likely love this. If you were looking for more of a traditional action RPG like Grim Dawn or something, then you might be disappointed with this one like I was. I don't like games where you are supposed to die over and over, it just makes me feel like I'm not making the progress I want to make. It wasn't the game's fault, I just had a different idea of what to expect.

Hades is a fast-paced and addictive roguelike that makes grinding feel fun and rewarding. Each run feels fresh thanks to the wide variety of upgrades and hero skill combinations, encouraging players to experiment and try new builds every time they play. The combat is smooth and satisfying, and discovering powerful or creative combos keeps the gameplay exciting. Even when failing a run, the progression system motivates you to keep going and improve. The art style, music, and voice acting also add a lot of personality and charm to the game. Overall, Hades is an excellent game that rewards persistence and creativity. Its replayability, strong combat, and engaging progression make it a highly enjoyable experience for players who love experimenting and grinding.

All these boons often amount to little more than a pallet swap. Do you want blue for water or yellow for lighting. That’s the thing that probably puts me off the most, the same boons all the time and even when you get new ones this one is not less pink than the last. So I guess this review is a caution for anyone else, if the above sounds contradictory to what you’ve heard about how “diverse” your run is, take caution.

Hades is extremely well-crafted, with sharp comedic writing and impressively dynamic dialogue that constantly reacts to your runs, deaths, and choices — that part is genuinely standout. I respect the craft and polish, but the core loop favors repetition (which I hate - I don't ever want to repeat / go back) and mastery over immersion and exploration, which kept it from being a personal favorite - the first game of 2025 that I have not finished (and I got Hades 2 on sale up next but is now uninstalled as well). 7.0 / 10.

The art is beautiful, the soundtrack rules, the voice acting is phenomenal. Play this game. Even if you think you're bad at games and it will be demoralizing, trust yourself. If you think the art/music is nice, if anything about it appeals to you, do it. There is no shame in many attempts. Wear them as a badge of honor to show the trials you've gone through. Yes it's hard at first. You will die a lot. It took 34 attempts to beat the final boss, 43 runs to properly meet one character (thanks, RNG!), and 60 runs to get to the end credits. Which is not the end of the story. I will continue playing to the end of the story, and maybe even beyond that. Not just because of all the things I listed, but because it's fun. Because I want to continue interacting with these characters and getting to know them. You'll play for 100 hours and still find new and interesting dialogues you haven't run across before. You'll find unique interactions due to items you're holding, characters you've met along the way, there's at least one character with special dialogues for turning certain menu options off and on. Everything is beautifully voice acted, the story is heartfelt and touching, the characters are extremely well-written. If you don't like them at first, give them time. Every character opens up into hidden depths the longer you play, even the ones you think couldn't possibly. It's hard at first, but once you get the hang of it, you'll grow, you'll improve, you'll be incredible. And you'll always wonder, "Is there a special dialogue if I do THIS?" And almost certainly there is. Now go find it! Early-game tips (spoilers only for character names, mechanics, and early-game tactics): [spoiler] Give a nectar to Athena so you get her keepsake and equip it a LOT in early runs, to get her dash boon where you can. That will help IMMENSELY as you get better at the game. You'll find other tactics that work for you over time, but the most useful thing to start is that dash boon. I also like the keepsake for Dusa and Skelly for early-game runs. [/spoiler]

In Hades, dying isn't a failure; it’s a [b]family reunion from hell[/b]. Your goal? To kick down the front door of the underworld and sprint toward the sun, only to be repeatedly murdered by a hydra, [b]a butterfly ball[/b], or your own hubris. Every time you perish and crawl back through the blood-red pool of the House of Hades, the story moves forward. It’s the only game where getting skewered by a spear feels like a great way to catch up on office gossip. It is a poetic tragedy wrapped in a neon seizure. You will die. You will cry. You will realize that the real "Hades" was the daddy issues we made along the way. This game is a [b]10/10[/b], where the primary mechanic is being stabbed to death by your dad’s coworkers.

Far from the 10/10 GOTY contender I'd always heard it was and built up in my mind. But it's still pretty fun and satisfying to beat once it finally clicks, as any good rogue-lite game should be. I enjoyed it enough to get the main story's ending (with 10 successful runs), but I'm not sure how much more of my time I'll feel like devoting to it in the future. It's a quite good game that's annoyingly close to being great. As Pixel a Day said in a [url=https://www.youtube.com/shorts/O8kX58gARRY]recent YouTube short[/url], Hades doesn't do anything badly and its worst aspects are perfectly competent, at minimum. The story is so paper thin that it's hardly ever surprising, though; I was mainly surprised by the amount of universal praise that gets heaped onto the game for its story, if anything. "Dad is a huge grouch who harbors a lot of resentment that he takes out on me. Oh wait, there's a - [i]gasp[/i] - deeper reason for it?! No way!" The REAL draw of the game is its gameplay loop, naturally. Enter a room, kill the enemies, claim a reward, check out the occasional optional thingy, proceed to the next room, repeat that several times until you beat the boss of the region, then repeat that process in the next region. Go all the way to the end or die trying, either way returning to the home base to chat with side characters and upgrade yourself (and decorate the house). I honestly don't have a lot to say about it other than...it's fun! My biggest criticism of the gameplay relates to the boons granted by the gods along each run. These are critical to the buildcraft aspect of the game, acting as a major way for each run to feel unique in how you slay your foes. But there are a lot of boons that are so obviously stronger than others regardless of which weapon you're using. I always feel like I'm chasing that one Athena boon every run (Divine Dash of course), and any time I get forced into taking Aphrodite boons, I bemoan my bad luck. The amount of unique voice lines is impressive and the brief glimpses we get into these interpretations of the mythical Greek figures are usually pretty fun, though once I reached a certain play time, I kind of wished I could turn them off to save a bit of time in my runs. You don't need me to tell you how gorgeous the art direction is; it speaks for itself. I'm definitely down to play the sequel, though from what I understand it's generally just Hades 1, but bigger. So I'm not sure how I'll feel about it in comparison to this one. Still, I recommend this to people who like action rogue-lites or want to try them out. I would just caution them about the amount of hype the game has been given over the years, because it directly impacted my opinion. 7/10

[h1] Game for mobile phones [/h1] It is a good game for a price of a shawarma (if you buy it on sale), but it's not a game that will keep you hooked for many hours (if you like to use your brain a little). Gameplay is boring and repetitive. The entire gameplay comes down to clicking one button - X or Y (it depends on the abilities you chose). There are several weapons, but it does not change your playstyle (clicking X or Y). There are many abilities, but you should choose those that improve one of your attacks (X or Y). If there are no enemies with armor you can literally stand still and press one button (X or Y), because you can stun-lock them. If there are bosses or enemies with armor it's also worth considering pressing the dash button. Some bosses are boring, because they have a lot of hp and it takes a long time to kill them. The hole idea of Meta progression was designed to keep your attention away from unchanging gameplay. The same goes for a "great" plot that definitely isn't half-filler. There are some pros: game price, visuals, sounds and friendliness towards people with only one finger on their hand.

I would recommend Hades 1 if you like a hybrid blend of an action roguelite game plus visual novel for downtime. The only real caution I have is to expect a brawler focus for Hades 1 & Hades 2 being more cast-plus magic-centric. Playing the sequel certainly helped me realize this game has a prearranged format it tends to stick with to make some fairly predictable runs, although part of the fun is getting better to the point you climb into the high heat tiers once clearing your first run. Certainly can appreciate that Hades 2 has some more variety (some wildly stronger than others as in 1, albeit can be run-defining beyond god keepsakes guaranteeing a god in the god pool of 4). I would highly recommend looking into the community online, as in other roguelikes, learning what works well requires a fair bit of trial and error, although you can certainly learn a lot more by doing some research into great run synergies plus using the codex to sculpt your blessing choices. This becomes a lot easier with the inclusion of rerolls once enough keys have been invested into the Mirror of Night. A basic tip anyone could use since it's often skipped past: select the toggle of the skills in the Mirror of Night to show a green alternate of the standard (these can be really helpful compared to their standard counterparts; pick and choose). Also, don't be afraid of handing out some nectar plus ambrosia; you get a keepsake the first time and even a usable summon for select characters you meet. You will have plenty of resources the more you play to open up options plus complete prophecies (gameplay milestones and/or challenges). As in most of these games, getting a run through the first couple of times will be the toughest aspect to start, albeit there's a lot to enjoy once you can upgrade enough to clear your first run. Hades 1 hits well for me despite not having much of an interest in roguelikes typically, although SuperGiant certainly knows how to make a great format of it, which I find is just overall further refined in Hades 2.

It is a good game, great combat mechanic with a variety of weapons that helps alleviate the innate boredom of rogue-like genre. That being said, incorporating a story element into a roguelike requires the player to either be kneecapped to make the story happen at the dev-intended pace or implement an RNG-based dialogue system where story progression may or may not occur in your next run and when each run takes upwards of 40 minutes to complete. And Hades 1 embraces the latter option to probably the most extreme end all the while doing so via the most lovely voices lent by regular actors and actresses at Supergiant Games. The way in which story progression, especially that in the epilogue is implemented in Hades 1 leaves far, far too much to desire and I find myself growing to hate the game the longer it keeps the "RNG dialogue-hunting" charade up. The worst part about being (or at least pretending to be) an "RNG dialogue hunter" is that the majority of the story-locked dialogue only 'procs' the first time you meet the related gods and if the needed dialogue occurs, very cool but if it does not, you will spend the next 30-odd minutes finishing the run in disappointment in hope of 'maybe it'll proc the next run'. The common advice for 'how do I proc dialogue of XYZ god to progress their questline' is usually 'just keep bashing your head against the wall and eventually it will occur' and it leaves sours my experience with the game.

So, I ended up caving into playing Hades after enough recommendations from some of my friends when I decided that I would play the first game (this one) so that I could hopefully get to playing Hades II some point soon after it's official release. While I haven't got to the second part of that yet, that is because Hades has captured my attention more than I expected. Admittedly, some of the 40 hours I spent we're slowed by my slow learning curve to the mechanics and adapting to playing a game on controller for the first time in a couple years - but the majority has been very engaged progression through the story and completing the prophecies (longer term quests). In truth, it does not feel like I have already spent 40+ hours in the game - the game has got me into flow state where time passes quicker than you feel because of the enjoyment. And even now - there is still some more that I'm choosing to experience before starting Hades II because I feel positively invested in the extended story. I'm also going to dance around some of these following things because I fear my descriptions would fail me and not do my experience justice. Firstly, the sound design is amazing and really adds to the environment. It comes across as thoughtfully engineered to really add to and enhance the vibes of the moment by moment. Second, as much as I wasn't 100% sure whether the art style was one that could be sold to me specifically, experiencing it through playing the game has dispelled those concerns. Next, gameplay maintains enough controlled variation to make the addictive gameplay loop stay fresh and prevent it going stale. 'Endgame' modifier runs also mean there is enough depth to demonstrate skill progression and means that you're unlikely to hit the skill ceiling before completing the rest of the game. Finally, the story is not just limited to the 'main story' as the sprawling set of specific interactions and parallel character driven stories means there is so much to engage with while being structured in a way as to not overwhelm you. Is the game perfect- not quite. There are some elements which you have to somewhat brute force / trial and error to find out how they work (such as the companions) and there are a couple of points where I think the interactions miss the specific story beat for the moment. In these cases however, they do not overshadow the rest of the game and are perfectly acceptable as issues in context. Overall, it takes me to the conclusion that the game is one that I would highly recommend experiencing for yourself. (Just be careful to make sure you have a controller on hand).

Game is decent. The variety and the nuanced timing of the different weapons, and the occasional run-altering boon synergy, are its strengths. They kept me coming back for the "postgame" challenges. But even this aspect feels better than it really is because of the frantic-by-design gameplay that doesn't offer time to think too much about what you're doing—if there are enough shiny objects, the player remains effectively distracted. Compared to their past efforts, the music and even the art direction feel tepid. Enemy designs and abilities are seldom interesting. The much-lauded dialogue, characterization, theming, and overall narrative are so trite that I can only recall them because they are built from the most well-worn tropes. The grind for progression feels artificial and padded with a million different currencies to pour into a million different buckets. The hub and its interactions feel comically underdeveloped. This is very much the pathology of a developer spread too thinly. There are also still bugs and glitches and hangups (especially if the player has unexpectedly high move speed—boss fights do NOT like it), and straight up bad design decisions (namely, the prevalence of projectiles with fast or homing projectiles who SHOOT AT THE PLAYER FROM OFFSCREEN), to contend with. I did keep coming back... though the 150 hours I've spent with it feel much, much longer than those spent with any number of other games.

Supergiant has perhaps the most spotless record of any dev out there, every game they put out is a masterpiece in its own right. Hades is no different there and Supergiant's house style of ultra-polished art and audio design is on full display. What I really like about Hades is that its never not fun to play. Even before you have any unlocks or boons, just the base weapons right from the jump feel great to use. Your dash is crisp, enemy attacks are appropriately telegraphed, and you're rarely faced with a situation that feels cheap. That goes a long way towards making the core loop of multiple runs never feel like a chore. On top of that the boon system is brilliant in that each boon has such an immediately impactful effect on your build that I would often look forward to the next run just for another chance at a different boon combination with a new weapon. The way the difficulty ramps up via heat level modifiers (another Supergiant staple that I love) feels so much more organic that just NG+ or whatever. Whether its presentation, design or just how it feels in your hands, Hades hits every mark.

TL;DR: I imagine the world would be a lot better of a place if we all had to climb out of hell before we got to see it. --------------- I didn't think I was going to end up liking Hades as much as I did when I first really got into it earlier this year. I'd given it a few tries on release, I played Bastion, Transistor is kinda sitting in my backlog not really going anywhere but also not QUITE interesting enough for me to want to jump into, and this... This is something else entirely. It didn't click for me until I was about five or six runs in, trying to figure out what I was doing wrong, and then finally something changed. Up until that point, I had never rolled both Ares and Artemis in a single run, through pure happenstance. I would get one or the other, but never both. I'd happened to have already had Ares' regular attack buff, and Artemis had the "all damage has a crit chance" boon on the table, and I suddenly thought of something that I hadn't considered previously: "Does that include the Doom damage?" Prior to this I'd been struggling a lot to stay alive in my runs, and it wasn't even that I was necessarily getting bad boons, or hadn't been upgrading myself, or anything like that. Rather, I had been searching and trying to find what I usually do in Roguelikes and Roguelites, a sort of "What is the way the game wants me to play this game?" Some kind of set of rules that the game follows that I have to follow as well, and this was sort of a watershed moment for me in Hades. Hades isn't a particularly mechanically complex game and its real appeal is, like everything Supergiant puts out, its charm, presentation and emotional appeal to the player. Its core loop is collecting resources, getting meta-progression, and slowly, carefully working towards the *opportunity* to make good choices that shift the battle in your favor. However, I think maybe this was what I was missing: "To make good choices". See, the beauty of Hades' mechanics is that the player is given an organic option to grow a given run's complexity on their own terms. There is no "right way". It's not like in The Binding Of Isaac, where some items you pick will absolutely ruin your run, or Dungeons of Dredmor where RNG can just decide that today you are screwed. Everything, EVERYTHING in the game is designed in some small way to help you and if a choice feels right to you, like it's going to make the experience of survival more comfortable, then you should always take it. There's never a wrong answer. There are suboptimal answers, but not wrong ones. I'm actually amazed that there aren't wrong answers because by all rights there should be. Healing in the game is incredibly sparse. You start runs very weak and enemies scale up pretty hard. I suppose there's a theoretical intentional poor set of choices you could make that would send you back home pretty quickly, but the ease with which you can make helpful choices is worked deep into the boon system, and even then your execution capability can still compensate for a few bad choices here and there. I'd describe Hades as a sort of tsundere of a game. It comes off at a glance as wanting you to fail, to crush you with the weight of the task that sits before you. But, within each run, there is a glimmer of an idea, that you could get a little further each time, that you can make small changes and preparations to tilt the odds in your favor, that you can *grow stronger*. It slowly reveals itself to actually like you, the player, quite a bit, and to want you to succeed. I think, maybe, that's a very thematically appropriate way to present the game's story and conflict, which I can't spoil meaningfully through this type of review because of what it takes to see it unfold piece by piece, dialogue by dialogue. It's just nice. Zagreus is just nice. He's a nice guy. More protagonists need to be his kind of nice, where he stands on business when it matters, but is otherwise pretty chill. Also, whoever thought up the Extreme Measures version of the Elysium boss fight deserves a raise.

Gameplay: The weapon–boon combinations are really fun and flexible, and there’s a lot of variety in how you can play...even though in the end most builds more or less converge on setting up Privileged Status. As for character design, my personal favorites are Demeter (“You grant life to all things, and you take life from all things—seemingly preferring the latter”), Nyx (her gentle husky voice is wonderful😭), and Chaos. Chaos especially feels like peak character design to me...They really embody chaos, fragmentation, and the breaking of rational boundaries. Their presence is stunningly beautiful, yet also evokes a faint sense of sanity loss as you take it in. Story: The story was a lot warmer than I expected...With an Ancient Greek setting, I thought it’d be way more twisted, but anyway this works well too. After all, even Virgil wrote: “Omnia vincit Amor et nos cedamus Amori.”

Hades is definitely one of the best games I've ever played, and by far the best rogue-like. There's so much abilities, powers, characters, and things to do that you can play for hours without the game getting boring, and everybody should get to experience this game. So for the game play, Hades is a rogue-like (more rogue-lite) dungeon crawler where you take on the role of the prince of the underworld, who must escape to find out about his past. The combat is very fluid and very fun. You can use a variety of weapons like a sword, spear, shield, and bow to hack and slash your way through chambers filled with enemies. You will also get to choose what chamber you go to next, and what reward it will yield. There's also many different powers and abilities you can get, like blessings from Olympians, weapon upgrades, and different currencies. All of these things, along with the 4 different levels you progress through, make it so every run feels unique, and you can play for hours without the game feeling repetitive or boring. Also the music and art style were amazing. You can tell that the game's art style was thoroughly made with an insane attention to detail, and the hand painted art style compliments the game and characters so well. The music was also so good, with each soundtrack perfectly matching the environments and setting the overall mood, and also they are also just plain awesome. And the story? Perfect. The way how each setback, each death, just unfolds more of the story is incredible. I won't say too much so you can experience it yourself, but it's very good. Also, every character is fully voice acted. Every single one. They all have different personalities and backstories too, which adds yet another layer of depth to the game. and you can even choose certain ones to strengthen your bond with. So this is normally the part where I put something bad, but the issue is I have literally nothing bad to say about Hades. Well, except for the fact that it ends. But since the developers couldn't have any negative aspects of the game, they decided to add an entire post-game, with it's own unique plot and events. I haven't played it yet ( my almost 38 hours were to just finish the main game), but I heard that it is still very good. So yeah Hades is my definition of a perfect game. In conclusion, please, do yourself a favor and just play Hades. It is by far worth the price, and even if you tried to speedrun the game and skip the entire story and character interactions, you would still get your moneys worth from this game. Hades deserves a Grammy, Oscar, and many game awards, but I can't give them those. What I can give them is a 10/10 for my final rating.

[b]Score: 8.3/10[/b] Hades was my first roguelike, and it honestly set the bar way too high. The story is my favorite part. The dialogue is genuinely funny, the characters are great, and I loved how Greek mythology is handled here. Unlocking things never felt boring either. New story moments, decorations, weapon aspects. Every run gives you something new to look forward to. The combat is smooth and satisfying, especially when you get a good combination of boons. Yes, it does get repetitive eventually… somewhere after 100+ runs. But it still feels worth continuing, since there are new dialogues even after all those runs. [b]Positives[/b] - Excellent writing and characters with lots of personality - Clever, engaging take on Greek mythology - Smooth, satisfying combat that feels great moment to moment [b]Negatives[/b] - The gameplay loop can become repetitive over time

My review after 100% achievements of the game is that I still feel like I have only touched half of the game. There are still so many things I still need to complete and many achievements to be earn. This is how great this game is. I played a lot of roguelike games but mainly card based or turn-based. This is my first time playing action roguelike game and I was blown away completely. This game is super hard but as you progress, you will feel that you've actually earned the progress. Unlike card based or turn-based, sometime it's all based on luck, Hades actually make you learn and improve your own skill. There is still RNG based skill called Boon but they are secondary compared to how you play with your own skill. This game also taught me how I weirdly hold controller in order to execute some impossible moves. I've bought this game across multiple platforms, with the Steam version being the most recent and of course definitive version. It's so much fun and having a prior intrigue of Greek mythology really helps the appeal of this game. I think you could still have plenty of fun even if the mythology isn't entirely your thing. The writing in this game is great. It's humorous at times but doesn't try too hard to make you laugh. The story and character development keep the replay value healthy despite running thru the same areas again and again. On paper, the replay value doesn't sound as good as it actually is. They did a great job of designing weapons, abilities, and progressive enhancements to keep things fresh. You're not going to care that you're repeating levels because the gameplay will be different with each weapon and the various skills. After hundreds of hours and multiple playthroughs on both difficulties I feel like this will be one of those games I won't tire of revisiting every other year or so. The game could be a bit difficult at first. After several attempts you will get better and more powerful combinations will be revealed. Achievements are not difficult but require a lot of patience. The devs really mastered the gameplay loop of a roguelite - after each attempt, you get a bit more story and a slight upgrade that gets you doing another run to unlock more. There's plenty of content and challenge, and achievements that are satisfying to earn too. Easily one of the best roguelikes I've ever played.

This is one of the most balanced games ever in terms of difficulty. Not simple enough to autopilot nor do you need an extensive wiki/youtube guide to understand the game. Other roguelite games I have played allow for much deeper character builds but also the possibility of losing a character multiple hours into a run. Hades strikes a perfect balance between casual and hardcore game experiences.
