So, 100%. My first game on Steam, fully completed. I think I'll make posts like this for every game I finish. I know no one cares, but personally, I want to keep a kind of diary of perfected games. This was a rather lengthy journey of 138 hours, with a short break for respite. This game has become one of the finest roguelikes for me, and the series as a whole is immensely compelling. The wealth of dialogue is a delight, as is the sheer number of weapons and their variations, ensuring that any shade can find a style of combat that suits them. Throughout the entire ordeal, one cannot miss how the creators were clearly passionate about their craft. The story is exceedingly well-woven, and every hero's motivation is perfectly clear and understandable. This leaves no frustrating questions about the characters, and the tapestry of the world remains intact. The game's visuals are incredibly striking. The art of the ancient Greek structures, the overall aesthetic, the design of the characters and foes—it's all a constant pleasure. Each region is distinct in its colour palette, its roster of adversaries, and even its pace, so the action never grows stale, right until the very end. A separate tribute must be paid to the composers. These mortals knew their craft, and the music resonated with me immensely. I hold a particular preference for "Lament of Orpheus," the tabs for which the developers have kindly released unto the world, so any who wish may learn to play it. For me, this is one of the best and most meticulously-wrought roguelikes. I am truly glad I spent my time upon it. I give it a 9.5 out of 10. I deduct a mere 0.5 because the gameplay grew ever so slightly repetitive around the 130th hour, but I suppose that is an inescapable fate. That is all. My thanks if you have read my thoughts on this game. Blood and darkness... Fear is for the weak!

Rarely has achieving 100% on a game been such a consistent source of entertainment and marvel at a game's near-perfect construction (prophecy of Night and Darkness being the forgivable exception). As many others have noted, the voice-acting and scripting of your interactions with the pantheon of Greek gods is of a really high quality throughout - and you really have to play the hell out of the game for any of these interactions to repeat. Add to that some of the best music and songs in gaming, imaginative and credible use of the source material, hours of fulfilling endgame content, wide variety of enemies, intelligent (but beatable) bosses, fun gameplay and a real sense of achievement through victory due to the tight balancing, means this is a real throroughbred that you need in your library. The almost unbelievable attention to detail in this game is something every designer should take note of. There's a reason the reviews for this game are overwhelmingly positive and that is because it is a bona fide masterpiece.

Hades is an outstanding roguelite that shines brightest in its story, voicelines, art style, and systems for progression and combat. Based on the title, it is no secret that it is based on the Greek gods, and characters are expanded on from that premise. Story and voicelines should essentially be discussed together, as almost all of the story is uncovered through character interactions. The voice actors and actresses did an amazing and extremely thorough job as, over the course of my journey from the start of this game to the end, I don't recall ever hearing the same voiceline twice. The story is uncovered through talking with the other characters, giving them gifts, increasing their trust and successfully completing runs. There are several smaller stories contained within the larger story and it is satisfying to see them develop and play out. The larger and smaller stories are extremely compelling, leaving the player wanting to see more. The art style is very interesting, using large shadows and vibrant colors for contrast to create a comic book aesthetic. It is highly stylized and helps to make the world feel unique and interesting. This art style makes both the levels and the hub between runs interesting in different ways - the levels look intense and mysterious while the hub, with its customization, is more warm and cozy. Also, the characters can be absolute thirst traps, so consider that a simultaneous warning and invitation. Progression and combat are handled well, with the player being able to unlock a large mix of persistent buffs, equippable "keepsake" items to provide extra unique buffs, weapons, and weapon variations. In addition, once the player can clear the game normally, they are given access to certain difficulty modifiers to make the game harder in exchange for more loot. The player is not obligated to increase the difficulty, but is rewarded for doing so, which is a great way to add another level of variance to the game loop. Combat is very fast, rewarding quick movements, reflexes and enemy knowledge on a micro level and rewarding strategy and knowledge of item and upgrade combinations to achieve satisfying results on a macro level. I'd say I only have one negative thing to say about Hades. Even though I mentioned the unique combinations of weapons, weapon variants, items and difficulty modifiers, the enemies and environments that the player battles through largely remain the same. For some people, this may still make the repetitiveness of the runs start to feel stale over time. By the same token, there also comes a point where, once the stories are complete, the player will eventually run out of stuff to do, and then it is likely time to move on. I don't think this is a bad thing, though - the player can enjoy the experience, leave and then return in the future if they want to relive it. Most games should not go on forever, those that do start to feel less like a game and more like a job. Overall, I highly recommend Hades to those looking for a satisfying story and some fast, challenging gameplay.

Finally typing up a review for this after having just done so for the sequel. It's been almost two years since I 100%'ed the original Hades, and almost four years since I had finished the true ending. I played Hades in roughly three phases: 1) In early 2021 I played for about a week until I finally managed my first clear. I enjoyed it quite a bit, but didn't really grasp the mechanics well enough to understand what future progression would feel like. The soundtrack was an absolute banger, and it made sense to me why everyone was praising this so much but the grind towards that first clear was enough for now. 2) It took me until late 2021 to go back for more. Over the course of about two months managed to finish the main story. That's when it truly clicked and I got good – now regularly clearing full runs rather than struggling to do so occasionally. But finishing all the remaining prophecies after the true ending felt very daunting and grindy, so I was satisfied with leaving it at that. 3) In January 2024, now deeply committed to my "try to 100% every game I enjoy" approach, I decided to finally tackle this one. It still felt daunting, and I was even mildly worried I'd burn myself out and take away from my love for the game. But that didn't happen, on the contrary. No longer worried about spoilers I looked up how to proceed certain prophecies, as well as guides for the different weapons and aspects. In my second phase I had gotten good with a few specific setups, but for full completion I now needed to engage with everything the game had to offer. Only now did I really understand the full depth of what this masterpiece actually had to offer, and it didn't take long before it felt like I was breezing through towards 100% completion just the same way I was towards the full ending earlier. During that third phase I also enjoyed the Noclip documentary about the development of the game – the passion and craftsmanship on display made appreciate the game even more. After 100 hours in Hades and another 100 hours in Hades 2 I'm probably saturated for a while – but their good vibes are always with me in the form of the soundtracks.

[h1][b]Hades – Highly Recommended[/b][/h1] [b]After 27 hours of playtime[/b], and as someone who has never really been into roguelike games, I can confidently say Hades is fantastic. This was my first game in the genre, and I was immediately hooked by how addictive and rewarding it is. [h2][b]Visuals & Art Style[/b][/h2] The art style is outstanding. The colors, animations, and character designs are polished and stylish, all heavily inspired by Greek mythology. Every area and character feels unique and full of personality. [h2][b]Story & Setting[/b][/h2] You play as Zagreus attempting to escape the Underworld from your father, Hades. The story unfolds naturally as you play, with plenty of dialogue that adds depth without ever feeling overwhelming or slowing the game down. [h2][b]Combat & Weapons[/b][/h2] Combat is fast, smooth, and incredibly satisfying. There are multiple weapons, each with its own moveset and playstyle, letting you choose between ranged, melee, or aggressive close-quarters builds. [h2][b]Progression & Customization[/b][/h2] Progression is where the game really shines. Each run lets you customize your build using different god powers, giving you the freedom to experiment and play the game your own way. No two runs feel the same. [h2][b]Difficulty & Replayability[/b][/h2] This isn’t a game you beat quickly—you’ll die a lot. But every run makes you stronger and better, which keeps you coming back. It’s frustrating, fun, and extremely addictive once it clicks. [u][b]Pros[/b][/u] • Excellent art style and presentation • Addictive combat and progression • Great weapon and build variety • Strong story and character dialogue • High replay value [u][b]Cons[/b][/u] • Can be frustrating at times • Repeated deaths aren’t for everyone [h1][b]Final Verdict[/b][/h1] If you’ve ever been curious about roguelike games, Hades is an excellent place to start. Even if the genre isn’t usually your thing, this game’s combat, progression, and presentation make it incredibly easy to get hooked. [h1][b]Highly recommended—especially if you catch it on sale.[/b][/h1] 🔥🎮

Completed 100% Overall grade : 9/10 I purchased this game on sale due to the hype about the release of the second one. It is a roguelike in which you play as the son of the god of the dead trying to escape his father's realm facing hordes of enemies and collecting "boon" power-ups from the gods of Olympus to become more powerful. PROS: - Progression: The game has an amazing progression system that makes it so every run you unlock something new. It might be small or big but it still helps overall. Every run I would go a bit further and became a bit stronger. Even after you beat the game once you get a new "endless" progression system where you can get more rewards by making the run harder. - Dialogue and NPCs: The game feels like it has endless dialogue with it's array of fun and plentiful characters. They will either say the next line that's queued up or, more likely, comment on something you have done. Even in the hub there was always someone to talk to and some quest to progress. For a game like this where you essentially do the same thing over and over this was great to see. - Quests and Collectables: During my runs I always made it a priority to do the quests or collect resources that helped me upgrade my hub. It kept me busy and entertained, no need to say more. - Boons and Weapons: The boon powers you get from the gods are all fun and different, and you have a tone of ways to combine them and even together with the many weapons to create very powerful and fun builds. You can also use some items and talents to affect these boons so there are many layers of options. That being said, I didn't enjoy using all of the weapons but opinions online vary. CONS: - Lack of level and enemy variety: The game focuses on quality over quantity. And it is filled to the brim with content for sure. However if you will excuse the spoiler, the game has only a few levels and just as many bosses. Sure all of them (except for 1 very boring boss) change depending on your actions and progression, but compared to other roguelikes that have several times that number of levels it can feel a bit predictable after 10-20 runs. The mobs are also mostly the same every playthrough so you will focus on beating them as fast as possible to get to the next reward and dopamine hit. - Strong presence of "woke" political ideals: The game features the ancient Greek pantheon and mythology. And yet many of the characters are featured having skin shades a lot darker than they should be. There are also many LQBT themes and characters. The game also beats you over the head with the importance of consent, even for some very trivial things. That being said it's not as bad as some other games, which is reflected in it's overwhelmingly positive grade, but I know there are those among you who don't tolerate any of this so I felt it needed to be pointed out. Overall I recommend this game, it gave me about 100 hours of fun, quick action and it's worth the price tag. Even better, it's often on sale.

I rarely write reviews, but Hades absolutely deserves the additional praise. I'm sure it has been said a thousand times already, but if you are here because you checked a box for action roguelike or roguelite you should absolutely check this title out, and if not you should check it out even sooner. There are few games that deliver on that concept as handily as Supergiant's Hades. If you've never played this style of game you're in for a treat. I would 100% recommend this as an entry point into the genre, I envy your opportunity to start here. This belongs in a hall of fame with other champions such as TBOI. If this franchise is not already on every list of the top 10 games in this category I would be shocked. Well done. Review: Elegant simplicity of initial game play meets exceptional attention to detail in every aspect and subtle satisfying growth in complexity as the game progresses. This game nails every element that keeps you coming back again and again in a great roguelite. 5 years after release and it still stands out. I am confident I will still be revisiting this game for years to come. Hades 2 looks just as brilliant and receives glowing reviews as well. That game caught my eye first, and I am extremely happy with my decision to play this one before starting the next installment. It was absolutely worth visiting first, and the main complaint seems to be that Hades 2 did not break the mold cast by Hades enough. I can't wait to check it out, more of the same with a few new tricks and some additional polish based on player feedback sounds perfect to me! The storytelling is clever, often relying on, but rarely (if ever) suffering from,character exposition. The tale of Prince Zagreus attempting to leave the nest and the story of his motivations comes across in cleverly executed triggered events which mostly take the form of bite-sized often humorous banter between characters. The blending of a few reenactments and witty dialogue in the retelling of what brought the protagonist to his current state really shines. Hades may not hold the number one spot for depth of story in my library, but it hits it out of the park on lore and theme. This game absolutely delivers a solid and engaging story in a clever way. Honestly the polished, exciting, and dynamic game play alone would shine enough to have hidden a lot of sins, but this game has nothing to hide. 10/10 Note: I'm not an all-in completionist by nature. I usually play games intensely for a moderate duration until something else captures my attention and I move on to the next exciting thing. That said, I am confident that I will be 100%-ing hades at least once, likely again at the 10 year anniversary. TLDR: Buy this game... You'll wish you had bought it yesterday and downloaded it already... You're welcome.

Hades is a really fun game. Seems to me like the perfect harnessing of the pick-3 semi-random build schtick in that it gives you enough levers to nudge the randomness around so that you very rarely feel like you've been screwed over by RNG. The really impressive part of this game, however, is the narrative. It takes the same roguelike setup we've seen many times and constructs a world around it that incorporates every single game mechanic in a way that is not only narratively believable but often emotionally engaging. Many of the bosses are full characters in themselves. You develop relationships with them. You loathe some of them (♥♥♥♥ Theseus), but you respect or love just as many of them. There's an all-encompasing feeling of rightness to the game that is constantly surprising. It will introduce a new mechanic to you, and you will engage with it at first on that mechanical level. And by the second or third time you see it, it will dawn on you that is *exactly* what makes sense for this world. And the game just never stops doing that. The best no-spoiler example I've got is the double boon rooms you start running into. They are a fantastic mechanical proposition, because they carry an extremely potent reward, but they are usually challenging enough to really cost you something. Just on that level, it's a really interesting choice to have to make. But then you realize that all of these gods are petty, jealous, vindictive little ♥♥♥♥♥, and *of course* they'd fly into a rage and try and kill you for a moment if you announced somebody else was your favorite. The whole game is like that. The characters and the world pull the extremely impressive trick of transforming what ought to be extremely reality-disrupting gamification and turning them into synergistic narrative threads from which to tell a compelling story. I've completely lost track of how many times I said to myself nearly the exact thing Zagreus says in-game in response to something, each time making me realize that my mechanical experience as a player of this game and his narrative experience as the protagonist of that game are so often on exactly the same page. Anyway, it's real good. Play it.

Replayed on PC. Excellent rogue-like that hooks you in quick with so much build variety and depth for an unforgettable experience. Pros: - Addictive Gameplay - Boss Design - Build Variety - Art Design - Characters - Unique Story Structure - Challenge-Reward System - Music - Humor Cons: - True ending requirements (The grind adds to the tediousness) - Area repetition (Can become tedious when going for the true ending) I’m not typically a fan of rogue-likes but Hades is an exception. There’s so much to praise that the game does well so I’ll highlight a few things that really stick out: build variety, unique characters, and the core gameplay loop. Each weapon is customizable via different aspects, boons, and hammer enchantments where each run is almost always different from the last. You start to learn and craft your favorite builds as you progress. There are so many different weapons and builds to find your favorite playstyle. As for characters, the gods themselves each have their own character traits with so much different dialogue where it’s fun to see what new things they’ll say depending on what you’ve done throughout each run. In addition to that, NPC’s you speak with can have small character arcs filled with good writing that result in rewards and character pay-off. It’s a great way to handle story in a game built around 25 - 40 minute runs. Speaking of the length per run, the gameplay loop is utterly addictive which in combination with the build variety and randomness of choices you can make, is hard to replicate runs with power-ups unless you know exactly what you’re trying to do. Something else to note is that between each run, you get stronger by using the resources you pick up which makes consecutive runs easier and you can even make the game harder with challenges that actively give you rewards that you’ll want to use to unlock more stuff. Many ideas work in tandem with one another and that’s exactly why this game was praised at release and will continue to be praised as one of the best indie’s ever made. My only complaints are that (1) going through the same areas can get a bit old even with the variety of different arenas & combat challenges within them and (2) requiring to grind out items to get the true ending. Overall, it’s an amazing game and still addictive even after playing the sequel as Zagreus has a different playstyle, albeit more simplistic, compared to what Hades 2 iterates on with the main character. If you’re a fan of rogue-likes, this is a no-brainer to pick up, even at full price, due to the overall quality, length, discovery, and character writing. 9.5/10.

Hades is one of those rare games that grabs you from the first run and somehow keeps getting better every time you die. Supergiant Games has absolutely nailed the roguelike formula — tight, satisfying combat, layered storytelling, and gorgeous presentation all woven together seamlessly. Every escape attempt as Zagreus feels unique thanks to the huge variety of weapons, boons, and upgrades from the Olympian gods. The writing is sharp, full of personality, and makes every character feel alive (and weirdly relatable — even the god of death). What really stands out is how the narrative evolves through repeated failure — the game expects you to die, and uses it to deepen the story and world instead of punishing you. The art direction is stunning, the voice acting is top-tier, and Darren Korb’s soundtrack absolutely rips — it’s easily one of the best game soundtracks out there. Whether you’re a roguelike veteran or new to the genre, Hades is pure, addictive brilliance. There’s always something new to discover, and the gameplay loop is so satisfying it’s almost dangerous. Pros: - Incredibly polished combat - Deep and rewarding progression - Amazing writing and characters - One of the best soundtracks in gaming Cons: - You will lose sleep trying to “just do one more run” Final Verdict: A masterpiece of design and storytelling. Worth every drop of ichor.

[b]ROGUISH EXCELLENCE WITH A RIDICULOUS ENDGAME[/b] [u]The Good[/u] Supremely addictive core gameplay loop - the DNA of previous SuperGiant games is clearly on display with some amazing additions to randomise and elevate each run. Amazing production values coupled with an engaging cast of characters, charming and voiced with aplomb. Plenty to do and "getting gud" is certainly a thing here. [u]The Bad[/u] Holy GRIND but the requirements to unlock the true ending is REDONKULOUS and takes too much time. The RNG is a real killer and if you're after "seeing it all" (as I was), you might just give up at a certain point (as I did), even after modding certain elements to accelerate it all (as I did). Of course it's a genre thing, but I do think there could have been a smarter way to stage all this out. [u]The Summary[/u] I got this on the recent sale and it was more than worth every penny. Seldom does a game grab and engage you in all respects (gameplay/story/art/music) but Hades is a sublime package through-and-through, and highly, highly recommended.

Hades is a masterpiece, a perfect blend of lightning-fast combat, rich storytelling, and stunning presentation. Every run feels fresh thanks to the endless mix of divine boons, weapons and upgrades, creating a gameplay loop that never gets old. The soundtrack is electrifying, the art direction is gorgeous, and the world design drips with atmosphere. Boss fights are intense and perfectly balanced, testing both skill and patience, while the Pact of Punishment modifiers keep the challenge alive for veterans. What truly elevates Hades, though, is its cast: every character, from Zagreus and the Olympian gods to the denizens of the House of Hades, is beautifully written, voiced, and full of heart. Their intertwined stories give weight to every death and make each escape attempt feel meaningful. Supergiant Games has crafted an experience that’s as punishing as it is rewarding: elegant, emotional, and endlessly replayable. See you in hell, where every defeat only makes the next victory divine.

The embellished repetition upon which this game is built is a well-calculated facade masking its own nature [repeat with marginal progress and small variants]. If you aim to enjoy some quality hours, its great and finely built, as the nuanced texts mingle with new interesting mechanics. For longer periods, please let me withdraw.

Hades is a game that doesn't seem to miss on anything it tries to accomplish. A perfect example on how to weave an appreciatively simple story and excellent cast of unique characters based on Greek myth (there’s also surprisingly dense dialogue here and quality to match it that can make even crpg games blush) with the exciting randomness of the roguelike action genre. By offering different perks, skills, weapons and dungeon layouts, custom difficulty, enemy variety or sometimes even boss encounters each run is truly unique by nature, and by completing or dying during it you unlock further dialogue or resources that fuel your next try. It’s simple a gameplay loop that urges you to play and play some more but what really keeps you engaged is the quality that it offers. Hearing everyone sing its praises the cynic in me really tried hard to find a smidge to point at and complain about but damnable game didn't seem to stumble in my 100h playtime, it simply was that laser focused on being plain fun and a joy to play - always a new build to try or some fun character to listen to. And the OST is a bop. So what I mean to say is: Hades is worth you time. Play this, seriously.

[h1][b][i]Hades[/i][/b][/h1] [hr][/hr] I really enjoyed almost everything about this game. The story is great, and the characters are even better. Dusa especially ended up being one of my favorites. Having to purposely die just to get new dialogue can be frustrating, and when new events pile up, it takes forever to see the ones you actually care about. The voice acting, art, and portraits are top-notch. The soundtrack is amazing too, though after seventy runs you might end up muting it and putting on your own music. Even with the grind, this is still one of the best roguelikes around. It’s stylish, and worth every escape attempt. A masterpiece that can drag a bit, but never loses its heart.

The story keeps you untertained, and each character have depth that you unravel during your interactions with them. The game has an great replayability, with the possibility to ramp up the difficulty in late game.

[h2]Gameplay-story synergy[/h2] In Hades, you're tasked with escaping from home and your overbearing lord father (but not really) to see the outside world. In doing so, you accidentally find your estranged mother, who, plot twist, doesn't know that you're alive. To maintain ludonarrative consistency with the game's roguelite mechanics, you keep escaping over and over, even though the Greek air is disagreeable to your personal health -- our main man, Zagreus, is hopelessly addicted to making bad decisions. Along the way, your heavenly aunts, uncles & cousins offer to help because (a) they dislike your father (b) they're convinced you're legit trying to escape to visit them. Eventually they find out your deception as well as the whereabouts of your estranged mother (in whom they have a vested interest), resulting in peak mythological family drama...

Maybe my most played on Steamdeck so I thought I would review it since I have been playing the second game. This game is easy to pickup and honestly insanely addictive. It follows the formula of a roguelite. You go out each night and gain temporary upgrades that change how your weapons hit enemies whether its knockback water from poseidon or deflect from athena. Every time you die, you get to spend some type of currency on permanent upgrades that follow you between runs. Due to this repetition, most other roguelites get boring quick or rely solely on gameplay. Hades has a great story with super memorable characters and due to subject matter -dying and respawning is recognized by the world and its characters. An NPC might mention something that just happened or have some natural progression in dialogue as you chip away at the game run after run. Even if you are not demolishing the enemies, it is fun to just listen to the gods talk to you about things. You will hardly ever hear a repeated line which keeps the game fresh. It is perfect for when you don't want to play a long form game and sometimes I tryharded and other times I just mindlessly needed something before bed. Before you know it, you have many many permanent/persistent upgrades and the runs become easier and easier so you can have resources and resolve for the later run areas that are still hard. Eventually clearing runs feels more than doable with the right build that night. Once you do complete a run, its not over. There are so many bonus handicaps and other challenges. It is fun to try out the different weapons and weapon variants. Completing more runs unlocks a little more of the story until you get the conclusion. It is one of the defining games in this genre. I am a poser but I hold it up there with Binding of Isaac in that this game got alot of people and devs onto this style of design. The second one is shaping up to be everything the first game was and more.

I enjoy the structure of the game a great deal. During and after a run, whether you win or lose, you generally make progress in the story and overall meta progression. I think the voice acting, music and sound design are absolutely outstanding. I enjoy the story, how it unfolds and progresses a lot. While I enjoyed the combat the majority of the time, it could feel repetitive compared to other roguelikes now and again. When it comes to (difficulty) accessibility, I appreciate the developers making the game more accessible to players who might not be as proficient at the combat part for whatever reason through God Mode, which gives the player more damage resistance that grows gradually with every death. This makes the story accessible in a way few other games with combat do. On the other end of the difficulty spectrum, the developers give players a variety of options to increase the difficulty, which I think helps keep the combat engaging in the later stages. In part as a consequence of the aforementioned structure, the game does not offer interesting replay value to me personally, neither in the form of continued runs after having finished the story and unlocked everything or starting over entirely. Overall, in my opinion Hades is a well-rounded game that excels at mixing the roguelike formula with an engaging story. It is definitely worth playing or at least trying for anyone with even a slight interest in what it has to offer.

[h3][b]I don’t say this lightly: [i]Hades[/i] is easily one of the best games of all time.[/b] [/h3] Every few years, a game emerges that is so outrageously good, so groundbreaking, that it redefines the art form itself. History divides into “Before X Game” and “After X Game.” [i]Hades[/i] is unquestionably one of those games. It almost feels like a disservice to give it a mere 10/10—games like this break the scales we use to measure them. That’s why it unironically earns a very rare, symbolic 11/10 from me. What still blows my mind is how the game [i]sees you.[/i] Every obscure thing you do somehow gets acknowledged. A specific example that sticks with me: I used the "Extreme Measures" Pact of Punishment, which changes boss fights and makes them harder. Then, the next run, I removed those modifiers and picked different ones. Not only did the game notice that I picked that specific pact of punishment, but it also noticed that I had [i]removed it[/i] in my next run — it wove that change into the narrative through dialogue seamlessly. The boss commented on how they had “better gear last time” but would still defeat me even now. That level of dynamic response happens [i]constantly[/i]. It's genuinely mind-boggling how cohesive the entire narrative is, nothing feels out of place or gamey[i]. [/i]Even after 100+ hours and unlocking all the achievements, I’ve yet to hear a [i]single repeated line of dialogue[/i]. And when you learn there are about [b]22,000 lines in total—8,500 from Zagreus himself—it makes sense.[/b] Which brings me to a fun little fact that I feel morally obliged to mention every time I get the chance: the guy responsible for almost all the music and sound effects in every Supergiant game, [b]Darren Korb [/b](living legend btw), is also the [i]voice actor[/i] for Zagreus. So yes, the main character literally [i]sings[/i] his own story. A single brilliant man is responsible for the majority of the audio in Hades. Fun fact for next time you play. I don’t say this lightly either, but [i]Hades[/i] might be one of the best [i]designed[/i] games ever made. Its gameplay and system design are out of this world. I’d bet the developers would agree that part of that brilliance comes from its early access phase — you can’t reach this level of polish and balance without thousands of players giving direct feedback and data. That’s not to downplay the developers’ genius. They’re still responsible for ninety percent of the design choices. Without going full game-dev-mode in my analysis, it’s staggering how intricately the systems interlock. Take boons, for example. They’re designed modularly, meaning the player discovers their own weird, golden combinations through experimentation. Every run feels like finding buried treasure. And if you’re paying even a little attention, you’ll stumble into a new build [i]every damn time.[/i] Please, do yourself a favor and don’t look up “optimal strategies.” Not only are most of them flat-out wrong, but they suck all the joy out of discovery and turn the game into number-crunching on a spreadsheet. [i]Hades[/i] is meant to be played with curiosity, not calculation. As Sully famously said in [i]Uncharted 3;[/i] "Greatness is what you do with the hand you're dealt" and the game rewards you for learning how to play with that hand — and that’s what makes it endlessly rewarding. Something in [i]Hades [/i]hit me on a personal level — probably deeper than the developers ever intended. The story of Zagreus is about persistence in the face of futility. Despite fighting through literal hell, defeating the God of Death himself, and finally reaching the surface and tasting the freedom you've been desperately chasing, [i]the Fates themselves[/i] pull the strings making you die and go back to square one[i].[/i] You must return. And yet, despite all that, despite it being borderline impossible for you to escape, you rise again. Over and over. You fight through the same torment, fully aware that you’ll fail, that the metaphorical boulder will roll back down. But you do it anyway. That’s why the real protagonist of Hades isn’t Zagreus — it’s [b]Sisyphus[/b]! Well... not literally (he’s actually in the game, cheerful as ever), but spiritually. The game embodies the same existential defiance Albert Camus wrote about in [i]The Myth of Sisyphus[/i]t: finding meaning through the struggle itself. For me, that hit frighteningly close to home. Without getting personal, I can say this: the idea of endlessly striving despite inevitable failure has never felt more human — or more beautiful — than it does in [i]Hades[/i]. And those reasons are 1% of why [i]Hades[/i] is so special. [h1]11/10.[/h1]

[i]Find more of my reviews on my curator page: [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45817624-Kasurot-Recommends/]Kasurot Recommends[/url][/i] --- [h2]Short Summary[/h2] Defy the god of the dead in this divine roguelike. Fast-paced action, brilliant writing, and a deeply compelling story of family make escaping hell irresistible. [h2]The Takeaway[/h2] [list] [*] [h3]Bright Spots / What Works[/h3] Exhilarating fast-paced isometric action, an incredibly deep and synergistic Boon system granted by Olympian gods, and a highly addictive roguelike structure perfected. [*] [h3]What Might Not Suit You[/h3] The core roguelike loop involves repetition of areas, run success can sometimes feel influenced by random Boon offerings, and unlocking final story secrets requires a dedicated late-game grind. [*] [h3]What It's About[/h3] A surprisingly resonant story exploring family dysfunction and reconciliation within Greek myth, emphasizing persistence against failure and Zagreus's fight for self-determination. [*] [h3]How It Plays[/h3] Gameplay masterfully drives the narrative forward through its death/rebirth cycle, provides incredibly addictive and stylish action, and facilitates rich character interactions both during runs and in the hub. [*] [h3]Core Tone[/h3] A brilliant mix of witty, charming character dialogue and intense, action-packed gameplay, all underpinned by surprisingly heartfelt emotional depth. [*] [h3]Series & Genre Context[/h3] Developed by Supergiant Games, [b]Hades[/b] represents a culmination of their signature style (seen in [b]Bastion[/b], [b]Transistor[/b], [b]Pyre[/b]) applied to the roguelike genre. It became a critical darling and commercial success, significantly popularizing narrative integration within roguelikes. [*] [h3]Technical Snapshot[/h3] The PC version is exceptionally well-optimized, running flawlessly on a wide variety of hardware with a crisp, distinct art style. It offers essential graphics settings, supports various resolutions and input methods (controller highly recommended but KBM viable with remapping), and includes minor accessibility options like subtitle adjustments. [/list] [h2]Main Review[/h2] In [b]Hades[/b], you embody the rebellious Prince Zagreus, immortal son of the eponymous god, utterly determined to escape his father's domain in the Underworld. This defiant quest serves as the backdrop for a surprisingly deep exploration of family dysfunction, persistence, and self-determination within the colorful tapestry of Greek mythology. As Zagreus, you collect powerful Boons from your Olympian relatives, unravel long-hidden family secrets through countless attempts, and gradually forge unexpected connections within the House of Hades and beyond. The defining gameplay experience is a masterclass in isometric action fused with addictive roguelike design. Combat is incredibly fast, fluid, and responsive, built around distinct weapon styles and a crucial dash mechanic. Each escape attempt sees you gaining temporary Boons from various gods, which combine in complex and satisfying ways, allowing for immense build variety. Death is not an end but a narrative beat, sending you back to the beginning but armed with permanent resources and new story insights, making the core loop of trying, dying, and improving utterly compelling. The Underworld and its inhabitants burst with personality, carried by sharp, witty writing and phenomenal voice acting. The dominant tone expertly balances this charming character interaction and sarcastic humor with the high-octane intensity of combat encounters, complemented by Darren Korb's iconic, driving rock soundtrack. Yet, beneath the style and action lies a genuinely heartfelt story. The narrative unfolds incrementally through clever integration with the roguelike structure; failure itself becomes the primary engine for pacing, revealing new dialogue, advancing relationships, and driving the plot forward one death at a time. [b]Hades[/b] is a landmark title, widely regarded as one of the greatest roguelikes ever made and a pinnacle of independent game development. Supergiant Games perfected the fusion of engaging, repeatable gameplay with a deeply compelling, character-driven narrative that evolves organically through the genre's inherent structure. Its brilliant writing, exceptional art, stellar music, and addictive core loop earned it universal acclaim, significantly influencing subsequent roguelikes and demonstrating the powerful storytelling potential within the genre. [h2]The Verdict[/h2] This game is an absolute triumph and a must-play for fans of action games, roguelikes, compelling stories, and Greek mythology. While the inherent repetition of the genre might feel grindy to some, and run success involves an element of luck, these are minor aspects within an extraordinarily polished and rewarding package. Its structure offers tremendous replay value through different weapons, builds, and escalating challenges. [i]If you seek a divine blend of action, story, and style that respects your time while demanding mastery, descend into Hades – you won't want to leave.[/i]

“I didn’t escape, but I fell in love with dying.” After 18 hours, Hades has completely hooked me. Every run feels meaningful even when I fail (which is often), the game rewards me with story progression, character dialogue, and new upgrades that make me want to jump right back in. The combat is fast, fluid, and incredibly satisfying. Each weapon changes the playstyle dramatically, and the boons from the Olympian gods keep every run fresh. One moment I’m a lightning-throwing blur blessed by Zeus, the next I’m dashing through enemies with Aphrodite’s charms it never gets old. What surprised me most is how story and roguelike mechanics blend so naturally. The voice acting is top-tier, the characters are all charming (even the ones trying to kill me), and Zagreus’ personality grows on you fast. The art style and soundtrack are also pure perfection. If you’re into roguelikes, Greek mythology, or just want a game that respects your time and effort Hades is a must-play. Even after 18 hours, I still feel like I’m only scratching the surface. 10/10 — “Just one more run.”

Insanely overrated game imo that is more flashy than anything and doesn't hold a candle to Isaac from a mechanical and content point of view. I feel like I'm the only person who could not get into Hades and does not understand the extremely high praise. The artstyle is complete overkill. Combined with the isometric perspective, it's far too visually overwhelming, to the point of making my vision blurry and giving me eye fatigue even half-way into a single run, which sucks a lot when you are trying to focus on fighting things. The visual complexity feels like they give you too much of a good thing to the point of it becoming bad again. There are so many colors, effects and other unnecessary nonsense on-screen that simply feel distracting. In addition to this the playstyle wears on your hands very fast and feels rather braindead. You spam dodges for very generous i-frames, and you are gonna do that A LOT considering how visually cluttered the game is and how you can abuse spam attack and dodge at the same time. The balancing feels weird. Normal enemies are a complete pushover and can be stunlocked and steamrolled. On the other hand bosses have insane health pools and attacks that are barely telegraphed, so you get slowly wittled down while chipping at them for five minutes non-stop. Then there are regular enemies with a yellow aura around them, who are complete damage-sponges that are immune to any kind of stagger. Awful and unfun balancing. The gameplay loop and amount of content feels very repetitive. I am already bored after just a few runs. You always fight the exact same boss in the same area with the same handful of different enemies per area while getting dripfed miniscule amounts of lore or story during or in between said runs. I highly doubt it even comes cloes to the variety and unlockable content of other rogue-like games such as TBoI. It seems the rogue-like mechanics mostly boil down to what reward you get per room and the meta currencies instead of having a wide deck of meaningful options mid-run, which seems rather disappointing for something that is supposed to be one of the most praised games of this genre. Besides mildly differing weapons and blessings there is nothing meaningful to make each run feel unique and fresh. The Overwhelmingly Positive reviews seem like a bit of an exaggeration. All Hades has strongly going for it are the story and attention to detail in environments and dialogue. The characters do look tacky and overdesigned, but that one is probably more of a subjective thing. Otherwise I seriously do not understand the high ratings this game received. Somehow it even has more reviews than TBoI. I am truly and utterly baffled.

Revisiting this game in preparation for Hades II (yes I'm a year late) Ultimately it's hard to *not* recommend this game. Even if you're not even a fan of roguelites/dungeon games, the game is worth experiencing just for the amazing artwork, music and a refreshing contemporary take on the classic Greek myth. It's dialogue system is extremely detailed, and the game often reacts to what you are doing as a player. I couldn't help but to be amazed every time I noticed a subtle detail like this. For example, if you beat your previous record time, a character will notice and give compliments in your next run. The story progression is done in a really clever way, slowly unlocking new pieces as you finish or even lose runs. The combat itself is tight, the controls are precise and work for both keyboard and controller really well. There are good amount of enemy variety, requiring different tactics to beat them. Certain enemies reward aggression, while others demand more defensive and opportunistic combat style. The different weapon aspects all feel unique, yet some feel considerably weaker than others. Really my main issue with this game is the way you build your character during runs. The skills (boons) you get are completely randomized, and many times I felt like I lost the run to pure bad luck because I didn't get any of the build-defining boons, or I had severe anti-synergy in my build. Many games of this genre have solved this issue by some kind of shop mechanic, but in Hades the shop still only contains only one boon, and sometimes a literal blind bag. Later on, there are ways to mitigate this by re-rolls, but they are extremely limited. This is probably just a me-issue, because I think the roguelikes I've played have generally allowed for a wider range of exploration and experimentation with different builds.

A VERY WEAK ROGUELIKE I read reviews saying this is a great roguelike and the best indie game ever, so I bought it expecting a truly great experience. And the game's style really won me over. It looks really good, especially for an indie game. But that's where the positives end for me. The game is criminally lacking in everything a truly high-quality roguelike should have: Very few enemies and bosses. Once you've completed the game, you've practically seen everything. The enemies are almost always the same and don't change at all throughout the game. This quickly becomes boring, as do the bosses, of which there are also very few. Roughly speaking, there are only four bosses and a few variations, not particularly different from each other. Even the boss models are identical, only slightly different in color. There are only four zones, and the locations within them are rather bland and not very distinctive from each other. The game seems to have several types of weapons, but they all feel almost the same. Here are a few melee weapons, here are a couple of ranged ones. But ultimately, it all boils down to frantic button mashing without any strategy. It's unlikely you'll be able to create any crazy builds; everything about it is boring. Many enemies have armor, meaning they don't react to your attacks until you remove it. It's unclear why it's there, other than to artificially stretch the gameplay. Speaking of artificially stretching the gameplay, there's everyone's favorite metaprogression, where you'll spend dozens of hours collecting resources to boost your stats. It's certainly very engaging (not). I'd like to point out that often, with a large number of enemies, everything goes to hell, and it's completely unclear where or who's throwing something up your ass. There's a plot here. Why? I don't know. Often, reading all these endless dialogues is uninteresting and makes you want to skip. Apparently, the point was that roguelikes usually have little or no plot. And here, supposedly, they decided to break the system. Well, probably because roguelikes are played for the gameplay, not for a second-rate plot written by some students. There's a lot more I could write about this game, but I don't feel like it. In short, it's a very weak roguelike that doesn't live up to the standards of the genre. Perhaps if they'd made a decent single-player adventure lasting a few hours, I'd have far fewer complaints.

Bought the game for the 5th anniversary while it was on discount. I got my first clear at about 6 hours, and finished the game 27 hours in. It does a great job at tying together story and gameplay (and I do mean great, every gameplay mechanic exists for a reason). The combat isn't super flashy or complex: you have a basic attack, dodge attack, special and a ranged attack. You can chain together the attacks really easily, and you're encouraged to do so. The difficulty comes from the enemies, who all have pretty different movesets and feel distinguished, although some of them can be annoying. Other aspects like the music and background are well made but don't stand out too much. Although, the music could be a bit more varied. You can also decorate your spawn area but this costs a currency that's in high demand, which means that I haven't meaningfully interacted with it until now - after I've finished the game. Not a notable part of the game. There is also a system to build friendships with characters, but it's very difficult to max out a friendship because you don't get much of the required resource, and oftentimes, you don't see the character once you do get it. It has good replayability, given that it's key to finishing the game, but YOU need to be the one to try out new things. The game won't force you to try out new builds or force you to work under certain conditions. You can increase difficulty by adding new mechanics to get more rewards. There are lots of collectionist objectives if you like that, and I want to continue improving my character and their weapon. Overall, great game, everybody is slightly British, but it doesn't feel like the game actually starts until you've finished. Good enemy design, not many times where I've felt annoyed instead of challenged. The best part of this game is early game, when you still get a rush after defeating a boss (this may change in late game).

English version : Hades might just be my favorite roguelike series. The gameplay is fast, intense, and challenging without ever feeling impossible, even if you don’t have a perfect build. You can create tons of fun and powerful combinations that feel strong without being completely broken (well, at least most of them). The story is engaging, and every new run brings something fresh, new character interactions, new bits of lore, and new resources which helps avoid that “I just wasted my time” feeling that some roguelikes can give. On top of that, the game is gorgeous, the soundtrack is fantastic, and the final boss fight is great. The only minor downside for me is that there’s only one main path to follow but there’s enough variation within each run to make them all feel unique. For completionists, getting the platinum isn’t particularly difficult, just a bit long, since it requires quite a lot of runs. Still, because every attempt brings something new, it never really feels repetitive (though it can drag a little toward the end). As a small tip: for achievements that require certain boons, don’t forget that some keepsakes can guarantee a specific god to appear ! All in all, a fantastic game (especially on the Steam Deck !) that’s absolutely worth trying out. French version : Hades est peut être ma série de rogue like favorite. Le jeu est rapide, nerveux, dur sans être totalement infaisable sans un build qui roule sur le jeu, permet des builds avec des combinaisons drôles et fortes sans être complètement fumées (pour la plupart). L'histoire est sympa et chaque nouvelle run amène quelque chose de nouveau en termes d'interactions entre les personnages, donc évite le côté répétitif, et de ressources, donc évite l'impression d'avoir juste perdu son temps. En plus de ça, le jeu est beau, les musiques sont vraiment sympas et le boss de fin est très cool. Le seul côté que je trouve dommage est le fait qu'il n'y ait qu'un chemin possible, mais il y a assez de changements qui peuvent arriver au cours des runs pour que chacune soit unique. Pour les complétistes, le platinum n'est pas particulièrement dur, il est surtout un peu long et nécessite beaucoup de runs, mais encore une fois, le fait d'avoir toujours quelque chose de nouveau entre chaque partie évite la répétitivité (même si sur la fin, ça peut sembler un peu long). Pour les succès qui impliquent d'avoir des bienfaits de certains Dieux, n'oubliez pas que certains accessoires peuvent garantir l'apparition de certains Dieux) Bref, un jeu très sympa (notamment sur steam deck pour ceux qui en ont) qui vaut clairement le coup d'être essayé !

I'm a certified roguelike hater, but Hades was a pretty good experience overall. A lot of roguelikes feel like the developers made a solid set of core mechanics, and instead of finishing their game, lazily turn it into a roguelike and use that as an excuse for why there isn't much content in the game. I never felt this way, even once with Hades. From start to finish, Hades never feels like it lets up on giving you new, interesting voice-acted dialogue, power ups to Zagreus' kit, and story revelations. It's almost designed like more of a full-fledged singleplayer game with a story that has a start and an end. As you continue to do runs, whether or not they are successful, you will continue to power up to the point where success is decently likely even if you're only of an average skill level. All of this I think cumulates in what is probably the most fun roguelike experience for newcomers to the genre. I do feel like the actual options you have wear a bit thin after a while--there isn't really a lot of emergent behaviour coming from item combinations like in Binding of Isaac. Once you've completed one run, there isn't much in the way of new levels or bosses outside of some buffed up versions of the main 4 bosses that you can optionally enable. That feels like a worth-it trade off for me though, I'm more interested in a memorable experience I can complete in a finite amount of time, rather than a super hardcore roguelike I can play for thousands of runs.

I’ve played a lot of games, but Hades honestly hooked me in a way very few have. From the moment you take control of Zagreus, trying to escape the Underworld, you realize it’s not just another hack-and-slash roguelike — it’s a beautifully crafted mix of fast, satisfying combat and surprisingly emotional storytelling. The gameplay loop is insanely addictive. You die a lot — and I mean a lot — but every death actually feels worth it. You get stronger, unlock new weapons, and experiment with different god boons, which completely change your playstyle. One run you’re shooting lightning with Zeus’s blessings, the next you’re setting everything on fire with Dionysus’ boons. It keeps things exciting, and no two runs ever feel the same. The characters are a big part of what makes Hades special. The Greek gods aren’t just background figures — they have distinct personalities, funny dialogue, and they actually react to your choices. Zagreus himself is charming and witty, and his interactions with Hades, Achilles, and even the gods on Olympus make the story feel alive. Over time, you start caring about the relationships more than just the next escape attempt. Visually, the game is stunning. The art style pops with color, and every part of the Underworld feels handcrafted. The music is perfect too — it kicks in during intense battles and somehow manages to make dying feel epic. What I love most is how Hades respects your time. Even short sessions feel rewarding, and the sense of progression never stops. It’s tough, sure, but fair — and when you finally beat Hades for the first time, it’s such a satisfying moment. Overall, Hades is one of those games that just gets everything right: gameplay, story, art, and replayability. Whether you’re into Greek mythology, fast-paced combat, or just want a game that keeps you coming back for “one more run,” Hades delivers all of it.

Recipe for Potato Dumplings (Varenyky) Ingredients: For the dough: Wheat flour – 500 g Water – 200 ml Egg – 1 Salt – 1 tsp For the filling: Potatoes – 1 kg Onions – 2 Lard or butter – 50 g Salt – to taste Ground black pepper – to taste Preparation steps: Making the dough: Sifting the flour: Sift the flour into a large bowl. Making the dough: Add salt and the egg to the flour. Gradually pour in the water, constantly stirring. Knead the dough until it becomes smooth and elastic. Resting the dough: Wrap the dough in plastic wrap or cover it with a towel and let it rest for 30 minutes. Preparing the filling: Boiling the potatoes: Peel the potatoes, cut them into large pieces, and boil until tender in salted water. Preparing the onions: While the potatoes are boiling, finely chop the onions. Sauté the onions in lard or butter until golden brown. Making the potato puree: Drain the potatoes and mash them. Add the sautéed onions, salt, and pepper to taste, and mix well. Forming the dumplings: Rolling out the dough: Roll out the dough into a thin sheet about 2-3 mm thick. Use a glass or cutter to cut out circles approximately 7-8 cm in diameter. Forming the dumplings: Place a spoonful of potato filling on each circle of dough. Fold the dough in half and pinch the edges tightly to seal the dumplings. Cooking the dumplings: Boiling water: Bring a large pot of water to a boil, add salt. Cooking the dumplings: Gently drop the dumplings into the boiling water, stirring carefully to prevent sticking. Cook until done (approximately 5-7 minutes after they float to the surface). Serving: Removing the dumplings: Remove the dumplings with a slotted spoon and place them on a plate. Serving: Serve the dumplings hot, optionally drizzling with melted butter, sour cream, or sautéed onions. Enjoy your meal!

It's indeed a well-made game. It just doesn't click with me. I didn't like the weight of reactions in the game rather than decision-making. Yeah, you get to choose the abilities on every floor, and that's one hell of a decision. I enjoyed the trial and error in that strategy-making. But the rest of the game feels like rather linear, finger-numbing iterations of reactions. Even though it claims to be rogue-like, the situations don't change much, and the experiences wear off relatively quickly. On top of that, there's a lot of emphasis on the accumulation of in-game capital, which I think takes away the pure joy of roguelikes. You might say you can avoid using the system, but the mere existence of that game design suggests that the game is more about players' labour, not luck. To me, roguelikes should feel like trying my luck and skills. It's probably the outcome of integrating roguelike aspects into an action game, though. Labour in an action game can justify your poor action skills. I couldn't get past the inflation of damage race, realising my limit of actions and the need for hours of labour, so I quit.

It took a while to click for me, because I usually am not into hack and slash type of games, but I'm very glad it did. This is definitely one of the top roguelikes out there. They absolutely nailed the Greek mythology theme here which gives it its own personality and sets it apart from other games in the genre. The collection of voiced NPCs, each with an insane amount of dialogue really make the game feel alive. As for the gameplay, it feels tight to play and there is enough variety in the available powerups as well as the unlockables that each run feels fresh. Apart from the unlocks that you pay for with currencies, there is also a meta progression where new stuff will simply show up from time to time unexpectedly (similar to Isaac). These can range from new room types, bosses, gameplay systems or NPCs that give powerful rewards when you encounter them. This way of slowly drip feeding you new content makes the game even more addictive. Finally the artstyle and sound direction are top notch, and the music ties very well into the Greek theme. My only complaint here is that the delivery of some the main character's voice lines can be a bit dry sometimes. All in all, this is an easy recommendation for anyone interested in roguelikes or hack & slash games.

Hades is certainly a unique experience. When I first started playing it, I thought it was going to become my second favorite game, after Subnautica. As I ventured further through the Underworld and unlocked more weapons, the fun just kept increasing. But, Hades has a fundamental flaw. The story is really interesting and the characters are really well designed. Especially from an artistic point of view. The art in this game is just amazing, everything looks SO good. The artists clearly put a lot of work into crafting this rougelike. The soundtrack is really good for bosses, and there are some pretty neat tracks here and there, but overall it isn't near the level of Dead Cells or Death's Door. That's ok though - the soundtrack is still good, and not every game needs to have songs that will stick in my head for an eternity because of how good they are. Overall, Hades is just amazing. But enough of that, let's get to the fundamental flaw I mentioned earlier. Repeating the same thing over and over is bound to get boring eventually. Even if you have six weapons to choose from, you always go through the same four areas and fight the same four bosses with them. That makes sense in the context of the story, but it also makes Hades get a bit boring more quickly than Dead Cells, for example, which is another rougelike, but IT has several biomes and bosses to choose from at each stage of the game. That being said tho... Hades is still totally worth buying. When you start to get bored you can just play something else and come back to it in a few weeks or months. Steam doesn't delete your games when you take a break from them. So, in conclusion: Hades is peak, but taking breaks from it from time to time is recommended to prevent it from getting slightly boring.

I want to like this game, but it feels too repetitive and one-note for me. Yes, there are a variety of weapons and boons, which alter your attack and defense mechanics, to unlock and explore. However, regardless of what you're using, the gameplay loop is simple -- Attack, dodge the ridiculous amounts of crap the game throws at you, attack, dodge, attack, dodge, dodge, dodge. No matter how many upgrades you collect, you never feel like a powerful character. Attacks barely chip away at the health of all but the weakest enemies, so every fight is a monotonous slog. And each time you die, you get a tiny little bit of story that seems to go nowhere, you put a few points into skill upgrades that seem to make little difference, any you go out and face the same groups of enemies again and again. Maybe the game gets better after hundreds of runs, but I just don't have the patience for that. I was hoping for something akin to the experience of a good rogue-like such as Binding of Isaac, or a good action-RPG like Diablo 2/3, where the experiences changes dramatically based on the items and abilities you find and/or choose. This is not that, so if that's what you're looking for, move along.

Absolutely superb. Every track fits the mood perfectly, from the adrenaline-pumping combat themes to the hauntingly beautiful melodies in quieter moments. And the art design is just wow. It’s stylish, vibrant, and full of personality. The level design keeps things fresh and challenging without ever feeling unfair. Hades isn’t just a great roguelike—it’s a masterclass in storytelling, design, and replayability. I can’t recommend it enough. 10/10

This mod lets you add a bunch of the difficulty modifiers to your desired difficulty and do them all at once. It cuts out the biggest area of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. After doing this, and making the game difficult to a level that suites me, it was a wonderful game. All that said, it took me 39 runs to clear the main story. 15 runs before my first clear. Never played rogue-likes before, I was always more of a NFS or FPS kinda guy. Picked it up at the recommendation of a friend years back, and it's unlocked a whole new world for me. Clocked 800+ hours across PC, PS4 and Switch, 100% completion across all three. Now, let's get to the review- Isometric view, with very tight controls and easy to learn/hard to master combat. I have seen a few people play it slow, I've seen many people play it fast, and I honestly prefer the latter. Pick up a weapon (it's just the one initially, you can unlock upto a total of 6, which in turn have 4 'aspects' each, so 24 different types of playstyles - safe to say, youll definitely find something that you like), and just run through. Go crazy. Do you like to move around tactfully and pick off enemies long range? Or would you rather run in headfirst and just go to town killing the wretches of the underworld? Better yet, use the hidden aspect of the bow and arrow, and just hold the special button. IT'S UPTO YOU. The gameplay is phenomenal. Honestly the only criticism I have is that I'm not good enough like proper speed-runners to finish a run in under 10 minutes lol. Let's see what else...the graphics do a good job of depicting the underworld and it's various regions. The enemy designs, the NPC art, everything is on point. What does stand out is the music. Damn. Just....yeah, play it.

This sat on my library for a couple years, but now with the release of Hades II I finally gave this a proper go. The TLDR is that Hades is really really solid. Perhaps the most replayable roguelike along with slay the spire that I've played, where the skill ceiling is even higher as all enemies are technically beatable without any upgrades. The length of a run is pretty optimal and overall run variety is great. There are six well balanced weapons along with randomized dungeons and loot that keep the runs fresh for a long, long time. Even after beating your first runs the game manages to introduce new enemies and sufficiently buff the exiting bosses. Eventually you'll reach the skill where you reach the final boss constantly, after which you can increase the difficulty gradually via the pact of punishment system. This ensures that you can always have a challenge without making things neither too easy nor hard. Honestly it feels like I've only scratched the surface despite beating the main story just now, there are still many things I'm yet to unlock and I've barely touched four of the six weapons. Finally I'll say that to my surprise the overall story / narrative is quite enjoyable. The voice acting is quite stoic, but the overall depth you have with different characters is very impressive. So far I feel like I've heard more unique than reused voicelines, and I'm already like 35 runs deep.

“Don’t worry BT, I’m not going anywhere.” I was never really an Xbox girl, it was the one system that eluded me when I was growing up. It made me feel rather left out sometimes since most of my friends mostly stuck to Xbox, but I was pretty happy with my Playstation, and the only exclusive I really felt like I was missing out on was Halo. This changed when Titanfall dropped, this insanely sick looking movement shooter where you can also control a giant mech. I had just entered my Gurren Lagann phase at the time so the idea of controlling a giant unstoppable machine was incredibly appealing to my young mind, and I wanted to hop on asap. Unfortunately, I never really could and it’s only now that I’ve finally been able to experience the sequel thanks to the steam release! I could finally see if my excitement was worth it as a teenager and if the game still held up today! I booted up the single player campaign and got to work. As is true in all universes, war is hell.You play as Jack Cooper, a pretty generic rifleman working in the Militia. The Militia fights against the IMC, a ruthless enemy force that seeks to take over The Frontier, a star system located far away from Earth, and establish total control. Accompanying this war are giant mechs known as Titan piloted by soldiers simply called pilots who serve as the leading force in the war. You want to be a pilot, and thus you begin your training to work your way up to pilot status. Your training is unfortunately cut short though as you`re suddenly thrust into a battle that devastates most of your crew, including your own captain. After waking up from the hells of war, you stumble upon your captain's old Titan, BT-7274 whose control has been relinquished to you. You`re then tasked with acquiring a device known as The Arc, a devastating planet ending weapon that the IMC seeks to get their hands on and totally destroy Harmony, the main homeworld of The Militia, and take total control of The Frontier. Wasting no time, you and BT set off to acquire the arc and stop the IMC from establishing ruthless dominion over the stars. It`s a pretty standard FPS plot so no real notes here. If you played any modern shooter like Call of Duty you kinda know what to expect here, and the campaign is short enough to where it doesn`t really get expanded on too much. The main crux of the campaign anyway is your relationship with BT, who goes from a simple mech to your best friend, though I found the growth of their bond to be established rather quickly. Granted, I know that`s just a consequence of the short length, but at the same time it means that I didn’t get rather attached to the characters all too much with me only liking BT as much as I do because I have a bias for funny robot characters. Still, these complaints aren’t really too high since it does get the job done well enough, I’ve just always been rather ambivalent to war stories they never really did too much for me personally. Despite the standard war story though, Titanfall 2 has a surprisingly great campaign packed in here. It starts off with a fairly basic tutorial, but soon you’ll be learning how to do some crazy movement such as wall running. This is where Titanfall 2 starts to shine as movement is kind of the name of the game here. If you play this like a standard shooter you will have a rather boring time, its gun mechanics are pretty simple and hiding behind cover waiting to heal before taking more shots is really the best it gets defense wise. If you really wanna have fun with this system though, you gotta start moving and this is where a good majority of my fun came from. Jumping between wall to wall, sliding under platforms, shooting things at high speed while you bunny hop around, you feel like an unstoppable god and every single level is built around this mechanic with walls stationed everywhere letting you stay in the air longer than you stay on the ground. Enemy bullets just fly past you as you zoom through the skies taking down anything that moves like an unstoppable god with the only thing stopping you being the ground that lies below your feet. Turning on your cloak to sneak up behind a full group before shooting a grenade from mid-air right in the middle of their formation, sliding down a corridor full speed and shooting the army right in front of you as they stand no chance at the reign of gunfire that comes at them full speed, blasting enemies in the face while running across the walls, jumping across them constantly in order to stay afloat, dominating the skies that reign above you, this game is incredibly exhilarating and it’s movement system made the short campaign feel like an utter blast start to finish. No space is wasted here, every single object has been placed in just the right position to let you take full advantage of your movement abilities, and the real fun of the game comes from messing around with this playground and improving your skills to get cooler and cooler looking skills. Alongside the standard shooting gameplay is the Titan gameplay. Throughout the game you’ll be in control of BT, gunning down other titans as you tower over everything below you, feeling like a literal walking tank that just can’t be stopped. Now I still enjoyed my time with the Titan gameplay, don't get me wrong, but this was definitely where I felt the game was at its weakest. It’s not a bad gameplay style but compared to the way faster on the ground movement, the slower tank gameplay with the titan definitely stuck out, and it made each of their sections feel a bit sameish because of it. I found the same general strategy ended up working for most of the fights too with you just choosing the loadout that you like best before switching out to the one with the special attack you like most when it’s charged up. It’s cathartic for sure, and when it’s done in short bursts it's incredibly fun, but there’s a few sections that can drag on a little bit, and it can make these sections just feel a bit of a slug compared to the rest of the standard gameplay. This is also where all the boss fights come into play where the same strategy once again works out, and I found myself rather disappointed that the movement system isn‘t really taken advantage of for a boss fight. It’s really my one main gripe with this campaign and while the Titan isn’t the majority of your gameplay, it still is often enough to where I felt a little bothered, and it makes me wish most of their sections were a little shorter. In terms of level variety, Titanfall 2 has a fantastic mix here and I greatly enjoyed the ideas each level brought to the table. There’s a lot of creativity jam packed into these 30 minute long stages, and each one is just the right length so they don’t end up getting boring by the end. There’s one where you’re hopping along conveyor belts that are building houses, scrambling along the walls and pipes in order to find stable ground. There’s another where you’re platforming through the skies, hanging on for dear life as the ship twists and turns trying to throw you off, with an endless wave of enemies coming at you. Then there’s the best level in the game, Effect and Cause, which sees you obtaining an artifact that lets you shift between the past and the future in order to successfully reach the end. This level is phenomenal with you constantly shifting between the two in moments of intensity, whether it be shifting it to give you easier enemies to fight or shifting in order to have stable ground to land on during a wall run. This gimmick alone sold me on the rest of the campaign, and I really wanna give it special mention because it’s easily the highlight of your entire runtime, and not a single second felt wasted during the time jumps. Titanfall 2 is just one of those games that feels effortless to play. From the moment it starts, it throws you into this fast-paced flow where you’re running on walls, sliding around, and shooting without even thinking twice. It’s quick, but never confusing, you always feel in control. The campaign itself is short but it’s actually a good thing here. There’s no filler, no dragged-out missions—just a tight, well-paced story. And somehow, by the end, it hits way harder than you’d expect.The final part of the game is where everything comes together—the action ramps up, the music kicks in, and emotionally it just lands perfectly. Combat is probably the best part. The gunplay feels smooth, Titans feel powerful, and switching between the two styles keeps things fresh the whole time. Nothing feels clunky or forced.It's a 10/10 for me. And one more thing BT ISN'T JUST A MACHINE.

Finished the campaign on Hard, Master and got all achievements. This game honestly has such a great story. BT is easily one of the most memorable companions in any shooter I’ve played. As someone who plays a lot of Apex, the multiplayer here felt familiar straight away, but Titanfall 2’s movement just feels more complete. Wall running, grenade boosting, all the movement tech makes the gameplay insanely fun. Apex has touched some of it before, but nowhere near like this. One thing I weirdly loved was the weapon sway while moving your camera around. Small detail, but it makes the guns feel more alive and weighty. I barely notice anything like that in Apex. The campaign is around 4 to 5 hours depending on difficulty, but it’s one of those short games that never really wastes your time. Every level feels unique and polished. Is it worth €30? Honestly, yeah. Great campaign, solid multiplayer, amazing movement, and just an overall polished experience. If you’re an Apex Legends fan, this is basically a must-play. [h1]🤖💔 “Short, but unforgettable.” 🚀🔥[/h1] Titanfall 2 delivers one of the most tightly crafted and emotionally impactful campaigns in recent memory — even if it doesn’t stick around for long. The campaign may be brief, but it wastes zero time. Every mission introduces new ideas, mechanics, or twists that keep the experience feeling fresh from start to finish. The pacing is exceptional — there’s no filler, just a constant stream of engaging, well-designed moments. At the heart of it all is the relationship between Jack Cooper and BT. What starts as a simple pilot-and-Titan dynamic evolves into something genuinely meaningful. The writing is sharp, the dialogue lands, and by the end, it hits harder than you’d expect from a shooter. Gameplay is just as strong. Movement is fluid, gunplay is responsive, and the Titan mechanics add a satisfying layer of power and strategy. The game constantly mixes pilot agility with Titan combat in ways that feel natural and exciting. It’s not trying to be massive — it’s trying to be memorable. And it succeeds. A short campaign, but easily one of the best — and most emotional — FPS experiences out there.

Recently COMPLETE THE 1.5/5 You know, this game has real potential, but we need to talk about the Titan mechanics first. If the player view is first person, they should have used a third person view for the Titan to give it the right feel. Instead, they added all this camera bobbing just to make the pilot and Titan perspectives seem different. It is honestly terrible, since you just transfer from one first person view to another. When you get inside the Titan, the camera shakes so violently that it makes your head spin. The movement mechanics are just awful. It seriously feels like you are sitting on top of a shaking ladder. The controls for the Titan feel like a basic mobile game, and it could have been so much better if they actually built it properly. Besides that, the game is incredibly repetitive. The environments are repetitive, and you fight the exact same enemies over and over. The developers just forced these weird gaps where they let you use the Titan, take it away, and then give it back again. The camera movement is so bad that I actively tried to avoid piloting the Titan. Honestly, the game would have been much better if they removed the Titans completely. The Titan serves no real purpose here other than acting as a basic damage multiplier.
