rating this on the singleplayer campaign because: 1) thats all ive played thus far, and 2) that's what's most likely to stick around in the future. it was a short campaign, but really good. i knew nothing going in other than "this game has freerunning, its older (game is from 2016, played in jan2026), you can control mechs, and people seem to play it for multiplayer a lot". it shows its age a bit in several minor ways, but even in 2026, im pretty happy with what i played. the gameplay isnt without its minor qualms, but nothing annoying. mouse was snappy with no acceleration or damping, controls were all responsive, fov was more than enough, game is very efficient on cpu and gpu even with multiple browsers full of tabs in the background. go in blind, maybe play the first game first, for story. I didnt think i'd care about the story at all in this, but coming out, it's what i cared about most. it took me maybe 10-15 hours of non-rushing and sorta screwing around here and there. gunplay is... acceptable. its not bad by any means, but ammo scarcity and encouraging you to play scrappily and swap weapons because there's no ammo of what you've been using, and not remembering ammo or even guns between missions is ass, but wasnt impactful at all. just kind of a minor annoyance in this game. if i had to put a value on this game, specifically for just the singleplayer campaign, i'd say it's worth.... honestly, 10-20 usd, maybe more, depending on your expectations. it WAS very short, but i rarely finish games these days because im so picky, and i actually finished this in two casual evening sessions. not sure if i'd play multiplayer of this. i'll give it a try, but i have some ideas how it'll go.... so yeah: value: 10-20 usd visuals: A, older but very creative sound: A-, very good, some very small wishes gameplay: A, actually fun story: A+, almost cried overall: solid A AGAIN: GO IN BLIND, DONT EVEN WATCH THE TRAILER edit: i just read about the history of tf1, apex, and ea... and dude? ♥♥♥♥ ea SO much. this is, once again, ea just destroying anything they touch. damnit. im upset that this is what's happened, and now im upset that im in on the knowledge that this is what's happened. titanfall fans: i see you, now. you are valid. Stop giving EA money.

Verdict: One of the most mechanically refined shooters ever made, with a campaign that still sets the bar for FPS design. Titanfall 2’s greatest strength is how fluidly it blends movement, gunplay, and verticality. Wall-running, sliding, and grappling are not gimmicks—they are fundamental to how combat flows. The result is a shooter where positioning and momentum matter as much as aim. The single-player campaign deserves special mention. Each level introduces a new mechanic and fully explores it before moving on, avoiding repetition while constantly teaching the player something new. The relationship between pilot and Titan is handled with surprising emotional weight, elevating the narrative beyond typical FPS storytelling. Multiplayer remains fast, skill-based, and rewarding, though the player base can feel uneven at times due to matchmaking population swings. Still, when matches click, few shooters offer the same sense of kinetic satisfaction. What Works Well Exceptional movement mechanics One of the best FPS campaigns ever made Clear visual and mechanical readability High skill ceiling without feeling unfair What Needs Improvement Multiplayer population inconsistency Limited long-term content support Final Thoughts: Titanfall 2 is a masterclass in FPS design. It may not have the ongoing support of newer titles, but its core gameplay remains unmatched.

Thousands of hours later, I’m still chasing this feeling I’ve put thousands of hours into Titanfall 2 across PC and Xbox, and I still haven’t found another FPS that feels quite like this. The movement is the obvious standout, but it’s more than just speed. Titanfall 2 teaches you rhythm. Wall-runs, slides, grapples, momentum chains. once it clicks, the game stops feeling like inputs and starts feeling like instinct. Going back to other shooters after this is… difficult. Everything feels heavier. Slower. More grounded than it needs to be. i will forever be left hollow without titanfall 3 The Titans are just as important. They aren’t a gimmick or a streak — they’re a second phase of the match. Calling one down still feels meaningful even after hundreds (thousands) of drops. You fight with your Titan, not just inside it, and that design choice carries way more weight than most games manage. The campaign is short, but it respects your time. No filler, no wasted moments — just smart level design, creative mechanics, and a story that lands harder than you expect. It’s one of those campaigns people still bring up years later, and that doesn’t happen by accident. What really stands out, looking back, is how confident this game is. It doesn’t pad itself. It doesn’t slow you down. It doesn’t ask you to wait. It trusts the player to move fast, think fast, and learn fast. A lot of games have taken pieces of Titanfall 2 since then — the gunfeel, the polish, the universe — but none of them quite capture the full picture. It turns out that removing just a little of the movement, a little of the scale, or a little of the risk changes the whole experience. I liked this game enough to permanently tattoo a symbol from it on my body, in the same place the character has it. That kind of commitment doesn’t come from hype. It comes from time. Titanfall 2 didn’t just hold up. It set a bar most shooters still haven’t reached. If you’ve never played it, you should. And if you have — welcome back, Pilot. [h3]APEX[/h3] ★★★☆ 7, awesome Titanfall 2’s campaign is one of the most polished among the multiplayer-focused titles, perfectly blending platformer, pilot combat, and Titan combat without a single dull moment. Titanfall 2’s pilot has no fall damage and can wall-run, slide, and double-jump, allowing them to perform high-speed acrobatics in platformer and combat. The Arc Tool puzzle and platformer utilizing time machine are intuitive without being too predictable, giving life to the middle of the campaign where similar landscapes tend to repeat. Pilot combat allows you to fight while using movement skills, so flying through the air to ambush enemies is rather good, but utilizing that speed in a tussle—like the pipe facility battle—is more thrilling. And what about Titan combat? Switching between various weapon loadouts, the weighty impact of combat is visceral. Especially in the mission of “Titanfall,” when you wield the Ronin and slice through Titans, the thrill becomes almost euphoric. Its boss battles could be the only downside. Rather than featuring unique mechanics, they essentially consist of versions of previously encountered Titans with merely higher health. It's difficult to dismount from BT and fight as a pilot, and since they differ little from common Titan combat, they fail to fully realize Titanfall 2’s potential.

Titanfall 2 is a triumph of imagination, heart, and sheer mechanical brilliance. It takes the foundation of a fast-paced shooter and elevates it with movement so smooth and intuitive that simply traversing the world feels exhilarating. Wall-running, sliding, grappling, and soaring between firefights creates a constant sense of momentum that few games have ever matched. The true soul of the game, however, lies in its campaign. What could have been a standard sci-fi story becomes something genuinely memorable thanks to the bond between Pilot Jack Cooper and BT-7274. BT is not just a Titan—you feel his presence as a partner who learns, adapts, and protects you. His calm, analytical voice contrasts beautifully with the chaos of battle, and when he says “Trust me,” it carries real emotional weight. It’s a line that perfectly captures the relationship you build together: absolute faith forged through combat, sacrifice, and shared survival. Each mission feels handcrafted, introducing new mechanics and ideas that keep the experience constantly fresh. Whether it’s clever level design or unforgettable gameplay twists, Titanfall 2 never settles for “good enough.” It pushes forward, confident in its creativity, and rewards the player for keeping up. The multiplayer continues this excellence, offering intense, skill-driven matches that feel just as fluid and satisfying as the campaign. Dropping a Titan into the battlefield never loses its impact, and every encounter feels dynamic and alive. Titanfall 2 is more than an outstanding shooter—it’s a reminder of what games can achieve when gameplay, storytelling, and emotion work in perfect sync. Like BT himself, the game looks you straight in the eye and says, “Trust me,” and it absolutely earns it.

I can't speak to the multiplayer of this game, but as for the single player- I have a handful of criticisms. the final boss is too easy and a bit anticlimactic, the overarching story is cliche at best, and none of the characters stand out much aside from perhaps the interactions between the main character cooper and his titan BT. it's also a bit on the short side clocking in at 4 hours for one playthrough on standard difficulty. in light of how dead the multiplayer is I can't say you should buy it full price. with those out of the way everything else about this game is practically perfect. simply moving feels wonderful. the gunplay feels wonderful. the gameplay variety and pacing are interlinked in a way that makes the mere act of progressing the story feel fluid. everything in the game seems to be in the service of momentum. every new tool, each level specific gimmick, the basic moveset of the character itself, all of it is there to help you keep moving around and hardly ever stop if you so wish. each setpiece is wonderfully created and awe inspiring. they are a scifi game and wear that on their sleeve, showing you sights and sounds that can probably never be recreated in reality. more than once I had audibly said "woah" or "that's cool"- and most games don't get that kind of response from me. it is the epitome of everything a linear military shooter can be. if the campaign was twice as long I'd say buy it even at full price but as is the length of it means you gotta wait for a better price ratio. but do play it someday if you've got any interest whatsoever in this kind of game. you will not be disappointed.

Titanfall 2 is one of the most underrated shooters of the last decade, delivering an exceptional blend of fast-paced action and a surprisingly emotional single-player campaign. The campaign is the game’s biggest surprise. You play as Jack Cooper, a rifleman who forms a bond with BT-7274, a Vanguard-class Titan. What starts as a straightforward sci-fi shooter evolves into a clever, varied experience filled with standout level design. Missions constantly introduce new mechanics such as time-shifting between past and present or gravity-defying platforming that keep gameplay fresh and inventive. The relationship between Cooper and BT adds genuine heart, making the story far more memorable than most FPS campaigns. Gameplay is where Titanfall 2 truly shines. The movement system—wall-running, sliding, double-jumping feels incredibly fluid and rewarding, encouraging speed and creativity rather than slow, cover-based combat. Pilots and Titans are both satisfying to control, and switching between agile infantry combat and the raw power of Titans creates an exciting rhythm that few shooters can match. Visually, the game still holds up well, with detailed environments, strong art direction, and smooth performance. The soundtrack complements the action perfectly, enhancing both the epic scale of Titan battles and the quieter character moments. A fantastic shooter on the Steam Deck and one of the best FPS games you can play....

This review is gonna be from someone who might have a little less than rose tinted lenses, and a realistic point of view. (Also I wanna put this at the top, there is an Indie Game that just got funded heavily at the time of writing this called "Diesel Knights." There is a playtest on steam right now! It is titanfall but with a diesel punk setting that has a passionate dev! Please please check it out ^ww^) Short-er review/tl;dr This game is genuinely a great game if you like fast paced movement shooters, but also recognize the skill gap it has and dwindling playerbase. As of writing this you can still play and find games, while also having a blast with nice community members. It may not be absolutely perfect like others say, with some gaps of interest when it comes to differing mechanics and loadouts. BUT it is def a game to give a good 50 hours to really see/feel what this game has to offer. Even If the graphics and setting are dated compared to today, the gameplay certainly is not. --------------------------------------------- The campaign might not live up to your expectations as everyone makes it out to be, but once again it is very good and should be experienced at least once. If you are expecting a COD campaign where you build relationships with multiple characters, or just that overall feeling like you're in a movie, this isn't exactly that. However you spend a lot of time with your titan and he's fun :3 The multiplayer is where you're going to spending a lot of time, and there are videos out there explaining it's pro's and cons. I am someone who enjoys games but doesn't get glazed over and ignores it's flaws. And ofc I am myself and have my own opinions so don't let any of these scare you. Again this is a great great game! There is a skill gap like I said and you really have to move past it. If you are new to shooters, especially movement shooters, it's gonna be harder. TF2 has that problem where mostly dedicated fans have stuck around with thousands of hours, mastering every inch of the game. Maybe it's just me but I haven't noticed it too much, however maybe that's just because of my skill level. The movement is smooth and fluid, but needs time to learn and again get to a certain skill level. It can feel clunky and not listen to you from time to time. It's almost like a beast you have to tame, but also respect it and let it take over you. (Does that make sense?) The guns are great! I like diverse guns that determine and change your playstyle to use effectively. There might not be as many as I'd like, but there are fun unique ones. At the same time there are guns that are "overpowered," which really mean easier to use/forgiving that a lot of people use. But some guns are genuinely way stronger in the hands of a master of them (Like the wingman I am learning. 2 shot body - 1 shot head revolver with good range and pinpoint precision. But tiny reticle you have to have good aim to use.) This might just be me, but if you play a game over and over and over again, you get this feeling of everything feeling the exact same in a different stale way. I felt it sooner in this game that other games have for me. Maybe it's the few npc voice lines, or something else. That just may be something you might feel too and I wanted to mention it here. But the thing that is super nice and I haven't really seen in other games are just the kinds of npc's included in every match. If Battlefield solves the feeling of a map feeling lifeless by adding more players, this game nails it with the kinds and amounts of npc's it adds. It really feels like a battlefield you're jumping into. They don't really get in the way, and there are enough different kinds where it feels like it's own unique setting. Sorry if this review isn't perfect and not worded well, it's just a glimpse of my experience. Thanks for reading! I hope it gave more insight to help you determine buying it or not. If it's on sale def pick it up and enjoy it for what it is! Have an amazing day!! --------------------------------------------- Like I said Diesel Knights is being developed full time from Jan 1st 2026 and is planning on having a 1.0 at the end of the year. The community is great and passionate and so is the dev. I cannot emphasize the hype and hopium us titanfall fans are having, and hopefully enjoy in the future. Join the knights today!

Titanfall 2 isn’t just a video game—it’s a masterclass in what a first-person shooter should be. From the moment you take your first wall-run to the second you call down your Titan from the sky like a god answering your prayers, the game grips you with unmatched intensity and never lets go. Respawn Entertainment took everything that worked in the original Titanfall and refined it to near perfection, delivering an experience that feels impossibly smooth, endlessly exciting, and confidently unique in a genre that often plays it safe. The campaign alone deserves legendary status. In an era where many shooters treat single-player as an afterthought, Titanfall 2 delivers one of the most creative, emotional, and brilliantly designed campaigns in FPS history. Each mission introduces new mechanics that constantly evolve gameplay, ensuring nothing ever feels stale. The bond between pilot Jack Cooper and the Titan BT-7274 is shockingly heartfelt, turning a game about giant robots and guns into a story with genuine emotional weight. Few games manage to balance spectacle and soul this well—Titanfall 2 absolutely nails it. Movement is where Titanfall 2 truly ascends. Wall-running, sliding, double-jumping, and grappling flow together with such elegance that once you master it, every other shooter feels painfully slow by comparison. Combat is fast, fluid, and skill-based, rewarding creativity and precision over cheap tactics. Whether you’re sprinting across rooftops or launching yourself through the air into a perfectly timed kill, the game makes you feel unstoppable without ever feeling unfair. Multiplayer is just as incredible, delivering chaotic, high-energy matches that remain addictive even years later. Titans crashing onto the battlefield shift the momentum instantly, creating thrilling power spikes that never get old. Every Titan class feels distinct, every weapon is satisfying, and the mix of AI grunts with real players keeps matches lively and cinematic. It’s pure controlled chaos—and it works beautifully. In the end, Titanfall 2 stands as one of the most criminally underrated games of all time. It’s bold, polished, emotional, and ridiculously fun, proving that innovation and heart can still thrive in blockbuster shooters. Whether you’re here for the story, the movement, or the multiplayer mayhem, Titanfall 2 delivers on every front with confidence and style. This isn’t just a great FPS—it’s a genre-defining masterpiece that deserves eternal respect. 🚀🤖

This game had the potential to be the standard of shooter games for years to come. Shooter games were PERFECTED here and instead the people chose hero shooters, tac shooters, BR’s, and whatever the hell CoD decides to release every year. The interaction between all of the games mechanics, including pilots, titans, ability and weapon customization, movement, and map design create a phenomenal experience throughout every match. No holding angles for 2 minutes straight, no being forced to swap off heroes because they instantly lose to another hero, no battle royale. You get to play how you want whenever you want and the game rewards that with pure speed, power, and an adrenaline rush like nothing else. Casual hang outs turning into hardcore lobbies after some trash talk, then transitioning into skill expression showing off with movement or great gun skill. Not many games nowadays foster that sort of community packaged in an arcade oriented shooter. At the time of writing, the multiplayer is hit or miss due to long queue times and extremely high skilled players. I recommend picking this up for the campaign. It does not error. It simply [b]hangs indefinitely[/b], waiting for something that never happens. This occurs regardless of: [list] [*]Native Steam vs Wine [*]Proton version [*]Overlay state [*]Network configuration [/list] [h2]Steam Flatpak[/h2] Flatpak Steam performs even worse: [list] [*]EA App often refuses to install [*]Background services are blocked by sandboxing [*]No useful error messages are provided [/list] These are known Flatpak limitations, and EA has made [b]no effort[/b] to support or mitigate them. [h2]The real issue[/h2] Titanfall 2: [list] [*]Runs well once started [*]Has good performance [*]Uses a solid engine [/list] [b]But the EA App is mandatory, deeply integrated, and fundamentally unreliable on Linux.[/b] When the EA App fails: [list] [*]The game fails [*]No error is shown [*]No actionable logs are provided [*]No official Linux support exists [/list] [h2]Conclusion[/h2] This game is being held hostage by its launcher. If you are on Linux: [list] [*]You may get lucky [*]Or you may lose hours or days troubleshooting [*]With no guarantee it will ever work [/list] That is not acceptable for a paid product. The single-player mode of Titanfall 2 takes up to 6–8 hours, and every moment is full of fresh experiences. The player controls a young pilot and works with his companion BT-7274 – an advanced robot. This is the best PvP FPS game I have ever played, and likely ever will play. This is the best traditional FPS Campaign I have ever played, and likely ever will play. The 238 hours I have on this game now represents maybe 1/5th of my total time on this game, if not then less. I owned this game on PS4 for years until I finally saved up enough to play it on PC. I have been playing Titanfall 2 since 2018, and it has never once moved from my Top Spot of PVP experiences. If you look at my list of games I have 100%ed, this is the only one. This will remain the only one for what is likely a very VERY Long time. It is perfection. The Campaign is short, tropey, and has as many twists as an interstate. Despite that, however, it does the best job with characterization I have ever seen in a FPS campaign. BT FEELS alive, the way he reacts to Jack Cooper even nonverbally sell that and help found the relationship to end all relationships. Despite my playtime I do not feel apt to really review the Multiplayer on a high level. What I CAN say is that it is the best execution of asymmetrical PVP I have ever seen. Titan V Titan? A tactical teamfight. Pilot V Pilot? A fast-paced and beautiful dance of skirmishes. Pilot V Titan? You are a single man taking down a tank and BOY DOES IT FEEL LIKE IT. I have no further words for this game. When it goes on sale, BUY IT. 100% it. The Blue Ribbon is easy, pretty much just a collectables hunt, and the game is a timeless masterpiece. If it ever moves from the top of my FPS list, the second coming of Christ is here. 10/10.

[h1] 100% Achievement Review [/h1] Probably one of the greatest first-person shooter stories to every exist, and I mean it beats Halo: ODST. And that's really saying something from me. Let me first start off by saying THANK GOD THERE ARE NO MULTIPLAYER ACHIEVEMENTS. There's only one, and it requires you to just join an online match. Which is amazing, because the servers are usually empty/ filled with modded and hacked lobbies. The movement, is one of the smoothest, most satisfying things EVER. The wall running, the sliding ,these games redefined the shooter genre with this type of movement and gun play, and it just made it that much more fun to play. After a while of doing parkour to collect collectables, honestly you would wish there’s more to collect. And the training ground where you have to beat your commanders time, is one of the most fun parts about this game. People are insane doing speed runs of it, I tip my hat off to them. The story is probably one of the best things EA has released, and if you think about it, that's really something. You need to experience the story. I’m literally not going to say anything because it’s that good that you need to experience it. Most of the achievements are story related, some of them are challenged based which for shooters are usually really annoying, but for this game was incredibly fun to work towards. It seems hard to do when you first look at the list, but you’ll realize that you can achieve these if you just wanna play the game. I didn’t spend a lot of time because I’d already played it twice on my Xbox and on the EA launcher, but I wanted to hang this one on the wall of 100% so I could feel special. This is a certified 10/10 game from me. I will never forget you BT.

Titanfall 2 is a game I never thought I would be interested in. I'm not a big fan of combat-heavy run-and-gunners, so I didn't hold out my hope too hard for this one. I was completely surprised. Not only is the campaign spectacular, the characters incredibly well-written, and the climax incredibly satisfying, but the combat blew me away, as well. Between the excellent parkour puzzles and the variety of weapons available, I can't decide what my favourite part of it is. There's a play style for every type of gamer available here and I couldn't be happier with that. Though the campaign is unfortunately short, it uses the 5-7 hours it spans perfectly. The relationship between Cooper and BT is one of the most strongly-written character dynamics I've seen, and the characters you're fighting feel so real, so much so that I got emotional seeing the voice actors being credited at the end. I'm not much for multiplayer, so I can't comment on that section of the game, but I think the campaign already makes Titanfall 2 an enriching, worthwhile experience.

Titanfall 2 is a fast, stylish shooter about parkour, giant robots, and does something rare: it tells a complete, memorable story in a tight package. There’s no bloated open world. No checklist obsession. No cinematic excess. Just clever level design, strong pacing, and one time-manipulation level that casually reminds the industry what creativity looks like. And then it emotionally blindsides you with a war machine who understands sacrifice better than the humans around him . BT is a Titan. He is programmed for combat, tactics, and survival. He speaks in calm, precise statements. He does not joke. He does not hesitate. And yet somehow, he is the most emotionally intelligent character in the entire game. BT listens. BT trusts you. He doesn’t say “I care.” He says, “Protocol 3: Protect the Pilot.” And somehow that hits harder. The art style does the heavy lifting. Strong silhouettes, bold colors, and readable environments make the game look sharp without needing ultra-realistic textures. The movement is incredible, wall-running, sliding, double-jumping - it’s pure momentum-driven joy. Combat on foot feels sharp and skillful. Calling down your Titan feels powerful every single time. Vince Zampella didn’t chase trends. He set standards. A timeless shooter, still ahead of its time.

Good game. Only played the single player so my review will reflect that. I also haven't played the first game. This game is like a Marvel movie: entertaining but deep down there's very little substance. Perhaps that's not the best analogy nowadays since this game definitely is far from slop, but you know what I mean. Mechanically this game is exceptional. Of course the movement is the standout feature and it's super smooth and effortless. The gunplay is great too and I don't even like military style ADS shooters but I liked it here. The guns are very well balanced and while I had my favorites, you're honestly fine with anything. Titan combat is very well done too, you do feel a bit slow but never so much that it felt clunky, just heavy and powerful. I did find Titan combat quite unbalanced, it feels to me like some of the kits are blatantly better than others but I'm not an expert. Level design is also very good. You can navigate very easily just by feel, the game invisibly guides you in the right direction. Yes most of the levels are linear, but it's nice to not have to look at waypoints and maps constantly. However a lot of the "platforming" sections relied very heavily on wall running to the point where it got stale. Like obviously the game is a FPS first, but there's only so many times you can wall run down a straight hallway and have it be fun, and the game goes way over that limit. Where this one loses points is in the difficulty, enemy variety, and story. The game is super easy. I even anticipated this, knowing it's an AAA game made for consoles and played on hard mode, but it didn't matter. Enemies die in a few shots at most, and many guns can easily one-shot with a headshot. They also take a while to react to your presence and their aim is pretty bad, a clear indicator that this game was designed for consoles first. Oddly enough the Titan combat was the more difficult part of the game because of limited cover/healing and long-ish cooldowns on your abilities limiting your damage output. Enemy Titans also don't evaporate in 0.2 seconds meaning they can actually shoot you back and deal heavy damage if you don't immediately take evasive action. Enemy variety is just really bad. There are maybe like 12 enemies if you count each different type of Titan, but in reality the number is closer to 5 or 6. The game is quite short and it's not like you're constantly fighting, a good amount of time is dedicated to platforming and exploration, but even so I was hoping for more variety by the end and never got it. The story is just... not it. It's incredibly generic and not one of the characters are compelling. There just isn't enough time spent with any of the characters to justify caring about them, maybe with the exception of BT but even then it's a stretch. Most of them kind of just appear, say some things, and then the game is over. Worst of all though, the villains fall totally flat. I didn't hate the villains because I barely knew who they were. They talk trash at you and that's about it. Because of this the boss fights lacked emotional weight and by the end it was obvious that they were just there to check a box and not for story reasons. Performance is a dream. Yeah it's a nearly 10 year old game at the time of review, but I got a rock solid 120fps at 4K with max settings. My GPU (RTX 3080) hovered around 70% utilization too so there was more in the tank. The game looks fantastic too. It's been nearly 10 years but graphics haven't gotten that much better since then, it holds up really well. I'm just glad I don't have to rely on fake frames and fake resolution to enjoy this game. I wish the game was just longer in general. I would have kept playing despite my objections about the story and enemy variety. The game simply feels good and is fun to play. Now I know why the fans of this series feel so slighted by the cancellation of Titanfall 3. Overall I expected a pretty shallow "broad appeal" type of AAA experience and that's what I got, but I did enjoy it. The strong points are really strong and the weak points are not so weak as to ruin the game (probably due to its length but I digress). The game has some unique things going for it which make it worth a play. Not rushing to replay it any time soon but I'm glad I picked it up. Got it on sale for $5 and I definitely can't complain about that.

Good campaign, excellent gameplay. I won't talk much of the campaign, It is reviewed enough already. The lack of a ranked system is honestly a plus for me. You play it purely for fun, and you can be sure that your opposing team does the same. There is no mindless, grindy and toxic ranked abyss that comes with most FPS games. The pilot combat is so fast, fluid and intense that you feel like you have been doped. The only way I've felt something similar was in a fever dream. Titans are cool, Nothing more needs to be said. It is probably the most fast paced and fun FPS game I've ever played. However, its not all daisies and sunshine, You have to select the most populated server in your region as opposed to the closest server with the lowest ping in order to shave off the matchmaking time, which is not ideal. Even then it can take anywhere between 2 mins to when the game kicks you to main menu for "inactivity". Out of all the game modes, I have only been able to play Attrition, All other modes are dead. (attrition is pretty fun though) Once you get in a match and finish it, if you quickly queue again, you will get into another match relatively quickly. But, you will encounter atleast half of the same guys as your previous match. Also in every single match there are a couple sweats that literally dominate, in the strictest sense of the word, everyone else in the lobby. If I had to compare it, it would be like Immortals in a bronze game. I feel more than a bit annoyed when killed by one of these sweats, and more than a bit elated when I kill one of them. It is an excellent game that is worth your time, I'd suggest giving it a try while multiplayer is still functional.

Titanfall 2 might be a few years old at this point, but jumping back into it on PC (using Bazzite) reminded me why people still talk about it. The visuals still hold up surprisingly well, and the game is incredibly well-optimized. With its modified Source engine, I was able to run it at 4K120 on my setup, and the Steam Deck had no problem pushing around 90fps. The movement system is still the star of the show. Wall-runs, slides, jumps - everything feels smooth, fast, and extremely fun. The mission design also mixes things up nicely with traversal sections, tight shoot-outs, and big Titan fights. The interactions between pilots and Titans give the game a nice bit of personality, and while the weapon selection isn’t massive, it works really well - especially during Titan battles. I only dipped into the multiplayer for a short time, but even then, the arena-style matches were a blast. On the downside, the story and soundtrack didn’t really stick with me once the credits rolled. The campaign is also on the shorter side, which isn’t terrible, but I definitely wouldn’t have minded a bit more. And of course, the EA launcher on PC is still… well, the EA launcher. Achievement hunters might also find the "... becomes the master" achievement annoying to clear. Despite a few drawbacks, Titanfall 2 still delivers one of the most fun and fluid FPS experiences out there. If you haven’t played it yet - or haven’t revisited it in a while - it’s absolutely worth the time. Rating: 4/5

After blowing through the single player game in one Sunday morning/afternoon (approx 9 hrs) I emphatically say "HELL YES" to recommending Titanfall 2. I finally got around to playing this one after watching an online post putting Titanfall 2 in someone's top ten games. The long Thanksgiving weekend seemed liked a good time to give it a go and I'm so glad I did. My first impression was that the graphics looked a little dated but nothing that took away from the experience. The tutorial that showed the basic movement and weapon usage was quick and painless. I was moving around quite effortlessly before I knew it. Once I got access to the Titan, I was hooked. The controls were buttery smooth and the gun play was extremely satisfying. The story was easy to follow and always directed you what to do next. The missions had great variety & pacing, although some of the jumping missions were a little too much. The penalty for dying was not severe (normal difficulty) so I was able to get through the levels with minimal deaths. The end game was a challenging conclusion and the story did a nice job of wrapping everything up. Overall, a very enjoyable experience for anyone who likes FPS and/or mech games.

I searched for other types while excluding Attrition, but it just endlessly searched without ever putting me into a lobby. The second is that the combat is just chaotic. The maps are decent sized and well designed, but combat seems to be relegated to rooftops or wall running. If you aren’t good at either (like me), you probably won’t enjoy it all that much. Titanfall 2 – A Masterpiece That Deserved More Love Stands as one of the most unexpectedly brilliant shooters of its generation. Combining fluid movement, tight gunplay, and a surprisingly heartfelt story, it delivers an experience that feels both exhilarating and refreshingly unique. The campaign is the true highlight. It’s creative, fast-paced, and full of clever level design twists that keep you constantly surprised. But what makes it shine is the relationship between the pilot, Jack Cooper, and his Titan, BT-7274. Their bond adds emotional weight to a genre that rarely goes beyond explosions and firefights. Even today, Titanfall 2 feels fast, smooth, and incredibly fun. It’s one of those rare games that rewards both skill and creativity, making every fight memorable. In short: Titanfall 2 isn’t just a great game—it’s a modern classic that deserved far more attention. If you love fast, skill-based shooters with heart, this game delivers in every way. 9.5/10

I'm writing this review some 9 years after Titanfall 2's release, and yet it remains one of the best looking and best playing single player First Person Shooters ever made. It's genuinely remarkable how good this still looks, and it does so whilst running at very high frame rates on pretty much anything. Stutterstruggle is not an issue with Titanfall 2, as it runs on Valve's Source Engine, not Unreal. Zero stutters, zero hitches, just super fluid frame rates. Amazing what the combination of great art and a great engine can achieve, something we don't see much of anymore. The game also plays amazingly well. It has a perfect blend of high speed traversal with double jumps, wall running etc, with a big variety of unique sci-fi weaponry which all feel satisfying to use. They all sound great too, in fact the sound in general is top tier with a great cinematic soundtrack and a very densely layered sound mix. The campaign itself is also flat out great. The story is fine but the real heart of the story is the friendship between the main character and the mech. Dialogue is nicely done, just enough banter without ever getting annoying. It's too bad we never got a sequel to this, although it would probably have been on Unreal and looked and ran far worse than this. Still we'll always have Titanfall 2, which I expect will remain one an FPS high point for many years to come. Don't skip this one just because it's a few years old, it's still a phenomenal game from start to finish.

Jesus I wasn't ready for this, but I hated coming back to this game... Despite the low time listed I played this a lot when I still had my old EA account. I remember having a good enough time coming back to the campaign every so often, but this go around? Ugh... The campaign's gameplay is painfully "gamey." I know, that sounds like a nothing statement, but the novelty of stompy mech game clearly whitewashed much of my memory. 2025 me is just not okay with the amount of sterile "this is a video game" type moments. Here is obligatory too literal robot humor. Ha, funny. Here is the obligatory time travel level. Woo, go 2016. Here's the overblown "mwa ha ha, we so EEE-Vile" villains, complete with corporate mercenaries protecting the toxic waste facilities of their actual death chamber factory. I can't believe I can accurately write that statement, it's like the game was a parody of itself... The gunplay is...adequate, but it's not really inventive. Going back, there aren't really fun guns. Just, the guns every game had at the time. Sure, they might have sci-fi skins, but here's the revolver! It revolvers. Here's the machine gun! It go dudda-dudda-dudda. There are a few neat guns, but nothing beats the carbine for me...in a setting with big, stompy mech battles... The platforming is...functional? After playing Jedi Survivor, it's clear that Respawn is competent at hiding the seams of their platforming segments, but only just. What I mean is that...it's clear that this part is a ramp and it acts like ramps do. Here is the blatant roadblock to movement that must be double-jumped or wall-ran. It's functional, is what I'm saying. Not as blatant as, I don't know, Star Wars Outlaws going "this is a yellow spot, so you can climb it" type stuff, but not by enough to wow me. The mech battles are fine, but again, not really excellent. It's just the Gears-core chunky boi shooter with a mech theme on it, almost completely separate from the too-mobile for its own good pilot combat. I never had a moment where I went...oh! That mech is hunkered down, let me get out and rodeo it as my pilot. I just shot it with my mech til it died. I never pined for my mech in a shootout. Any challenge was just "oh! I died...darn. What got me? Some bull? Cool." I really like BT (the bot) and Cooper (the guy) and their interactions, but that's about all that really stuck with me after all of this time. The stuff that should be core memories of my time with the game just slide off of my neurons. That's all the campaign. The multiplayer has been anemic since I started playing years ago, so I can't say much about it, other than that Respawn never figured out how to make pilots work as bots, so that's probably why they don't exist. In hindsight, that was probably why Titanfall 1 was multiplayer only, too. I don't hate the game. I'm not mad at it, but this has aged poorly for me and I have requested a refund, because I have zero interest in playing the game ever again. That doesn't take my fond memories of my time away from me or anything. I can still fondly recall staying up to beat the campaign when it first came out, even as I can appreciate that the game isn't as good as I remember. If you don't have rose-tinted goggles for this, you can skip it. There's clearly a reason they never made a Titanfall 3 and it had nothing to do with a lack of interest for one.

Titanfall 2 Underrated King of Movement and Mech Mayhem Titanfall 2 isn’t just a shooter — it’s a full-blown adrenaline machine that refuses to slow down. From the second you wall-run into a slide, double-jump over a grenade, and drop a Titan from orbit like it’s your own personal meteor strike, you realize this game plays in a league of its own. The combat is fast, fluid, and absurdly satisfying. Gunplay feels crisp, every weapon has personality, and the game somehow balances acrobatic pilots with gigantic metal death machines without breaking a sweat. One moment you’re zipping across rooftops like cyber-parkour royalty, and the next you’re stomping around in a Titan, turning enemies into glowing confetti. And let’s talk mobility — because wow. Titanfall 2 makes movement feel like a superpower. Wall-running, grappling, sliding… it’s so smooth that every other FPS feels a little sluggish afterward. Once you get the rhythm, it’s like the game plugs directly into your brain. Then there’s the multiplayer — yes, it's still alive, and yes, it’s still ridiculously addictive. Every match feels like a highlight reel waiting to happen. Even years later, the community keeps the game humming, and jumping into a lobby still feels like meeting old friends who all learned how to sprint on walls. Titanfall 2 is a modern FPS classic — overlooked, underappreciated, but endlessly fun. Whether you're dropping Titans, styling on enemies with acrobatics, or just living out your mech-pilot fantasy, this game delivers pure, high-octane joy from start to finish. Rating 4.5/5

Titanfall 2 tam anlamıyla hız, akıcılık ve adrenalin dolu bir FPS. Kampanya beklemediğim kadar iyi çıktı — özellikle hikâye odaklı FPS severler için gerçekten keyifli bir deneyim sunuyor. Pilot olmak, duvarlara koşmak, parkur hareketleri… Bir süre sonra oyunun temposuna kapılıp geri dönmek istemiyorsun. Titanlar oyunun yıldızı! Onlarla savaşmak, farklı Titan sınıflarını kullanmak (Scorch, Ion, Northstar vb.) inanılmaz tatmin edici. Multiplayer modu ise hâlâ çoğu modern oyunun yapamadığını başarıyor: hızlı, pürüzsüz ve rekabetçi. Haritalar çeşitlilik ve strateji sunuyor. Düşmanlara karşı çevik hareketlerle, Titan’ınıyla zekice oynamak beni defalarca güldürdü. Özellikle bir duvardan süzülüp Titan’ın kollarıyla parçalayınca… Hah, o anları unutmak zor! -- Titanfall 2 is pure speed, fluidity, and adrenaline in FPS form. The single-player campaign surprised me — it’s genuinely fun and a rare treat for story-focused FPS players. Being a Pilot, wall-running, and nailing those parkour moves just feels amazing; you get sucked into the pace almost instantly. Titans are the real stars here! Jumping into giant mech combat, mastering different Titan classes (like Scorch, Ion, Northstar, etc.) is incredibly satisfying. And the multiplayer? It still delivers what many modern shooters fail to: fast, smooth, competitive gameplay. Maps are varied and strategic. Outmaneuvering enemies with slick movement, then turning the tide with your Titan? Some of the best moments I’ve had in shooters. Those smooth transitions from Pilot agility to Titan destruction… chef’s kiss!

Titans are no different, you can easily be decimated by a random pilot running around; all that means is you can also do it to them. EA doesn't deserve Titanfall. This is one of the most beloved FPS games for a reason. The campaign is fantastic, the movement has an incredibly high skill ceiling, the guns are awesome, Titan combat is really fleshed out and integrates amazingly into the game's singleplayer and multiplayer, there's not really any microtransactions, and there's no skill-based matchmaking. You start out sucking at the game, and as you get better, you really [i]feel[/i] your improvement as you begin to stand out against the other players in the lobby. It's very gratifying and refreshing compared to the dozens of modern FPS games where you are basically guaranteed to have a 50% winrate no matter how good you are due to their ELO systems. The overwhelming community love and support for this game that has grown even past the game's heyday is something that is extremely undervalued by soulless megacorp Electronic Arts. I guess it's just less risky and probably more profitable to continue to milk Apex Legends until the Titanfall franchise fades into irrelevance.

Not my thing. And I think there are 3 reasons for that: 1. The plot hook was not strong enough for me. Not like I expected something extraordinary or anything, but... When that captain died, it was extremely forced and almost nonsensical. Neither he, nor the Titan had any observable substantial damage. Aside from missing batteries, which also made little sense. 2. The shooting felt weird. Almost weightless, I guess, like there was no real impact force behind the bullets. Which is strange, because visually the enemies were exploding into pieces. It also sounded muffled, and playing with in-game and even system settings did not seem to change that. Both of these issues seemed to persists for multiple weapons, and even inside the Titan. 3. Runs at around 60 with periodic dips on ultra settings (one of the early cutscenes dipped to 12FPS somehow), even on 7900XTX. But problem is that it's just too detailed for my brain. I had similar issue with some multiplayer maps in F.E.A.R. especially some "tropical" one or whatever. So many little details, so many happening, and everything is so sharp, that it's borderline sensory overload for me, resulting in a very tiring experience of just trying to focus on something. One of the best FPS games out there. The combat feels incredible—whether you’re on foot or piloting a Titan, every battle is pure adrenaline. A quick restart usually fixes it, though.

Honestly, this game is truly underrated. That 2009–2016 era of FPS games was something special, and coming back to Titanfall 2 just reminds me how unmatched it really was. The combat is slick and incredibly fluid, movement just feels great even if a little floaty. I’m still not the biggest fan of some of the guns (a few lean a bit too hard into sci fi gimmick territory for me with a few interesting ones I wont lie), but the moment to moment gameplay more than makes up for it. The story isn’t the most original premise you’ll ever see, but it never tries to be anything it isn’t. It’s confident, tight, and surprisingly heartfelt. The banter with BT hits that perfect balance of dry humour, warmth, and weight a nice emotional break from the game’s overall darker tone. It's genuinely one of the better buddy dynamic narratives in shooters. And the level design? Honestly incredible. There are moments here that feel like master class set pieces taking advantage of unique mechanics in ways that are memorable without feeling like gimmicks. Levels like that one (you know the one) are still talked about for a reason, and even outside the standout moments, the campaign’s pacing and creativity keep things constantly engaging. It's got some decent performances by its voice actors which is always appreciated. It’s short, punchy, and doesn’t waste your time a rare thing now. Titanfall 2 really deserved better support and recognition at launch, because even today it stands toe to toe with the best shooters ever made.

Every now and then, a shooter comes along that reminds you why you fell in love with the genre in the first place. Titanfall 2 is that game. It’s fast, fluid, smart, and bursting with heart — all the things modern shooters often forget to be. A Campaign That Actually Cares When people talk about Titanfall 2, they always mention the campaign — and for good reason. It’s short, but every mission feels handcrafted, creative, and full of personality. You’re not just running through corridors shooting bad guys; you’re wall-running through collapsing factories, time-traveling through battles, and building a bond with your Titan, BT-7274, that hits way harder than you’d expect from a mech made of metal and code. BT isn’t just a robot. He’s your partner, your tank, your best friend. By the end of the story, you care. It’s a rare thing in an FPS where emotional storytelling usually takes a back seat to explosions.

Nearly a decade later, Titanfall 2 still stands as one of the best shooters ever made. Its parkour-style movement feels smoother than most modern games, turning every firefight into a fluid dance of speed and precision. The campaign — especially the unforgettable Effect and Cause mission — remains a masterclass in storytelling and design, with the bond between Jack Cooper and BT-7274 as heartfelt as ever. Multiplayer may not have the massive player base it once did, but it’s thriving thanks to a passionate community and private servers. The balance between agile Pilots and powerful Titans is still unmatched, offering a level of variety and intensity few games can touch. Verdict: 10/10 — A timeless classic that proves great design never ages.

[quote] Please consider following my [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/41005226/]Curation page[/url]. I cover a wide range of genres both paid and unpaid, providing unbiased opinions as well as regular giveaway events. [/quote] [b]Video Review[/b] https://youtu.be/k9z5lmeUlNs [h2]Still Holds Up![/h2] Titanfall 2... Let’s just say it was a masterpiece that redefined how we looked at the FPS genre. At a time when most major publishers (including EA itself) were dragging the scene down with buggy releases and half-hearted sequels as many still do to this day, like with Battlefield and Homefront, Titanfall 2 stood out as a breath of fresh air and hope. It took a step back to focus on what mattered: a strong, story-driven campaign, meaningful character connections, and fast-paced, fluid game play with online co-op matches, without that toxic, racist competitive feel. None of that Press F to pay respects nonsense, just pure, engaging design. With talented voice actors like Matt Mercer, fantastic writing and character development, cinematic missions, and smooth game play, Titanfall 2 delivered passion and polish in a way EA hadn’t previously managed since Mass Effect 2 or even TimeSplitters. Simply put, Titanfall 2 was (and still is) incredible. It reshaped the FPS genre by proving that speed, parkour mobility, and mech combat could coexist beautifully, without dragging each other down or holding each other back, offering both intensity and heart in equal measure. [h2]The Issue[/h2] There isn't a Titan Fall 2, and Titan Fall 1 got shut down and removed from store pages. A shame. [h2]Conclusion[/h2] I first played Titanfall years ago, and back then it was fantastic. Coming back to it now, I wanted to see how it’s aged, and honestly, for $2, it’s worth every penny. Sure, some elements feel a bit dated, like the classic brotherhood and sacrifice storyline that inevitably leads to the big “Nooo!!!” moment, but that was the popular style of the time, and it still works well today. Even after all these years, Titanfall 2 manages to deliver the same thrilling, cinematic experience it always did. It goes on sale often, and if you’re looking for a short but good single-player campaign with great game play and heart, it’s absolutely worth picking up.

Titanfall 2 is a first person shooter that combines fast infantry movement with mech combat. You play Jack Cooper, a rifleman who becomes the pilot of the Titan BT-7274. The campaign mixes parkour, shooting, and Titan battles. It is compact and varied. Movement is the core strength. Wall running, sliding, and double jumps create high speed navigation. Gunplay is tight with clear weapon feedback. Titan combat shifts to heavier weapons and shield management. The contrast keeps missions active. The campaign is short but well designed. Each level introduces a mechanic and uses it fully. Set pieces are inventive and avoid repetition. The story is straightforward with a focus on the pilot Titan partnership. It delivers momentum without downtime. Multiplayer is fast with a skill based learning curve. Pilots fight with mobility and gadgets, while Titans act as temporary power spikes. Modes encourage objective play. Match flow stays dynamic due to quick time to action. Progression unlocks weapons, Titans, and cosmetics. Performance and netcode are solid. Maps support movement routes and vertical play. The player base may fluctuate, affecting matchmaking speed. Private matches and co-op Frontier Defense add extra value. Overall, Titanfall 2 provides a refined shooter with strong movement and a standout campaign. It suits players who want speed, mechanical skill, and short but high quality single player content.

Ten out of ten. No caveats. Pure, unfiltered joy. From the very first frame, Titanfall® 2 makes you feel like a gamer who’s rediscovered what video games can do when design, heart, and ambition collide. The campaign is a masterclass in pacing and imagination — short, cinematic, and astonishingly clever. It never forgets you’re playing a game: puzzles that make movement feel brilliant, set pieces that reward curiosity, and an emotional core (the Pilot–Titan bond) that actually lands. “Toy story meets adrenaline” is the closest shorthand I can offer — it’s earnest, surprising, and somehow deeply human while also being ridiculous in the best possible way. Multiplayer? Flawless in its fundamentals. Movement in this game is the star: wall-running, double-jumps, slides, and fluid parkour create a ballet of chaos where skill expression feels meaningful from minute one. Gunplay is tight and responsive — every encounter has weight. The Titans add a spectacular layer of spectacle and strategy; they’re not just bigger guns, they’re whole different games that mesh perfectly with Pilot combat. Maps are smartly designed to reward both verticality and tactical cleverness, so every match feels fresh. Technical polish and audio-visual presentation are top-tier. The game runs beautifully, the art direction is bold without being overbearing, and the soundtrack elevates every sequence without trying to be louder than the moment. Sound effects — from the whine of a Titan’s servos to the satisfying click of a well-timed reload — are little pleasures that keep stacking up. What I love most: Titanfall® 2 never plays it safe. Its single-player is short but sculpted, daring to experiment in ways other AAA shooters won’t. Its multiplayer respects the player’s time and skill, offering frantic, high-skill matches that remain approachable and endlessly replayable. It’s rare to find a game that nails both the emotional, crafted one-player experience and the razor-sharp competitive playground — and does both exceptionally. Pros * Brilliant, inventive single-player campaign with genuine heart. * Peak mobility and movement mechanics — pure fun. * Satisfying, precise gunplay and excellent weapon feel. * Titans add strategic depth and cinematic spectacle. * Beautiful audio-visual design and excellent polish. Cons (nitpicks) * Campaign is on the shorter side — but every mission is a highlight. * Some online modes can be intense for newcomers — but the learning curve is part of the joy. Final verdict: If you love shooters, movement-based gameplay, or just brilliant game design, skip the hesitation and play Titanfall® 2. It’s one of those rare games that sticks with you — inventive, emotional, and endlessly replayable. This is a must-play.

Graphics / Visuals: 8/10 – For its time, Titanfall 2 still looks sharp, with fluid animations and stylish environments. Sound / Music / Atmosphere: 8/10 – The audio design sells the chaos of Titan combat, and the soundtrack keeps the adrenaline high. Single‑Player Gameplay: 7/10 – The campaign is excellent in concept and pacing, though a few sections feel slightly undercooked. Multiplayer Gameplay: 9/10 – Fast‑paced, original, and endlessly satisfying. You can clearly see the DNA that later evolved into Apex Legends. Story / Narrative: 7/10 – BT and Cooper carry the plot with charm, but the wider IMC vs. Militia conflict is fairly standard. Content & Replay Value: 7/10 – The campaign is short and sweet; multiplayer is where the longevity lies. Technical Performance: 7/10 – Stable, smooth, and still runs well years later. Achievements / Progression: 10/10 – A dream for hunters: brisk, skill‑based, and no pointless grind. Titanfall 2 is one of those rare shooters where both the single‑player and multiplayer shine. The campaign is a rollercoaster of inventive mechanics and set‑pieces, never overstaying its welcome. In fact, as an achievement hunter, I almost felt it ended too quickly — just as I was fully immersed, the credits rolled. Multiplayer, on the other hand, is a gem of originality. The fluid parkour, Titan loadouts, and fast‑paced combat make it feel like Apex Legends’ older sibling — same bloodline, same energy, just in a slightly different form. I’d happily sink dozens more hours into it, but my backlog and bucket list of games keep pulling me forward. For me, Titanfall 2 was a fast, exhilarating ride: a campaign that impressed, a multiplayer that still feels fresh, and an achievement list that respected my time. Fourteen hours to 100% completion, and every minute was worth it.

Things I like: - Among the best movement mechanics of any first-person shooter. Personally, I think Echo Point Nova is the only one that beats it. - Giant, pilotable robots. Enough said. - The gameplay is fast-paced & addictive. - The maps are large & spacious, and possess enough variety amongst themselves to force the player to change strategies, keeping the gameplay interesting. - The Holo Pilot is an effective way to confuse the enemy. - Legion is love. Legion is life. - Most other shooters tend to copy abilities from other titles and do little to make them unique. In Titanfall 2, however, the abilities of the pilots & titans are truly innovative. For example, Scorch is not your typical "flamethrower" class like the Pyro from Team Fortress 2 or Firebreak from Black Ops 3; he launches giant thermite grenades, gas canisters that explode upon ignition, and entire swaths of thermite along the ground. You don't find that ♥♥♥♥ in any other game. You also don't find the gravity star in any other game. - The music & sound engineering are great. - The voice actors convey a sense of authenticity--it's as if they're actually there and not pretending to be someone they're not. For example, grunts sound terrified & under stress whilst in battle responding to the environment around them, Briggs actually sounds committed & considerate of her people like her character is supposed to be, and Marder genuinely sounds like the cold, posh, and single-minded general he is. - Lots of skins to choose from. - Technologies do not feel class-exclusive and have a way of blending into other aspects of the game/world. For example, the smart pistol's target-finding technology is scaled up for Legion's Smart Core, the Phase Shift technology is scaled up for Ronin's Phase Dash & scaled down for the Phase Rewind boost, the electric smoke grenade technology is scaled up as a universal Titan countermeasure, and the Cloak technology is scaled up for the Cloak Drones in Frontier Defense. - Apart from the cosmetic paid DLC, there are no microtransactions. - The game is made with the Source engine and runs it very well. Good job. Things I HATE: - This game NEEDS a sequel and players have been vocally asking for one for years, but neither the developer (Respawn) nor the publisher (Electronic Arts) appear interested in providing one. - Respawn is too focused on developing Apex Legends--an objectively inferior game that shouldn't even be remotely considered part of the Titanfall IP--to continue meaningful contribution to Titanfall 2 content & improvement. - The game is published by EA and requires an EA launcher & account. - There was a period of time where the servers were getting DDoS'ed and neither EA nor Respawn put in the effort to fix it despite vocal player outcry lasting years. Thankfully, this has since been resolved, but the slowness to act has permanently stained the relationship between the players & the dev team. Things I don't like: - The campaign is too short. - There is no support for crossplay, even as similarly aged titles have already added it to themselves. - There is no support for local nor offline multiplayer. - There is no support for community-run servers outside of third-party mods like the Northstar client. - Many of the more interesting gamemodes, like Marked For Death, cannot be directly queued for. They must be queued via a rotating "mixtape". - You cannot queue for some modes (e.g., Frontier Defense, Coliseum) and the other gamemodes at the same time, forcing the playerbase to divide into one really populated queue for normal multiplayer and a couple other queues for Coliseum & FD that hardly get any traffic. - There are not enough weapons to choose from, especially shotguns, and not enough ways to customize them. - Skin customization on the Pilot, Titan, and weapons thereof is limited to one zone each. You cannot customize the skin by applying textures to multiple zones on the model, nor can you create your own textures & recolors. - Whilst I understand the Titans were given locked loadouts for balancing reasons, a fully customizable Titan loadout like in Titanfall 1 would make Titans less predictable. Diesel Knights & ShatterRush, two indie titles inspired by Titanfall, are already capitalizing on this. - Unlike Titanfall 1, you cannot change the voice of your Titan OS. Like Titanfall 1, too many of the OS voices are female. - There are some attention-to-detail things that feel overlooked, including (but not limited to): nose arts not perfectly wrapping around the Titan's model, limbs & accessories clipping through each other (e.g., Legion's left shoulder in the loadout screen), the training pod intro not being present on the Glitch map, the announcers feeling less lively than those in Titanfall 1, the other team being represented by a random faction logo that the players A) probably didn't choose and B) wouldn't make sense lore-wise for your faction to be fighting, the lack of video feeds over comms like in Titanfall 1, and Monarch only having one execution to choose from. - Boosts replacing Titanfall 1's burn cards probably wasn't a good idea. Many of the boosts have a niche purpose (e.g., Amped Weapons requiring you to stay alive, Hard Cover requiring you to be in a defensive situation), and Holo Pilot Nova is straight up useless--just use the regular Holo Pilot. - Respawn should have added all of the maps from Titanfall 1 to the Titanfall 2 map roster. - [spoiler] Some characters are oddly written. For example: Ash toys with Jack through the factory when it would make more sense for Kane's character to do that, and her obsession with "focus" as the Vinson Dynamics announcer is cringeworthy. Barker, though he is charming, doesn't sound drunk enough. I was really curious about trying this game after hearing so much praise about the campaign, so when I saw it once for like 2.99, I snagged it to give it a spin. I guess I should mention that I'm not that fond of milsims. Specifically anything resembling COD or Battlefield, that kind of thing. Those types of games made me believe in my younger years that I didn't like shooter games, because they were so prevalent. To me, they just all feel and look the same and I bounce off of them easily, even though boomer shooters ended up becoming one of my favourite genres after I gave Doom '16 a go many years ago. Titanfall's mould kind of fits that of a milsim, but what it does with that foundation elevates it to a point where i can confidently say I really enjoyed the game. Schmooving along the walls was super fun, it gave it the same edge and versatility that comes with movement shooters in general and added some flair to the otherwise standard modern shooter gunplay. The gameplay segments where you are piloting BT interachangeably kept the game from getting stale, I loved the different loadouts for him and experimenting with them, just pure fun taking out baddies with traps or giant 5m wide shotgun blasts. Tbh you acquire them so quickly throughout that I don't think you even get time to properly play with them for too long before you get another one, but silver lining of that is maybe that could be good for replays? At first the game wasn't grabbing me with the story, the first 30-ish mins kind of threw me off but in the end, I ended up liking the narrative even though i think Cooper was a bit of a milquetoast protagonist. I can't help but think they could've fleshed out his character a bit more, cause he does speak but very sparingly and doesn't have much of a sway to his personality. Maybe the intent was to make him kind of a blank slate for the player? Despite this, I think the game established an interesting concept with the Titans and how they're linked to their pilots. I would be interested in learning more about it, tbh. I'm a sucker for themes involving robots or AI becoming sentient and learning what it means to be human, and this has licks of it here and there. The latter half of the campaign especially goes all out with the setpieces and genuinely makes you feel awesome playing it, especially during the mech piloting parts. Apart from my dislike of the milsim theming, I'm gonna parrot what everyone else says about this game; It's too damn short! And whether or not we'll get TF3 is so far out of reach at this point that it'd probably be better to not hold my breath. But yeah, I just wish there was more of it!! I also wish they went a bit more out there with the weapons, I know there are some that are a bit wacky like the fire throwing stars or the volt gun, although I think we could've had even crazier ones. It's a scifi setting afterall, make some gimmick guns! Another thing I'm not too pleased about is that most of the characters are pretty bland and forgettable, like I didn't remember much about the big bad or his cronies that much except some of the boss fights, like the Ash one. That aside though, it's still a great game, definitely worth playing. Wish we got another part to this series, guess I'll join the TF3 waiting queue right beside the Half Life 3 one.

TITANFALL 2 review I was coerced into playing this game by the funny owl. I barely remembered their review and I'm quite glad I didn't. I fully agree that it's much better to go in blind. Even with the small amount that was shown to me it adds up significantly. If you are planning to buy this game for the campaign please do yourself a favor and not look at anything beforehand. This campaign is short and sweet. Never outstaying its welcome. I loved it and wished I had played it on master difficulty. The game recommended hard difficulty so that's what I went with and felt some encounters were easy. That won't be the case for everyone. So please enjoy at your own pace. Which is a lot to enjoy! A favorite of mine is when a first person shooter can incorporate silly or wacky or more correctly defined sci-fi weapons into a setting and not feel out of place. Especially when the reasoning behind such strong weapons is the fact that an army is expected to be using said weapons on infantry and titans alike. From guns that shoot electrified shots to ninja stars that embed themselves into titans to explode with thermite or sci-fi purple gravity it's a delight going into every fight not knowing what weapon it will throw at you next. Now for the elephant(s) in the room. Price and multiplayer. I did not buy this game full price. I seldom ever do. I paid a whopping 4.86 after tax. Less than $5, most people's lunches cost more. This game is easily worth more for just the campaign. If the game is on sale for less than $15 it is a must buy. If its a steam sale and less than $5 like i got it then why are you still reading go play this. Not everyone has extra money(or time) for video games. And this hits the mark in terms of dollar/minute of entertainment. i have not played the multiplayer and truth be told I don't have a want to anytime soon. I will update the review if that ever happens. That being said, finding out the original game was a multiplayer only experience is quite baffling with how enjoyable this game's campaign is. I hope to one day play again. To enjoy the multiplayer or get reacquainted with the controls if the third is ever released. ok edit woah played the multiplayer and absolutely love it. this is amazing

“Titanfall 2” is a fun and hard-hitting action FPS that becomes genuinely riveting toward the end thanks to strong direction and despite a barebones sci-fi story that serves as little more than scaffolding for the action set pieces (and ends on a somewhat unsatisfying note). But what really makes the game stand out is its level design. The campaign missions not only look great, they’re packed with creative mechanics and weapon variety, with each chapter introducing something fresh. Of course, this is partly “helped” by the game’s undeniable brevity and relatively low difficulty, even on “Master.” Still, “Titanfall 2” is a fantastic palate cleanser between bigger, more demanding titles, and a fun game to spend a couple of afternoons with. I’m not big on multiplayer matches, but from the little I experienced, I can absolutely see the appeal—it could be worth the price of admission on its own if you’ve got the right squad to jump in with (or against).

I began my Titanfall journey with Titanfall 2, on the Xbox One. I played a lot of the game, sucking at PvP but absolutely adoring the campaign and PvE Frontier Defense mode. I enjoyed my time on Xbox, even during the height of the hacking attacks the game suffered. In a rare show of care these days, Respawn came back to fix the issue and left again, leaving the game in the community's hands. Titanfall 2 is vastly different from the first, focused more on preset classes for players (Pilots with special abilities, and particular Titans with specific armaments and such) though in my opinion it has made the game so much more open, and made the game even more memorable than the first (sorry Atlas, I still love you bunches). While the game was kneecapped prior to release, the community, though small, is extremely passionate, and I'm proud of what it has accomplished since Titanfall 2's release and abandonment. The game is fun, the community is excellent, and your Titan is your best friend. Titanfall 2 will not die as long as us Pilots remain. Titanfall 2 is a masterpiece of the FPS genre, boasting an incredibly fluid and exhilarating parkour movement system that, when combined with its satisfying gunplay, creates a gameplay loop that remains unmatched years after its release. Its single-player campaign, while tragically short, delivers one of the most emotionally resonant stories in gaming through the heartfelt bond between pilot Jack Cooper and his Titan, BT-7274, making it an unforgettable experience that consistently goes on sale for a criminally low price. Though its multiplayer can be daunting for newcomers due to a dedicated, highly-skilled player base and its potential was squandered by EA's poor release scheduling, the game stands as a shining, must-play testament to innovative design and is worth every penny for its campaign alone.

After all these years, it’s still the best first-person shooter by a huge margin. I can’t believe people prefer to play the same repetitive Call of Duty or Battlefield games with no special gameplay or story, while a masterpiece like Titanfall 2 is collecting dust—just because EA was stupid enough to destroy their only masterpiece with their own hands. Even after losing this game, they’re now losing Apex as well. With simple ideas—like adding Jack Cooper as a character in Apex, or even just releasing a few skins for Titanfall 2—they could have kept the community alive. But instead, they decided to focus on Battlefield and their other useless games. If you’re interested, read this review from me, a young FPS gamer who’s been playing shooters for almost 10 years. Gameplay The core gameplay of Titanfall 2 is a masterpiece. Not because it was the first game to combine this kind of movement with an FPS, but because it did it in the best possible way. This movement system doesn’t add any disadvantages—it only improves the experience. The campaign missions are incredible, combining amazing level design with masterful gunplay and movement. The online gameplay was so good that Apex later took many of its mechanics, and other shooters copied elements of it too. It’s a joy to see that there are still skilled players keeping the online alive. The gameplay truly showcases what a masterpiece looks like. Story The story is genuinely engaging. Jack Cooper starts as just an ordinary soldier, and the plot develops in a way that turns him into the pilot of BT-7274. But what really shines is the evolution of the bond between the two. Earlier, BT even tells Cooper about his long relationship with Captain Tai Lastimosa, and we realize that the bond between pilots and their Titans is not ordinary at all. The way this relationship develops is beautiful. Cooper clearly doesn’t know anything about being a pilot at first, and the dialogue reflects that. But together, they learn. BT becomes a true friend, and Cooper becomes a true pilot. Just as BT’s first lines explain the protocols, his final lines end with the same—and with that unforgettable “Trust me.” I’m sure no one has ever felt such emotions for a robot before. Issues Aside from the campaign being short, my biggest problem was the weak boss fights. Except for Viper—who was absolutely amazing—the others were weak, almost indistinguishable from fighting a normal Titan. But still, when you defeat Ash, you get that satisfying feeling of victory. Final Thoughts I bought this game for 5 dollars, and it feels like I committed a sin. The game is absolutely beautiful, and you enjoy every moment of it. The campaign is amazing, and the multiplayer is still alive even today. Definitely buy this game if it’s on sale—it’s absolutely worth it. Trust me.

For those who don't know, or haven't noticed, some people are being blocked from playing online in the game because current CPUs are experiencing an issue that prevents the game from connecting to the EA server. To resolve this, open System Properties. Press Win + R, type sysdm.cpl, and press Enter. Or search for 'Edit the system environment variables' in the Start menu. Open Environment Variables. In the System Properties window, go to the Advanced tab. Click on Environment Variables… at the bottom. Create a new System Variable. Under System variables, click New…. For Variable name, enter: OPENSSL_ia32cap. For Variable value, enter: ~0x200000200000000. The game will be fixed and you can play online on the EA server.

Titanfall 2 is still talked about to this day as one of the best fps campaign ever made. With fun, fluid gameplay both inside and outside of a mech, a crazy action-packed and otherwise trippy ride with unexpected elements sprinkled throughout, and overwhelmingly positive reviews, this is a must play for all. Pros: + Fun and fluid gameplay mechanics, including wall running, thoughtful weapons and instant time travel + Extremely satisfying combat and movement. Most satisfying I’ve played in an fps game + Great plot and gameplay sequences + Menus and transitions are clean and snappy with almost no load time + Great graphical options and visuals + Extremely well optimized game, even on 4K res + Aged well and has been one of the greatest fps campaigns for a long time + Checkpoints are for the most part generous + Good pacing between boots on ground and mech + You have a knife that can hack things and also steer large ships + Fun multiplayer + Better than Call of Duty. CoD had also tried and failed to copy this game Cons: - Launching this game via Steam is an abysmal, terrible process. Launching this game via the mandatory EA app is only slightly better, but gets better after the first time. The game still sometimes launches windowed or minimized, even after selecting full screen in the settings multiple times. I had to install the game twice for it to even launch the first time. It does not play well with Steam - The writing and characters are quite lame and juvenile. Generic voice overs, the mech pesters you often, predictable lines taken from movies, and lame generic artificial intelligence not understanding human thoughts and feelings lame humor - Some mech against mech sequences seemed poorly designed - Humanizing robots, even giving them genders - Has a bug for 11th gen Intel processors that will lock multiplayer access on both Windows and Linux. The fix is a searchable and easy OS hack. This bug is a con, as it remains unpatched. - Has DLC - No HDR calibration - Published by scummy piss poor EA - Requires EA app Mixed: ~ Multiplayer has ai bots As an additional note; the swap between boots on ground and mech combat is a nice blend and was executed well. The mechs have various weapons and kits to unlock and choose from, which was a nice touch. However, I found myself favoring boots on ground not only because it was faster and provided more opportunity to avoid taking damage, but also because some mech sequences were set up awkwardly in a way where you can get surrounded and melted easily. In conclusion, you should buy it and you should play it. It isn't perfect, and I’m not sure about the best fps game ever made, but I do believe it nearly perfected the fast-based fps genre. Overall Rating: 4 out of 5
