Note: The vast majority of my playtime is on console (500+ hours as a guesstimate). Onto the review. I would consider this game in the top ten FPS's of all time. [h1]Multiplayer[/h1] Titanfall 2 multiplayer is by far one of the most rewarding pvp experiences I've played. [h2]Pilot Gameplay[/h2] The final balance patch left a couple weapons as obvious outliers (CAR and Spitfire) but asides from them the vast majority of the weapons are viable in even not so skilled hands. Because of the well balanced weapons the true show of skill in this game is in movement, it [i]is[/i] a movement shooter after all. With the engine being a heavily modified version of Source, movement tech is baked into it's DNA. Grapple pilot, gravity star jumping, b-hopping, rocket boosting, edge boosting, stim pilot, and many variations of strafe tech are some of the options available to you if you want to go fast. These movement options and tech come together to form the smoothest and best feeling movement system I've ever felt in a game, and as much as I love games like Ghostrunner, Neon White, and Mirror's Edge, Titanfall 2 manages to somehow make the player feel like they have the weight of a real person while still making the wallrunning and sliding fast and smooth. Movement in this game is intuitive enough that a new player can get to an intermediate level after maybe 3-4 sessions but still deep enough that truly mastering it can take months if not years. Every match is a race against yourself to keep up your speed while still maintaining the skill to hit your shots. Speaking of shots, I realize I haven't talked much about gunplay. That's mostly because there's not much to talk about, it's good. These are former Call of Duty devs who made this game so you can expect it to feel nice, with a very satisfying hitmarker sound. [h2]Titan Gameplay[/h2] What can I say, big robots are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awesome. Obviously one can tell that Titans are the star of the show just based on the name of the game. Each of the seven Titans have unique abilities that suit a wide variety of playstyles, with further customization with the choice of five kits for each titan that bolster or modify one ability or general gameplay for the Titan. Titan gameplay at its core has you trying to be as resourceful and efficient as possible while you walk around in your giant metal machine. Just because the health bar at the top of your screen looks big, doesn't mean it actually is, in a battle between Titans if you misuse your abilities or fail to utilize proper cover you'll be dead just like that and then you'll have to farm up your meter to call your Titan again. Each Titan can do serious damage relatively quickly so utilizing your defensive cooldown and cover will make or break a fight unless a teammate comes to help. Pilots have decent anti-Titan weaponry as well, not incredibly damaging but enough to make a difference if you don't make sure to pick them off as they come at you like mosquitoes. Each team will usually start to receive their Titans at a similar time, but sometimes one player will get theirs early, if they call it then they're no better than target practice as six enemy pilots plink-plonk them with heavy weaponry, but if the entire team gets their Titans fast then the opposing team is in for a bad time as the group of Titans cover each others weaknesses. This game of cat and mouse will make you start to be strategic with not only your weaponry in-Titan, but also when to use your Titan at all. Regardless of all that complex thought though, shooting things in a giant robot is and always will be fun. [h2]Maps/Map Design[/h2] The maps in Titanfall 2 are good, simple as that. There are a nice variety of maps which all have decent design from both a Pilot and Titan perspective, though some obviously lean more one way than the other which can put a damper on the mood if you keep getting maps more designed for the part of gameplay you're not in the mood for. This issue is solved by playing either Titan Brawl or Pilots Vs Pilots but sadly the population of the game isn't high enough to find a reliable amount of matches. One other issue is that there simply are not enough maps! I'm not going to act like there aren't [i]enough[/i], but there certainly could be more. [h2]Frontier Defense[/h2] This is getting a separate section because I think it's worth mentioning the game's only full pve co-op experience. Frontier Defense is a relatively simple 1-4 player wave based horde/objective defense mode, with four difficulties selectable before starting, that ends at wave five. Each wave the game chooses a preset with predetermined types of and amounts of enemies (grunts, robots/drones, and various types of Titans). You start of as a Pilot and then get your Titan at the end of wave one. At the end of each wave the money you got from bonuses and killing enemies can be used to buy a few simple upgrades like turrets, stunning arc traps, or batteries to replenish your Titan's health. The replayability of this mode is solely dependent on how much you like semi-mindlessly shooting enemies. Because of the predetermined wave types once you figure out a type it becomes pretty easy as you'll know how to play the wave just based on the wave's starting tagline. The maps used for this mode are recycled multiplayer maps and sadly there's only nine, which for a gamemode as simple as this is not good at all. Having such a low pool of maps in such a simple gamemode means that getting unlucky and playing Homestead three times in a row can very quickly kill and drive to play the mode. With no more updates that means the only remedy is fan-made/adapted maps on a modded client. Regardless, it is still fun to just chill with some music on when you have nothing else to do (or more likely when you can't find a regular MP match). [h1]Campaign[/h1] Onto what is widely considered the best part of the game. I'm going to keep this section light to avoid spoilers for future players. This campaign is among the top three FPS campaigns of all time for me and among my general top ten campaigns as well. It consists of one tutorial mission/prolouge and eight main story missions and should take around 5-8 hours depending on how thorough you are in each mission. The campaign was designed gameplay first and it shows, each mission is fun and unique with a great balance of Titan and Pilot gameplay and mechanics, mission four (Effect and Cause) in particular is a fan favorite for it's simple but very well utilized primary mechanic. Despite being designed with gameplay as a priority, the narrative isn't by any means bad or even just ok, I'd call it great. It's a relatively simple story without much nuance, but the characters are very likeable, the dialogue is never cringe-inducing or awkward in feel, and the overarching themes are pretty timeless. [h1]Final Words[/h1] This game (and franchise) is truly a one of a kind experience and I'm not sure we will ever get anything like it again, sadly it was put to bed too early by EA when they decided to release it directly between Battlefield 1 and Call of Duty Infinite Warfare, two goliaths not just in the genre but the entire industry, and then also deciding to cancel the third game in the series. Luckily this game is still here and available to purchase unlike the first, it's community is small but fiercely devoted and you'll always be able to find someone to talk with about it whether it be for gameplay advice or lore discussion. I highly recommend--implore, even--anyone reading this review to pick up this game for the meager $3.99 it goes on sale for every other week. You will not regret it. Trust me.

Titanfall 2 I never played the first Titanfall, but with the sequel including a full campaign, this was a fresh and exciting experience. For a 2016 release, the game still feels steady—graphics, movement, lighting, weapons, and voice work all hold up to AAA standards. The campaign is on the shorter side. At around 12 hours with all collectibles, I found myself wanting more. Still, every moment was enjoyable, and it never felt padded. Tutorials were quick and helpful, though the on-screen hints sometimes broke immersion. What stood out most was the relationship between the pilot and BT. Their banter grows into a genuine camaraderie, grounding the fast-paced action with personality and humor. The variety of loadouts for BT adds replayability, letting you approach combat with different styles. Boss encounters were another highlight, each bringing unique challenges that kept the gameplay fresh. No crashes, no major issues—just a tight, polished shooter with heart. Titanfall 2 may be short, but it delivers a memorable campaign worth experiencing. —The Ember Archives https://store.steampowered.com/curator/45601239/

Titanfall 2 isn’t just a game—it’s a caffeine shot directly to the soul with a robot best friend who makes you look cooler than you’ll ever be in real life. ====== The Good ====== The campaign feels like someone spliced a sci-fi blockbuster with an emotional buddy cop flick, where your partner weighs 20 tons and throws you around like a baseball. Movement is so fluid that you spend most of your time convinced parkour should be a daily commute option. You wall-run once and suddenly hate the concept of stairs. Titans aren’t just mechs; they’re giant hugs made of metal and rockets. Calling one down from orbit is basically nature’s way of giving you a high-five for surviving 30 seconds longer than expected. ===== The Multiplayer ===== Picture dodgeball, except everyone has automatic weapons, high-tech armor, and the ability to run on walls. The maps are designed so cleverly you’ll swear you’re a genius for chaining six acrobatics in a row—right before someone half your age blasts you out of the air. It’s chaos, but beautiful, cinematic chaos. ===== The Verdict ===== Titanfall 2 is that friend who convinces you to go out on a random night, and suddenly you’re ziplining off a building, piloting a tank-sized robot, and possibly crying about a robot who understands friendship better than most humans. It’s fun, it’s fast, and it’s criminally underrated. Think "shiny parkour ballet with explosions"—and then multiply it by pure joy.

Titanfall 2 is hands down the best game I have ever played. I used to play on PlayStation back in the day, and now here on PC, I keep coming back to it. The main stand out feature in my opinion is the movement mechanics, no other game has even come close to achieving what Titanfall 2 has done. You can go whole games without ever touching the floor and you wont even realise. Throwing yourself through the air and gliding across walls feels completely natural paired with a tactical like a grappling hook of stim boost. Its simultaneously extremely fast paced and very satisfying. The gunplay complements the movement perfectly, by no means is it realistic, but who needs realism when your 20 meters in the air quickscoping someone across the map. Or flying past someone, moving just as fast as you, both attempting to kill the other. Almost every gun is balanced and can be used well, the only complaint I have about the guns is the pesky Car and Spitfire, which are slightly unbalanced. But what makes Titanfall really unique is, obviously, the TItans. Somehow going from being a tiny, fragile but speedy pilot to a tanky, slow but extremely powerful TItan, works really well. You would think that the game would become unbalanced as soon as a couple of people get their titans but no, it meshes perfectly. I can't really explain how it works it just does. Outside of multiplayer the campaign is amazing, BT-7274 is NOT a clanker, far from it, his personailty is unmached, and the bond Jack Cooper and BT develop through the story feels genuine. Each mission feels distinct with its own mechanic for that level including time travel and moving parts to the extreme. The story is great and as the player you feel involved and impactful. The only donwside is the length of the campaign, with it being only 6-8 hours but that just means everything feels purpousful, there is no filler missions. I have played the campaign so many times and would happily play it again. If you've never tried it, you owe it to yourself to experience this masterpiece.

[h1]Titanfall 2[/h1] [h3][Overview][/h3] Titanfall 2 is a sci-fi FPS that incorporates parkour elements and mech combat. In the campaign, you play as Jack Cooper, a militia rifleman who commandeers a Titan known as BT-7274 following the death of its original Pilot. Cooper and BT form a loyal bond as they fight through various battles while on their mission to prevent a mega-corporation known as the IMC from releasing a devastating super-weapon. [h3][Recommended Tweaks][/h3] - Add launch options to enable Raw Mouse Input & Borderless Windowed mode: +m_rawinput 1 -window -noborder [h3][Positives][/h3] - Great gameplay. Movement feels incredibly smooth, gunplay is great, you get useful abilities, etc. - Good weapon selection and variety. Guns feel weighty and impactful which is great. - Good graphics and art style. Definitely one of the best looking Source engine games out there. - Great campaign. The levels are very solid, and the boss battles are decent. - The Time Gauntlet and Arc Tool are both great, albeit short-lived gimmicks in the campaign. It would’ve been nice to see them both used more. The sections of the game that utilize them felt like they took inspiration from 3D puzzle-platformers which I found enjoyable. - Being able to pick your preferred dialog options in the campaign is nice. [h3][Mixed][/h3] - The campaign’s difficulty is far too easy. I’d recommend playing on Hard at least, but I found Master to be the most well-balanced. - The campaign is really solid, but it definitely felt like it was meant to be more than it was. It’s too short for its own good, and it would’ve benefited with more time to further flesh out its unique gameplay ideas and narrative. - The controls, while solid, can get in the way at times. Wall-running can be especially finicky. - $30 is steep if you’re only playing for the campaign, but the game goes on sale fairly often. [h3][Negatives][/h3] - Requires an EA account and the EA App. - Multiplayer is filled with cheaters. - Some of the deeper story and lore is weak. Most of the campaign characters are generic. The good guys are generic future militia soldiers, the bad guys are generic mercenaries, and there’s also a generic evil corporation at the head of it all. Not very interesting for the most part. The bond between Cooper and BT is the only main compelling part of the story, and it’s a shame it wasn’t expanded upon further. - Depth of field is pretty obnoxious in some of the cutscenes. It’s also forced on with no way to disable it. [h3][Conclusion][/h3] Titanfall 2 is one of the most fluid and satisfying FPS games I’ve ever played. The gameplay is fantastic, and the campaign is excellent as well. Multiplayer is unique, but full of cheaters. Overall great game. 8/10 Follow my [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/44976971/]Steam Curator[/url] page!

[quote]Just saying, but I do have a curator page. If you like my remarks about games, you can find more of them here: https://store.steampowered.com/curator/44130985-TDP%27s-Gaming-Escapades [/quote] Modern first person shooters used to be good. They used to have fantastic single player campaigns featuring gripping stories, fun gameplay and/or incredibly likeable characters. But then the focus shifted to prioritizing multiplayer modes as they brought in more money and players. So the campaigns became an afterthought, getting weaker and weaker with every release, while more resources were dedicated to the development of multiplayer modes. Several games have tried to break this norm, such as the modern DOOM and Wolfenstein games. I recently played those games and ended up having mostly negative impressions of them, partly due to how their gameplay styles were structured and partly due to the story presentations. Then I tried Titanfall 2 after neglecting that game for a very long time and... I honestly can't believe EA published this. [h2]Activision execs are utter morons for causing these guys to leave Infinity Ward[/h2] Titanfall 2 is created by Respawn Entertainment; A studio consisting of various veteran members of Infinity Ward who had previously worked on Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 1 and 2. This bit of info alone should tell you how good the single player campaign is in this game. Titanfall 2's campaign is without a single shred of doubt, one of the best campaigns in the FPS genre. It can be finished in about 4 hours, yet its level of quality is truly praiseworthy. The pacing is very well-done, with story events never feeling rushed or dragged out. All of the major plotpoints happen while you are witnessing them, instead of keeping them as backgorund developments. The game constantly introduces new things to prevent its gameplay from going stale. The scale of events gradually rises through the campaign, turning what starts like your ordinary sci-fi shooter into an adrenaline fueled, all-out war to ensure a whole planet's survival, with lots of moments that catch you truly off guard. The final missions of the game in particular have some of the hypest events and setpieces that I have ever seen in a first person shooter. I wish I could tell you about them, but I don't want to spoil anything. But that's not the whole thing, as the campaign is also full of emotion and personality. A part of this is thanks to the NPCs reacting to what you do, like cheering you on after doing seemingly impossible feats. And the other part is because of the inclusion of a very unusual, yet fantastic companion that is by your side through the entirety of the game... Someone who needs their own section in this review. [h2]"Trust me."[/h2] Throughout the campaign, you are accompanied by a vanguard class titan called BT-7274. Contrary to many titan models in the game's world, BT can act on his own and respond to whatever that happens around him, while also being capable of verbal communication with others. And the developers have used this to great effect. One can describe BT as a gentle giant. He's literally a machine of mass destruction, armed to the teeth and with the ability to flatten any normal human with ease, but acts and talks in a very calm and collected manner at all times, even when he should be freaking out. Not only that, BT proves himself to be an exceptional ally, always watching after the main character and being there when the situation requires his immediate intervention. He is already incredibly likeable, but then the dialogue options are introduced and take the friendship between him and the player to the next level. At many points in the game, you will be given the option to have a brief conversation with BT, either to ask him a question or to respond to what he has just said or done. Basically, a pop-up will appear on the bottom of the screen, containing two dialogue options for you to choose from. These conversations are completely optional and do not affect the story progression, but going with them causes you to deepen your bonds with BT. There's also some fun to be had, as BT's incapability of understanding puns ends up with hilarious responses coming from him. To top this all off, some of the most exhilarating moments in the campaign comes from him going against an enemy titan. All of these have turned BT into one of the most likeable and memorable characters in the FPS genre, if not all of gaming. I cannot express how much I love this character and how badly I want him to return. [h2]A pilot can only be stopped by an equal or overwhelming force...[/h2] So, we now know the campaign is fantastic. What if I told you the gameplay is equally fantastic and incredibly fun as well? Titanfall 2 has intergrated movement into one of its core gameplay elements, and uses it to full extent during platforming and combat. Sure, you can treat the combat sequences like a normal Call of Duty, but it becomes ten times more fun when you try to do more with what you are given. The parkour abilities, coupled with smooth controls, fluid gunplay and the ability to reload while running, allow you to run around, gun down everyone you see in style and feel like a total badass. Your melee attacks can knock down everyone in one hit, making it extremely fun to just run around and punch or jump kick anyone you see. The gameplay while piloting the titan is also equally fun, as you clearly feeling like you are controlling a machine of mass destruction and whenever you run into other titans, the resulting combat is nothing short of exhilarating. The game even successfully tries to lean you into its preferred playstyle, as the levels and platforming hazards are smartly designed in a way to make you better without you even realizing it. The game is training you on how to use the movement options and your titan's loadouts through the whole campaign, so by the end of the game, you have a complete understanding of the game's movement system and not only you are almost ready for the online modes, but a second playthrough will prove to be even more fun than the first. [h2]Unfortunately, nothing is flawless...[/h2] And I said all this, without even talking about the multiplayer modes! Which, again, should tell you how good the campaign mode is. As for why I didn't bother with the online modes... well... first, I don't have the time to play online and second, I don't want to deal with its problems. The online portion of this game acts... wonky, and not because of the netcode. Titanfall 1 & 2 have mostly been neglected by EA, and something always happens from time to time. The EA App might cause issues, the servers might get DDOS'd for prolonged periods of time, or your CPU might cause incompatibility issues and lock you out of online services. But I implore you to not let these stop you from getting this game. Titanfall 2 goes for as cheap as 3 USD, and it's a hell of a bargain for the campaign alone. Online mode issues aside, there are also some possible performance issues in the game as well. Titanfall 2 runs on a heavily modified version of the Source Engine, which I personally know as one of the engines with consistently good performance output. But while the game looks really good, runs pretty well and the loading screens are insanely fast, problems such as random stuttering, launch problems, freezing and crashing might arise depending on your hardware. [h2]TL;DR[/h2] A fantastic first person shooter, featuring a very fun gameplay alongside a gripping single-player campaign mode with one of the best companion characters in the genre. You might not want to miss this

[h1]Story/Campaign[/h1] (will be used interchangeably) It's very solid, however it's way too short, not enough time for the player to get sufficient experience to get used to the titan's abilities, in my opinion at least lol, and can't quite get a feel for all of the weapons, not even in the gauntlet training mode. Hard mode as a beginner was properly challenging, it took me less than 10 hours (around 8 maybe) to beat the entire story, there are still collectibles to collect which is a cool thing but it doesn't really add much to the game beside achievements. There is also an incredible bug that still haven't been fixed, it occurs in "Trial By Fire" mission, after getting into the stronghold/building, if you happen to hit the checkpoint when you get inside and then die at any point after entering, your ally will be bugged and you have to restart the entire mission, sure it takes like 4 minutes or less to get to the same point but for you to find out that your ally is supposed to follow you through the building and for them not to do it completely ruined the mood for the rest of the missions and the arch with your titan. It's pretty frustrating that you been wasting time trying to make your ally move with the electrified smoke to give them the illusion of safety. It does work and you need to push them. [h1]Multiplayer[/h1] Due to level locked equipment, including perks, it's not a really enjoyable experience with experimenting, my best guess is it's influenced by Call of Duty's level system at the time. At least every pilot/tactical is available from the get go. There are also lot of modes in game which is pretty cool. [h2]PvP[/h2] The "stock" beginner weapons are really good but it sucks that you don't have many options to choose from. Also the game developed a meta since it's release, nearly everyone runs the same titans (Tone, Ronin) and guns (CAR, Kraber, etc). Also the latter mentioned Kraber sniper rifle is OHK (One Hit Kill) but has some travel time, sorta balances out and unfortunately melee is also OHK for some whatever reason Respawn Ent. thought it would be an awesome idea. My other gripe with PvP is the atrocious balancing, I thought Team Fortress 2's and Counter-Strike's balancing were awful, the brought up examples are games I have lot of experience with and think have awful to terrible matchmaker got topped by Titanfall 2's, contrary to popular belief, being stopped by G40 (Prestige level 40, meaning they are like 400 level + whatever else) something vets/tryhards is not fun and you not learn anything from it just because how crazy a movement shooter can go. Sure this game has a worse MM due to the lack of players while the said examples have more but all 3 fails to give consistent matchmaking, CS2 suffers from botched ratings(premier)/rankings(old comp mode), you having a hidden rating that you can only consciously keep track of but still giving you matches with 3k to 13k rated players in the same lobby or team even. Team Fortress 2 has a falsely advertised SBMM, but even though having mostly botted player count still provides a semi decent play and said MM is a downgrade of what it had previously. Back to Titanfall 2 my other gripe is that the game mostly being played in TDM, which itself is a fine mode but there are at least 7 more gamemodes, and I do queue for all gamemodes but I have to go out of my way and untick TDM for it to give me other gamemode matches. [h2]PvE aka Frontier Defense[/h2] So far on Easy mode the game is fairly fun! Grab some friends, this is the only game mode I would advocate for a game purchase and nothing else honestly. Regular/Normal feels largely the same as Easy, I haven't noticed a difference, but Hard is like proper Hard, this game mode is amazing genuinely. [h1]Closing words, TL;DR, S.C.R.E.W. Titanfall 2 is hands down one of the most fun shooters I’ve ever played. It’s super fast-paced, so it might not be for everyone, but once you get into it, nothing else really compares. Honestly, I’d still call it the best multiplayer game out there, and it blows my mind how underrated it is - the small player count just doesn’t make sense for how good it is. The Titans are the star of the show. They’re designed to feel grounded and believable, like a real machines you could imagine existing in the world. Piloting one is incredible - you can really feel the weight behind every step and shot. It’s like running around in a giant war crime machine swatting away mosquitoes. On the flip side, fighting a Titan as a pilot feels intense - they’re like towering golems that can one-shot you, so you’ve got to be smart and fast to survive. That balance makes every fight feel thrilling. The game’s age doesn’t matter at all - it still outshines most modern shooters. The campaign is good, but multiplayer is where it really shines. The only downsides are the occasional camper with a Kraber and the fact that cheaters used to be a problem, though these days they’re pretty rare. Overall, Titanfall 2 is a masterpiece that deserved way more love than it got.

One of the best shooters I've played in recent years. First of all, I appreciate that the game does not waste my time with endless cut scenes and exposition as well as 1 hour tutorials. As soon as you start the game, you get told the basics of the story pretty quickly, and then you are thrown into a small tutorial that serves not only as a way for you to test the game mechanics, but it also accesses your proficiency with said mechanics and gives you a recommended difficulty level. This tutorial is in the form of a small obstacle course where you have to move as fast as you can while also killing every enemy that you see. As you finish it for the first time, you immediately think "I can do it faster now that I know a few tricks" and you go again. Eventually, I settled for a time after a few tries and took the "Hard" difficulty recommendation, and I can tell you that after finishing the game I was thankful for it. There are parts of the game that were somewhat harder and required a few tries, but even then it was nothing over the top. If I had been left to choose it for myself, the game would probably be a walk in the park and I wouldn't have enjoyed it as much. I know this must not have even easy to implement, but it was honestly one of the best design choices the team made and I wish it would be this easy to pick a difficulty in other games without having to either go for a lower one and never adjusting it, or go for a higher one and end up struggling with the game to the point where you stop enjoying it and just drop it. Besides that, the game has a lot more going for it. First of all, the movement. It feels so good to run across the maps while jumping and riding walls, trying to flank the enemies before they flank you. Its so fluid, I was left wondering whether I was playing Titanfall or a new Mirror's Edge game. Then, we have the Titans themselves. It feels amazing to pilot one of these things and crushing everyone that is unfortunate enough to cross your path while your piloting it. And the game keeps giving you different Titan variations as you progress through the story, allowing you to test all of them and choose which one you prefer for the current scenario. You also end up having a few boss fights in these things and when I was in one it was quite tense. These were probably the missions that I had to repeat the most, the enemy Titans do not joke around when fighting you one on one. But each time I restarted the fight, I learned something new that allowed me to push forward, so it wasn't an annoyance retrying these a few times. The level design itself is also amazing. Besides the tutorial level and the missions where you get to pilot the different Titans, there was also one where you get a device that allows you to time travel between the current time period and the past, using it to solve puzzles but also for combat. One moment you're in the present surrounded by soldiers and in the next you have outmaneuvered them by traveling to the past, repositioning, and traveling back to the present. I can also remember a mission towards the end where you get stripped of your weapons and Titan and have to make through it somehow. Finally, the shooting. It feels amazing. I don't remember a lot of games, let alone single player games, that have such a satisfying feeling. Each time you pull the trigger its like a dopamine injection straight to your brain, and when you land a head shot its even more satisfying. I don't know why it is so hard for other games to replicate this feeling, but it felt amazing from start to finish to shoot each and every weapon I found in the game. I definitely recommend you to try this game for yourself, and if after one hour you haven't found it fun, just refund it. The game doesn't take that long to complete too, which to me is a god send when every game nowadays wants you to invest 30+ hours just to roll credits.

A very polished, linear FPS from the gamergate era that I found in the Steam bargain bin. I paid close to $1 per hour of game play-- a great value. TItanfall 2 is nice to look at and ran smoothly at 4K resolution on my 5-year-old rig. It also has fantastic combat and a great soundtrack. My only two gripes are that it relies too heavily on themes borrowed from other games, and there is very little character building. Still; it's an enjoyable romp with guns, mechs and wall running.

Sometimes I get tired or burned out from long, exhausting games. In those moments, I really appreciate shorter titles with a clear goal, a concise story, and solid execution across the board. Titanfall 2 delivers exactly that — in about 5 hours (short by today’s standards), you get a well-made FPS shooter that does almost everything above average. My only real complaint would be the boss fights. They don’t feel challenging, exciting, or unique — they’re basically just like fighting regular enemies. Other than that, if you’re looking for a short, story-driven FPS shooter, this is definitely worth a shot.

I’ve been playing Forza Horizon 5 for a while now, and honestly it’s one of the most enjoyable racing games I’ve played. What I like the most is how easy it is to make money and collect cars. The game keeps rewarding you with credits, wheelspins, and free cars, so it never feels too grindy. Even after a few hours of playing, my garage was already full of amazing cars. The map looks beautiful and there’s always something fun to do, whether it’s racing, exploring, or just driving around. It’s also a game that pretty much anyone can enjoy. Kids can have fun with the simple controls and colorful world, while adults can enjoy the huge variety of cars and events. The only part I found difficult was drifting. It definitely takes practice to get the timing and control right, especially during drift zones. At first I kept spinning out, but after some time it became really satisfying. Overall, Forza Horizon 5 is a super fun game with great graphics, lots of content, and a rewarding progression system. Definitely worth playing if you enjoy racing games.

As we're heading to Horizon Festival's next destination, I feel like I should say a few words about this game before hopping behind the wheel of my Lancer VI for the last time in Mexico. I made acquaintance with the Forza series from Forza Motorsport 4 on my second-hand Xbox360 back in the day. It was brilliant. Hugging apexes in roaring Ferraris, drifting high in the alps in JDM classics - it was new, fresh, and bloody well done. The same feeling carried over to Horizon. Road racing, hugging tight corners with your loyal beast purring underneath you, pulling insane G's. Drifting, late night sessions with the boys, pushing each other into walls because none of you knew how to properly drift. With an addition of... offroad (excluding Horizon 1), exploring the map in 1,000 horsepower buggies and SUV's while listening to fast-paced Drum & Bass. Playground Games did a damn good job with Horizon 3 and 4, being my all-time favorite Forza games. But Horizon 5? There are good and bad things about it. Can't complain, overall experience was amazing. Heart-stopping near misses, clean and dirty overtakes, PvP and PvE racing with little kids trying to push you off the track or ram you into walls - it was fun, generally. Generally. My main complaint is how barren the map feels. Don't get me wrong, I have countless laps around the whole map of Mexico in my Lancer, with tight corners and long straights diversifying the experience. It's just that the middle of the map feels empty. Same feel, despite where you drive. Vast fields, tight roads, little huts scattered around the land. It was not enough. It still felt empty and uneventful. As if the whole map was designed around the Battle Royale mode, which, let's admit it, was a flop. The City. It felt rural. For a major city on the map it felt just ancient. Empty. Small. Suffice it to say that after completing every single race in that area I never even considered driving around the city [i] just because [/i]. Simple as that. I have high hopes for Tokyo, and I am very excited to drift through the neon-filled streets of a MODERN city, just like in Horizon 3. Car Sounds. Now, pardon me. This section is going to be pretty short, as I have just one major complaint. Why in the ♥♥♥♥ are they re-using sounds for the same car brand over and over again? Lambos and Ferraris sound the EXACT same no matter the model. Overall.. The game is great. Late-night drives solo or with friends, competing for the first place with randoms whose ego urges them to push you off the course, custom-tuning your cars to your liking, racing through the vast landscapes with Hospital Records blasting fast-paced tunes in your ear and the engine of your AMG GT R roaring like a wild beast beneath you - all those granted me plenty of good memories, fun moments and an overall great impression of the game despite its flaws. Rating: 7.5/10. I'll see you in Japan, fellow drivers. Let's race, clean and dirty, for one to emerge victorious!

As a long term fan of the Forza Horizon series, I was extremely hyped for this game (and am for the 6th game too). This game definitely wasn't 'bad' by any means but in my personal opinion it didn't iterate nearly enough and the things it did iterate on weren't enough to solve its shortcomings. Firstly, I don't care what anybody says, the map is awful. There is nothing remotely interesting to find or see on this map, its just dirt. For a map only 30% bigger than the last game without making it any more diverse was a let down for me, thankfully it seems like Forza Horizon 6 will fix that. Another thing I dislike is that there's no penalty or losing, you can't make mistakes in this game because it rewards you no matter what you do, hell even simply not playing the game will reward you with a bunch of wheelspins in your message center for when you decide to come back. You start out with extremely good cars and 40 minutes in you could probably buy one of the fastest cars in the game, it's not fun to progress in this game because your just baby fed EVERYTHING. The last few points I have made have sounded negative so Id like to be a bit positive before ending this review, its not a 'bad' game, its still really fun to drive around, play with friends, explore the map even if its not great, the visuals are nice, the cars are nice, the game is extremely optimized, its not bad... just not enough over Forza Horizon 4, which is why it still gets a thumbs up.

Forza Horizon 5 takes the foundation of its predecessor and refines it into the ultimate celebration of car culture, moving the festival to the vibrant, sprawling landscapes of Mexico. It doesn’t try to reinvent the wheel. Instead, it focuses on scale, spectacle, and a much more cinematic sense of discovery. The first thing that hits you is just how gorgeous the game is. Even half a decade after its release, it remains a technical benchmark for the genre. Though it’s a bit of a bittersweet realization knowing my current PC probably won't be able to handle the jump to Horizon 6. The map is a massive part of that beauty. While some players felt it lacked elevation, I didn’t find that to be the case at all. The world has its highs and lows, pun intended, from the towering volcano to the coastal flats. And while the seasons are admittedly less dramatic than the snowy UK winters of the last game, that simply comes with the territory, pun intended again. It’s a natural trade-off for such a diverse Mexican setting. Where the game truly steps up is in its presentation of the races themselves. In many open-world racers, tracks feel like empty streets with a few arrows taped to a pole, but here, every race feels like a physical event. When you arrive, the track is built out with grandstands, professional start-finish lines, and festival branding. It feels like a real, organized competition. The coolest part is that once the race is over, all that infrastructure is gone, and the road returns to being a normal highway. It adds a layer of immersion that makes the world feel alive. The progression system remains largely the same as the fourth game, which is great for those who value their time, but it does introduce some smart improvements. The new Expeditions are a highlight. These are scripted, objective-based journeys that act as gateways to new festival sites. They give the game a better sense of pacing and make expanding the festival feel like a genuine milestone rather than just ticking off a checklist. Of course, the core of the experience is still the cars. There is an insane amount of them to choose from, and they all look, sound, and drive exceptionally well. At the end of the day, Forza Horizon 5 isn't trying to be a grueling simulation. It’s a masterclass in pure, accessible fun. It’s a near-perfect refinement of the formula that makes you feel like the star of the show from the moment you hit the gas. This ties into the game's greatest strength. The power fantasy. You are treated like absolute royalty from the jump. You can miss your braking point, scrape every wall, and crash through every corner, yet the commentators and fans still treat you like a god-tier superstar. It’s a pure, guilt-free power fantasy that prioritizes your enjoyment over punishing your mistakes. Even when your driving is less than professional, the game refuses to break the illusion that you are the greatest to ever do it. As for the post-launch content, the two big DLCs: Hot Wheels and Rally Adventure, are both high-quality additions with plenty of content. They are objectively good expansions that offer a lot of variety, though if I’m being honest, I personally fancied the ones in Horizon 4 a bit more. There was just something about the atmosphere of Fortune Island and the charm of LEGO Valley that felt a bit more special to me, even if the Mexico expansions are technically more polished. It’s a shame the game is still often perceived as a mixed bag by some. For me, it was a great game while it lasted, offering a masterclass in pure, accessible fun. But with the community's eyes already turning toward the future and the hopes of Japan, it feels like it’s finally time for the series to move on. Unfortunately, because of my hardware, I won’t be joining that next trip. For now, I’m happily stuck in Mexico, and there are far worse places to be stranded.

[h1]Forza Horizon 5: A masterpiece that’s always there for you[/h1] Forza Horizon 5 is more than just a racing game; it’s an absolute [b]masterpiece[/b]. What I love most is how it fits literally any mood. Whether you're feeling down, stressed, or just pure joy — this game takes you as you are. You can just hop in, start driving, and let the world wash over you. It’s like a digital comfort zone. [h2]Mexico & The Vibe[/h2] Setting the game in Mexico was such a [u]perfect call[/u]. The map is incredibly immersive and just beautiful to look at. And man, the music... the main menu theme alone is something I could listen to for hours. It sets the vibe perfectly before you even turn the key. [h2]The Details Matter[/h2] You can really tell the devs poured their hearts into the technical side: [list] [*][b]Engine Sounds:[/b] Each of the [b]900+ cars[/b] sounds unique. I love how the exhaust note changes depending on your surroundings — the way it echoes when you blast through a tunnel is just spot on. [*][b]Total Freedom:[/b] The game never tells you "no." Want a high-speed street race? Go for it. Feeling like some rally or off-roading? It’s all there. Want to weave through traffic or just chill and explore the map? [i]The choice is always yours.[/i] [/list] [h2]The Downsides...[/h2] However, the game isn't perfect, and there are a couple of things that break the immersion: [list] [*][b]The "Ghost Town" Feeling:[/b] Despite how beautiful Mexico is, the map often feels [i]empty[/i]. The cities are ghost towns with almost no pedestrians, and the traffic is way too thin. Sometimes you can drive for miles without seeing another soul, which makes the world feel a bit lifeless at times. [*][b]Lack of Progression:[/b] Because the game constantly showers you with cars and rewards, [b]nothing feels earned anymore[/b]. You don't really build a bond with your cars because they're just handed to you like candy. It loses that "soul" when everything is given to you right away. [spoiler]Supposedly, they’re fixing the progression in FH6 — we’ll have to wait and see.[/spoiler] [/list] [h1]Verdict[/h1] Even with these flaws, the [i]Forza Horizon[/i] series is easily the best in the business right now. It’s a world you just want to keep coming back to! [b]Highly recommended![/b]

Forza Horizon 5 is a visually impressive racing game, but it’s not without its flaws. At first glance, the game looks amazing. The graphics are top-tier, with detailed cars and beautiful lighting. Driving feels smooth and responsive, and there’s a huge variety of cars to choose from. If you enjoy racing mechanics alone, the game definitely delivers. However, one of the biggest downsides is the map. The game is set in Mexico, and while it sounds interesting on paper, in practice it feels a bit bland. Large parts of the map look very similar, with a lot of empty space and not enough variety to keep things exciting. Compared to previous entries, the environment just doesn’t feel as memorable. The overall action also feels weaker. Events can become repetitive, and there’s less of that “wow” factor that keeps you constantly engaged. It sometimes feels like you’re just driving around without a strong sense of purpose. On the positive side, there’s still a lot of content, and the game runs very well. Multiplayer and seasonal events add some replay value, but they don’t fully fix the core issue with the map and overall excitement. In the end, Forza Horizon 5 is a solid racing game with great visuals and mechanics, but the uninspiring map and weaker sense of action hold it back from being truly amazing. Rating: 6/10 Forza horizon 4 better

Forza Horizon 5 is a polished game with great graphics and satisfying controls. There is no denying that it is very well made and offers a plethora of activities and races. There are a number of issues nonetheless: the open-world proposed here is less interesting than in Forza Horizon 4, and though it is nice to be able to drive around an open world, it makes specific races very generic. The different types of races are distinct, but individual races tend to blend into one another. There are bugs that can potentially prevent completionists from achieving 100%. Time-gated activities are a nuisance. The dialogues are just as corny as in the previous game. But the two main reasons I'm giving this a thumbs-down without the slightest hesitation is that (1) the developers must stop trying to force online play and social feature down the throat of players who don't want it; and (2) a game that is not free-to-play should never heavily advertise or taunt players with DLC-locked content. The map is littered with markers for activities, with no clear indication as to which is player-created or which is behind a paywall. The in-game autoshow where you buy cars has DLC-paywalled cars in the middle of those you can get normally from the game mechanics. These deleterious aspects of modern games really needed to die out yesterday.

Look, racing games are exactly what you expect. Drive between point a & point b typically as fast as possible, with various modes or event types adding layers of nuance. I grew up on the genre, with my dad always supplying the house with Mario Kart & Need for Speed games. That core block of Underground - Carbon (plus Pro Street for myself) is really the basis for a lot of my preferences with racing games, and as time went on, the Need for Speed series seem to have either drifted away from the core premise that kept me stuck to the series (likely ushered by the decline in car culture come the 2010s), or lost the polish that I felt the games once had compared to others. After Pro Street, I mostly fizzled out on racing games until a few years back having picked up FH4 on a decent Steam discount, serving as my introduction to the series. To me, Forza Horizon 5 really takes what was already there in 4, and cranks the polishing up to 11 with further refinement in visual and audio fidelity. This game looks & sounds fantastic, it's consistently one of the games that Microsoft uses to showcase hardware (and for good reason.) The map feels huge & densely packed, especially in the more jungle-like areas. But, simultaneously flat & empty as most of the map decoration "budget" appears to go towards flora, and while hilly, the areas feel like they're in their own contained little bubbles (as in, hills are in the "hilly area" and not really in other sections of the map.) The urban environments, while in scale do appear larger then what 4 has to offer, feels invisible the way that it's tucked into a valley. Beyond the map, the narrative is absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. The narrative has absolutely zero level of friction, coming across as a luke warm delivery for another reason to just hop in the car and drive fast. And don't get me wrong, I know what genre I'm playing— I don't expect really much in terms of a narrative. But the writing here feels like it is the absolute bare minimum they could get away with. Undoubtedly one of the weakest elements of the game. Beyond that, I sort of despise the lack of "CaRPG" elements that are present in prior mentioned Need for Speed games. Starting out with a beater that you race, upgrade, trick out and eventually buy up into higher classes of cars with introduces some layer of progression to these style of games that I think brings a little spice to the game. Instead, Forza Horizon 5 just hands out cars like candy, and you can run 90% of the game in some super car if you really want to. I understand the accessibility to cars is a turn on for some people, but for me personally, that stuff should wait until "end game" where you've gained some rep as a racer. My complaints are mostly minute though, and are moreso issues with the delivery of the systems. The game at the end of the day is pretty fun & enjoyable, even if it makes me roll my eyes at times (especially when they just substitute Spanish words in the writing seemingly at random. Do Spanish speakers actually enjoy this?) Driving around in my car of choice is, for the vast majority of the time, a really slick and polished experience. Otherwise, I wouldn't have chased 3 stars on everything on the map. If you have any interest in cars or racing games, Forza Horizon 5 is a great, approachable game that I'm sure you'll enjoy. 6 looks to be a really exciting entry as well, I presume it'll probably mechanically be very similar.

Overview After 134 hours with Forza Horizon 5, it is clear this is a game that knows how to keep you hooked. It is smooth, polished, and easy to enjoy, but the longer you play, the more certain cracks start to show beneath the surface. Pros Visually Impressive World Mexico looks stunning. The environments are varied, from deserts and jungles to coastlines, and everything is detailed and well crafted. From a visual standpoint, it is hard to complain. Driving Feels Just Right The handling is where the game really shines. It is accessible without being boring, and whether you are racing seriously or just cruising, it feels consistently good. Massive Car Collection There is a huge range of vehicles to choose from. You are never really short on options, and experimenting with different builds keeps things interesting. Freedom in Gameplay You are not forced into anything. You can race, explore, tune, or just drive around. That flexibility makes it easy to pick up anytime. Long Lasting Appeal Even after 134 hours, it still has moments that pull you back in. The core gameplay loop is strong enough to hold attention over time. Cons World Feels Empty Over Time While the map looks beautiful, it can start to feel lifeless. Outside of events, there is not much happening dynamically, which makes long drives feel a bit hollow after a while. Repetitive Event Structure Many races and challenges start blending into each other. You notice the repetition more the longer you play. Weak Story Presence The story is minimal and forgettable. It does not add much to the overall experience. Online Inconsistencies Multiplayer is not always reliable. Connection issues and matchmaking problems can take away from the experience. AI Balance Issues The AI can feel uneven, either too easy or oddly difficult at times. Underwhelming Engine Sounds A noticeable drawback. Many cars lack distinct, powerful sound profiles, which takes away from the immersion, especially for a car focused game. Final Verdict Forza Horizon 5 gets the fundamentals right, driving, visuals, and accessibility, but it does not always maintain depth in the long run. It is a great game to jump into, but over time, the emptiness of the world and repetition start to stand out. Still, if you enjoy open world racing, it is worth experiencing.

I totally want to spend money on the Hotwheels DLC so that I can feel even more immersed in this masterpiece of a game. SOME THINGS I REALLY LIKE ABOUT THIS GAME: 1. I love how the devs included lots of characters to interact with the player, I like how they are constantly talking non stop in the background, even when you're racing, to make the game more challenging by providing a distraction. Very smart move by the devs, keeps you immersed in the story. Moreover, I enjoy how these characters all have boring and totally bland personalities, the wet blanket manner of speaking really helps the player to not feel afraid, after all, we wouldn't want any of the other characters to have more personality than US, would we, precious? 2. I like how the male characters in this game are totally watered down and unintimidating. Sometimes when I see men, I get VERY intimidated. Not in this game. The devs at Playground games know that the only good man is a neutered man. Soft spoken, non confrontational, and a little bit (or a lotta bit) dopey. The women call the shots in this game, and rightfully so. The devs are obviously very big Tolkien fans: "Men? Men are weak." - Lady Elronda 3. No incentive to progress. This might seem counter intuitive...just hear me out. Usually racing games lock cars behind progress, but thats not fair, because some demographics are at a disadvantage. That triggers me. I also hate feeling the PRESSURE of having to compete or achieve something, why not just make all cars available from the start? Well thats exactly what these brilliant devs did! Don't want to actually try? No problem, just do some custom race to speedrun past all levels and get rich, then buy all the cars in the game within 2 days and you're golden. Its so refreshing to have a competition free environment in a racing game. I hate competition. In forza everyone's a winner! 4. Racing AI is either a rocket ship that leaves you in the dust, or a snail that drives slower than you're grandma. I know this one REALLY sounds like it can't possibly be positive, but just think about it. It's a metaphor for life really, you see....because.. in life, sometimes...you either speed past everyone with ease...or you get left in the dust like an aging turtle. Wow, that's deep. That's innovative. That's FORZA.

Наиграв столько, сколько я писал отзыв про 4-ю форзу, я могу сказать лишь одно - форза 4 гораздо лучше пятерки. Форза 4 это одна из лучших релизов этой франшизы, если не лучшая, так как там идеально практически все, от огромнейшего автопарка ( чем эта часть не обделена ), до окружения, детализации и графики, так как в сравнении с предыдущей частью скачек в графическом дизайне значительный, в то время между 4-й и 5-й разница практически незаметна. В 5-й форзе было странным выбрать жаркую и сухую Мексику после Британии. В Британии заметна смена климата, постоянные дожди и густые туманы весной и осенью, огромное количество снега зимой, и умеренно теплое лето. В то же время в Мексике нету понятия смены климата, так как страна расположена близко к экватору и смена сезона заметна лишь в изменении температуры в пару градусов, что уже говорить про игру. Огромная карта с Мегаполисом Гуанхуато, которая больше 4-ки на 50%, но трафик главного города - ранее утро, когда еще никого практически нету на дорогах, езда загородом - постапокалипсис. Странная прогрессия. Получить гиперкар класса S2, можно буквально в первые часы игры, в то время как у стариков NFS это было бы табу. Резко пропадает интерес играть с такими вроде-бы не сильно заметными но минусами. И вот слаживается ощущение, неужели форза как франшиза, которая вошла в историю аркадных гонок и автосимуляторов начинает, франшиза которая известна своим огромным автопарком, которой позавидует любая другая студия, делающая игры про машинки в таких масштабах, франшиза студия которой делает сотни тысяч фотографий для новых локаций, франшиза создающая максимально реалистичный звук каждой машины в разных условиях, и разном окружении... начинает скатываться? НЕТ. Форза 5 это все ещё та игра, которая дает на клыка NFS, The Crew и прочих. Игра, к которой должны стремится все разработчики автосимов и аркадных гонок, ведь именно на Playground Games держится вся уникальность Форзы, отличающая её от других игр жанра. В этой игре есть Eventlab где ты можешь создать то что у тебя в голове, чем игроки часто пользуются создавая порой абсурдные вещи. Это та франшиза, у которой миллионая фанбаза, желающая уже увидеть на свет Форзу 6. Вообщем, что можно сказать про Forza Horizon 5? Да это все еще ебущая во все щели своих конкурентов игра, и я более чем уверен что 6-я часть станет еще лучше её предшественников. 7.5/10

Forza Horizon 5 offers an enormous amount of content, and it’s easy to feel overwhelmed if you’re not already familiar with the series. The game throws a huge variety of events, challenges, collectibles, and progression systems at you right from the start, which can make it tough to know where to focus. That said, once you settle into its rhythm, the experience is incredibly fun and rewarding. Using an analog controller makes a noticeable difference. The driving feels more natural and responsive, especially during high‑speed turns or off‑road sections. I’m still working out how to map manual shifting to the paddle or quick‑action buttons, but for anyone playing on the easier difficulty settings, automatic transmission works perfectly well while you get your bearings. Despite the learning curve and the sheer volume of things to do, the game shines as a joyful, fast‑paced open‑world racer. Whether you’re exploring the map, tuning cars, or jumping into races, it’s consistently entertaining. If you’re even slightly curious, it’s absolutely worth giving it a try.

Just wait for/buy 6 at this point, Horizon Mexico was a mistake. After TWO DECADES of being a Forza fan, it gets really hard to understand what Playground Games was doing for the entirety of FH5. All of the issues from FH4 were compounded on and grief was only added to, the multiplayer was gutted and players scattered via strange instancing choices and lack of a ranked racing mode, and countless visual bugs and balance issues on dozens and dozens of cars went unfixed for the entirety of the game's lifespan. The shallow bowl of a map pushes all of the interesting landmarks to the edges in service of a battle royale mode that died in the water, leaving half of the map a scrub brush desert with nothing going on in the immediate area. The landmarks you do see are all walled off invisibly, made insufferable to drive around and impossible to drive on due to some strange deal with the Mexican government (unlike all the previous games where ruins tended to be fun playgrounds for you to ramp your car off of/crash into/dodge around.) Instead of really leaning into Mexico and getting interesting regional things like GM models that we never saw in America, we got milquetoast story missions that ended up being boring chores, all written with pandering and patronizing toddler-friendly dialogue that makes me marvel at how stupid and insufferable some of the Horizon staff are,.... and about five or six cars that were important to Mexican culture at all. All these things make Horizon 5 grate on your nerves the longer and longer you stick around, like a stale marriage where neither party is really having fun anymore. I'm still ripping around Mexico in the leadup to FH6, but it's literally only because I'm craving some open world cruising and spending some time with the handful of Eventlab tracks that the community put more work into than the devs typically do per-event, cleaning up the last few crumbs of good content I can polish off this disappointing hold-over of a game. I hope to God they cut the FOMO out of the festival playlist like the cancer it is next game, and actually spend time adding interesting content, quirky/historical vehicles, and good mechanics post-launch instead of just adding rich people SUVs that don't even go offroad and the next horsepower-spamming hypercar from any of the same handful of manufacturers we've seen over and over and over in these titles and/or recycling content from BETTER GAMES that came before. Y'all know what the community wants. Do it.

Forza Horizon 5 takes everything great about Horizon 4 and elevates it to a whole new level. After playing it, it’s hard not to fall in love with the sheer freedom and excitement this game delivers. 🚗 Gameplay & Driving Driving in FH5 is even smoother and more responsive than ever. Each car feels distinct, and the improved handling makes races, drifts, and stunts incredibly satisfying. Whether you’re a casual racer or a speed demon, the game adapts perfectly to your style. The addition of new customization and tuning options lets you make each car truly yours — from performance upgrades to aesthetic details. 🌍 World & Atmosphere The open world is stunning. Set in a vibrant and massive representation of Mexico, every corner of the map feels alive. Dynamic weather and seasonal events keep exploration fresh and exciting. Every drive feels like a new adventure, whether you’re racing across deserts, jungles, beaches, or cities. The map is packed with secrets, challenges, and scenic routes that reward exploration, making it hard to put the game down. 🎯 Content & Variety There is always something to do: Races and championships Seasonal events Showcases and stunt challenges Expansive car roster to collect The game constantly gives you new reasons to play, and the rewards feel meaningful. 🏁 Final Thoughts Forza Horizon 5 is the ultimate open-world racing experience. It’s polished, beautiful, and endlessly fun. After playing, it’s hard to imagine wanting any other racing game. For fans of driving games, this is an essential experience.

As someone who grew up playing the Forza franchise, this review is going to be a little biased. The short and sweet is, do not start with this game if you're trying to get into Horizon. I would start with either Horizon 1, 4, or 6 once that comes out. All the issues I have with this game are entirely progression based, with the game feeling too easy. It's too easy to get super cars, with you just being given one for free pretty early on. In Horizon 1, you'd have to grind for tens of hours before you even get ONE. In the first couple hours of this game, you get several for nearly free. It kinda trivializes all the early races, and makes the main story feel more bland in my opinion. Thankfully it sounds like they're moving away from that in Horizon 6. The story is alright, it's a Forza game. The story doesn't have to be good. You do play as a British person tho, so that takes away points from me. Being able to see parts of Mexican car culture is great, though. That's the one thing this game does do really well. It does feel kinda sensationalized, but the point is to celebrate Mexico so it makes sense. Other than that, the game is REALLY good. The controls are amazing, and honestly the best they've ever been. The game is very pretty despite the really basic map. The music is always amazing in a Forza Horizon game, actually added songs to my playlist from this game. A lot of the models are reused unfortunately, but that's not a terrible thing if you're here for gameplay. It's definitely one of the weaker entries in the series, but it's still a great game made by amazing developers. 7/10

Forza Horizon 5 is the rare racing game that feels just as much like a professional photography sim as it does a high-speed motorsport festival. The open world of Mexico is breathtaking, but the real magic happens in Photo Mode. The game’s ability to render realistic bokeh and depth of field is incredible—you can practically treat it like a studio session with an 85mm lens, capturing every sharp detail against the soft, sun-drenched landscapes. It’s a dream for anyone who appreciates clean, high-resolution visuals. The car roster is massive and diverse, featuring plenty of 90s Japanese and European icons that are perfect for those who love that specific era’s aesthetic. Beyond the solo content, it’s a fantastic social experience. Cruising in a convoy with a partner or a group of friends turns the game into a digital road trip, whether you're tackling high-stakes races or just exploring the minimalist beauty of the desert at sunset. It’s polished, joyful, and easily the best "hangout" game currently available.

Forza Horizon 5 is a well-made open-world racing game that offers a lot of content and a great overall experience. The game is set in Mexico, and the map is large and varied, with everything from deserts and jungles to cities and coastlines. The visuals are a standout, and the changing weather helps keep races feeling fresh. The driving is smooth and easy to get into, but still has enough depth for players who want to tune and customise their cars. There’s a huge range of vehicles to choose from, and each one feels a bit different, which keeps things interesting. However, the game isn’t perfect. After a while, the races and events can start to feel repetitive, and there isn’t much of a story to keep you engaged. If you’ve played previous Forza Horizon games, this one might feel quite similar, rather than something completely new. Online features are a nice addition, but they can be inconsistent at times, with occasional connection issues. The soundtrack is decent, but can get repetitive during longer sessions, and some players may not like the focus on paid DLC. Overall, Forza Horizon 5 is a polished and enjoyable racing game with a lot to offer, even if it doesn’t change much from earlier titles. It’s a solid choice for both casual players and racing fans.

Forza Horizon 5 proudly carries on the legacy of Forza Horizon 4, and it is one of the reasons why I already pre-ordered Forza Horizon 6. The cars, the map, the visuals, and the overall world are all fantastic. The only small criticism I have is that the game gives you access to too many cars and activities right from the beginning, and it can feel a bit overwhelming. Maybe that is subjective, and for many players that is actually a great thing. Still, I am really glad that progression will return in the sixth game, because that is something I truly missed.

I really wanted to like Forza Horizon 5, but after around 90 hours, I honestly can’t recommend it. While it looks good on the surface, the overall experience feels like a step back compared to Forza Horizon 4 in several important areas. To start with some positives, the graphics are nice—clean, colorful, and well-optimized—but nothing groundbreaking for a modern title. The photo mode is also genuinely enjoyable and one of the better features of the game if you like capturing your cars in different environments. Another decent addition is the inclusion of Donut Media content, which adds a bit of variety, although it’s still nothing particularly special in the long run. That said, the negatives quickly outweigh the positives. The sound design is a clear downgrade. Many cars sound worse than they did before, especially VW and Audi 5-cylinder engines (Golf R32, Audi Quattro, RS3, RS2, etc.), along with several Porsche models. Overall, a large portion of the cars have very generic engine sounds, which seriously hurts immersion. The Mexico map looks beautiful, but it feels completely lifeless. Roads are often empty, and many areas repeat the same patterns. After some time, everything starts to feel dull, and there’s very little that keeps exploration interesting or rewarding. Customization is another weak point. Car customization feels almost identical to Horizon 4, if not slightly worse in some cases. On top of that, character customization is extremely limited and dull—you can’t really create your driver the way you want, only the way the game allows you to. For a newer title, this lack of evolution is disappointing. The backstage and auction systems are frustrating and unnecessarily restrictive. If you want specific cars like a 911 GT3 RS (2023) or a GR Yaris, you’re forced into grinding or paying for passes and points. Even worse, after all that effort, the car might not even feel as good as you expected. The monetization model is also unacceptable. Even if you buy the Ultimate or Premium Edition, you still have to pay extra for additional car packs. That completely defeats the purpose of those editions. Cars like multiple GT3 variants or something like a Golf 8R should have been included as free updates, not locked behind extra payments. It feels like a clear cash grab. The “career” or story mode is another major disappointment. It feels like a failed attempt at creating something meaningful, but in reality, it’s shallow and completely pointless. There’s no real sense of progression or engagement—it’s just there without adding anything valuable to the experience. The Hot Wheels expansion is also underwhelming. It’s decent, but nothing memorable. Compared to the LEGO expansion from Horizon 4, it feels like a downgrade in creativity and fun. Overall, despite having a huge number of cars, the game lacks real substance. Within about 50 hours, you’ve pretty much seen everything it has to offer. After that, there’s little motivation to keep playing, as the world doesn’t pull you back in and the gameplay loop becomes repetitive. It’s disappointing, especially considering how high expectations were. In the end, this feels like one of the weakest Horizon titles so far.

On a technical level, this is a good game. You will have a good time But it's worse than FH3 and FH4 in many ways. I'm recommending it for that alone - The map is really bland and generic - the locations from Mexico are beautiful but the actual road feel of racing through these locations lacks variety. I still find myself booting up FH3 / FH4 if I want to just drive around and vibe. I can't stress enough how much this harms the game because it affects every aspect of the game - the tracks, the driving around for fun, or just driving to the next event - Song selection is quite hit or miss - there's some really good ones mixed in with some mediocre ones, which is a shame given how good the song selection has been (dare I say) iconic in the previous games. Another big hit to the feel of the game because Horizon is basically a music festival with cars - Some cars are gatekept behind weekly chores and if you miss them you have to grind ridiculous amounts of credits to auction snipe them. Honestly introducing this in FH4 was a mistake and I feel they should remove it for FH6 - Later on they added car pack DLCs but it feels like they kind of just gutted the car collection from FH4 just to drip feed it through the weekly chores (see above) and to resell the remaining later after people complained about weekly chores. So the way to get cars beyond the initial collection is to grind with time and pay with money - Story makes no sense because you aren't working your way up in the world anymore, somehow you just have access to high end cars immediately which can be a plus for some people but it causes the game to lack direction - Depiction of mexicans in the game is really cringe because they do this spanglish thing where they keep inserting random spanish words into english dialogue. Either give us normal english (which mexicans are capable of speaking) or mexican dialogue with english subs. The spanglish just feels culturally inappropriate - Lack of mexican car culture in general - other than 1 sidequest and a few references, the game doesn't celebrate the region's car culture as much as previous games. I enjoyed learning about how the beetle was called 'vocho' and how it's beloved in Mexico but that's about it. In general Mexico just felt like flavor of the week dripped onto a generic Horizon game, instead of an opportunity to let all of us in the rest of the world to experience their culture through the game. It's not a net negative but it's huge missed potential

[h3]Forza Horzion 5, it’s fun, it’s chaotic, but prepare for an overwhelming amount of content[/h3] For brief context, I’ve played every Forza Motorsport game from 1 all the way through to 8, but I have only played Horizon 1 and 2. Safe to say that jumping into Horizon 5 was wild. From the very first second, you’re dropped out of a plane into loud music, massive jumps, and cars being gifted to you left, right, and center. It’s a huge contrast to Forza Motorsport, which starts calm, measured, and almost meditative. Horizon 5 immediately throws you into action, and honestly, it’s fun, both to race and just to drive around freely. But at the same time, it can feel a little confusing and exhausting with just how much is going on. [h2]The Good[/h2] Firstly, and most importantly, The driving is fun and easy. Coming from Forza Motorsport, I can feel the difference when using a controller. Horizon is more arcade-like, but not ridiculously so. Cars feel distinct, off-road and on-road handling is satisfying, and tuning makes a real difference in car handling. The showcase events like racing a train or racing three jet skis are insane but thrilling. The number of cars available is also insane with over 900 cars. Hypercars, hatchbacks, forgotten relics, trucks, lorries, rally cars, you name it. I’ve driven everything from a parade float to a tiny micro car that can only fit one person, to a JDM legend like the Nissan Skyline, to a 1000hp hypercar like the Koenigsegg. After 30 hours, I have about 150 cars as it’s extremely easy to acquire cars in this game (more on that later) and that’s only scratching the surface. The variety here is unmatched. This game is easily the best I’ve ever played in terms of the number of cars on offer. But let’s talk about the world that Horizon is set in; Mexico is huge and varied, beaches, jungles, mountains, deserts, airfields, winding villages. The game encourages exploration, and even though the streets feel mostly empty and NPCs sit behind invisible walls, it’s still fun to cruise around and discover things. In terms of the Graphics and the audio, they are both very nice, lighting through the trees looks great and I find the engine sounds to be pretty good (although not perfect). Weather effects are cool in theory while driving around but can be inconsistent (rain suddenly stops in seconds). Music is mostly ignorable if you just want engine sounds, but including a classical radio station this time is hilarious. One last positive that I want to mention, Forza is known for being impressively inclusive, during the character customisation, you can add prosthetic limbs, you can add hearing aids, and putting your male character in a dress is hilarious, but I guess it’s also good inclusivity. Also, the game calling you by your own name is a nice touch. [h2]The Bad[/h2] My main issue is going to seem strange to some, but it’s to do with the amount of content in Horizon 5, There’s so much. Hundreds of races, thousands of accolades, hundreds of cars to collect, collectibles to find on the map, and festival playlists to complete weekly and monthly. At first, it’s very confusing, I didn’t know for a while what I was supposed to be doing. Accolades come for literally everything, sometimes completely random and if you are trying to do everything 100%? Well, that feels like a monumental task, possibly taking hundreds or even thousands of hours. Also, the progression feels hollow. Being gifted dozens of cars in the first few hours is fun, but it removes the sense of achievement you get from working your way up from old, slow cars to a hypercar, maybe I just miss the days of old racing games that force you to work your way up so once you finally get round to driving a Ferrari or Lamborghini, you really feel like you’ve earned it. I personally would have preferred a slower, earned progression. But in terms of story… Well… What story? Honestly, it’s just an excuse for racing. Dialogue is cringey (looking at you, Ramiro), forgettable, and mostly unneeded. The game likes to remind you that you are in Mexico by throwing in a totally random Spanish word into the dialogue like “amigo”. Also there seemed to be many references to Horizon 4 that went over my head because I never played it. The map itself, while varied, has nothing in it that really stands out. There’s no open city, only a tiny village with tight roads. Streets are mostly empty; NPCs are behind invisible walls. The world feels more like a showcase sandbox than a living place. And finally, if you are someone that like me that likes to get achievements, well… be prepared for a gigantic task ahead, because in Horizon 5 the achievements are ridiculously grindy, especially online achievements involving game modes like The Eliminator. Winning The Eliminator feels like a mix of luck and excessive map knowledge. Also, some festival playlist achievements require waiting weeks or maybe even months for challenges to appear. Maybe that’s fun for hardcore fans of the game, but exhausting for anyone else. [h2]Final Thoughts[/h2] I’m about 30 hours in and have finished the main Hall of Fame “story.” Now it’s a do-whatever sandbox, which can feel freeing but also overwhelming. For me, Horizon 5 is best for casual players and car enthusiasts.
