TLDR: great game but definitely fits the "Forza Horizon 4.5" nickname I've played every forza horizon game, most of which I have over 200 hours on and I think this one's just ok. Its definitely a covid game. Out of every game in the series, this one is the smallest jump in terms of what this game adds to the series. FH1 was the first and has the best progression in the series. FH2 added more cars, a new handling model, and cross country races. FH3 added bodykits, event blueprints, and had the best expansions imo. FH4 added seasons, a festival playlist, and a basic level editor via "Super 7". FH5 adds... not much more tbh. The most significant addition is fleshing out the level editor, and allowing you to add items to races instead of just the Super 7 stuff. The handlings improved. This game has the most *stuff* in the series. Most cars, most tracks/events, most bodykits, most pr stunts. Although, because this game is set in mexico, the seasons are actually downgraded compared to fh4. Instead of having 4 distinct season, each with there own interesting changes. In fh5 they just kinda mesh together. The most it changes is some parts of the map have a bit more water now and the top of the mountain has some snow. Thats about it. Speaking of snow, I do find it odd that this is the only game with snow tires that are separate from rally tires, yet there almost entirely useless. They had the chance to make a Blizzard Mountain expansion 2 but never did. And more generally, the class system is the most unbalanced in this game. horsepower doesnt effect PI much at higher classes. So having 900hp cars in S1 is common, meanwhile tires spike PI way to much. To make things worse, most tracks favor speed over handling, so trying for a handling setup puts you at a heavy disadvantage. Rally cars don't fair much better. Most cars can get mud tires. Not a problem by itself but they usually cost less PI than rally tires, while also handling better than rally tires offroad. The idea behind this is that rally tires handle better on road, hence why it costs more PI. In reality, because most rally tracks are mostly or entirely offroad, mud tires just gives you free PI and better handling. To make things worse, because mud tires are cheaper, many famous rally cars can't hit the top of S1. So you can get a fully upgraded rally car with 900+hp and be stuck at like 862 PI. But, while I made a long rant about the problems with the game, said problems are relatively small. The seasons problem doesnt take to much away from the game, and the cars being unbalanced only effects online races and rivals mode. Outside of those 2 problems, its fh4, but more. and considering you cant buy that game anymore (rip but not playground games's fault), this game is an easy recommendation.

Forza Horizon 5 excels at one thing: demonstrating how the Horizon series has lost all the soul from which it was originally birthed. Horizon of the past was a festival and truly felt like it—there were characters, a story they were part of, and a passion they all shared. What once was a festival has evolved into a Fortnite lobby alongside so many other games, and I'm sure it's very profitable. So I suppose I was too harsh originally—it does excel at two things. A great example of a game which feels alive, immersive, and exciting is the original Forza Horizon, which occupies less than 1/20 the disk space required by Horizon 5 and remains on my computer to be played often. I will excuse large downloads for games like Microsoft Flight Simulator and Red Dead Redemption 2, but those are rich, expansive experiences that absorb players in a world which feels real and connected. Somehow, Forza Horizon 5 takes up more disk space than both these games, which, as I implied, could be excused if it were a reasonable analogue to Microsoft Flight Sim for driving games. It is not. The world in which you drive feels ostentatious yet sterile, a perfect match for the driving itself. If you enjoy driving quick, snappy sportscars on winding roads I suggest you look elsewhere. If you enjoy off-roading, Forza Horizon 5 has endless options; every car performs the same both on and off the road. I bought the game on sale for $29.99 expecting a decent driving experience which I could idly enjoy while listening to something in the background, and unfortunately it fell short of my limited expectations. If you're wondering about my playtime, I blame it on the fugue of boredom which overcame me and ended with me walking away in a trance, leaving the game running to go pick lint out of my bellybutton (or something equally exciting). But, in the end, I was a fool. Why had I expected anything different? And where was the love I once held for skins in Fortnite? Maybe I grew up, and out of what makes Forza Horizon 5 so great...maybe it's not a bad game, more akin to a shirt you wore at 12 years old when you were a different person and much smaller, much too small for the shirts worn by your adult self. It's hard to say, but I don't recommend purchasing.

Still a really good, solid game to consider, even at this time. For [b] casual [/b] players, the map is always beautiful and very spacious - each time you drive, even often on the same roads, but at variable scenery (whether it's at the beach, atop of mountains, through the rainforest, or simply over the stretching desert roads) - these driving experiences will never ever feel the same each time, it's always different. Relaxed, cruising at controlled, enjoyable speeds, and simply appreciating the splendid views - that's the perfect recipe for a nice, 'spirited driving' experience. From a [b] competitive [/b] standpoint, it's very easy, even for beginners, to obtain top tier cars and as well to apply free, community-made tunes shared by other players - to build a whole, challenge-worthy but widely varied garage, for relatively non-expensive in-game currencies, also easy to earn and not so timely. Sometimes however, a few online race tracks might feel 'unforgiving', or the race itself might feel 'unfair' - mainly because of the tricky nature of challenging routes (no room for error or 'skill issues'), and/or also due to other players as well (too good/bad or 'lucky'). Regardless, as in other games, trying to complete the race is always a must for learning, and so is having good sportsmanship, as I very often noticed, is also present in this game (for instance, racers often using 'Link' (in-game, quick chat feature), to simply say 'sorry' when they make mistakes affecting/impacting other racers). The game never lacks [b] content [/b], as quite regularly, new challenges/events are added to unlock exclusive and amazing cars (voted by players - very cool), which all players can then get for free (for points earned), and players can even claim any previous ones which they missed (requires a 'backstage pass' which costs higher points, but still free to unlock one previously missed, exclusive car per 'season' - from any earlier season - also very cool). This is yet another reason why many players, including myself often come back to the game. I'd say that the [b] price [/b] is also very fair and reasonable - for the amount of content and gameplay, so it's very much worth its value, and even more so - at the 50% off discounted price, especially during certain Steam sales events. I'd recommend playing this game using a controller, and of course, on a decent, average gaming rig (this game is also already optimized for your device after each update - very convenient) [b] Overall [/b], I'd highly recommend this game, especially if you are fond of driving, racing or such simulation games. Even I still find it to be the most visually immersive driving game - with good, engaging and some random gameplay as well. Online competition and completing challenges are quite fun sometimes, but, I think it's much better to appreciate the drive along the relaxing views, one place at a time, y'know, and I'd suggest giving this a try too, from time to time. At this point of time, if you are considering getting the game, it'd be much more worthwhile if you'd continue playing - because 150 GB is quite demanding. Another way is you could also use the Steam storage management feature (in settings) to transfer the game to another storage drive and play again later. Forza Horizon 6 is also right around the corner (next year), so you could also consider skipping straight to that, however, expect full price for quite some while after release, before eventually the getting lower prices from much later sales events. However, as seen from several recent games, the graphical recreation and maps of Japan have already been really impressive, and now it's only imaginable what FH6 is going to be like. Only time will tell, but it probably won't disappoint, that's for sure. So, if you don't have FH5 already, I'd still recommend getting it as of right now, and I don't think that it would not be worth it. But again, certain things considered, it's always your choice. Well, that's a pretty long review... I guess I might as well become a game critic now :3 Nah but anyways, thanks for reading, I hope that in some way, you have gotten something out of this :> I wish you a very happy gaming holiday!

Two years ago I started playing the series with Forza Horizon 4. I was six years late, but when I finally played it I fell in love. I never had the money for an Xbox or a good PC, so for years I just watched other people play. I built a PC and started FH4 on integrated graphics. I saved up, bought a GPU, and later picked up Forza Horizon 5 on sale. I played FH5 three years after its release, and it became my most-played game. Even now I haven’t completed everything, there are too many challenges, too many boards, too many cars. FH4 has about 700 cars; FH5 has around 900. It never ends. The story writing is basic and the voice acting is bad, they’re there but you will not care about them because the fun is completing the challenges. The Hot Wheels DLC, Rally DLC and the free DLCs (like the donut media one) are great: lots of content, lots of fun. What is annoying is the Premium Edition situation. Years later they still release small car packs with only 4–5 cars each. After 900 hours of playing if you want to have everything you have to buy the Ultimate Car Pack Collection. The map is huge but often feels empty. Too much desert, too much jungle, and too many long, empty roads. If the Rally DLC map were part of the main map, the world would feel better it has better, more fun curves. The seasons doesn't make sense. It’s Mexico, so it basically like “hot” or “raining,” and that loses a lot of the seasonal atmosphere that FH4 had. I definitely recommend it, the game is fun if you play alone and its fun if you play with friends, it is just like previous titles but with some better mechanics and more content.

After spending around 177 hours in Forza Horizon 5, I can confidently say that it is one of the most engaging open-world racing games I have played. The map set in Mexico is vibrant, diverse, and full of life, offering deserts, jungles, beaches, and mountains that make every drive feel fresh. The graphics are impressive, with detailed environments and cars that look almost real, especially when weather effects or lighting change the atmosphere. The gameplay is accessible but still rewarding. Whether you enjoy drifting, racing on asphalt, going off-road, or simply exploring the world, the game gives you complete freedom. The large collection of cars and the tuning system add depth, letting players experiment with different builds and driving styles. This makes the experience fun even after many hours of play. However, the game also has a few weaknesses. After long sessions, some activities start to feel repetitive, and certain story missions lack impact. The formula does not innovate much compared to previous titles, so experienced players may notice familiar patterns. Even so, Forza Horizon 5 remains an excellent racing game. Its beautiful world, huge variety of cars, and relaxed but exciting gameplay make it worth playing for many hours. For me, it has been a memorable experience, and it still has plenty to offer even after 177 hours on the road.

### Review of Forza Horizon 5 **Rating: ★★★★★ (5/5)** Forza Horizon 5 is nothing short of an absolute joyride! From the moment I booted up the game, I was captivated by the stunning visuals of Mexico’s diverse landscapes. The level of detail is incredible, from the sun-soaked beaches to the lush jungles and bustling cities. It feels like a vibrant, living world that invites exploration at every turn. The game offers a fantastic range of cars—everything from classic muscle cars to sleek modern sportscars. The customization options allow you to truly make your vehicle your own, which adds a personal touch to the racing experience. The driving mechanics feel smooth and responsive, making it easy to jump into a race or just cruise around enjoying the scenery. One of my favorite features is the dynamic weather system and seasonal changes. Each season brings a new flavor to gameplay, whether I’m racing through a rainstorm or enjoying a sunny day. The variety keeps the experience fresh and exciting. Multiplayer is also a blast! Racing against friends or participating in community events feels competitive yet laid-back, allowing for fun, social interactions while doing what we love—driving. Overall, Forza Horizon 5 is a masterpiece that captures the spirit of racing while providing endless opportunities for exploration and creativity. Whether you’re a die-hard car enthusiast or just looking for an engaging game to unwind with, I can't recommend it enough!

A solid 8.5/10 from me.Highly Recommended.

This is one of those moments when it's tough to rate a game due to Steam forcing you to go for black or white, when in reality this game cannot be polarized in such a manner due to it having many shades of gray. Yes, I do have nearly 500 hours for this game at the time of the review, which probably means that I sort of like it, but like I've said, that's only partly true. Don't get me wrong, it's very fun if you are a casual petrolhead, and if you like collecting stuff in general. It helps a lot that the game is very easy on the eyes, especially on low-end of the specification spectrum. I'm getting almost consistent 60fps on my device with an integrated GPU, more specifically AMD Radeon 680M, and the game still looks extremelly pretty. Additionally, you can adjust the difficulty according to your needs. If you want a challenge, you can have a challenge, but if you want to sit back and relax, and easily do (most of) the weekly challenges, you can do that as well. On the negative side of things, the most annoying one is predatory behavior of the developer, releasing a bunch of rather expensive (for what you get) car packs, that cost money to get even though you've splurged on the Premium edition. You will probably want to grab them if you are a completionist, but at the same time you'll probably think three times before spending what you've paid on the full game for less than 10% of the cars in the game in total (extra car packs are about 100 cars in total, and the entire game has almost 1000 cars). Also, when the game got released for PS5 in April of 2025, PC version on sale costed more than what it was back in 2023 when I got the game. The situation got a bit better during the sales in late 2025, but it's still not at the point where it was two years ago or even one year ago. Yes, you can do most of the stuff while playing as a single player, but there is a challenge here and there where you need to hop into multiplayer games, and that's where another big problem in the game becomes apparent. You'll encounter lots (and I mean LOTS) of people who want to ruin your fun just for ♥♥♥♥ and giggles, and there's no easy way to report them. You would need to upload a video on developer's website as proof, and that requires a lot of hassle for something that should be fairly straightforward. Other issues would be inability to control the weather and day/night cycles in offline mode. Yes, you can do it through blueprints, but I would prefer it during free roam. Then there's a huge problem of short lifespan of Forza games, you can probably expect that the servers for FH5 will be live until the end of 2027 or something like that. The game's plot is also extremelly silly and way overcomplicated. NPCs talk way too much. If you can look past these issues, and if you prefer arcade racing games as opposed to realistic simulations, this game might be for you. If you always wanted to fit offroad wheels to your average Ferrari or Lambo and go bonkers in an off-road race, then this game is definitely for you. Hey, you cannot crack your oil casket if the entire undercarriage of the car is not even modelled, right? Definitelly scratching that itch, but I still miss TDU and TDU 2.

Forza Horizon 5 delivers one of the most impressive open-world racing experiences available today, blending stunning visuals, a vibrant world, and an enormous selection of vehicles into a game that’s both accessible and deeply rewarding. Set in a beautifully realized version of Mexico, the map is not only vast but genuinely diverse—featuring deserts, jungles, beaches, ancient temples, and bustling cities. Every area feels handcrafted with attention to detail, and the environmental variety keeps exploration exciting even dozens of hours in.

Racing, much like rallying, can be a monotonous grind. Day after day, year after year, even when you’re doing 300 km/h, the numbers on the timer only move by fractions of a second. So don’t expect too much from this game. If your heart doesn’t skip a beat when your camera brushes past a tire; if an engine backfire in neutral doesn’t make your right foot twitch; if an upshift and an overtake don’t make your whole body tense—then this isn’t the game for you. Better to save your time and money than blame the game for being “boring.” But if those moments speak to you, Welcome to Forza Horizon 5. May every corner remind you why racing is beautiful.

Forza Horizon 5 is an incredible racing game, with perhaps the most jam-packed open-world from Playground Games to date and a massive collection of cars available. Playground Games continues to strike a perfect balance between simulation and arcade-like car handling and physics, which is in the same spirit as FH3 and FH4. That being said, FH5 brings very little new to the table in comparison with FH3 and FH4. For example, seasons were introduced in FH4 which was an amazing feature since it transformed the map from week-to-week and made the world feel alive. In FH5, seasons are also present, but since the game takes place in Mexico there is very very little difference from season to season. The only difference is amount of rain and humidity, and it gets repetitive quickly. The Horizon Festival is drastically smaller or at least less relevant than in the previous Horizon games, which makes the world feel more empty in many areas. In other words, FH5 is on paper larger, prettier and better than any past Horizon title, but it doesn't always feel that way. In a sense, FH5 lacks any real character in comparison with past Horizon titles. That being said, there are many things that FH5 does better than its predecessors. Car sounds for example are better than ever before, and although the car sounds aren't always unique across different cars, they are significantly better than they were in FH4 and change depending on the upgrades you apply to a car. There are more upgrade options than ever before which is another welcome addition, and lastly, the game looks stunning. Even if you have the smallest enthusiasm for cars and racing, Forza Horizon 5 will likely prove extremely enjoyable for you. For returning players like myself, it's another solid Forza Horizon, although with not that many new additions as one might want. All in all however, Forza Horizon 5 is an incredible game that I can't recommend enough. 8.9 / 10

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️ Forza Horizon 5 — Still the King of Open-World Racing Forza Horizon 5 nails what a racing game should feel like fast, fun, and loaded with things to do. The game throws you into a massive open world based on Mexico, and there’s always something happening: street races, off-road events, drift zones, drag strips, Horizon Stories, seasonal challenges, collectibles, and a huge amount of community-made events. You never run out of things to race or unlock. Car handling strikes a great balance between arcade and semi-sim, the car list is huge, and the visuals are top-tier. The weather effects, lighting, and overall vibe make the world feel alive, and the soundtrack fits perfectly with the Horizon festival atmosphere. ✔️ Likes Tons of events, races, challenges, and content to keep you busy for hundreds of hours. Huge car list with fun tuning and customization options. Beautiful graphics and one of the best open worlds in any racing game. Solid balance between casual and more realistic driving. Seasonal updates and community creations keep the game fresh. ❌ Dislikes — Mexico Map Some regions feel too open or repetitive, especially the desert areas. Heavier focus on off-road/dirt compared to FH4 may not satisfy asphalt-focused players. City areas like Guanajuato are great but too small, not enough dense street-racing zones. Several biomes feel underused with big empty spaces unless tied to seasonal events. Jungle and sandstorm areas can hurt visibility and make some races feel messy. Overall, the map is huge but not as tightly designed or balanced as FH4’s.

Forza Horizon 5 — Review Forza Horizon 5 is an open-world racing masterpiece that blends eye-popping visuals, a massive and varied world, and an incredibly deep car-collecting and tuning system. It’s one of the best entries in the Horizon series, striking a near-perfect balance between arcade fun and realistic driving feeling. What Makes It Great Stunning World & Setting The game is set in a beautifully rendered version of Mexico. The map is diverse, with deserts, jungles, volcanoes, coastal highways, and more. The attention to detail in the landscapes makes every drive feel fresh and visually rewarding. Spectacular Graphics & Sound Forza Horizon 5 takes full advantage of modern hardware to deliver high-fidelity graphics, realistic textures, and vibrant lighting. On top of that, the audio design is excellent — engine roars, environmental ambience, and tire sounds feel rich and immersive. Huge and Varied Car Roster There are hundreds of cars — from classic muscle to hypercars — and you can really customize them. The tuning options are deep, letting you tweak performance parts to match your driving style. Accessible but Skillful Driving Whether you’re new to racing games or a veteran, Forza Horizon 5 welcomes you. You can play with driving assists, or go more hardcore by turning them off. The driving feels smooth and responsive, making it fun to explore or race. Variety of Activities There’s always something to do: races, challenges, seasonal events, drift zones, and more. The Horizon Adventure system gives structure, but you’re also free to just drive around and enjoy the world. Long-Term Engagement With seasonal updates, a constantly changing open world, and live events, the game has a lot of replay value. Players keep coming back, especially if they like collecting cars or competing in different modes. Accessibility Features The game does a great job with accessibility: many players appreciate how inclusive its options are. Minor Drawbacks (But Not Dealbreakers) While the map is huge and varied, some players feel that parts of it can be a bit repetitive. The story and mission design are not very deep — it’s not really a narrative-driven game; the focus is more on driving, exploring, and having fun. For some, the in-game economy and reward system (like wheel spins) might feel a little grindy. Verdict If you love racing games, Forza Horizon 5 is a dream come true. It’s visually stunning, loaded with content, and offers a driving experience that’s both accessible and rewarding. Whether you want to race hard, drift around just for the fun of it, or explore the open world at your own pace — this game delivers. Highly recommended for: Players who love car variety and tuning Fans of open-world games Those who enjoy long-term multiplayer and seasonal content Anyone who just wants to hop in a car and drive through beautiful landscapes Less ideal for: Gamers looking for a strong, character-driven narrative Players who dislike long grinds or “gambling-like” reward mechanics

Forza Horizon 5 hit me way harder than I expected. The whole vibe is just electric - Mexico feels like one massive sun-soaked festival where something’s popping off every 100 meters. Events, races, wheelspins, new cars, seasonal stuff… the game floods you with content to the point where 100 hours barely scratch the surface. And yeah, I’m already 80+ hours in, still glued to it like it’s day one. Gameplay? Super fun. The handling felt a bit sticky at first, especially on a controller, but that actually made it more addictive. Those cursed corners made me want to bump the difficulty, retry events, and actually learn how to take turns on a high-end car like a human being. The soundtrack slaps too - different stations, different moods, never gets dull. I’m not a racing game person at all, I just love cars so the physics threw me off at first. But as soon as I got used to it, it turned into a whole advantage. Especially once you dive into the tuning and customization. It’s ridiculous how deep it goes. You can tweak weight, build parameters, tire pressure, engine setups - it all genuinely changes how each car feels. The game both looks and sounds insane. Wet roads at night? Peak visuals. Absolute perfection. The sound design/engines/weather, everything just elevates it even more. Favorite activities? I’m basic in the best way. Give me road races, closed-circuit races, anything on asphalt. Off-road? Miss me with that. But jumping into a new car and discovering how it behaves is pure dopamine. The more I unlock, the more I want to play - it’s that kind of loop. Now, the one thing that actually tilts me sometimes is the Drivatars. These bots straight up break the laws of physics, break my confidence and sometimes break my will to live. They get traction in places where your car just slides into the shadow realm. The fix? Either race real people online or mentally tune out the bots entirely and focus on your own run. If you stare at their behavior too long, it gets frustrating fast on high difficulty levels. I’d recommend Forza Horizon 5 to anyone who loves cars, tuning, or arcadey racing vibes. No matter skill level, it just grabs you and doesn’t let go.

Like in my prior review of Forza Horizon 4, I have A LOT more hours in this game than my Steam hours suggest due to having owned the Xbox version of this game since it first came out 4 years ago. After seeing the Ultimate edition of the Steam version on sale for a surprisingly low price, I had to snatch it up purely for the benefit of having a copy of this game that's not completely tied to Microsoft's operating systems due to it being confirmed playable on Steam Deck/Linux via Proton. Now that my reasons for having bought this game twice are out of the way, here's my actual review. I've been a fan of the Forza Horizon games since the 3rd entry. While Gran Turismo and Forza's parent series, Forza Motorsport, have been increasingly losing me due to shifting their focus towards E-Sports over the main appeal they've always had for me, which is just simply getting to live out the escapist fantasy of collecting and driving rare and exotic cars that you're not even likely to see on the road, let alone drive, with beautiful graphics and solid, realistic physics, Forza Horizon has not only been filling the niche that those two series have been leaving for me but doing a damn fine job at it. For people who don't really care about accurately simulating real world motorsports, this series has proven to be a true automotive playground and Forza Horizon 5 is no exception. The amount of stuff there is to do in just the base game alone is more than worth the price of entry IMHO. Not just because of the sheer size of the game's open world and the amount of cars to collect but because of all the different race routes, stunt spots, story missions and other activities. You can very EASILY get lost in this game for hours at a time! The only real complaints I have about this game have really just been that some of the DLC's that are not included in the Ultimate bundle are questionably priced (looking at you, Universal car pack) and the story characters are admittedly pretty bland to the point of being annoying at times. Still though, this is still a Forza Horizon game at its core so I wholeheartedly recommend it both to existing fans and people looking to try the series out!

[h3]Just another racing game ? well, not really[/h3] I was kinda hesitant for a long time, wondering if I should even buy it. I thought it was just another racing game, but it surprised me from the start. The open-world feels alive and there’s always something going on. Even in “story” mode it feels like being online (well, technically you are online), with random events popping up and the chance to spot other players in ghost mode on the map and interact with them. The story is nice, it keeps you excited, even if some story races are insanely hard to get 3 stars. Icons of Speed Past Midnight is the only time in my life I hated a Supra, but it is what it is. Different environments across the map, like jungle, mountains, desert, not sure if Mexico is like this, but it looks amazing. Side challenges around the map, treasure chests or barn‑finds where you get legendary cars, are also nice, a cool way to reward players in story mode. [h3]Hot Wheels DLC? Absolutely worth it. [/h3] The DLC takes you to some floating islands up in the sky, each with its own environment: a forest‑canopy island, a snowy/volcano‑tundra island, and a canyon‑desert island. There are insane loops, jumps, magnet‑tracks, water‑slide tracks and wild gravity‑defying stuff. The challenges and races are amazing, and I actually completed them, it was really short, but fun. It took me about 30h to hit 100 % completion. I started playing this instead of the story mode, because why not 😂 Overall, cool DLC, worth it. ...though I’ll be honest, the sharp turns on this map were a pain in the a** sometimes 😂 [h3] Conclusion. Should I play It ? [/h3] Well, even if it’s not the best racing game, it’s definitely one of the best, that’s for sure. For a game released in 2021, it still competes with 2025 racing games. So yeah, I would 100% recommend it, it’s worth your time, and it’s crazy fun. Forza Horizon 5 is one of those rare games that grabs you from the very first race and never lets go. Set in a breathtaking recreation of Mexico, the world is not only massive but alive—filled with vibrant cities, lush jungles, sun-soaked beaches, and even an active volcano. Every location feels handcrafted with incredible attention to detail, making exploration just as fun as the racing itself. The handling strikes a perfect balance between realism and accessibility. Whether you're a seasoned sim-racer or just in it for casual fun, the game adapts beautifully. Each car feels unique, and with hundreds of vehicles to unlock, tune, and customize, you’ll never run out of new toys to play with. The Horizon Festival’s events are consistently exciting, varied, and full of personality. From high-speed road races to off-road adventures and outrageous showcase events, there’s always something new to do. Online play is smoother than ever, and joining Horizon Arcade or seasonal events with friends feels effortless and rewarding. Visually, Forza Horizon 5 is absolutely stunning—arguably one of the best-looking racing games ever made. Combined with dynamic weather, dramatic lighting, and an incredible soundtrack, the experience is pure joy from start to finish. In short, Forza Horizon 5 is a must-play. It’s the ultimate open-world racing game—fun, fast, gorgeous, and endlessly entertaining. If you love racing games, this is the new gold standard.

Forza Horizon 5 is easily one of the most enjoyable open-world racing games I’ve played in a long time. The map, inspired by Mexico, is huge and packed with variety—dense forests, long beaches, desert areas, small towns, and even a volcano. No matter where you go, the world feels lively and full of detail. The driving strikes a great balance: it’s realistic enough to feel satisfying, but still forgiving enough that anyone can jump in and have fun. The car list is massive, with everything from old classics to the latest supercars, so there’s always something new to try. Exploring the map and switching between different types of events keeps the game from ever feeling repetitive. Progression is relaxed and lets you tackle things in whatever order you prefer. There’s always something to do, thanks to the rotating seasons, weekly challenges, and online events. Visually, the game looks fantastic, and it runs smoothly even on less powerful setups. Not everything is perfect—online features can sometimes be a bit unreliable—but it’s a small complaint in the grand scheme of things. Verdict: Forza Horizon 5 is a blast from start to finish. Its world, cars, and sheer amount of content make it an easy recommendation for anyone who enjoys racing games. ⭐ 10/10 – A beautiful and endlessly entertaining open-world racer.

Forza Horizon 5 is an open-world racing game developed by Playground Games and published by Xbox Game Studios. Set in a vast, fictionalized version of Mexico, it expands on the formula of its predecessors with improved visuals, refined physics, and a seamless blend of arcade accessibility and simulation detail. The core gameplay revolves around freedom of exploration. Players can race on-road, off-road, or through city streets, jungles, deserts, and mountain terrain. The map is massive and diverse, offering dynamic weather systems and seasonal variations that significantly alter driving conditions. Car handling strikes a balance between realism and fun. Every vehicle feels distinct, yet controllable across multiple surfaces. Tuning options, upgrades, and customization systems allow players to fine-tune performance and appearance to match their driving style. The feedback loop of earning, modifying, and mastering cars remains deeply satisfying. Visually, Forza Horizon 5 sets a benchmark for open-world graphics. The lighting, skyboxes, and environmental detail are exceptional, from volcanic peaks to coastal highways. On modern hardware, the game maintains high frame rates and resolution with minimal loading, making exploration fluid and uninterrupted. The soundtrack and audio design are equally polished. Ambient sounds, engine roars, and radio stations create atmosphere and variety. The adaptive music system reinforces pacing—quiet between races, energetic during events. Voice acting and festival chatter maintain the game’s upbeat tone. Multiplayer integration is seamless through the “Horizon Life” system. Players can join events, convoys, and races instantly without interrupting single-player flow. The community-driven seasonal challenges, creative modes, and online leaderboards extend longevity far beyond the main campaign. Overall, Forza Horizon 5 is one of the most complete open-world racing experiences ever made. It combines technical excellence with freedom, accessibility, and an infectious sense of discovery. For both casual drivers and car enthusiasts, it represents the high point of the Horizon series—a world built for speed, creativity, and constant motion.

Absolute masterpiece. In my opinion, the game feels and looks better then Forza Horizon 4. Forza Horizon 4 also had some really really impressive graphics and great cartoony artstyle, but in my opinion, It doesn't hit as hard as Forza Horizon 5 does. The game is perfect. Perfect realistic art style (people may disagree with me on this, but i prefer realistic graphics art styles compared to more cartoony ones, much like how it was in Forza Horizon 4), the graphics in my opinion are one of the best graphics ever made for a video game. The only games that look better or are on par with Forza Horizon 5 is something like Ready or Not (one of the only good UE5 titles where the devs actually cared for its artstyle and AMAZING performance, which is unbelievable to be said about UE5 titles), the upcoming GTA 6 and RDR2. AMAZING realism on the cars' engine sounds,(stuff like the Jesko and a few others can be improved, but still pretty good) the engine sounds of the vehicles are outstanding, so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ realistic. Me being able to hear cars i hear outside mostly daily ingame to super/hyper/track cars i dream of having or only just glaze them is a feeling that can't be matched. The hate the game got at launch wasn't really deserved, even though the launch wasn't the best, It has gotten much better now. The vehicle physics are also really great, not THAT realistic, but more arcadey. In this aspect, unlike the graphics, I think that the game being less realistic in vehicle physics is way more fun and adds onto the charm of the game instead of it being super realistic. The vehicle physics have realism, but not that much, I personally think it's perfect. PERFORMANCE IS ABSOLUTELY MINDBLOWING, a game made in 2021 that looks THIS GOOD and performs this AMAZINGLY is too good to be true, I average 90-105 FPS on High Settings with 8x MSAA (the MSAA implementation on this game is very good btw, doesnt look like a blurry mess on 1080p like how TAA and FXAA do, while performing better then them somehow in this game specifically) and sometimes see rare dips to 70-80 FPS, really playable, no studders even with a HDD! (I'm running the game on my 1TB 5400 RPM hard drive, and see no issues besides loading times), and my gaming laptop with an i7 10750H and a 3050 TI Laptop GPU (4gb vram) see no issues whatsoever! The story is also really great for an arcade racing game, had a LOT of fun on it and teaches you stuff regarding how racing is made to be fun, not to take it seriously. The DLCs, Playlists and events are also really well done. The Hot Wheels and Rally Adventure DLCs are very well done and had a lot of fun playing them! The Playlists feature is also pretty smart, it lets me get my favorite dream vehicles i want like the recent Mercedes AMG E63 S which was put on the last few playlists was one of my dream cars that I really wanted, and the playlist feature finally made my dream come true! I also got a few Porsches i wanted from it. Events are pretty great too, even community ones! Absolutely reccomend, i bought this game at full price cuz i couldn't wait for a discount. Note that i also played the game on one of my friends' PCs, and because of how good the game was, i decided to purchase it on Steam at full price (premium edition). 10/10, would reccomend if you're into these games.

FH5 is a tough title for me. I love racing games, but because I've never owned an Xbox console I've never played any of the Horizon games. It feels like a 9/10 game but is hindered by an overwhelming career/story mode and cluttered UI. I still recommend it, but it's not for me. On one hand, the visuals, location, soundtrack, and car roster are all top tier. You'll pretty much be able to find a little of everything in this game, as you'd expect. The things I don't like are minimal, and maybe down to personal preferences, but they still ruled my experience. First, I just don't vibe with Horizon's physics in this title. The cars seem to just skate over any surface, and while cars can seem like they have weight when throwing them into corners, they also just bounce off walls, cars, or other immovable parts of the environment. If I think about all my favorite racing titles, they all make you feel like what you're driving is centered in the world. I rarely felt that way in this game. Most importantly of my criticisms comes down the gameplay: there is simply TOO MUCH to do. You are constantly being pulled in different directions, which seems like the ultimate game experience because you'll never run out of things to do. For me I was looking for more of a linear story, with side quests thrown in, but there's seemingly no "continue" point. This isn't helped by the fact that, from the start, you have a huge budget and are given one of every class of vehicle. Not to mention you get a new car after every other race, you're soon flooded with too much choice.

🏆 "The Ultimate Open-World Racing Experience" ⏱️ ~20+ hours played 👍 Helpful Review I’ve played a lot of racing games over the years — arcade, sim, open world — but Forza Horizon 5 hits a level of polish and freedom that very few games ever reach. From the very first drive, it feels incredible. The controls are buttery smooth, every car has its own personality, and the sense of speed is addictive. But what truly makes this game special is how it manages to be both relaxing and thrilling at the same time. One moment you’re drifting through mountain roads with a sunset in the background; the next, you’re blasting through a sandstorm in a million-dollar hypercar. It’s pure joy. The map — a stunning recreation of Mexico — is honestly one of the most beautiful open worlds I’ve ever seen in any game, racing or otherwise. The diversity is insane: jungles, volcanoes, cities, deserts, beaches… all seamlessly connected. You can drive for hours and still find new places, new routes, and new surprises. Customization is another huge win here. You can tune, paint, and modify your cars in countless ways, down to the smallest detail. The community paints and liveries are basically art. Combine that with a massive car list — classics, supercars, off-road beasts — and it’s impossible to get bored. Online play is smooth, fun, and totally integrated into the experience. No endless menus or waiting lobbies — just hop in, and you’re racing with friends or randoms in seconds. The Horizon Festival feels alive, and that feeling of being part of something bigger makes the world feel dynamic and social. The music is top-notch, the atmosphere is unmatched, and the performance (especially on PC) is fantastic. Even after hundreds of hours, I still find myself launching the game just to cruise around, take photos, and enjoy the scenery. If you love cars, freedom, or just beautiful worlds to get lost in, Forza Horizon 5 is the best it gets. It’s not just a racing game — it’s an experience you feel. ⭐ 10/10 — “Just one more drive.”

After spending about 120 hours in Forza Horizon 5 and unlocking almost all of the achievements, I feel like I have experienced nearly everything the game has to offer. First of all, the game is visually stunning. The map based on Mexico is beautiful, the car selection is huge, and the driving physics are still some of the best in the arcade-racing genre. However, after a long time playing, the gameplay starts to feel repetitive. Many events begin to feel the same, and this is something that also reminds me of Forza Horizon 4. The core gameplay loop hasn’t changed much between the two games. The DLCs are a mixed experience. The Rally Adventure DLC is actually quite interesting. The rally mechanics, dirt roads, and more technical driving create a refreshing change of pace compared to the base game. It feels more focused and challenging, which I appreciated. On the other hand, the Hot Wheels DLC was less interesting for me. While the tracks look impressive and creative, the gameplay quickly becomes more about spectacle than driving skill, and the novelty wears off faster than expected. One mode that I personally didn’t enjoy is “The Eliminator”. While the idea of a battle-royale style racing mode is creative, in practice it often feels frustrating and somewhat random. Encounters can depend too much on luck, car drops, or map positioning rather than pure driving skill. Because of this, the mode never really felt satisfying or balanced to me, even though I appreciate the attempt to add something different. Another downside is the lack of a meaningful story. There are some narrative elements, but they are very light and mostly serve as short introductions to events. Compared to how big the game world is, the story content feels minimal. Overall, Forza Horizon 5 is still a very polished and enjoyable racing game, especially in the first dozens of hours. But after completing most of the achievements and spending over 120 hours in the game, the repetition and lack of deeper progression or story can make it feel a bit monotonous. Still, for fans of arcade racing and car collecting, it remains a solid experience.

I really thought I would enjoy this game, but after about an hour of playing, several aspects have made me decide to refund it. Here are a few of the issues I’ve experienced: - The driving dynamics feel very arcade-like. I understand that some players enjoy this, but personally, it’s not for me. Cars can take turns at 180 mph without any real difficulty, showing almost no body roll or believable suspension physics, which makes the handling feel floaty and unrealistic. - All automatic cars seem to behave as if they have dual-clutch transmissions, which feels both unnatural and unrealistic. The shift times are unrealistically fast for many of these cars, and there’s a strange clutch-like behavior even on true automatics, causing the engine to rev to around 3,000 RPM just to get the car moving. - The tutorial is long, drawn out, and lacks any sense of excitement or uniqueness. - The cutscenes are unskippable, which makes the pacing even worse. They’re not engaging or exciting, and for a racing game, I’d rather be driving than watching awfully drawn-out scenes. - The voice acting feels cheesy and low quality, making the story hard to take seriously. - The character creation process feels mediocre and unnecessary. It places emphasis on identity-focused elements that don’t contribute to the gameplay experience, making the overall design feel misplaced in a racing title where driving should be the main focus. I understand this is a Forza Horizon game and not a Forza Motorsport game, but even then, it’s not Need for Speed. - The music choices feel uninspired and outdated. Games from the late 2000s and early 2010s had far stronger and more memorable soundtracks that added real energy and atmosphere to the experience. This game’s music just doesn’t capture that same vibe, and I ended up muting the music as soon as I started playing. - The engine power figures are completely unrealistic. For example, no Ford Bronco I’m aware of makes 40 pounds of boost and 600 lb-ft of torque, even when tuned. Overall, the combination of these issues makes the game unenjoyable for me. Compared to the older Horizon games, it just doesn’t feel as good or as fun to play. It’s not what I was expecting. I recognize that some of these points may seem minor to others, but they reflect my personal expectations and preferences as a player.

PROs + Great racing game with a large variety of races and cars. Truly overwhelming in terms of scale. + Diverse biomes with alternating seasons. + New challenges weekly (most of which are fun) + Great car handling and physics. a sweet spot between simulation and arcade. Makes you work hard to master each car. And you can truly feel the differences between tuned cars. + Multiple difficulty levels for each player. Allows you fine grained control over the difficulty. Also allows you to grow as a racer. (games like NFS have very few modes, and the highest difficulty is either not hard enough, or rubber-banding physics-bending AI) --> this is not the case in this game. + Events, Class Tiers and Tuning makes all the cars viable and usable. Also encourages us to play at different Tier levels, all races are skilled and fun, and the skill levels are very balanced and controllable. + Not pay-walled or pay-to-win! + Lots of post game content, careers, jobs, events, adventures, makes the game worth every cent. CONs + Poor map design, very sparsely populated. large open spaces, very very boring. I don't know how you managed to make Mexico (a place so full of life) sooooo boring. THINGS THAT NEED FIXING : + Poorly optimized for PC controls. Forza Horizon 5 — Gorgeous Cars, Disgusting Online System I genuinely want Forza Horizon to keep getting better — this series has been with me for years and given me countless moments of joy. That’s why it hurts to see how badly Forza Horizon 5 handles its online experience. Let’s be fair: Forza Horizon 5 could’ve been the best open-world racing game ever made. The cars look amazing, the map is huge, the driving feels great — until you go online. The moment you join a multiplayer race, it turns into a demolition derby. People ram you at full speed, shove you off the track, block you on purpose — and laugh while doing it. Want to report them? Good luck. You’ll have to record a video, take screenshots, manually type in their nickname, and then pray that someone at Playground Games actually bothers to look. Spoiler: they don’t. In the end, the system punishes fair players with frustration and rewards griefers with total freedom. What’s worse is that other racing games already solved this years ago. iRacing uses a Safety Rating system that automatically penalizes dangerous driving and off-track behavior; Gran Turismo 7 tracks contact frequency and “sportsmanship scores.” And Forza Horizon 5? Still living in the 2010s, pretending that “manual reports” are enough to keep races fair. If Playground Games actually cares about online racing, here’s what they should do: Add an in-game instant report tool that automatically saves the last five minutes of gameplay; Use diverse, data-driven calculation methods (relative speed, collision angle, impact frequency, trajectory changes after contact, etc.) to detect intentional ramming; Toughen penalties for high-speed or deliberate collisions — ghost offenders, kick them from lobbies, or restrict ranked play; Or just remove player-to-player collisions entirely in public lobbies if you can’t manage them properly. It’s 2025. Other games already use advanced algorithms and unique detection methods to maintain fair, clean racing — yet Horizon 5 still relies on player “self-discipline.” If you can’t even guarantee basic online fairness, stop pretending to be an MMO. Focus on what Forza Horizon used to be — a pure, joyful single-player racing experience. ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- 总的来说地平线算是这十几二十年历程里综合最优秀的赛车游戏，陪伴了我近十年的时光，但是不得不说，如果线上游戏维持当前的监管水平那playground还是别做把地平线网游化，增强社交属性的春秋大梦了（乐 玩家在比赛里乱撞、恶意挡路成，举报流程又繁琐得一匹——录视频、截图、输入昵称，还要填写违规行为，甚至还要专门的术语，处理速度短则几天长则半年，大概率是最后没人理。 我就纳了闷了，是别的赛车游戏没有安全评分或算法识别恶意驾驶的例子吗，这么大家公司不会学习吗？《地平线5》多少年了却还停留在不知道多久的过去？？？ 解决方法说白了，要么加入游戏内即时举报和自动录像，完善监管 ; 要么彻底取消玩家碰撞体积 又想要车辆碰撞的趣味性又不维护在线环境，世上没这种好事 2025年了，靠玩家“自觉”维护公平多少有点贻笑大方了

There's a lot with this game so I'm just gonna to a pros and cons list: Pros: - As of 2025 standards, the game is visually stunning. - Weekly/Monthly challenges so there's reason to come back in check in. - Some of these cars are FUN to drive. Had the urge to get a racing game just for some mindless fun. Don't have a Switch so Mario Kart was out of the question. Got FH4 on sale a while back, then got FH5 after playing 4 for a while. For the uninitiated, Forza Horizon is unique in that its racing falls somewhere between a complete arcade racer with totally unrealistic handling (like Grand Theft Auto), and racing sims like Gran Turismo. It's much harder to 'drift' your way to victory because you need to follow a racing line just like in real racing, but the driving feels more 'floaty' than an actual sim which makes it more accessible. Add to that the large, gorgeous open world and you get the most unparalleled sense of freedom any racing game has to offer. P.S. I actually slightly prefer FH4 to FH5 although both are great

Forza Horizon 5 is one of those games that never really gets old. From the moment you drop into Mexico, everything just feels alive — the lighting, the weather, the sound of engines bouncing off canyons and jungles. The map is massive but never empty; every corner has a race, a barn find, or just a reason to floor it. The driving physics strike that perfect balance between realism and fun. Every car feels different — from rally monsters sliding through the desert to hypercars screaming down the highway. The tuning and customization go deep, but even if you’re not into that, the game’s accessible enough to just jump in and enjoy. Online play is smooth, and the community events keep it fresh. The only real downside is the progression can feel a bit too generous — you earn cars so fast that collecting loses some meaning. Still, that’s a small complaint in a game this polished. Forza Horizon 5 isn’t just a racing game — it’s a celebration of driving. Whether you’re cruising for the views or chasing leaderboard times, it’s easily one of the best open-world racers ever made.

🏎️ Forza Horizon 5 – Personal Review I’ve played a lot of racing games over the years, but Forza Horizon 5 is easily one of the best I’ve ever experienced. From the moment you drop out of that plane into Mexico, the game grabs you and doesn’t let go. It’s not just a racing game — it’s an open-world celebration of cars, speed, and freedom. 🌎 World & Visuals Let’s start with the obvious: this game is absolutely stunning. The Mexican map is huge, diverse, and alive. You can go from racing through a dusty desert to tearing through a rainforest, climbing a volcano, or speeding across the coast — all without a single loading screen. The lighting, weather effects, and car detail are next-level. Sometimes I just drive around with no destination because the world feels so alive. 🚗 Driving & Gameplay The driving is near perfect. It finds that sweet spot between realism and fun — you feel the weight of the cars, the grip of the tires, but it’s never frustrating. Whether you’re drifting, off-roading, or street racing, the controls feel smooth and responsive. Every car has its own character, and tuning them adds even more depth. The variety of events is huge — street races, off-road challenges, stunt jumps, drift zones, drag races, and even fun seasonal events. And the freedom to just do whatever you want is what makes Forza Horizon 5 stand out. You can spend hours just exploring, collecting cars, and customizing them to perfection. 💬 Online & Replayability Online play is solid for the most part — though you’ll run into the occasional disconnect or lag spike. The Horizon Life system makes the world feel alive, with other players zooming by and sharing the same open world. Seasonal events, community challenges, and constant updates keep the game fresh even years later. ⚙️ Minor Downsides It’s hard to find serious flaws here. Some bugs and server issues can pop up occasionally, and the AI can feel too forgiving at times. The in-game economy also leans a bit toward grinding if you’re not using wheelspins or lucky draws. But honestly, none of that ruins the experience — it’s still pure fun almost every time I play. 💬 Final Thoughts Forza Horizon 5 is everything a racing game should be — fast, gorgeous, accessible, and endlessly replayable. It’s one of those games you can lose hours in without even realizing it. Whether you’re a hardcore car fan or just want to relax and cruise through an open world, this game delivers in every way. ⭐ Final Rating: 9.5/10 Breathtaking visuals, incredible driving feel, and endless freedom. Forza Horizon 5 is the gold standard for open-world racing — it’s pure joy on four wheels.

The game features stunning graphics, over a thousand cars, and still manages to be genuinely fun to play. However, the map feels small — set in Mexico, more than two-thirds of the activities focus on rally, off-road, or stunt events, which doesn’t really fit with around 80% of the cars available. The game also puts a huge emphasis on tuning, yet offers no proper tools to test or understand the effects of your adjustments. For example, there’s no power/torque vs RPM graph available when tuning gear ratios, even though such data clearly exists in the engine upgrade screen. The single-player content is limited, and the stories are rather cringe, pushing most of the experience toward multiplayer and user-generated content, which often varies in quality. On top of that, game modes and menus feel confusing and cluttered, hurting the overall flow. Worse still, with each new car added since launch featuring fewer upgrade and tuning options, it’s hard not to feel like you’re playing an early access title rather than a full-fledged AAA game.

[h2]The epitome of modern open-world simcade... with flaws[/h2] [b]Purchased Premium Edition & played on Steam Deck LCD[/b] There’s nothing that I can say about this game that hasn’t already been said. [i]Forza Horizon 5[/i] will be remembered less as the great open-world 2021 racing game of the year, and more as the placeholder until the next [i]Horizon[/i]; filled with empty deserts, FOMO seasonal playlists, and META cars locked behind either DLC paywalls, or long-since gone time-limited events that cease to return. It really leaves you feeling like it’s a “what could’ve been game," whilst paying little homage to the culture of the country it took place in, with there being only two Mexican cars in the entire roster. Additionally, the content gets very overwhelming at times, flooding you with tasks leaving you no room to breathe and enjoy the scenery until you’ve completed them all. [i]FH5[/i]’s biggest redeeming factor was its ability to make you miss its predecessor, when there was a simpler currency system pre-accolades, where there were proper seasons, and what felt like a much more colorful game in [i]Forza Horizon 4[/i] than its 5th rendition counterpart. Conversely, there is no [i]Forza Horizon[/i] game that I wouldn’t buy, as there isn’t a close alternative- not even by the likes of [i]The Crew[/i] or the [i]Need for Speed[/i] franchise (which EA has shelved at the time of writing this): neither having the semblance of [i]Forza[/i]’s atmosphere. Despite this game leaving more to be desired, it really shines when it comes to rallying. The simcade physics with simulation steering turned on, is quite an enjoyable experience whilst offroading. Both expansion packs can be summed up as "nothing short of amazing." Not to mention the variety of traditional, or sometimes purely fun nonsensical, vehicle builds that you can race competitively against other players. Most of all, [i]FH5[/i] is a really easy title to pick up and run on low to mid range hardware such as the Steam Deck. It was and still is worth my time to play until the inevitable release of [i]Forza Horizon 6[/i]’s Japan, and I’m sure it will be worth yours as well. [i]Forza Horizon 5[/i] is a fun experience in the dying genre of racing games in spite of its flaws, and you should definitely buy it when it’s on sale. I highly implore purchasing all the DLC given that Microsoft is very stingy with their licensing, because DLCs, along with the base game, do eventually get removed from all storefronts making them impossible to find keys for thereafter.

Before getting deeper into this review, I want to mention, that I've never even thought, I'd ever play and enjoy a car racing game, as I'm mostly into RPGs and MMOs. With that being said though, Forza Horizon 5 is a very enjoyable racing game. To be completely honest, one of the most enjoyable games I've played in a long time. With only 18.5 hours in currently, I'm far from being an expert on this subject, but this game honestly feels like a RPG packaged as a racing game. You gain levels and currency through participating in races, which you unlock, as you gain more accolade points through various activities and unlock more parts of the Horizon Festival. And that honestly feels pretty much like doing quests and exploration in an RPG. I do like that approach very much. The driving feels very good, the handling of the various cars do have weight to them, without feeling floaty or overly realistic, in my opinion, its the perfect middleground between realism and arcade, which I also appreciate very much, as I think I probably wouldn't enjoy realism as much as the more "arcadey" approach Forza Horizon 5 has. Racing rarely gets boring either, as the game keeps recommending me higher and higher difficulties, as I keep winning races, and thanks to me repeating races until I can reach 1st place, I currently play on the Expert difficulty level, which really makes it challenging, ngl. The learning curve from Highly Skilled to Expert was exceptionally steep, so that it was a bit frustrating at first, but I'm slowly getting the hang of it after some hours of practice! There also seems so much to be done, when looking at the ingame map, I sometimes get a bit overwhelmed with the sheer amount of things to do, and I'm far away from having even unlocked every type of race or activity and at the beginning that did bother me a little bit, but as time went on I realized, that this game does not require you to do anything in a specific order or way, and it just gives you "overwhelming" freedom to just do anything and unlock more, anytime you want to. So I just do random races I see on the map and unlock more of the Horizon Festival as I feel like. So far I haven't tried any online races, but that's also a part of the game, I'm looking forward to, once I have refined my driving skills! That being said though, the game is a open world with a online lobby, as in, you do see other people as you play the game when connected to the net. You can form convoys and do activities together, or just drive around and have fun. I honestly haven't engaged in that, that much yet, as I'm heading from race to race, but it does seem like a fun feature for more social players that want to engage in activites with other players. c: With only 18 hours in right now, I am very far from having seen everything this game offers, this review probably misses a lot of features. Like Tuning. Customization options. And probably much more. But those are things, I haven't had that many experiences yet with, so theres no way I could review those appropriately. What I am going to say now though, at the finish line of my review is, that I really can recommend this game to anyone looking for a change of pace in their games. I literally got into this game from a very different genre of games and had a lot of joy so far. I don't even like cars. But this game's fun mechanics and challenging gameplay on the higher difficulties, keeps me engaged and looking for more. A truly great experience so far. I grabbed this game in the steam Autumn sale, and honestly, it was very much worth it already. I'm also very much looking forward to Forza Horizon 6 next year! I will probably update this review, as I progress more and experience more parts and features of this game.

I’ve spent a good number of hours in FH5 and honestly, it’s one of the most satisfying racing games I’ve played in years. The Mexico map is massive and never feels boring — deserts, jungles, highways, cities, sandstorms — every drive feels different. The car handling is spot on. Whether you’re cruising casually or pushing hard in races, the controls feel smooth and predictable. Arcade enough to enjoy, but realistic enough to keep you engaged. Car sounds are amazing, especially with headphones on. Graphics are stunning even on medium settings, and the day–night and weather changes add a lot to the immersion. The festivals, events, and challenges keep coming, so there’s always something to do even if you don’t want to race competitively. Multiplayer works well most of the time, and free roaming with random players is surprisingly fun. Car collection is addictive, and tuning/customization gives plenty of freedom. Minor bugs and occasional online hiccups exist, but nothing that ruins the experience. Overall, FH5 is not just a racing game — it’s a chill, fun driving experience you can keep coming back to. If you enjoy cars even a little, this game is a must-have. Highly recommended. 🚗🔥

In a vacuum the game is great and would absolutely satisfy a great deal of players. It is even suitable for those that may not be that into cars or sim racing. I myself am in this camp, and it is why I bought Forza 5 to begin with. However, my grievances with it, and why I have chosen to request a refund are purely grounded in the technicality of the game's "playable" status on Steam Deck. The warning reads "some functionality is not accessible when using the default controller configuration, requiring the use of the touch screen or virtual keyboard, or a community configuration." Fair enough, unless that 'some functionality' is the connection of your steam account to a Microsoft account, without which you cannot play this game at all. Having spent approximately half of my playtime experiencing the various ways in which this warning is disingenuous for this particular game, I cannot in good faith recommend it. During initial setup, Microsoft's authentication dialogue boxes scale incorrectly, rendering critical UI elements inaccessible on the Deck's native display. Text entry fields and confirmation buttons appear off-screen or unusable, and were highly unresponsive even when I did find them in the end. Indeed, I did manage to get this to work after roughly 6 attempts, using a USB dock, mouse, keyboard, and the time honoured tradition of button mashing. Even with these peripherals—which most Deck users won't have available portably— this initial start up was a massive pain in the bumper. The playable badge promises that a game works on Deck with some warts and jank that one must account for. And again, fair enough. But I believe that Valve should revoke playable Steam Deck status for Forza 5 until Microsoft fixes their UI scaling for the authentication flow. Because for those unlucky enough not to get past this verification roadblock, the game isn't actually playable. It's also kinda silly that the game with a €50 'Premium' edition which doesn't even get you the complete experience can get such intricate monetisation and hamster wheel mechanics right, yet no one seems to have thought 'yo, wouldn't it be useful if people could actually connect to this extraneous service of ours that no one actually likes?' Come on Microsoft. But I recognise that this is me being pedantic rather than pointing out objective technical failures.

Forza Horizon 5 feels like a [b]tech demo[/b]. [h2]the core and technical aspects[/h2] the core of the game - driving and racing the cars - is incredibly well done and has clearly had a lot of effort and time invested towards it over the course of the franchise's lifespan. the simcade engine is the best of its kind and no other competitor comes close. driving remains immensely satisfying irrespective of the type of vehicle you're maneuvering, the terrain surface you're on, or weather conditions you're under. the game consistently looks, sounds, and performs very well. [hr][/hr] but it ends there. it's as if the developers had invested a lot of time and care into creating an incredibly solid base for a racing game, but then skimped out on all the additional aspects that wouldn't have required nearly as much effort or resources, but that would've greatly contributed to the quality of the final product. that's where the tech demo analogy comes from. first case in point: [h2]the map[/h2] the team was clearly capable of creating a large, varied, beautiful, and functional open world map. Mexico certainly ticks all of those boxes, and more: the volcano, the jungles, the many long, winding and twisting roads with great verticality, the beach town, the stadium and test track - i could go on. [b]on paper it's perfect[/b]. i much prefer it to the predecessor's Edinburgh. but holy sh*t is it [b]empty[/b]. the NPC vehicle traffic is so incredibly sparse. there are [i]zero[/i] pedestrians, like, at all. there's no people. there's no proper intersections, no parking garages, no gas stations, no traffic lights. there's no [i]things happening[/i]. no airplanes in the sky, boats on water, no service vehicles, no wildlife (outside of howler monkeys? and some birds), no events. the one urban area in the game feels like a complete ghost town. it's embarrassing. it looks and feels completely fake. this has been the case throughout the entirety of the franchise's lifespan. The Crew perfected the open-world racing map in 2018. so why can't Forza Horizon? [h2]story[/h2] terrible and completely dispensable in every possible aspect. ninety five percent of the storylines revolve around you driving a vehicle from point A to point B on the map while some at best completely forgettable and at worst extremely annoying character yaps about some boring ♥♥♥♥ in an irritatingly fake and forced spanish accent with involuntary spansih lingo sprinkled in occasionally. it's all totally dry, inoffensive, and boring, with zero character, no emotion, and a total lack of any plot. just absolutely terrible. the only slightly redeemable aspect are some of the scripted "Showcase" events, which seem more like technical presentations rather than parts of the story. [h2]progression[/h2] there is none. the currency model is optimized... - for the 10 year old playing the game on the living room Xbox whose parents bought it for him at $80, and who certainly wouldn't appreciate driving a beat-down Ford for the first 10 hours of the game. and that's fine. but there has to be a fine line, a compromise? the game showers you with rewards at every possible step. you earn credits as a reward for completing races, showcases, and events - and cars (and their upgrades) [i]do[/i] cost credits - but that aspect very quickly becomes totally irrelevant as you're constantly rewarded with Wheelspins, which in turn give you credits and cars in extreme abundance. the new "Accolades" system is a diamond in the rough - a good idea in isolation, which ultimately suffers from being part of a larger, flawed system. the one aspect of progression that's done right is what the game aptly calls [i]Hard To Find[/i] cars - ones that cannot be purchased outright using credits nor won in a wheelspin. instead, they appear for limited time in either the [i]Forzathon Shop[/i] or as a reward in a seasonal Festival Playlist. and it is this limited nature and the FOMO associated with it is what makes you want to play the game and acquire the car, and what ultimately makes it that much more satisfying once you do. -- but even so it's hard to make these cars appear special or unique next to their cheap, readily available 150,000 CR supercar counterparts. so - if there's no story to follow or get invested into, and little feeling of progression as you play - what's left? [hr][/hr] well, it's not all bleak. again, the activities that benefit most from the game's great foundation are thankfully the ones you'll spend most of your time on - racing (whether against AI or online versus real opponents) and simply cruising around the map. and they're very polished, really enjoyable, and in my opinion enough to just barely overshadow all the negatives. at its core, Forza Horizon 5 is still very enjoyable. it just sucks that i can't help but keep wondering just how much better it would've been with a bit more effort.
