Forza Horizon 5: The Participation Trophy of Racing Games I booted up Forza Horizon 5 thinking, “This might finally be it, the racing game I’ve been waiting years for.” Instead, I got what can only be described as Fast & the Frivolous. Let’s start with the positives. The game is stunning. It’s so pretty it makes real life look like it’s still rendering. The controls? Tight. Soundtrack? Fire, if your Spotify playlist is curated by a hyper-caffeinated intern trying to appeal to twelve demographics at once. But here's where the tire marks start to skid. The moment I finished the tutorial, the game tossed me the keys to not one, but several million-dollar cars. I didn’t earn them. I didn’t buy them. I basically blinked and suddenly I owned more Lamborghinis than common sense. At one point I thought, “Did I accidentally buy the DLC where Jeff Bezos plays the role of your race team manager?” Nope. Just standard gameplay. The whole experience feels like showing up to your first day of work and being made CEO for spelling your name right on the application. Where’s the grind? Where’s the thrill of clawing your way up from a beat-up PT Cruiser with mismatched panels and three working spark plugs? Where’s the part where you duct tape a spoiler on and feel proud about it? Instead, Forza seems to have been designed by the same committee responsible for modern school award ceremonies. “You showed up! Here’s a Bugatti!” And don’t even get me started on the in-game commercials. You’re mid-drift and suddenly you’re getting bombarded with adverts for DLC and other in game events you likely want no part in. I wanted to race, not attend a digital flee market. Also, if you dare to have WeMod installed, not running, just installed, Forza will throw a tantrum like a toddler who’s been told they can’t lick the dog. I had to perform a full digital exorcism just to get the game to stop auto-closing itself. I’m playing offline, Forza. Calm down. I’m not trying to hack into NASA. Look, maybe I’m bitter. Maybe it’s because my kids expect trophies for showing up, too. Maybe I’m just nostalgic for the days of Gran Turismo and Need for Speed, where you actually worked for your success. And when you finally got your dream car, it meant something. In summary, if you want a game that throws exotic cars at you like Halloween candy and congratulates you for breathing, Forza Horizon 5 is your jam. But if you're looking for a meaningful climb from rags to RPMs, this one feels more like riding shotgun in someone else’s power fantasy.

My friend's Dungeons and Dragons characters have more compelling backstories and arcs than Forza, and he's not even close to being a writer! How are they so bad? Is the game fun? Yes. Is it rewarding? Well... Forza Horizon 5 is fun at first glance the driving feels good, the car list is massive, and visually it's stunning. But it quickly becomes clear that the game lacks any meaningful progression. Within the first hour, you're given dozens of cars, including supercars, with no reason to even use most of them. The constant flow of free vehicles kills any sense of reward or accomplishment. The "festival" theme feels hollow. There's no sense of rising through ranks, no rivals, no endgame – you arrive as the best and stay there. Maybe I’m biased because I just replayed Need for Speed: ProStreet, which I consider to have one of the best progression systems and festival atmospheres ever made. In comparison, the "festival" in Horizon 5 feels pointless. Now let’s talk about the map. What is this? Horizon 3 (Australia) and Horizon 4 (UK) had fantastic, memorable worlds. I loved how seasons in FH4 changed the vibe and even your driving strategy. Here, you're just driving across a giant flat plate. Nothing feels iconic or immersive. The city is painfully bland. After playing FH3 and FH4, I actually wanted to visit Australia and Scotland. After FH5? Mexico feels like a post-apocalyptic wasteland from Fallout. And while we’re at it, why is the festival in Mexico? The game tries way too hard to inject Mexican culture with awkward Spanglish dialogue and forced enthusiasm. I thought the cutscenes in NFS Unbound were cringe, turns out, FH5 takes that crown with ease. And honestly, Mexico doesn’t even have a well-known car culture. Can we please go back to America, Europe, or Japan? As a sandbox? It’s decent. As a racing game? It fails to deliver any real structure, challenge, or progression. It’s all sugar, no substance.

[h1] TL;DR of [b]MY EXPERIENCE[/b][/h1] [h3] because I couldn't bother reading reviews for this game[/h3] [b]Performance:[/b] actually well optimized (played it on a 2060 and later on a 3060, both 8gb, 16-32gb RAM and Ry5 3600X) [b]Content:[/b] there is no street racing scene, the cities are minuscule and only a little larger than Lance Strolls brain. Also, I wish we could increase the amount of laps on official races. The Mexico map is so cross-country/off-road heavy that it gets frustrating. [b]Difficulty:[/b] yes, everything you read is true, the AI cheats and has infinite grip on corners, even at 200mph. It is not a "skill issue", difficulty in these games should be about how early/late AI reacts to the driving line, not actually messing with the cars stats. A 100mph bot-driven Civic shouldn't have more grip and speed than a player-driven one. [b]FOMO:[/b] it depends solely on what you want to drive. Personally, I despise the time-gated events this game has, just use an unlock tool to get the cars you want, you won't get banned [b]Customization/tuning:[/b] good enough, although it's not possible to edit the Tunes and Designs you download from other people (makes no sense to me, but ok) [b]Headtracking and VR:[/b] non-existant. I find it absurd that nobody thought that at least headtracking should be implemented in a game like Forza, but alas, the wonders of workarounds exist. You can use Opentrack to simulate mouse movement, although it is VERY janky. To the Leadership Team and Executive Producers at Playground Games / Xbox Game Studios, I am writing to you today as a deeply invested and long-time customer of the Forza Horizon series, specifically regarding my profound disappointment with the current state of Forza Horizon 5's global leaderboards. While I genuinely appreciate the incredible work put into the game's core design, breathtaking visuals, and engaging gameplay – evident in the sheer joy I find perfecting tunes for vehicles like my 1956 F-100 and 2020 Bronco R, and exploring the vibrant map – a fundamental aspect of the online experience is severely broken. The pervasive presence of cheated and impossible times on the global leaderboards for various events, including those like "Oasis Cross Country," is, frankly, criminal. As a Customer Care Senior Specialist in my professional life, I understand the critical importance of delivering on a product's promise. When I, and countless other players, pay hard-earned money for Forza Horizon 5, we are implicitly promised a fair and fun online racing environment. Currently, that promise is being demonstrably broken. It is a straight lie to customers to present a competitive online landscape that is so thoroughly contaminated. Encountering times like 21 seconds on a complex cross-country track, which is humanly impossible in any car or class, is not merely frustrating; it actively devalues every legitimate effort, saps the motivation to compete, and turns what should be an exhilarating challenge into a disheartening exercise in futility. From a customer's perspective, and leveraging my understanding of product delivery, this feels akin to "selling a broken record like it was new." The core online competitive experience, a significant draw for many players, is compromised by a seemingly unaddressed issue. This severely erodes customer trust and, if left unaddressed, will inevitably cause long-term damage to the brand's reputation among its most dedicated players. I was, along with millions of other loyal users, eagerly anticipating the upcoming release of Forza Horizon 6, prepared to invest my hard-earned money into what I hoped would be a refined and fair online experience. However, due to the persistent and unaddressed integrity issues in Forza Horizon 5, I will now actively raise awareness within the gaming community, urging others not to purchase the next installment. Furthermore, I will be seeking legal assistance to explore avenues regarding the broken promises and the ongoing pattern of delivering products with fundamental flaws, even in new releases. I urge you to implement more robust anti-cheat measures, conduct aggressive and regular leaderboard purges, and prioritize restoring the competitive integrity of Forza Horizon 5's online leaderboards. The current situation is a disservice to your loyal player base and undermines the fantastic work your development teams have poured into the game itself. I sincerely hope that you will take this feedback to heart and take concrete steps to rectify this critical issue. The future enjoyment and trust of your committed customers depend on it. Sincerely, A Disappointed but Hopeful Player

I understand if people want a bit of mindless fun after a long day. I'm not here to Pooh Pooh anybody's good time in a video game. But for me this game just feels manipulative. The constant glazing by all the two dimensional characters that talk to you. The constant points that flash In the middle of the screen after doing just about anything. Did you drive near an opponent? POINTS! Turned a corner? POINTS! Hit a cactus? POINTS! Drafting, drifting, driving fast? POINTS! But the game just isn't for me. The driving itself is not engaging enough to be fun on its own. The game looks good and I would love to enjoy it, but I only really want to do street or circuit races. I just don't care about the other types that you are forced to play to progress and that take up a lot of the game. If all you want is engaging races with some gorgeous graphics in an interesting environment unfortunately what the game offers is very shallow. My dream game would be a (mostly) illegal street racing game with Forza Motorsport driving mechanics and all the pizzazz of Forza Horizon, but with less shallowness in the world buliding and preferably a much more straightforward monetization with some clearly defined DLC packs. Not this mixing up of the terms where you can mistakenly buy a premium edition that doesn't have everything. So basically what I'm praying for is the production value of Forza Horizon, its seamless fun, plus the driving mechanics of Forza Motorsport.

[h1] ---{ Detail Notes }--- [/h1] I've not touched a forza horizon title in years yet what draw me back to even want to play this game then the past games, was not only the car collection but the map was more up my ally of nice blue seas nicely enough designed roads from what i saw. So pick it up 2024 December in the winter sale and since then well you can see, in basically 6 months put into 375 hours into it. And so i've come to tell you this game is totally worth it, had lot more fun then even in the crew 2 ever gave me. So if you were looking for a open world car game, i'll hands down say this is it, this is the golden eagle of them all at moment for you. But if you want me to dig at it more here then. The cars all feel weighty and not all but so far found out of my 468 cars 282 feel so different to drive and well some so different it require me to have to change how i drive them mainly ones that have so much lose of grip in lower gears and other things that makes them so unique then any other car i've gotten. In case bad at working it out that's so far i've found 186 that feel same as another to drive. I guess with so many cars there was bound to be alikes in the game. Have in mind there are 902 total to drive so am just getting to scratching the bellow the surface of the collection of cars to have fun with, some not likely to get for a while seeing how there are 20M CR player snipping cars to get too. (DLC included in that car total btw, not sure what the total is without DLC included) The graphics of the game look pretty neat more so when you turn raytracying tho downside i get blinded few times, the light glare from the sunlight and such can be over the top at rare times, guess its not perfectly optimised but when its not filling your vision it looks goooooooood, more so on those chome cars. And at night can look so pretty at times in fact i understand more why people want the next instalment to be japan. Like just seeing the player created japan citys at night with as best neon lights or just well placed street lights we have to use, it for sure can look so beautiful, you would want to stop drifting/driveing around to admire it all. The main gameplay consists of 5 different stuff but only 4 race types : Those 4 other races types Cross country (All mainly offroad fully), Dirt racing (mix of dirt roads and none dirt roads basically rally cross, few dirt racing events are fully dirt but quite a handful are more tarmac then actually dirt racing), Road racing (Bit more legal racing events no traffic but more acted like its official day race just set on street roads) and lastly Street racing. (The same as road racing but more set at night or dusk and duh traffic enabled while you race so would have to be careful of your turns) My fav was the sub event in the street racing type were you only race 1 single ai midnight battle they called it where when you win you gain the car you were racing along side like pinkslips racing, i hope in the next game they do more of those cause 4 wasn't enough, i wanted more of those events in the game. They were surprising more fun then i thought they would be when i was heading to my first one. And the other thing to do is skill base types this is where your jumps and drift skill zones and how fast you can be and such will be. Now lastly wanna quickly as i can talk about where most of my gaming hours has also gone into, and that is the online activities you have Trails and Tours (These are like the same events just that they have some differences in how they play out, but they are still PvE races with other players) / Open races / Playground games / Hide and Seek / Battle royal / and lastly Arcades. But only two of those are actually good fun, one mid where yeah its ok and can be done sole if no players join you. The rest are pretty bad. What are those two good ones then? The Trails and Tours and the Open races MP mode. Arcades are the ok but not really grand MP mode and as said even if no one joins, i have been able to beat them sole at least as long as it's a decent car for the job. The other MP modes nah there are totally unbalanced sadly and so are trash. They have refused to improve the bad ones, more so the hide and seek, where the hider has like a 98% win rate. So its viewed as the most hated one of them all with how unbalanced it is. As said mentioned above tho spite the lacking MP quality well other then those 3 good ones you can still convoy up with random or a friend and have blast. End of the day this game is still a pretty great game to play, i for real wouldn't of put this amount of hours within less of a year if i wasn't having such a good time with it. I started Forza Horizon 5 on its release day, November 5, 2021. It was my first ever Forza Horizon game, and I dove into it casually—no rush, just enjoying the ride. Fast forward 287.4 hours later, I’ve completed the game with 100% of achievements on Steam, and what a journey it’s been. From the start, what really hooked me were the stunning visuals, tight driving mechanics, and the massive open world. The game’s version of Mexico is vast, vibrant, and full of life, easily one of the most beautiful and enjoyable maps I’ve explored in a racing game. I’ve played other similar titles like The Crew 2, but Forza Horizon 5 quickly became my favorite. One of the best aspects is how player-friendly the progression feels. I spent most of my time driving the Lamborghini Sesto Elemento Forza Edition—an absolute beast—and never felt rushed or pressured. You can go at your own pace, whether you're chasing seasonal goals or just cruising for fun. That said, some achievements are time-gated, particularly those tied to the Festival Playlist, which updates weekly every Thursday. To complete these, you’ll need consistency and patience, especially for challenges like the smashables, which only appear once per series (a month-long rotation). If you stay on top of them, they’re manageable, but missing one can set you back quite a bit. PvP and online-related achievements require dedication and strategy, but they’re far from impossible with some persistence and good matchmaking. In the end, I’d give Forza Horizon 5 a 9/10. It’s a phenomenal game with endless content and polish, but interestingly enough, before this game I tried Forza Horizon 4 and ended up liking it even more—perhaps for its setting or its slightly different vibe. Still, if you’re into open-world racing and want a game that respects your time while delivering top-tier fun, Forza Horizon 5 is hard to beat.

Forza Horizon 5 doesn’t just build on the success of its predecessor—it roars past it. Set in a vibrant, hyper-detailed version of Mexico, this is the most visually stunning, content-packed, and downright fun open-world racer yet. Playground Games has taken everything that made Horizon 4 a classic and turned the volume all the way up. If you’ve played Forza Horizon before, you’ll feel right at home—but better. The core arcade-sim hybrid handling is still here and still top-notch. Cars feel weighty, responsive, and grounded, whether you’re tearing across sand dunes in a trophy truck or hugging corners in a McLaren. Racing in Horizon 5 is endlessly satisfying. Whether it’s a street race at sunset, a cross-country rally through the jungle, or an impromptu drag race on a deserted airstrip, every drive feels exhilarating. The map is huge and diverse, and there's always something to do just around the next corner. Let’s not beat around the cactus—Horizon 5’s version of Mexico is breathtaking. The map is Playground Games’ biggest and most varied yet. Lush rainforests, sprawling cities, ancient ruins, dry deserts, active volcanoes, and tropical beaches all blend into a seamless playground of speed. Dynamic weather (including sandstorms and tropical storms), time of day, and lighting make every area feel alive. Simply driving around feels rewarding. With over 500 cars at launch, from exotics and muscle cars to off-road monsters and classic tuners, the car list is stacked. Each vehicle is faithfully modeled, and the tuning and upgrade system gives gearheads plenty to obsess over. Paint jobs, widebody kits, engine swaps, and even horns and sound systems can be customized. Want to turn a Beetle into a dragster? Go for it. The campaign is much more player-directed this time. You build your Horizon Festival by unlocking new outposts across Mexico, and each expansion adds different types of races and events (street, dirt, cross-country, etc.). It gives the game a sense of purpose without being restrictive. Expeditions are a standout—story-driven adventures that mix exploration with racing and give the world context. EventLab allows players to create their own races, mini-games, and even stunt challenges. Some user creations are wild, like Hot Wheels-style tracks or demolition derbies. Multiplayer is packed with content: Horizon Open, Eliminator (a battle royale with cars), co-op races, and community events. Online integration is smooth. You’ll see real players seamlessly driving around your world. Quick matchmaking and tons of seasonal content keep things fresh. Weekly playlists and challenges encourage you to come back regularly for rewards—but thankfully, they feel optional rather than obligatory. However, there’s some bloat and UI clutter when it comes to menus and notifications. The game can be overwhelming at first with how much it throws at you. Forza Horizon 5 isn’t just a racing game—it’s a celebration of cars, culture, and creativity. From its stunning Mexican backdrop to its overflowing content, it’s hard to find a game more joyful and well-crafted. While it builds heavily on the foundation of Horizon 4, it does so with enough new ideas, polish, and sheer scale that it firmly earns its place at the front of the pack. If you love cars or just love having fun behind a digital wheel, Forza Horizon 5 is the best it’s ever been. Rating: 8/10

Set in a breathtakingly recreated version of Mexico, this entry builds on everything its predecessors did right and delivers one of the most visually impressive and content-rich racing experiences ever made. Driving in Forza Horizon 5 is pure joy. Whether you're drifting through tight turns or flying off-road in a rally car, the handling is refined and responsive. Coming from FH4, which I got for cheap coin when the delisting was announced and having a hell lotta fun with it, I was a little cautios with FH5, cause the reviews were not so favourable. And they were correct, that it's not as memorable and disctinct as FH4 is. But you know what?! I have a hell lotta fun with it. :D Having (for whatever reason) only started racing with keyboard, I must say, the feeling of handling the car is way better than in FH4. Also I was instantly sucked into the world and have spend a ton of hours in the few days I possess the game, so they implemented the "formula" perfectly. Drifting, a severe pain point in FH4 for me (due to keyboard, left and right steering is always 100% only), is more relaxed here and thus way more fun. The stories are thrilling and it's really tough to switch the game off at night. So what else can I ask for from a game? If you're owning FH4, there currently a promotion with an extra 15% discount and I don't regret any coin I spent on this title. Let's see if I'm beating the 500+ hours I spent in Horizon UK. Edit: Aaaaand they changed the "Forzathon" (a Coop event, for those who don't know, now called "Horizon Arcade"), so that the tasks are tailored to the number of players participating in the event. That means, if I'm the only player, I can finish it anyway. Impossible in FH4! A simple, yet compelling change!

It was actually fun working through them, and overall, this has been a good game for me. My first Forza experience was Horizon 4, which I enjoyed enough to grab this one too—this time the Premium Edition. Would I say it was worth it? Not really. But since I got it on a discount, I don’t regret the purchase too much. There’s not much to say that screenshots or trailers can show - you just have to play it to really get the feel. It’s a game focused on multiplayer, tuning your cars, and just enjoying massive variety. While the cosmetic tuning options aren’t as deep as what you get in something like NFS Unbound, there’s still plenty of performance and visual customization to mess with. There’s a huge car list and lots of fun racing. The Rally Adventure and Hot Wheels DLCs are nice additions too - they bring more content and variety to the game, and feel like worthwhile expansions. If you enjoy open-world racing games with a big community and tons of cars, Forza Horizon 5 is definitely worth checking out.

[h3]⚠️ If you have an NVIDIA graphics card, you'll probably want to read this.[/h3] After more than 100 hours of gameplay, I can state that Forza Horizon 5 is without a doubt one of the most complete and entertaining racing games I have ever played. One of the aspects I appreciate most is the amount of content available: there is always something to do, such as races, challenges, seasonal events or even just driving around the map enjoying the scenery, which can often be therapeutic. Also, the visuals are a show: the map, inspired by Mexico, is rich in detail and has an atmosphere that makes you want to explore. The graphics are amazing, and Photo Mode stands out as a powerful tool to capture all this beauty, offering advanced options for camera control, focus and exposure. The gameplay maintains that arcade feel the series does so well, easy to learn and pick up, but with enough depth for those who like to tweak every little detail of the controls or the car. Driving feels smooth and responsive, making the game accessible to newcomers and still rewarding for experienced players. But unfortunately not everything is perfect. If you, like me, use an NVIDIA graphics card, it is worth knowing that the game still suffers from random and unpredictable crashes. I have lost several online races and even stopped playing for a few days out of pure frustration and despite trying dozens of fixes found on the internet nothing worked. It is frustrating to see this kind of issue persist in a title released in 2021. In the end I partially recommend Forza Horizon 5, especially if it is on sale. It is a great game with many strengths but one that still suffers from technical problems that should no longer exist.
